title: Theology names speech about God, and stands to faith as science to understanding
english: Theology, by the etymology of the word, means speech about God. Taken generally, it names every teaching that treats of God and of divine things. And because God can be treated of in two ways — first from principles known by the natural light, then from principles which God has made known in a supernatural manner — a twofold theology is commonly distinguished: one natural, the other supernatural.

Natural theology is that part of philosophy which treats chiefly of immaterial being and of God. Aristotle himself calls metaphysics by this name in the first book of the Metaphysics. Supernatural theology, however, is that teaching about God which has its origin from divine revelation. This theology is called theology absolutely and by antonomasia. It is of this alone that we must treat from here on.

Further, the habit that rests on revelation is twofold. One is that by which we simply believe and embrace what is contained in the word of God; and this habit is nothing other than faith itself. The other is that by which a person is fitted to explain distinctly the things that faith believes, to assert and defend them with various reasons, and from them to draw legitimate consequences. This habit is properly called theology.

Theology, taken in this way, stands to faith as science stands to understanding. For faith is the habit of the principles; theology is the habit of the conclusions. The primary and principal object of faith is certain truths immediately and expressly revealed by God. The proper objects of theology are those revealed only mediately and virtually — that is, those gathered by reasoning from those first immediately revealed truths. So theology, though distinguished from faith, still presupposes faith and in a way includes it. But faith does not necessarily bring theology along with it.

title: Theology is not required of every person for salvation, yet the church cannot stand without it
english: Many things are commonly disputed about theology in the schools. But what we now propose to teach on this subject will be referred to these heads: first, what and how great is the necessity of theology; second, what is its nature, where we must inquire into its genus and difference; third, what is the dignity of theology and its excellence above the remaining sciences.

As to the first: it is certain that theology is not in itself necessary for each person unto salvation — that is, it is not necessary that all who come to eternal life be endowed with theological science. For in the church all are not teachers, as the Apostle teaches ([[1 Corinthians 12:29 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 12:29]]); nor are they for that reason deprived of salvation. For the salvation of individuals, faith suffices; a fuller and wider knowledge of the things of faith is not necessarily required.

Nevertheless theology — that is, such a science of divine things as can defend, explain, and commend the faith itself — is necessary in the church, so that the church may stand and be preserved, and so that individuals may obtain salvation. This the Apostle teaches ([[Ephesians 4:11-14 >> Bible:Ephesians 4:11-14]]), where besides other things he affirms that Christ appointed teachers in his church for the perfecting of the saints and the building up of the body of Christ, and so that we may not be children tossed and carried about by every wind of teaching. From this it is plain that there is danger, if there are no teachers in the church, that its frame be dissolved, the building fall, and private persons fall away from the faith, carried off by many and various errors. And the same Apostle requires as a necessary condition in a bishop that he be able to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict ([[Titus 1:9 >> Bible:Titus 1:9]]) — which cannot be done by one who is not more learned in sacred things than the common run of the faithful.

title: The church has never lacked teachers above the faithful people; faith itself requires theological science in the church
english: And certainly the church never existed without such men, who by doctrine in divine things stood above the pious and faithful people. For of old doctors of that kind were the patriarchs and the prophets, who had their own schools and disciples — those called in Scripture the sons of the prophets. A school of that kind is thought to have been the hill of God mentioned in ([[1 Samuel 10 >> Bible:1 Samuel 10]]). And it is thought to have taken that name because divine teaching was handed down there. Likewise in ([[2 Chronicles 34 >> Bible:2 Chronicles 34]]) mention is made of the Mishneh, in which Huldah the prophetess is said to have lived. That word is translated by many as school, or college, which our French version has followed. For from the usage of the Chaldee and Rabbinic tongue the root signifies to learn and to teach. Whence the Talmudic text is called by the Hebrews the Mishnah, as if you were to say doctrine, or discipline, by a certain antonomasia.

After the times of the prophets also the Jewish church had its own theologians, who were called Wise Men, Masters, and Scribes. With that title Ezra himself is marked in the book that bears his name. And of this same kind were those who in the Gospel are called doctors and experts of the law. From them Christ, taking away the key of knowledge, handed it to the apostles, and to pastors and teachers, who for their part are their successors.

But besides ordinary bishops and pastors, in whom at least some knowledge of theology is required, the Christian church from the beginning has had its own schools, and doctors professing sacred teaching in them and expounding the divine writings. Especially famous was the Alexandrian school, in which, if Jerome is believed in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, there had been in an unbroken series, from the times of the evangelist Mark down to Jerome's own times, ecclesiastical doctors. Of whom Pantaenus is especially remembered, and Clement of Alexandria, who succeeded him.

And certainly from the very necessity of faith the necessity of theological science is inferred. For faith cannot be propagated and endure unless there are those who teach, commend, and defend the faith. But it is not for every believer to do this — only for those who are skilled in Scripture and in divine things. So for the preservation of the faith and of the church, and consequently for the salvation of men, theology is necessary: that is, in the church there must be men skilled in divine things, who generate, foster, and nourish faith in others — though it is not necessary that each person be so taught and skilled.

title: Theology is not a science by Aristotle's strict definition, yet it is rightly called science by the evidence of the consequence
english: So much, then, is clear about the necessity of theology. But now, that we may hold clearly and distinctly what it is, we must first inquire into its genus. The first question, therefore, is whether our theology is a science. On which we say that theology is not a science accurately speaking, and according to the definition of science laid down by Aristotle. For science according to Aristotle is an evident assent: but theological conclusions are not evident. And that is because they are gathered from inevident principles. For faith is the habit of the theological principles. But faith is an inevident habit. For the Apostle opposes faith to sight: ([[2 Corinthians 5:7 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 5:7]]) — By faith, he says, we walk, not by sight. And ([[Hebrews 11:1 >> Bible:Hebrews 11:1]]) teaches that faith is of things that are not seen. Faith, he says, is the substance of things hoped for, and the argument of things that are not seen.

Now those things are said to be evident which of themselves move the intellect to the knowledge of them — that is, which of themselves persuade and commend themselves to the mind, and by their own light so strike and convince the mind that it cannot but assent to them. That this does not suit the mysteries of our faith is plain. For they are not things known of themselves, whose truth of itself lays itself open to our mind. But that we assent to them, we do because of the authority and testimony of God, who revealed and confirmed them by his Word.

But here a distinction must be made between the evidence of the consequent and the evidence of the consequence. For theological conclusions are indeed not evident: yet the consequence by which they are drawn from their principles is evident. From inevident premises, to be sure — but they are gathered evidently. For example: that Christ is true God and true man is a principle of faith, which of itself is not evident, but is believed because of God's testimony alone. Yet from it it evidently follows that in Christ there are two wills, one divine and the other human. And so in this respect theology lacks nothing toward the true character of a science.

Although, however, theology is not a science properly and strictly speaking, and according to all the conditions of science laid down by Aristotle, still there is no habit of the mind to which it more nearly approaches, and to which it ought rather to be referred. For it is a certain knowledge evidently deduced from certain principles, which, though they are inevident, are no less certain than if they were evident. And so it is rightly and fittingly called a science, nor can it be designated by any more apt name.

title: Theology is one science by species under divine revelation, and is practical rather than merely speculative
english: Further, theology is one science by species, not many. For although it treats of things that are very diverse — for example, of God, of angels, of man, of virtues and vices, which seem to belong to altogether different sciences — still all those things agree in one common formal reason, under which they confront and are objected to theology. That common reason is divine revelation. For the things I have named do not fall under the theologian's consideration in any way whatever, but only insofar as they can be known through divine revelation. For example, concerning the nature, powers, and duty of man the theologian does not teach whatever can be taught, but only those things which he has learned and gathered from the word of God.

Here it must also be noted that not whatever God reveals in any manner whatever pertains to the object of theology. For God may have revealed certain things privately to many persons, which do not fall under this science. But here by revelation we understand that which is common to the whole church, and which was made for its common usefulness, and which God willed to be consigned in writing. For the theologian ought to prove his assertions not from private revelations made to this person or that, but from sacred Scripture.

Further, theology does not seem to be a science merely speculative, nor merely practical, but practical and speculative at once. And that is because theology treats of many things that belong to practical science as well as to speculative. For it contemplates God and the divine mysteries, which do not fall under action; and it also gives precepts of life, and teaches what manners are worthy of a Christian man.

Nevertheless we judge theology to be practical rather than speculative. For the whole of theology is occupied in the explanation and defense of the things contained in the Scriptures. But the teaching contained in the Scriptures, from the scope of God himself who teaches and reveals, is referred to action — namely to the love of God and of neighbor. Nor has anyone attained the scope of this teaching who does not refer whatever he has learned from the word of God to that end. For Christ affirms in ([[Matthew 22:37-40 >> Bible:Matthew 22:37-40]]) that the law and the prophets hang on these two commandments: you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and your neighbor as yourself. Then Paul says in ([[Romans 15:4 >> Bible:Romans 15:4]]) that whatever things were written were written for our learning, that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope. But above all his words in ([[2 Timothy 3:16-17 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16-17]]) are to be weighed: All Scripture is inspired by God, and is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for discipline which is in righteousness; that the man of God may be perfect, and thoroughly furnished unto every good work.

To this belongs the fact that the Gospel is called by the same Paul a teaching according to godliness ([[1 Timothy 6:3 >> Bible:1 Timothy 6:3]]). For that is for no other reason than that the chief scope of the Gospel is to form us unto godliness. Indeed those articles which seem most to pertain to contemplation — namely concerning the divinity and incarnation of the Son of God — are called by the Apostle in specie the mystery of godliness, in chapter 3 of the same epistle ([[1 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:1 Timothy 3:16]]). Add that the habit of the theological principles is faith. But true faith is a practical habit. And the habit of the principles and the habit of the conclusions are of the same genus.

title: The object of theology is God as the savior of men, not deity considered apart from that respect
english: As for the object of theology, it is to be noted that sometimes the object of a science is said to be whatever the science considers in any way. So the object of theology is not one. For it considers many and very diverse things: God, the church, angels, the sacraments. Yet all these agree in one common appellation, insofar as they fall under the theologian's consideration. For whatever the theologian treats can be called divine things. For they are either God himself, or other things ordered in some way to God. Nor is anything properly considered by the theologian except with some respect to God. So if anyone asks about the object of theology, it can not ineptly be answered that that object is divine things.

But for the most part the object of any science is said to be that of which the science principally intends to give us knowledge, and on account of which it considers all the rest — because, namely, they lead to a fuller and more perfect acquaintance with it. Of this kind the object of theology is God, which almost all confess, and which the very word theology teaches, which, as was noted above, means speech about God. But it is not agreed whether that object is God simply, as God is, or rather under some certain respect. The former is defended by the more celebrated scholastics following Thomas Aquinas, and they state that the object of theology is God as God is, and, as they speak, under the reason of deity. But this seems to us too loose and general. Nor is the scope of theology to lead us simply into the knowledge of God as God is; rather it treats of God with some respect to men.

Therefore the object of theology can more conveniently be said to be God, as God is, and the savior of men. For the whole of Scripture proposes God to us under this respect. And it principally intends to teach us what benefits of God are toward men, and what worship and obedience he in turn requires of them. But if it touches any other things, it does so in order to declare and confirm these more. For example, when it teaches that there are three Persons in God — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — its scope is not simply to teach us this truth; but by it it wills to inform us more clearly and richly concerning the manner of our redemption and salvation, which was procured for us through Christ, and is applied and sealed to us through the Spirit. And likewise the attributes of God, such as justice and mercy, are narrated in the Scriptures in relation to men, so that they may know how far the justice of God is to be feared by them, and what refuge they ought to seek in his mercy.

title: Theology's dignity appears from its object — above metaphysics, and wide through creatures, ethics, and history
english: Further, once the nature of theology is known, it is ready to hand to gather what its dignity is, and its excellence above the remaining sciences. And first, indeed, those things already said about the object of theology show it sufficiently. For the dignity of the sciences is usually measured by the dignity of their object. But the object of theology, as has been said, is God Most High, who surpasses all other things infinitely in dignity, since he himself is of infinite essence and perfection.

First philosophy does indeed treat of God, but concerning so great an object it hands down few and slight things compared with those handed down in this discipline. For theology narrates the nature and attributes of God far more richly and clearly than metaphysics. Then it opens many mysteries about God altogether unknown to the philosophers — as that there are three persons in God though the essence is one, and that the Son of God was incarnate and died for us, and many like things.

Then also, although God is the principal object of theology — because, as we have just taught, it considers nothing except in order and respect to God — still theology treats of many things besides God, and there is no science that extends itself to more things, or whose object lies open so widely. For it discourses on many excellent matters concerning spiritual creatures, namely angels both good and evil, of which human reason can scarcely attain anything. There we have a perfect ethics, and a rule of living well far holier and more sublime than any precepts of the wise of this age. Nor does theology lack political and economic precepts, many of which can be drawn from sacred Scripture.

Add that through this discipline a person is led into a true knowledge of himself, and learns those things about himself which cannot be taught from elsewhere. For this alone opens the origin of the human race, and the various states of man. And since it is easy to notice in human nature a great misery and disturbance, theology alone teaches its cause and remedy, and opens so great a magnitude of the evil. Over which matter philosophy long ago seethed and panted in vain.

Indeed sacred teaching embraces not a few geographical and historical matters, which pour great light on history and geography. And without its torch shining ahead, the beginnings of the world would be unknown, and the origins of almost all nations, nor would chronology have any certain beginning, and the first and most venerable antiquity would lie wholly hidden. Finally sacred Scripture, the fountain of our theology and its first rule, scatters here and there certain physical matters which not lightly assist natural science — as, for example, that saying of Solomon in the first chapter of Ecclesiastes ([[Ecclesiastes 1:7 >> Bible:Ecclesiastes 1:7]]), concerning the origin of springs and rivers from the sea, and their perpetual return by a circle into the same sea.

title: Theology is also commended by its author — God, not Aristotle or Euclid
english: But as much as this science is commended from its object, so much also does its author commend it. For the remaining sciences glory in some illustrious man as their chief author. Aristotle is held the prince of the philosophers, and Hippocrates of the physicians; and the mathematical disciplines acknowledge Euclid as their parent. But theology claims God for itself as author, from whom this sacred teaching has flowed forth. For prophecy was not brought in of old by the will of man, as the Apostle Peter says ([[2 Peter 1:21 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:21]]); but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit, who first consigned it in writing.

Not without the deity, indeed, were the good arts and disciplines invented; and the light of reason itself descends from the Father of lights ([[James 1:17 >> Bible:James 1:17]]), who is the mover and governor of nature. But the principles on which theology rests are the express sayings and oracles of God, by which those things are made manifest which could not have become known except by a light higher than reason.

title: Theology surpasses the other sciences in certainty, both in the object and in the habit of faith
english: Hence it comes about that theology surpasses all the remaining sciences in certainty. For those rest on human reason, which can be deceived and is liable to error. But theology reclines upon the truth of God, who can neither be deceived nor deceive. Many indeed waver about theological truths, and to them the principles and conclusions of theology seem less certain than the things handed down in the human sciences. But that does not hinder them from being in themselves most certain — just as the sun does not cease to be most splendid, though the blind and the bleary-eyed either do not perceive its light at all, or perceive it only obscurely.

But here it must be noticed that when we set theology as more certain than the other sciences, we do not so understand it as if that certainty were only on the side of the object. For the things which God has revealed are not only most certain in themselves, but can also be known more certainly through the habit of faith and of theology than any truths known through the light of reason alone. So that one who is strengthened in faith and in the science of divine things is more certain, and more persuaded, concerning the divine truths than he is concerning any other truth. And thus the habit of faith and of theology, in itself and from its own species, excels in certainty the habit of the merely natural sciences — although not all participate that habit equally, and it is firmer in one person and less firm in another.

title: Theology's dignity shines most in its end and use — perfect beatitude, not a particular good of this life
english: But in no matter does the dignity and excellence of theology shine forth more than in the excellence of its end and use. For among practical disciplines, the further and more universal the end of any discipline is, the more worthy and excellent that discipline is. So politics excels military science, because the end of military science is victory, which is a means to obtaining public peace and tranquillity — which is the end of political science, and some greater good. But the end of this science is the highest and last of all: namely the perfect beatitude of man, to which the ends of all the other arts and disciplines are subordinated.

The remaining disciplines and arts care for some particular good of man. Medicine, for example, the health of the body; jurisprudence, estates; politics, public peace and tranquillity. But none of these suffices to make a person blessed. Theology, however, cares for the whole happiness of man, and supplies whatever things are desired for living well and blessedly.

Philosophy also strives toward that, indeed. But it attains its scope less fully, and whatever goods it tries to procure for a person are contained within the compass of this life. But theology offers eternal life and happiness, and renders them to those who follow its leading. And so it teaches how to order the present life, that we may be blessed not only for the state of this life, but in such a way that it leads through to everlasting beatitude.

title: Theology is wisely called wisdom: hardest mysteries, and independent of every other science
english: Therefore by highest right this sacred discipline ought to be called wisdom. For according to Aristotle himself, wisdom is the science of the most excellent things. But as is clear from what has been said, theology treats of the most excellent things: namely of God and of his wonderful works, both in creation and in our redemption. Then also of things of the greatest moment with respect to us, and which it is of the highest interest for us to know — namely of our highest happiness, and of life rightly ordered according to God, which is the way to attaining that happiness. Nor does it treat only of the most excellent things, but also in the most excellent manner: namely not from the inventions of human reason, but from divine revelation.

Besides, among the marks of wisdom it is commonly reckoned that it is occupied about things most difficult and remote from sense; next, that it does not depend on another science; and finally that it directs and judges the other sciences, as their arbiter and mistress. All of which fit theology exactly.

For first it opens to us mysteries far most difficult, which in themselves are not only remote from the senses, but far surpass the capacity of the human mind. For they are, as the Apostle says, things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have ascended into the heart of man; but God has revealed them to us by his Spirit, who searches all things, even the depths of God ([[1 Corinthians 2:9-10 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:9-10]]).

Second, theology does not depend on any other science. For one science is said to depend on another in two ways. First, when a certain science takes its principles from another, which principles are conclusions of that superior science. So the art of fortifying cities depends on geometry; for geometrical conclusions are the principles of that art. Then, when the end of one science is referred to the end of another science. So military science depends on politics; since the military end is referred to the political end, and is a means to attaining it. But in both of those ways theology is plainly independent. For since the end of theology is the last end of man — namely his eternal beatitude — it cannot be referred to any end, but all things are necessarily referred to it. Then also there is no human science from which theology takes its principles; but it has them immediately from the revelation of God, whose are the utterances and pronouncements.

title: Theology uses the natural sciences as mistress, judges them, and rightly bears the title Wisdom
english: But you will say: theologians in their arguments often use propositions which are not revealed, but known by the light of reason alone; and many argumentations are found in theology in which only one of the premises is revealed, while the other is one of the conclusions of some natural science. I answer that when theology takes certain things from other sciences, it does not do so from necessity, but to illustrate the matter more, and to accommodate itself to weak persons. For by itself alone it is sufficient to itself, and can prove all necessary conclusions from revealed principles. So when it borrows anything from the natural sciences, it does not do so as an inferior compelled to run back to a superior, but as a mistress who freely uses the faculties of her handmaids.

And in truth theology is the arbiter and mistress of the other sciences, which directs them and judges concerning them, herself to be judged by no other science. For all the remaining disciplines are to be measured by her rule, so that whatever they have not consonant with theology is rejected, and nothing is admitted which does not agree with the principles of theology.

And so various errors in philosophy have been detected — as, for example, concerning the origin of the world, which some of the philosophers thought eternal, others made from matter; but none thought it created from nothing, as it truly is, except with theology showing and leading by the hand. And in many other matters where the philosophers stuck fast and did not have the thing sufficiently explored, theology set it in the open and took away all doubt — as is plain in the business of divine providence and of the immortality of the soul.

Therefore by right and merit sacred teaching is to be adorned with the title Wisdom, which is also often attributed to it in Scripture: as when the Apostle calls the Gospel the wisdom which is in a mystery; and says that it is to the nations foolishness, and to the Jews a stumbling-block; but to those who believe, the power of God and the wisdom of God ([[1 Corinthians 1:18-24 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 1:18-24]]; [[1 Corinthians 2:6-8 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:6-8]]).

title: Faith is assent to God speaking, moved by divine authority — and not every assent counts as faith
english: Faith, taken theologically in general, is the assent we give to God speaking, when we are certainly persuaded that something is true, moved to it by divine authority. By this, faith is distinguished from opinion, which is a timid and uncertain assent. Likewise from science, which is indeed a certain assent, but one that rests on demonstration or some evident argument, not on anyone's testimony. Finally from human faith, which rests in the authority of men.

Therefore not every assent, even when given to things contained in the word of God, is to be counted as faith. For if someone holds some doctrine of religion with certainty and firmness — for example the creation of all things out of nothing — yet is not driven to it by divine revelation, but by some reason that seems necessary to him, to that extent he does not have faith. Nor does the one who believes the history of the Israelite people from the report of Josephus the historian, and does not give faith to the sacred historians. The same can be said of those who cling to the true and orthodox religion, but only from custom, and moved to it by the authority of their ancestors alone.

But various species or grades of faith may be assigned from the Scriptures. In some people faith remains in the theoretical intellect alone: and so they give a bare and simple assent to what is proposed in the word of God, yet are not moved thereby to act rightly, nor are they made better. So Simon Magus believed Philip's preaching, yet his heart was not right, and he was in the bitterest gall and the bond of injustice, as is recorded in Acts 8. So also those had believed in the name of Christ to whom nevertheless Christ did not entrust himself, because he knew all people thoroughly, as we read in John 2. And even the demons themselves share in this in their own way, who are said in James to believe and tremble (James 2:19).

title: Historical faith names idle assent; temporary faith is shallow joy that collapses under the cross
english: This is the faith that our writers call historical. It does not take that name from its object, as though it belonged only to things narrated historically in the Scriptures. For those who have this faith believe as true whatever is contained in the sacred writings — promises, doctrines, and precepts no less than histories and narratives. Many of the ungodly do not doubt the truth of the Gospel promises, and even the demons do not call them into question. But this faith is called historical from the way it turns about its object. Just as when we read histories that do not concern us, we contemplate them bare and are not inwardly affected or moved by them: so those who have that faith which the word of God teaches speculate without purpose and do not apply them to practice.

Whether this faith ought to be called true is asked. The Doctors of the Roman Church affirm it. And this can be granted them in some sense. For that faith believes only what is true, and believes it in earnest, not fictively and with pretense. Yet only that faith seems to us absolutely deserving to be called true which is justifying and saving — which we deny that historical faith to be.

From this faith another grade of faith does not differ far, which may be observed in Scripture. For there are those in whom faith not only illumines the theoretical mind, but also affects the practical mind to some extent; so that they do not merely believe the Gospel truth simply, but are tickled with some joy from it, and in some measure abstain from their vices and worldly desires. Yet by that faith their mind is only lightly imbued; it has not penetrated deeply enough, nor taken root in the heart. Nor do they renounce their own vices and desires wholly truly and sincerely, and love of the world and of earthly things always clings in the breast. Hence it comes about that if a somewhat heavier cross must be borne, and persecution rushes in, they take offense and cast away the faith. Which they also often do when they yield to their desires and are weighed down by the cares of this life.

These are the ones Christ marks in the parable: those who at once receive the Word of God with joy, yet have no root in themselves, but are temporary; and when affliction or persecution arises because of the word, they are immediately offended (Matthew 13:20-21). Such also are those of whom Peter writes in his second letter: who, after they had first escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, are again entangled in them and overcome; so that their last condition is worse than the first (2 Peter 2:20). And of this kind also are those whom the Apostle so severely threatens in Hebrews 6 and 10. Our schools call this faith temporary, taking the name from Christ's words which we have just cited.

title: Miracle-working faith is a special gift; justifying faith is named; Rome confuses it with historical faith
english: But there is also a certain faith which is counted among the peculiar gifts of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:9), and which does not fall to all who are in the Church, but to a few, as it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit. This is the faith through which miracles are wrought, from which it has also received its name. And it is found in the one who, called by God to work miracles and having a promise concerning this matter — as the Apostles had from the mouth of Christ, and many others from an inward revelation of the Spirit — does not hesitate or distrust, but is certainly persuaded that God is able and willing to accomplish those stupendous works through him. Of this faith Christ speaks in Mark 11:22 when he says to the disciples, Have faith in God. Amen I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, Be taken up and cast into the sea, and does not doubt in his heart but believes that what he says will happen, it will be done for him, whatever he says (Mark 11:22-23). He also reproaches the disciples for the defect of this faith in Matthew 17:20, when he refers the cause why they could not cast out the demon to their unbelief. And to this the Apostle looks in 1 Corinthians 13:2: If I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.

Finally there is another faith, to which Scripture attributes our righteousness and salvation, to which it urgently and often exhorts us, and which it adorns with the highest praises and elogies. And this is the faith which we name justifying, saving, living, and true.

But here we have a dispute with the Doctors of the Roman Church: for they confuse justifying faith with that which we have just called historical, and put no distinction between them, but want them to be plainly one and the same. Then they also teach that the faith of miracles is nothing other than a certain excellent grade of justifying faith.

title: Justifying faith must be distinguished from historical faith; Rome's reply helps; miracle faith is not an eminent grade of justifying faith
english: But that justifying faith ought to be distinguished from historical faith is not hard to prove. For if historical faith were the same as justifying faith, then whoever had historical faith would by that very fact have justifying faith. Yet many hypocrites and ungodly people are endowed with historical faith who nevertheless lack justifying faith. For of this faith Scripture says that whoever believes does not perish but has eternal life (John 3:16), and that Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4); and that in the Gospel the righteousness of God is revealed to all and upon all who believe (Romans 1:16-17). From which it is plain that no one is endowed with such faith who is not a partaker of righteousness and salvation. And therefore to those who are in a state of perdition and remain in sin, if they are said to believe, another faith must be assigned.

And certainly what the Pontificians say about these places helps our sentence. For they say that when Scripture says whoever believes has eternal life, it ought to be understood of those who believe as they ought and with the whole heart; and that the reason many believe in the Son and yet do not have life is that they believe badly, and not with the whole heart, and not as they ought — as may be seen in Bellarmine, book one On Justification, chapter ten, paragraph Adde quod. But who can with any reason affirm that it is the same faith by which someone believes well and by which someone believes badly; by which someone believes as he ought and by which someone believes as he ought not? Or that the faith by which someone believes badly, and not with the whole heart, and not as he ought, is the justifying faith which the Apostle says is imputed for righteousness (Romans 4)?

Next, that the faith of miracles is not an eminent grade of justifying faith is also manifest from this: that some are gifted with that faith who nevertheless do not have justifying faith. For to many who will say to Christ, Did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works? Christ will answer, I never knew you, as Christ himself witnesses (Matthew 7:22). Add that the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 12:9 numbers the faith of signs among the various charisms of the Spirit, which the Pontificians call graces given freely (gratiae gratis datae). Yet an eminent grade of justifying faith belongs to grace that makes acceptable (gratia gratum faciens). For it is given for the salvation of the one who has it — not, like those free gifts of the Spirit, for the salvation of others. Then if the faith of miracles were an excellent grade of justifying faith, Christ, when reproaching the disciples for the defect of that faith, would not say to them, If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mountain, Move from here, and it would move, and nothing would be impossible for you (Matthew 17:20). For a grain of mustard seed denotes something very small in the Scriptures, and it amounts to the same as if Christ said, If you had even a tiny bit of faith.

title: Justifying faith applies the word to practice; it includes the lesser species as the perfect includes the imperfect; assurance of pardon is not its primary act
english: Now justifying faith is that by which not only the theoretical intellect is illumined, so that it certainly believes the things taught by the word of God, but also the practical mind of man is so affected that it refers those things to practice and applies them to itself. For the truly faithful person so believes, for example, the promises of the Gospel concerning remission of sins and eternal happiness and glory, that he firmly and effectually judges his highest good and blessedness — to which he must aspire with all his strength — to be placed in them; so he gives faith to the mysteries of our redemption that he plainly thinks consolation and peace of conscience are to be sought for himself in them; finally he so considers the divine commandments that he certainly resolves within himself that life is to be lived according to them.

From which it can be clear that justifying faith is so diverse from historical and temporary faith that it includes all their virtue; and is so distinguished from them as the perfect from the imperfect — or by that distinction by which a higher grade differs from a lower. For justifying faith stands to the remaining species of faith as the rational soul stands to the sensitive and vegetative; whose force and faculties — life, sense, and motion — it eminently embraces, and adds the grade of reason. For so also justifying faith makes us believe all things taught by the word of God, which historical faith performs. And if God should promise something special and call someone to work a miracle, then it also supplies the force of miraculous faith; nor does the one who already believes the word of God as he ought, if a special promise is directed to him, need a new habit in order to give assent to it. Hence it is that the Apostle, commending the force and efficacy of saving faith, attributes to it various miraculous works which holy men once wrought, or which were done for their sake: saying that by faith the fathers crossed the Red Sea, and by faith the walls of Jericho fell, and by faith some stopped the mouths of lions and quenched the power of fire (Hebrews 11). But above the remaining species of faith, justifying faith has this: that it more brightly irradiates the theoretical mind, more fully imbues the practical, penetrates more deeply, and begets a sharper sense of truth and a firmer assent in our souls than historical or temporary faith. Then also whatever it has drawn from the word of God it refers to action and to the ordering of life; and in the way we have said, it applies it to itself.

Which application is indeed to be understood rightly, and in the sense already set out. Not, however, as though the proper act of justifying faith, by which it is discerned from the other species of faith, consisted in this: that someone should bring himself to think that his sins are remitted, and that he is a child of God predestined to life, and will certainly be a partaker of salvation. For this persuasion, if it is legitimate, necessarily presupposes faith and arises from it; and therefore cannot be its primary act. For since remission of sins and eternal life are promised in the Gospel to no one absolutely, but under the condition of faith and repentance: in order that we may be certain of the grace of God and of our salvation, it is necessary that it first be clear to us concerning our faith and repentance. From which it is manifest that that certainty of faith is a consequent, not faith itself; or if someone wishes it to belong to faith, at least that it is not its primary act.

title: Faith's object is what God has revealed; Bellarmine misstates it; primary and secondary objects; explicit and implicit faith; revelation measures explicitness; implicit faith is no pretext for ignorance
english: But that the nature of faith may be more fully understood, it is necessary to discuss its object and subject, cause and effects a little more widely. And indeed from what has been said it is plain that the object of faith is the things that have been revealed by God, and insofar as they have been revealed by God. So that the material object of faith is the things contained in the word of God; but the formal object is the divine authority and truth itself.

Therefore Bellarmine does not dispute rightly against our writers, as though they altogether restricted the object of saving faith to the bare promise of remission of sins. For we set the object of that faith as not only the things promised in the Gospel, but also whatever else is taught, narrated, and commanded in the word of God. Which the Apostle teaches in Hebrews 11, where speaking of justifying faith he says that by faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that the things which are seen were not made of things which appear (Hebrews 11:3). And likewise that Noah by faith believed the divine warning about the coming flood, by which, being moved with fear, he built an ark for the saving of his house (Hebrews 11:7).

But here it must be noted that not all things which are set before our faith belong equally to its object. For just as in the objects of the human sciences some things are those whose knowledge is chiefly intended, and those are called the principal object — as, for example, in Logic the syllogism and demonstration — while others are proposed only for the elucidation of those former things, and so that they may be known more easily and more richly, and these are the secondary and less principal object of the science: so also the matter stands in the doctrine of faith. For some things are set before faith primarily and chiefly, and some secondarily and less chiefly. Now that principal object is the things without which one cannot arrive at salvation, nor can life be rightly ordered: such as those called the articles of faith, summing up the mysteries of salvation, and also the divine precepts. But the word of God contains many other things which pertain only to the confirmation of those and to a fuller knowledge of them — as, for example, the various histories and miracles narrated in the Scriptures — and those are the secondary object of faith.

Further, the things that belong to the principal object of faith must be believed distinctly; for the rest it is enough if they are believed confusedly. Those things are believed distinctly which faith apprehends separately and one by one. And this is the faith which is called explicit. Confusedly, those which are not apprehended in particular, but only in some common principle in which they are contained: and this is the faith which they call implicit. For example, one who believes that the book of Judges is divinely inspired, and yet has not read it, nor heard anything from it recited: he indeed believes that the histories contained there are true, but implicitly and confusedly. But one who reads those histories, and knows one by one what is narrated in that book about Samson and Gideon and the other leaders of the Israelite people, has an explicit and distinct faith of them.

But since God has not at once and once for all manifested the whole doctrine of redemption and salvation to men, but in many ways and in many parts — and first more obscurely, then more clearly — it follows that according to the various differences of times faith ought to have been more or less explicit. For revelation is the measure of faith: and the more things are distinctly revealed, the more things faith must be extended to. And therefore from us, to whom the Gospel has been clearly made known, an explicit faith of many articles is required as necessary, for which under the Old Testament an implicit faith formerly sufficed.

But here too it must be observed that when we say an implicit faith of many things contained in the word of God is sufficient, this ought not to be taken as though it were praiseworthy to rest in any sort of knowledge of the principal heads of faith, and as though no fuller knowledge were to be sought. For although a distinct faith of a few articles is required as plainly necessary to salvation, yet this also is certain: that each person is bound to use every effort, according to the manner of his calling, to advance more and more in the doctrine of salvation, and to be more fully and richly instructed in the word of God. To which the Apostle diligently exhorts the faithful (Colossians 2:2 and 3:16). And therefore those gravely err and sin who, under the pretext of implicit faith, foster the stupid and crass ignorance of the people.

title: Scripture's authority is sharply disputed; Rome grants God as author in itself but hangs our knowledge on the Church; ours say Scripture itself suffices
english: The authority of Scripture is sharply disputed between the Orthodox and the Pontificians. The question is: whence sacred Scripture has its authority. Both sides, however, understand by the authority of Scripture that dignity according to which it merits faith in everything it says in any way, and the highest obedience from faith in the things it commands and forbids.

But here the Pontificians make a distinction. They grant that Scripture in itself has its authority from nowhere else than from God; yet they contend that that authority, as it concerns us, hangs on the Church's testimony. This is their mind: that Scripture is worthy of all faith and reverence because it proceeded from God, the fountain of all truth and the supreme Lord of all; yet that one cannot know certainly and without doubt that Scripture came forth from God from any other ground than that the Church witnesses it. Thus, that Scripture is of irrefragable truth and has the highest empire over consciences comes from its having God as author; but that it is certainly acknowledged to have God as author already hangs on the Church's testimony.

But our writers do not hang the authority of sacred Scripture, either in itself or as it concerns us, on the Church's testimony and authority. For they assert that the sacred books can be acknowledged to have come forth from God from another ground than the voice of the witnessing Church; and that when the faithful receive these books as divine, they do not do so because of the Church's authority; but that Scripture itself is enough to furnish knowledge of itself.

title: Parties agree whence authority belongs, not how it is known; plan of inquiry; four questions about Scripture's light, the Spirit, the Church, and faith's foundation
english: The parties therefore agree whence Scripture's own authority belongs to it; they do not agree whence it is known that such authority belongs to it. And so the state of the controversy seems easy and ready. Yet when one comes to the fight, and each side explains its mind more clearly and in particular, then great obscurity and confusion arise in this question; and one can scarcely assign in what the parties properly disagree.

Therefore, so that, as far as in us lies, we may bring some light to this most celebrated question, we will try to set out the whole matter more carefully. And first we will investigate and set out the way in which Scripture becomes known to us as divine. Then we will inquire into the Pontificians' sentence, which is not so ready and prompt to acknowledge and perceive as it might seem. And finally, once the state of the controversy has been drawn out from that, we will explain what the Pontificians' error is in this part, and will refute it.

Further, concerning the way by which we come to knowledge of sacred Scripture, four things chiefly will have to be discussed. First: whether sacred Scripture has some light by which it presents itself to be acknowledged, and what that light is and of what kind. Second: what parts the Holy Spirit has in this business, and how far His work is necessary for someone to acknowledge the Word of God and Scripture. Third: what is to be attributed to the Church in this matter, and how much its testimony avails. Fourth: finally, on what foundation especially that faith rests which we give to Scripture as true and divine.

title: Scripture has light in itself apart from the Church; that light is evidence of truth; metaphysical versus moral evidence
english: As for the first point: in this question our writers lay down as a foundation that sacred Scripture has in itself a certain light by which, with all authority of the Church set aside, it can become known through itself. And certainly Scripture in many places compares itself to light. But this noted only in general brings little light to this controversy. Therefore it is necessary to set out more distinctly what that light and evidence of Scripture is. For by that light we understand nothing but a certain evidence of truth which the faithful perceive in Scripture, and by which Scripture proves its own divinity to their minds.

Further, a twofold evidence can be distinguished: one which may be called mathematical or metaphysical; another which can be called moral. I call metaphysical evidence that which belongs to first principles known of themselves, and to conclusions demonstrated through principles of that kind. Moral evidence, however, is that which is seen in things that cannot indeed be demonstrated, yet are urged by such marks and arguments that a prudent and skilled man cannot doubt them or wrest dissent from himself. So it is that the Aeneid was written by Virgil, and the orations against Verres, Catiline, and Antony by Cicero.

title: Scripture's evidence is not metaphysical demonstration; its light is moral evidence that induces the pious and prudent
english: The evidence that belongs to Scripture is not of the former kind. For that Scripture is divinely inspired is not a thing known of itself, as these principles are — The whole is greater than its part; The same thing cannot at once be and not be. Nor can that be demonstrated logically or mathematically, as experience shows. For no one has ever been able to bring any demonstration of this truth. Add that if the matter stood so, the assent we would give to sacred Scripture would be science, not faith, since the definition of science itself is that it is a demonstrative habit.

Therefore sacred Scripture has no other light or evidence besides that moral evidence we have named. For although it is not known of itself, nor can it properly be demonstrated, that sacred Scripture came forth from God, yet this is urged by so many and so probable arguments, and Scripture has in itself so many and so marked notes and indications of its divinity, that from them a pious and prudent man is effectively led to believe that it is true and divine.

title: The first transmitters prove Scripture divine: prophets and apostles were not impostors seeking gain, unlike Muhammad
english: And so that we may bring forward here certain specimens of those arguments: that the Scripture which we hold as sacred is truly such, and divinely inspired, is proved from the condition of those who first handed it down and recommended it as divine. For if sacred Scripture is not true and divine, then the sacred writers, who profess that they wrote as God inspired them, and who testify that the things they write were either seen by them or divinely revealed to them, must have been impostors whose design was to deceive men and mock the world.

But this suspicion cannot fall on the Prophets and Apostles, by whose work Scripture has been consigned to us. For those who mean to deceive aim at that either from desire of gain, or for the sake of some pleasure, or in hope of some glory and of obtaining pleasure. Thus those who were authors of some superstition certainly won wealth and dignities for themselves by their inventions — as, for example, Muhammad, who by deceiving the world with his fables arrogated the highest empire to himself and his own. But such a thing cannot be affixed to the Prophets and Apostles except very shamelessly and against every appearance of truth.

For if the matter is estimated by the sense of men, nearly all of them were most miserable, and of a cast-down and despised condition; nor by their preaching did they produce for themselves any riches in the world, or any empire and glory among men. On the contrary, that doctrine which they asserted by word and writings stirred up against them the hatred of their fellow-citizens and of outsiders, and made them liable to infinite reproaches and insults; nay, it cast them into certain danger of life, so that most of them sealed their writings with their own blood.

title: They did not stumble into suffering by inadvertence; Moses refused dynastic gain and recorded his own faults
english: Nor can it be said that they fell into such hardships by thoughtlessness. For when they took up their office they foresaw these calamities, and voluntarily handed themselves over to be exercised and tormented by so many evils. Moses indeed was leader and priest of the Israelite people; yet how little he cared for himself and his own is plain from this: that he did not transmit the principate and the priesthood to his posterity, but designated his servant Joshua as leader of the people after him, and, at God's command, inaugurated his brother Aaron as priest.

And how far the sacred writers were from vain glory is plain from this: that if anything great or illustrious was done or said by them, they refer it wholly to God as received from Him; nay, in those very writings which they commend as divinely inspired they candidly note their own blemishes and defects; and if anything in them was slight and humble and without glory, they do not disguise it. Thus Moses recorded his own diffidence and the penalty of that diffidence which God imposed on him; and likewise his brother Aaron's idolatry and his sister Mary's murmurings.

title: The world's rapid faith in the Gospel makes Scripture's divinity credible; Paul from Jerusalem to Illyricum
english: Next, that the doctrine and that Scripture which we hold as divine are truly divine is made very credible by the faith which the world has given them. For in a few years the Gospel of Christ pervaded almost the whole world; and as soon as it began to be preached to the nations, it found countless followers everywhere, of every age, sex, and condition — so much so that one Paul, from Jerusalem even to Illyricum, in a very short space of time filled all things with the Gospel of Christ, as he himself writes to the Romans (Romans 15:19). But that could not have come about except from a divine force that accompanied that sacred doctrine, and, as the same Paul notes in the place cited, from the power of the divine Spirit engraving it on men's hearts and confirming it with various prodigies and signs.

title: Everything stood against reception; rude messengers and fierce enemies prove the growth came from God's power alone
english: For if the matter is considered in itself, everything ought to have stood in the way of men receiving that doctrine, and Scripture which is its foundation. First, the genius of the doctrine itself. For it sets before us to be believed very many mysteries which human sense judges folly; and it commands and exacts things that most of all repugn human affections — namely that we bear Christ's cross, deny ourselves, and for Christ crucified be ready to leave wealth and pleasures and pour out our life (Matthew 16:24).

Next, those who announced that doctrine to men did not use art and eloquence, by which men's minds are usually bent. Nor did they prevail among men by authority, or by fame of wisdom and learning. Nor were they powerful men who could terrify by threats and arms and compel people to embrace their doctrine; but most of them were rude and unlettered men, earning their living by mechanical arts, from the nation of the Jews, despised and hated by all others, and held for barbarians and ignorant by those who were then thought wise and learned. Add that they were preaching to men nursed in another religion, and occupied by many and great prejudices. For the superstition from which they were being turned away they had received from their ancestors, and they saw it established by the consent of peoples, the vote of the wise, and great authority then.

Finally, it can scarcely be said how many and how sharp and powerful enemies the doctrine contained in our scriptures had. For the teachers of the Jews and the philosophers of the nations assailed it with great effort. The former opposed their own authority; the latter exercised against it all the sharpness of their ingenium and unfolded their eloquence. And besides, the magistrates and princes of the age most atrociously persecuted those who had embraced it, and raged against them with every kind of punishment. Since therefore nothing aided it humanly, and on the contrary it had all things adverse, it is necessary that its increase and propagation be ascribed to the power of the one God. For if any other sect and religion has crept widely and found many followers, that was done by human means. Muhammadanism spread briefly from Arabia through many provinces; but that was done by arms and open force. Next, that doctrine in many things flatters the flesh.

title: Martyrs' constancy, number, and condition mark something divine in Scripture
english: Besides, something divine in Scripture is argued by the constancy, number, and condition of the martyrs who sealed it with their own blood. For since by nature nothing is dearer to a man than life, how did it come about that so many men willingly sought death for the defence of Scripture and of the doctrine it hands down, unless from a certain divine force that had settled thoroughly in their minds? Rage has sometimes been spent on certain heretics and the superstitious, and a few examples can perhaps be found of those who from a certain fierceness and obstinacy of mind chose rather to die than to suffer themselves to be moved from an error once seized. But there is no error, no superstition and human doctrine, that has had followers so obstinate that, when by denying their impiety they could escape safe and unharmed, they nevertheless refused not to endure punishments and torments. But when the Apostolic and prophetic doctrine, and Scripture, first began to be propagated through the world — and could not yet be reckoned established by the tradition of the ancestors and by custom, the deepest roots by which human institutes usually cling to men's minds — not a few only were found, but infinite myriads of men, of every age, sex, and condition, men, women, boys, old men, the lettered and the unlettered, who endured every harshest kind of death rather than deny Scripture's doctrine: although by that denial alone they could not only redeem life, but also enjoy their goods and honors with fellow-citizens by equal right. Nor can they be reckoned to have rushed into certain death by fierceness or stupidity or some disease of mind: since they often extorted from the enemies themselves testimony of a rightly composed mind and of a blameless life, and in death itself attested the highest modesty, the highest humanity, and presence of mind. In which, certainly, unless someone willingly shuts his eyes, the finger of God can easily be noted.

title: Miracles confirm Law and Gospel; God would not lend omnipotence to a lying claim
english: Besides, that the doctrine handed down in the Scriptures — and so Scripture, which is its foundation — is divine and flowed from God is proved from the miracles done in confirmation of that doctrine. For since Scripture and heavenly doctrine have two chief parts, Law and Gospel: the law was confirmed by those wonders that happened in the desert — that the living voice of God speaking was heard from the midst of fire, that for forty years manna rained in the desert, that water was often led out from the rock, and that the Israelites' clothes were not worn out in that whole time, and more of that kind. To the Gospel almost infinite miracles of Christ bore witness; then those visible and plainly stupendous gifts of the Holy Spirit poured out on the first believers, so that suddenly they spoke in various and foreign tongues, healed any diseases, expelled demons, and performed very many other wonders. Since such things are above nature's powers, it is necessary that God exercised his power in them. But it is unholy to think God willed to use his omnipotence to make faith for a Scripture and doctrine falsely and injuriously ascribed to him, as if he had willed by compact with men to lie.

title: How we know the miracles happened: writers known; either deceived or deceiving
english: But you will say: those miracles are indeed said to have been done, yet how can we know they really were done? For it seems no less uncertain whether those miracles are true than whether that Scripture is divine in whose confirmation they are said to have been done. I answer that those things really happened can be proved efficaciously from our scriptures themselves. For our writers wrote those things in such a manner that they cannot have lied in this matter. For the one denying or doubting that what our writers Moses and Paul narrate about those miracles is true, I will ask, for example, whether he wills to call into doubt that there was a certain Moses who gave laws to the Israelite people and wrote certain volumes; and likewise that there was a certain Paul who preached Christian doctrine and wrote certain epistles ascribed to him. About this matter certainly no one has hitherto doubted, nor have the atheists themselves willed or dared to deny it. And really that is witnessed by a fame so constant, so perennial, so received by the consent of all — even of adversaries — that to doubt about this would plainly be to rave. For frequent mention of Moses and of his writings is made among the Gentiles. Nor do Jews and Muhammadans, most hostile enemies of the Christian religion, deny or doubt that our Apostles were and wrote. If someone would stubbornly wish to call that into doubt, he would have to be driven to bring a cause of his doubt, and some reason why he does not give faith to the concordant testimony of the whole world — and why he believes rather that Pliny and Titus Livius were and wrote than Moses and Paul. And certainly we labor in vain in proving this, since the matter is in confession. For those who reject God's word do not deny that those authors whom we hold as sacred were or wrote, but blaspheme that they did not write true things.

Come then, let us see whether it can be that those things narrated by Moses and Paul about those miracles are not true. Certainly, if they are not true, either those men were deceived in writing, thinking things had happened which really had not; or they wrote with a mind to deceive and tried to thrust false things for true. The former cannot be said. For they do not report those things as received from elsewhere, but testify them as done or seen by themselves. Therefore Moses must have willed to deceive the Israelites, and Paul the Corinthians, Galatians, and others. And so profane men feel who accuse Moses and Paul of imposture. It remains to see whether they were impostors who tried to persuade those to whom they were writing, and into whose hands they were handing their writings, that these and those prodigies and miracles had been done, when nevertheless nothing of them had been done.

title: Impostors hide from witnesses; Moses and Paul appeal to eyes and ears among their hearers
english: Certainly impostors, and those whose mind is to deceive, are accustomed so to forge their lies that they cannot easily be charged with lying by those they want deceived. Thus Numa, who instituted most of the rites of Roman superstition, feigned that he had conversations by night with the nymph Egeria — truly alone with her alone, where no one could be a witness. In Muhammad's Qur'an also certain portentous things are narrated, yet not as done before men's eyes, but whose credit would rest with him alone. But if someone narrated portents and dreams, and nevertheless appealed about their truth to the senses of those he addressed — as if he were already recounting that by Moses the waters flowed back and grain rained while we were looking on, and willed to persuade us of that itself — this would no longer be imposture, but a certain kind of dementia plainly unusual and incredible; nor can this fall on one who is not altogether raving and stirred by black bile. Now those wonders held in Moses — that the sea was split, that the voice of God speaking was heard from mount Sinai, that in the desert it rained manna and quails, that torrents of water burst from the rock, and more of the same kind — those wonders, I say, Moses does not commemorate as things that happened at other times or in distant places: but he narrates them as having happened in that very time and in that very place where he was writing, indeed while those for whom he was writing were seeing and attending, and into whose hands he was handing his writings. And about the truth of those miracles he appeals to the eyes and ears of the Israelites. You have seen, he often says, and you have heard; and by that name he heavily and often rebukes their mind as ungrateful toward God.

Likewise the Apostle Paul, when he had among the Corinthians certain rivals and envious men who were trying to call his apostleship into doubt and render it suspect, appeals about the truth of his apostleship to miracles and signs done in their midst. The signs of apostleship, he says, were published among you with all patience, through signs and wonders and powers (2 Corinthians 12:12). And in chapters 12, 13, and 14 of the former epistle he discusses the miraculous gifts of the Holy Spirit — the gift of healings, the working of powers, the gift of prophecy, and the gift of speaking and interpreting foreign tongues by the Spirit's sudden breath — as things known and customary in their midst: he exhorts them to peace, warns them not to envy one another because of such gifts, and also rebukes that they sometimes used such gifts ambitiously; and he orders that thereafter they do it toward edification, and he prescribes the lawful use of those gifts.

title: If the miracle reports were lies, craft fails and madness cannot explain the world's faith
english: If therefore all those things are lies and fictions, certainly Moses and Paul were not, as the profane charge, crafty dealers and cunning men whose purpose was to deceive men and impose on the world. For no one can be deceived in things about which appeal is made to his ears, eyes, and experience. But it is necessary that they were — far be the blasphemous saying — men plainly raging and insane. And yet their writings, with the atheists themselves as judges, prove enough that they were of sound mind. For they speak things coherent with themselves, and in which much prudence and wisdom is to be discerned.

Next, let us feign they were insane men who wrote with the highest madness or imprudence and presented those lies as true, which they could be charged openly and by all. Whence then did it come about that the Israelites looked up to Moses, and the Corinthians, Romans, Galatians, and others to Paul, as divine and holy men, and received their discipline with so great reverence — although in many things it is ungrateful to the flesh, burdensome, and repugnant to human affections — and that no profit returned therefrom to those who thus willed to be deceived, if the matter is valued from men's sense? Certainly no miracle, nor any portent, is more incredible than this: that the doctrine of insane men, and their thick and foul lies, without any aid either divine or human, obtained so great faith among those very people for whom it was impossible not to recognize and notice their insanity and lies.

And here that ancient dilemma has place: the miracles narrated in the Scriptures are true, or not true. If true, the doctrine and scripture to whose confirmation they were applied are true also. But if they are not true, it is more than a miracle that a doctrine so abhorrent from men's sense, and stuffed with so many lies which anyone was ready to charge, was nonetheless received with so great ardor without any help divine or human, and retained with so great constancy through exiles, crosses, and tortures, while those eminent in the world by power and prudence were raging and indignant.

Since therefore what Moses and Paul recount about miracles done in confirmation of the Law and the Gospel is written in such a manner that those to whom they were writing could at once recognize whether they were saying true or false — since they are things about which appeal is made to their experience and senses — and yet so great faith was given to those writings by those who first received them, and thereafter even to this day, it is plainly necessary that they wrote true things, and that the miracles they narrate are true, and therefore that Scripture and the doctrine in whose confirmation God willed those things to happen are true.

title: Adversaries themselves confess Moses' and Christ's miracles; Jews invent magic or the Name
english: But besides, that the miracles reported as done by Moses are true, and likewise those attributed to Christ and his Apostles, is clear from the adversaries' own confession. For as to Christ, the Jews who are most hostile enemies of the Christian name neither formerly dared, nor even now dare, to deny that Christ performed miracles: but they have invented I know not what to elude the force of the argument we draw therefrom — namely either that Christ did those things by magic art which he had learned in Egypt, or by virtue of that tetragrammaton Name whose right pronunciation and exposition he held. For they fable that whoever knows how to pronounce that name rightly can by its force do any wonderful works. The vanity of that invention is clear of itself, and there is no need to refute it. Here we only note that the truth of Christ's miracles is not a little confirmed thereby: since the Jews who most envy his glory neither dare nor are able openly to deny that those things were done. And likewise very many of the Gentiles bore testimony to Moses and acknowledged the truth of the Mosaic history, as is to be seen in the books of Josephus against Apion, and of Eusebius on the Preparation of the Gospel.

title: Prophets' predictions prove Christian doctrine and Scripture's divine origin
english: Especially do the Prophets' predictions prove the truth of Christian doctrine, and argue Scripture's divine origin. For it belongs to God alone to foreknow future contingencies certainly and distinctly, and things that will come to pass only after many ages. And therefore no one can predict such things except by the afflatus of the divine Spirit. But the Prophets predicted many things for which no causes appeared in the nature of things, and which were fulfilled long after their death. Thus Isaiah named Cyrus, and predicted his empire and wondrous felicity, a hundred and fifty years before Cyrus was born. Thus Jeremiah the Prophet precisely numbered the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity before the Jews were led away to Babylon. Thus finally Daniel prophesied very clearly concerning the Monarchy of the Persians and of the Greeks, concerning the successors of Alexander the Great, and concerning Antiochus especially Epiphanes who profaned the temple of God.

title: Gospel events clearly foretold; Isaiah 53 and Daniel 9 show stunning Messianic consensus
english: But what is chief: what the Gospel teaches us concerning the nativity, life, passion, death, and burial of Jesus Christ, concerning his resurrection and ascension into heaven; likewise concerning the fruit of his death and passion, the calling of the Gentiles, the desolation of the Jewish nation, and the abrogation of the ceremonial worship, with nearly all the details of these things, are found clearly and openly predicted in the Prophets. Among other things Isaiah chapter 53 is notable, where he speaks of the death and passion of Christ our Redeemer, and of his offering for the sins of the world, so expressly and clearly that he seems to narrate a thing already done, not to predict a future one (Isaiah 53). And Daniel chapter 9 expressly designates the time at which Christ was to come, and at once to be cut off, and to put an end to sacrifices — namely after seventy weeks of years, which the dreadful destruction of the whole Jewish nation was to follow (Daniel 9): so that for one comparing the oracles of Moses and the Prophets concerning the Messiah with the Gospel history of Christ, a wondrous and plainly stupendous consensus at once appears. Whence it is manifestly proved both that the Prophets' books are divine, since they contain predictions of things that happened after so great a space of time, and that the Gospel history is true and divine, since God through the Prophets bore testimony to it so many ages beforehand.

title: Jews attest the prophecies were not forged; hatred could not make them erase Daniel
english: Further, that these oracles were not forged by Christians the Jews testify — enemies of the Christians, and yet the keenest assertors and defenders of the prophetic books. And besides, that that greatest hatred of the Christian religion could not compel them to erase from their books those oracles so greatly adverse to themselves — this itself, I say, frees them from the crime of which certain Gentiles wished to render them suspect, as if they had inserted into their books those oracles concerning Cyrus and Alexander the Great in order to court those kings' favor. For if they had thought so much allowed to them, those oracles by which Christians so greatly press them would not have remained untouched, especially that of Daniel concerning the time of Christ's advent and his cutting off. Nor will anyone ever suspect such a thing of the Jews who has ascertained with how great religion — not to say superstition — toward the sacred books they conduct themselves, even to such a degree that they keep the syllables and apices of each book numbered, and appoint a public fast if by chance a Scripture codex has fallen to the ground through carelessness. Add that whoever will attentively read through and consider the books of the Prophets Daniel and Isaiah will easily recognize that in them all things cohere and are woven with the same thread and genius, nor is anything found that anyone could deservedly suspect to have been added and inserted there against the author's mind and sense — and that could be torn away from them without the ruin and gap of the whole work.

title: Antiquity, providence preserving Scripture, and the sects' consensus jointly commend its authority
english: Besides these, many arguments can be taken toward conciliating Scripture's authority and veneration from Scripture's antiquity, from God's care in preserving it, and from the world's hatred toward it, and God's just judgment against its haters and despisers. For the books of Moses, which are as it were the basis and foundation of the whole of Scripture, are by far the most ancient of all that exist. Indeed there are no writings that equal the antiquity of Solomon and David. And yet almost the whole world long waged war against Scripture and tried to abolish it — as in Jewish times that Antiochus Epiphanes, and in Christian memory the Roman Emperors, whose power was so great and whose empire so widely extended. But as much as the world worked to abolish it, so much did God's providence watch that it should remain safe and entire hitherto.

Nor is the consensus of the nations — indeed of the various sects — of small moment in this matter. Since today three chief sects thrive, afterward subdivided into many others — namely the Jewish, the Christian, and the Mahometan — which occupy the greatest part of the world. Jews, Christians, and Mahometans all acknowledge the authority of the Old Testament. The Jews indeed reject the New Testament, but the Mahometans hold it in esteem with us, and at least venerate Christ as God's greatest Prophet. What then could compel so many peoples, disagreeing among themselves in customs and sects, and mutually pursuing one another with the keenest hatreds, to approve these books as sacred and divine, unless the force of truth itself and a certain divine efficacy?

Which arguments, although perhaps not all equally valid if taken singly by themselves, nevertheless when taken together have the greatest force toward proving Scripture's excellence and conciliating authority to it. Nay, those superior ones which we have explained more widely we judge to be such that by them Scripture's authority can validly be asserted and proved even against atheists and the profane, who can retort and oppose nothing that has any force, and whose vanity it is not hard to show.

title: Scripture bears intrinsic divinity notes a well-disposed mind perceives, as critics scent an author
