(1) all persons can/ought by certain faith believe their sins remitted and themselves just before God;
(2) with the same firmness as believing Christ is God's Son and world's Redeemer;
(3) such persuasion so necessary that without it none is truly faithful/just;
(4) true saving faith consists in that persuasion as its proper chief act — justifying even those who are wicked without good works.
Le Blanc names Bellarmine and Becanus as sources who suppose or expressly fasten these on the Reformed.
translator_notes: OCR: CXXIX 1675 PDF 243; Thesis I calumny catalogue.

title: Issue is common-consent dogma — not whether some Reformed gave occasion for the charge
english: The real question is not whether some Reformed gave occasion for the charge.
It is whether Reformed theologians teach those four points by common consent as received faith-articles nearly all subscribe — as the opponent claims. Le Blanc says affirming that is calumny.

Defense needs only many celebrated Orthodox Reformed who reject the imputation; a few who taught or seemed to imply it does not prove school-wide dogma while others contradict without being branded heterodox.
translator_notes: OCR: CXXX 1675 PDF 243; issue = common consent, not occasional occasion.

title: First calumny answered: remitted-sins persuasion is not Reformed formal act of faith
english: Briefly, taking the charges in reverse: it is calumny to say Reformed theologians teach by common consent that faith's formal justifying act is each believer's certain persuasion that sins are remitted and he is just before God — and that without that persuasion none is truly faithful, as if denying a fundamental article.

Perkins, Davenant, Ames, Mestrezat, Du Moulin, Walaeus, and Wittich following Widmar expressly deny that saving faith's formal act is already-obtained-grace certainty; it is rather fleeing to God and leaning on him for mercy through Christ — and the former trust can be absent even from the justified for a time, as also the Presbyterian Anglican Confession teaches.
Musculus and Peter Martyr likewise place faith's essence in Spirit-wrought firm heart-assent that draws fiducia, hope, charity, and good works — not in remitted-sins persuasion.
translator_notes: OCR: CXXXI 1675 PDF 243-244; CXXXII absent in print. First calumny / formal act.

title: Second point: own-justification certainty is not held as firm as faith that Christ is God's Son
english: Not all Reformed doctors teach that each believer must be as firmly sure of personal justification and eternal salvation as of the dogma that Christ is God's Son and the world's Redeemer — so calling that common consent is false accusation.

Many Reformed already grant that own-salvation persuasion can be separated from faith for a long time and belongs only to faith's accidental perfection — so it cannot bind with the same firmness as the Christ-article, which no one can lose even briefly and still remain truly faithful.
translator_notes: OCR: CXXXIII 1675 PDF 244; equal-certainty charge. CXXXII not in 1675.

title: British Dort deputies: assurance persuasion may be vivid, languid, or null — below dogmatic faith
english: The British Dort deputies, chiefly Bishop George of Llandaff and Davenant, state for their church: assurance-persuasion lacks certainty that forever rules out contrary fear — sometimes vivid, sometimes weak, sometimes null in heavy temptation.

Its weakness comes first because personal trust sits below dogmatic faith: Catholic articles bind assent as immediate principles, while special-faith truth is only assumed; the conclusion cannot be firmer than its weaker premise — experimental marks often doubted or clouded by temptation.
translator_notes: OCR: CXXXIV 1675 PDF 244; British Dort judgment on assurance degrees.

title: Opponent misreads Dort V.9 as equating assurance with divine-faith certainty
english: Given that the British deputies' votes shaped Dort's Canons and their judgment stands in the acts, the opponent has little ground to read Dort V.9 as defining own-grace persuasion equal in kind and certainty to divine faith in immediately revealed articles.

Dort V.9 says the faithful can and are certain, according to the measure of faith, that they remain living church members, have remission, and eternal life — not that this certainty matches assent to the chief revealed articles.
Readers should ask whether the carping Learned Man reads Dort better than the deputies who drafted and first signed its decrees.
translator_notes: OCR: CXXXV 1675 PDF 244-245; Dort V.9 vs British deputies' sense.

title: Ames with the British: 'my sins are remitted' is a deduced conclusion, lesser certainty than principles
english: Ames aligns with the British: answering Bellarmine's framed question — can one without special revelation be certain with divine-faith certainty that sins are remitted? — Ames says Bellarmine fails to distinguish degrees: principles immediately revealed versus deduced conclusions, and faith-in-itself versus fiducia in apprehension or hope.
Once ambiguities are cleared, Ames defends the affirmative against Rome's denial — but not with equal certainty across all that is called divine faith.
Because 'my sins are remitted' is a deduced conclusion, not an immediately revealed principle, faith holds it with lesser certainty than the principles.
translator_notes: OCR: CXXXVI 1675 PDF 245; Ames vs Bellarmine on certainty degrees.

title: Ames: faith-in-itself requires greater certainty than fiducia born from faith
english: Ames further distinguishes faith-in-itself from fiducia that rises from faith — the trust by which we grasp a present good or hope a future one.
Greater certainty belongs to faith itself than to that born fiducia, even when the fiducia is loosely called faith.
So when believers are said to be divinely certain of accepted grace or coming salvation, Ames means fiducia from faith, not justifying faith as such — and that fiducia has lesser certainty.
translator_notes: OCR: CXXXVII 1675 PDF 245; Ames faith vs fiducia certainty.

title: Many Reformers: calling assurance an act of faith does not equalize it with 'Christ is God's Son'
english: Many Reformers expressly teach graded certainty within faith: some assents rest on revelation alone; others mix revelation with report, reason, or sensory experience — yet both count as acts of faith.

Equal firmness does not follow: maximum certainty belongs to revelation-alone articles; mixed conclusions vary with the weaker premise — as Le Blanc already taught, and many Reformed doctors openly say.
So calling own-grace persuasion an act of faith does not prove common Reformed consent that it matches certainty that Christ is God's Son and the world's Redeemer.
translator_notes: OCR: CXXXVIII 1675 PDF 245; graded certainty within faith acts.

title: Even Rome: not every 'divine faith' assent equals Catholic dogmatic certainty — Catharinus & Vasquez
english: Even inside the Roman school, not every assent labeled divine faith matches Catholic dogmatic certainty.

At Trent, Catharinus held a just man can be divinely certain of his own grace; Vasquez calls divine faith both the penitent's trust of pardon-to-come and the justified man's trust of pardon obtained — yet neither equates that private faith with Catholic certainty.

Trent's canon that none can know with faith-certainty he has obtained grace added 'to which falsehood cannot be subject' with an eye to Catharinus — who afterward still kept his view and re-read the decree.
translator_notes: OCR: CXXXIX 1675 PDF 245-246; Catharinus/Vasquez/Trent.

title: Rivet and Daillé citations: dispute heat can force soft readings; they would not desert Ames/British sense
english: The opponent's Rivet and Daillé citations fail: from a few words he claims they gave own-grace fiducia the same certainty as faith in the fundamentals.
Even the most learned, caught in dispute heat, let slip things that need softening back to a sound sense.
Le Blanc doubts that, if warned, those doctors would have left the Ames/British sentence already laid out.
translator_notes: OCR: CXL 1675 PDF 246; Rivet & Daillé under dispute-heat caveat.

title: Two celebrities' opinions are not common Reformed consent against Ames and the British deputies
english: Even granting Daillé and Rivet differed from Ames and the British — giving own-remission fiducia the same certainty as article-faith — that does not make their view common Reformed consent.
Both men held peculiar opinions many Reformed opposed.
Why weigh Reformers by those two rather than by Ames and the Anglican deputies to Dort?
translator_notes: OCR: CXLI 1675 PDF 246; two witnesses vs Ames/British measure.

title: Last charge: opponent reads 'all and each men' as 'all the faithful' and cites Pareus
english: Last calumny charge: Le Blanc said Rome calumniously pins on the Reformed a common-consent teaching that all and each men can and ought by certain faith believe their sins remitted and themselves just.
The opponent re-reads 'all and each men' as 'all the faithful,' then cites Pareus to make that the real Reformed common doctrine — hence not calumny.
translator_notes: OCR: CXLII 1675 PDF 246; last charge via Pareus re-reading.

title: 'All men' means Gospel hearers in external communion — even the vicious — not only the faithful
english: Pareus was unnecessary: Le Blanc's own theses already prove Reformed common doctrine that each of the faithful can and ought be certain of grace without special revelation, and that such certainty is commonly called faith-certainty — so lack of it marks infirmity, not unbelief of the fundamentals.
The opponent's conjecture fails: 'all and each men' did not mean only the faithful.
Nor did Le Blanc mean Rome charges a duty on absolutely every human without exception; he meant all Gospel hearers in external church communion — even those who are wicked.
translator_notes: OCR: CXLIII 1675 PDF 246; homines = Gospel hearers in external communion.

title: Rome assumes even the vicious must believe themselves just; Reformed teach they are on the path of perdition until living faith
english: Le Blanc did not claim Rome expressly says the Reformed teach every Gospel hearer in external communion — however he lives — must by certain faith believe himself just; rather Rome's anti-Reformed disputations manifestly assume that.
The opponent's book keeps pressing that, for Calvinists, even those who are wicked and dying flagitious need only firm belief that grace if that were the formal justifying act.

If that assumption were right, every external church member would be bound to believe himself just whatever his life; but Reformed sense is the opposite: such persons must believe they are on the path of perdition until they truly renounce vice and believe with a faith efficacious through love (Galatians 5:6) — only then may they believe themselves just and reconciled through Christ. The contrary is atrocious calumny.
translator_notes: OCR: CXLIV 1675 PDF 246-247; vicious-in-communion calumny vs living faith.

title: Pars I close: Le Blanc kept common Reformed doctrine; Rome's four imputations are calumny; opponent's charges fall
english: Pars I close: Le Blanc has not deserted common Reformed doctrine or foisted a private opinion as school teaching.
His complaint stands: Rome calumniously imputes the four points as if by Reformed common consent.
The opponent's charges of deceitful dissimulation and of Le Blanc's own calumny are undeserved; the eloquent declamations built on that rotten base collapse without needing a line-by-line chase.
translator_notes: OCR: CXLV 1675 PDF 247; Pars I close. Next: PARS SECUNDA Roman comparison.

title: Pars II opens: Roman absolute faith is Spirit-moved assent to all God has revealed
english: Pars II opens the Roman comparison: for Rome's doctors, faith taken absolutely is Spirit-moved and Spirit-inspired assent to everything God has revealed to human beings.
The motive of that assent is the truth and authority of God who reveals.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II I 1675 PDF 247; Roman absolute faith = Spirit-moved assent.

title: Same faith is dead/idle apart from love, or living/effective joined to good works
english: Rome distinguishes two states of that same faith: it may stand apart from God's love and other pious works — as in many sinners — or be joined to love and good works.
Apart from love it is called dead and idle; joined to love it is living and effective.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II II 1675 PDF 247; dead/idle vs living/effective.

title: Jaubert: credere Deo without charity is dead; credere in Deum living in the just alone
english: Jaubert of Arles, against Molinaeus's Clypeum, unfolds the split at length.
Credere Deo is supernatural mind-assent to whatever God revealed because God said it — possible without charity, and then called dead for lack of charity's life.
Credere in Deum is living faith animated by charity, found only in the just, and through it the person hopes for the fulfillment of the promises.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II III 1675 PDF 247; Jaubert bifariam; living faith works through love.

title: Formed vs unformed: charity is external improper form making faith meritorious
english: The usual Roman School distinction is formed versus unformed faith: unformed is faith alone without charity; formed is faith joined to charity and love.

Charity is called faith's form — not an internal form that constitutes its essence, but an external, improper form that gives faith a relative standing: it profits to eternal life and is, they say, meritorious of salvation.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II IV 1675 PDF 247-248; formed/unformed; external form.

title: Estius: charity perfects faith so it merits; one habit is not another's subject
english: Estius: charity is not faith's essential form, and one habit is not another's subject.
Rather, through charity faith is perfected and formed so as to be meritorious and to profit to eternal salvation — as charity is called the form of all other virtues.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II V 1675 PDF 248; Estius on metaphorical form.

title: Valencia: charity is metaphorical form only; faith and charity are distinct virtues
english: Gregory of Valencia agrees: theologians say charity perfects faith as a form, yet not as an essential or even accidental proper form — faith and charity are species-distinct virtues perfecting different powers.
Charity may only metaphorically be called faith's form by analogy to a proper form that perfects its subject.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II VI 1675 PDF 248; Valencia metaphorical form.

title: Scripture cue: faith working through love and James's dead faith make charity like soul to body
english: Their cue for calling charity faith's form is Scripture: Paul describes saving faith as faith that works through love, and James calls faith without charity's works dead.
Form is what something lives and acts by; so charity stands to faith as soul to body.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II VII 1675 PDF 248; Gal 5:6 and James dead-faith cue.

title: Dead faith is still God's gift and true in itself; the wicked assent inwardly but use faith badly
english: Rome still calls dead, unformed faith a divine gift that merits the name of true faith — even while saying its holders do not believe well or as they ought.
Bad Christians' assent to the Word is inwardly real and God-inspired, yet they misuse faith, miss its due end, and omit what faith commands.
Stapleton: the act without charity is good in itself, but not well done because it is not aimed at the ultimate good.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II VIII 1675 PDF 248; Bellarmine/Stapleton on dead faith as gift.

title: Dead faith can be called true or not by respect; only charity-animated faith truly profits
english: Rome allows dead faith to be called true or not by respect, and can reserve the title of true faith for formed faith.
The Ethicen opponent's analogy: a legitimate king, bishop, or baptized believer may still fail the perfection due to the name — yet the name is not simply denied.

So faith left in those who fell from baptismal grace by other sins than unbelief is true faith; yet in a good sense only charity-animated faith is called true, because that alone profits, makes us God's children, and seats Christ in the heart — backed by Fathers and Rome's public Office.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II IX 1675 PDF 248-249; Ethicen author; true by perfection vs by essence.

title: Stapleton: dead faith fictive for perfect justice, not fictive as to faith's own virtue
english: Stapleton likewise: dead, unformed faith may be called feigned or hypocritical with respect to the life and truth of perfect justice.
It is not feigned with respect to faith itself and the virtue proper to faith.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II X 1675 PDF 249; Stapleton fictive vs proper virtue.

title: Scholastics dispute whether unformed faith is a virtue: name-fight, not thing-fight
english: Scholastics split on whether unformed faith is a virtue: Thomas says no; Durandus and Bonaventure say even dead faith is a virtue — but the fight is largely about the name.
Affirmers take virtue generally as a habit of mind agreeing with right reason and divine law; in that sense Rome does not deny unformed faith is a virtue, binding the intellect in obedience of faith.
Deniers reserve virtue for what makes one live rightly and simply good; on that sense all concede that without charity neither faith nor any morally good habit is a virtue.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XI 1675 PDF 249-250; Thomas vs Durandus/Bonaventure.

title: Living and dead faith are one species; charity adds only external relative perfection
english: Rome refuses to make living and dead faith different species: they differ only by accidental perfection and remain one faith in species.
Faith may be found with or without charity while keeping its essence; charity when present adds only an external, relative perfection.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XII 1675 PDF 250; one species; accidental perfection.

title: Same-number faith with/without charity is common teaching, not defined dogma like same-species
english: Common Roman teaching even allows the same numerical faith to be formed or unformed as charity comes and goes — Peter's faith intrinsically the same under either label.
Same-species living/dead faith is defined dogma; same-number continuity is common and approved by modern doctors, but not equal in certainty and not a dogma — some older Scholastics opposed it.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XIII 1675 PDF 250; same-species dogma vs same-number opinion.

title: Valencia/Tapper/Estius: Trent defined species-same faith without charity; number-same is certain but not defined
english: Valencia: accidents do not multiply the essence — formed or not is accidental to faith — so same-species faith with or without charity is of the faith.
Trent settled against heretics that true Catholic theological faith can exist without charity in faithful sinners; it did not define numerical identity.
Numerical sameness is now so common that the opposite is called rash; Tapper and Estius concur that species-sameness is de fide and number-sameness highly probable.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XIV 1675 PDF 250; Valencia/Tapper/Estius; Trent scope.

title: Rome rejects calling dead faith historical: it assents to all God's Word on God's testimony
english: Rome refuses the Protestant label historical for dead faith.
Dead faith does not traffic in histories alone: it assents to histories, dogmas, and promises in God's Word alike.
And it does not believe on human historian-authority, but on the testimony of God speaking and revealing in the Word.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XV 1675 PDF 250; reject historical label.

title: All Rome: only living, charity-formed faith actually justifies; Aquinas and Becanus
english: Setting the historical label aside: all Roman doctors confess dead faith without charity does not profit to salvation or justice, and no faith actually saves and justifies unless it is living and effective through love.
Aquinas: unformed faith is not a virtue; formed faith is, because we are justified only through what has the nature of a virtue.
Becanus for Catholics generally: faith can exist unformed, but justifies only when formed by charity.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XVI 1675 PDF 250-251; Aquinas/Becanus; only formed justifies. Next: XVII+.

title: Dead unformed faith still first disposition to justice (Stapleton)
english: Even after granting with Stapleton that dead unformed faith profits neither salvation nor justice, Roman doctors still call faith as such, charity present or absent, the first and most necessary disposition toward justice.

In itself faith is the soul first act of union with God; by not-yet-formed faith charity is sought so that faith may later be formed, provided the prayer faith prompts is used (Stapleton, De Justif. 8.17).
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XVII 1675 PDF 249-250; dead faith as disposition (Stapleton).

title: Absolute faith is justification foundation and root (Jaubert/Arnold)
english: Rome therefore calls absolute faith, Spirit-moved assent to the whole Word, the foundation and root of justification: from it justice before God begins to sprout, and without it no one reaches justice.

Yet bare assent without charity cannot carry anyone to justice or salvation, any more than a foundation without walls and roof makes a house; Jaubert via Arnold says faith without charity-working is a roofless house and fruitless tree (Adv. Molinaei Clypeum 1.40.5).
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XVIII PDF 250; absolute faith as foundation (Jaubert).

title: Only formed faith actually justifies; unformed may be called justifying as disposition
english: Common Roman teaching: only formed living faith actually justifies; yet not-yet-formed faith is still a necessary prerequisite disposition and may be called justifying in that preparatory sense, though alone it remains useless and justifies no one.

On Paul justified by, from, and through faith, some Romans read living formed faith working through love; others take faith absolutely as the first disposition without which justification cannot be reached. Stapleton records both without rejecting either (De Justif. 8.16-17).
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XIX PDF 250; formed alone actu justifies; unformed as dispositio.

title: Unformed justifying faith means active faith birthing charity, not idle speculation (Vasquez)
english: When Romans call not-yet-formed faith justifying as root and foundation, they do not mean idle speculative faith, but an active faith that begins to work through good works, somehow generates charity, and presses toward it without yet fully possessing it.

Vasquez: only the faith-act that stirs affection counts as root and foundation in act (Disp. 210.7.54); Stapleton likewise ties not-yet-formed faith to obtaining charity through the prayer faith prompts (De Justif. 8.17).
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XX PDF 250; Vasquez actuosa faith vs inert.

title: Justifying faith object includes all revealed: promises, threats, precepts, dogmas
english: Roman doctors place in justifying faith object everything revealed to the Church in God's Wordrdrd: grace-promises, but also threats, precepts, and dogmas.
Faith saves and justifies not only by embracing grace-promises, but also by assenting to dogmas, believing mysteries, and receiving threats and precepts with fitting obedience and reverence.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXI PDF 250; object = all revealed content.

title: Principal object still Christ grace and mercy (Stapleton; Trent sess.6)
english: Rome still grants that justifying faith chief object is God grace and mercy in Christ offered in the Gospel to believing penitents; Stapleton confirms this from Trent sess. 6 c. 6.

Christ the Mediator and his redemption are principal when faith disposes to justification, yet not the sole proper object; faith also regards the other revealed objects while that disposition is underway.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXII PDF 251; Stapleton + Trent principal object.

title: Special mercy certain promise is presumption, not faith necessary object (Bellarmine)
english: Roman doctors refuse to count a certain promise of special mercy among justifying faith objects; Bellarmine treats that as presumption rather than faith (De Justif. 1.4; 1.8).

Vasquez and others deny special mercy is a necessary faith-object, as they say heretics invent, while still requiring particular trust in divine promise for justification; what they reject is that each must believe his own sins already remitted as faith necessary object.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXIII PDF 251; Bellarmine vs special mercy object.

title: Proper act of justifying faith is assent; notitia denied as faith act (Bellarmine)
english: Rome unanimously locates justifying faith proper act in assent to everything God revealed in the Word delivered to the Church, because of divine authority and testimony.

They deny that knowledge (acquaintance, understanding, or awareness) is faith act; Bellarmine even says faith stands against scientific understanding and is better defined by ignorance than by knowledge (De Justif. 1.7).ge (De Justif. 1.7).ge (De Justif. 1.7).
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXIV PDF 251; assent vs notitia (Bellarmine).

title: Notitia means evident distinct knowledge; rude confused apprehension suffices for faith
english: When Romans deny faith is notitia and oppose faith to scientia, they mean evident or at least distinct accurate cognition, not every grasp of the object.

Believers need not see evidence in the mysteries themselves, nor have the clear grasp of teachers who explain and defend them; a rude confused apprehension, as in the unlearned who believe Trinity and Incarnation, is enough, and faith properly sits in assent rather than in that apprehension.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXV PDF 251; notitia = evident/distinct knowledge.

title: Faith never without some apprehension; apprehension precedes faith but is not faith
english: Rome still grants that faith never lacks some apprehension, at least rude and confused, of what is believed.
In the believer there are two: apprehension and judgment or assent; apprehension properly is not faith but something that precedes it.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXVI PDF 251; apprehension precedes assent.

title: Implicit Church-faith alone insufficient; explicit Creed articles required for salvation
english: Rome concedes that merely believing in general what the Church believes, with no explicit grasp of any mystery, does not suffice for salvation.

Private persons may hold many dogmas only implicitly, but each believer needs some express explicit cognition of at least the principal Creed articles; that cognition may still be crude and confused...
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXVII PDF 251-252; explicit Creed vs implicit rest.

title: Accurate divine science useful and laudable though not required for salvation
english: Even while holding that implicit faith in most dogmas, and only rude confused notitia of the principal articles, can suffice for salvation, Rome does not deny the usefulness of deeper divine science.
Such science kindles love of God; learners who advance deserve praise, while perpetual learners who never reach truth deserve blame.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXVIII PDF 252; science useful not necessary.

title: Bellarmine De Justif. 1.7 summarizes apprehension, double assent, faith vs science
english: Bellarmine De Justif. 1.7 gathers the preceding points: believer has apprehension plus assent; rude rustic apprehension is not properly notitia; distinct theological notitia is not required for faith.

He splits assent into evidence-following (notitia) and authority-following (faith), citing Augustine; mysteries above reason are believed not understood, so faith is better defined by ignorance than science, yet divine science remains useful and laudable.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXIX PDF 252; Bellarmine cap.7 summary.

title: Vasquez: justifying faith is assent not perfect understanding; against Calvin exact knowledge
english: Vasquez Disp. 209.3: justifying faith is assent, not perfect understanding of the mysteries.

Against a Calvinist-sounding demand for accurate distinct cognition able to explain and defend dogmas, he holds that rude believers assenting on testimony alone have enough for justifying faith; only explored exact science is excluded, not every notitia.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXX PDF 252; Vasquez vs Calvin exact knowledge.

title: Valencia: explicit faith for Apostles Creed; implicit enough for other truths in laypeople
english: Valencia distinguishes explicit faith (immediate assent to a truth) from implicit faith (assent wrapped inside another act with a different immediate object), as when believing Scripture is God Word implies all it contains.

In the time of grace everyone must explicitly believe the Apostles Creed articles; other scriptural or defined truths may be held only implicitly by lay faithful not charged to teach and confirm others.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXXI PDF 252; Valencia explicit Creed.

title: Estius: explicit faith of life-necessary articles and publicly taught dogmas
english: Estius: every Christian owes distinct explicit faith to articles whose distinct cognition is needed to order life rightly.

Dogmas publicly obvious in church teaching — by preaching, feasts, ceremonies — must be held explicitly by all not justly hindered from hearing them, especially where the Church presses hard against grave heresies (Sent. 3 Dist. 25 q. 2).
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXXII PDF 252-253; Estius explicit duties.

title: Today Rome denies persuasion of own remitted sins as faith-act; Cologne/Cassander dissent noted
english: Present Roman consensus refuses to make persuasion that one has obtained mercy and remitted sins part of the faith that justifies; such persuasion is treated as rash presumption, not the act by which one is justified.

Cassander cites earlier Cologne Enchiridion theologians who required believing not only general remission for penitents in Christ, but also that one own sins are remitted through faith, together with a new penitent affection.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXXIII PDF 253; Rome vs Cologne on remitted-sins persuasion.

title: Catharinus: private divine faith of remitted sins possible without being Catholic faith-act
english: Catharinus denies that persuasion of obtained pardon is an act of Catholic faith or a requirement for justification.

Yet he allows the justified, without special revelation, a private divine faith that their sins are remitted when they experience in themselves the conditions under which God promised remission; Vasquez notes such assent can be divine faith if drawn from revealed principles plus evident experience (Disp. 209.3).
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXXIV PDF 253; Catharinus private divine faith.

title: Vasquez: persuasion of being justified can be private divine faith and somehow aids justification
english: Vasquez classifies duly believing one sins are remitted and that one is justified as private divine faith, specifically different from Catholic dogmatic faith (Disp. 209.4).

Such belief can arise from conjectures under the Spirit impulse rather than as a revealed proper object; even when it does not remove all fear without special revelation, it is God gift and somehow helps toward justification.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXXV PDF 253; Vasquez private faith of justification.

title: Cassander: adoption-certainty follows justification; not required to obtain it
english: Cassander grants that justifying faith naturally yields certainty of adoption and reconciliation, and a sensed grace wrought by the Spirit.
Yet that certainty of remitted sins follows justification; it is not a condition required to obtain justification or under which remission is promised.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXXVI PDF 253; Cassander certainty follows justification.

title: Common Rome: fiducia of mercy to be obtained is not justifying faith act but distinct from faith
english: Roman school common teaching: fiducia of pardon and mercy still to be obtained from God is not an act of justifying faith but something distinct from faith.
They urge this hard against Protestants in the faith-nature disputations of Bellarmine, Valencia, Stapleton, and others.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXXVII PDF 253; fiducia not faith-act.

title: Yet Trent lists hope and fiducia of divine mercy among dispositions to justification
english: Rome still counts that fiducia among the necessary prerequisite dispositions to justification; Trent sess. 6 c. 6 lists hope and trust of divine mercy among adult dispositions.

Trent sequence: grace-stirred hearing-faith, free movement to God, belief of revealed promises especially justification of the ungodly in Christ, salutary fear, turning to mercy, hope with trust God will be propitious for Christ sake, and beginning to love him as justice fountain.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXXVIII PDF 253-254; Trent hope/fiducia as disposition.

title: Fiducia not act of absolute faith but included in living formed faith (credere in Deum)
english: When Romans say fiducia is not a faith-act, they mean absolute faith in its proper nature, not living formed faith (believing in God))), which alone actually saves and which includes fiducia and love among its acts.

Jaubert (Clypeus 1.40.8-11) and Lombard via Augustine: living faith is not assent alone but also mercy-trust flowing from charity; believing in God means loving, going into, clinging, and being incorporated into his members.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XXXIX PDF 254; fiducia in living faith (Jaubert).

title: Vasquez: private faith of the promise necessary alongside Catholic faith for hope and justification
english: Vasquez not only puts fiducia inside living faith but names as faith the penitent persuasion that God will remit one sins and justify him.

Beside Catholic faith of universal dogmas and promises he requires a private promise-faith that God will not fail with efficacious help; without that peculiar faith, hope of pardon — itself a necessary disposition — cannot stand, so Trent sess. 6 c. 8 faith as salvation beginning/root covers both Catholic and private promise-faith (Disp. 210.5).
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XL PDF 254; Vasquez private promise-faith + Trent 6.8.

title: Romans distinguish two special applications of promises (Jaubert)
english: Roman doctors do not simply deny special self-application of grace and salvation promises; they distinguish two appropriations.
Divine-faith certainty that one is already among God true sons they reject; moral certainty with trust expecting fulfillment they approve (Jaubert, Clypeus 1.40.9).
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XLI PDF 254; twofold application (Jaubert).

title: Both schools: Spirit-wrought faith is idle or love-working
english: From this slice and what precedes, both Roman and Reformed schools agree Spirit-authored divine faith is either idle without good works or active working through love.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XLII PDF 254-255; shared idle vs love-working.

title: Romans with Reformed: idle faith dead, hypocritical, useless to save
english: Rome with the Reformed grants idle workless faith is rightly called dead and hypocritical, useless for salvation and justice, saves and justifies no one, and is not believing well as one ought.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XLIII PDF 255; idle faith useless.

title: Reformed grant historic faith a Spirit gift and intellect perfection
english: Reformed freely grant Rome that historic faith — assent to the Word that does not yet move the will to good deeds — is among God gifts and an intellect perfection lighting saving truth.
Those so gifted are greatly culpable for not using that light for their own salvation, since by nature it shows the way of justice and salvation.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XLIV PDF 255; historic faith as gift.

title: True faith name-fight: Reformed reserve true for saving; Rome allows both senses
english: Whether dead idle faith is true faith is largely a matter of terminology: Reformed reserve true for saving faith; Rome often allows true also for real Spirit-gifted assent.
Even Romans who restrict true to living faith still call dead faith true as non-feigned assent, Scriptural faith, and a Spirit gift lighting saving good — which Reformed do not deny.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XLV PDF 255; true-faith name dispute.

title: Historic vs dogmatic: Romans misread Reformed historic faith
english: Rome dislikes the Reformed historic label and prefers dogmatic, but most Romans misread historic as mere human assent to Scripture stories.
Reformed historic faith names divine assent to the whole Word that remains idle and speculative — commonly called dead faith.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XLVI PDF 255; historic misread.

title: Formed and unformed: external form for salvation-profit, not essence
english: Reformed reject informis/formata as if charity were faith inner form; Rome means only an external form that makes faith profit for salvation, not essence.
Aside from the barbarous, unscriptural phrasing, Le Blanc finds nothing else to blame in that Roman usage.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XLVII PDF 255; formed/unformed.

title: Seeming clash: same species as dead faith yet dead faith profits nothing
english: Rome common teaching that saving justifying faith is not specifically distinct from dead unformed faith seems to clash with their own admission that dead faith profits nothing for salvation or justice.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XLVIII PDF 255; same-species tension.

title: Resolution: same species or number; only living faith actually justifies
english: Rome holds living formed faith the same kind (even the same number) as dead, yet living sses by external accidental perfection; only living efficacious faith actually saves and justifies.
Salvation-texts they refer to living formed faith; not-yet-formed as disposition means active faith beginning to work and birth charity, not idle speculation (Stapleton; Vasquez).
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II XLIX PDF 255-256; same species resolution.

title: Whole question reduces to specific vs accidental difference — small once living alone saves
english: Rome can say justifying faith is not specifically other than dogmatic/historic yet still join Reformed in granting only living efficacious faith actually saves.
The dispute shrinks to specific/generic vs merely accidental difference — scholastic and small once both sides attribute salvation to living not dead faith.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II L PDF 256; accidental vs specific.

title: If Romans call dead faith justifying, they mean remote disposition only
english: When some Romans label dead idle faith justifying, they mean remote disposition, not actual justification.
Reformed press only that living efficacious faith disposes infallibly and proximately — and Rome agrees on that point.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LI PDF 256; remote disposition.

title: Definition clash: Roman firm assent vs Reformed fiducia definitions
english: Rome unanimously defines faith as firm assent to all God has revealed because of the Revealer authority; Reformed definitions of justifying faith look more varied.
Some Reformed keep assent but add efficacy and focus on grace-promises; most define by fiducia applying Christ merit, or heart-rest in God as author of eternal life.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LII PDF 256; definition diversity.

title: Rome defines faith absolutely (living and dead); Reformed define the living add-on
english: Rome scopes the definition to absolute faith common to living and dead — a definition Reformed also use for faith as genus.
Reformed justifying-faith definitions mostly name only what living faith adds beyond faith in general.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LIII PDF 256; absolute vs justifying scope.

title: Loose Roman and tight Reformed definitions do not negate shared content
english: Rome's loose definition does not deny that living faith is practical and effective trust, including mercy.
Reformed tight definitions do not deny firm assent to the whole Word; they spotlight what most distinguishes living justifying faith from historic dead faith.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LIV PDF 256; loose vs tight definitions.

title: Object: both sides — whole Word, yet grace-promises principal (Stapleton/Trent)
english: Reformed grant Rome that justifying faith object covers all God Word contains; Rome wrongly charges a promises-only restriction.
Rome likewise grants Gospel promises as principal (Stapleton from Trent) while refusing restriction to promises alone — so little controversy remains here.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LV PDF 256-257; object breadth.

title: Special mercy object: antecedent remitted vs to-be-remitted (Cassander/Cologne)
english: The live fight is whether special mercy is justifying faith object and chief part — Protestants usually yes, Rome no.

Special mercy may be antecedent (already remitted) or still to be obtained; some Reformed and even Cologne/Cassander treat antecedent remitted-sins persuasion as justifying, but many Reformed put to-be-remitted trust as the justifying object.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LVI PDF 257; special mercy twofold.

title: Vasquez requires such to-be-remitted faith; most Romans deny particular remitted/to-be-remitted as faith object
english: Vasquez requires such faith that is to be remitted;
Most Roman doctors still deny special mercy however taken as faith object — denying particular remitted or certainly-to-be-remitted belief as faith proper act.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LVII PDF 257; Vasquez vs majority.

title: Yet Rome requires mercy-fiducia for justification — partly logomachy
english: Rome still requires resting trust on divine mercy with hope of remission, so some of the clash is a fight over words.

Reformed special mercy as object usually means non-antecedent mercy under trust is counted as faith; Romans deny chiefly antecedent mercy as a faith object while distinguishing faith from trust, yet still require trust in divine mercy for justification.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LVIII PDF 257; fiducia still required.

title: Reflex certainty of already-received grace: Reformed secondary act; Rome allows sure fiducia
english: Most Reformed make antecedent remitted-sins certainty a reflexive secondary faith-act after justification, not the primary justifying act — which Rome denies as faith.
Yet Rome allows so sure a fiducia of obtained remission that it expels doubt and anxiety, nearly Protestant; and Catharinus/Vasquez even call that persuasion an act of private divine faith.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LIX PDF 257; reflexive certainty.

title: Notitia: Rome grants apprehension, explicit chief articles, and useful growth in knowledge
english: On the concept of understanding, Rome grants Reformed that some apprehension is needed to conceive faith, and explicit knowledge of chief articles for saving faith.cles for saving faith.cles for saving faith.
Implicit or rude cognition may suffice for many dogmas, yet clearer knowledge is useful and praiseworthy and should be pressed according to calling and capacity.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LX PDF 257-258; notitia shared ground.

title: Reformed grant essence in assent not notitia; notitia not strict science
english: Reformed grant Rome that faith essence is assent rather than notitia, though some knowledge is included or presupposed.
That included knowledge is not strict science (evident cognition through causes) nor even always distinct accurate perception of mode.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LXI PDF 258; essence in assent.

title: Not every dogma needs explicit grasp; privates need not pastor-level defense
english: Reformed do not require from every believer explicit apprehension of every dogma; knowing fundamental principal mysteries expressly is enough.
Even for those principal mysteries, privates need not the distinct accurate intelligence by which doctors and pastors defend and prove them.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LXII PDF 258; explicit vs private.

title: Rome disputes in vain as if Reformed put faith in notitia and exact science
english: Rome argues in vain as if Reformed located faith in notitia rather than assent, and as if every believer must have exact accurate distinct cognition able to explain and defend mysteries like a doctor or minister.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LXIII PDF 258; vain notitia charge.

title: Reformed should not over-read Bellarmine ignorance over science line
english: Reformed should not charge Rome with requiring zero cognition for private faith or preferring ignorance to knowledge.
Bellarmine faith better by ignorance than science is harsh phrasing, but means science as evident knowledge we lack regarding faith-objects — not dissent from Reformed doctrine.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LXIV PDF 258; Bellarmine science.

title: Assent: common to historic and living; specific justifying act beyond bare assent (Ames)
english: A few Reformed deny assent is a faith-act; most number it among faith acts. Rome puts principal act in assent to the whole Word; Reformed deny that for living faith specifically.

Rome speaks of absolute faith; Reformed say assent is common to historic and living, so the specific saving act lies beyond bare assent — Ames means assent does not mark off saving from historic faith.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LXV PDF 258; assent locus.

title: Special application as practical use of the Word — Rome agrees faith must be efficacious
english: Reformed commonly teach special application of grace and salvation promises; Rome seems to reject it.
But if application means living faith is not idle speculation but turns the Word to practice and the believer use, Rome already grants faith must be efficacious and active to justify and save.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LXVI PDF 258; practical application.

title: Persuasion-application: same twofold Roman distinction as in XLI
english: If special application means persuasion that grace and salvation promises specially belong to me, Rome rejects it only with the XLI distinction.
Divine-faith certainty of already being among God sons is condemned; moral certainty with trust expecting fulfillment is approved.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LXVII PDF 258-259; persuasion distinction.

title: Issue is whether application is faith-act or only fiducia-act (Vasquez names it faith)
english: The real question is not whether the believer may/should apply grace promises, but whether that application is a faith-act (Reformed) or only a trust-act (Rome)
Even so, some Romans including Vasquez still name that persuasion about obtained or future grace as faith.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LXVIII PDF 259; faith vs fiducia act.

title: Most Reformed join fiducia to faith; Rome distinguishes absolute faith but includes fiducia in living faith
english: Most Reformed admit application belongs to fiducia yet call it a faith-act because they join fiducia to faith; a minority treat fiducia as effect only.
Rome distinguishes fiducia from absolute faith, but expressly includes fiducia in living faith.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LXIX PDF 259; fiducia and faith.

title: Love likewise: not absolute-faith act for Rome, yet included in living formed faith
english: On dilectio some Reformed deny it is a faith-act, others affirm; all Romans say love is not an absolute-faith act but another virtue.
Yet they freely grant living formed faith includes love, and credere in Deum means loving God and tending into God.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LXX PDF 259; dilectio parallel.

title: Closing logomachy: both sides agree living faith includes trust and love
english: Much of the fiducia/love fight is verbal: Reformed mean living faith as distinct from historic when they number trust and love among faith acts.

Rome denies those as acts of absolute faith common to dead and living, yet grants that living faith as such includes trust and love as its acts — so the Roman comparison block closes in shared substance.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars II LXXI PDF 259; logomachy close before De Facultate.

title: Reformed disagree: some place faith subject in intellect alone (Molinaeus, Baron)
english: Reformed are not of one mind on which faculty is faith's subject.
Molinaeus and Baron place the proper subject in intellect alone: no faith-act is elicited by the mind.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 260; Molinaeus Th. 18-19; Baron Exerc. 3.2.5.

title: Amyraut: faith's subject is intellect beyond controversy
english: Amyraut (Theses de Fide 1.15ff) treats intellect as faith's seat beyond serious dispute.
To have faith = to believe = to be persuaded of truth; persuasion enters by reasons into the intellect.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 260; Amyraut part 1 th. 15+.

title: Intellect-only party: whole form of faith resides in mind assent
english: For this party the whole essence of faith sits in intellect alone.
Proper acts: know the Word and assent — both intellective, none other.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 260; closes intellect-only essence claim.

title: Yet they mean practical intellect: assent moves the will by effects
english: Intellect here = practical mind: faith's proper act is practical assent that moves the will.
Subjectively in the intellect, yet effective in the will through inseparable effects.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 260; Tilenus setup.

title: Tilenus: primarily in intellect, secondarily in will as it moves it
english: Tilenus: faith primarily and properly in intellect; secondarily in will as mover.
Like moral knowledge: subjective in mind, effective in will when it commands action.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 260-261; Tilenus Disp. de Fide.

title: Baron: faith in intellect by essence, yet belongs to will by origin, annexed act, fruits
english: Baron: essence in intellect (even fiducia), yet faith touches will by origin, annexed love-act, and fruits.
Assent is often called will-commanded and free (Augustine: none believe unwilling); love co-instant; sanctification follows.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 261; Baron art. nn.5,7; Augustine.

title: All grant will-fruits; Amyraut denies will-command needed for assent
english: Reformed agree faith's fruits touch the will; they quarrel whether assent is will-commanded.
Amyraut: faith follows Spirit-disposed intellect like sensation follows a fit organ — no will-imperium needed.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 261; Amyraut de Causa Fidei.

title: Others with Baron: pious affection must precede assent (Ames)
english: Baron's side: some will-affection must precede assent.
Ames: pious affection toward God is among assent's antecedents (Medulla 1.5).
translator_notes: OCR PDF 261; Ames Medulla 1.5.

title: Chamier: faith is voluntary intellect-act commanded by will (Thomas)
english: Chamier (Panstratia 3.12.4): faith is a will-commanded intellect act (with Thomas).
Science assents by evidence; theology's obscure truths need the will to move assent — else no assent at all.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 261; Chamier Panstr. 3.12.4; Thomas.

title: Ames places faith essentially in will alone (five concurrents)
english: Ames (Medulla 2.5): faith's constituting acts are acts of the will; knowledge does not constitute; assent is effect.
Essentially in will alone — nearly the reverse of the intellect-only party.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 261-262; Ames five concurrents.

title: Ames in Bellarmine Enervatus: will-seat with antecedent intellect assent — seeming clash
english: Ames (Bellarmine Enervatus 4.4.1) seats justifying faith in will yet requires antecedent intellect-assent and grants consequent intellect virtue.
Apparent clash with assent-as-effect is eased if assent follows pious affection but precedes resting/election acts.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 262; Ames Bellarm. Enerv. 4.4.1.

title: Middle Reformed view (most common): faith in both faculties as aggregate
english: Most Reformed take a middle: justifying faith formally in both intellect and will.
Not one simple habit — an aggregate of intellect- and will-elicited acts.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 262; common Reformed media via.

title: Chamier: faith is love (credere in Deum = loving) hence will-act
english: Chamier: faith is in intellect and will; syllogism — love is act of will; faith is love; therefore act of will.
True faith = believing in God = loving by believing (Augustine).
translator_notes: OCR PDF 262; Chamier + Augustine.

title: Wendelin: faith not simple virtue — knowledge, assent, trust span powers
english: Wendelin: same will-argument; faith is not a simple virtue.
Parts (knowledge, assent, trust) do not all belong to one power.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 262; Wendelin Theol. Christ. 1.24.

title: Bucanus: subject is the soul — mind knows/judges; will/heart embraces
english: Bucanus: faith's subject is the human soul.
Mind: knowledge, judgment, consent to Word/promise; will and heart: apprehension/embrace.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 262; Bucanus Loc. 10.18.

title: Rivet: intellect + will; justifying faith an aggregated habit
english: Rivet: justifying faith's subject is intellect and will (knowledge/assent vs trust).
Justifying faith is one habit through the joining of parts, not one simple numerical habit.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 262; Rivet Synopsis Disp. 31.14,16.

title: Alting and many: promise offered to mind and will as true and good
english: Alting: faith's subject is partly intellect, partly will — grace-promise known as true and embraced as good.
Walaeus, Trelcatius, Paraeus, and many agree (Alting Loci 1.13).
translator_notes: OCR PDF 262-263; Alting; Walaeus, Trelcatius, Paraeus.

title: Le Blanc's own: saving faith depends somehow on will as free good work (1 Peter 1)
english: Le Blanc's own first point: saving faith somehow depends on the will by origin.
It is a free good work God rewards with salvation (1 Peter 1) — hence voluntary.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 263; Le Blanc's voice begins; 1 Pet 1.

title: Yet true faith is not bare arbitrary assent without solid reasons
english: True faith is not bare arbitrary assent without reason.
Word-objects are obscure in themselves, yet believers are moved by fit reasons that God truly testifies.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 263; assent not arbitrary.

title: Perceiving those reasons depends on grace-changed will affections
english: Grasping faith's reasons somehow hangs on the will: as one is affected, so one judges.
Grace must change will-affections so the mind can weigh motives; faith rises from judged truth, not bare will-imperium — yet pious affection opens the door.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 263; grace-changed affections.

title: From will as cause ≠ in will as subject (like commanded contemplation)
english: Will-dependence does not by itself make the will faith's subject.
Like free contemplation: commanded by will, yet elicited and seated in mind alone.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 263; cause≠subject.

title: Faith precisely vs other virtues: simple assent habit in intellect alone
english: Take faith precisely against hope/charity: one simple deep simple assent to the Worddd.
So taken, seat is intellect alone — truth is intellect's object, good is will's.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 263; precise sense.

title: Living faith as aggregate: includes love, desire, trust — will also subject (Galatians 5:6)
english: Usually 'faith' names an aggregate: assent plus love, desire of grace, and resting trust.
That living/saving/formed faith (faith working through love, Galatians 5:6) has will as subject too.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 263; Gal 5:6 living/formed faith.

title: Conciliation of intellect-only and both-faculties; Ames will-only improbable
english: Intellect-only and both-faculties views can be reconciled by the twofold sense.
Ames's will-only view is improbable: dropping assent as faith-act rewrites the word's common sense.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 263; rejects Ames extreme.

title: Rome: faith subjectively in intellect alone, yet will commands assent (Estius; 1 Corinthians 1:18; 2 Corinthians 10; Romans 4)
english: Rome places faith subjectively in intellect alone, yet grants will concurs as commanding principle (Estius Sent. 3 dist. 23)...
Religious objects rarely admit reason's exam (1 Corinthians 1:18); will must lead assent into Christ's obedience (2 Corinthians 10), as Abraham did not consider his dead body (Romans 4).
translator_notes: OCR PDF 263-264; Estius; 1 Cor 1:18; 2 Cor 10; Rom 4.

title: Thomas and Sylvester: believe with the heart = by will (Romans 10:10)
english: Thomas on Romans 10:10: believing with the heart = by the will; one can do outward cult unwilling, but not believe.
Sylvester: heart-belief excludes fiction and marks will-commanded saving faith vs coerced demonic/sign-faith (Romans 10:10).
translator_notes: OCR PDF 264; Thomas + Sylvester on Rom 10:10.

title: Rome's intellect-only subject is of absolute faith; living formed faith occupies will too
english: Rome's intellect-only claim covers absolute faith in itself.
Living formed faith, even for them, seats trust and love in the will as elicited acts.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 264; absolute vs living/formed.

title: Contarini and Cajetan: faith begins and ends in will; Bonaventure both powers
english: Contarini: faith begins in obedient will, yields intellect-assent and promise-trust, and ends again in will.
Cajetan (John 6) and Bonaventure: believing in God joins intellect and will / cognitive and affective powers.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 264; Contarini, Cajetan, Bonaventure.

title: Verbal clash: absolute-faith subject vs living-faith subject
english: Some Reformed concede intellect-alone as proper subject; most claim both faculties — Rome usually denies.
Much is verbal: Rome means absolute faith (dead or living); Reformed mean living faith, which Rome also seats partly in will via trust and love.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 264-265; logomachy on subject.

title: Whole subject-of-faith dispute is philosophical, not piety
english: Le Blanc: the subject-of-faith fight is philosophical, not piety.
Piety needs living embrace of the Gospel; mind-vs-will faculty questions can wait for philosophers.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 265; closes subject locus as non-piety.

title: Next: faith's connection with love and works — Reformed: inseparable
english: Shift: connection of faith with love and good works.
Reformed consensus: true saving faith is inseparable from charity — light never without heat.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 265; opens connection locus.

title: Reformed grant illuminated yet vicious assent — but refuse true/saving name (James)
english: Reformed grant Spirit-lit theoretical assent in the vicious — yet deny it the true/saving name.
James: such faith does not save; 'true' is reserved for living efficacious faith inseparable from charity (James 2).
translator_notes: OCR PDF 265; James on unprofitable faith.

title: Rome: true saving faith separable from charity and works
english: Rome: true saving faith can exist without charity and works — and remain after charity is cast away.
Spirit-moved real assent counts as true faith even when dead and unformed.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 265; Roman separability.

title: Rome still titles dead faith saving/justifying as remote disposition
english: Rome admits dead faith does not actually save, yet still titles it saving/justifying as remote disposition.
On that naming, saving faith can exist apart from charity and works.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 265; remote title.

title: Can living faith separate from charity? Divided vs composed sense
english: Rome distinguishes: in divided sense living faith can become dead by losing charity.
In composed sense living (=actually saving) faith cannot exist without charity.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 265; divided vs composed.

title: Common ground + name fight over calling remote-disposing faith saving
english: Both sides: Spirit-gifted assent without charity exists in the wicked and actually saves no one; Reformed allow remote preparation.
Name-fight: should remote-disposing faith be called true/saving? Better style reserves those names for faith that actually saves.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 265-266; name vs thing.

title: Rome grants living faith never without charity; Reformed grant fall from living love
english: Rome grants: living faith never without charity; no actually-saving faith without works of love.
Reformed also grant: once-living faith can lose love, cease justifying for a time, and leave the person unaccepted.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 266; mutual concessions on living faith.

title: Polish Thorun Confession: regenerate can lose true faith while in known sin
english: Polish Reformers at Thorn: false charge that the once-justified cannot lose grace while sinning at will.
Regenerate persevering in known sin retain for that time nor true faith nor the grace of justification — new damnation-guilt unless renewed to repentance.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 266; Thorun Confession 4.2.11.

title: Paraeus and Baron: habitual faith in mortal fallers does not justify
english: Losing true faith in known sin means separation from love — faith ceases saving/justifying.
Paraeus and Baron: habitual-only faith in mortal fallers is interrupted and does not justify for that time.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 266; Paraeus; Baron on mortal sin.

title: David's fall shows living faith can separate from charity's works for a time
english: Saints' falls prove living justifying faith can for a time lose charity's works without becoming absolute unbelief.
David's months of adultery and Uriah's murder (2 Samuel 11) kept Word-assent yet not saving love — under the guilt of damnation for that interval.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 266; David/Uriah example.

title: British Dort judgment on David and Peter: justifying faith can cease for a time
english: British Dort theologians: regenerate David and Peter could fall into damnable guilt and lose present fitness for heaven.

Election made their final salvation certain; yet if death had taken them impenitent in those sins, neither could have been saved — justifying faith can cease for the interval before renewed repentance.
translator_notes: OCR PDF 266-267; British judgment at Dort on art. 5; closes De Facultate.

title: Justificare in Scripture usually forensic: declare just, not make just
english: Justificare (Heb. hitsdik, Gk. Dikaioo) is usually forensic in Scripture.
It means declaring or acknowledging as just the one accused—not making the unjust just.

title: God justified by men; wisdom justified by her children
english: Wherever God is justified by men (Ps 51), the sense is forensic victory in judgment.
Mt 11: wisdom justified by her children; Lk 7: people baptized by John justified God against Pharisees.

title: Man justifying himself: asserting innocence
english: Same forensic sense when a man justifies himself—asserts innocence or claims righteousness.
Lk 10 lawyer; Lk 16 Pharisees who justify themselves before men.

title: Justify as a judge's act: defend the humble; condemn bribery
english: Justify also names a judge's act: Ps 82 justify the humble and orphan.
Isa 5 woe on judges who justify the wicked for bribes.

title: Justification opposed to condemnation
english: Clearest forensic use: justification set against condemnation (Prov 17; Matt 12).
Job 9: self-justification still meets the mouth's condemnation.

title: Some Protestants make forensic sense perpetual; most allow real change
english: Some Protestants claim forensic sense is perpetual and never means real change.
Most (and Le Blanc) disagree: Dan 12 justify many = instruct unto righteousness.

title: Ecclesiasticus 18: do not wait until death to be justified
english: Ecclus 18:22 resists a bare forensic gloss.
Aim: repent and become holy now—vernacular: do not wait till death to be good.

title: Rom 8:30: learned Protestants include sanctification under justification
english: Rom 8:30: some top Protestants read justify as Spirit-wrought making holy, not bare acquittal.
Inhering holiness must sit somewhere in the chain; stuffing it under glorify is forced.

title: 1 Cor 6:11: justified with washed and sanctified—real change
english: 1 Cor 6:11: justified listed with washed and sanctified—Spirit renews inwardly.
Bare penalty-acquittal would anticlimax after washed; washing includes real cleansing.

title: Titus 3: regeneration needed that we may be justified
english: Titus 3: God regenerates by the Spirit so that, justified by grace, we hope for life.
If regeneration is prerequisite to being counted justified, justification here includes sanctification.

title: Beza: justification broadly includes imputation and sanctifying efficacy
english: Beza, Zanchi, Bullinger, Leyden: justification can include inward righteousness given.
Beza: broad justification = imputation plus Spirit's sanctifying efficacy.

title: Zanchi: second sense of justify is to make the unjust just
english: Zanchi: justify (1) acquit vs condemn; (2) make the unjust just—parallel to sanctify.
Cites 1 Cor 6:11 washed / sanctified / justified.

title: Thysius / Leyden: justification sometimes seems to embrace sanctification
english: Leyden Thysius: given tight connection, justification sometimes seems to embrace sanctification as consequent.
Cites Rom 8:30; Tit 3:7.

title: Bullinger: washed, sanctified, justified name the same thing diversely
english: Bullinger on 1 Cor 6:11: different words for the same truth.
Washed→baptism; sanctified→Spirit; justified→justifying faith.

title: Calvin: regeneration under justification possible but not necessary
english: Calvin: Rom 8 / Tit 3 could stretch justification to regeneration's continuous grace—but usual Pauline sense is free imputation.
He allows rare wider use; nothing blocks restricting to remission.

title: Apoc 22:11: justify means grow more just, not bare declaration
english: Almost all Protestants deny forensic sense at Rev 22:11.
Justify there = grow more just/pious from already just—progress in righteousness.

title: Roman doctors: Becanus—justify three ways in Scripture
english: Roman consensus (Becanus): Scripture uses justify three ways—make just, make more just, declare just.
Justification likewise: acquisition, increase, or declaration of righteousness.

title: Bellarmine: acquisition, increase, and forensic declaration
english: Bellarmine: justification = acquire righteousness, increase it, or forensically declare it.
Summer-heat analogy: not only cold→hot but hot→hotter = just→more just.

title: Romans admit forensic sense: Rom 2:13 factores legis
english: Romans themselves grant forensic justify at Rom 2:13 (Estius: held/declared just).
Tapper + Augustine: sometimes pronounce/reckon just, not only gift with righteousness.

title: Rom 8:33 forensic: God who justifies vs accusation
english: Rom 8:33: many Roman interpreters read justify forensically against accusation/condemnation.
Toletus, Pererius, Sasbout/Estius: judge-pronouncing the elect just.

title: Protestant schools adopt only the forensic sense in justification disputes
english: Protestant school disputes adopt only the forensic sense of justification.
Before God it means absolving the sinner from due penalties—condonation of punishment.

title: Protestants distinguish justification from sanctification; Chamier on word swap
english: Protestants distinguish justification (absolution) from sanctification (inward cleansing)—inseparable yet distinct.
Chamier allows occasional Scriptural word-swap; Rev 22:11 is inherent-progress sense.

title: Denying justification by inherent works does not deny true grace-wrought righteousness
english: Denying justification by inherent works does not deny the real righteousness that comes from grace, which God accepts and rewards.
Point: no inherent work survives strict justice without mercy—acquittal is mere grace in Christ.

title: Imputed Christ's righteousness: passion and obedience made ours
english: Imputed Christ's righteousness is his passion and obedience given as truly ours.
By its merit we are loosed from the law's curse—exclusion and eternal fire.

title: Faith alone means living efficacious faith as sole instrument
english: Sola fide means living, work-bearing faith—not dead or idle faith—as the sole condition and instrument.
Romans agree on the thing itself when calumny is stripped away.

title: Protestants not abusing words: distinct names for distinct benefits
english: Two inseparable but different benefits deserve two school names: justification vs sanctification.
Scripture most often uses justify for judicial absolution / being reputed just.

title: Roman school: justification includes real abolition and infused righteousness
english: Romans: justification = not only penalty remitted but sin abolished and inward righteousness obtained.
First vs second justification: make the ungodly just; then make the just more just.

title: Roman inherent righteousness: accepted and rewarded, not strict-law standing
english: Roman justify-by-inherent-righteousness does not mean surviving strict law without mercy.
Means grace-given inherent righteousness God accepts and will reward with kingdom glory.

title: Denying imputed justification: form of just/holy from new inward righteousness
english: Romans denying imputed justification still grant Christ's merit frees from hell's pains.
They deny imputation is the form of the name just/holy—that comes from new Spirit-wrought righteousness.

title: Not by faith alone but also by works: conversion acts and growth
english: Roman not-faith-alone-but-works does not mean properly meriting remission.
Means: bare assent is not the sole condition—conversion acts needed; the justified grow by works—Protestants concede the substance.

title: Chemnitz: no fight over words if Fathers teach reconciliation rightly
english: If remission is free in Christ's merit alone, extending justify to cover inward renewal is no crime.
Chemnitz: no word-fights with Fathers who rightly teach reconciliation, remission, adoption.

title: Brentius takes justification to include renovation; Protestants spare him
english: Brentius folded renovation into justification; Melanchthon pushed back on the mechanism.
Gerhard: wider Latin sense of the term is not itself the Pontifical error—Protestants spare Brentius.

title: Borrheus and Reformers: Scripture sometimes uses justification for sanctification
english: Even many Reformers grant Scripture sometimes uses justification to cover sanctification.
Borrhaus (if citations hold): Pauline justify/glorify packs reconciliation, Christ's righteousness, regenerating gift—dissension verbal, not real.

title: Open question: Paul's justify—forensic only or also inward renewal?
english: Still open: in Paul, is justify only forensic absolution (Protestants) or also Spirit-wrought renewal (Romans)?
Where doctrine agrees and analogy of faith holds, leave lexical liberty—Protestants already differ among themselves on Dan 12, Rom 8, etc.

title: Either sense of justify still fits Paul: free absolution and free sanctification
english: On contested Paul texts, either interpretation still yields an Apostolic, analogy-of-faith sense.
Absolution and sanctification alike are free by Christ's grace and faith—not of works.

title: What is not of grace is of works—so sanctification is not of works
english: Paul: grace and works mutually exclude (Rom 11:6).
Sanctification is free singular grace—hence not of works.

title: Of works means according to debt—new holiness is free, not owed
english: Of works = according to debt (Rom 4:4 wage).
New holiness in Christ is free—so we are not sanctified of works.

title: Salvation includes liberation and image-renewal—yet not of works (Eph; 2 Tim; Tit)
english: Salvation in Ephesians, 2 Timothy, and Titus includes liberation and image-renewal—not remission only.ot remission only.ot remission only.
Yet Paul says not saved of works; so even a wide justify still means by grace through faith, not works.

title: Titus 3: renovation by the Spirit opposed to works of righteousness we did
english: Titus 3: Spirit's renovating wash—not works of righteousness we did—is the saving means.
Therefore sanctification itself must not be called of our righteous works.

title: Eph 2: good works are fruit of new creation—so sanctification too is by faith not works
english: Eph 2: good works are fruit of new creation—hence not salvation's cause.
Same logic: works follow sanctification (Augustine's order for justification)—sanctified by grace/faith, not works.

title: Without works of the law we are also sanctified—same Pauline sense as justification
english: As we are justified without works of the law, so we are sanctified without them—same contrast between obligation and grace.
God counts living charity-working faith holy despite legal shortfalls—parallel to forensic absolution of the guilty believer.

title: Without Mosaic ceremonies we are justified and sanctified (Galatians)
english: Justify without works of the law especially means without Mosaic ceremonies (Galatians).
Same for sanctification: ceremonies not required to be holy before God.

title: Either acceptation of justification: free by faith; quarreling superfluous
english: Whether justify = bare acquittal or also inward righteousness, we are still free by faith, not of works/law.
Paul's aim stands either way—living love-working faith, not Do this and live; lexical quarrel is superfluous.

title: Scripture: justified by faith; theologians dispute the sense
english: Scripture plainly says we are justified by / through / from faith.
Theologians still dispute the sense; this tract seeks clarity amid the clash.

title: What faith justifies: bare assent can exist without obedience
english: Scripture sometimes calls 'faith' bare assent without obedience.
John 12:42 leaders and Simon Magus believed yet stayed unconfessing or corrupt.

title: Usually 'faith' means living assent that bears love, trust, obedience
english: Usually 'faith' means assent that yields love, trust, and obedience.
Only that faith is tied to salvation, adoption, and victory—not bare belief.

title: Dead vs living faith: believe God vs believe in God (Augustine)
english: Speculative assent ('believe God') is dead; practical trust-love ('believe in God') lives.
Augustine: believing in God is loving and joining his members; James: faith without works is dead.

title: Historic/dead faith cannot justify—James and Galatians
english: Historic/dead faith—possible even in demons—cannot justify.
Paul equates justifying faith with love-working faith, new creation, and obedience.

title: Living faith justifies us—but is not the righteousness we stand in
english: Only living, efficacious faith is in view when Scripture says we are justified by faith.
Even that faith is not the righteousness we stand in before God—it flees to mercy.

title: Faith does not justify by its own merit or dignity
english: Faith does not justify by its own merit; grace alone binds God to the believer.
If faith earned justification, it would be debt not free grace (Rom 3–4).

title: Orthodox: faith does not justify as a meritorious work—mode still disputed
english: Denying that faith justifies 'as a work' means it is not formal/meritorious cause.
Reformed agree on that—but still dispute how faith justifies.

title: Some: faith only senses a justification already done before belief
english: Some say faith only senses a justification already done—eternal or at the promise of Christ.
On that view faith's only role is to make us know and feel secure about it.

title: Justification is actual remission in time—not the eternal will to justify
english: Justification is actual remission, not the eternal will to remit.
Decree precedes faith; actual justification follows faith in time.

title: Remission = ceasing to be liable to punishment—requires repentance and faith
english: Remission means ceasing to be liable to sin's punishment—same substance as justification.
While one persists in sin without conversion and faith, wrath remains; sins are not yet remitted.

title: Eternal decree frees elect by giving converting grace in time—not by suspending the law
english: The eternal decree frees the elect by giving converting grace in time—not by voiding the law.
Scripture ties remission to living faith, repentance, and turning (Rom 10; Acts; Prov; Ezek).

title: Remission is a promised benefit under condition—not an eternal decree already done
english: Remission is a conditional gospel promise, not a finished eternal decree before faith.
We pray 'forgive us' for what is future to us—not for a past absolute decree.

title: No Scripture makes justification an eternal decree; it follows faith and the Spirit
english: Scripture never equates justification with an eternal decree.
It is a temporal gift after faith/conversion, done by the poured-out Spirit (Tit 3; 1 Cor 6).

title: 1 Cor 6: once you were such—but you were washed, sanctified, justified
english: Paul contrasts their justified state with their former vices (1 Cor 6).
That contrast collapses if they were already justified while still immersed in sin.

title: Rom 8:30 golden chain: calling precedes justification
english: Rom 8:30 orders calling before justification in the golden chain.
Justification sits between calling and glorification—not before faith's call.

title: If justified before conversion: absurd—death/life and love collapse
english: Actual justification before conversion yields absurdities against the apostles.
Justified = passed from death to life; unconverted lovelessness still 'remains in death.'

title: Justified = God's child; persisting sinner = of the devil—cannot both be true
english: The justified are God's children; unrepentant sinners are of the devil (1 John 3).
Pre-faith justification would make someone God's child and the devil's at once.

title: If already justified, death cannot shut one from heaven—yet Paul bars the unrepentant vicious
english: Full remission fits one for heaven if death comes in that state.
Paul bars the unrepentant vicious from the kingdom—so they are not yet justified.

title: No one actually justified until the Spirit applies Christ by faith and repentance
english: Actual justification waits until the Spirit applies Christ by creating faith and repentance.
Westminster/Anglican art. And most Reformers who call faith the means agree.

title: How faith concurs: instrumental, relative/objective, or covenant condition
english: Most: faith is the instrumental cause receiving Christ's offered righteousness.
Others: relative/objective apprehension; others: gospel covenant condition.

title: Simplest: faith justifies because it is imputed to the believer for righteousness
english: Simplest: faith justifies because it is imputed to the believer for righteousness (Rom 4).
God counts the living believer just for Christ's death and obedience.

title: Covenant-condition view comes to the same: living love-working faith required
english: Faith-as-covenant-condition means the same: cling to Christ with living love-working faith.
Under that—not another—condition the gospel promises salvation and remission.

title: Instrument language must mean moral condition—not physical tool or mere notice
english: Calling faith an 'instrument' cannot mean a physical tool—only a moral prerequisite condition.
'Apprehend/receive' is metaphor for God's granting remission to living believers—not mere notice of prior justification.

title: Faith is the gospel condition for being held just—then: does faith alone justify?
