title: David and Peter prove regenerate can fall—and remain death-liable while impenitent
english: David and Peter show regenerate saints can plunge into grievous sin under God’s permission for humility.
While they rest impenitent they owe damnable guilt, lose present fitness for heaven, and must not pretend safety.

title: Fourth British thesis: the wanderer must return by renewed faith and repentance
english: God’s fixed order: a wandering believer must first return by renewed faith and repentance.
Only then can he be brought to the heavenly goal.

title: Means as sure as the end: elect dying in impenitent vice are not saved
english: Election’s end travels a fixed road of means; the broad path of impenitent vice never reaches heaven.
Paul’s shipwreck word and David/Peter show: elect dying unrepentant in grave sin would not be saved.

title: Fifth thesis: between grave guilt and renewed repentance the sinner stands damnable yet to-be-absolved
english: Between grave guilt and renewed faith-repentance the sinner stands damnable by deserving.
Christ’s merit and God’s purpose mark him for absolution—but not actually absolved until pardon is sought in living faith.

title: Bremen at Dort: grave falls cost good conscience; lighter daily sins do not
english: Bremen’s Dort eleventh thesis matches Britain: grave falls strip conscience, purity, and joy.
Daily lighter slips do not work that loss.

title: Paraeus: fallen faith is sick—habitual only, and does not justify until repentance
english: Paraeus: David-like falls cost heart-cleanness, joy, and conscience; justifying faith then lies sick.
Only habitual faith remains—and God still imputes until repentance restores the act of receiving pardon.

title: Polish Thorn declaration: sins against conscience forfeit justifying grace for a time
english: At Thorn the Poles deny once-justified antinomian security: a relapse that wounds the conscience forfeits justifying grace and the Spirit for that time.hat time.hat time.
Infirmity-slips differ; without special exciting grace unto late repentance such falls leave the sinner damnable in deed.

title: Ames and Crocius: sin that wastes the conscience vs sin that does not
english: Reformed schools (Ames, Crocius) split sins that waste the conscience from those that do not.
Conscience-wasting sin cannot share true piety; infirmity-slips can remain in a godly good conscience.

title: Ursinus/Paraeus: reigning vs non-reigning sin
english: Ursinus (via Paraeus): reigning sin is unresisted and actually death-liable—found in all the unregenerate and in some regenerate falls.
Non-reigning sin is Spirit-resisted; saints keep faith and comfort amid remaining infirmities they hate.

title: Reformed map: two kinds—lighter compatible with holiness; graver death-liable until repentance
english: Reformed doctors thus own two kinds: lighter faults compatible with holiness even at death.
Graver falls, until repentance, make one actually death-liable and unfit for heaven.

title: Reformed reject Rome’s intrinsic venials—yet allow a commodious use of the names
english: Reformed deny Rome’s claim that some sins are by nature non-mortal.
They still allow mortal/venial labels when taken in a careful, commodious sense.

title: Commodious sense: venial by event (pardoned) vs mortal by event (actually damning)
english: First commodious use: ‘venial’ for sins actually pardoned through faith and repentance—even if huge in themselves.
‘Mortal’ then marks sins that in fact damn through unbelief and impenitence—Rome’s ‘from the event.’

title: Venial from cause: infirmity and ignorance obtain mercy more readily than destined malice
english: Second sense: sins of infirmity and ignorance are ‘venial’ as nearer mercy—Paul’s persecuting ignorance.
Destined-malice sins win pardon harder and more often meet eternal death; Rainolds backs the distinction.

title: Gomarus and Piscator: only the sin against the Spirit is mortal as irremissible
english: Some Reformed reserve ‘mortal’ for the irremissible sin against the Spirit—all else ‘venial’ as remissible.
That matches 1 John’s sin unto death and Gomarus/Piscator’s usage.

title: Ursinus: reigning sin singularly mortal; non-reigning singularly venial
english: Ursinus/Paraeus: call reigning sin singularly mortal—the unresisted, actually fall that leads to death against conscience.
Non-reigning remains singularly venial: Spirit-resisted infirmities where faith and comfort still dwell.

title: Davenant: conscience-wasting falls are singularly mortal; defects in good works are not
english: Davenant: singularly mortal are falls that wound the conscience and bind believers under death-guilt.
Flaws mixed into good works, though truly sinful by law’s rigor, are not appropriately called mortal.

title: Davenant’s triple ‘mortal’: irremissible Spirit-sin; remissible kingdom-barring guilt
english: Davenant’s first mortal: only the Spirit-sin’s irrevocable death-desert.
Second: remissible yet kingdom-barring guilt—Paul’s flesh-work catalogs until repentance restores life.

title: Second class widened: all Spirit-opposed fleshly acts until repentance
english: The second mortal class covers every flesh-obedient act—outer or inner—until repentance quits the hellward road.
Romans 8: flesh-living dies; Spirit-mortifying lives.

title: Third sense: law-rigor ‘mortal’ remains that do not damn those in Christ walking not after the flesh
english: Third ‘mortal’: deserts of remaining corruption under law-rigor-rigor-rigor that mercy in Christ does not impute unto death.
Romans 8’s ‘no condemnation’ holds for those not walking after the flesh—grave fleshly falls still need renewed repentance.

title: Davenant’s close: defects in regenerate works are not appropriately second-sense mortal
english: Davenant’s hinge: work-adhering defects are true sins by law, yet not appropriately ‘mortal’ in the second sense.
They add no new death-guilt while the new man resists the old Adam’s tumult—unlike capital falls needing fresh repentance.

title: Baron of Aberdeen: every sin mortal of itself; in the regenerate some mortal, some venial
english: Baron’s Aberdeen disputation joins Reformed consent: every sin is mortal of itself; none venial except by accident.
Yet in the regenerate he still distinguishes heavier falls that threaten wrath from daily lighter faults that leave favor and pardon-confidence intact.

title: Baron’s first assertions: all sin mortal of itself; reprobate sins mortal; elect atrocious sins still deadly
english: Baron’s opening axioms: no venial sin by nature; reprobate sins mortal both by desert and by event.
Elect atrocious, falls that wound the conscience still actually cut favor-degree and would forever shut heaven if persevered in—against flat ‘all elect sins are venial.’

title: Baron’s fourth assertion: some regenerate sins rightly called venial under the gracious covenant
english: Under the gracious covenant Baron names some regenerate sins ‘venial’: they do not cut kingdom-hope or prior favor-degree.
He classes involuntary lust-motions, work-adhering blemishes, and small-matter faults—backed by James, John, and Ecclesiastes on universal stumbling.

title: Baron’s fifth–sixth: non-exclusion is from mercy; comparative lightness explains why some are venial
english: Absolutely, non-exclusion from favor is mercy, not the sin’s nature.
Comparatively, lighter regenerate faults are lighter in themselves—so grace’s covenant punishes them more mildly than conscience-wasting atrocities.

title: First difference: avoidability—habitual and assisting grace can shun atrocities, not daily lighter faults
english: Baron’s first cut: avoidability under grace.
Habitual plus assisting grace can keep the regenerate from Paul’s listed atrocities; daily ‘venial’ slips no saint outruns for life.

title: Second difference: obligation—works-covenant exacts all; grace-covenant still binds toward perfection
english: Works-covenant: strict, precise duty to shun even the lightest fault under eternal peril.
Grace-covenant does not erase that aim—it still obliges striving, grieving shortfall, and daily plea for pardon.

title: Grace softens rigor: precise duty for attainable measure; vow-and-endeavor for degrees beyond ordinary grace
english: Grace removes the law’s terror without erasing the duty: attainable ordinary-grace obedience is still exacted under eternal peril.
Beyond that, ‘degrees’ perfection is owed in vow and endeavor—not as a strict act-condition of life.

title: Evangelical equity: precise duty to quit mortal sins; not to live without every lightest fault
english: Even under gospel equity: quit ‘mortal’ sins in act—repent and stay clear (John 5:14).
Living without every lightest ‘venial’ slip is degrees-perfection, not the precise life-condition.

title: Third difference: act-deformity—three scholastic venial species excused before a gracious Judge
english: Venial acts carry less deformity: something softens the offense before a gracious Judge.
Baron tracks the three scholastic species—by genus, by surprise, by small matter—each ‘light’ only comparatively or by accident.

title: Fourth difference: repentance required—ordinary for venial; singular after David- and Peter-like falls
english: Daily ordinary repentance clears venial faults.
Mortal falls demand rare, exact, extraordinary repentance—David after adultery and murder; Peter after denial.

title: Mortal guilt needs special confession and sorrow; venial mostly covered by general humble acknowledgment
english: Mortal guilt: name it, confess it, grieve it specially.
Most venials hide from us—so a humble general corruption-plea (‘cleanse me from secret faults’) can cover them, without canceling special sorrow for noticed slips.

title: Mortal repentance must be perfectly practical cessation; venial repentance cannot be
english: Mortal repentance must actually quit the whole class—or grace and glory are lost (Paul’s vice-lists).
Venial repentance cannot be ‘perfectly practical’ in that sense: no one lives without such faults, yet the godly are not thereby damned.

title: Fifth difference: effects—mortal falls bring heavier losses under the grace-covenant than lighter faults
english: Effects differ: mortal falls cost the regenerate far more than daily lighter faults.
Baron will track three covenant-ordered damages that trail mortal—not venial—slips.

title: First damage: temporary loss of prior favor-degree—hatred while the fall lasts, election unrevoked
english: First loss: while a grave fall lasts, the regenerate loses the prior degree of divine favor and incurs hatred.
God's purpose for election remains; present pleasing to Him is not.is not.is not.

title: In mortal state even prayers displease; lighter daily faults do not cast out gospel acceptance
english: During a mortal fall even regenerate prayers and thanks are unacceptable for the time.
Daily lighter faults do not cast out Spirit-walk acceptance: God in Christ receives imperfect obedience, eyes off its clinging blemishes.

title: Second damage: mortal falls block remitted peace and Spirit-gifts; lighter faults do not
english: Atrocious falls bind God’s goodwill: while they last, remission-sense, conscience-peace, and Spirit-gifts are blocked.
Daily lighter faults leave ordinary saving testimonies flowing—though even they deserve unworthiness by nature.

title: Why the difference: mortal falls quit covenant-necessary obedience; lighter faults do not
english: Mortal falls break the obedience required by the covenant for further gifts and the beatific vision—until extraordinary practical repentance.
Lighter infirmity-slips leave that precise salvation-obedience standing: Spirit-walk and whole-hearted following still named.

title: Second effect: multiple loss of intenseness of inherent faith, hope, and charity
english: Second mortal effect: grace inherent by the Spirit is multiply diminished.
faith, hope, and love that are within habits are not erased, yet weakened outwardly in fervor and inwardly in entity—within a room for opposing actions to restore

title: Habit remnants may remain, but justifying acts and peace cease in mortal falls—not in lighter slips
english: Even if habit-remnants linger after capital falls, acts of justification and peace stop
Infirmity’s lighter slips leave faith, hope, and Spirit-wrought confidence still acting with mercy-trust and pardon-sense.

title: Third effect: present fitness for heaven lost in mortal guilt—not by lighter faults under grace
english: Third mortal effect: present kingdom-fitness is lost while defilement and unfinished course remain.
Under grace’s providence, lighter faults alone do not strip that fitness—even if death finds someone only in them.

title: Augustana theologians: all sins mortal by nature; in regenerate some mortiferous, some not
english: Lutheran consensus: every sin mortal by nature—none venial in the unregenerate.
In the regenerate they still mark mortiferous or reigning falls (against conscience, from malice) versus non-mortiferous infirmity slips that do not cast out Spirit and faith.

title: Gerhard: venial/mortal labels track mercy and person, not the act’s nature—with four cautions
english: Gerhard: ‘venial/mortal’ labels track Trinitarian mercy toward the regenerate, not the act’s nature under law.
Four marks of resisting infirmity, then four cautions—prefer ‘mortiferous/reigning’ and ‘infirmity-falls’ over the Roman names.

title: Gerhard vs Bellarmine: some regenerate sins exclude from the kingdom in act; others do not cast out Spirit
english: Against Bellarmine Gerhard grants a real sin-discrimination among the regenerate.
Ignorance/infirmity blemish spiritual life if resisted in Christ; cast out Spirit, faith, and life.

title: Most Roman doctors hold some sins venial by nature—yet not as a defined article of faith
english: Dominant Roman school: some sins venial by nature—no eternal-death guilt, no extinguished spiritual life.
Not yet a defined article: celebrated Roman voices still hold every sin mortal of itself, venial only by mercy.

title: Roman doctors still grant: even ‘venial’ sins in those dying outside grace meet eternal penalties justly
english: Rome still grants: so-called venial sins, in those who die outside grace, are justly punished forever.
Eternal penalty for the graceless end is not denied even for the ‘light’ class.

title: Reformed concede unequal malice and unequal penalties among sins
english: Reformed freely grant graded malice among sins—not Stoic equality.
Penalties likewise unequal: some far milder, some far heavier at the last judgment.

title: Reformed grant grave conscience-wasting sins vs lighter faults compatible with peace and seeing God
english: Reformed mark serious sins that bar piety, peace, and salvation-confidence while they last.
Lighter daily faults leave good conscience, the holiness-measure needed to see God, and lawful pardon-trust.

title: Most Reformed: some falls add new eternal-death guilt until repentance; lighter faults do not
english: Most Reformed: capital falls add new death-guilt and bar heaven until real repentance—death mid-crime would damn.
Lighter thoughts, laughter, idle words, and work-blemishes add no such new guilt even if death finds them.

title: Many Protestants admit a good-sense mortal/venial distinction for grave vs lighter regenerate sins
english: Augustana across the board, and some Reformed, keep a good-sense mortal/venial vocabulary.
Mortal = a guilt that destroys conscience and brings new death; venial = lighter faults compatible with peace, pardon-sense, and heaven-fitness even at death.

title: Status controversiae: are any sins non-excluding and non-deserving of eternal death by nature?
english: The live quarrel narrows to one question: sins venial by nature—non-excluding, non-deserving eternal death even under rigid right?
Rome generally yes; Protestants no.

title: First Protestant reason: every sin defiles; nothing defiled enters heaven apart from mercy
english: First proof: shut out mercy, and even the lightest fault forever bars heaven—so by nature it is mortal.
Defilement is universal; nothing unclean enters; cleansing and pardon alone reopen the gate.

title: Second reason: after judgment every unrepented sin—even idle words—meets eternal penalty
english: Second proof: post-judgment, no temporal penalties remain—so idle words in the impenitent meet everlasting pain.
If God justly forever-punishes them, they deserve it; theologians already say he punishes below desert—so ‘mortal’ fits.

title: Third reason: what may never be remitted may justly be forever punished—even in the just, absolutely speaking
english: Third proof: never-remissible, therefore justly forever-punishable.
Remission is mercy by definition—so absolutely, even for the just, God could withhold pardon of the lightest faults and punish them forever.

title: Fourth reason: the legal covenant demanded flawless obedience—any lightest fault lost life and incurred curse
english: Legal covenant with upright Adam: life only by number-perfect obedience—any lightest fault lost life and drew the curse.
No pardon-lane under law-alone; repentance and remission belong to the gospel covenant—so every sin is mortal by nature.

title: Fifth reason: every sin—even ‘venial’—offends infinite Majesty and deserves objectively and extensively infinite penalty
english: Closing proof: even so-called venial sin strikes infinite Majesty—objective infinite malice—and leaves an unending stain apart from mercy.
Due penalty is infinite in object and in everlasting extent; therefore every sin is mortal by nature under justice.

title: Sin excludes from favor and binds under just penalty—debtor before God
english: Sin against God’s nature and law offends infinite Majesty and shuts a man out of favor.
Justice then holds him debtor to the penalties that such offense requires.

title: Remission defined: the debt is paid and liability to penalty ceases
english: Remission is the debt paid and penalty-liability ended; retention = still bound to punishment.
So pardon is the end of exclusion-from-favor and of law-threatened obnoxiousness.

title: Eternal decree to remit vs actual remission in time—do not confuse them
english: Eternal decree prepares every grace the elect will enjoy—including pardon.
Yet decree ≠ actual remission: God remits only by making them cease to be liable for penalty.

title: No remission without Christ’s satisfaction as surety under justice and wisdom
english: Justice and wisdom required a fitting mode: no immunity without satisfaction to avenging justice.
Only through Christ the surety’s death and passion—never without that merit in view.

title: Satisfaction must be applied: adults receive fruit only by true repentance and living faith
english: Satisfaction alone does not equal remitted sins until applied under God’s institution.
For reasoning adults: true repentance plus living, love-working faith mediate the fruit.

title: No release from wrath until sin is retracted by serious repentance joined to faith
english: Christ’s death frees no one from provoked wrath while he still perseveres in sin.
Eternal law: renounce sin with contrite faith, and the penalty-obligation lifts.

title: Gospel always sets faith and repentance as prior conditions of remission
english: Gospel never detaches pardon from prior faith and repentance—Luke 13; Acts 3:19; Prov. 28:13.
John 3: belief escapes judgment; unbelief already judged, wrath remaining.

title: Divine wisdom abhors pardon for the obstinate who trample Christ’s blood
english: Wisdom will not spare the obstinate who will not leave sin.
Nor share Christ’s death-benefit with those who trample his blood and refuse him as Savior.

title: Heavier vs lighter sins need different repentance—special contrition vs general humble confession
english: Daily lighter faults versus works of the flesh that cannot coexist with true holiness—two modes of repentance.of repentance.of repentance.
Heavier: special contrition; lighter: humble general confession of corruption (Ps 19).

title: Heavier-sin repentance must be perfectly practical; lighter cannot be—Baron of Aberdeen
english: Heavier pardon requires truly practical repentance—genuine cessation, or no grace or glory.
Lighter faults cannot be fully abandoned in this life; pious salvation is not thereby lost (Baron)...

title: From man’s side: active faith and worthy repentance-works; what then is God’s remitting action?
english: Man’s side: active efficacious faith fleeing to grace in Christ, plus repentance-worthy works.
God’s act of remission is best understood by asking how the opposing relationship of guilt is established.lt is established.lt is established.

title: Guilt is a relation resulting from sin by eternal law—no new temporal condemning sentence needed
english: Guilt = relational liability under eternal law once sin is posited—debtor while he remains in sin.
No extra temporal condemning act required; relations result from the foundation (white-wall likeness).

title: Remission: guilt-relation ceases; reconciling relation arises by the gospel law of faith and repentance
english: Remission = guilt-relation ends; a reconciling, life-accepting relation rises in its place.
similar relational structure under the eternal gospel law of contrition, mercy-seeking, and living faith.

title: Bringing to repentance and generating living faith suffices—no separate temporal absolving sentence required
english: Grace that brings true repentance and living faith is enough for actual absolution and reconciliation.
No extra temporal courtroom sentence—any more than guilt needed a fresh condemning sentence.

title: Elect sins not remitted from eternity—only in time when contracted guilt is actually loosed
english: Decree ≠ execution: elect pardon is not eternal-actual but temporal-actual.
Guilt is contracted in time (original + actual); only then can it be actually loosed.

title: ‘God does not will to punish’ is ambiguous—actual remission vs decree to transfer into a non-punishable state
english: ‘'God will not punish' has two meanings: (1) already in the order of faith and repentance → actual remission; (2) only decreed to be moved there → not yet.
Paul pre-conversion shows decree-not-to-punish without actual pardon while still in perdition.

title: No one has sins actually remitted before true faith and serious repentance
english: Actual remission never precedes true faith and serious repentance.
Serving sin / unbelief = wrath remaining and death—cannot coexist with actual pardon.

title: Pre-faith actual remission would void gospel conditions and contradict alien enmity (Col 1:21; 1 John 3)
english: If elect already had actual pardon pre-faith, gospel conditions of faith/repentance would be empty.
Col 1:21 enmity and 1 John 3’s ‘still in death’ cannot be called blessed covered-sin status.

title: Cross-payment does not actually cancel anyone’s debt until applied by faith and repentance
english: Surety-payment on the cross opens a mediated path; it does not automatically clear each person’s debt.
Sufficient price is ours only when faith-and-repentance apply it—until then liability remains.

title: Alting’s two modes of ‘deleted’ sins: decree/death vs effective application—absolute pre-faith talk is dangerous
english: Alting’s two senses: decree-and-cross vs efficacious application at believing.
Absolute ‘remitted before faith’ still misleads hearers toward actual granted pardon—dangerous and calumny-prone.

title: Only past sins of which one seriously repents are actually remitted—not future uncommitted sins
english: Actual remission at faith/repentance covers past sins seriously repented—not futures not yet done.
No guilt-relation without committed sin;n;n; pre-fall Adam needing pardon is a contradiction.

title: Future-sin blanket remission would call David pardoned while compounding adultery and Uriah’s murder
english: No repentance of uncommitted sin → no remission; persevering sinners stay bound.
Blanket future-pardon would bless David mid-adultery and Uriah-plot—against 1 John and Christian sense.

title: Union with Christ covers sins retractable by present faith-repentance—not sins not yet incurred
english: Faith-union applies Christ’s sufficient price to sins already incurred and sincerely retracted.
Not to unincurred futures; no absolute ‘paid in Christ’ without the condition-acts for that sin.

title: Believers have a ready remedy for future falls—not already-remitted futures; Maresius’s dangerous speech
english: Ready Christ-remedy for future falls requires renewed faith-repentance acts—not already-done pardon.
Even Maresius’s ‘extend justification by new faith-acts’ implies pre-act non-application; bold statements invite calumny

title: Many in Rome deny image-adoration and call the charge a Protestant calumny—so the true Roman doctrine must be sought
english: Many Romans—lay and some doctors—deny they adore images and call the charge a calumny.
They claim their Church gives adoration-cult only to the one true God.
So Le Blanc will dig out Rome’s real doctrine on image-cult, lest Reformers be falsely blamed for inventing it.

title: True Roman doctrine on images is drawn from general Councils, universal practice, and common doctor-consensus
english: Three wells yield Rome’s real teaching on images: general Councils Rome owns, her universal practice, and the received doctors’ consensus.
What those three agree on may safely be called Roman dogma.

title: Three Councils Rome counts as universal on images: Nicaea II (787), Constantinople (869), and Trent
english: Rome owns three ‘universal’ Councils on images: Nicaea II (787), Constantinople (869), and Trent in the sixteenth century.

title: Nicaea II’s constant teaching: Christ’s and the saints’ images are to be adored—and doubters are anathematized
english: Nicaea II (Rome’s ‘seventh’) steadily teaches that Christ’s and the saints’ images are to be adored and saluted.
Whoever hesitates about that adoration is anathematized.

title: Tarasius and the Synod receive and adore image-pictures in Christ’s and the saints’ names—‘so the whole holy Synod believes and teaches’
english: At Nicaea II Tarasius, with the Synod, receives image-pictures by ancient tradition and adores them in Christ’s and the saints’ names.
The whole Synod seals it: ‘thus we believe and teach.’

title: Nicaea II’s fathers distinguish adoration from mere veneration—and call hypocrites those who venerate but refuse to adore
english: The Synod’s adoration is more than bare veneration.
Those who say they venerate images but will not adore them are branded hypocrites who insult the saints.

title: Yet Nicaea II reserves latria—faith, hope, trust, invocation—to the one true God alone
english: The same Council walls off ‘latria’—inward faith, hope, trust, invocation—as God’s peculiar cult.
Tarasius: we adore images, yet we refer latria and faith only to the one true God.

title: Anastasius: ‘adore’ need not mean latria—Moses adds ‘only’ to latria-service, not to bare adoration
english: Anastasius: do not stumble at the word ‘adore’—we even ‘adore’ men and angels without giving divine latria.
Moses’ ‘alone’ (Deuteronomy 6:13; Matthew 4:10) binds latria-service to God, not the bare verb ‘adore.’

title: Synodical letter: Scripture says ‘adore’ absolutely, but ‘serve/cult’ with ‘alone’—so latria is referred to God only
english: The Synod’s letter to the emperors: Scripture’s ‘‘adore’ is used without ‘alone’,ne’,ne’,,’ so the word is equivocal.
‘Serve/cult’ carries ‘alone’—hence latria is ascribed and referred to God only (Deuteronomy 6:13; Matthew 4:10).

title: Image-adoration is called ‘honorary’—outward honor-signs; refuse them and you are a hypocrite even if you claim to ‘venerate’
english: They brand image-adoration ‘honorary’—an outward emphasis of honor, not latria.
Kiss, bow, and the other signs are required; refuse them while claiming ‘veneration’ and you are still a hypocrite.

title: Nicaea II names the honor-signs: kisses, embraces, lights, incense—honor passes to the prototype
english: Nicaea II lists kisses, embraces, lights, and incense as the honor owed to images.
Images stand in churches not only to remind, but to receive honorary adoration (not latria).
Honor paid to the image ‘results’ upon the prototype.

title: Synodical letter: to ‘adore’ images is to kiss and love them—Greek prosechein/proskunein as embrace and strong love
english: The synodical letter equates ‘adoring’ images with kissing and loving them.
Greek usage (proskunein and related terms) is pressed to mean embrace and strong affection, not latria.

title: Constantinople VIII (869): Christ’s image to be honored like the Gospels—refuse adoration and miss His face at the Second Coming
english: The ‘eighth’ Council ranks Christ’s image with Gospel-veneration: paint teaches as syllables teach.
Refuse to adore Christ’s image, and you are cursed not to see His face at His return.
Greek Gospel-book rites explain the parallel.

title: Trent Session 25: keep images; honor them by kiss and bow—honor passes to prototypes; no divinity or trust in the image itself
english: Trent Session 25 keeps Christ’s and the saints’ images in churches and bids due honor—kiss, bare head, prostration.
No divinity or trust is to be pinned on the wood; honor is referred to the prototypes (Nicaea II).

title: Sum of Roman Councils: relative honorary adoration is owed—kiss, bow, incense—not latria; ask nothing from the image
english: Roman Councils agree: images are owed cult—kiss, salute, bow, incense, lights—and may be called ‘adoration.’
But only subordinate adoration referred to the prototype—not latria, not petitions, not trust or divinity in the image.

title: What that adoration really is is clearest from Rome’s solemn universal temple-practice, approved or silently allowed by pastors and Pope
english: Rome’s real image-adoration is best read from her public temple practice.
Bishops, pastors, and Pope either approve or stay silent while the people make it part of piety.

title: Received practice: salute, kiss, kneel, offer incense and lights; set images on altars; process, vow, gift, and pilgrimage to them
english: Beyond Council-approved kiss and kneel come altar-placement, rich adornment, street processions, vows, offerings, and pilgrimages to images.

title: Coster the Jesuit defends kneeling prayer before Christ’s image, adorning images, candles, and carrying statues in processions
english: Jesuit Coster publicly defends kneeling prayer before Christ’s image, rich adornment, saint-candles, and statue processions as commendable Church custom.

title: Molanus of Louvain likewise defends carrying images in processions, setting them on altars, and clothing them in gold and precious garments
english: Louvain’s Molanus champions processions, altar-images, and gold-and-garment adornment against the ‘superstition’ charge.

title: Yet public prayers addressed to the images themselves seem to clash with Nicaea II and Trent’s ban on seeking anything from an image
english: Practice strains the Councils: Nicaea II and Trent bar seeking from an image, yet Rome’s public use aims prayers at the images themselves.

title: Breviary prayer (Pius V / Trent) addresses the Cross as distinct from Christ—‘O Cross … save the present throng’
english: The restored Roman Breviary aims a feast prayer at the Cross as distinct from Christ: ‘O Cross … save the present throng.’

title: ‘Vexilla Regis’ praises the Cross apart from Christ, then prays: ‘O cross, hail, only hope… grant pardon to the guilty’
english: The Passion hymn Vexilla Regis first praises the Cross as distinct from Christ, then prays to it as ‘only hope’ for justice and pardon.

title: Aquinas infers latria for Christ’s Cross (and even for other cross-effigies by representation) from ‘O cross, hail, only hope’
english: Aquinas reads the hymn as prayer to the cross-as-distinct and concludes the true Cross is owed latria (representation plus contact), and other cross-images latria by representation alone (ST III q.25 a.4).

title: Calling ‘cross’ a mere metonymy for Christ breaks where the hymn opposes and distinguishes the cross from Christ
english: Modern metonymy (‘cross’ = Christ) cannot rescue texts that oppose, distinguish, and praise the cross by bodily contact apart from Christ.

title: John XXII’s Veronica prayer (with huge indulgences) is aimed at Christ’s face-image on the sudarium, asking it to purge and lead to the blessed
english: John XXII’s indulged Veronica prayer is directed to the sudarium face-image itself—asking the ‘holy face’ / ‘blessed image’ to purge, enlighten, and bring the devout to Christ’s pure face.

title: Cross-consecration in the Roman Pontifical asks Christ’s true Cross to sanctify a stone/metal cross so its ‘merit’ frees souls—against Trent’s ‘no virtue in images’
english: Trent denies inherent virtue in images; yet Pontifical cross-blessing asks Christ to load a new stone/metal cross with true-Cross holiness so its ‘merit’ cleanses souls—and the Veronica prayer already ascribed light-giving power to an image.

title: Another Pontifical prayer asks the Father to make the held cross-sign a saving remedy and shield—implying God-given virtue in the material cross
english: A second Pontifical prayer asks the Father to make the held cross a saving remedy and shield.
If the prayer is trusted, the material cross must be thought to receive real virtue from God—Trent’s denial notwithstanding.

title: Papal consecration of wax Agnus Dei images begs God to give them power against devil, storm, plague, and epilepsy
english: Wax Agnus Dei tokens—symbolic ‘Lamb’ images—are consecrated with papal prayers that they receive power against demons, storms, plague, and epilepsy (cf. John 1:29).

title: Urban V’s verses with Agnus Dei gifts claim the wax lamb repels lightning, breaks sin, guards childbirth—so these imagelets escape Trent’s ‘no virtue’ class
english: Urban V’s gift-verses treat the wax Agnus as lightning-ward, sin-breaking, and childbirth-guarding.
On the Pope’s own mind, such imagelets sit outside Trent’s ‘images have no cult-virtue’ rule—or expose its hollow edge.

title: Doctors who ‘deny’ image-adoration mean only absolute latria—they still allow the relative honor the Councils sanction
english: Some Roman doctors ‘deny’ image-adoration and cry calumny—yet Nicaea II, Constantinople VIII, and Trent anathematize refusal to adore images.
Their escape: they deny only absolute latria to images, while still allowing the Councils’ relative honor-cult.

title: Others teach images of God and Christ are to be adored with latria—yet call it relative or per accidens, so Councils still ‘agree’
english: Some leading Schoolmen even assign latria to images of God and Christ.
They salvage Council language by calling that latria relative or per accidens—joined to the prototype—not absolute latria per se.

title: Despite diverse talk, Roman doctors agree with the Councils: images are owed cult and ‘adoration,’ with bow, kiss, incense, and lights as legitimate signs
english: Beneath the quarrel, Roman doctors lock step with the Councils on three points: images are for cult not bare memory; ‘adoration’ is a fair name; bare head, kiss, kneel, incense, and lights are lawful honor-signs.

title: Vasquez: Catholic truth is that images are owed adoration-signs; iconomachs who withhold kiss and bow are heretics under Nicaea II
english: Vasquez: owed image-adoration (kiss, lights, incense, bare head) is Catholic truth.
Seventh-Synod ‘iconomachs’ who kept images for memory but refused bodily honor-signs were condemned—veneration without adoration is not enough.

title: Vasquez clears Holcot, Durandus, and Pico: they still required embrace and kiss—calling refusal to adore images in any way an intolerable crime
english: Holcot, Durandus, and Pico, on Vasquez’s reading, still required kiss and bare head—even if they called it improper adoration of the image.
Vasquez: to teach images must not be adored at all is crime and intolerable error.

title: Consensus that images are somehow to be cultivated and adored—yet Schoolmen still quarrel over the mode and nature of that cult
english: Roman Schoolmen agree images somehow deserve kiss, incense, lights, and kneeling.
They still split on the mode and nature of that cult—Vasquez: unity against iconomachs, diversity on how adoration works.

title: Three School distinctions opened: honor per se vs per accidens (king, purple, accidents)
english: Schoolmen preface the quarrel with distinctions: honor per se vs per accidents.
Per se: the subject that carries the reason of veneration; per accidents: what is merely joined to it.
King example: the man who is king is honored per se; purple and other adjuncts only per accidents—royal dignity is the reason, not an accidental add-on.

title: Second distinction: honor propter se vs propter aliud—rational nature vs sacred signs
english: Second cut: honor on account of itself vs on account of another.
Only rational nature is venerable propter se; sacred signs are venerable only propter aliud, because their excellence hangs entirely on the holy thing they represent.

title: Third distinction: honor proprie vs improprie—legate, funeral statue; from Bellarmine
english: Third cut: proper vs improper honor.
Proper: honored by reason of itself; improper: honored in another's place — legate for the king; funeral statue for the corpse.
Bellarmine, De Ecclesia triumphante II.20, is the source for all three distinctions.

title: Question: are images adored properly or only improperly? Some older Scholastics say only improperly
english: Roman School question: proper or only improper adoration of images?
Some older Scholastics allow kiss, prostration, and honor-signs, yet call that adoration improper or abusive—acts toward images terminate on the prototype, not the image.

title: Durandus, Holcot, Pico: improper-only view rejected as rash by recent Scholastics
english: Durandus, Holcot, and Pico are tagged with the improper-only view.
Recent Schoolmen — Vasquez, Suarez, Bellarmine, Valencia, Puteanus — reject it as rash and insist images are adored properly and truly.

title: Agreement that images are adored properly—but split on whether the image alone can be integral object
english: Recent Schoolmen agree images are properly adored, but quarrel over the mode.
All say images are not adored for themselves but for the exemplar.
The live question: can the image alone be an integral, proximate object of a distinct adoration—like a legate honored for the king yet with his own inferior honor?

title: Vasquez rejects image-alone adoration as superstitious—must co-venerate the prototype
english: Vasquez brands image-alone adoration superstitious: a rational creature must not subject itself to an irrational one.
An image without its prototype cannot lawfully be adored; the adorant must also venerate the exemplar in and through the image as terminus.
Cited: Vasquez on ST III, disp. 108, c. 3.

title: Suarez and others allow images adored as proximate terminus without directly adoring the exemplar
english: Many disagree with Vasquez: images may be adored without simultaneously adoring the exemplar, as proximate terminus.
Suarez: images cannot be adored except because of the exemplar, yet can be adored in themselves and properly without directly adoring the exemplar as quod.
Cited: Suarez on ST III, disp. 54, sect. 5.

title: Bellarmine: images of Christ and the Saints venerated per se and properly, not only as stand-ins
english: Bellarmine's proposition: images of Christ and the Saints are venerated per se and properly.
They terminate veneration as considered in themselves—not only as stand-ins for the exemplar (De Ecclesia triumphante II.21).

title: Puteanus: the material object of our adoration can be the image alone
english: Puteanus agrees: Christ's image—and any saint's—can be adored so that the material object is the image alone (on ST III q.25 a.3).

title: Bellarmine on the genus of image-cult: imperfect, analogical dulia/hyperdulia/latria
english: What genus of cult terminates on the image alone? Bellarmine: an imperfect, analogical cult.
Images get neither proper latria, hyperdulia, nor dulia—those belong to intelligent natures—but inferior reductive analogues keyed to what they represent.
Cited: De Ecclesia triumphante II.25.

title: Puteanus: image of Christ alone gets relative latria, not absolute
english: Puteanus's line: when Christ's image alone is the material object, the latria owed is relative, not absolute.
Absolute latria tracks uncreated excellence in the thing; respective latria tracks excellence only by relation.

title: Same rule for Mary and the Saints: respective hyperdulia and dulia
english: On Puteanus's scheme: Marian images get respective hyperdulia; other saints' images get respective dulia—not the absolute grades.

title: Further question: one act adorning image and exemplar together? Peresius and Catharinus deny
english: Next quarrel: can one act adore image and exemplar together as one mental object?
Peresius de Ayala and Ambrosius Catharinus say no—image-adoration is always a distinct act from exemplar-adoration.

title: Suarez: one act can adore prototype in the image via representative presence
english: Majority Roman line (Suarez): one act can adore image-for-prototype and prototype-in-image together as adequate object.
The image does not really contain the prototype, but contains it in representative being—so the mind takes both as one without mistaking paint for Christ.

title: Vasquez: images may—and must—be adored only with the exemplar, never alone
english: Vasquez goes further: images can and must be adored only with the exemplar—never alone even in thought.
Apart from the joined exemplar the image is not capable of veneration; together they make the integral proximate terminus.

title: Vasquez's ground: no irrational thing is capable of honor per se—alone-adoration risks idolatry
english: Vasquez's ground: nothing irrational is capable of honor per se, because adoration is willed submission to a superior excellence.
Image-alone veneration can be branded folly or idolatry—servitude to the irrational, or attributing deity or dignity to it (Gentile error, not Christian religion).

title: Vasquez: adoration's one act has exterior mark plus interior affect of submission
english: Vasquez: one adoration-act has two parts—exterior mark (kneel, bare the head) plus interior affect of submission.
Without the affect, the gesture is not cult (it could be a joke); both together make one honor-act, as virtue's interior and exterior do.

title: Does the interior affect terminate on the image too? Vasquez: only the exterior mark does
english: Follow-up: when one act covers both, does the interior affect terminate on the image too?
Vasquez: only the exterior mark terminates on the image; the interior affect aims at the exemplar alone, and the mark is transmitted to it (

title: Suarez counters: interior submission also terminates on the image in the one joint act
english: Suarez answers Vasquez: in the joint act, interior submission terminates on the image too—not only the sensible mark.
One interior-and-exterior act adores prototype-in-image and image-for-prototype as one object, truly and properly—not merely abusively.

title: From joint-act hypothesis: images share the exemplar's cult genus—dulia, hyperdulia, even latria
english: If one act covers image and exemplar, images share the exemplar's cult genus.
Saints' images: dulia; Mary's: hyperdulia; God's and Christ's: latria—as Aquinas and most Scholastics teach.

title: Bellarmine's first escape from idolatry: improper latria when the mind stays fixed on the exemplar alone
english: How can image-latria avoid idolatry? Bellarmine's first route: improper latria.
Mind fixed only on the exemplar while Good-Friday crucifix rites use the image as stand-in—latria properly goes to Christ alone, improperly said of the image.

title: Bellarmine's second route: proper latria per accidents—yet do not tell the people images are owed latria
english: Bellarmine's second route: proper latria per accidents—Christ adored as shining in the image, like king-plus-clothes.
Latria per se to the image remains forbidden; yet he forbids telling the people that images are owed latria, preferring the contrary for popular speech (II.22-23).

title: Vasquez's latria fix: interior submission to God alone; images get only the exterior mark
english: Vasquez's fix: one act, but split—interior submission aims only at the exemplar or God; the image gets only the exterior mark.
Latria names the interior servitude-affect toward God, not the bare gesture—so II Nicaea rightly denies latria to images.

title: Vasquez still allows saying images are adored with latria—per accidents, via exterior signs
english: Vasquez still allows absolute speech that images are adored with latria—but only per accidents.
Exterior signs drawn from latria-servitude toward the exemplar make the image latria-adored with the prototype, not per se.

title: Suarez closes the Roman locus: true proper latria of Christ's image with Christ—relative toward the image, absolute toward Christ
english: Suarez closes the Roman locus: one true proper latria-act can terminate on Christ and his image together.
Per se the act aims first at Christ; the image is only co-adored concomitantly—like royal purple with the king—so Councils forbidding creature-latria are not breached.
Toward Christ the act is absolute latria; toward the image, respective latria for God's sake, not the creature's.

title: Roman Councils deny absolute god-cult of images, yet require relative cult of Christ, Mary, and saints
english: Roman Councils refuse to call images gods or to vest them with absolute, highest cult.
Yet they steadily require some cult of Christ’s, Mary’s, and the saints’ images—for the prototype, not for the image as such.

title: Roman image-cult is rightly called adoratio; praxis is prostration, kneeling, uncovering, kiss, candles, incense
english: School and Councils name the image-cult adoratio without embarrassment.
The living praxis is bodily: prostration, genuflection, bare head, kiss, candles, and incense.

title: Protestants do not calumniate Rome by charging image-adoration—Councils anathematize the contrary
english: Rome’s own school teaches image-adoration; her Councils anathematize refusal.
Calling that adoration is not Protestant slander—it is Rome’s self-description.

title: Relative/inferior adoration does not clear Rome—Protestants never charged absolute god-cult of images
english: Rome’s refuge—only relative, inferior adoration—is the very thing Protestants meant.
Even thoughtful pagans denied their statues were gods; Protestants do not charge Rome with that stupidity.
So the accusation tracks Rome’s own relative cult, not a forged absolute one.

title: Suarez’s three modes of adoration toward an image: exemplar alone; exemplar+image as one; image alone for the exemplar’s sake
english: Rome agrees images get some adoratio, yet Schoolmen split on how.
Suarez lists three modes: mind wholly on the exemplar; exemplar and image as one adequate object; image alone as matter, exemplar as reason.
Thomas III, disp. 54.4 is his locus.

title: Older Scholastics allow only mode one (improper adoration); recent School rejects that as rash
english: Older Schoolmen: bodily honors yes, but intention only on the exemplar—so image-adoration is improper/abusive.
Recent School throws that out as rash and insists images are adored properly and truly.

title: Some allow modes one and two, but reject mode three (image alone as per-se adored thing)
english: Middle party: modes one and two are licit—adoration may terminate on exemplar-plus-image as one total object.
Mode three (image alone as the per-se adored thing) they brand illicit, even when the exemplar is the reason.

title: Others reject mode two and allow modes one and three—image loved per se as a means for the end
english: Opposite party: drop mode two’s single total object; keep modes one and three.
Image may be the per-se terminus, yet only because of the exemplar—like loving a means for an end.

title: Majority of Roman theologians: all three Suarez modes are right and pious
english: The Roman majority blesses all three Suarez modes as right and pious.
Adoration may terminate on exemplar alone, image alone, or both as one total object.

title: Among joint-act adorers: some send only the exterior sign to the image; others the interior submission too—latria/dulia/hyperdulia debate
english: Joint-act camp still splits: Vasquez-style exterior-only toward the image vs interior submission aimed at both.
Many then assign latria/dulia/hyperdulia to Christ’s, saints’, and Mary’s images; others keep image-cult a lower, analogical order.

title: Beneath School diversity, three Roman agreements: some cult owed; rightly called adoratio; bodily honors licit
english: Diversity aside, Rome’s Doctors lock three points: some cult is owed to the images; adoratio is the right word; uncovering, kneeling, lights, and incense are legitimate.

title: Status controversiae: Protestants reject all such cult as superstition; Rome affirms it under anathema and solemn praxis
english: Protestants unanimously refuse every such rite as superstition against God’s word.
The quarrel’s status is simply whether kneeling, bare head, incense, and candles before images please God—Rome says yes under anathema and universal praxis.

title: Protestant ground: Decalogue Non facies tibi sculptile—no likeness of heavenly or earthly things to be adored
english: The engine is the Decalogue ban on making and adoring any likeness of heaven, earth, or waters.
Christ’s and the saints’ images are exactly such heavenly likenesses—so the precept strips them of cult.

title: Roman reply A: Vazquez and others call the ban a positive ceremonial law abrogated by the Gospel
english: First Roman escape: grant the ban’s breadth, then reclassify it as positive ceremonial law canceled by the Gospel.
Vazquez (Thomas III, disp. 104) leads; Lorinus, Catharinus, Ayala, and Soto follow.

title: If the image-ban is a separate positive precept, Rome’s Decalogue becomes an eleven-word Hendralogus
english: Separate the image-ban from Non habebis Deos alienos and you mint an eleventh precept.
Moses still calls the Law’s breviary ten words—so Rome’s split (plus her two covetings) drives a Hendralogus, not a Decalogue.

title: No NT word marks the image-ban ceremonial—unlike the Sabbath shadow in Colossians 2.16
english: Colossians 2.16 flags Sabbath/feast shadows as ceremonial; nothing parallel softens the image-ban.
The NT never whispers that Christians may now cult God or saints in images.

title: The ban is moral and perpetual—Gentiles are reproached for image-cult, not for breaching Moses’ positive rites
english: Prophets blame Gentiles for making and culting images—proof the ban is moral for all, not a Jew-only positive rite.
Gentiles are not charged with breaking Moses’ ceremonial code, but with violating nature’s moral law.

title: Romans 1: Gentile wise men charged with exchanging God’s glory for corruptible image-likenesses
english: Romans 1 puts Gentile image-making under NT indictment, not OT ceremonial only.
Paul’s charge: swapping incorruptible God’s glory for likenesses of man, birds, beasts, and serpents.

title: Gentile sages were not crude corporealists—they used images as thin symbolic signs, yet still fell under Paul’s charge
english: Don’t rescue Romans 1 by saying only crude corporealists are meant.
Egypt’s sages treated images as thin symbolic signs—not literal God-bodies—and Paul still brands that folly.

title: Plutarch and Varro: Egyptian animals and human-shaped gods are mystical vessels, not crude bodies of deity
english: Plutarch’s Isis treatise reads Egyptian animal cult as mystical symbolism of divine virtues.
Varro (via Augustine, Civ. 7.5): human-shaped gods are vessels signifying rational soul— Liber’s wine-jar for the vine.

title: Maximus of Tyre: statues of words, men, beasts, gold and ivory help reach a God beyond sense
english: Maximus asks whether gods should have statues, then answers with a ladder of aids—words, men, beasts, precious figures—toward a God beyond sense.

title: Even mystical-symbolic image-cult is moral sin—Decalogue binds all men forever against exposing God’s likenesses for cult
english: Symbolic paganism still counts as grave sin—mystical intention does not sanitize image-cult.
The Decalogue’s ban is moral and perpetual for every human likeness set out for cult.

title: Primitive Doctors: Decalogue is the moral-natural sum—only the Sabbath’s seventh-day rigor is ceremonial
english: Fathers read the Decalogue as the moral-natural sum binding everyone.
Only Sabbath’s exact seventh-day stoppage is ceremonial; sanctifying a holy day remains moral

title: Irenaeus, Tertullian, Cyprian, Augustine: second commandment and Decalogue still bind Christians (Sabbath flesh excepted)
english: Irenaeus: Decalogue words remain, extended not dissolved by the Incarnation.
Tertullian universalizes the ban on likeness-making; Cyprian applies the second commandment to Christians; Augustine keeps the whole Decalogue except carnal Sabbath.

title: Most Roman doctors admit the ban is moral—but shrink it to forbidding only absolute god-cult of images
english: Mainstream Rome drops Vazquez’s ceremonial dodge and owns the ban as moral for Christians.
Their new escape: the precept only bars absolute god-cult of an image—relative, inferior cult of God’s and the saints’ images supposedly survives.

title: Relative cult is exactly what the precept forbids—no sane painter treats the panel as absolute God
english: Everyday sense: anyone who paints God and bows to the panel means relative honor through it—not absolute godhood of paint.
The precept targets precisely that relative move; absolute tablet-worship is too absurd to need its own ban.

title: Scripture condemns relative image-cult too—transgressors meant to honor the true God through their images
english: Biblical offenders often intended relative cult of the true God through images—and are still condemned.
So the mandate reaches subordinate/relative adoration, not only absolute god-cult.

title: Golden calf: Israel meant Jehovah under a bovine symbol—plural Elohim with singular sense; not literal bovine deity
english: The calf was Egypt-style bovine symbolism aimed at Jehovah, not a sudden belief that jewelry had become God.
Plural Elohim with singular force is ordinary Hebrew—even of the true God (Gen 20.13; 2 Sam 7.23).
Calling the image by the prototype’s name is stock; absolute bovine deity is psychologically incredible.

title: Aaron’s feast: Cras solemnitas Jehovae—honor of the cast image referred to the true patriarchal God
english: Aaron’s proclamation names Jehovah’s feast, not a rival god’s.
So the calf-honor was explicitly referred to the patriarchal true God.

title: Micah’s graven/molten image vowed to Jehovah—relative cult still called a most grave crime
english: Micah’s household shrine: silver vowed to Jehovah, Levite priest, hope of Jehovah’s blessing.
The cult is textbook relative—and Scripture still brands it a most grave crime.

title: Jeroboam’s calves: Jehu’s zeal for Jehovah coexisted with Bethel and Dan—cult referred to the true God
english: Jehu can burn for Jehovah against Baal and still keep Jeroboam’s calves.
Those calves were image-vehicles of Jehovah-cult—relative, and still sinful.

title: Joram’s calf-cult judged less than Baal-statues—because it claimed the true God, wrongly imaged
english: Spirit ranks Joram’s calf-sin below Baal-sun worship: calves claimed Jehovah; Baal swapped in a creature.
That ranking collapses if the calves were taken as literal gods or Apis—so relative Jehovah-cult is the better reading, and still condemned.

title: Jeroboam’s political craft: minimize religious change so ten tribes stay—cannot have swapped Jehovah for Apis
english: Jeroboam’s aim was political: stop Jerusalem pilgrimages without revolting the tribes.
Swapping Jehovah for Apis or a brand-new calf-god would have been religious overthrow, not crafty minimal change.

title: Ecce Dii tui Israel: plural form with singular sense; naming the image God means symbol, as papal ‘God the Father’ panels today
english: Plural Dii on the calves tracks Hebrew idiom, not a pantheon.
Calling the symbol God mirrors modern panels labeled God the Father—representation, not literal identity.

title: Bellarmines Ps 106 forgotten God does not prove absolute calf-cult—Scripture calls willful disobedience forgetting God
english: Bellarmines Ps 106 forgetfulness does not equal atheism about Jehovah.
Scripture also calls thieves and adulterers forgetters of God while they still profess him—same idiom covers calf-cult disobedience.

title: Deos alienos & conflatiles: unauthorized Jehovah-images still count as alien gods because God never willed that mode
english: Prophetic Deos alienos still fits relative Jehovah-calves: God never authorized that mode.
Human-invented image-cult of the true God is as offensive as foreign-god cult.

title: Some Roman doctors grant Jeroboam meant the true God—and still call the cult illicit, a blade that cuts today’s images too
english: Honest Roman voices admit relative Jehovah-calf cult can still be idolatry—wrong mode, unauthorized images.
They concede the same knife can cut today’s image-cult if God has not approved it.

title: Claim that Jeroboam culted Apis is free invention—Scripture never says so; his craft aimed away from Jerusalem, not from Jehovah
english: Apis-in-the-calves is assertion without Scripture.
Jeroboam’s counsel was anti-Jerusalem, not anti-Jehovah—sudden Egypt-reversion is psychologically forced.

title: Ten-tribe politics: proposing Apis would be madness—far likelier Jehovah under calf-symbols like cherubim or the bronze serpent
english: A Mosaic people would revolt at Apis; empire-hope rules that out.
Better parallel: calves as presence-symbols like cherubim or the bronze serpent.

title: Jeroboam never denied Jehovah—calf-cult was relative, referred to him, and still branded gravest idolatry
english: No rival deity was preached—only Jehovah via calf-symbols.
Scripture’s idolatry verdict on that relative cult proves the law bans relative image-adoration too.

title: Calf as strong-God symbol like Apis attributes—Scripture still allows relative reference and gravest condemnation together
english: Optional reading: ox-strength as Jehovah’s power symbol, Apis-style attributes.
Either way Scripture holds together relative reference to Jehovah and gravest condemnation.

title: Rome’s sacrifice-only censure of Jeroboam clashes with her own per-accidens latria of divine images
english: Rome says Jeroboam’s fatal step was sacrifice—latria’s chief exterior act.
Yet she already allows per-accidens / relative / concomitant latria of God’s images in other acts—so why not in sacrifice on the same terms?

title: Vazquez’s sacrifice exception (protestation of omnipotence) would ban every relative latria-act toward images
english: Vazquez fences sacrifice off because it protests omnipotence and dominion.
But every latria-act protests some uncreated excellence—so the fence would outlaw all relative image-latria, not sacrifice alone.

title: Thomas puts hope of salvation in the cross—an image—so hope’s protestation is no weaker than sacrifice’s
english: Hope’s claim on God is as strong a protestation as sacrifice’s.
Thomas still assigns worship to the true cross and its image because hope of salvation is set there—O crux Ave spes unica.

title: Hezekiah smashed the bronze serpent because Israel burned incense to it—piety praised
english: 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah destroys Moses’ bronze serpent for incense-cult.
Scripture praises that piety—so even minimal religious cult of an image is banned.

title: If any image deserved honor, the bronze serpent did—yet incense alone brought it down; Nicaea II’s lights clash with that
english: Bronze serpent had divine mandate, saving use, memorial force, and Christ-typology—best-case image.
Incense alone justified smashing it; Nicaea II’s incense-and-lights approach collides with that verdict.

title: If the precept only bans absolute god-cult, it never touched the wise Gentiles’ relative simulacrum-cult
english: Narrow the precept to absolute god-cult and pagan sages walk free—they already distinguished sign from god.
Their relative referral is the same structure Rome now claims.

title: Celsus and Arnobius’s opponents: statues are dedications and social bridles, not gods with sense
english: Celsus: only a fool thinks the polished metal is God—statues are dedications to gods.
Arnobius’s pagan spokesmen: ancients knew signs lack sense; images bridle the crowd toward civil virtue under felt divine presence.

title: Pagan confession: we adore visible images unto the honor of the invisible God—Recognitiones and Lactantius
english: Pagan line in the Clementine Recognitions: visible images for invisible God’s honor.
Lactantius records the same: fear the named gods, not the crafted things.

title: FINIS: even if the crowd sometimes took signs for gods, the institutors’ relative cult still violates the likeness-ban—so say the primitive Doctors
english: Institutors of pagan cult knew gold is not God per se—they venerated divinity through it.
Alien-gods precept may catch their false companions; the institutors’ relative cult still violates the prohibition against images—so say the primitive Doctors
Pars altera closes here; next frontier is Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu.

title: Cult has three acts: intellect of excellence, will’s inward bow, and outward signs of subjection
english: Roman doctors (Bellarmino first) say cult wraps three acts.
Intellect grasps the excellence; will bows inward and wills a protest of that excellence and our subjection.
Outward signs follow—head bowed, knee bent, or the like.

title: Three excellences, three cults: latria for God, civil honor for natural dignity, dulia for supernatural grace and glory
english: Cult species track excellence species—three for this debate.
Latria answers infinite divine excellence; civil observance answers natural human dignity.
Dulia answers the mid-rank supernatural grace and glory of the Saints.

title: Scholastics split dulia: hyperdulia for Mary as Lady and Queen, proper dulia for the other Saints
english: Mary’s maternity of the Son of God lifts her above other Saints as Lady and Queen.
Hence Schoolmen bisect dulia: hyperdulia for her, proper dulia for the rest.

title: Dulia/hyperdulia names lack conciliar sanction; Pérez dislikes ‘dulia’ as implying servitude to fellow-servants
english: School use of dulia/hyperdulia is not yet fixed by Roman Councils.
Pérez (via Bellarmino) dislikes calling saint-cult ‘dulia,’ since the word means servitude and we are conservi, not their slaves.

title: Even latria/dulia champions admit scriptural mix-up of the terms, yet defend the School distinction as anti-equivocation coinage
english: Even latria/dulia partisans admit the Greek terms blur in pagan use and Scripture—latreia sometimes of human service, duleia often of God’s own cult.
They still defend the School coinage: the thing differs, so the names must, to kill equivocation.
As the old Church coined homoousios against heretics, so the later Church may rebaptize words against later errors.

title: ‘Fellow-servants’ still fits dulia: Scripture’s honorable subjection (Galatians 5) and imperfect ‘service’ by example and intercession
english: Being conservi does not bar dulia: Scripture also uses dulia for honorable subjection—“through love serve one another” (Galatians 5:13).
Imperfectly we are their servants by their example and intercession—and by the majesty and glory that still outrank us pilgrims.

title: The three cult-species are analogical, not univocal under one genus
english: Roman doctors deny one univocal genus for the three cults—only analogy of proportion.
As ‘excellence’ is not univocal of God and creatures, neither is ‘cult’ owed for excellence.

title: ‘Religious’ cult of Saints: denied strictly (religion’s object is God), allowed broadly or secondarily
english: Strictly, religion’s object is God’s cult—so saint-cult is another species of observance.
Broadly (or secondarily) they still call saint-honor religious, as opposed to mere civil polity.

title: Are Saints ‘to be adored’? Strict latria—no; broader human cult—yes
english: ‘Adoration’ strict = latria for God alone—Saints out.
‘Adoration’ broad = creaturely honor—Saints in, and their cult may wear the name.

title: Scholastic ‘adoration’: whole cult, or the special bodily signs (prostration, genuflection) Thomas ranks first among exterior latria acts
english: Scholastics stretch ‘adoration’ from the whole cult-package to a special exterior act.
Thomas (2a2ae q.84) puts bodily exhibition—prostration, genuflection—first among exterior latria acts.
Strict adoration = outward submission-signs springing from inward affection.

title: Interior latria vs dulia: supreme will-prostration to God as first principle and last end, vs lesser creaturely inclination
english: Interiorly latria and dulia part cleanly.
Latria is the will’s highest prostration to God as first principle, last end, and supreme good.
Dulia is a lesser bow to more-than-human yet still creaturely excellence.

title: Exterior acts mostly shared—except sacrifice, temples, altars, and priests reserved to latria
english: Outwardly almost every cult-sign is shared between dulia and latria.
They reserve sacrifice—and temples, altars, priests tied to it—to latria alone.
No one may offer sacrifice or dedicate those things except to God.

title: No sacrifice to Saints—yet Masses ‘of’ Saints offer Christ’s body to God for their honor, merit, and intercession
english: Rome refuses sacrifice to Saints, yet allows sacrifice to God in their honor.
Masses named for Saints still immolate Christ’s true body to the Father.
Such Masses commemorate the Saint and plead by his merit and intercession.

title: Though sacrifice is withheld, votive offerings and dedicatory gifts fill Saints’ named churches and chapels
english: Sacrifice aside, Rome still loads Saints with oblations and consecrated gifts.
These mark benefits thought received from or through them—crowding their named shrines.

title: Temples ‘of’ Saints: many deny building them to Saints, yet name churches after them as thanks to God and plea to the Patron
english: Doctors deny temples built to Saints—yet churches everywhere bear Saints’ names.
Explanations diverge; one line: sacrifice still goes to God in thanks for the Saint’s glory, while the Patron is appealed as advocate.

title: Bellarmino: sacred houses may be built to Saints as basilicas (relic-chests), not as temples of sacrifice—else idolatry
english: Bellarmino allows sacred houses to Saints—as basilicas, not sacrifice-temples.
Temple-ratio to Saints would be idolatry; basilica-ratio is a great relic-chest and memorial.
Mass of Peter ≠ Basilica of Peter: Mass to God, basilica the Saint’s monument.

title: Pontificale simply calls them ‘Churches’ dedicated in Saints’ honor and name—without Bellarmino’s temple/basilica split
english: The Pontificale skips temple/basilica jargon and simply consecrates ‘Churches’ in Saints’ honor and name.
Litanies name the title Saint; the bishop asks God to purify the church in that Saint’s memory.

title: Popular books still say temples and altars are dedicated to Mary without scruple—Alexis de Salo and the Liège Manual
english: Popular Roman books freely say temples and altars are consecrated to Mary and the Saints.
Alexis de Salo’s Method and the Liège Sodality Manual put that praxis in print—altars first to God, yet in Mary’s honor and memory.

title: Bellarmino’s basilica-as-relic-chest is not limited to relic sites—basilicas also summon the named Patron for cult and prayer
english: Do not over-read Bellarmino’s relic-chest image as relic-only.
He also allows basilicas so the name itself summons worshippers to honor and pray to that Patron.

title: Sacred houses may rise where Saints lived or wrought wonders—even for Angels and Mary without bodily relics, or by image and name alone
english: Relics are not required: houses may mark dwellings, deeds, or apparitions.
Mary and the Angels get churches without bodily relics; image or bare name can carry the memorial.

title: Altars ‘of’ Saints: same stone is God’s altar and a martyr’s tomb—dedication to Saints only under tomb-ratio, else idolatry
english: One stone: altar to God, tomb over a martyr’s bones—every altar a Saint’s sepulcher.
Dedication ‘to Saints’ is licit only as tomb-ratio; altar-ratio to Saints would be idolatry.

title: Practice jars Bellarmino: countless Marian altars bear her name without her tomb or relics
english: Roman practice undercuts Bellarmino’s tomb-only rule.
Marian altars everywhere take her name without her sepulcher or relics.

title: Pontificale consecrates the same altar twice—once as sepulcher, once as altar—with distinct forms
english: The Pontificale splits consecration: sepulcher-form and altar-form for the same stone.
That public rite is not Bellarmino’s tomb-only permission scheme.

title: Every altar is also sanctified in honor of God, Mary, and all Saints—beyond any single tomb-ratio
english: Each altar gets a title Saint (possible tomb-ratio)—and also a general sanctification to God, Mary, and all Saints.
That universal honor outruns Bellarmino’s tumulus-only leave.

title: No priests to Saints—yet confraternities and sodalities uniquely adore and invoke them, especially Mary
english: Rome bars priests of Saints, yet proliferates confraternities and sodalities.
Those societies specially adore and invoke their patrons—Mary foremost.

title: Feasts ranked as God’s own cult—yet Saint-days abound; many say they are God’s feasts in Saints’ memory
english: Feasts are classed with Godward cult—yet Saint-days fill the calendar.
Many resolve it: feasts (like temples and Masses) go to God, in the Saints’ memory and honor.

title: Bellarmino: feast-honor terminates also on the Saints secondarily—dulia under ‘religion’ in the general sense
english: Bellarmino lets feast-honor terminate on Saints also—primarily God, secondarily Saints.
He calls that dulia, and ‘religion’ only in the broad genus, not the special Godward virtue.

title: Vows to Saints are common; Thomas’s escape: the Saint-promise is vow-matter, the God-promise is the formal vow
english: Saint-vows (especially Marian) are everyday Roman praxis—yet vows are latria-acts.
Thomas’s patch: the Saint gets promise-matter; God alone gets the formal vow (tacitly guaranteeing fulfillment).

title: Bellarmino rejects Thomas here: Saint-vows aim to honor Saints, and some formulas vow to God and Saints together
english: Bellarmino: Thomas fits prelate-obedience vows, not Saint-directed fasts and pilgrimages that mean to honor Saints.
Some formulas vow to God and Mary and all Saints at once—so the Saint-clause is inside the formal vow.

title: Cajetan/Bellarmino: vows to Saints as ‘gods by participation’—vows made to God in the Saints
english: Backup line (Cajetan via Bellarmino): vow to Saints as gods-by-participation where God dwells in glory.
Thus the vow is to God in the Saints—as cursing Saints blasphemes God in them.

title: Those vows still terminate on Saints too—like alms to Christ in the poor; same promise, different end (latria vs dulia)
english: Even ‘God-in-the-Saints’ vows still land on the Saints—as alms to Christ in the poor land on the poor.
Same true promise, different end: God as first author (latria) vs Saints as mediators (dulia).

title: Others keep Thomas: ‘vow’ analogically covers God-promises and Saint-promises—absolute vs relative
english: Another School path: Church usage stretches ‘vow’ analogically to Saint-promises.
God-vows absolute; Saint-vows relative—ending finally in God’s glory.

title: Popular Manual of Mary’s sodality: vows honor her as witness and terminate the promise in her
english: Bellarmino’s terminating Saint-vows are not niche—they sit in popular sodality manuals.
Mary’s Manual: vow to God with Mary as witness and intercessor—and terminate the promise in her.

title: Oaths are latria-acts—yet swearing by Saints is allowed secondarily as divine truth shines in them (Thomas 2a2ae q.89 a.6)
english: Oaths belong to worship—yet Rome swears by Saints...
Scholastics allow it secondarily: swear by the divine truth shining in them (Thomas 2a2ae q.89 a.6), not by the Saints as such.

title: Singular ‘adoration’: bodily submission-signs; Vázquez defends sacred adoration of Saints as Catholic tradition
english: Rome pushes a named ‘adoration’: exterior submission from true inward reverence—prostration, genuflection, bare head.
Vázquez (on Thomas III) calls sacred Saint-adoration Catholic by perpetual use and tradition.

title: Popular Method books demand frequent bows and genuflections to Mary privately and in church—Alexis de Salo’s program
english: Handbooks pressed on the people push Marian adoration—bows and genuflections at home and in church.
Alexis de Salo’s approved Method trains deep reverences to the Queen of heaven and maps them into practice.

title: Mendoza: Mary may receive latria by contact with Christ—secondary and respective, if scandal is avoided (Cajetan on Thomas)
english: The standard teaching is: Saints receive dulia, Mary receives hyperdulia—yet Mendoza asks if she may also take latria.
Three dignities: holiness (dulia), maternity (hyperdulia), contact with Christ (latria), as cross and nails do.
Cajetan’s Thomas: allowed as secondary respective latria if scandal is kept off—so Mendoza concludes.

title: Suárez agrees contact-latria is speculative, not for common public use—prefer absolute inferior cult for her own holiness and maternity
english: Suárez too allows extrinsic contact-latria—Mary touched Christ and cooperated in redemption more than cross or nails.
Speculatively fine; publicly he bars common use lest divine excellence be ascribed, and lest inferior absolute cult for her own holiness and maternity be the greater honor.

title: No real contradiction: deniers refuse absolute supreme adoration; affirmers mean adoration below the supreme
english: Famous Jesuits say Saints are to be adored; many Romans say only God is—yet Le Blanc finds no contradiction.
Deniers mean absolute supreme latria; affirmers mean inferior adoration the deniers still allow.

title: Chief cult-part: invocation—Saints know at least what touches their beatitude, including living prayers for their help
english: Invocation is the chief Roman cult of Saints and Angels—spoken aloud or by heart alone.
School premise: reigning Saints need not know all earthly events, yet know what touches their beatitude—including cult and pleas for their aid.
Hence it is certain for them that the dead Saints hear the living’s prayers.
Next frontier is Romana XLI–LXXVII (how they hear; merits; patrons; Marian dominion), then Pars Secunda Reformata.

title: How Saints hear living prayers—opinions vary; Costerus: by angels, migrants, and divine revelation for their glory
english: How Saints hear the living’s prayers is unsettled among Roman doctors.
Costerus: heaven knows earthly deeds by angel messengers and by the newly departed—and especially by revelation of what advances the Saints’ glory.
God hides from them nothing that can heighten that joy; living prayers and glory-works belong to that class.

title: Living vs beatified: occult inspiration vs vision in the divine essence; distance no bar if God opens hearts
english: Living learn hidden things by occult inspiration; the beatified see them in God’s essence as in a mirror—more perfectly than in themselves.
No bodily bulk or distance bars Saints from prayers, acts, and opened thoughts.
Unwilling minds stay closed except to God alone, who searches hearts.

title: Holden: pure spirit by natural reason knows all corporeal natures and motions—denying prayer-hearing is crass ignorance
english: Holden (Paris): natural reason shows a pure spirit knows every corporeal nature, motion, and act.
Calling heaven deaf to mortal prayer is, for him, dense ignorance.

title: Bellarmino’s two probable views: see all relevant things in God from beatitude’s start, or revelation when we pray
english: Bellarmino favors two lines: Saints see in God from beatitude’s dawn all that touches them—including our prayers—or God reveals prayers only when we offer them.
He leans to the first as simply likelier; the second as better for answering heretics.

title: Second premise: Saints know needs, pray with greater charity, and are mediators of intercession not redemption
english: Roman premise two: heaven knows living needs and prays with greater charity than on earth.
They plead both for the Church militant and for individuals who seek their patronage.
Called intercessors and advocates—mediators of intercession, never of redemption.

title: Saints do not intercede immediately—their petitions rest on Christ’s merit (Bellarmino)
english: Intercession is not immediate: it rests on Christ’s merit.
Bellarmino: Saints obtain from God for us only through Christ.

title: Only Christ mediates redemption; yet Saints’ merits move God to grant favors—Mass ‘through the merits of Saints’
english: Christ alone mediates redemption; Saints still ‘benefit’ by merits that move God—without strict right or promise.
Mass liturgy asks ‘through the merits of Saints,’ holding their deeds and sufferings before God’s eyes.

title: Living ruled by Angels and blessed human spirits—Costerus: Saints as administrators of God’s goods
english: Roman school: Angels and blessed human spirits both rule the living.
Costerus: reigning Saints administer earthly goods—compel the impious, rescue the pious—matching angelic wonders.

title: Patron Saints by realm, craft, and need—Luke, Ivo, Crispin; sea, childbirth, plague, toothache
english: Every realm, town, and craft keeps a singular patron Saint.
Luke for doctors, Ivo for lawyers, Crispin for shoemakers; James for Spain, Mark for Venice.
Special needs: Paul and Nicholas at sea; Margaret in childbirth; Roch in plague; Apollonia for toothache.

title: Any Saint may aid any need; particular patrons arise from craft, death, gifts, miracles, or name-play
english: Any Saint can intercede for any need; the faithful may approach any.
God did not fence offices so tightly—patrons stick by craft, martyrdom, gifts, miracles, or even name-affinity.
Luke for medicine; Paul and Nicholas for seafarers (Acts shipwreck; Myra miracle).

title: How to invoke: pray God to give/free; ask Saints to take patronage and obtain from God—Miserere vs Ora pro nobis
english: Trent Catechism: God and Saints are not asked the same way.
Ask God to give goods or free from evils; ask Saints, favorable with Godto take patronage and obtain from Him.
Formulas: to God ‘Have mercy / Hear us’; to a Saint ‘Pray for us.’

title: Bellarmino/Perron: no asking Saints as authors of grace—absolute prayer to God alone; relative ‘pray for us’ to Saints
english: Bellarmino: never ask Saints as authors of glory or grace—only that they obtain from God.
Perron: absolute prayer (author of goods) for God alone; relative prayer (‘pray for us’) for Saints.

title: Yet public hymns and litanies ask Mary to pity, free, and give goods—not merely to pray
english: Public hymns still ask Mary to pity, free, and confer goods—not only to pray.
Ave Maris Stella, Alma Redemptoris, and Bonaventure-style litanies even say ‘Spare us / Free us, Lady’ and ‘Have mercy.’
