title: Hymns to John the Baptist and John the Apostle ask cleansing, healing, and vision of the Word
english: Baptist hymns beg pity, loosing of faults, and cleansing of polluted lips.
Apostle John is asked to lift plague and scandal and grant sight of the Word’s face.

title: Martin, Benedict, Nicholas hymns: foster prelates, clothe with justice, grant perennial kingdoms and life’s aid
english: Martin’s hymn asks him to foster the feast, clarify prelates, and clothe us as he once shared his cloak.
Benedict: help climb the narrow way to perennial kingdoms; Nicholas: strip death’s losses and grant life’s aid unto glory.

title: Bellarmino reconciles bold verbs: ‘save me / give me’ mean by praying and merits, not as author
english: Bellarmino: the ban is on sense, not wording.
You may say ‘Save me / Give me’ to a Saint if you mean by his prayers and merits—not as author of the gift.

title: Roman Catechism correction: one may also ask Saints themselves to pity and help by grace and deprecation
english: After ‘Ora pro nobis,’ the Catechism corrects: you may also ask Saints themselves to pity you.
Moved by our misery, they help before God by their grace and prayer.

title: Bellarmino’s ‘by praying only’ sense fails prayers that ask by command, precept, and power
english: Bellarmino’s ‘they only pray it in’ reading does not fit public texts.
Some hymns ask Saints to act by command, precept, and power—not merely by obtaining.

title: Apostles’ and Peter’s hymns: ‘loose us by command’; Peter binds and opens heaven by word
english: Apostles’ hymn: shut/open heaven by word; loose sins ‘by command.’
Peter is asked to loose sin-bonds by the power given him; the Baptist to clear the heart’s hard stones by his merits.

title: Reason: what God grants by prayer is not done by Saintly command—authors treat Saints as sub-God givers (Costerus)
english: Reason: God’s gifts answered by prayer are not done by a Saint’s command.
Hymn authors treat Saints as under-God givers and administrators—Costerus: ask them both to intercede and to help.
His Ave Maris Stella gloss: loose by prayers, merits, authority, empire.

title: Much cult is titles and eulogies—Mary called Queen, Door of heaven, Refuge of sinners, ‘by thee the world is saved’
english: Much Roman Saint-cult is piled titles and eulogies—especially Mary’s.
She is absolute Queen, Door of heaven, Refuge of sinners, Help of Christians.
Hymns even say: through her the world is saved and life given.

title: Paris Breviary Assumption: Mary alone slew heresies; Bellatrix who crushes the serpent; Mediatrix hymns
english: Paris Assumption texts: Mary alone slew all heresies; near God of hosts she is ‘our Bellatrix’ who crushes the serpent.
Philip of Valois vowed horse and arms to her after Flanders.
Public hymn: Mediatrix, washer of crimes; Bonaventure litanies: Salvation and Beatitude.

title: Private doctors pile titles: Viegas, Voragine, Costerus, Salazar, Mendoza—Queen by natural maternal right
english: Private doctors escalate: prince of all creatures; ruler in heaven, world, and hell; Queen of Queens.
Salazar/Mendoza: proper Queen and Empress by natural maternal right—not metaphor—plus spiritual empire over souls.

title: Empire even over reigning Christ—old rhythmic prose and Paris Missal: ‘by mother’s right command the Redeemer’
english: They claim empire not only over creatures but over Christ reigning in glory.
Old rhythmic prose and Paris Missal: mother stands over the Son—‘by mother’s right command the Redeemer.’

title: Though erased from some Missals, doctors still defend: Damian, Albert, Pelbart, Bustis—Virgin’s empire even over God
english: Erased from some Missals, restored in others—and many doctors still defend the claim.
Damian: she commands at God’s tribunal as Lady not handmaid; Albert: prays as daughter, commands as mother.
Bustis: ‘By the Virgin’s empire all things serve—even God.’

title: Modern Jesuits unashamed: Costerus, Salazar, de Argento—maternal power over Christ; Mary as Domina Dei
english: Recent Jesuits double down: Costerus—mother heard by authority, not as a servant.
Salazar: lasting maternal/royal power over Christ, used especially when she intercedes.
De Argento: throne above God’s; title Domina Dei—God subjected to her dominion.

title: Dea title in poems and prose—Lipsius, Mendoza, Catharinus, Bembo; Bustis prefer ‘Queen of mercy’
english: Many even give Mary the name Goddess—in verse (Lipsius) and prose (Mendoza, Beroaldus, Catharinus).
Bembo for Leo X speaks of ‘the Goddess’ at Loreto; Bustis allow ‘Goddess of Goddesses’ but prefer Queen of mercy.

title: Alexis de Salo & Tanner: God in the Virgin not only by essence/power/presence or grace but by Identity
english: Alexis de Salo and Tanner: God dwells in Mary beyond essence, power, presence, or grace—by Identity.

title: Marian dominion is real power: she dispenses all grace—Salazar, Lapide, Pelbart as treasurer of divine gifts
english: Marian dominion is real power, not an empty title—she dispenses God’s grace to all.
Salazar: every grace-flow via Mary as moon; Lapide: treasurer of divine graces; Pelbart: no Spirit-gift without her dispensation.

title: Mary as God’s cellarer and neck of the body—Salazar: other Saints’ influx only as moon mediating
english: Bustis: God made Mary His cellarer—nothing reaches us but by her hands.
Alexis: she is the Church’s neck and grace-basin; Osorius: every good hangs on her.
Salazar: other Saints’ help only through Mary as mediating moon.

title: Even temporal goods: Salazar’s householder analogy—Mary holds the keys of worldly expenses
english: Not only spiritual goods: Salazar compares Mary to a trusted wife holding the household keys.
God gives her guardianship of temporal goods—worldly outlays pass through her hands.

title: Some say Mary made and governs the world—Biel, Alanus, Salazar after Bonaventure
english: Some go further: Mary as cause who made, conserves, and governs the world.
Biel and Alanus speak so; Salazar after Bonaventure: by her disposition the world she founded with God perseveres.

title: Bernardinus of Siena: Mary did more for God than God for man—Rivet and Drelincourt collect the sayings
english: Bernardinus of Siena: Mary did more for God than God for humankind—so God is much obliged to us for her sake.
Rivet and Drelincourt gather such sayings; Le Blanc sends the curious reader there.

title: Private only, yet not disapproved: sainted speakers, approved books, pastors fostering popular devotion
english: These sayings are private, not conciliar definitions—yet Rome does not disapprove.
Evidence: the harshest speakers are canonized; books carry episcopal and even papal approbation; pastors foster them in popular devotion.

title: When Protestants object, grave Romans excuse rather than openly damn—Bellarmino, Richelieu, Camus
english: Protestant objections meet excuse, not open damnation, from heavy Roman names.
Bellarmino, Richelieu, and Camus vs Drelincourt illustrate the pattern.

title: Expurgatory Indices leave Marian extremes untouched while cutting Augustine’s anti-temple-to-Saints lines
english: Expurgatory Indices scrub suspects—but leave these Marian extremes untouched.
They even cut Augustine’s lines against temples to Saints/Angels, while Bernardinus, Bembo, Costerus, Catharinus pass.

title: Relics and images deferred; of faith that Saints may be invoked—yet not necessary that each Catholic actually invoke them (Holden)
english: Relics and images matter most for Saint-honor but are reserved for a later dispute.
Of faith: Saints may be licitly invoked—yet not that every Catholic must actually invoke them.
Holden: invocation is useful, not a binding actual duty; some Catholics are saved who never invoked Saints.
Romana closes at LXXVII; next frontier is Pars Secunda (Reformata).

title: Sum of the Roman doctrine: a middle cult between divine majesty and merely civil honor
english: Le Blanc opens Pars Secunda by compressing the Roman account he has already given.
Rome, on that account, assigns angels and canonized people a middle honor.
That honor sits above civic respect for outstanding neighbors and below the worship God's majesty requires.
The lower comparison is with rank, power, and natural gifts, not with anything beyond nature.

title: Roman cult of Saints is analogical, and only loosely called religious or adoration
english: Rome does not put Saint-honor in the same univocal class as worship that belongs to God alone.
The link is analogy, not identity of kind.
Religious and adoration may be used of it only in a looser, less proper sense.
In the stricter use, adoration stays reserved for God.

title: Latria and dulia, with hyperdulia for Mary, though Scripture does not keep the distinction exactly
english: The Schools coined Latria for worship of God and Dulia for honor of holy angels and people.
Dulia is then split: Hyperdulia for the Blessed Virgin, and Dulia in the strict sense for the other Saints.
They admit Scripture itself does not keep that Latria–Dulia split with exactness.

title: Interior acts differ easily from divine worship; exterior signs mostly do not, except sacrifice
english: On Rome's account, inward acts of Saint-honor are easy to tell apart from inner worship of God
outward signs are mostly shared by both religions.
The stated exception is sacrifice, together with altars, temples, and priests that belong to it.

title: No sacrifice to a creature, yet Masses in Saints' honor that commend the offering by their merits
english: Rome refuses a sacrifice properly so called to any creature.
It still honors saints by offering sacrifice to God in their name.
The Mass does more than give thanks: the saint is invoked, and Christ's body and blood, as they hold it, is commended to God by that saint's merits and prayers.
The secret prayers of Andrew and James are cited as the working formulas.

title: Altars as tombs, yet every altar sanctified to Mary and all Saints; temples as basilicas
english: Rome's doctors will not consecrate an altar to a Saint as an altar, but they will as a tomb.
In practice every altar is sanctified to God and also to the Virgin and all the Saints.
Temples are not built for Saints precisely as temples, yet they are raised and dedicated as sacred houses and basilicas where Saints are ritually honored and invoked.

title: The Roman practice: relics, images, feasts, sodalities, and vows
english: Across the Roman Church, Saints are honored in churches named for them.
The rites include bows and kneeling before relics, statues, and images, with candles, incense, and offerings.
Feast days, named confraternities, and vows made and paid to the Saints belong to the same practice.

title: Invocation is the chief part: Saints as guardians who hear even silent prayers
english: The main Roman act toward the Saints is calling on them, in private and in public.
They are supposed to intercede for the Church at large and for each believer.
They are treated as guardians who see each person's need and hear prayers that are never spoken aloud.

title: Saints invoked as intercessors, yet often with the same formulas used toward God
english: Roman doctors say Saints are asked to obtain goods from God, not to be the authors who give them.
In practice people still ask Saints outright for every bodily and spiritual good.
They use the same prayer-forms as toward God, and explain the difference as a difference of sense.

title: Reformers do not deny all honor to Saints; greater excellence deserves greater honor
english: Rome often says the Reformed refuse the Saints every kind of honor.
Le Blanc answers that they unanimously say the opposite.
Created excellence, as well as divine excellence, is owed its own honor.
Grace and glory outrank civil rank and natural gifts, and the honor should rise with them.

title: Saint-honor differs only in degree from civil honor, but in kind from divine worship
english: However high the respect due to people adorned with saving grace and crowned with glory, the Reformed hold it differs from ordinary civil honor only by degree.
The people compared are those who excel by office, rank, or natural excellence.
From the honor God's majesty requires, the same respect differs in its whole kind.

title: The name may be civil, after Augustine, taken from the heavenly city rather than the earthly
english: What the honor is called matters less to them than what it consists in and how it is shown.
They refuse the bare name religious, because religion properly looks only to God's cult.
They prefer civil, or Augustine's phrase, a cult of fellowship and love.
Civil here is taken from the heavenly city of grace and glory, and it still outranks earthly civic respect in degree.

title: Rambour: religious honor for God alone; civil honor of the heavenly city for Saints and angels
english: Rambour divides honor into religious honor owed to God alone and civil honor given to creatures.
Civil honor of the earthly city covers reverence, love, and fear even toward people outside the faith.
Civil honor of the heavenly city is how the household of faith is treated, including mutual esteem in Romans 12 and Philippians 2.
Saints and angels receive that second civil honor: charity and fellowship, not servitude, by praise, love, imitation, and the stirring of zeal.

title: Voetius: the honor is human and civil; one commonwealth of pilgrims and those in the homeland
english: Voetius denies that honor of holy angels and people is religious cult or servitude; it is human and civil.
Against Bellarmine he notes that the Saints were human and, with the angels, fellow-citizens who share one commonwealth with us.
Bellarmine mixes the city of nature with the city of grace.
Pilgrims and those already home are one people, so honor paid to heavenly citizens is still civil, though higher in degree.

title: Chamier: formally civil even when the cause is supernatural glory
english: Chamier splits civil cult into what it is in itself and what causes it.
A cult can be formally civil even when its cause is supernatural.
Honor of the Saints reigning with Christ is of that sort: not causally civil, because their dignity is supernatural, yet wholly distinct from religious cult, and so formally civil.
He allows the alternative name officiosus, dutiful.

title: Chamier: the honor flows from religion as a commanded act, not as the elicited act of religion
english: Chamier will not call Saint-honor religious; he calls it civil or dutiful.
He still says it flows from religion as a commanded act, not as the act religion itself elicits.
Worship of God is religion, as loving is love; civil cult only comes from that worship, as the Samaritan's care of wounds came from love.
An effect of religion is not religion itself.

title: Drelincourt: religious in the strict sense is God alone; in a wider sense, honor paid for God's sake
english: Drelincourt uses religious in a strict sense for what binds the soul to God and sets the manner of worshiping him.
In that sense only God is worshiped religiously, and Saint-honor is the same kind as honor of living believers, higher only in degree.
In a wider sense, religious covers whatever hangs on religion and is done to honor God.
In that wider sense he allows the honor of blessed spirits and of Christ's mother to be called religious.

title: Reformers commonly reject the Latria–Dulia split, because one cult is properly religious and Scripture mixes the words
english: Reformed doctors generally reject dividing religious cult into Latria and Dulia.
Only the cult proper to God deserves the name religious in the proper and simple sense; creature-honor is religious only improperly.
Scripture also mixes the words: latreia sometimes means human service, and douleia is often kept for God's cult alone.

title: Some Reformed, with Chamier, may reserve latria and dulia as names of different kinds, not degrees
english: Some Reformed writers will still keep Latria for God's cult and Dulia for creature-honor, as a useful distinction.
Chamier allows the Greek words only if they name different kinds, not higher and lower degrees.
Religious cult and civil cult are not synonyms and not analogues of one another.

title: Vossius: the Latria–Dulia split is not scriptural or classical, yet not wholly rejected
english: Vossius says neither Scripture nor the classics observe a Latria for God and a Dulia for creatures, as Valla and Vives also grant.
Taken strictly, douleia fits God more than the Saints, since religious service makes us God's servants; Perezius saw this, and Bellarmine's objection fails.
He still does not condemn the distinction, as a guard against ambiguous names, and because Augustine did not refuse it.
The quarrel with Rome is the thing, not the word: they do not leave God's cult whole, but hand a large part of divine honor to the Saints.

title: Only such cult is lawful toward the blessed as suits an absent creature
english: The next question is what honor the Reformed actually grant the blessed, whether human or angelic.
Their general rule is that nothing may be shown them beyond what fits a creature who is absent, or as good as absent.
There is no mutual commerce with such a creature on which a richer cult could rest.

title: Divine cult is whatever cannot truly suit a creature, even if the worshiper denies he takes the object for God
english: Whatever Scripture counts as divine worship is first stripped away from honor of the blessed.
A cult is divine even if the worshiper does not consciously take its object for the supreme God, the first principle and last end.
It is enough that the act cannot really suit a creature, because it assumes something divine in that creature.
The worshiper's mistaken explanation does not change the nature of the act.

title: A cult is divine which treats its object as present everywhere and able to hear every silent prayer at once
english: Divine cult, on this account, treats its object as watching every worshiper, in every place and time, though unseen.
It also treats that object as hearing countless different prayers at once, including unspoken ones, and as able to help each person in a single moment.
Calling the object only God's friend and minister does not change the act.
Majesty and power of that size belong to God alone, whatever people imagine.

title: Feasts, sacred houses, gifts, oaths, vows, and prayers for grace are as divine as sacrifice
english: Feasts, sacred buildings, dedicated gifts, oaths, vows, and prayers for bodily goods and especially for grace and glory count, for the Reformed, as signs of God's own cult, no less than sacrifice.
Rome itself would not excuse sacrifice to a creature by calling it relative, or offered to God's friend so as to be referred at last to God.
The same plea does not excuse dedicating churches, offering gifts, vowing, swearing, or asking grace and glory of a creature.

title: Sacred houses may not be dedicated to angels or Saints for cult, though ancient memorials of martyrs are not condemned
english: Dedicating a sacred building to angels or to Saints in heaven is held altogether unlawful.
The ban covers not only offering them sacrifice there, but honoring and invoking them with any rites.
The old custom is not condemned when churches kept the martyrs' memory, thanked God for their victories, and offered the Eucharist to God, which honored holy men greatly.
Rivet's note on the Apology for the Blessed Virgin is the reference.

title: Feasts are not consecrated to angels or Saints, though a solemn commemoration, as in the English liturgy, is allowed
english: Feast days may not be consecrated to angels or the blessed, because feasts belong to God's solemn worship.
A set day may still solemnly remember certain Saints, thank God for benefits given to them and through them, and propose their virtues for imitation.
Such days are consecrated to God alone, even while they honor holy men.
The English liturgy, which remembers apostles and other holy men, is the example.

title: Swearing by Saints is as forbidden as sacrificing to them
english: Swearing by the Saints is rejected outright.
An oath by any creature is as forbidden as a sacrifice to that creature, because Scripture condemns both swearing by what is not God and sacrificing to any but God.
A secondary oath, on the ground that divine truth shines in the Saints, has no more excuse than a secondary sacrifice on the ground that God's power and goodness appear in them.

title: Vows belong to the Lord alone, not to Saints as gods by participation or as obtainers of goods
english: Vows, Scripture says, are to be made and paid to the Lord alone.
To vow to Saints as gods by participation, or as those who obtain what we need, is as contrary to true piety as offering them sacrifices under the same title.

title: Praying to Saints in the same forms used to God is treason against the divine majesty
english: Using toward the Saints the same prayer-forms used toward God, and asking them for grace, glory, and any bodily or spiritual good, is treated as an offense against God's majesty.
It does not help to call the Saints not the first authors but only givers and stewards under God.
The same pretext would not excuse sacrificing to them.

title: Many honors lawful toward the living are not lawful toward the spirits of the dead
english: It is not only divine worship that may not be moved over to angels or Saints in heaven.
Many honors that are lawful toward people living with us on earth are, by reason and piety, forbidden toward the spirits of the dead.

title: Bowing and kneeling suit the present, not a Saint in America or China, still less one in heaven
english: Greeting, uncovering the head, and bowing are used toward holy people we actually live with, and only when they are present.
It would be absurd to bow or kneel in France, at home or in church, to honor a holy man traveling in the Americas or in China.
Saints reigning with Christ are as far from us as heaven from earth, so those signs toward them are held contrary to reason.

title: Chamier: absent-capable honors are due; genuflection, greeting, and gifts to the needy are not
english: Chamier holds that honor of the Saints is the same in kind as honor of the living, and differs only by being stronger or weaker.
Degree does not change the species.
Acts that can be paid to people who are absent are due; genuflection, greeting, and bowing, which need presence, are not.
Still less are gifts for the needy, such as clothes, lights, bread, and wine.

title: Asking the living to pray with us does not extend to the dead, with whom we cannot communicate
english: Asking trusted pious people to pray with us and for us belongs to honor among those with whom we have real dealings.
No one addresses, aloud or in the heart, a pious man too far away for even a letter, as if someone in Jerusalem had silently begged the help of Paul's prayers while Paul was in prison at Rome.
For that reason Protestants do not ask the dead in Christ, as they ask the living, to help them before God.
The blessed are far off in glory, and there is no way left to tell them what we feel.

title: To suppose the Saints see all men and hear all thoughts is to give them something divine
english: If the Saints in glory are supposed to see everyone everywhere at once, hear their prayers, know their thoughts, give the help asked, and notice everything done in their honor, something divine has been given them.
The signs of honor in question then cease to be human cult and become divine cult.

title: What remains is pious memory, praise, and imitation of faith, hope, and the other virtues
english: Asked what honor of the Saints is left, Le Blanc answers from the Reformed doctors.
It is frequent pious remembrance, a high estimate, praise when there is occasion, and a careful recall of their virtues and great deeds.
Above all it is following their example, receiving their teaching, and striving to match their hope, faith, love, zeal, courage, patience, and humility.

title: Spanheim: Mary's honor is grateful thought, preaching of her virtues, and commendation of her glory
english: Spanheim's account of the honor due to Mary is also the pattern for other Saints.
First comes honoring remembrance that God, in sheer goodness, made her the mother of the Lord who is Father of all.
Second, preaching the virtues Scripture records in her, as an example.
Third, commending the glory and blessedness she enjoys in heaven.

title: Drelincourt: memory, thanks for gifts given through her, her faith, her example, and her blessedness
english: Drelincourt's honor of the Virgin begins with reverent memory, speech, and delight in her praises.
Next the whole heart praises God for grace and benefits given through her.
Her words are believed, her faith is embraced, and the Spirit's lessons through her are followed.
She is an example of believing and of living, her Christian virtues are imitated, and her blessedness is extolled.

title: Rivet: angels, if present, would be received; being unseen and not everywhere, they are not greeted
english: Rivet treats honor of rational creatures, angels and humans, together.
If angels are present we do not know when or where, unless they appear visibly as they once did.
Some are often near and helpful, but there is no conversation with them, they are not everywhere, and they do not search the heart, so we neither speak to them nor greet them with outward signs.
The patriarchs did greet angels whom they received as men; apart from that, angels are spoken of with honor, and their obedience is magnified for imitation.

title: Rivet: the holy memory of great servants, praise without flattery, and nothing that requires them to hear
english: People illustrious for virtue, above all for piety toward God and service of the Church, have a holy and venerable memory.
They are spoken of reverently, their virtues are recalled, they are proposed for imitation, and they receive due praise.
Any further honor must be such as can be paid to people we do not see and who do not hear us.
That kind is worth more because it cannot be flattery or self-interest.

title: Honor rises with God's gifts; the dead are not served as masters but followed as fellow heirs
english: Rivet next warns that we should raise the degrees of observance and veneration in proportion to the gifts God has given such persons and to their greater or lesser excellence. We are not to make the praises due them all equal, but to give each what is his own, according to the measure we recognize in him.
But we do not serve with servitude properly so called anyone who has no need of our works and to whom we can be of no use.
For we are not the servants of the saints who have died. We are to be sharers of the same inheritance with them, and to press on in their footsteps as far as we can.
That is what they most wanted while they lived on earth, when they went before us by example, imitating Christ so that we might imitate them.

title: Rivet on the Virgin: every honor fit for the absent, short of religious worship
english: Rivet ends by saying that we honor the most Blessed Virgin first of all, in proportion to the very great gifts God gave her.

"If she were living among us on earth," he writes, "we would think it a great honor to take her into our home as John did and to give her every duty that children owe their parents, since she became the mother of our firstborn brother. We would speak to her with reverence, greet her with veneration, and take her most holy counsel to heart."

"But she is not living among us on earth. We neither see nor hear her, and we must not believe that she is infinite or present everywhere. She is now in heaven, having served God's purpose in her own generation, as Scripture says of her father David. So we revere and honor the most Blessed Virgin in every way that the absent can rightly be honored and glorified, except religious worship, which belongs to him alone who is present everywhere, who is almighty, and who searches hearts and minds."

"In this we obey his will when we call the Lord's mother blessed, blessed among women, and for many reasons: she believed; it was done to her as the angel had said; after bearing the Son of God she cared for him and nursed him as a baby and gave him every service of the best of mothers; she acknowledged him as her Savior even when he was crying in the cradle; she trusted his words when many spoke against him; and after a whole earthly life spent in exercises of holiness and rare piety, most pleasing to God, she fell asleep devoutly in the Lord and gave back her most holy soul to God."

"In heaven she enjoys the blessedness God promised to those who worship him, and in that chosen vessel it stands out, as God knows, even in degrees of glory, in proportion to the grace she received here. We praise such a woman, keep her memory with grateful hearts, and speak of her with reverence. We hold her up to all Christians, and above all to devout women, as a model of the virtues, and we urge everyone to imitate her in whatever is to be imitated." (Apology for the Most Holy Virgin Mary, book 2, chapter 1.)

title: Daillé: refusing prayer to angels is not contempt but loyalty to God alone
english: John Daillé teaches the same in his book On the Object of Religious Worship.

"When we decline to adore the angels and the other blessed spirits, or to honor them with prayers and other religious honors," he writes, "this does not come from any contempt for them. It comes from our conscience about the duty we owe to the one God, best and greatest, to whom alone, we believe, prayers and the other acts of religious worship are to be offered."

"With this worship of God kept intact, we gladly confess the rest: the excellence of God's work in all the heavenly spirits is great, and great too are the wisdom, faith, love, holiness, and, finally, the blessedness of the most Blessed Mary, of Christ's holy martyrs, and of his faithful ministers. We celebrate their outstanding deeds, words, and struggles in the cause of godliness often and gladly, whenever there is occasion, and we commend them to ourselves and our people for imitation, each as far as he is able. And we never speak their name or memory except with praise. All of this shows that God's saints, angels and men alike, are honored by us as is fitting and held in high esteem."

title: Daillé: honor of the saints consists in praise and imitation
english: Daillé then holds that the honor we rightly give to the angels and to the saints received into heaven is, by the judgment of both the inspired and the church writers, entirely contained in two things: in good report and in imitation, that is, praise and imitation.

The first means thinking and speaking well and highly of them as outstanding servants of God. The second means imitating faithfully and earnestly their way of life and the obedience they gave to their Lord and God, who is ours as well. (On the Object of Religious Worship, book 3, chapter 1.)

title: Cautions in praising the saints: no divine titles, no unrevealed patronage or hearing of prayers
english: In this good report or praise of the saints, angels and men, the teachers of the Reformed school think we must take care not to give them, in our eagerness to exalt them, titles and tributes owed to God and Christ alone. Nor should we intrude into things we have not seen and credit them with anything that the word of God does not establish.

Holy Scripture neither teaches nor hints that the saints who have died in Christ govern human affairs or have been appointed by God as patrons and guardians of the living. So the Reformed refuse to celebrate them in that role. Nor will they credit the saints with praying for individual believers, or with being able to hear and answer the prayers of many people at once, since no divine revelation has disclosed this.

title: Whether the saints pray for the Church in general: Drelincourt suspends judgment
english: Whether the saints at least pray for the Church Militant in general, some among the Reformed will not affirm as certain and suspend judgment on the question.

One is Charles Drelincourt, cited often already, who judges it uncertain whether the saints pray for the Church. He places this among God's hidden things, not revealed to us, because Scripture nowhere teaches it clearly and expressly. (On the Honor to Be Shown to the Blessed Virgin, volume 2, page 106, number 179 and following.)

title: Chamier: the general prayer of saints is likely but not proven
english: Chamier likewise takes up the question whether the souls of the saints pray for us in general, that is, for the Christian Church as a whole and for the whole body of believers. He declares that no certain argument establishes it, though he grants it has some likelihood, and he leaves the matter open for each to decide for himself. (Panstratia, volume 2, book 8, chapter 5.)

title: Rivet: the reigning saints pray in general for the Church still fighting
english: Others readily grant, and think it probable, that the saints reigning with Christ in heaven pray at least in general for the Church fighting here, since this seems wholly in keeping with the love that burns in them and with the communion between the two Churches, the Church Militant and the Church Triumphant.

Andrew Rivet states his view this way: "We do not deny that the Church of the saints who reign with Christ cares for the members still fighting here. But that care is general. It does not come from knowing each person's condition but from their general knowledge: they know that the whole Church has not yet been received where they reign, and that some are always fighting on earth. We do not doubt that they pray to God for the preservation and completion of these, just as they always ask for the growth of his kingdom." (Summary of Controversies, second treatise, question 48.)

title: Du Moulin: the blessed know the Church is pressed, and so are concerned for it
english: Peter du Moulin is of the same mind. "The blessed spirits," he says, "do not see what happens here and do not know individuals, yet they know that the Church is hard pressed by its enemies and faces endless struggles. Since glorification has increased their love rather than lessened it, it is fitting that they should be concerned for the Church Militant." (Treasury of Sedan Theses, volume 1, Theses on the Saints, part 3, thesis 3.)

title: The saints are not our intercessors and advocates: that title is Christ's alone
english: However that may be, the Reformed theologians agree in denying that the saints are, or can rightly be called, our intercessors and advocates.

Only he deserves the title of our intercessor with God who can hear and take in the prayers of all people and of each one, at once and at all times, and whose office it is to offer and commend them to God. That, they hold, fits our Lord Jesus Christ alone. Nor would anyone call the believers living here our intercessors and advocates merely because, out of mutual love, we ought to pray for one another.

title: No merits of the saints, yet the godly may draw God's favor on the whole body
english: The Reformed also refuse to credit the good things that come to us to the merits of the saints, or to ask anything of God through their merits. The saints owed all that they were to divine grace, and so, strictly speaking, they could merit nothing either for themselves or for others.

Yet they do not therefore deny that, by virtue of the communion of saints, the good and godly works that individual members of the Church do by God's grace in some way call down and draw God's blessing and favor on the whole body. Indeed, God sometimes spares the ungodly themselves for the sake of the godly and righteous who live among them, and gives them time and means to repent, just as the Lord declared to Abraham that he would have spared Sodom and Gomorrah if even ten righteous people had been found there.

title: No controversy over whether the blessed deserve some honor
english: From what these theses and the earlier ones have set out so far, it is clear that there is no dispute here over whether the blessed, both men and angels, deserve some kind of reverence and honor and ought to receive it from us. The teachers of the Reformed school readily admit and teach this, and the contrary cannot be laid to their charge except by slander.

title: Both sides agree the honor of saints is not of one species with divine worship
english: It is also clear from this that the teachers of the Roman school agree with the Reformed that the honor owed to holy men and angels does not fall under one univocal genus with divine worship, and so is not of the same species. Nor is that honor religious in the proper and strict sense, but only in a broader and less proper sense. In that sense, eminent theologians among the Reformed expressly allow that the honor owed to the saints may be called religious.

title: Latria and dulia: a school distinction both sides can tolerate
english: We have also shown that the teachers of the Roman school admit that the division of religious worship into latria and dulia is an invention of the schools, and that Scripture does not strictly keep the difference between these words as the Roman school uses them. Dulia is more often confined there to the worship proper to God, while latria is sometimes extended to service rendered to human beings.

The teachers of the Reformed school, for their part, do not much object if, for clarity's sake, latria is assigned to divine worship and dulia to the respect with which creatures may and should be honored.

title: The real question: shrines, rites, oaths, vows, relative honor, and prayer addressed to saints
english: The whole difficulty and question therefore comes down to this: what does the honor consist in that may lawfully be given to holy and blessed creatures, and above all to the most Blessed Virgin Mary?

May churches not only be named after saints and angels to tell them apart, but also be built for the purpose of publicly invoking in them the angels and holy men already received into heaven, and of honoring them with various rites: kneeling and bowing before them as though they were watching us, burning incense to them, lighting candles, and offering all kinds of gifts?

May one swear by them and make vows to them relatively to God, that is, insofar as God's truth shines in them and God dwells in them through glory? And finally, may we ask them to pray for us, and not simply ask, but address prayers to them, meant in a different sense, to be sure, yet framed in the same words and formulas as those we address to God?
The teachers of the Roman school affirm all this, and the Roman Church confirms it by its practice; the Protestants with one voice deny it.

title: Saints as guardians and mediators, and Mary as Queen of Heaven, rejected by Protestants
english: A further point in dispute is whether it is lawful to celebrate the saints who have died in Christ as guardians and patrons of the human race, entrusted by God with the government of our affairs, and to treat them as mediators and intercessors with God who can at all times hear and take in the prayers of all people, whether spoken in the heart or with the lips, offer and commend them to God, and help with their own suffrages and merits.

Above all, the question is whether the Blessed Virgin should be acknowledged and proclaimed Queen of Heaven and of the whole world and Lady of all creatures, as the one through whom the world was saved and who alone has destroyed all heresies, and whether she should be hailed as Mother of mercy, Mother and fountain of grace, our life and our hope. The practice of the Roman Church approves all of this; the Protestants reject and condemn it.

title: Further scandalous titles: goddess, tutelary deities, Mary's dominion over her Son
english: The Protestants are also offended by many other tributes heaped on the Blessed Virgin and the saints. These come from private teachers, it is true, but the Roman Church neither disapproves nor forbids them.

So the Virgin Mary is given the title of goddess, and the saints are called tutelary deities, as in an inscription I remember reading a few years ago in the church at Troyes dedicated to Saint Peter: "Peter, Helen, Mastidia, tutelary deities of Troyes."

The Virgin Mary is credited with command and dominion over her own Son and with power to dispense under God all the gifts of grace and nature and to share them with whomever she wills. She is called the enlightener of hearts and the cause of things; she is even said to have founded and made the world and to preserve and govern all that is in it. There is more of this kind, which we pass over for now for brevity's sake.
translator_notes: Mastidia (Mâthie) is a local saint of Troyes; the inscription is quoted as Le Blanc remembers it.

title: First argument: worship without God's word is will-worship
english: The Protestants hold that the blessed spirits, whether of men or of angels, are not to be honored with the worship the Roman Church gives them: churches and altars built and dedicated in their honor, candles lit to them, incense burned, knees bent before them as though they were watching; vows made to them, offerings of every kind presented, oaths sworn by their name; and, finally, solemn prayers by which people run to them for help, and hymns sung to them publicly in thanksgiving for benefits received from God, and anything else of the kind.

Neither the blessed angels, I say, nor the saints who have died in Christ are to be worshiped in this way. The Protestants prove it first from the fact that such worship ought not to have been devised by human beings apart from God's word. Otherwise it will be offered without faith, since without God's word no one can be sure that it pleases God and is accepted by him.

So if it is clear that worship of this kind rests on no command or revelation of God, it may rightly be rejected as one of the forms of self-made worship that the Apostle condemns. And it is plain that this whole worship has no foundation in God's word, since in all of Scripture, Old Testament or New, there is no command for it and no example of it.

title: Old Testament: no worship of angels, though they ministered often to Israel
english: As for the Old Testament, the teachers of the Roman Church themselves admit that the worship they usually give to departed saints was not practiced in the Old Testament Church. The reason they give is that at that time the souls of the saints did not yet enjoy the heavenly glory and blessedness to which they were raised after Christ's coming, but were held in a kind of prison, which they call the limbo of the Fathers.

But at least there is no reason why the worship they give to angels, if it is lawful, should not have been given to angels under the Old Testament. In fact, if angels are ever to be worshiped, that was the time above all: God mostly used the ministry of angels in governing his ancient people, and they appeared frequently in the Jewish Church, because God often used them as his messengers to the faithful. In the Church of the New Testament, by contrast, God has spoken to us through the Son, to whom, and not to angels, he has subjected the world to come, as the Apostle teaches in Hebrews 2:5.

Yet neither from Holy Scripture nor from any record of the history of the Jewish nation can it be shown that even the smallest part of public worship was given to angels: that any chapel or oratory was consecrated in their honor, any feast kept, or a single candle lit or grain of incense offered to them; or that in the public assemblies of the faithful any prayers were addressed to them, hymns sung, or any form of adoration shown at all. On the contrary, everyone agrees beyond doubt that the opposite is plainly the case. And nothing would have stood in the way; indeed, it would have been most fitting for the Jews to honor angels with such worship, if it were lawful for us.
translator_notes: The 1675 print reads Heb. 2. 3; the words cited are Hebrews 2:5, so the English gives 2:5.

title: New Testament: Christ and the Apostles instituted no new worship of angels or saints
english: Under the New Testament, Christ and the Apostles changed nothing at all in this respect. They instituted no new worship by which angels and the spirits of the righteous, admitted to the sight of God's face, were from then on to be worshiped. There is no command, no example, not even the slightest hint of it anywhere in the New Testament. Nowhere are we told there to invoke angels or departed saints, to run to them for help, to sing hymns to them publicly, or to honor them with frankincense and incense, altars and churches, or any other outward acts of adoration.

title: Nor does the tradition of the first three centuries know such worship
english: Not only is there deep silence about these things in the writings of the New Testament; nothing of the kind can be extracted from the church's tradition of the first three centuries either.

There were many distinguished Christian writers in that period whose works survive and are in people's hands: among the Latins, Tertullian, Cyprian, Lactantius, and Arnobius; among the Greeks, Justin, Athenagoras, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and many others. Nowhere in them do we read that any worship like that of the present Roman Church was once given, or is now to be given, to angels and dead saints. On the contrary, many quite obvious signs point the other way.

title: First sign: early writers kept the souls of the faithful outside heaven until the resurrection
english: First, most of the church writers who lived in the second and third centuries after Christ held that the souls of all believers, even the holiest, are kept in certain places outside heaven until the last day of judgment and are not admitted to the heavenly homeland until they receive their bodies back at the resurrection.

Some of them, it is true, give the martyrs a special place by a unique privilege, namely paradise, as they call it. But by that name they by no means mean the highest heaven itself, where the martyrs would see the Lord face to face. They mean a region below heaven, happier and more pleasant, indeed, than Abraham's bosom, where the souls of the other godly rest, yet not capable of heavenly glory. John Daillé, of renowned memory, shows this at length against Cardinals Bellarmine and Perron.

It follows that in those first centuries of Christianity the doctrine of the worship and invocation of saints now prevailing in the Roman Church had not yet been received as apostolic tradition. That worship rests on the assumption that the saints enjoy the highest glory and blessedness. Since, according to the Roman school, the souls of the saints were not admitted to that glory before Christ's coming, they admit that the saints were not yet solemnly worshiped and invoked. (On Punishments and Satisfactions, book 5, chapters 3 to 6; and On the Object of Religious Worship, book 3, chapter 22.)

title: Second sign: ancient liturgies prayed for all the dead, even apostles and the Virgin
english: Second, the oldest surviving liturgies show that those early Christians offered prayers and supplications to God for absolutely all the dead, even for the holiest, for the martyrs, for the apostles, and even for the Virgin Mother of God herself. In those liturgies they ask God to give them rest in the land of the living, to grant them the good things he has promised, and to give them rest and a good remembrance. They are not simply offering thanks for them, as Bellarmine vainly argues.

But ever since the religious worship and invocation of the saints was publicly received, Augustine's saying has been treated almost as an oracle: "He wrongs a martyr who prays for a martyr." And no one will ever bring himself to use the solemn invocation that the Roman Church teaches is owed to the saints reigning with Christ toward people who need to be commended to God by our prayers.

title: Third sign: against pagans the early Christians owned one God and no subordinate cult
english: Further, the pagan philosophers professed to acknowledge only one supreme God and said that the others they called gods were servants of that one supreme deity, worshiped only in second place after him. They charged the Christians with being content to worship the supreme God and neglecting the lesser powers under him, to whom, they said, a veneration of their own was also due.

Those early Christians frankly admitted that they did in fact worship only one supreme God, and they defended this as lawful and right. They did not grant that even the smallest part of religious worship was owed to God's good and holy servants, nor did they divide religious worship into supreme and subordinate, or absolute and relative. Yet honesty, charity, and prudence would have required exactly that of them if they had held the same view of the worship of saints and angels as the present Roman Church.

title: Arnobius: the first God suffices; his court is honored in him without naming each
english: To this pagan charge the early Christians answered with Arnobius: "For the duty of worshiping the divine, the first God is enough for us, the Father of all things and their Lord, the founder and ruler of everything. In him we worship all that is to be worshiped; we adore what it is right to adore; and what calls for the homage of veneration we honor with our veneration."

"Since we hold fast to the head of divinity itself, from which the divinity of all divine beings, whatever they are, is derived, we think it pointless to go through them person by person. We do not know who they are or what names they have, and we cannot have any clear, firm, or tested knowledge of how many of them there are."

He then illustrates this with the very comparison from princes' courts that the pagans used on this point: "In earthly kingdoms no necessity forces us to pay homage by name to the members of the royal family along with the princes. In the honor paid to the kings themselves, everything connected with them feels itself silently included. In the same way, whoever these gods are whom you set before us, if they are royal offspring sprung from the sovereign head, they understand that, even if they receive no worship from us by name, they are honored together with their king and included in the veneration given to him." (Arnobius, Against the Nations, book 3, beginning.)

title: Origen: imitating the angels wins their favor; God's friends follow him as a shadow
english: Origen teaches the same when he deals with a similar argument. Celsus had argued that one must never fall away from the worship of God and that the soul must be intent on him in every action and thought, but that this did not prevent the various powers set under God from being appeased and won over, since this too redounds to the honor of the supreme deity.

That distinguished teacher of the ancient Church replies: "For the angels of God to be well disposed toward us and to do everything for us, it is enough, first, that we love God and that our disposition, as far as human nature can, imitates the judgment of the angels themselves, who imitate God; and second, that we lay hold of the Son of God, the Word, as far as we are able."

And again: "There is one God whom we must win over, the Lord of all things, and to have him favorable we must pray to him; he is won over by godliness and every virtue. But if anyone also wants others besides him, God above all, to be favorable, let him consider that, as the shadow moves when the body moves, so when someone has the supreme God favorable, it follows that he has all God's friends favorable too: angels, souls, and spirits."

"For they perceive who are worthy of God's favor. They not only wish such people well but also work alongside those who want to worship God; they seek his favor and pray and plead together with us. So we dare to say that whenever people who have firmly resolved to choose and follow what is better pray to God, countless holy powers pray with them uncalled, offering themselves as companions to our frail and mortal race, contending, so to speak, at our side and laboring with us in this struggle." (Against Celsus, book 5; and Against Celsus, book 8.)

title: Origen: prayer to God alone through the Son; invoking angels is irrational
english: Here it should be carefully noted that Origen says the countless holy powers, by which he means the angels and blessed spirits, do pray together with those who want to worship God, but uncalled, without being summoned. He teaches not only in general that one God is to be adored and religiously worshiped, undivided and inseparable, but also that our prayers are to be directed to him alone, and that no kind of prayer or invocation is to be used toward the blessed angels or any other creatures whatever.

"Away," he says, "with this advice of Celsus, who bids us pray to daemons" (that is, in the Platonists' usage, spirits who serve the supreme God); "he is not to be listened to in the least. Prayers are to be offered to God, best and greatest, alone; and also to the only-begotten Word of God, the firstborn of all creation, who as High Priest is to be asked to carry our prayer, when it reaches him, to his God and our God, his Father and our Father." (Against Celsus, book 8.)

In book 5 of the same work he says: "It is fitting to send up every supplication, prayer, entreaty, and thanksgiving to the supreme God, the Lord of all things, through the living Word and God, the High Priest who is above all angels. We will also pray to the Word himself, entreat him, give him thanks, and offer him prayers, provided we can understand the difference between prayer in the proper sense and prayer in a loose sense."

"For it is contrary to reason that angels should be invoked by us, since we have by no means received knowledge of them; that is something beyond human reach. And even granting that knowledge of them, wonderful and hidden as it is, could be grasped, that very knowledge, by showing their nature and over whom or what each of them is set and appointed, will forbid us to dare pray to anyone but the Lord who is over all and amply sufficient for all things, through our Savior, the Son of God."

title: Origen: even the stars, which he thought pray to God, may not be prayed to
english: It should also be noted here that Origen, like many other teachers of the Christian school in that age, thought the sun, the moon, and the other stars were rational living beings, endowed with virtue and enlightened with the light of knowledge by the Wisdom that is the radiance of eternal light. He does not oppose Celsus at all when Celsus praises them as the most glorious heralds of things above and truly heavenly angels, and he himself was fully convinced that the sun, moon, and stars offer prayers to God, the Lord of all things, through his only-begotten Son.

So if, in Origen's view, God's angels deserve some religious worship, the sun, moon, and stars ought by the same reasoning to be thought worthy of it as well. Yet when Celsus complains that the Jews do not worship the sun, moon, and planets, Origen not only denies in general that it is right to revere and bow down to those creatures, that is, to worship and adore them; he also declares it unlawful to make supplication to them or sing hymns to them. "We judge," he says, "that it is not fitting to pray to those who themselves pray."

He adds that the sun and the stars themselves want it so: they would rather send us on to God, to whom they themselves pray, than draw us down to themselves, or split off from God the power of prayer we have and take part of it for themselves. Later he adds that since the Lord is everywhere with us and near us, it is absurd to seek to pray to something that does not reach to all things, whether the sun, the moon, or any other star.

Finally, when Celsus writes that we would seem to honor the great God more if we also sang hymns to the sun, he answers that he knows the opposite is true: "We sing hymns to the only God, the Lord of all things, and to his only-begotten, God the Word." (Against Celsus, book 5.)
translator_notes: The Greek pair is reconstructed from a damaged scan as σέβειν καὶ προσκυνεῖν, which the Latin glosses as colere atque adorare.

title: Against Perron: Origen excludes relative as well as absolute prayer to angels
english: Nor can anyone say with Cardinal Perron that when Origen denies that angels are to be prayed to and invoked, he means the kind of prayer they call absolute, not the kind called relative, which is the only kind the Roman school says may be used toward angels.

Celsus himself, whom Origen is answering, did not think that angels, or daemons, as he calls them with Plato, were to be worshiped with supreme and absolute worship, but with a worship referred to the supreme God, whose servants they were. So against the Christians he argued that they should be invoked, not with absolute prayer, as if they were the first and highest givers of good things, but only with relative prayer, as those who obtain and dispense those goods under the supreme God.

Since Origen denies that they are to be invoked in the way Celsus and other pagan philosophers wanted, it is plain that, according to Origen, neither absolute nor relative invocation may be used toward them. Moreover, when Origen says they pray for us uncalled, without being summoned, he shows clearly enough that they are not even to be asked to pray to God for us. That denies them relative prayer, not merely absolute prayer.

title: Origen grants angels only the honor of praise and imitation
english: So Origen, pressed by Celsus's objections that Christians despised the servants of the supreme God and the angelic powers and gave them no honor at all, grants that no other honor is to be given them than the honor that consists in praise and imitation. "We call them blessed," he says, "and we speak well of those to whom God has entrusted the welfare of human beings, yet we do not give them the honor owed to God." (Against Celsus the Philosopher, book 8, cited several times already.)

In the passage from book 5 of the same work quoted above, he also states that we are to imitate the angels as far as human nature allows, and that this will be enough for those blessed spirits to wish us well and to take pains for us in everything. But nowhere does he mention that we solicit their prayers by praying to them, or that any of the things used in the Roman Church today are done in their honor, though that would have served his purpose best and would have refuted the pagan slander even more fully.

title: Origen's therapeia toward Gabriel and Michael is acknowledgment and imitation, not invocation
english: So when Origen, in that eighth book against Celsus, suggests that a certain therapeia, that is, a kind of honor and respect, is owed to God's true servants, Gabriel, Michael, and the other angels and archangels, that therapeia, by Origen's own teaching, can in no way consist in adoring or invoking them, which he insists is owed entirely and undivided to the one supreme God. It consists in acknowledging and celebrating their blessedness, glory, and holiness, and in devoutly imitating their obedience and love toward God. These are the ways in which he admits we may honor the holy angels.

title: Scripture: one God adored and served; the Roman reply of latria and dulia
english: But to return to Holy Scripture: not only does it contain no command or example concerning the worship of angels or of the dead saints, but it often teaches that one God is to be adored and that he alone is to be served. So no religious worship at all is to be given either to angels or to the saints who have died in Christ.

The teachers of the Roman school reply that Scripture forbids us only to give creatures that supreme and absolute worship by which someone is worshiped as first principle and last end, the worship for which they have reserved the name latria. It does not, they say, forbid us to show God's servants and friends, such as the angels and the spirits of the just received into heavenly glory, that lower religious worship which they call dulia.

title: What Scripture forbids: acts of religious adoration toward creatures under any pretext
english: When Holy Scripture forbids us to adore creatures and serve them, it is not merely ruling out that we should take creatures for the first principle and last end and worship them in that capacity. It rules out our performing, on any pretext at all, acts of religious adoration toward them: calling on someone in public worship, singing him hymns, burning incense, dedicating churches and feast days, swearing by his name, making vows to him, and the like.

title: Romans 1: the pagan sages served the creature though they held it a minister of the supreme God
english: That this is how things stand is plainly proved by the Apostle's charge against the pagan philosophers: they "worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator," that is, they gave divine worship to the creature beside the Creator, or rather than the Creator, because they worshiped the sun, the moon and the stars, the heroes and the genii with religious worship (Romans 1:25).

Yet it is certain that those pagan philosophers did not take the sun, the heroes and the genii for supreme gods. They took them for servants of that supreme God whom they called the Father of men and gods, and whom they believed was honored also in those lesser divinities.
translator_notes: The 1675 print reads Rom. 1. 26; the words cited are Romans 1:25, so the English gives 1:25.

title: Orosius and the Recognitions: pagans own one God with many ministers
english: So Orosius reports that the pagans used to say they did not follow many gods, but venerated many servants under one great God.

So too the old author of the Recognitions brings in the same pagans saying: "We also say that there is one God, who is Lord of all. But these too are gods. For just as there is one Caesar, who has many judges under him, such as prefects, consuls, tribunes and the other authorities, in the same way we think that, since there is one God of all, these too have been appointed gods in this world on the pattern of the authorities we have named. They are subject to the greater one, but they govern us and all that is in this world." (Orosius, Histories, book 6, beginning; Clement, Recognitions, book 5.)

title: Celsus and Hierocles: lesser powers honored so that the supreme God is never left
english: This is why Celsus, as Origen reports him, says that whoever venerates many gods does something pleasing to the supreme God by that very act, insofar as he worships one who is subject to the greatest God. He adds: "No one may be honored except those whom God wills to be honored; so whoever venerates his subjects does not offend him to whom all belong."

So he wants the lesser powers under the supreme God to be worshiped in such a way "that God is never in any way abandoned, not by night, not by day, not in private, not in public, not in any thought, not in any work, but that with these or without them the soul is always intent on God." Later he says: "In this way you will seem to venerate the great God the more, if you honor these too with hymns and praises." (Origen, Against Celsus, book 8.)

With this agrees what Hierocles teaches: "The gods are to be acknowledged and worshiped as distinct from their author and parent, but their dignity is not to be raised beyond measure; in the end their worship is to be referred to their one maker, whom you may properly call the God of gods, as supreme and best." (Hierocles, On the Pythagorean Verses, page 10.)

title: So relative intent does not clear the worship given to angels and saints of latria
english: The pagan philosophers just mentioned worshiped the sun, the moon and the genii only with some lower worship, not as supreme gods but only as servants of the supreme God, and they referred all that worship to the honor of the supreme God himself, as the testimonies cited make plain. Yet the Apostle says that they served the creature, that is, that they gave latria and divine worship to the creature.

It is therefore clear that those who give latria to angels and to departed saints are not cleared of the charge. They worship them with prayers and hymns, with vows and with oaths sworn by their names, with various offerings, and with churches and feast days dedicated to their honor. That holds even if they protest that they give all this to the saints and angels not as to supreme gods, but as to God's servants and friends, and so to gods only by participation, and that relative to the supreme God himself, to whose honor all this finally goes and is referred.

title: Not sacrifice alone: Scripture condemns even the sacred kiss (Job 31)
english: Nor can anyone say that the reason the Apostle accuses the pagans of giving latria to creatures is that they offered them sacrifices, which everyone admits belong to the worship of latria. For Holy Scripture condemns the Gentiles not only for sacrificing to creatures, but even for worshiping them with a sacred kiss.

The holy man Job protests that he was innocent of this crime: "If I looked at the sun when it shone, and at the moon moving in brightness, and my heart rejoiced, or rather was secretly enticed, and I kissed my hand with my mouth" (Job 31:26-27).
translator_notes: The 1675 print cites Job 31. 26; the words quoted run through 31:27, so the English cites 31:26-27.
Pass B clarified 2026-10-09: the denial governs the causal clause (quoniam obtulerunt eis sacrificia), not the accusation itself; nemotron misread the earlier wording as a polarity flip.

title: If relative latria is lawful, why not relative sacrifice? The Fathers reserved prayer and hymns too
english: Besides, if on the premises of the teachers of the Roman school it is lawful to worship creatures even with latria, provided it is relative and not absolute, no solid reason can be given why it should not be lawful to sacrifice to them relatively as well.

If it is good and pious to make vows to the angels and saints who reign with Christ and to swear by them, because God dwells in them by glory, divine truth shines out in them, and they are in a sense gods by participation, why should it be impious and forbidden to offer them sacrifices on that same ground and in that same respect?

Nor did the ancient teachers of the Church reserve only sacrifices for the divine worship that may not be given to creatures. As we saw above, they reserved prayers and hymns as well, which they hold are to be addressed to God alone, the Lord of all.

title: Colossians 2:18: Paul forbids the threskeia of angels, and so the cult of saints a fortiori
english: Holy Scripture does not only say in general that one God is to be worshiped and that latria is not to be given to creatures. It also forbids in particular that we give any threskeia, that is, any religious worship, to angels. And if it is not lawful to worship angels religiously, much less will it be lawful to give that worship to departed saints, since angels surpass human beings in the excellence of their nature and are not inferior to the saints in grace and glory.

The Apostle Paul expressly condemns the threskeia, or religious worship, of angels: "Let no one lead you astray who delights in humility and the worship of angels, walking in things he has not seen, that is, intruding into things he has not seen, puffed up without reason by the mind of his flesh" (Colossians 2:18). Here the Apostle forbids, without qualification, the threskeia, the religious worship, of angels.

It cannot reasonably be denied that people practice this threskeia, that is, worship angels religiously, when they build churches in honor of angels, dedicate feast days to them, invoke them solemnly in holy places, seek their patronage and protection with prayers, and bend the knee and fall to the ground as if the angels were present and watching. So, on Paul's view, such people have either been led astray by those seducers or are rashly puffed up by the mind of their flesh.
translator_notes: Le Blanc quotes Colossians 2:18 without a reference; the English supplies it.

title: Had any angel-cult been lawful, Paul would have distinguished it from the abuse
english: If, in the Apostle's judgment, worship of this kind had been owed to angels, and if he had thought it lawful to consecrate feasts and chapels to angels, to sing hymns to them in the public assemblies of the faithful, to invoke them, and to fall down before them, he would not have condemned the worship of angels without qualification.

Had impostors brought some excess into the religious worship of angels among the Colossians, he would have marked it out plainly and would somehow have separated lawful worship of angels from unlawful. That is certainly what the teachers of the Roman school would do if some sect arose now that, in their judgment, gave the angels too much in this respect.

title: Perron's evasion: the 'religion of angels' as the law given through angels
english: The teachers of the Roman Church give various answers to this and invent various shifts, but anyone who weighs the matter without partisanship or prejudice will see at once how empty they are.

Cardinal Perron will not have "the religion of angels" mean the religion by which angels are worshiped. He takes it rather to mean the religion handed down by angels, and he guesses that the name stands for the Jewish religion, that is, the rites of Moses, because elsewhere Paul says the law was "ordained through angels in the hand of a mediator" (Galatians 3:19). On his reading, then, the Apostle's aim is to call the Colossians back from Jewish worship and the ceremonies of the law of Moses. (Perron, Reply to the King of Great Britain, book 5, chapter 6.)
translator_notes: The 1675 margin gives only Gal. 3; the words cited are Galatians 3:19, so the English gives 3:19.
Perron's work is his Réplique à la réponse du sérénissime roi de la Grande-Bretagne (1620); the margin cites book 5, chapter 6.

title: Perron's reading is new: the Fathers and Rome's own interpreters read it as worship of angels
english: First, this invention of Perron's is plainly new; no Christian had heard of it before his time.

The ancients, such as Origen, Chrysostom, Hilary writing under Ambrose's name, Pelagius writing under Jerome's name, Theodoret, Theophylact and Oecumenius, all take "the religion of angels" to mean a religion with angels as its object. And not one interpreter of the Roman Church before Perron took Paul's words in Perron's sense.

Nor could even so great a cardinal's authority win that invention over the most learned men of his own church after him. They rejected it outright as empty, among them the Jesuit Petavius, a distinguished student of antiquity (Theological Dogmas, tome 3, book 2, chapter 9, paragraph 16).
translator_notes: Hilarius sub Ambrosii nomine is the Latin commentator on Paul now called Ambrosiaster; Pelagius sub Hieronymi nomine is Pelagius' Pauline commentary transmitted under Jerome's name.

title: The law of Moses is never called 'religion of angels', and Colossians 2:16-18 forbids the reading
english: Certainly Scripture nowhere calls the law of Moses "the religion (threskeia) of angels." No author of any kind, secular or churchly, can be found who uses that name for it.

And even if the name were common, it could not fit this passage of Paul. In the verses just before, Paul had already armed the Colossians in plain, explicit words against the deceit of the Judaizing impostors: "Let no one judge you in food or in drink, or in respect of a feast day, or of the new moon, or of the sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is of Christ" (Colossians 2:16-17). What point would there be in repeating the same thing in those dark and ambiguous words?

Paul also says that those who brought in the religion of angels walk in things they have not seen (Colossians 2:18): that is, they set foot in what they do not know and chatter about the unknown. That fits the worshipers of angels very well, for they pour out a great many unverified claims about the nature, orders and duties of angels. It does not fit men devoted to the law of Moses, since the discipline of Moses had been set out precisely in the sacred books and laid open to anyone who wished to learn it.
translator_notes: The 1675 print gives no margin here; the quoted words are Colossians 2:16-17 and the phrase 'walk in what they have not seen' is Colossians 2:18, supplied in the English.

title: Rome's second evasion, that Paul condemns only false angel-worship, fails: he forbids it outright
english: So the theologians of the Roman school fall back on another defense to protect their church's belief and practice against so explicit a law of the Apostle. The answer of most of them, and of the more learned, comes to this: the Apostle does not condemn the religious worship and invocation of angels or of saints, but only a false, superstitious and idolatrous worship and adoration, such as they say Simon Magus and Cerinthus and the followers of each taught.

But that is pure invention on their part, with no footing in the Apostle's words or teaching. Nowhere does he teach or so much as hint that there is a pious and lawful religion (threskeia) of angels and that he condemns only the excessive and idolatrous kind. He condemns the religion of angels plainly and as a whole.

So whatever errors the old heretics held about the nature, duties and worship of angels, that does not stop people today from breaking Paul's prohibition when they pursue angels with religious worship and offer any kind of threskeia to angels and saints. The Apostle forbids the threskeia of angels absolutely, not merely the kind Simon or Cerinthus are said to have offered them.

It is plain that those who worship angels and saints with vows, prayers, hymns, basilicas, oratories, feasts, gifts and offerings of every kind, as is the established custom in the Roman Church, do offer them threskeia. It follows that what the Roman Church does here is condemned by the Apostle no less than what Simon or Cerinthus, or any heretics like them, are reported to have done.

title: Rome's third reply: worship of ministers is not divine. But the Colossian errorists also took angels for ministers
english: The teachers of the Roman school answer that whatever rites and acts they use in worshiping angels and saints, that worship is not divine. They worship angels and saints, they say, not as gods but as God's servants and our intercessors with God, whereas threskeia, or religion, is the worship that belongs to God and is given to someone as God.

But the Apostle's own text shows well enough that the people he rebukes there, and warns us against, did not take angels for gods. They took them for messengers and servants of the supreme God, and for our mediators and advocates with God. The very name they gave them shows this, since "angel" means messenger.

Besides, those seducers professed to be Christians, and they worshiped angels on the pretext of humility, as if they were unworthy to come to God directly and so needed the mediation and intercession of angels with him. So it is clear enough that they worshiped angels with a subordinate worship, lower than the worship they thought due to the supreme God. On the Apostle's meaning, then, people who worship angels with a lower worship, without taking them for gods, are still giving angels threskeia.

title: The Angelici and Laodicea: Theodoret on praying to angels in Phrygia and Pisidia
english: What kind of religion toward angels those false Christians had, whom the ancients called Angelici, we can learn from the Synod of Laodicea. One of its canons was taken into the Code of Canons of the Universal Church: "Christians ought not to forsake the Church of God and go off to name angels and hold assemblies, which is forbidden."

What "naming angels" meant to that council Theodoret explains in his commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians, on the very passage we are pressing. "Those who defended the law," he says, "also led people to worship angels, saying that the law had been given through them. This vice lasted a long time in Phrygia and Pisidia. That is why the synod that met at Laodicea in Phrygia forbade by law that anyone pray to angels. And to this day one can see oratories of Saint Michael among them and their neighbors. They urged this practice out of humility, as they claimed, saying that the God of all things cannot be seen or reached or grasped, and that we ought to win God's goodwill for ourselves through angels."
translator_notes: The canon is Laodicea canon 35; the quotation from Theodoret is his commentary on Colossians 2:18.

title: So Laodicea and Theodoret condemn naming and praying to angels, and Petavius admits Rome does both
english: So in the judgment of the fathers of the Synod of Laodicea, and of Theodoret who expounds their canon, to name angels and pray to angels in order to win God's goodwill through them is to give angels unlawful worship and to sin against the Apostle's command, which condemns the cult and religion of angels.

Building oratories to angels, and to Saint Michael himself, belongs to the custom of the old heretics, not to the practice of the orthodox Church. How well that fits the present practice of the Roman Church I leave everyone to judge. For that church, as the Jesuit Dionysius Petavius admits and observes, "seeks the protection and patronage of angels with prayers and vows, and puts them forward as mediators with God; it also raises oratories and basilicas in their honor, and dedicates festal and joyful days to their worship" (Theological Dogmas, book 2, chapter 9, number 13).

title: Estius' claim that the Michael oratories were converted pagan shrines has no basis in Theodoret
english: Estius' remark is so absurd that it needs no refutation. He says that by the oratories dedicated to Saint Michael Theodoret does not mean places the heretics consecrated to their unlawful worship of angels, but places once defiled by the heretics' idolatry and later turned into oratories of Saint Michael by the prudence of the catholic bishops.

One would have to imagine Theodoret out of his mind to have him say what Estius maintains: that the old heretics used to pray to angels, the Synod of Laodicea forbade it, and therefore the place where they prayed to angels was changed into oratories of Saint Michael by the wise counsel of the orthodox. Besides, Theodoret does not hint at any such conversion of places, or at any such supposed prudence of bishops.

Theodoret's purpose forces itself even on unwilling readers. He means to prove what he had said, that the vice of those who called on angels lasted a long time in Phrygia and Pisidia, from the fact that down to his own day oratories dedicated by them to Michael could be seen among the Phrygians and their neighbors the Pisidians. No such oratories were found in the rest of the Christian world (Theodoret, Commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 2).
translator_notes: Estius is Willem Hessels van Est (Guilielmus Estius, d. 1613), Catholic commentator on the Pauline epistles.

title: Prayer is a chief part of divine worship, so angels and saints are not to be invoked
