english: That neither angels nor the blessed spirits of the just are to be prayed to or invoked is settled by this: Scripture counts prayer and invocation a principal part of divine worship and a chief and special duty of our religion toward God.

That is why Scripture calls God's temple "the house of prayer" (Isaiah 56:7; Matthew 21:13), and sets the prayers and supplications of the faithful before us as a kind of spiritual sacrifice (Psalm 141:2; Hebrews 13:15). And we are taught to call only on him in whom our faith rests, as the Apostle says: "How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed?" (Romans 10:14).

title: Rome's distinction: absolute prayer to God, relative prayer to the saints as intercessors
english: The teachers of the Roman Church reply that the prayer Scripture sets forth as part of the worship proper to God is absolute prayer, by which someone is asked as himself the author and giver of good things. It is not relative prayer, by which we ask someone to pray to God for us and obtain from God what we need.

They say they call on angels and saints not as authors of good things but only as those who obtain them for us, our intercessors with God. So they ask nothing more of angels and saints than that they pray to God for us, just as, without any wrong to God, we ask our fellow believers who live with us on earth to help us before God with their prayers.

title: But Rome's public hymns ask the saints directly for what only God gives
english: But when the Roman Church calls on angels and saints, it does not simply say to them, "Pray for us," or ask only that they intercede for us with God. It addresses them in many prayers of exactly the same form as those we are used to making to God.

It does this not only in the private devotion of the faithful but in public, solemn worship. To the Blessed Virgin it says: "Protect us from the enemy, and receive us at the hour of death. Grant us a pure life, prepare us a safe road. Make us free of our faults, gentle and chaste." To John the Baptist: "Look on us with pity, and wash away our faults." And to John the Apostle: "Take away the plague, remove the sore, and tend the sick; drive out disease, strike down the enemy, and take away the stumbling block."
Many like things are said to other saints too, as we showed at length in the first part of these theses.
translator_notes: The first two lines to the Virgin are the Maria mater gratiae doxology; the next lines are from Ave maris stella.

title: Rome's retort that the words mean only intercession: then why use the words of absolute prayer?
english: They retort that when they pray to the saints in that way, they do not mean that the saints give and bestow those good things themselves by any power of their own, but only that the saints obtain them from God by their merits and prayers. So, although the words say something else, all they mean is that the saints obtain from God by intercession what is asked.

But surely nothing forces them to think one thing and say another. If they ask the saints only to pray to God for them, why do they address the saints in the words of absolute prayer? Why are they not content to repeat to the saints the familiar "Pray for us"?

title: We may ask living saints to pray for us, but no one would address them as Rome addresses Mary, Benedict or Nicholas
english: Everyone admits it is lawful to ask holy people living here with us to pray to God for us. Yet no one would be tolerated who said to a holy man on earth what is commonly said to the Virgin Mary: "Take away our ills, bestow heavenly gifts; make us free of our faults, gentle and chaste." Or what is said to Saint Benedict: "You who grant us to climb the narrow road, give us the everlasting kingdom." Or what the hymn to Saint Nicholas says: "Take away the loss that death brings, bestow the helps of life, so that after the exile of the flesh we may be with you in glory."

If anyone had spoken that way to the apostles themselves, they would have stopped such a prayer as impious and told him to ask for those things from the Lord, not from them. Are we to think, then, that what they would have rejected as impious and sacrilegious while they lived on earth can please them now?
translator_notes: The Benedict line alludes to the narrow way of Matthew 7:14.

title: Some prayers even ask the saints to act by their own delegated power and command
english: Besides, in the usage of the Roman Church there are quite a few prayers addressed to the saints in which they are asked not only for the goods of grace and glory, but also to give these to us by the power entrusted to them, by their own order and command. That is plainly something other than obtaining such goods for us from God by their prayers.

So the apostles together are addressed: "You who shut heaven by your word and loose its bolts, loose us from all our sins by your command, we pray." And: "Health and sickness of all are subject to your command; heal those sick in their ways, restoring us to virtue." And again: "Command that we, guilty men, be loosed from our guilt, we pray." And to the Apostle Peter in particular: "By the power given you, loose the chains of sin, you who by your word shut heaven to all and open it."
We proved this more fully above as well.
translator_notes: The first lines to the apostles are from the breviary hymn Exultet caelum laudibus.

title: Mutual prayer among the living gives no warrant for invoking the departed
english: Even if the Roman Church asked nothing of the saints except that they pray to God for us, that could not be defended as lawful by the example of the prayers believers ask of one another, when under some need they ask their brothers to help them before God with their prayers.

Scripture tells us both to help our brothers with our prayers and to ask the same help from them. It does not follow that someone living in Europe could, without folly or even impiety, speak aloud or in his heart to a holy man living among the Chinese or in the Americas, ask him as if he could see and hear to intercede with God for him, and obtain what he feels he needs.

How then can we conclude from it that we may piously and reasonably ask the saints who have died in Christ, aloud or only in the heart's desire, to pray to God for us? They have been carried up into the heavenly paradise and are as far from us as the highest heaven is from the earth. Until we enjoy the same blessedness, we have no dealings with them and no means of sharing our thoughts.

So from the prayers that believers fighting side by side on earth ask of one another, it no more follows that we may invoke the saints already received into heaven than it once followed, on the Roman Church's own teaching, that the believers then living should have invoked the souls of the fathers held in Limbo.
translator_notes: The 1675 print reads 'non aliud a Sanctis petere' where sense needs 'peteret'; the English follows the sense ('asked').

title: Rome assumes the saints see and hear all who pray to them; that is walking in what we have not seen
english: The theologians of the Roman school assume that the spirits of the just, once admitted into heaven, know and perceive what happens on earth despite so vast a distance. They assume that each saint can at one and the same time hear the prayers of everyone who calls on him and see their needs, and can also look into their inmost thoughts and the hidden desires of their hearts and know them with certainty.

But this should not have been assumed without the word of God and sure reasoning. To declare it on the strength of our guesses and suspicions is simply to set foot in things we have not seen (Colossians 2:18).

title: The burden of proof lies on those who claim the saints hear us
english: Nor is it our task to prove the contrary, though much could be brought from Scripture on the point. For us to refrain from begging the prayers and suffrages of departed saints, it is enough that we do not know whether they hear us and do not find it revealed in God's word.

Those who say it is so must prove what they say. They are bound to demonstrate the knowledge of our affairs that they ascribe to the souls of the saints, by an argument that cannot be answered or by some clear word of Scripture. Otherwise their devotion toward the holy souls of the saints will totter altogether and be practiced without faith.

title: Prophets and apostles knew hidden things by revelation for their office; it does not follow the dead see all
english: Anyone who sifts the proofs they bring from Scripture to establish so great a matter will easily see how weak and light they are.

First, they prove that the saints reigning with Christ in heaven know what happens on earth, and so hear the prayers of all who call on them and see into their thoughts and hearts, from the fact that some men while still alive knew things absent and future, and even the secrets of the heart. Elisha, for example, said to his servant Gehazi, "Did not my heart go with you when the man came down from his chariot to meet you?" (2 Kings 5:26). Samuel said to Saul, "I will tell you all that is in your heart," and spoke of his father's asses that he had lost (1 Samuel 9:19-20). Peter knew, though he was not present, that Ananias and Sapphira had kept back part of the price of the field (Acts 5:1-9). Paul looked into the heart of the lame beggar and saw that he had faith to be healed (Acts 14:9).

But what sort of inference is this: prophets and apostles knew certain hidden things that belonged to their office, because God revealed them; therefore the souls of the blessed, received into heavenly glory, know what happens on earth, see the needs of all who call on them, and hear their prayers, whether spoken aloud or formed only in the heart's desire? What does follow is that God can reveal to the blessed spirits of the just whatever needs, actions and thoughts of men living here he pleases. Whether he does so cannot be concluded from it at all.
translator_notes: The 1675 margin gives chapters only (2 Reg. 5; 1 Sam. 9; Act. 5; Act. 14); the English supplies verses.

title: Appeal to the saints' office as patrons proves the unknown by the equally unknown
english: Suppose someone says that the office God has given the departed saints requires them to know our affairs, since God has appointed them our patrons and intercessors. He proves the unknown by what is just as unknown.

God's word nowhere teaches that the saints who enjoy heavenly glory have been given us by God as guardians and mediators to intercede for us with him. On the contrary, the opposite is gathered quite clearly from Scripture.

Nor can it be said that hearing the prayers of those who call on them belongs to the saints' blessedness on the ground that it adds to their glory. If calling on the saints who have died in Christ is superstitious and unlawful, a human invention, then knowing who calls on them adds nothing to the saints' glory. It ought first to have been proved that God is pleased and accepts it when the saints who reign with him are invoked, before anyone could suppose with any show of probability that such invocation adds to their glory.

title: Rome's proof from Matthew 22 and Luke 15: the just are equal to angels, and angels know sinners' repentance
english: The theologians of the Roman school also argue that the saints triumphant in heaven are not ignorant of what men do or of what happens to them in this lower world, and that even men's thoughts are not hidden from them, because these things do not escape the knowledge of the angels.

For Christ himself testifies that the just in heaven will be "equal to the angels" (isangeloi), "as the angels of God," in the twenty-second chapter of Matthew (Matthew 22:30; compare Luke 20:36). Since they are to be equal to the angels, they argue, we must not think that angels surpass them in knowledge of our affairs.

And they take it to follow that what happens on earth, even the inner movements and feelings of human hearts, is known to the angels of heaven, because the angels are said to rejoice "over one sinner who repents more than over ninety-nine righteous persons" (Luke 15:7, 10). If the angels see sinners' repentance, they certainly know what happens in the world, not only outwardly but inwardly too, in the sinner's heart, where true repentance and sorrow for sin reside.
translator_notes: Isangeloi is Luke 20:36; Matthew 22:30 has 'as the angels of God'. The words about ninety-nine just are Luke 15:7, joined to the angels of 15:10 (the margin gives Luc. 15. 10).

title: Angels serve us by office and so know our repentance; nothing shows the dead have that office. Pars Secunda closes
english: It is no wonder that angels, who are "ministering spirits sent to serve for the sake of those who will inherit salvation" (Hebrews 1:14), know what concerns us, above all the repentance and conversion of sinners, which they are commanded by God to help bring about. Their office keeps them with us and about us. But, as we have already said, it cannot be shown from God's word that God has entrusted a like office to the blessed souls of the just.

Nor is Christ's saying that the just will be "equal to the angels" in heaven to the point. That equality or likeness to the angels must not be stretched beyond Christ's purpose, which is to teach that after the resurrection the just will live the life of angels, in that they will no longer be subject to the needs and weaknesses of this life and will neither marry nor be given in marriage, as anyone who reads Christ's words in Matthew can see (Matthew 22:30).

Further, when Christ says in general terms that there is joy among the angels over the conversion of one sinner, it does not follow that each angel knows each man's thoughts and hears his prayers. In the same way we can truly say that there is great joy in the Church of God when one sinner turns to God, and yet it does not follow that every member of the Church knows the thoughts, words and deeds of all the others.
translator_notes: The 1675 margin reads Heb. 1. 13; the words quoted are Hebrews 1:14, so the English gives 1:14.

title: All Roman doctors confess that the first man was not liable to death before sin
english: All the teachers of the Roman Church admit that the first man, before he sinned, was not subject to death as we all now are, but was in some sense immortal.
Against the Pelagians they hold by common consent that the necessity of dying which now lies on us arose from sin, and would have had no place if man had remained in his original integrity.

title: Two senses of mortal and immortal: must die or can die; cannot die or need not die
english: To make their view on this clearer, they point out that in the state of integrity the first man was mortal in one sense and immortal in another.

A person can be called mortal in two ways, and immortal in two ways. In the first way, a mortal is one who must die; in the second, one who can die. Likewise, in the first way an immortal is one who cannot die; in the second, one who does not have to die.

title: Adam was mortal only as able to die, and immortal only as able not to die
english: In their view Adam in his first state was not mortal in the first sense, only in the second. There was no necessity at all that he die, and had he persevered in original righteousness he would never actually have died. Yet it was possible for him to die, as in fact happened after his fall. Through sin he and all his descendants became mortal in the first sense, because he brought on himself the necessity of dying.

In the same way, man in the state of innocence was not immortal in the first sense, for he was not such that he simply could not die. He was immortal in the second sense: he was able not to die, and had he stayed faithful in obeying God he would never have tasted death.

title: The risen saints will be immortal in both senses, unlike Adam in innocence
english: From this one can see how the first man's immortality in the state of integrity differs from the immortality the just will have after the blessed resurrection.

After the resurrection the saints will not be mortal in any way. They will not only be free from the necessity of dying; they will be altogether unable to die, or to bring death or mortality on themselves by sinning. So they will be immortal in both senses: they will not only be able not to die, they will be unable to die, and death will never have any power over them.
translator_notes: The final clause echoes Romans 6:9 ('death hath no more dominion over him'), said there of the risen Christ; the print gives no reference.

title: Rome's doctors agree Adam could avoid death, but dispute whether he could not die
english: In explaining this, however, the teachers of the Roman Church differ somewhat among themselves. They all agree that Adam in his unfallen state was able not to die, and that had he not sinned he would in fact never have died.
But they dispute whether we should say only that Adam, while he remained upright, was able not to die, or whether we may also say that in that state he was unable to die.

title: Some say unfallen man could always die by violence, though providence would have prevented it
english: Some say that man could always have died, even while his innocence stood, and that the first man's immortality consisted only in his not being subject to the necessity of dying, as we now are through sin.

For although man remained in integrity, they say, he could have died if someone who had abandoned the first innocence had done violence to his body by sword, by fire, or in any other way at all. Nothing of the kind would actually have happened, since God by his providence would have turned every danger aside.

title: They add that elemental strife would at last have killed unfallen man, unless God translated him (Scotus)
english: They even add that the first man and all his descendants would in the end have died by a necessity of nature, because of the conflict of the elements that make up the human body, unless God had carried them over into a state of immortality before that happened. Such a death, had it occurred, would have been no more a punishment for man than for the beasts; for both it would have been natural.

It follows that man, even persisting in integrity, always had the capacity to die. It could not truly be said of him that in that state he was unable to die, although he was able not to die and was not subject to the necessity of dying.
Estius attributes this view to Scotus and certain others (Estius on the Sentences, book 2, distinction 19, number 2).
translator_notes: Estius is Willem Hessels van Est, commentator on Peter Lombard's Sentences.

title: Estius himself holds that unfallen man could not die, by the order God established
english: Estius himself, in the same place and in the next number, declares that he and many others hold a different view. He thinks we must say outright that while his first innocence stood man was unable to die.
It was not merely that man, persisting in obedience to God, would in fact not have died. The order of things God had once established necessarily required it, and it could not have been otherwise.

title: Estius: man was made free, lord of things and God's friend, so no harm could befall him in God's friendship
english: To explain this, he points out that God did not make man a merely servile creature, as he made the nature of the brutes. They are therefore naturally subject to death and may be killed for men's use; indeed, some of them give way to others by death to serve as food. God made man, like the angels, free by nature and lord of other things, and besides that, through grace and righteousness, a kind of companion and friend of God himself.

From this, he says, it is clear enough that man was so made that nothing hostile would befall him as long as he remained in God's friendship. Two pairs would always go together and follow from each other: being good and being happy, and likewise being innocent and being free of misery.
And this law is so permanent, because divine justice requires it, that if it were removed the order of the universe would be disfigured.

title: By absolute power God could have made man mortal in body; Adam could die in the divided sense, not the composite
english: He says, however, that all this must be understood of the order God once established. "If we speak of God's absolute power," he says, "there is no doubt that as Lord of all creation he could, without wronging it, have so made human nature that, although man kept his innocence in his soul, in the condition of his body he would have been like the brute animals, subject to death and the rest no less than they are."

So, although Adam in the state of innocence could sin and through sin become subject to death, and in that sense (the divided sense) it is true that unfallen Adam could die, Estius insists that the same statement is false in the composite sense, because he could not die as long as he kept his innocence.

title: However they explain it, Rome's theologians now agree the first man's immortality was supernatural
english: However the theologians of the Roman school explain this immortality of the first man, they all now seem to agree on one point: it must be called supernatural, not natural, in the sense in which natural is opposed to supernatural.

Bellarmine above all affirms this and tries to prove it with many arguments (On the Grace of the First Man, chapter 9), as does Becanus (Summa of Scholastic Theology, tome 1, treatise 5, chapter 4, question 1).
translator_notes: Becanus is the Jesuit Martin Becanus (d. 1624), Summa theologiae scholasticae.

title: The contrary view, that immortality was man's natural condition, was condemned by Pius V and Gregory XIII
english: In the last century there were indeed some among the teachers of the Roman Church itself who held that the first man's immortality was not a gift of grace but his natural condition.

But the Roman popes Pius V and Gregory XIII condemned this view in a special bull in which they condemned many articles of certain recent theologians. Article 75 among them reads: "The immortality of the first man was not a gift of grace, but his natural condition." So Bellarmine himself testifies (On the Grace of the First Man).
translator_notes: The bull is Pius V's condemnation of propositions of Michael Baius (Ex omnibus afflictionibus, 1567), renewed by Gregory XIII (1579). Le Blanc numbers the article 75 after Bellarmine; later collections number it differently.

title: Estius' answer: Adam's immortality was in one way natural, in another above nature
english: To make the view of the Roman school's teachers on this question clearer, I think it worth setting out what William Estius teaches on it, very precisely and clearly, in his commentary on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 19, number 9.

There he answers the question "Whether the immortality of the first state was natural to man" with many different distinctions. He teaches that it was natural to man in one respect and above nature in another, just as death is natural to fallen man in one respect and against nature in another.

title: First sense: natural as belonging to nature's first institution
english: First, what is present from nature's first institution is called natural. In this sense he says that immortality was natural to the first man and death against nature, since man was created immortal at the beginning, that is, free from the necessity of dying.

title: Second sense: natural as what every appetite seeks
english: Again, what each thing's appetite naturally tends toward is called natural. In this sense too he grants that immortality is natural to man and death against nature, because everyone by nature longs for immortality and shrinks from death.

title: Third sense: natural as what one has from birth, whether good or not
english: Natural can also mean what each person has from birth, whether it is good for nature, suited to it and in keeping with natural appetite, or not. In this sense too, he admits, immortality was natural to the first man and mortality is natural to us. He was created immortal; we are born subject to death.

title: Fourth sense: natural as having its cause in nature; the body's temperament and the tree of life
english: He adds that what has its cause in nature itself is called natural. "In this way too," he says, "immortality was in a manner natural to the first man. For it rested on the excellent balance of the human body as its inner cause and on the tree of life as its outer cause, and each of these was a natural cause of that effect."
translator_notes: The tree of life is that of Genesis 2:9; the print gives no reference.

title: Yet Estius calls it simply supernatural: from original righteousness and the earthy body; Baius rightly condemned
english: But Estius teaches that in another respect this same immortality was supernatural to man. Partly because of righteousness, on which the body's good constitution, and so immortality itself, depended. "That righteousness," he says, "was supernatural, inasmuch as through it the soul was subject to God and clung to him as its supernatural good and end. As long as that subjection lasted, the soul had a certain supernatural power by which it could keep the body from all corruption." And partly because of the body, that is, the matter from which man was made. Since that matter was earthy, it held in itself no cause of immortality, but rather of mortality.

"So although the first man," he says, "had in his very nature some cause of immortality, it was not a full and complete one. On the contrary, if in thought we set his supernatural gifts aside and consider only what was natural in him, he was mortal, so that he would have had to die. For he was made of contraries, and the dissolution of the compound necessarily follows from their conflict in the end. In this way, then, immortality was supernatural to the first man.

"But the supernatural is properly opposed not to what is called natural in the first, second or third of the senses just listed, but only to what is natural in the fourth sense. In that sense the first man's immortality cannot be called simply natural, because, as we said, natural causes alone were not enough to give it to him. So the immortality of unfallen man should be called supernatural, absolutely speaking, rather than natural.

"That is why the Apostolic See rightly condemned the proposition that the first man's immortality was not a gift of grace but a natural condition, especially if it means that immortality was so owed to human nature that God could not have created it mortal. That is clearly utterly false."
translator_notes: The condemned proposition is the Baius article cited in thesis XII.

title: The Reformed agree: unfallen man could not-die, but only the risen blessed cannot die
english: As for the teachers of the Reformed school, they too hold by common consent that man in the state of innocence was immortal in some measure, and they explain that immortality in much the same way.

Like the teachers of the Roman Church, they distinguish the immortality by which someone is unable to die from the immortality by which someone is able not to die and is free from the necessity of dying. In the first sense, they teach, only the blessed after the resurrection will be immortal. Man in his unfallen state was immortal only in the second sense: he had the possibility of dying, which the blessed do not have, but not the necessity of dying, which we now have through sin.

title: Placaeus: Adam was neither immortal as the risen will be nor mortal as we are
english: Josué de la Place (Placaeus) puts it this way in thesis 32 of his Theses on the State of Adam before the Fall: "Adam's immortality was not the kind we shall have after the blessed resurrection, since he was able to sin and so able to die. Nor was his mortality the kind we have now in this state of sin, since he was able to avoid sin and so able to avoid death."
translator_notes: Josué de la Place (Placaeus) taught at Saumur; the theses cited are from the Saumur Theses theologicae.

title: Pareus' four senses of immortality: unfallen Adam's was the power of not dying, given union with a perfect soul
english: Pareus likewise says that the immortality by which man before sin was immortal in body was a power of not dying, that is, the absence of the act of dying, on the supposition of its union with a soul perfect from its origin, although man's body was mortal in itself.

"Immortality," he says, "means first an inability to die that is absolute and by nature. In this sense God alone has immortality, and in this sense the Fathers deny, and we deny, that man was immortal by nature. Second, an inability to die by the grace of creation: so angels and human souls are immortal. Third, an inability to die by the grace of a gift: so the bodies of the blessed will have immortality. Fourth, a power of not dying, that is, the absence of the act of dying, on some supposition, though the thing is mortal in itself. In this sense man before sin was immortal in body, on the supposition of its union with an immortal soul perfect from its origin." (Pareus, against Bellarmine, On the Grace of the First Man, chapter 9.)
translator_notes: 'God alone has immortality' echoes 1 Timothy 6:16; the print gives no reference.

title: Tilenus: posse non mori is of nature, non posse mori of glory
english: Tilenus says the same in his Disputation on the External State of the First Man, ninth thesis: "It should be understood that the first man's immortality was not wholly of the same kind as the glorious immortality of the blessed. For as being able not to sin is one thing and being unable to sin another, so being able not to die is one thing and being unable to die another. The first belongs to nature, the second to glory. The first kind of immortality removes the act of dying but does not rule out the power to die; the second abolishes and extinguishes both."
translator_notes: Daniel Tilenus (1563-1633) taught at Sedan before Le Blanc.

title: Tilenus holds this immortality natural rather than supernatural, yet by God's covenant, not the body's own power
english: The Reformed, however, maintain that the immortality man had in his first integrity should be called natural rather than supernatural, and that the first man really was in some sense immortal by nature. This is what Tilenus teaches in the eighth thesis of the disputation just cited, where he says that man is truly called immortal by nature.

Yet in the second thesis, explaining his meaning more precisely, he teaches that the first man's body was in itself corruptible, since it was made up of contrary qualities in conflict with one another, but that by God's covenant it would have been incorruptible had man continued in obedience to God without sin.

title: Placaeus: the power of not dying was as natural to Adam as the power of not sinning
english: Josué de la Place says the same in the thesis already cited: "The power of not dying was as natural to Adam as the power of not sinning. The reign of death is no more from nature than the reign of sin. He had the possibility of dying from nature, but the necessity of dying from sin."

He gives this reason: it is fitting that the physical powers follow the condition of the moral powers, which rule in man. From this he concludes that in Adam life and righteousness stood on the same footing, and so, since righteousness was natural to him, the power of not dying must have been natural too.
translator_notes: 'Reign of death ... reign of sin' echoes Romans 5:14 and 5:21; the print gives no reference.

title: Pareus: natural to integral nature, and to the whole man, not to the body in itself
english: Pareus distinguishes between nature unfallen and nature corrupted. He says that with respect to unfallen nature Adam's immortality was natural, but that with respect to corrupted nature it is not immortality but mortality, that is, the necessity of dying, that is rightly called natural.

He also distinguishes between unfallen man and man's body considered in itself, and holds that immortality was natural to the man, not to the body in itself (on Bellarmine, On the Grace of the First Man, chapter 9). In chapter 5 he teaches that whatever belonged of itself to the principles of nature for its perfection, and without which nature was not first made in its principles, was natural to unfallen man.

title: Both schools agree: before sin man was free of the necessity of dying, yet able to sin and to die
english: In this question one thing is entirely certain and, as appears from what has been said, approved by the common consent of both the Roman and the Reformed schools: before sin man was free from the necessity of dying, yet so placed that he could sin, and so could also die. And man was immortal in no other sense than this.

title: Rome too allows this immortality natural in two senses: implanted from origin, and perfecting nature
english: Nor do the theologians of the Roman school deny, as we showed above, that the immortality the first man had before sin can be called natural in a certain respect and sense. It can be so called insofar as "natural" means what was implanted from the first origin, not something added from outside and laid on top. It can also be so called insofar as "natural" is opposed to what is against nature and means what adorns and perfects that same nature.

title: The only question left: is it, simply speaking, natural or supernatural?
english: The only question left is whether, simply speaking, this immortality should be called natural rather than supernatural with respect to unfallen man. The Protestants say yes; the teachers of the Roman school say no.

title: With Pareus' definition of natural, the dispute is only about a word
english: But for those Protestants who define "natural" with Pareus as "that without which nature was not first made in its principles," the question is only about a word. For in that sense, as we have seen, the teachers of the Roman school admit that immortality was natural to the first man.
translator_notes: Pareus' definition is the one cited from his chapter 5 in thesis XXV.

title: A real dispute remains only with Protestants who think unfallen man needed no supernatural help to escape death
english: The only real disagreement left will be between those Protestants who hold that unfallen man could have escaped death forever without any supernatural help, and the Roman school, which by common consent denies it.

title: So long as death is from sin and life was joined to righteousness by God's decree, the question matters little
english: Still, provided it is agreed that the necessity of dying that now lies on us comes not from nature but from sin, and that had man persevered in his original integrity, life would always have been joined to his righteousness by God's most wise and most just decree, this question does not seem very important.

title: Two Reformed views; Amyraut: unfallen man would have lived forever, but only an earthly life
english: To make my own view on this clearer: I find two opinions in the Reformed schools about the unending life unfallen man would have had.

Some hold that if the first man had remained in obedience to God, according to the covenant of nature God made with him, he would indeed have lived forever, but only with an earthly, animal life that would never have been changed into a heavenly and glorious one. This is what Moses Amyraut teaches in his Theses on the Three Divine Covenants.
translator_notes: Moses Amyraut's Theses de tribus foederibus divinis were disputed at Saumur.

title: The commoner view: after a span on earth man would have been changed into heavenly glory
english: The more common opinion holds that if man had never fallen from his original integrity, he would at last have been taken up into a blessed and glorious immortality in heaven, after spending some span of time on this earth, as God's wisdom saw fit.
This would have happened through a change like the one the godly and holy will undergo who are found alive on earth at the last judgment.
translator_notes: The change of the living echoes 1 Corinthians 15:51-52 and 1 Thessalonians 4:17; the print gives no reference.

title: On that view man would never have lived forever without supernatural help
english: This opinion is both the more common and the more probable. On it, plainly, man could never have gone on living forever unless God helped him beyond nature, since the change that was to carry him up into heavenly life would itself have been a supernatural change, not a natural one.

title: Le Blanc: an endless earthly life without supernatural help is improbable; he follows Pierre du Moulin. De Primi Hominis Immortalitate closes
english: But that man could have lived forever an earthly, animal life without any supernatural gift or help, as the first opinion maintains, seems to me in no way probable. I cannot see how a body made of the elements, and so naturally and in itself corruptible, could be kept from corruption forever without some help above nature.

Here I follow the judgment of Pierre du Moulin, who also has no doubt that man, however perfect the natural balance of his body, needs supernatural help and God's continual aid to keep that good balance (eukrasia) (Du Moulin, On the State of Innocence, thesis 50).
translator_notes: Pierre du Moulin (Molinaeus) taught at Sedan; the theses cited are his disputations on the state of innocence.

title: Rome's common teaching: Adam before the fall had true righteousness and holiness (Trent, Session 5)
english: The common teaching of the Roman Church is that the first man, before he sinned at the devil's prompting, was endowed with true righteousness and holiness, on account of which he was pleasing and acceptable to God for eternal life.

The Council of Trent itself teaches this plainly in its fifth session, in the decree on original sin. There it pronounces anathema on anyone who does not confess that the first man, Adam, when he had broken God's command in paradise, at once lost the holiness and righteousness in which he had been placed. It pronounces it too on anyone who asserts that the holiness and righteousness Adam received from God and then lost, he lost for himself alone and not for us as well.
translator_notes: Trent, Session 5 (1546), Decree on Original Sin, canons 1 and 2. The command in paradise is that of Genesis 2:16-17; the print gives no reference.

title: What that righteousness included: true knowledge and pure love of God, and a body and appetite obeying the spirit without struggle
english: In the view of the Roman Church's teachers, that righteousness and holiness did not consist only in man's mind being filled with a true knowledge of God, enough for gaining eternal blessedness, and in his will embracing God with pure and chaste love.

It also consisted in this: the flesh obeyed the spirit and the body the soul without difficulty or resistance, and the sensual appetite followed reason's lead so fully that it never rebelled against it or pulled the man in different directions.

So Adam in that unfallen state felt within himself no struggle of flesh against spirit, and no rebellion of his members against the law of his mind, such as we often feel. He moved toward good and turned away from evil without conflict or difficulty, and he did not have in him the concupiscence spoken of above, with which we are now born and which stays with us until death.
translator_notes: The law of the members against the law of the mind is from Romans 7:23, and the struggle of flesh and spirit echoes Galatians 5:17; the print gives no references.

title: Was it natural? Rome's three senses of natural: from birth, agreeable to nature, flowing from nature's principles
english: The question is whether this righteousness and holiness was natural to the first man or not. To answer it, the teachers of the Roman Church point out that "natural" is used in several ways.

First, whatever one has from birth is called natural, and in this sense natural is opposed to acquired. Second, what suits nature, what does not destroy nature but rather adorns and perfects it, is called natural; in this sense natural is opposed to what is against nature.

Third, what is either a part of nature, or flows from nature's principles, or is fitted to flow from them, is called natural. In this sense the body and the soul, the powers of sense and of understanding, and the acts those powers perform without help that goes beyond nature, are called natural, and so natural is opposed to supernatural.

title: Some Roman doctors held it natural in every sense, even as opposed to supernatural (Medina)
english: Some teachers of the Roman Church, however, maintain that the righteousness and holiness which the whole Roman Church agrees was found in our first parents before sin was natural in every sense. It was natural, they say, not only as natural is distinguished from acquired or from what is against nature, but also as it is opposed to supernatural. That righteousness was not supernatural grace; it belonged to the natural state of man not yet corrupted, and was a condition owed to unfallen nature.

Medina bears witness to this on the Prima Secundae, question 18, article 2: "Some teachers understand by 'man placed in a purely natural state' man placed in unfallen nature, with a gift and strength that heals nature, so that he could remain in the good and in the practice of the virtues and persevere if he chose. This opinion is without doubt Augustine's."

These are the remarkably learned men who, as Bellarmine reports, think that Thomas himself held the same view along with the other more reputable authors, and that on this point they held the opposite of what Bellarmine himself teaches.
translator_notes: Bartolomé de Medina (1527-1580), Dominican commentator on Thomas Aquinas' Summa, Prima Secundae.

title: That view condemned by Pius V and Gregory XIII (Baius' articles 21 and 26)
english: Popes Pius V and Gregory XIII condemned this view in the last century. In their bull, which condemned many articles together, it appears as article 21: "Human nature's being lifted up and raised into partnership with the divine nature was owed to the integrity of man's first condition, and is therefore to be called natural, not supernatural."

Article 26 runs: "The integrity of man's first condition was not an exaltation of human nature beyond its due, but its natural condition." Bellarmine records this in chapter 1 of his single book On the Grace of the First Man.
translator_notes: The articles are from the propositions of Michael Baius condemned by Pius V (Ex omnibus afflictionibus, 1567) and again by Gregory XIII (1579). 'Partnership with the divine nature' echoes 2 Peter 1:4; the print gives no reference.

title: So Rome's common view: natural as agreeable to nature and as present from origin, but not as opposed to supernatural
english: The common view of the Roman Church's teachers, then, is that the righteousness and holiness with which the first man was adorned before the fall can indeed be called natural in two senses. It is natural as opposed to what is against nature, meaning what suits nature and does not destroy it but adorns and perfects it. It is natural too as opposed to what is acquired, meaning what is there from the origin, or from birth.

For they grant that our first parent was created in righteousness, and so they call the righteousness he had in his unfallen state original righteousness. But they deny that it was natural as natural is opposed to supernatural, because in their view it did not flow from nature's principles but was God's free gift, which raised man above his natural condition.

title: Supernatural per se and per accidens: Elijah's chariot and Samson's strength; the blind man's sight and Solomon's wisdom
english: To make their meaning clearer on this point, they note that something is called supernatural in two ways, in itself (per se) and by circumstance (per accidens).

What by its very kind is not fitted to flow from nature's principles is supernatural in itself, like Elijah's going up to heaven in a fiery chariot, Samson's strength, and other things of that sort. What is sometimes obtained by a divine miracle, though otherwise it usually flows from nature's principles, is supernatural by circumstance. Such was the sight the Lord gave back to the man born blind, the wisdom God gave Solomon, and many other things we read in Scripture.
translator_notes: The examples are Elijah (2 Kings 2:11), Samson (Judges 14-16), the man born blind (John 9) and Solomon's wisdom (1 Kings 3:12); the print gives no references.

title: Rome holds original righteousness supernatural in itself: unfallen nature could not by its own powers so know and love God, or so rule the body
english: They hold, then, that the gift of righteousness in the first man was supernatural not only by circumstance, because God gave it freely, directly and in a way beyond nature, but also in itself and by its kind, because the righteousness that adorned the first man neither flowed nor could flow from nature's principles, even uncorrupted nature.

Man, even before sin had infected him, could not by nature's own powers know and love God as fully as a righteousness and holiness that pleases God and is accepted by him requires for the reward of eternal life and blessedness.

Nor could nature's powers and gifts alone subject body to soul, and sense and appetite to reason, so perfectly that there was no rebellion of flesh against spirit in man, and that he felt no difficulty or resistance in doing good and no leaning toward doing evil. Yet that is how things stood in unfallen man, in whom there were no disordered movements of concupiscence rebelling against right reason.

title: Bellarmine's fourth proposition: Adam's rectitude was a supernatural gift; man's two propensions, from flesh and spirit, fight
english: This is what Bellarmine teaches in chapter 4 of his single book On the Grace of the First Man. His fourth proposition there reads: "The rectitude with which Adam was created, and without which all men have been born since his fall, was a supernatural gift."

To explain it, he first notes that by nature man is made of flesh and spirit, and so shares a nature partly with the beasts and partly with the angels. Because of the flesh, which he shares with the beasts, he has a leaning toward bodily, sensible good, which he pursues through sense and appetite. Because of the spirit, which he shares with the angels, he has a leaning toward spiritual, intelligible good, which he pursues through understanding and will.
From these different, even opposed, leanings a kind of conflict arises within one and the same man, and from that conflict a great difficulty in doing good, as one leaning hinders the other.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia primi hominis (one book, part of his Controversies), chapter 4.

title: Bellarmine: original righteousness a golden bridle; natural as from birth and as suiting nature, not as flowing from its principles
english: Next he says that at the beginning of creation divine providence, to remedy this sickness or weakness of human nature arising from the condition of matter, gave man a remarkable gift, original righteousness. By it, as by a golden bridle, the lower part was kept easily subject to the higher, and the higher to God.

The flesh was so subject to the spirit that it could not be moved against the spirit's will or rebel against it unless the spirit itself rebelled against God, though it was in the spirit's power to rebel against God or not.

From this he concludes that the first man's righteousness was natural in the sense that whatever one has from birth is natural, and in the sense that what suits nature is natural; but it was not natural in the sense in which natural is distinguished from supernatural and means what flows from nature's principles.

title: Bellarmine quoted: opponents call rectitude natural like health; Rome calls it supernatural in itself, so fallen man differs from pure-natural man as the stripped from the naked
english: "Our opponents," Bellarmine says, "hold that the rectitude in which Adam was created was natural to him in this last sense, that is, as natural is opposed to supernatural. They hold it was a kind of health owed to nature and fitted to arise from nature itself when well formed, that is, uncorrupted. Men who lost that rectitude in Adam now lack some natural good, they say, as a beast would lack one if it were born blind, lame or feverish. And if original righteousness were now restored by God to some man, they would call it a supernatural gift by circumstance, not in itself, as we said of the eyes given back to the man born blind.

"We, however, hold that this rectitude, even in the lower part, was a supernatural gift, and supernatural in itself, not by circumstance, so that it neither flowed nor could flow from nature's principles. And because that gift was supernatural, as we shall prove shortly, once it was taken away human nature, left to itself, began to feel the conflict of lower part against higher that would have been natural, that is, would have followed from the condition of matter, had God not added the gift of righteousness to man.

"So man's state after Adam's fall differs from his state in a purely natural condition no more than a man stripped differs from a man naked. Take away original guilt, and human nature is no worse, and suffers no more from ignorance and weakness, than it would be and would suffer if it had been made in a purely natural condition. The corruption of nature, then, came not from the lack of some natural gift, nor from the addition of some bad quality, but solely from the loss of the supernatural gift because of Adam's sin."
Bellarmine then proves that this is the common view of the scholastic teachers, old and more recent, by citing many of their testimonies.
translator_notes: Bellarmine, De gratia primi hominis, chapter 5, summarized at length by Le Blanc.

title: Roman doctors agree it was grace, but divide: some say it was somehow owed to innocent nature, since God could not create man bad or wretched
english: Although the teachers of the Roman Church now generally agree that man's righteousness and holiness in the state of integrity and innocence was a supernatural gift, grace in the proper sense, added on top of nature, there is still a notable difference of opinion among them.

Some of them hold that the first man's righteousness and holiness was supernatural and belonged to grace rather than to nature, yet was in some way owed to innocent nature. On their view it was impossible for God to make and create the first man without such grace, since that would have been at odds with God's goodness, justice and wisdom. Otherwise God would have created man either bad or wretched, or rather both.

A creature that neither knows God nor loves him with a pure and chaste love, as befits a rational creature, cannot help being bad and wretched. So too one whose bodily senses and appetite drag an unwilling, resisting reason down to lower things, and who do not obey the mind's commands and direction but rebel and riot against it. And it is contrary to God's goodness to make a man bad and a sinner, or at least wretched, through no fault of his own.

title: On that view only a debt founded on merit conflicts with grace
english: So they do not think that every kind of debt is at odds with grace, only a debt founded on good works and merits.

When God makes a rational creature, his goodness and wisdom require that he give it the gifts and supply the help it needs to love God with a pure and chaste love and to live a righteous, peaceful and blessed life. Even so, in their view, those gifts and that help belong not to nature but to grace in the proper sense, because they are in no way owed to the creature's merits, and the creature is not equal to them by itself unless God helps it beyond nature.

title: This is the Jansenists' teaching in their short Catechism on grace: a rational creature without grace would be disordered
english: This is the teaching of those who follow the doctrine and positions of Jansenius, as can be seen in the short Catechism on grace they published.

In its fourth chapter, after stating that the first man was created in a state of holiness and righteousness, of knowledge and love of God, with God at once forming his nature and giving him grace, they teach that man could not have been created in any other state. God can make nothing that is not well ordered, and a rational creature would be disordered unless it were created in a state of grace.

They prove this from the claim that an intellectual creature's essential order is to tend toward God as toward its center and its source. It cannot tend there except by the help grace supplies. It follows that such a creature, if deprived of grace before it was corrupted by sin, would be outside its proper order.
translator_notes: The 'short Catechism on grace' is the Jansenist Catéchisme de la grâce (1650).

title: Drawn from Jansenius' Augustinus: man could not be created in pure nature without grace; the grace of love was still grace though fitting
english: These points are taken from Jansenius himself, who in his posthumous book entitled Augustinus gathers this same teaching from Augustine at length, proves it and enlarges on it. He does so especially in the first and second books on the state of pure nature.

There he argues at length that man could not have been created in a state of pure nature without any grace at all. By the powers of nature alone, even uncorrupted nature, without the help of grace assisting nature, man cannot love God with any true love or be made blessed by any kind of contemplation and enjoyment of God. So if God were supposed to create man in a state of pure nature without any grace, he would necessarily create him both bad and wretched, which is wholly at odds with God's goodness and wisdom.

He teaches besides that the grace of love for God in which the first man was created keeps the full and true character of grace. God gives it to the innocent creature not as a debt of justice but because it befits the creature's weakness, and by the law of his own wisdom, kindness, holiness, mercy and rectitude. Otherwise all sins, and the creature's love spilling down into lower things, would be laid at God's own door, since he commanded it to bind its love to no one but God, its source and end.
These are Jansenius' own words, in book 1 On the State of Nature, chapter 20, whose title is "How the good will in which a rational creature must be made was grace."
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius, Augustinus (Louvain, 1640, posthumous), volume 2, De statu naturae purae, book 1, chapter 20.

title: Jansenius: debts of fittingness do not conflict with grace; knowledge and love of God are still grace even for the innocent
english: As can be seen in the same place, Jansenius holds that grace, even in the strictest sense, is not contradicted by any kind of debt, whether called connaturality, seemliness, fittingness or equity, so long as it arises from some other source than the creature's own right.

Nothing could be more connatural to a creature made in God's image than to be created with knowledge and love of God. On God's side, nothing could be more fitting, seemly and equitable than that a rational, innocent creature, ordered to God as its natural end, should be given what it needs to reach that end; in a sense God owed this to himself and to his attributes.

Yet that knowledge and love of God, without which no creature can enjoy God, deserves to be called grace even with respect to innocent creatures. It is owed to no merit of the creature, and knowledge and love of that kind surpass the powers of any created nature unless God helps it beyond nature.
translator_notes: 'Made in God's image' is Genesis 1:27; the print gives no reference.

title: The commoner Roman view: original righteousness wholly unowed, so a state of pure nature was possible
english: The more common view among the teachers of the Roman school goes another way. They hold that the righteousness and holiness of the first man was not only a supernatural gift, belonging to grace and not to nature, but also something wholly unowed to human nature, even innocent nature not yet sinful. So it would not have been at odds with God's wisdom, goodness and justice for man to be created without such righteousness.

That is why they count among man's possible states the state of pure nature, or, as they put it, of man in a purely natural condition. In that state, as they see it, man would be neither righteous nor unrighteous, neither guilty of any sin nor endowed with any grace.
translator_notes: The 1675 print reads 'quod ad naturam non ad gratiam pertinebat' ('which belonged to nature, not to grace'). Thesis XII and the argument require 'ad gratiam non ad naturam', so the translation follows that sense and treats the printed order as a printer's inversion.

title: Pure nature defined negatively: nothing added, good or bad, beyond what is owed
english: Jansenius, already mentioned, reports and explains the scholastics' view on this in book 1, chapter 1 of On the State of Pure Nature. On their account nature is called pure by a negative purity: nothing is added to it, good or bad, beyond what is owed to it. It has neither sin, nor the punishment that goes with sin, nor any gift of grace beyond nature.

title: Look at fallen nature without its guilt: pure nature differs as the naked from the stripped, negation from privation
english: To make it easy to see what such a state of nature includes, they tell us to look at fallen nature: whatever we find in it apart from the guilt of sin, they say, belongs to pure nature.

Their set rule is that pure nature differs from fallen nature as the naked man differs from the man stripped. The two differ only in that the one has lost what the other never had. So pure nature is like a negation, fallen nature like a privation.

title: So man in pure nature would lack any ordering to the vision of God, faith and charity, and the fight of flesh and spirit would be natural
english: So when they teach that God could create man in a state of pure nature with no prior sin at all, they mean that man would then be created without any ordering to eternal blessedness, that is, to the clear vision of God, and so would be made without faith in his intellect and without charity loving God.

They mean too that the conflict of flesh and spirit we experience would be wholly natural to such a man. The merely natural order would even require God to let those two opposed appetites clash back and forth, neither withdrawing his concurrence nor checking their mutual conflict and hostility by any added gift.

title: Pure-nature man would be as ignorant and weak as fallen man, and outwardly worse off, lacking Adam's tradition and the promise of Christ
english: So with regard to the inner powers of the soul, there would be as much ignorance in pure nature, as much weakness in thinking, judging and living well, and as much proneness to sin, as we experience in fallen nature. With regard to outward things there would be more.

The sense objects that stir up desire would be the same, and besides that, the evil counsel and example of wicked men would then urge men to evil more strongly. For in fallen nature the ease of sinning could be softened by what had come down by tradition from the head of the race to his descendants: the knowledge of God and of the virtues that had been given to Adam, the memory of God's promises and threats, the recollection of the former state and of the fall, and the promise of the coming Christ with the hope of his redemption.
So on this score blindness, a more widespread corruption of morals, and the tendency to sin would apparently have been greater in pure nature.
translator_notes: The promise of the coming Christ handed down from Adam alludes to Genesis 3:15; the print gives no reference. Thesis XXI continues the scholastics' account as reported by Jansenius.

title: Bellarmine: man in pure nature would be as we are, prone to vice, and could be denied healing grace
english: This is Bellarmine's teaching in chapter 7 of the book already cited. Answering the seventh objection there, he says that man created in a purely natural state would have been just as we are with respect to bodily mortality, the rebellion of the members, ignorance, difficulty and the like.

Later, answering the eighth objection, he denies that the natural drive of our flesh is more rebellious now than it would have been earlier without grace, and denies that man's purely natural endowments would have been any healthier before sin than they are now after it.

Further on he even grants that man could have been made in such a state of pure nature that he would have had a headlong bent toward vice and the drive of sensuality. And he insists that nothing absurd would follow if God refused a man so created the grace that heals these evils and that man needs to reach eternal blessedness.
translator_notes: Bellarmine, De gratia primi hominis, chapter 7, answers to the seventh and eighth objections.

title: Bellarmine denies such a man would be in the devil's power; Tapper says he could suffer every evil, even damnation, as punishment-free torment
english: In the same place, however, Bellarmine denies that a man so created in a purely natural state would for that reason be in the devil's power. Here he parts from Ruard Tapper.

Tapper holds that God can create man without original righteousness, and that such a man would then not only suffer the weaknesses already named, difficulty and ignorance, but would also be afflicted with every evil we experience, even damnation and harassment by demons.

"Man could be created without original righteousness," he says, "and be afflicted with all the evils we now experience: diseases, damnation, harassment by demons and all the rest. In him, though, they would not be punishments and penalties, only torments, as they are in the beasts." So Tapper writes in his explanation of the second article of the Louvain faculty, page 72, where he deals with original sin.
translator_notes: Ruard Tapper (1487-1559), dean of the Louvain theology faculty; his commentary explains the Louvain articles of 1544.

title: The Reformed agree: God made man upright, in righteousness and true holiness (Eccl. 7:29; Eph. 4:24)
english: The Protestants, and especially those among them called the Reformed, likewise teach by common consent that God created man in true righteousness and holiness, as the Preacher says: "God made man upright." That uprightness can consist in nothing else than conformity with God's will and law, which is what man's righteousness consists in.

They think Paul has the same thing in view when he urges believers to "put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness." He is plainly alluding there to the first creation, in which man is said to have been made in God's image and likeness. In Paul's mind that image includes the holiness and righteousness that Christ works in believers by his Spirit.
translator_notes: Ecclesiastes 7:29 and Ephesians 4:24 are quoted without reference in the print; the image and likeness is Genesis 1:26-27.

title: The Reformed: original righteousness also meant every faculty in order, with no disorder or conflict
english: They do not place the holiness and righteousness in which God made the first man only in his acknowledging God as his creator, as was fitting, and clinging to him with pure and sincere love. They place it also in the good constitution and order of all his faculties: the lower obeyed the higher and the higher obeyed God without difficulty or resistance, and he had no leaning to evil and no difficulty or reluctance in doing good, such as is now found in every single human being.

So in their view nothing in newly created man was disordered and nothing was excessive. There was no disorder (ataxia) in him and no conflict among his faculties. All of them, in the most perfect good order (eutaxia), agreed with one another and worked together toward one and the same end, the end for which God, the author of nature, had created him.

title: Natural not as part of man's essence but as created with him, like the body's proportion and beauty
english: They further maintain that this righteousness was natural to the first man before the fall and should be called natural. They do not mean that it was a part making up the essence of human nature, or that it flowed necessarily from the principles of human nature. They mean that it was created together with that nature and belonged to the native endowments of human nature before the fall. On their teaching, then, original righteousness was a natural gift, not a supernatural one.

It stood to the soul of unfallen man as the due proportion and beauty of the limbs, their strength and grace, then stood to his body. Those belonged to a natural, not a supernatural, perfection of man, even though they were not part of his essence and did not flow necessarily from the principles of human nature.

title: Survey of Reformed doctors, beginning with Tilenus: natural as opposed to supernatural, as natural as the substantial form
english: To make the Reformed school's view on this question clearer and surer, it will be worth setting out briefly how some of its leading teachers explain their meaning, all the more because there might seem to be some difference among them here.

Tilenus comes first. In the first part of his Syntagma of Theology, disputation 33, thesis 14, he says that original righteousness is rightly called natural in the sense in which natural and supernatural are set against each other and distinguished. In thesis 17 he says that this quality of original righteousness was as natural to our first parent as nature itself and the substantial form he received in creation. And in the thesis before that he says the quality shone out at once from God's original image in man, as accidents commonly do from their subjects.
translator_notes: Daniel Tilenus, Syntagma tripartitum disputationum theologicarum (Sedan).

title: Ames: original righteousness a moral condition owed to a nature made to act justly
english: William Ames, in volume 4, chapter 1 of his Bellarmine Disarmed, explains how original righteousness was natural to the first man: "We do not say that this righteousness was an essential part of physical nature or flowed from its principles in a physical way. We say it was a moral condition owed to that nature, which was created to act righteously."
translator_notes: William Ames, Bellarminus enervatus (1628), volume 4, book 1, chapter 1.

title: Placaeus: original rectitude a natural gift, propagated by generation; grace only as a free gift, not as Christ's favor to sinners
english: Josué de la Place, in the Syntagma of Saumur Theses, disputation on the state of Adam before the fall, thesis 18, says that the first man's original rectitude should be counted among natural gifts. It was nothing other than agreement with the law of nature, a perfection created together with nature and meant to be handed on by natural generation, and so a natural perfection answering to man's natural faculties.

In thesis 26 he grants that original righteousness was indeed a grace, in the sense of a free gift coming from the same three persons who created nature itself. But it was not a grace in the sense in which the word is opposed to nature and means the effects of the divine favor with which God follows sinners in Christ.
translator_notes: The theses are in the Syntagma thesium theologicarum in Academia Salmuriensi disputatarum.

title: Du Moulin: to know and love God was natural to Adam; his purity not a bridle laid on from outside
english: Pierre du Moulin explains his view on this as follows: "We maintain that before the fall it was natural for Adam to know and love God. In unfallen nature we recognize no leaning toward rebellion, for there was nothing that had to be held in check, though there was something that had to be governed. Nor do we think that Adam's purity before the fall was a bridle put on him from outside, or a rider set on his back, but a natural strength." (Disputation on the State of Innocence, thesis 25, in the Thesaurus of Sedan Theses.)
translator_notes: The 'bridle' answers Bellarmine's golden bridle (thesis X of this locus).

title: Pareus: supernatural above integral nature or above corrupt nature; original righteousness natural like sight; Bellarmine misstates the question
english: Pareus, commenting on chapter 1 of Bellarmine's book On the Grace of the First Man, says that the supernatural is whatever is in man, for his perfection, above the principles of nature or his native endowments. He divides nature into unfallen nature, as it was at creation before the fall, and corrupt nature, as it is in the state of sin. So, he notes, "supernatural" is used in two ways: for what is above unfallen nature, or for what is above corrupt nature. He grants that original righteousness was supernatural in the second way, since it surpassed corrupt nature, but denies that it was supernatural in the first way, since it did not go beyond the native endowments and perfections of unfallen nature.

On chapter 5 he says it can be defended that original righteousness was natural to the first man as a good of his nature, no less than the power of seeing or sensing. For bright knowledge of God and divine things came from his enlightened mind, and righteous and holy acts welled up from his righteous and holy will and heart as from a perfectly clear spring, no less naturally, though through free choice, than sight comes from the eye.

But he adds that there is no need to press this point. What was natural to Adam was not only whatever made up his nature or flowed of itself from the principles of that nature, but also whatever of itself accompanied the principles of nature for its perfection, and without which nature was not first made in its principles. That, he says, is the sense of "natural" our theologians chiefly have in mind when they maintain that original righteousness was natural to the first man.

From this he concludes that Bellarmine twists the point at issue when he says the question here is not whether original righteousness was natural to the first man in the sense of what is there from birth, which both sides grant, but whether it was natural as natural is distinguished from supernatural, meaning either what makes up nature or what is fitted to flow from nature's principles.
translator_notes: David Pareus, commentary against Bellarmine's De gratia primi hominis, chapters 1 and 5.

title: Rambour: original righteousness natural as native, not as flowing from nature's powers, like natural knowledge of God
english: Finally Abraham Rambour, in the Syntagma of Sedan Theses, disputation on the image of God in man and original righteousness, thesis 27, gives his view on the question in these words: "We hold that original righteousness includes the whole integrity and holiness of man, and that it was natural to him. Loving God and obeying him were planted in Adam's nature from the moment it existed, and man excelled in this gift from the moment he was made.

"We do not want this to be taken as though this holiness flowed from the powers of nature, but in the sense that this integrity was native to man, so that in him, by nature as God made him and while he stood in that state, there were no disordered movements. In the same way we call some knowledge of God natural, since nothing is so natural as what is so lodged in nature that it cannot be removed without, so to speak, nature's renouncing it on oath. This righteousness, then, shone in Adam as soon as he came into being, and he felt nothing in himself that resisted it."
translator_notes: The 1675 print reads 'huic justitiae tepugnans'; this is a misprint for 'repugnans' ('resisting'), which the translation follows. Abraham Rambour taught theology at Sedan.

title: Some Reformed make it natural as owed to nature's order; others, like Pareus, only as concreated and not superadded
english: From this it is plain that many of the Reformed openly teach that original righteousness was natural to the first man because it was a perfection of the natural order, owed to a rational creature not yet corrupted by sin, shining out, as it were, from the faculties of human nature, still taken to be pure and innocent, just as health and soundness shine out from a body that is in the condition nature intends.

Others, Pareus above all, seem to call that righteousness natural to the first man only because it was a perfection created together with him and belonged to his native, original endowments. When they deny it was supernatural, they mean only that it was not something added on top of man's first, native endowments.

title: Common Reformed view: God's goodness forbids creating man without original righteousness, prone to evil
english: However that may be, and on whatever ground original righteousness is said to have been natural to the first man, the common Reformed view seems to be that it is wholly at odds with God's goodness and wisdom for him to make man without original righteousness: a man who does not know and love God as he should, who leans and inclines toward evil, and in whom sense and appetite resist reason and rebel against God's law.

They do not believe that in a rational creature such a lack of love for God, such a headlong bent to evil and vice, and such a rebellion of sense and appetite against the mind and God's law, can be free of sin and guilt.

So they think it absurd, and an insult to the Creator, to say that this rebellion of the soul's lower faculties, with the proneness of the whole man to evil and his resistance to good that follow from it, is a consequence of man's being made of a rational soul and an organic body, something that results from that make-up necessarily and by the very nature of things unless God adds something above nature to subject reason to God and the lower part of the soul to reason.

title: So the Reformed think Rome's state of pure nature fictitious and impossible
english: They therefore regard as plainly fictitious and impossible the state of man "in a purely natural condition" that the Roman school so often speaks of. In it man is supposed to be uncorrupted by sin and yet empty of righteousness and holiness: not clinging to God with a pure and chaste love but dragged toward lower things by his own concupiscence, ignorant of what true blessedness requires, weak and unable to do good, and inclined headlong toward vice.

This can be gathered from the treatises of the Reformed teachers cited above, and of many others, where they argue about original righteousness against Bellarmine and other teachers of the Roman school.

title: Pareus will not deny God could create man without original righteousness, only that he could make man whole without wholeness
english: Pareus, however, does not venture to assert that human nature could not have been created without original righteousness. "We do not say," he writes, "that God could not have created human nature without original righteousness. Are we to put a boundary to God's power? What we do say is that when God made man whole, he could not deny himself by making a whole man without wholeness." (On Bellarmine, On the Grace of the First Man, book 1, chapter 6, reply to the fourth argument.)
translator_notes: 'He cannot deny himself' echoes 2 Timothy 2:13; the print gives no reference.

title: Many Reformed still grant Adam supernatural gifts; du Moulin: revealed knowledge and constant help were supernatural
english: Although the Reformed teachers maintain that original righteousness was natural to the first man, many of them at least will not say that he lacked all supernatural grace and that God adorned him with natural gifts only. This is especially clear in Pierre du Moulin, in the disputation on the state of innocence cited above, theses 49 and 50.

"We do not deny," he says, "that there were some supernatural gifts in Adam. If he drew any knowledge from revelation, or had anything that human nature, however pure, could not reach without a special and extraordinary gift of God, that was without doubt supernatural, and Adam would not have passed it on to his descendants even had he persevered in his integrity.

"Again, there is no doubt that a man, however perfect his body's natural balance, needs supernatural help and God's constant aid to keep that good balance (eukrasia). In the same way, though Adam's nature was pure and holy, it still needed continual supernatural help to keep that purity, since even lifeless and irrational things are upheld by God's inflowing power."
translator_notes: The 1675 print reads 'sustentur'; the translation takes it as 'sustententur' ('are sustained'). The eukrasia passage is the one Le Blanc cites in De Primi Hominis Immortalitate XXXV.

title: Rambour: grace raised Adam's natural gifts, making him a son and heir, not only a faithful servant
english: Rambour likewise recognizes supernatural gifts in Adam, in thesis 29 of the disputation just cited: "This does not mean that we take supernatural gifts away from Adam. God's grace adorned these same natural gifts and lifted them higher day by day, just as grace does not destroy nature but directs it and raises it higher than it can climb by its own strength.

"So the first man was not only an outstanding creature but also a son of God, adopted to enter into the heavenly inheritance. By nature he had the standing of a faithful servant who understood his Lord's will well and carried it out perfectly; by grace he also had the dignity of a son who hoped for his Father's blessing and inheritance."
translator_notes: Adam as 'son of God' recalls Luke 3:38, and the servant-son contrast Galatians 4:7; the print gives no references.

title: Tilenus: Rome slanders us as Pelagians; Adam's will was naturally upright but moved to act by grace, like a vine needing sun and rain
english: Similar things can be read in Tilenus: "The papists wickedly and slanderously pin the Pelagians' view on us, as though we held there were no supernatural gifts in the first man, when we expressly ascribe the theological virtues to him." (On Original Righteousness, thesis 38.)

A little earlier, explaining more precisely what the grace given to Adam consisted in, he says: "Adam's will had from nature the power to act righteously and holily; that it actually did so, and loved God above all things, came from its being moved effectively by grace.

"But a vine is not without a natural power to bear wine just because it needs outside help, such as sun, rain and tending, to bear it in fact. In the same way the uprightness of Adam's will and the good order (eutaxia) of his affections were still natural, even though in their actual exercise they were set to work and helped by moving grace."
translator_notes: 'Second act' is the scholastic term for a power in actual operation, as distinct from the power itself (first act).

title: Le Blanc: hard to see how faith, hope and love were supernatural yet righteousness natural; Rambour's statements do not fit together
