english: So Tilenus counts as supernatural grace in the first man both the actual help by which he was stirred to do good and the theological virtues, faith, hope and love, with which he was adorned. But it is hard to see how those virtues could have been supernatural gifts in Adam while his uprightness, or original righteousness, was natural to him. Or what righteousness and uprightness could please God and be accepted by him without faith, hope and love?

In the same way, in what we quoted earlier from Rambour, the things that very learned man asserts together do not seem to fit well: that the first man's righteousness and holiness was natural and not supernatural, and yet that it did not flow from the powers of nature. How can something not be supernatural if it does not flow from nature's powers?

Unless, that is, we say that he, like Pareus, calls supernatural whatever is acquired and added on top of native endowments, and calls original righteousness natural only because it was planted in man from his first origin, created together with him, and so belonged to his native endowments. That seems to be how he explains himself. Even so, what he adds does not quite square: that the first man's righteousness was natural to him as some knowledge of God is natural to us. The knowledge of God he calls natural does not go beyond nature's powers.
translator_notes: Faith, hope and love are the triad of 1 Corinthians 13:13; the print gives no reference.

title: Summary: both schools agree the first man had true righteousness and holiness, with nothing disordered
english: From what has been set out so far it is clear that the Roman and Reformed schools agree on this: before the fall the first man had true righteousness and holiness. Through it he knew God with his mind as he ought and loved him with his will, and he had nothing disordered in him, nothing at odds with God's law and will, nothing that would not freely submit to right reason.

title: Most Roman theologians agree with the Reformed that Adam was created in that righteousness
english: It is also clear from this that most theologians of the Roman school, at least, teach with the Reformed that the first man was created in that righteousness and holiness. He was therefore never without it; it was planted in him from his first origin.

title: Hence most Roman doctors grant it was natural in the sense of native, not acquired
english: It plainly follows that most teachers of the Roman Church grant, with the Protestants, that original righteousness was natural to the first man in the sense in which "natural" means the same as "native" and is opposed to what is acquired and added on top.

title: Some in Rome even hold, with most Reformed, that it was natural as opposed to supernatural
english: In fact, what we reported earlier shows that the Roman Church has its own teachers who side with most of the Reformed here. They hold that original righteousness was one of nature's gifts, not one of grace's, taking grace as the opposite of nature. On their view it was natural to the first man even in the sense that stands against "supernatural".
translator_notes: Le Blanc means Medina's 'certain doctors' and those condemned with Baius (theses IV-V).

title: Many in Rome grant the Reformed that God could not create man without it, so pure nature is a fiction
english: Again, as can be gathered from what has been said, a good many in the Roman Church grant the Reformed that original righteousness, whatever it should finally be called, natural or supernatural, was a perfection so owed to innocent man that God could not have created him without it without compromising his wisdom and goodness.

They grant too that the state of man in a purely natural condition, as the ordinary run of the Roman school describes it, in which man is supposed to be no sinner and yet empty of righteousness, prone to vice and struggling with a concupiscence that fights right reason, is a mere fiction, something God's goodness, justice and wisdom forbid ever to exist in reality.
translator_notes: The Jansenists of theses XII-XVI are the chief Roman examples.

title: The Protestants in turn grant it was not natural as constituting nature; many allow supernatural gifts and needed grace
english: The Protestants, for their part, grant the teachers of the Roman school that original righteousness was not natural to the first man in the sense of what makes up nature, or of what flows necessarily, that is physically, from the principles of human nature.

Many teachers of the Reformed school also do not deny that the first man had some supernatural gifts, and that even innocent man needed some grace in order to act rightly and righteously. Some of them even admit that original righteousness did not flow from the powers of nature.

title: The real controversy: natural or supernatural; real for some Reformed, verbal for others
english: The real dispute here, between the Roman school (with very few exceptions) and the Reformed school, is whether original righteousness was natural or supernatural to the first man. The Reformed teachers say by common consent that it was natural and not supernatural; almost all the Roman theologians, on the other hand, insist that it was supernatural and not natural.

With some theologians this dispute seems to be about substance, with others only about words. It is a dispute of substance with those who hold that original righteousness was a perfection of the natural order, answering to man's natural faculties and belonging to nature rather than to grace. When the Roman theologians call that righteousness supernatural, they really do mean the opposite.

With the others it is a dispute about words. They teach that original righteousness was natural to the first man only because it was created with him and should be counted among his native endowments, and when they deny that it was supernatural they mean only that it was not added to man over and above his first endowments. That the Roman teachers grant, or a great many of them do.

title: A further question: does God's wisdom forbid creating man without it, and is 'pure nature' a possible state?
english: There is a further question between the Reformed school and a great many Roman teachers: whether it is not contrary to God's wisdom and goodness for man to be created without original righteousness, and whether the state the Roman school calls "pure nature" should be counted among man's possible states.

In that state man would not be corrupted by sin, yet would lack true righteousness, would struggle with much ignorance and weakness, and would be drawn toward evil by his own concupiscence and by an appetite rebelling against reason, just as things are in the state of corrupt nature. The ordinary run of Roman teachers says yes; the Reformed school, with perhaps one or two exceptions, says no by common consent.

title: First absurdity: God would be the author of concupiscence, which John says is not of the Father; Bellarmine's rust analogy fails
english: Indeed, unless we hold this, the gravest absurdities follow. First, it will follow that God himself could be the author of the concupiscence by which the flesh fights against the spirit, since on this hypothesis he could have created man with it. Yet the Roman teachers grant that this concupiscence, even after original sin has been forgiven, has the character of a vice and of a moral evil that God finds displeasing and hateful, and John denies that it comes from the Father.

Bellarmine's reply does not remove the force of this argument. He says that concupiscence would have arisen from matter apart from God's intention, as rust arises on a sword, and the smith is not therefore its author. But the smith did not make the iron from which the rust comes, whereas God did create the matter of our bodies. And even so, rust cannot be on a sword fresh from the smith's hands unless the smith is at fault.
translator_notes: The flesh fighting the spirit is Galatians 5:17; John's denial that the lust of the flesh is 'of the Father' is 1 John 2:16. The print gives no references. Bellarmine's rust analogy is in De gratia primi hominis, chapter 5.

title: Otherwise God would be the author of sin, or a rational creature could commit every crime without guilt
english: Suppose God created a man with the same ignorance, the same leaning toward evil and resistance to good with which we are now born of Adam, and chose not to help him with any supernatural grace, as the scholastics commonly think could happen. That man would not love God or shape his acts and affections by the rule of right reason. He would give way to his desires in everything and would inevitably plunge into one crime after another as occasion arose, just as a child of Adam would do if he were left without any help from God's grace.

God would then be the author of sin, since he would have created a man who, through no fault of his own but simply because God chose to make him so, cannot avoid sin, rushes headlong into crimes of every kind by a flaw and drive in his nature, and cannot love his Creator as he ought.

Otherwise we would have to say there could be a rational creature not bound to know and love God, one that could defile itself with every impurity, give way to anger, excess and gluttony, assault its fellows with rape and murder, and do everything else the natural and eternal law forbids, and still not be guilty of any crime or sin. Both conclusions are utterly absurd and plainly involve impiety.
translator_notes: The 1675 print reads 'patrari' (passive) where the construction needs 'patrare'; the translation follows the active sense.

title: Granting that, whether original righteousness is called natural or supernatural matters less, if it is God's free gift
english: Once it is granted that God cannot create man without righteousness and holiness, the other question does not seem so important: whether the righteousness and holiness in which God made the first man, and without which God could not have created him, belongs to the endowments of nature or of grace, and should be called natural or supernatural. That holds provided we affirm, as everyone grants, that it is God's free gift, owed to no merit of the creature.

title: Yet reason favors calling it natural: what belongs to nature's right constitution and health is natural
english: Still, reason seems to require us to say that it belonged to the endowments of nature and was natural rather than supernatural. What belongs to the right constitution of a nature, without which that nature is neither healthy nor rightly formed, is natural, not supernatural.

Human nature without the holiness and righteousness that unfallen man had is not healthy but sick, and cannot be called rightly formed, if indeed the rebellion of the lower faculties against reason and the whole man's tendency to rebel against God are a disease and a defect of rational nature.

title: Second reason: what a rational creature needs to reach its natural end, knowing and loving God, is natural
english: Further, what an uncorrupted rational creature needs in order to reach its natural end is natural to it. The end of a rational creature is to know, love and worship God, for that is what God made it for.
It cannot reach that end if it is created without righteousness and holiness, that is, if it is thought of as stripped of the gifts we lost through Adam's sin.
translator_notes: The final printed sentence, 'Et si consideretur ut destituta donis illis quae per Adami peccatum amisimus', is a fragment; the translation reads it as restating the preceding condition.

title: Third reason: every natural faculty has its natural perfection, and for the moral faculties that is righteousness
english: Again, there is no natural faculty without a natural perfection that belongs to it. Man's moral faculties, which make him capable of virtue and vice, are as natural to him as his other faculties. What can their natural perfection be, if not the very righteousness and holiness now in question?

title: Fourth reason: conformity to the law of nature belongs to pure nature, so the righteousness that makes it possible is natural
english: Add that it belongs to the endowments of nature in a rational creature that is not corrupt but pure to conform to the law of nature and shape itself by its rules. So whatever it needs in order to conform to the law of nature and bring all its impulses under it does not go beyond the endowments and order of nature.

But a man without any righteousness or holiness, and subject to the weaknesses we are born with today, cannot shape himself by the law of nature. So the holiness and righteousness that remove such weaknesses must be counted among the gifts of uncorrupted nature.

title: So it is inconsistent to say righteousness was natural yet Adam needed supernatural help to act; God's constant help can be of the natural order
english: So it also seems not quite reasonable for some of the Reformed cited above to say that, although the righteousness and holiness in which the first man was created were natural to him, he still needed a supernatural help to move and stir him to do good.

It is certain that without God's constant help man never does any good, not only in spiritual matters but not even in civil and human ones, so that even before the fall man needed the continual help of God, in whom we live and move and have our being. But that help did not have to be of the supernatural order. Help that did not go beyond the order of nature as God first established it could have been enough. The help a creature not yet corrupted and spoiled needs in order to act in keeping with its nature and tend toward its natural end should be reckoned as belonging to the order of nature.
translator_notes: Acts 17:28 is quoted without reference in the print. Le Blanc answers du Moulin and Tilenus (theses XXXVII and XXXIX).

title: Still, God may have added supernatural gifts; Scripture is clear only that he revealed himself to Adam
english: It does not follow, however, that what many of the Reformed explicitly teach is false, namely that the first man had some supernatural gifts. God could have added to the endowments of man's first nature, and to the help it needed, whatever he pleased above nature. But what that was and how much, we do not venture to define, since Scripture is silent.
One thing Scripture does make certain: the first man had a certain supernatural knowledge, since God revealed himself to him beyond nature and taught him his will in express words.
translator_notes: God's express word to Adam is the command of Genesis 2:16-17; the print gives no reference.

title: Body and soul do not make conflict natural: right order subjects the body's leanings to the soul
english: It does not follow, from man's being made of an earthly body and a spiritual soul, that the conflict of sense and appetite with reason is natural in him, or that such conflict and rebellion can only be removed by a supernatural gift.

Man does naturally have two inclinations, one toward earthly good because he has a body, the other toward spiritual good because he has an intelligent soul. But as the soul far surpasses its body, so a rightly formed nature requires that the body's impulses and inclinations be subject to the soul's commands, and so that appetite obey reason. Where it is otherwise, nature is plainly out of order.
translator_notes: Le Blanc answers Bellarmine's two-propension argument (thesis IX).

title: Nor is the fall hard to explain if rectitude was natural: the higher part turned from God, and disorder followed. De Justitia Primi Hominis closes
english: Nor, granting that the rectitude created with man was itself natural and not supernatural, is it as hard as Bellarmine thinks to show how the corruption now in us, which forces reason to be subject to the passions, got into human nature.

That flaw began in the higher part of the soul, when it turned away from God and began to be carried toward the object of the sense appetite as though that were its end. The disorder (ataxia) of man's moral faculties followed from that. Their original rectitude lay in all their impulses and affections being directed, at the command of mind and reason, toward God as their highest end. Reason cannot turn aside from that end and put earthly goods in its place without being forced to serve sense and appetite, shamefully and against its own nature, since their object now stands for it in place of the highest end.

title: Roman teachers charge Calvin and the Reformed with taking free choice away from man
english: Most teachers of the Roman Church commonly accuse Calvin and those who share his religious position of removing free choice from man and stripping him of any freedom in what he does. At the least, they say, these men teach that sin destroyed free choice in man altogether.

One example is the Jesuit Bailly, in the catechism that Rivet answers in his Summary of Controversies (treatise 4, question 4). There Bailly argues against the Reformed as if they flatly denied that man has free choice.

Another is the Jesuit Martin Becanus. In his Summa of Scholastic Theology (treatise 1, chapter 2, question 9) he says that Lutherans and Calvinists hold that the sin of our first parent completely did away with free choice.
translator_notes: Bailius (Bailly) the Jesuit, Catechism, answered by Rivet, Summa Controversiarum, tract. 4, q. 4; Martin Becanus, Summa theologiae scholasticae, tract. 1, cap. 2, q. 9.

title: The Reformed hold that free choice belongs to the rational creature and was not lost by sin
english: Yet all the Reformed consistently hold that free choice, taken simply and in its own nature and essence, cannot be separated from a rational creature. So sin did not wholly remove man's power to act freely.

Indeed, man corrupted by sin acts no less freely in what he does than he did before sin. If he is left to himself and gives way to sin, he does it with complete freedom. If grace moves and rouses him to pursue a better life, those acts are free too, and the efficacy of God's grace takes nothing away from his will's freedom.

title: Free choice is not an act or habit but a faculty, belonging to man as he has intellect and will
english: They also agree that the free choice which cannot be separated from man is not an act or a habit. It is rather a faculty of the soul.
Even so, the name does not mean some faculty distinct from mind and will. Man has free choice because he has an intellect and a will.

title: Many Reformed oppose liberty only to compulsion and define it as freedom from compulsion
english: They do not all explain in the same way what the freedom consists in that makes man free in acting and gives his choice the name free.

To begin with, a good many of the Reformed teach that the freedom by which man is said to have free choice is not set against bondage, or against necessity as such, but against compulsion. They mostly talk as if compulsion were the only thing that destroys freedom, and they describe freedom as exemption from compulsion.

title: They add that the agent must act from counsel and reason, not mere impulse of nature
english: They do not mean, though, that everything that acts of its own accord and without compulsion acts freely. They grant that animals act of their own accord, yet they deny them freedom.

So for freedom they also require that the agent not simply be driven by nature's impulse but act from deliberation and reason. On their view, then, the full definition of freedom is exemption from compulsion in an agent who acts on the judgement of reason.

title: Wendelin and Ursinus define free choice as choosing without compulsion what the intellect shows
english: Thus Marcus Wendelin, explaining thesis 18 in his Christian Theology (book 1, chapter 5), defines free choice as "a disposition of the will by which, moving itself and without compulsion, it chooses or rejects what the intellect sets before it."

Zacharias Ursinus gives a similar definition in his Catechetical Explanations (part 1, question 8, number 1): "Free choice, then, is a faculty or power of willing or not willing, of choosing or rejecting, an object that the intellect sets before it, by its own movement and without compulsion."
translator_notes: Marcus Friedrich Wendelin, Christianae theologiae libri duo, book 1, chapter 5, thesis 18; Zacharias Ursinus, Explicationes catecheticae, part 1, question 8, number 1.

title: On this view freedom lies in willingness, not indifference; Wendelin says the blessed praise God freely though they cannot not praise
english: It follows from this view that freedom properly lies in the willingness with which the will follows the intellect's judgement. It does not lie in any indifference of the will or any power for opposites, since the will's freedom can exist without these, even though in fact the will is indifferent toward many of its acts. Wendelin teaches this in the same passage.

After giving the definition quoted above, he adds: "This is enough, in general, for freedom of choice. Some add that through free choice the will by its nature stays able to choose the opposite or something else, or to hold back from acting. That does not belong to free choice in general.

"For freedom of choice also exists without indifference to either of two opposites, which they call the freedom of contrariety. So it is also freedom when the will is fixed on one of two opposites. That is how it is with the blessed: they do good freely, yet being confirmed in good they cannot do evil.
"Indeed, not even the freedom of contradiction is strictly necessary to freedom of choice. The blessed praise God freely, and yet they cannot fail to praise him."
translator_notes: Liberty of contrariety is the power to choose either of two contraries (this or its opposite); liberty of contradiction is the power to act or not act.

title: Wendelin and Ursinus make every voluntary act free, so that God is freely good because not by compulsion
english: He and those who agree with him admit a difference among the will's acts: the will is fixed on some of them, while toward others it stays by nature able to go either way. Still they hold that the will should be called free with respect to both kinds, and that both kinds come freely from the will.

So they do distinguish between what is simply voluntary and what comes from choice, but they draw no line between the voluntary and the free. They want the two to cover the same ground, so that whatever is voluntary is free for that very reason. They do not think any necessity destroys the nature of freedom unless it also destroys the nature of the voluntary.

They therefore teach that God, though good by nature, is freely good, because his goodness is not forced but willed. Ursinus says this in the passage cited above: "What is free is called hekousion, that is, spontaneous. It is the opposite of akousion, the involuntary and forced, but not of anankaion, the necessary.

"Hekousion can go with anankaion, but not with akousion. God and the holy angels are good anankaios, that is, necessarily, yet not akousios, that is, under force; they are good most freely, because the source of their goodness is in themselves, a free will."
translator_notes: Ursinus' Greek terms are transliterated in Pass B: hekousion (voluntary), akousion (involuntary), anankaion (necessary).

title: Others oppose liberty also to natural necessity, determination by matter or by sense
english: Others state plainly and precisely that the freedom by which man is called free in acting is not exemption from compulsion alone, compulsion being the necessity imposed by an outside agent's force against the inclination of the thing compelled. That freedom, they say, is also opposed to natural necessity, that is, to being fixed by nature on one outcome.

This natural necessity, on their account, comes from matter, and in two ways. In one, the outward action does not depend on any inner act that commands it. Once the faculty is there and a material object is brought to it from outside, the action must take place, and with just this character and this strength. Everything without sense and reason is subject to this necessity.

In the other, the outward action does depend on an inner command, so that it can be held back and need not always happen the same way, yet what settles it comes only from something material. That is the case with animals. Their outward actions depend on sense and are directed by it, and they vary a great deal even toward one and the same object as their senses are affected in different ways, inwardly and outwardly. But their senses themselves are always moved and settled by some material object.

Man is free of both kinds of necessity. In the acts for which he is said to have free choice, he is not settled in acting by matter brought to him from outside, or even by material sense alone. Being an intellectual agent, he acts and desires on the judgement and command of reason.

title: Hence rational agents are masters of their actions, unlike things moved only by sense
english: This is where they locate freedom of choice. Those who act on reason's judgement know their end, set it before themselves, and direct and fit their actions to it, so that in a sense they are masters of what they do.

Lifeless things and animals that are led by sense alone, by contrast, do not know their end. So they do not direct themselves to it but only move toward it like slaves, who carry out orders without knowing why they are given or what they are for. They do not so much act for an end as get moved toward an end by a higher agent.

Besides, the sense and appetite of animals are tied to material things. Human will follows the lead of mind and reason, whose objects are not only things of sense but things of the intellect, not only present things but future ones. It ranges over every kind, mode and degree of good and is shut in, so to speak, by no limits. From this comes the great variety in what men desire and choose, and also in their outward actions.

title: Josué de la Place: freedom is exemption from compulsion, from matter, and from sense
english: This is set out more fully by Josué de la Place, professor at the Academy of Saumur a few years ago, in his treatise On Man's Free Choice. There he sums up what he had argued at length before: "The natural freedom of the will consists in this. Being free of compulsion and of the necessity of matter and of things of sense, it can take as its object, in any place and at any time, things immaterial as well as material, of the intellect as well as of sense, future as well as present, honourable as well as useful or pleasant, and their opposites, in short every order, degree and relation of goods and evils.

"It can choose the final end, the intermediate ends and the means that lead to them as it judges fit, that is, by the judgement of the practical mind. Without that judgement it would not even be rational, let alone free."

Later he repeats, as his own view, that not every necessity clashes with the will, meaning with freedom of choice, but only the necessity that comes from compulsion, or from matter without sense, or from sense without reason. Likewise he says freedom lies in exemption from three necessities: compulsion, being settled by matter, and being settled by sense.
translator_notes: Josué de la Place (Placaeus), professor at Saumur, treatise De libero hominis arbitrio.

title: Some exclude all natural necessity and require deliberation, distinguishing the voluntary from the free
english: Some, however, think that exemption from compulsion and from being settled by matter or sense is not enough for human actions to be free. In their view freedom also rules out every kind of natural necessity, even one that does not come from matter or sense.

Nor do they think it enough for a free action that a man act on reason's judgement in any way at all. The judgement must be the conclusion of some deliberation and weighing. Only those things are done freely by us, then, about which we can take counsel and deliberate.

Now there are some acts of our will to which it is fixed by nature and about which no one ever deliberates, such as the act by which we want to be happy and do not want to be miserable. They do not hold that the will is free in these. Nor do they think it acts as a free cause in the impulses that rise in it suddenly from some violent disturbance before our mind can collect itself and begin to deliberate.
That is why they distinguish the free from the voluntary and hold that the voluntary is the wider class, since not everything voluntary is free.

title: Rivet: freedom excludes natural necessity and requires prior deliberation
english: This is the teaching of Andrew Rivet, formerly professor at the Academy of Leiden, in his Summary of Controversies (treatise 4, question 3): "We acknowledge that the nature of freedom cannot coexist with compulsion in the proper sense, nor with natural necessity either, by which an agent is fixed by nature on one outcome. It is not enough for freedom that a man does something of his own accord, since natural causes do that too. Prior deliberation and a judgement of reason are required, and these have no place where nature's necessity settles the act."

Later he says: "We distinguish three points in freedom, by which we explain the nature of free choice in itself. 1. Freedom is in a subject, namely the will. Acting from its own inner principle without reasoning or deliberation, the will always acts of its own accord and without compulsion; acting with counsel and deliberation, it acts freely and without necessity.

"Without the first freedom, from compulsion, the nature of the will is destroyed, for necessity is laid on the will that it cannot be forced in what they call its elicited act. Without deliberation arising from the intellect's indifference, it cannot will freely, since it would then be fixed by nature on one outcome."

So with Thomas he calls free choice an elective power. And with Bellarmine he grants that it belongs to the essence of free choice that one has the option between different things and that the choice is made with a full and complete judgement of reason.
translator_notes: Andrew Rivet, Summa controversiarum, tract. 4, q. 3. An elicited act is one the will itself produces, as distinct from an act it commands another faculty to do.

title: Amyraut distinguishes motions of the will that follow deliberation from those that do not
english: Moses Amyraut, until recently professor at the Academy of Saumur, teaches much the same on this point in his treatise On Man's Free Choice (p. 61 and following). He first distinguishes two movements of the will.

One is not cut off from the knowledge that has its source in reason, but the knowledge from which it springs and grows did not itself come out of any prior weighing. The other is not only joined with knowledge but arises from knowledge that consultation (probouleusis) went before. That knowledge is simply the conclusion reached by deliberation, when several objects are considered and compared, or one and the same object is looked at in different ways, so that the mind, swung this way and that for a while by the weight of reasons, finally leans to one side.

Next he observes that the movement of the will that follows no weighing or deliberation by the mind is itself of two kinds. By one the will is carried toward the end, namely happiness and blessedness itself; by the other toward the means thought to lead to that end.
translator_notes: Moses Amyraut, De libero hominis arbitrio, p. 61 ff. Probouleusis is Aristotle's term for the deliberation that precedes choice.

title: Amyraut: neither movement belongs to free choice, which needs prior deliberation (prohairesis)
english: Then he shows that neither movement belongs to free choice. Not the first, because free choice is what Aristotle called prohairesis, and as he says, "every prohairesis is preceded by some probouleusis. No one deliberates about that final end; one is carried toward it not only by necessity but without any prior deliberation (aprobouleutos)."

Not the second either: though it differs from the first, it is just as much without prior deliberation. It is so sudden and so quick, whether it comes from some disturbance or bursts out at the sight of something great, unforeseen and unexpected, that it gets ahead of all weighing. He infers that such a movement is indeed hekousion, spontaneous and voluntary, but not prohairetikon, free and elective.

This is why it is rightly said that the first stirrings of our passions are not in our power. Only the things we take counsel about, whether we should take them up or leave them alone, are in our power, and we do not count as in our power what runs ahead of all deliberation.

So at last he concludes (p. 65): "What belongs to our choice, then, must be the things we can deliberate about. And we should say that those things come from our free choice which we have deliberated about in such a way that desire followed the deliberation and weighing. That, as we have often said, is where prohairesis lies."
translator_notes: Amyraut, De libero hominis arbitrio, p. 65. The Greek terms (prohairesis, probouleusis, hekousion, prohairetikon) come from Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.

title: Some also exclude the motive or impulsive necessity that God might impose
english: Beyond the necessity that comes from compulsion, from matter, from sense or from any other settling by nature, there is a necessity thought to come from an outside cause, God himself for instance, moving and driving the faculty in such a way that he lays on it a true necessity of acting. That is, he removes from the agent the power to act otherwise, even though the agent is supposed to act of his own accord and not unwillingly. The schools call this motive or impulsive necessity.

Some among the Reformed think that this necessity too clashes with human freedom. They hold that freedom cannot coexist with any necessity in the proper sense, what the schools call necessity of the consequent, as opposed to necessity of the consequence.

title: Ames: free choice is free from all necessity as to the exercise of its act, though it acts infallibly under God's ordination
english: William Ames, formerly theologian at the Academy of Franeker, takes this view. In his Bellarmine Disarmed (volume 4, book 4, chapter 1) he writes: "We grant that free choice, in what it does, is free from all necessity.
"Properly speaking it cannot act by necessity as regards the exercise of its act, even though, with respect to God's ordaining, it acts certainly and infallibly."
translator_notes: William Ames, Bellarminus enervatus, tom. 4, lib. 4, cap. 1.

title: Baron: the will is not bound by necessity of the consequent nor by any motive necessity from God
english: Robert Baron, formerly professor at the Academy of Aberdeen, holds the same in his General Metaphysics Adapted to the Use of Theology. Among much else he makes two claims there.

First, the will is not held or bound, in producing its acts, by necessity in the absolute sense, what they call necessity of the consequent. Second, the will, even of fallen man, is not held by any motive or impulsive necessity with respect to God.

"He too," Baron says, "gave men free choice. So he does not do away with that faculty entirely by laying necessity on it, either through his eternal decree or through a motion and bending in time." (Section 12, Disputation 1, On Freedom of Choice, number 17.)
translator_notes: Robert Baron, Metaphysica generalis, sect. 12, disp. 1, De libertate arbitrii, num. 17.

title: Le Blanc: the first view does not really differ from the second, only states it less distinctly
english: To give my own view as well: I think the first opinion, which defines freedom as exemption from compulsion in an agent acting on reason's judgement, does not differ in substance from the second, which opposes freedom not only to compulsion but also to the necessity that comes from matter or sense, called by some physical necessity.

The first opinion holds that exemption from compulsion does not deserve the name of freedom except in a being that uses reason. Plainly, then, it assumes that freedom requires the agent to follow reason's judgement and not to be settled by matter or sense. So the second opinion differs from the first only in being stated more precisely and more fully.

title: Both views wrongly confuse the free with the voluntary
english: Both views share one drawback: they wholly confuse the free with the voluntary and hold that every act of the will is free. In the common understanding of men and in ordinary usage, we call free only what is in our power, what could be otherwise, and what we are allowed to weigh and deliberate about.

But as shown above, there are acts of the will to which it is so fixed by nature that they cannot be otherwise in any way, and about which no deliberation can be held. Further, every act that comes from us freely can fall under precepts and be commanded or forbidden by some law, divine or human. That does not fit at all the acts toward which the will stands quite unchangeably, so that in no state could it, or ever can it, act otherwise.

Lastly, the men we are dealing with admit a great difference among the will's acts. Some are in our power, so that we can weigh and deliberate about them and, as the practical mind judges one way or another, do them, leave them undone, or even do the opposite; the others are of a quite different kind. Why, then, will they not give things that differ in nature different names too, and, following the usage of the schools, reserve 'free' for the first and 'voluntary' for the second? A wise man does not leave the common way of speaking without need.

title: Some distinguish free choice broadly taken (intellectual spontaneity) from free choice strictly taken
english: Among the learned men who seem to confuse the free and the voluntary, some point out that freedom of the will, or free choice, is taken in two ways, a broad one and a strict one.

Freedom of the will in general, or in the broad sense, is for them nothing but to hekousion noetikon, intellectual spontaneity, that is, spontaneity led by the light or judgement of the intellect. This general freedom of the will properly consists in the will's having mastery over its act to the extent that it can never be forced. Instead it moves or restrains itself, acts or refrains, as it pleases, for some definite reason, consideration or judgement.

title: On their view this broad freedom is exercised even toward the last end, and natural necessity does not lessen it
english: This, in their view, is the freedom the will exercises in all its acts. It does so not only when dealing with the means to the end, or with things that contribute little or nothing to the end, but also when dealing with the end itself.
So the necessity that flows from the will's nature and agrees with it, by which the will is set on pursuing the highest end, in no way destroys or lessens this freedom of the will.

title: Strict free choice concerns means and what is in our power, and includes indifference
english: Freedom in the stricter sense, or free choice, is by their own admission limited to means directed to the end, or to things that contribute little or nothing to it. It concerns ta eph' hemin, the things in our power, and Aristotle rightly defines it as the spontaneous arising from prior deliberation, or deliberative desire for things in our power.

In this sense acts are called free when they are purely contingent and we can do them or not do them as we choose. Taken so, freedom includes a kind of indifference. The will is free only in so far as it is indifferent, that is, able to act or not act toward the same object, and able to choose this, or something else, or its opposite.

In this sense God does not love himself freely, since he wills and loves himself by the necessity of his nature. Nor does man freely want to be happy and not want to be miserable, since he wills this, and cannot will otherwise, by a natural necessity.
translator_notes: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.3, defines choice as deliberate desire of things in our power.

title: Strang and Alexander More likewise distinguish free choice broadly and strictly taken
english: This is the teaching of John Strang, Doctor of Sacred Theology and principal professor at the Academy of Glasgow, in his treatise On the Will and Actions of God concerning Sin (book 3, chapter 14). After setting out and developing what we have described, he says he does not deny that the term free choice is rightly used in that strict sense, though in another and wider sense he maintains that all the will's acts are free.

The famous Alexander More draws the same kind of distinction in his On Grace and Free Choice (disputation 1, thesis 28). He offers two definitions, one of free choice in the wider sense and one of free choice in the strict sense.

In the first sense he describes free choice as "the endowment most proper to an intelligent nature, by which it wills or shuns nothing except what it has understood to be good or evil." In the second, it is "the will as it chooses means set before it by the intellect after deliberation."
translator_notes: John Strang, De voluntate et actionibus Dei circa peccatum, lib. 3, cap. 14; Alexander More, De gratia et libero arbitrio, disp. 1, thesis 28.

title: The dispute over whether all acts of the will are free is a mere quarrel about words
english: So it is clear, as Strang admits in the passage cited, that the dispute between those who say all the will's acts are free and those who deny it is merely a quarrel about words (logomachia).

Those who say so take freedom broadly, as the willingness with which the will readily follows the intellect's judgement; in that sense no one would deny that every act of the will without exception is free. Those who deny it take freedom as the openness and indifference by nature that the will has toward acts that come under weighing and deliberation. In that sense it is obvious, and everyone grants, that the will is not free with respect to some of its acts.

But the broader use of 'freedom' is less accepted and less common, and we should speak with the majority as far as we can. So when we speak without qualification, it is entirely proper to deny rather than affirm that the will is free in acts where it exercises only the first kind of freedom and not the second, strict kind.
translator_notes: Strang, De voluntate et actionibus Dei circa peccatum, book 3, chapter 14.

title: The third view is too timid in not claiming freedom from all necessity in the proper sense
english: Further, the third opinion seems overly timid in not daring to claim that human actions are free from every necessity in the proper sense. Its fear, of course, is that this would take something away from the unchangeableness of God's decrees, the efficacy of his grace, or the will's being settled by the judgement of practical reason.

But to keep the efficacy of providence and divine grace, the force and unchangeableness of God's decrees, and the mind's rights over the will, there is no need to subject man's free choice to any necessity in the proper sense. The most learned men among the Reformed show this, and we hope, God willing, to show it with them.

title: With Ames and Baron, Le Blanc opposes freedom to every necessity properly so called
english: So, with Ames and Robert Baron, we are not afraid to say that the freedom of human choice is opposed to every necessity in the proper sense. Strictly and properly speaking, no human act is free unless we grant that man has a real, inward power to act otherwise, or at least to hold back his act and stop acting.
By necessity in the proper sense we mean what fixes the agent on a given action in such a way that no real, inward power remains in him not to act or to act otherwise.

title: Indifference means a real power to act or not, which remains even after the agent has decided
english: So it is not wrong to place man's freedom in acting in a certain openness and indifference he has toward his acts.

Note, however, that this indifference does not mean, as some seem to suppose, the uncertain state of a man who wavers and has not yet settled which way to turn and lean. It means a real power to act or not act, and to arrange his action one way or another. That power remains even in someone who by his own judgement and choice has settled on these actions or those, and for whom it is fixed and decided to do this and nothing else.

title: The common definition, able to act or not when all requisites are present, has a good sense: simultaneity of power, not power of simultaneity
english: The common definition places human freedom in a man's being able, when everything needed for acting is present, to act or not act, or to do this or that. Some misuse it, but it can bear a good and suitable sense.

In all deliberate actions, which alone are free in the proper and strict sense, a man has a true and real power not to act or to act otherwise, not only before he acts but while he is acting. He cannot, of course, do two opposite things at once, or act and stop acting at the same time. Yet while he does the one, the power for the opposite act, or for stopping, remains in him.

The schoolmen express this by saying that free choice has a simultaneity of power for opposites, but not a power of simultaneity, that is, a power to have the opposites at once. The reason is that a power for one act is not opposed to a power for not doing it or for doing the contrary, whereas two contraries or contradictories cannot be in the same subject at once.

title: Strang grants that strict free choice has active indifference, free of all antecedent necessity, even under divine determination
english: Besides the authors of the fourth opinion, John Strang admits this in the same third book, chapter 15. He denies that this is the definition of freedom in general, but grants that it fits free choice in the stricter sense, in that, whatever the prerequisites for acting, free choice keeps an active indifference that frees it from all antecedent necessity, whether that comes from divine predetermination or from the nature of the will itself and some particular state of the object (p. 698). And this stricter use of 'freedom' is the most common, and should therefore be counted the most proper.

He explains the matter this way (p. 696): "In things that concern the end, or in matters indifferent, where the intellect need not judge that they are necessarily connected with the good in general, it is true in the divided sense, of elicited and of commanded actions alike, that the will keeps the power to do this or that, or to act or not act. It keeps it not only when everything prerequisite to action is present, but also when it has been settled to act, whether by God or by itself, and while it is acting.

"In such things, then, the will stays free, and acts altogether freely, not only before it is settled and acts but also when it is settled and acts. Even while acting it keeps the faculty by which it could refrain, although on the hypothesis that it is settled or acting it cannot fail to act. Whatever is, given that it is, is necessarily, though taken simply it is a contingent thing.

"So once divine determination is granted, whether by efficacious grace or in any other way, there follows a necessity of the consequence, namely that the act of the will to which God has settled it follows infallibly. But there is no necessity of the consequent, because the act remains contingent by its nature."
translator_notes: John Strang, De voluntate et actionibus Dei circa peccatum, book 3, chapter 15, pp. 696, 698. The 'divided sense' takes the power and the condition separately, as opposed to the 'composite sense' that takes them together.

title: Rivet accepts the definition in the divided sense, following Diego Alvarez
english: Andrew Rivet, too, does not object to calling free choice the faculty of the will by which, when everything prerequisite for acting is present, it can act or not act, provided this is taken in the divided sense and not the composite.

His words, in the Summary of Controversies (treatise 4, question 3), are: "That is, if one says that when all the antecedent requisites for the act are present, in order of reason or of time, free choice can act or not act, meaning that together with those same prerequisites there is in free choice the faculty and power by which it can act or not act if it wills, as Diego Alvarez distinguishes. For even God's efficacious motion, by which the will is settled on such an act, does not take from free choice the faculty to do that act or the contrary one. It only brings it about that free choice, though able to do or not do such an act, does it infallibly, yet freely."

He adds that created free choice, not only before it is settled on one act but at the very instant in which God settles it and it settles itself on that act, has at the same time the power by which it can produce the contrary act if it wills. It does not, however, have a power to have the contrary act at the same time, because two contrary acts cannot be in one power at once, only one after the other.
translator_notes: Andrew Rivet, Summa controversiarum, tract. 4, q. 3, citing the Dominican Diego Alvarez.

title: Crocius defines liberty as the will's natural property to choose and to take up or suspend action
english: Ludwig Crocius in particular, while he lived doctor and professor of theology at the School of Bremen, gives this definition of freedom and no other: "The freedom of the human will is its natural property by which it can choose what the intellect or sense sets before it under the aspect of good, and, when everything needed for acting is present, can will to take up an action or to hold it back." (Theological Syntagma, book 3, chapter 37, thesis 3.)

He adds there that the ancient Fathers spoke of free choice in the same sense. And in explaining the same thesis he notes that freedom, the will's natural property, is opposed to necessity, whether it comes from an outside cause that compels or from nature fixing the will inwardly and absolutely on one outcome.
translator_notes: Ludwig Crocius, Syntagma sacrae theologiae, book 3, chapter 37, thesis 3.

title: The power to do evil is no part of the essence of freedom: God, the confirmed angels and the blessed cannot sin, yet are free
english: When freedom is placed in a certain indifference of acting, in the free agent's being able to act or not act, to do this or that, we must take great care not to read this as if it belonged to the essence of freedom that the free agent can do either good or evil.

Being able to do evil is no part of freedom's perfection. It is rather an imperfection that goes along with freedom in a created person, something accidental to it. God, the freest of all agents, cannot do evil. Neither can the holy angels, from the time God confirmed them in grace.
This is also the privilege of the blessed souls once admitted to the vision of God: they can never sin again. Yet that does not mean the holy angels or the blessed souls have lost their freedom.

title: Conversely, the power to do good can be absent while freedom remains, as in demons, the damned and fallen man
english: On the other hand, being able to do good and to do what is acceptable and pleasing to God is a perfection that a free agent can lack while the nature and essence of freedom stay intact.

Everyone agrees that freedom in acting has remained in the demons, the angels of darkness, and that it does not wholly perish in men whom God has given over to eternal damnation. Yet neither the devil nor the damned can do good or do anything God approves.

Indeed, even in this life man corrupted by sin and lacking God's grace cannot achieve anything truly good and pleasing to God. As our Lord says, "Without me you can do nothing" (John 15:5), and the Apostle agrees: "Not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as from ourselves; our sufficiency is from God" (2 Corinthians 3:5). And still a man who is hardened and plainly abandoned by God keeps his freedom in acting.
translator_notes: Le Blanc gives the references after the thesis: John 15:5; 2 Corinthians 3:5.

title: God cannot create a rational creature unable to do good, but a creature can bring evil habits on itself
english: It does clash with God's goodness, justice and wisdom for him to form an intelligent or rational, and therefore free, creature that cannot do good and has some necessity of doing evil placed in it by God himself. God, supremely good and great, cannot create anything that is not good.

But a creature that God made good can become evil by its own fault and vice. By doing evil it can acquire habits that fix it on evil so firmly that it can no longer do good. Its will is then hardened in evil and cannot, without the help of divine grace, free itself from the snares it has willingly walked into.

title: A creature bound by its own fault to do evil still sins freely and can abstain from each particular sin
english: Yet a creature that its own fault has thrown into this necessity of doing evil does not on that account act unfreely in the evil it does. The corrupt habits that hamper its mind and will do not stop it from weighing and deliberating about what it does, nor stop its will from following the judgement of corrupt reason willingly, with no force compelling it.

In fact, one who cannot do good can still refrain from each particular evil act, and no necessity binds him to commit this sin or that. When the devil stirs and urges someone with temptations to rebel against God and obey the flesh, he could have left him untempted. When a man blinded and hardened by God's just judgement commits some crime, such as murder or adultery, he could have kept himself clean of that adultery and that murder, and he cannot plead any necessity for it.

title: To which faculty freedom belongs: the common Reformed view puts it formally in the will, radically in the intellect
english: Having set out the nature and essence of human freedom in this way, we still have to ask which of man's faculties it properly concerns and belongs to.

The more common view among the teachers of the Reformed school is that human freedom has its origin in mind and reason but is properly a disposition of the will. Man can choose among various things, embracing one now and rejecting it at another time, because he can judge things in various ways and grasp in them different aspects of good or evil. Even so, no act in man counts as free unless the will either produces it or at least commands it.

So only the will's acts are held to be free in themselves. Acts carried out through other faculties are free only to the extent that they depend on the will and happen with its consent, or at least its neglect and toleration. That is what the schools mean by saying that freedom is formally in the will alone, and in the intellect only as in its root.
Ludwig Crocius settles the matter so in the passage cited above: "The freedom ascribed to choice is properly a disposition of the will, though it has its root in the intellect and reason."
translator_notes: Crocius, Syntagma, book 3, chapter 37 (cited at §1784).

title: Amyraut: freedom in the acts of commanded faculties, of the will, and of the intellect, whose freedom is self-action
english: Some of the Reformed, however, reason differently about this. Among them is the distinguished Moses Amyraut. To explain his view on the question, he notes that freedom is ascribed to three kinds of acts: first, the acts of the faculties the will commands; second, the acts of the will itself; third, the acts of the intellect.

In the first respect, on his view, freedom is nothing but the ability to live or act as you will, for we count as free when, with nothing forcing or blocking us, we do what we want. In the second respect he defines freedom as "the ability to will as we judge should be willed, each person being settled on it by his own judgement and not another's." Bodily actions are counted free because they depend on a free source, the will; in the same way, he says, the will's actions are free because they too depend on a free source, the judgement of the intellect.

The intellect's freedom he places in its autopragia: the intellect acts from itself and through itself, and is autexousios, in control of its own operations, since it is neither forced by violence to perform them nor dependent on anyone else's command. So freedom, with respect to the acts of the mind and intellect, is a self-governing power of judging about things that comes neither from outside force nor from outside command. That learned man develops this more fully in his short book On Free Choice, section 1, p. 20 and following.
translator_notes: Moses Amyraut, De libero arbitrio, section 1, p. 20 ff.

title: Amyraut infers that freedom belongs first to the intellect, the governing part, not formally to the will
english: From this teaching it follows that the freedom found in outward actions depends in them on the will, while the freedom that belongs to the will's acts depends in them on the intellect. The intellect, however, is free in itself. So freedom belongs first and chiefly to the intellect and should be placed there as in its own natural seat.

Hence freedom is not, as many would have it, formally in the will alone while being in the intellect only as its cause and root. The same learned man teaches this and tries to prove it on p. 30 and following of his short book.

His main argument is that in his judgement the intellect is by nature more its own master than the will. The will follows the intellect's lead and is subject, as it were, to its rule, which is why the Greeks call the intellect to hegemonikon, the governing part. He thinks it absurd that freedom should be formally in the faculty under another's command rather than in the one bound by the laws of no other faculty.

title: Yet Amyraut concludes that freedom is formally in both faculties jointly, though the intellect's part is the weightier
english: Yet at the end of the same section he concludes that freedom, properly speaking, is not formally in the intellect or in the will taken separately, but in both faculties together. Man is not counted free simply in that he judges, nor simply in that he desires, but in that he desires on the judgement and counsel of reason. In the same way humanity is not formally in the understanding soul, nor in the sensitive nature alone, but in man as made up of those two natures.

On his view, then, free choice is not any one of the rational faculties in man, nor something with one part belonging more to the intellect and another more to the will. It is the character and disposition of both faculties, intellect and will, by which, as they work together on human actions, each in its own way, man as man is counted free.

Still, just as in defining man the element of reason counts far more than that of animal nature, so in defining free choice the intellect seems to weigh far more than appetite. Many other things desire, but among visible creatures man alone is thought to desire freely, because he alone has an intellect.

title: Amyraut: the practical intellect is the source of free action only when it judges after deliberation
english: He does not, however, make the intellect the source of freedom in man however it is taken, but only in so far as it pronounces on what is to be done or desired, not only in general but in the particular case, and so as to drive a man to act or hold him back from acting. In that respect it is called the practical intellect, which dictates in each particular matter what is to be done or not done, sought or shunned, here and now.

Even then he does not think any judgement of the practical intellect is enough for free action. He requires a judgement that is the conclusion of weighing and deliberation. On his view, then, the practical intellect is not the source of free actions in man in just any way, but only when it judges what to do probouleutos, that is, after deliberation and weighing have taken place. This can be seen in the section cited, p. 31 and following.
translator_notes: Amyraut, De libero arbitrio, section cited, p. 31 ff.

title: De la Place: the same freedom belongs to intellect and will, but more to the will, which commands
english: Josué de la Place, another very learned man and Amyraut's colleague while he lived, agrees with him that freedom is not formally in the will alone, and that the intellect as well as the will is a free faculty.

He differs from his colleague in this: Amyraut distinguishes the freedom that belongs to the intellect from the freedom that belongs to the will and gives each its own definition, whereas de la Place holds that the very freedom by which the will is called free also belongs to the intellect. On his view that freedom lies in exemption from three necessities: compulsion, being settled by matter, and being settled by sense. And that exemption, he judges, belongs to the intellect just as much.

His view is also opposed to Amyraut's in this: when will and intellect are compared, he thinks freedom lies more with the will. The reason is that he thinks command and mastery in man rest with the will rather than the intellect. The intellect does not move the will by its act as by a command, but by the object it sets before it; the will, by contrast, moves the mind and applies it to understanding by its act, as by a command.

Even so, that learned man thinks that some acts of our mind are free, and so morally good or evil, though they are not done at the will's command and do not depend on its consent as on their source. He counts faith, and the heresy opposed to it, among such acts. See his Posthumous Works, treatise On Free Choice, pp. 163-164.
translator_notes: Josué de la Place, Opuscula posthuma, treatise De libero arbitrio, pp. 163-164.

title: Alexander More: free choice is intellect and will together, whether 'appetitive mind' or 'intellective appetite'
english: Alexander More, the famous man already mentioned, holds with those learned men that intellect and will in a sense divide free choice between them. Free choice, he thinks, is nothing but intellect and will in so far as the two faculties work together and are held together by a kind of bond or marriage. Which of the two faculties it rests in more, he leaves open.

"For as the choice of the intellect ends in the will," he says, "so the freedom of the will has its root in the intellect." On his view, then, free choice can be called the intellect as it moves and affects the will, or the will as the intellect moves it. In Aristotle's own words, it is "either desiring mind or thinking desire" (On Grace and Free Choice, disputation 1, thesis 21).
translator_notes: Alexander More, De gratia et libero arbitrio, disp. 1, thesis 21; Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.2, 1139b4-5.

title: Le Blanc: no act is free unless it depends in some way on the will, which could have omitted it
english: For my part, I think no act of any faculty in man, not even of the mind itself, is free unless it depends in some way on the will and happens either at its command or with some kind of its consent. To put it more plainly: unless it is an act the man could have left undone if he had wished.

Who would call an act freely done by a man if he could not have made it otherwise however much he wanted to, and if his will is not supposed to have taken part in it in any way, directly or indirectly, mediately or immediately?

Again, since every free action can fall under a command and take on the character of virtue or vice, it must come in some way from the will. That is why the schools have so far agreed in accepting Augustine's maxim that sin is not sin unless it is voluntary, that is, unless the sinner's will is in some way its source and cause, which is how the common understanding of the faithful takes that saying.
translator_notes: Augustine, De vera religione 14.27: sin is so far a voluntary evil that it is not sin at all unless it is voluntary.

title: That does not make freedom formal in the will alone, since every free act also springs from deliberation
english: It does not follow, though, that freedom should be said to be formally in the will alone. Every free action owes its origin in some way to the will, but every free action also arises from some weighing and deliberation by the mind.

The intellect produces no action freely that the will could not have prevented, and in the same way no act of the will is free unless the mind was able to weigh and deliberate about it. With equal right, then, free actions must be traced to both mind and will. If one concludes from the first point that freedom is formally in the will, one can conclude from the second that it is formally in the intellect.

title: Le Blanc: freedom is formally neither in intellect nor will but in the man acting through both
english: My own view is rather that freedom is formally neither in the intellect nor in the will, but in man as he acts through intellect and will. Freedom, properly speaking, is not a disposition of this faculty or that. It arises from the mutual relation and joint working of several faculties, and so it cannot properly be ascribed to any one faculty, only to the subject (suppositum) in which those faculties are found.

Strictly speaking, then, neither mind nor will should be called free, but man himself, in so far as he uses those faculties in a certain way. When the will is called free, the statement is not, in the language of the schools, formal but causal: the will, joined to the intellect, is the cause of the actions for which man is said to act freely.

This point is not idle, as will appear later. It helps to resolve certain difficulties in which a good many entangle themselves by looking for the whole nature of freedom in the will rather than in the man as such.

title: Whether intellect or will contributes more to freedom is left undecided, as Aristotle left it
english: Whether the intellect contributes more to man's freedom than the will, or the will more than the intellect, is not something the theologian needs to settle. Aristotle himself, the prince of today's philosophers, did not inquire into it closely.
So we too, along with some very learned theologians, leave the question open.

title: Despite their differences the Reformed accept Bellarmine's definition of free choice, as Baron, Pareus and Ames show
english: However the teachers of the Reformed school differ in explaining the nature of freedom and the faculties it does or does not belong to, they readily accept Bellarmine's definition of free choice in On Grace and Free Choice (book 3, chapter 3): "Free choice is the free power, given or granted to an intelligent nature for the great glory of God, of choosing among things that lead to some end one rather than another, or of rejecting or accepting one and the same thing, as we judge fit."

Robert Baron shows this in his General Metaphysics (section 12, disputation On Freedom of Choice), where he not only approves the definition but explains it carefully part by part. Pareus does not reject it either. Commenting on that passage of Bellarmine, he makes some remarks on the definition and then admits that, on free choice considered absolutely, there is no dispute between us and Bellarmine.

The definition Pareus puts in its place as plainer and fuller is not far from Bellarmine's: free choice is "the power of willing, not willing, choosing or rejecting an object the intellect sets before it, without compulsion, by a spontaneous and deliberate movement, with the will able to will or not will the opposite." Likewise Ames grants that the definition can bear a sense that leaves no reason to quarrel over it (Bellarmine Disarmed, volume 4, book 4, chapter 1).
translator_notes: Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 3, chapter 3; Robert Baron, Metaphysica generalis, sect. 12; David Pareus on Bellarmine; William Ames, Bellarminus enervatus, tom. 4, lib. 4, cap. 1.

title: Roman questions about free choice touched only so far as they bear on present controversies
english: The teachers of the Roman School debate many questions among themselves about what free choice is and what makes it what it is. Most of these belong more to metaphysics than to theology, and there is no intention here of listing and sifting them all.
Only those will be touched, and briefly, that bear somehow on the controversies now inflaming the Christian schools and dividing them against one another.

title: The genus of free choice: act, habit, or power; all Rome now says a power
english: The usual disputes about the genus of free choice are passed over here: whether it is an act, a habit, or a power, and under which of the soul's contents it should be classed.

Some older writers did teach that free choice lies not in a power or a habit but in an act; Bellarmine assigns that view to Hervaeus, the commentator on the Sentences. Others held that it is neither act nor power but a natural habit arising from intellect and will, which was the view of Cardinal Bonaventure, a teacher of great fame in the Roman School.
Even so, the whole Roman School now agrees that free choice is a power and a faculty.
translator_notes: Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio, is the source of the attributions to Hervaeus and Bonaventure; Le Blanc gives no book or chapter.

title: Which power free choice is: a universal power, or a particular one distinct from intellect and will
english: Once free choice was granted to be a power, the next question was which power it is, and opinions differed.

Thomas and Bonaventure, on Bellarmine's testimony, report that some took it to be not one particular power of the soul but a universal power containing as its species every power of the soul, sentient or intellectual, that produces acts free in any way.
Others, such as Alexander of Hales, the noble scholastic who taught both Thomas Aquinas and Bonaventure, called it a particular power but one distinct from intellect and will.
This question too can be left aside, for all the schools now agree that free choice is not anything really distinct from intellect and will.

title: Whether free choice embraces both faculties or the will alone; Durandus gives freedom first to reason
english: A further question is whether free choice is made up of both faculties and belongs to both, or must be confined to the will alone.

Some held that it includes both mind and will. Durandus, a teacher of high standing in the Roman School, was of this view. He said that reason, and not the will only, is free 'formally', to use their term, and indeed that freedom belongs to reason first and more fully than to the will.

title: Gassendi: freedom first in the intellect, secondarily in the will, because reason is indifferent in judging
english: Pierre Gassendi, a man of great renown and provost of the church of Digne in Provence, adopts this view in his treatise on freedom, fortune, and fate, printed at the end of the second volume of his works. There he says freedom seems to him to be in the intellect first and in its own right, and in the will only secondarily and by dependence.

His ground is this. On the more common Roman view, as will shortly appear, freedom lies in a certain indifference and indeterminacy of a free power. Reason is indifferent when it judges what is to be done and can judge it one way or another, so any indifference the will has toward things it desires springs from the indifference in reason.

The will can refuse or accept one and the same object, and pick this or that among many. It can do so because reason can form different judgments of those objects as different aspects of good or evil appear in them.
translator_notes: Gassendi, De libertate, fortuna, fato (Opera, tom. 2).

title: Gassendi's mind free only as flexible toward objects; the intellect compared to a balance
english: He does not make the mind free in every respect. It is free only in that it stands somewhat indifferently toward a great many objects and is so pliable by nature that, while its object is truth, it can judge a matter now one way and now another and take now this judgment and now that one for true.
Yet it cannot refuse what appears true or accept what seems false. Nor can it change its judgment of anything unless the object presents a stronger or weaker appearance of truth or falsehood.

He therefore likens the human intellect to a pair of scales that tilts one way or the other as weight is added to or taken from either pan. Once one pan has gone down, it cannot rise again unless weight is put on the other.
The illustrious author develops this at greater length in the same volume, page 82.

title: Rome commonly rejects this: freedom formally in the will alone; free choice the will itself under an aspect
english: The Roman School, however, generally rejects this view. Most of its teachers hold that the intellect is not free formally, and that freedom belongs in its own right and formally to the will alone.

So they teach that free choice is no power other than the will. It is simply the will, regarded in a certain respect and manner. The will and free choice are thus one and the same power in reality, yet free choice is distinguished from the will by a distinction of reason.

title: The will reaches wider than free choice, in objects and in acts; the last end is willed naturally
english: In their view the will covers more ground than free choice, both in its objects and in its acts. Everything done by free choice is also done by the will, but the reverse does not hold.

Likewise every object of free choice is an object of the will, but not every object of the will falls to free choice. The highest end, happiness, is an object of the will, whereas free choice has for its object only the means to that end.
It follows that the acts by which we want to be happy and do not want to be wretched are acts of the will and not of free choice, since the will moves toward the last end by nature and not freely.

title: The intellect the root and condition sine qua non of the will's freedom
english: The scholastic theologians generally say the intellect is not free in itself and formally. Still they grant that it holds the root and cause of the will's freedom, at the least as the condition without which there would be none.

That freedom arises because the human intellect does more than set different objects before the will. It also weighs them against each other, sees different aspects of good and evil in a single object, and in a manner points them out to the will.
That is why the will can refuse or accept the same object and choose this or that among many, and in this the use of freedom consists.

title: Why they deny the intellect formal freedom: moral good and evil, praise and blame, belong to the will
english: Their main reason for denying the intellect formal freedom is that acting morally well or badly belongs to the faculty that is free formally and in itself.
In their judgment virtue and vice belong strictly to the will alone. No action deserves praise or blame, reward or punishment, except as it comes from the will.
Hence even the intellect's own operations count as sin or merit only so far as they are voluntary and in some fashion directed by the will.

title: The chief question: in what the freedom that makes choice free consists; Roman theologians disagree
english: The central point of the question appears to be where, strictly, the freedom lies that makes the will called free and in which the essence of free choice consists.
Theologians of the Roman Church are not entirely agreed on this. To make their differing opinions clearer, one must first set out the senses and distinctions of freedom that the schools employ.

title: Liberty opposed to servitude, compulsion, necessity; servitude proper and metaphorical
english: Freedom, then, stands over against three things: servitude, compulsion, and necessity.

Servitude, and with it the opposing freedom, is either literal or figurative. Literal servitude is the state of people who are slaves by legal condition and so are under their masters' power. Figurative servitude is when something is spoken of as lord over men.
Thus Scripture calls those who give themselves to their sins slaves of sin, and those whom God's just sentence has handed over to ruin and death are likewise called slaves of death and decay.

Against the slavery to sin Scripture sets another servitude, that of righteousness, which is freedom from sin; the schools call it the freedom of grace. Against the slavery of misery, that is, of death and decay, Scripture sets what it calls the freedom of the glory of the children of God.
translator_notes: Le Blanc cites no verses; the references are supplied for the scriptural phrases servants of sin, servitude of righteousness, and the glory of the children of God.

title: The freedom that names free choice is not freedom from servitude
english: The teachers of the Roman Church point out that the freedom under discussion, from which free choice takes its name, is not the freedom opposed to servitude, either literal or figurative.
Someone who is a slave by condition is not for that reason without free choice. Neither have those whom Scripture calls slaves of sin been robbed of it by sin.

title: Whether this freedom excludes only compulsion or also necessity; older scholastics: compulsion only
english: Nobody questions that this freedom shuts out compulsion before all else. The question is whether compulsion is the only thing it excludes, or necessity as well, and whether in a rational agent it is enough to be exempt from compulsion.
In fact a fair number of the older scholastics seem to have held that freedom of choice, taken in general, is opposed not to necessity as such but only to compulsion.

title: Bonaventure: necessity of compulsion destroys freedom, necessity of immutability does not
english: Bonaventure plainly held this view. On the second book of the Sentences, distinction 7, question 2, he writes: 'To the claim that willing freely and willing necessarily are opposed, the answer is that necessity is of two kinds. One comes from an outside cause, such as the necessity of compulsion, and this is opposed to willing freely. The other comes from an inner disposition, and this is not opposed to it but stands together with freedom. Such is the necessity in the free choice of the demons, who bind evil to themselves so tightly that they would by no means be parted from it.'

In distinction 25, question 2, he says: 'Free choice may be considered in two ways, as free or as deliberating. Taken as free, I grant that it can concern not only what is contingent but also what is necessary, as is evident in God, in Christ, in the angels, and in the blessed.

'There are two necessities, of compulsion and of immutability. The first conflicts with freedom of choice, the second does not. For choice is called free not because, in willing this, it can will the opposite, but because whatever it wills it seeks under its own command. It wills a thing in such a way that it wills itself to will it, and so in the very act of willing it moves itself and rules itself.
