For that reason it is called free, even though it is unchangeably directed to its object.'
A little later he adds: 'The act of free choice, taken as free, can not only concern what is necessary but can itself be necessary.'
translator_notes: Bonaventure, In II Sent. d. 7 and d. 25, as cited by Le Blanc.

title: Bonaventure took this from Alexander of Hales: necessity of compulsion against necessity of inevitability
english: Bonaventure learned this teaching from his master, Alexander of Hales, who in many places makes the essential freedom of free choice consist in freedom from compulsion.

His clearest statement runs: 'Necessity is of two kinds, of inevitability and of compulsion. The necessity of compulsion destroys free choice; the necessity of inevitability does not. So although there is a necessity of inevitability in the angels, they still have free choice.' (Summa, part 2, q. 72, memb. 3, art. 3.)

title: Aquinas: natural necessity does not conflict with freedom, which is opposed to violence or compulsion
english: Thomas Aquinas, another pupil of the same Alexander of Hales, held the same doctrine. 'Natural necessity,' he says, 'by which the will is said to will something necessarily, happiness for instance, does not conflict with freedom, as Augustine teaches in the first book of The City of God.

'Freedom of the will is opposed to violence or compulsion. There is no violence or compulsion when a thing moves according to the order of its own nature. Violence lies rather in hindering a natural motion, as when a heavy body is kept from falling toward the center.

'So the will seeks happiness freely, though it seeks it necessarily. In the same way God too loves himself freely by his will, even though he loves himself of necessity.' (De potentia, q. 10, art. 2, ad 1.)
translator_notes: Aquinas, Quaestiones disputatae de potentia, q. 10, a. 2, ad 1.

title: Aquinas: an act can be praiseworthy and meritorious though the will be determined to one thing
english: So he teaches that a deed may deserve praise or blame, merit or demerit, simply because it is spontaneous, voluntary, and not forced, even though the will is fixed on that one thing.

On the third book of the Sentences (margin: dist. 12, q. 2, art. 1, ad 3) he writes: 'The inability that comes from compulsion, which is the opposite of the voluntary, removes merit and demerit. Not so the inability that comes from perfection in good or in evil. That does not remove the voluntary; it presupposes a will confirmed in one direction.'

In the same book (margin: dist. 18, art. 2, ad 5) he explains how Christ could merit by a free choice fixed on one single act, namely the love of God: 'Even if it were fixed on one single act, such as loving God, which it cannot fail to do, it does not on that account lose its freedom or its claim to praise or merit. It goes toward that act spontaneously and not under force, and so remains in command of its act.'
translator_notes: The two references are printed in the margin; they are kept in brackets in the Latin lock and marked as marginal in the English.

title: Scotus: freedom consists with necessity, the will always acts freely, God loves himself freely though necessarily
english: Scotus does not differ on this point. He teaches three things about the will's freedom clearly and openly.

First, the will's freedom is fully compatible with necessity: 'Freedom remains in the will together with necessity of willing. For freedom of willing lies in this, that the will brings forth its act with delight and by choice and continues in it.'

Second, whether the will acts necessarily or contingently, it always acts freely and never by nature: 'The will always has its own manner of causing, namely freely.' Again: 'The will as will is a principle that acts freely. So the will can no more act by nature than nature, taken as a principle set over against will, can act freely.'

Third, this holds not only in creatures but in God himself, who loves himself with the greatest freedom though with a necessary will: 'The divine will necessarily wills its own goodness, and yet in willing it, it is free.' (Quodlibet 16, as cited by Jansenius in his Augustinus, On the Grace of Christ the Saviour, book 6, chapter 25.)

title: Later scholastics in the same line: Thomas of Strasbourg, Marsilius, Biel, Orbellis, Brulefer
english: These luminaries of the school were followed in the centuries just after them by a great many other scholastics.

Thomas of Strasbourg says: 'The necessity of compulsion removes merit; the necessity of immutability that comes from perfected virtue does not remove it but increases it.' Marsilius of Inghen says: 'What is necessary and inevitable, not by nature but by grace, does not cease to be praiseworthy.'

Gabriel Biel says: 'The act of blessedness is freely brought forth, and so is contingent though unchangeable and everlasting. It is free, I mean, by consent and delight, though not free to do the contrary, and that freedom is enough for merit.'

Nicholas de Orbellis borrows Bonaventure's words: free choice is called free simply, not because in willing one thing it can will the opposite, but because whatever it wills it seeks under its own command. It wills something in such a way that it wills itself to will it, so that in the act of willing it moves and rules itself, and for that reason it is called free even though it is unchangeably directed to its object.

Finally Stephen Brulefer teaches: 'The act of free choice as deliberating, though it may concern what is necessary, is always contingent. But the act of free choice as free can not only concern what is necessary but can itself be necessary.'
All these passages, and many more, are quoted at length by Jansenius in the sixth book on the grace of the Saviour, chapter 29 and following.

title: Some sixteenth-century Roman theologians kept the view: Alfonso de Castro and Joseph Angles
english: Even in the last century some theologians of the Roman School still held this view. Alfonso de Castro, a Franciscan, writes in his book on heresies under the heading Liberty: 'There is yet another freedom, opposed to necessity, or more accurately to compulsion.' He adds that when we call man's choice free, it is this freedom that is meant.

Joseph Angles, another Franciscan and bishop-designate of Bosa, later took over Alfonso's words as his own in his commentary on the second book of the Sentences. Having spoken of the freedom of grace and the freedom of glory, he says: 'Third, there is the freedom opposed to necessity, or more accurately to compulsion. This is the freedom of nature, which is our present subject.'

Later, after distinguishing freedom from compulsion, from sin, and from misery, he concludes: 'As regards freedom in the first sense, free choice exists equally in men and in angels. The reason is that the will of neither bad nor good angels, nor of bad men, can be forced.'

Further on he asks whether the act of free choice concerns only contingent things or necessary things as well. Following Bonaventure, he notes that free choice may be viewed either as free or as deliberating, and he draws two conclusions.

First: 'The act of free choice can concern and does concern necessary things. For there is free choice in God, in the angels, and in the blessed, and it issues in its act unchangeably and necessarily, since God is unchangeable by nature and angels and the blessed by glory.'

Second: 'If free choice is taken in the second sense, its act concerns contingent things. For we do not deliberate or take counsel about what is necessary or impossible, but about contingent things that it is in our power to do or leave undone.' (On distinctions 24 and 25, the single question on free choice, arts. 1-3.)
translator_notes: Alfonso de Castro, Adversus omnes haereses, s.v. Libertas; Joseph Angles, Flores theologicarum quaestionum in II Sent. (d. 24-25).

title: What these doctors mean: compulsion alone destroys freedom in one who acts by rational judgment
english: As the passages already quoted readily show, these teachers say that freedom of choice is opposed not to necessity as such but to compulsion. They do not mean, as their opponents seem to assume, that the nature and essence of freedom is simply exemption from compulsion.
They admit that many things act without being forced and yet do not act freely, for in their view nothing is a free agent unless it acts on the judgment of the intellect.

Their point is narrower. In one who acts on the judgment of reason, compulsion alone destroys freedom, and necessity does not. No one can act under force and freely at the same time, but someone can act freely even though he acts necessarily.

title: They do not say freedom is always joined to necessity; wayfarers have indifference, but freedom does not consist in it
english: Nor do they hold that freedom always comes with necessity, or that free choice, especially in man, is not indifferent and undetermined with regard to most of its acts.

They grant that people in this present life not only act freely but are so constituted that no natural necessity, or necessity strictly so called, binds them in acting. They can act or stop, do this or that, and perform opposite acts toward the same object.

What they deny is that freedom, considered simply, consists in that indifference and indeterminacy toward action or always goes with it. Freedom can remain and be kept without it, and it is sometimes found in one who is not indifferent at all but acts inevitably and unchangeably.
translator_notes: in via: the scholastic term for the state of pilgrims in this life, as against in patria (the blessed in heaven).

title: Besides liberty of contrariety and of contradiction, a liberty of complacency; Biel and Viguier
english: The schools speak of freedom of contrariety or specification, by which one can do this or that, or even perform opposite acts, and of freedom of contradiction or exercise, by which one can at least stop acting and hold the act back.

Beyond these two they set a freedom of complacency, or delight. It is found in someone who is moved to an action neither by outside force nor by blind animal impulse but by his own judgment, even though the light guiding him is so evident that he cannot bring himself to the opposite act or even to leave off the one he is doing.

Gabriel Biel gives this distinction in the words quoted earlier, and so does the more recent John Viguier, doctor and professor of theology at Toulouse. 'As to the will's indeterminacy or freedom regarding its last end,' he says, 'in heaven it is wholly determined and not free, either in specification or in exercise. It lacks the freedom of contradiction and of contrariety, yet it is free with the freedom of complacency, because it takes pleasure and delight in that object.' (Institutiones theologicae, ch. 3, §3, v. 1.)

title: Whoever acts on a sure judgment of reason acts freely, necessarily or contingently; Bonaventure and Scotus
english: They consider that anyone acting on a settled judgment of reason acts freely, whether he acts necessarily or contingently.

He always acts and seeks under his own command. He wills a thing in such a way that he wills himself to will it, and so approves his own will, turning back on it silently or openly. In this way, in the very act of willing he moves and rules himself, as Bonaventure puts it in the passage cited above.

Or, in Scotus's words, 'the will, through the firmness of its freedom, lays necessity on itself in bringing forth its act and in persevering in it, that is, in fixing itself on the act.' (Quodlibet 16.)

title: Jansenius revives the old scholastic view: freedom opposed only to compulsion
english: Cornelius Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, revived this view of the old scholastics in our own time and tried to explain it, as can be seen throughout the sixth book, on the grace of Christ the Saviour, of the volume he called Augustinus.

There he argues at length that freedom is opposed not to every necessity but only to the one that comes from outside force working against the agent's inclination, which we call compulsion. In someone who acts on the judgment of reason, he says, compulsion alone removes freedom; the necessity of inevitability and immutability does not.

So a free agent is not the opposite of a necessary agent, any more than a natural agent is the opposite of one acting contingently. The free agent is opposed only to the natural agent, just as the contingent agent is opposed only to the necessary one.

Therefore it is no more contradictory for one who acts freely to act necessarily than for something acting by nature to act contingently. A natural cause can be hindered in its action by another cause, and in the same way a free cause can be fixed on one course immovably and unchangeably.
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius, Augustinus (1640), tom. 3, De gratia Christi Salvatoris, lib. 6.

title: Jansenius: whatever is voluntary is free, since will and nature are opposite principles
english: For Jansenius, whatever acts on the judgment of reason acts freely. Since the will is a rational appetite, he holds that will and nature are flatly opposed, and that the will can no more act in the manner of nature than nature can act in the manner of a free cause.

Just as no action of a natural cause can be free, so no action of the will can be natural rather than free. The free therefore reaches exactly as far as the voluntary, and whatever is voluntary is free by that very fact, because the will always and by its essence keeps its own way of acting, distinct from that of nature.

title: Jansenius grants first impulses of the will are not free, because not in man's power
english: He does admit that some motions arise in the will that are not free for all that. These are the sudden ones that run ahead of reason's full judgment, usually called 'first-first motions'.

They come from the will without violence, yet they lack what he takes to be the chief thing in freedom. They are not in a man's power, they happen without reason's full attention, and they happen even against the will's wishes and resistance in some way, since when the will reflects on them it does not consent and would rather not have them in it at all. (On the Grace of Christ the Saviour, book 6, chapter 37.)
translator_notes: motus primo primi: the scholastic term for involuntary first stirrings of desire that precede deliberation.

title: The voluntary in a broad and a strict sense; in the strict sense it converts with the free, even in the blessed
english: On his principles, then, 'voluntary' has two senses.

First, a broader and less proper one, covering every motion that arises in the will in any way at all. In that sense the voluntary is wider than the free, since first-first motions are voluntary but not free.

Second, a strict and proper sense, in which those acts of the will, and only those, are voluntary that occur when reason is attending and has weighed the matter and judged it. Taken so, the voluntary and the free coincide, and the one is no wider than the other.
Since the will does not move toward the last end without a full and sure judgment of reason, it acts no less freely regarding that end than when it seeks the means that seem to lead there.

So it is not only people in this life who perform a free act of will when they want to be happy and not miserable. The blessed in heaven do so too when they cling with their whole will to God whom they see clearly. In both cases the will here follows a firm, certain, evident, and steadily approved judgment of the intellect, and when it reflects on itself it approves that act of its own to the utmost.

title: Jansenius: indifference is not of the essence of freedom; freedom is the agent's mastery of itself
english: He does not hold that the general character and proper essence of freedom includes any indifference or indeterminacy of the will toward the act called free, such that the will could do the opposite, or at least leave the act undone or hold it back.

In his view freedom consists only in this: the free agent rules itself and its act, and it acts and moves itself rather than being acted on and moved by another. He maintains that this holds even in acts to which the will is fixed necessarily and unchangeably.

title: Jansenius with Scotus: the necessity in such acts is concomitant, not antecedent
english: The necessity then present in the will, as he puts it in Scotus's words, 'does not come before the will, so that the will would be understood to fall under a necessity that drives it into the act and fixes it there. If that were so, the will would be acted upon and would not act, and freedom could not remain in such an act.

'It is a concomitant necessity, understood to fall under the will. The will, through the firmness of its freedom, lays necessity on itself in bringing forth its act and in persevering in it, that is, in fixing itself on the act.' (On the Grace of Christ the Saviour, book 6, chapter 37.)

title: Jansenius: reason and will reflect on their own acts, so the rational agent always moves itself
english: To show more plainly that a rational agent in some way acts and moves itself in everything it wills and desires, even when its act of will is necessary and unchangeable, he observes where the power of self-action and self-movement lies, the power that belongs to a free agent.

It lies in the fact that both reason and will, the faculties to which freedom belongs, can turn back on their own acts. Reason can judge its own judgment and ask whether it judged rightly. The will likewise can not only will and desire but also will its own willing and its own desire.

In every rational motion, necessary or not, such reflection on itself is always present, silently or openly. So in every motion a rational agent always moves itself and is master of itself, and in this way exercises its own freedom.

title: Jansenius: the blessed love God most freely; their necessity comes from the perfection of their freedom
english: In his account the proper signs of true freedom are doing what the agent likes, what pleases him, what seems good to him.

From this he concludes that the blessed in heaven, loving the God they see clearly, move themselves most perfectly, hold the most perfect command over their act, and so are supremely free. With the fullest and calmest judgment they judge that God must be loved by them, and they judge that in this they judge most soundly. Their will, in loving, wants to follow reason, wants to want this, and does not want to stop.

Whatever necessity shows in that act comes from the will itself and from the perfection of its mastery and freedom. The will creates that necessity for itself by moving and determining itself, not in the manner of nature but in the manner of the most perfect freedom.

title: Jansenius grants wayfarers indifference but makes it a sign of freedom, not its cause
english: That teacher will not have it belong to the proper essence of freedom that the will stand indifferently toward its acts, able to act or not act, to do this or even its opposite.

Yet with the old scholastics he openly admits that such indifference is present in the will of people still on their earthly way. Their freedom is exempt not only from compulsion but also from unchangeable voluntary necessity; it is open to either side.

What he denies is only that the general freedom of human choice consists in that indifference. The indifference is indeed a most certain sign of freedom in a rational creature, but it is not the cause or ground of freedom. It can therefore be present or absent at the will's discretion without any loss of freedom. (On the Grace of Christ the Saviour, book 6, chapter 34.)

title: The Jansenists' Manuale Catholicorum: freedom does not consist in indifference
english: Those who call themselves disciples of Augustine, and whom their opponents call Jansenists, took up this doctrine of Jansenius and still hold it. This can be seen in their book entitled Manual of Catholics, in the twenty-first apologetic and doctrinal thesis.

They write there: 'The essence of freedom in no way consists in indifference. For the holy Fathers say, Where there is will, there is freedom. Free choice, according to St Prosper, is the spontaneous appetite for a thing that pleases one. And according to St John of Damascus, freedom of choice is nothing other than the will.'

A little later they add: 'What is done voluntarily is done freely, even if it is done necessarily, for God loves himself necessarily and yet freely.' And again: 'Only the necessity of compulsion or violence, then, is incompatible with freedom, not simple necessity, unchangeable necessity, or the necessity of natural inclination.'
translator_notes: Manuale Catholicorum, apologetic and dogmatic thesis 21; the patristic sayings are as the Manual gives them.

title: The 'three columns': Jansenists accept a sense of the third condemned proposition, yet require freedom from necessity
english: In the paper they call 'of the three columns', where they separate the different senses of the five well-known propositions condemned by the popes Innocent X and Alexander VII, they assign to the third proposition the following sense as sound and accepted by them.

'To merit and demerit in the state of fallen nature, man does not need freedom from the necessity of infallibility. Freedom from compulsion together with the judgment of reason is enough, if one considers strictly the essence of freedom and of merit. Yet given the condition of that state, there is always an indifference of power by which the will, even under grace that is proximately necessary and efficacious of itself, is able not to will, though never so as not to will while under that same grace.'
Here they grant that in the state of fallen nature indifference of the will always goes with freedom.

That is why, in the articles presented to the bishop of Comminges, they do not hesitate to say: 'To merit and demerit in the state of fallen nature, freedom from compulsion is not enough; freedom from necessity is required. For although grace efficacious of itself determines the will to act infallibly and irresistibly, so that the will never actually dissents from it, it does not bring in necessity, since it does not remove the power of dissenting.'
translator_notes: The 'three columns' paper set the five propositions condemned by Innocent X (Cum occasione, 1653) and Alexander VII beside their admissible and inadmissible senses; Convenae is Comminges.

title: Rome condemned the view that freedom is opposed to compulsion only: Pius V and Gregory XIII
english: The view that freedom of choice is opposed only to compulsion and not to necessity has, however, been condemned by the popes of Rome.

Bellarmine mentions a decree of Pius V, later renewed by Gregory XIII, which censures these two propositions among many others: 'What is done voluntarily is done freely, even if it is done of necessity', and 'Only violence is incompatible with man's natural freedom.'
translator_notes: The decree is Pius V's bull Ex omnibus afflictionibus (1567) against Baius, confirmed by Gregory XIII (Provisionis nostrae, 1579); Le Blanc names neither bull; these are Baius's propositions 39 and 66.

title: Common Roman doctrine now: freedom requires immunity from necessity, at least absolute and natural
english: The common teaching of the Roman School today, then, is that freedom from compulsion is not enough for freedom of choice. There must also be freedom from necessity, at least from absolute and natural necessity, the kind by which things are fixed by nature on one course and simply cannot act otherwise than they do.
On this point both the more recent Thomists and the Molinists agree.

title: Hence the voluntary is a genus with two species, and the spontaneous a wider genus still
english: They therefore deny that what is voluntary is free when the will is necessarily fixed on it, as the will of the blessed spirits is fixed on loving the God they see clearly.

So they treat the voluntary as a genus with two species under it. One is the free, which is done with selection and preference. The other is the voluntary in the strict and proper sense, which is done gladly but not freely, because it is done necessarily and unchangeably.

Above the voluntary they place the spontaneous as its genus. For not only beings with intellect and will act of their own accord, but also brute animals without reason, and even lifeless things, such as a stone moving downward, since acting spontaneously means acting on nature's impulse.

title: They distinguish willingness or complacency from liberty, which is of contrariety or of contradiction
english: They thus separate willingness, or complacency, from freedom. They allow no freedom in the proper sense except two kinds.

One is freedom of contrariety or specification, by which a person can produce opposite acts toward the same object, or seek objects that are opposed or simply different. The other, at the least, is freedom of contradiction or exercise, by which a person can act and also hold back or check his action.

title: They require indifference and indetermination: the common description of freedom
english: They do not allow freedom without some indifference and indeterminacy in the free agent with respect to acting. Only those acts are free, they think, whose opposite we can do, or which we can at least leave undone and break off.
This follows the familiar description of freedom, which places it in this: given everything required beforehand for acting, the free agent can act or not act, and can do this or that.

title: Some recent Thomists make indifference a property of freedom, its essence independence and dominion
english: Some recent Thomists, however, note that indifference toward acting or not acting is a property of human freedom that cannot be separated from it, but that the essence of freedom does not lie there.

They place it rather in independence and in standing above finite goods, together with the power of governing, or in a kind of dominion by which the free agent directs itself and all that is its own to the last end.

This can be seen in the recent Dominican writer Vincent Baron, in the third part of his dogmatic theology, on the principles of human freedom and of God's knowledge, written against the Jesuit Théophile Raynaud (disputation 1, article 3, §1).
Yet by the more common positions of today's school, the very essence of freedom is to be placed in this indifference toward acting or not acting.
translator_notes: Vincent Baron OP, the Dominican; not the Reformed Robert Baron cited elsewhere in the theses.

title: The indifference they mean is not equilibrium but the real power of acting and not acting
english: When the teachers of the Roman Church speak of the indifference that either makes up the essence of freedom or at least necessarily goes with it, they do not mean a state in which the will wavers between two opposites, leaning no more to one than to the other, hanging as if in balance and pushed this way and that by the slightest weight.

They grant that freedom is present in someone who is not at all indifferent in that sense. His will may be strongly inclined to certain actions by deeply rooted habits, and he may have a settled purpose of acting this way and no other, from which he can be moved only with great difficulty.

The indifference in which, in their view, freedom of choice lies is nothing else than a real power of acting and not acting. It remains even in someone whose mind and will are fixed on acting by a firm and steady purpose.

title: Rome: freedom does not require indifference to good and evil; God, Christ, the angels, the damned
english: It should also be noted that in the common view of the Roman Church's teachers freedom does not require indeterminacy or indifference between acting well and acting badly. The ability to act well is no part of the essence of freedom, and still less the ability to act badly.

They hold that God is the freest of agents, yet he cannot act badly. Neither could Christ as man at any time. Nor can the angels and heavenly spirits now, who by God's singular favour are unchangeably confirmed in good, and they are none the less free for that.
Conversely, by their own admission, the devils and the spirits of the damned in hell can do nothing good, and yet they act freely and free choice has remained in them.

The reason is that, though the first are fixed on acting well and the second on acting badly, both can refrain from particular acts and choose among several goods or several evils. See Puteanus on the Prima Secundae, q. 10, arts. 1-4, doubt 3, and William Estius on the second book of the Sentences, dist. 14, §5.
translator_notes: Puteanus: presumably Joannes Puteanus (Jean Dupuy) of Toulouse, commentator on the Summa I-II.

title: The formula 'all prerequisites posited, can act and not act': first sense, simultaneity of power not power of simultaneity
english: The definition that calls freedom the power by which a free agent, given everything required beforehand for acting, can act and not act, do this and that, is not understood in the same way by every theologian of the Roman School. To see this, note that the words can bear several senses.
First, they could be taken to mean that the free agent can act and not act at once, performing opposite acts at the same moment. Everyone rejects this as plainly false.

All agree that in a free agent an act and the absence of that act, or an act and its opposite, cannot coexist at the same time. They therefore take the words to mean only that the free agent has at one and the same time the power for opposite acts, so that the power of acting and the power of not acting are both found in it together.
The schools express this by saying that what is ascribed to the free agent is simultaneity of power, not power of simultaneity.

title: Second sense: with all prerequisites, even divine motion, the act may not follow and its contrary may
english: A second possible sense of the description is this. Given everything required beforehand for some act of the free will, on the side of the object, on the side of God, and on the side of the intellect, that act can just as well not follow as follow, and an opposite act can even take its place.

An act cannot be combined or joined with its own absence or with the opposite act. But all that is required beforehand for some act of the human will, say conversion and the love of God, can be joined with the absence of that act and even with the act opposed to it, and often actually is.

Thus, whatever the light and even the attraction of the object, whatever the dictate and judgment of the intellect, and finally whatever divine motion urges toward conversion while still preceding the will's own actual determination, conversion may in fact not follow.

It often does happen that, with all these things exactly alike, conversion goes with them in one person and not at all in another, because the will determined itself one way in the first and otherwise in the second.

title: The Molinists accept the second sense: the composed sense true of the prerequisites, false of the act
english: This sense is approved and accepted by those in the Roman School called Molinists. They deny that anything which prepares the human will for consent and moves and drives it beforehand, whether on God's side or on the intellect's, is incompatible with the will's dissent.

They hold that any judgment of reason and even any divine motion can be combined not only with the act toward which they move and direct the will in advance, but also with the absence of that act, and indeed with the contrary act. So the same motion of divine grace brings about conversion to God in one person and not in another, because the first chose of his own accord to follow grace's leading and the second did not.
In different respects, then, they both deny and affirm that the free agent, given all that is required for acting, can act and not act, do this and that, in the composed sense.

If it is taken to mean that in the free agent an act can be combined with ceasing from it, or one act with its opposite, they grant that this composed sense is false and only the divided sense opposed to it is true. But if someone holds that the absence of the act, or the opposite act, can be combined not with the act itself but with all that is required for acting, then in their view that composed sense is true.

title: The recent Thomists deny both composed senses yet keep the power of not acting, as one sitting can walk
english: Those called the more recent Thomists think differently, for on their teaching both composed senses are false.

They hold that an act cannot be joined with its own absence or with the opposite act. Nor can the absence of the act, much less the contrary act, coexist with what is required beforehand for acting, among which is a certain divine premotion. Once what is required for an act is in place, the act follows certainly and infallibly, and it can never happen that it does not follow.

Yet they grant that, given all that is required for acting, the free agent can act and not act, do this and that. Though the absence or suspension of the act cannot stand with those prerequisites, the power of not acting, or of acting in the contrary way, fits with them perfectly well.

It is just as when the will actually consents: dissent cannot stand with that consent, but the power of dissenting remains. Again, the act of walking cannot go with the act of sitting, yet the power of walking does not conflict with it, and sitting does not remove that power from the one who sits.

In the same way the prerequisites for acting, whether on God's side or on the side of our intellect, carry the act along with them by necessary consequence, yet in no way remove the power of not acting. They do make the will act, but so that it acts while still able not to act, and without losing the power to act otherwise.

title: Diego Alvarez states the Thomist view and its definition of free choice
english: Diego Alvarez, archbishop of Trani and Salpi and the leading figure among the more recent Thomists, explains his view as follows.

'It must be held that freedom of choice necessarily requires this: given everything required before the act, whether in order of reason or of time, it can act or not act. That is, together with those same prerequisites there is present in free choice the faculty and power by which it can act or not act, if it wishes.

'The proof is this. If any of the things required for performing a given act took from free choice the faculty or power of not acting, or of performing the opposite act, it would be God's efficacious motion by which free choice is predetermined to that act. But such motion does not remove the faculty of not performing that act or of performing the contrary one. It brings about only this: free choice, though able to perform the act or not, does in fact perform it infallibly and freely...

'Yet it is not part of the nature or definition of free choice that, given all that is required in advance in the order of causality for performing a given act, it can leave that same act undone in the composed sense, if the composition is made between those prerequisites and the absence of that act, or the contrary act.

'So these two things cannot coexist: that in free choice, at some instant of time, all that is required in advance in the order of causality for producing a given act is present, and yet it does not produce that act but produces the contrary. And freedom of choice nevertheless stands together with this impossibility.' (Summary of the work on the aids of divine grace, book 4, chapter 14, nos. 5 and 6.)

To avoid all ambiguity, then, the proper definition of free choice on his account is: 'Free choice is the faculty of will and reason for acting or not acting, either way, and for doing one thing or another.'
translator_notes: Diego Alvarez OP, De auxiliis divinae gratiae (1610), lib. 4 (summa), cap. 14, nn. 5-6. Le Blanc's '....' marks his own omission in the quotation.

title: No controversy over whether free choice exists: the Reformed hold it survives the fall, weakened and enslaved
english: The foregoing theses have set out, as briefly and clearly as we could, the doctrine of man's free choice taken absolutely and in itself: first as the teachers of the Reformed School hold it, then as the teachers of the Roman School understand it.

Above all, they showed that there is no dispute over whether man has free choice at all. Every Reformed theologian grants that man was given free choice when God first made him, and that the same free choice survived in man after the fall and was not wholly destroyed or lost. The fall badly weakened it and brought it into slavery to sin, until Christ's grace sets it free.

title: Both Schools agree free choice is a faculty, not really distinct from intellect and will; two questions remain
english: Second, what we set out earlier makes it clear that both schools agree that free choice is neither an act nor a habit but belongs among the soul's faculties, and yet is not a faculty really distinct from intellect and will.

The questions of any weight now raised about the nature of man's free choice come down to two. With respect to which faculty is man said to have free choice? And what does the freedom consist in, on account of which our choice is called free?

title: The remaining dispute lies between individual doctors, not between the Schools
english: As the earlier theses show, whatever dispute remains on those questions is not really between one school and the other. It is between individual teachers who, in both schools, think and reason about these matters in different ways.

Hardly any view on them prevails in one school without having some defenders in the other. And at least no view is rejected by teachers of the opposing school without being attacked as well by some teachers of its own school.

title: The common view in both Schools: freedom rooted in the intellect, formally in the will alone
english: To start here: when people ask which faculty free choice belongs to, a large share of the theologians of both schools hold that the freedom of human choice does in some way take its origin from reason and rests on the practical judgment's indetermination, or on a kind of self-action (αὐτοπραγία) in it, yet resides in the will alone as its subject.

The Schools put it this way: freedom is in the intellect only as its root, or as a cause without which it could not be, but it is formally in the will alone. On that view free choice is simply the will, whether insofar as it follows reason's judgment and dictate, or insofar as, among several means that reason points out, it takes one and refuses another, accepting this or not accepting it.

title: Dissent: Durandus and Gassendi; Placaeus and Amyraut; Le Blanc's view that the subject of freedom is the man
english: Just as some Reformed teachers depart from that more common view, it has also had critics in the Roman School, both long ago and recently: Durandus in the past and Gassendi now. In their view freedom is not in the will alone but in the intellect as well, and indeed more, and first, in the intellect than in the will.

Admittedly the Reformed teachers handle this question more freely, and their senses and opinions vary more widely. Some make freedom common to will and intellect, yet hold that it belongs with the stronger claim to the will, as Josué de la Place (Placaeus) does, while others give that claim to the intellect, which is the view of Moïse Amyraut.

Others insist that freedom is not a property of one faculty or another but something that arises in man from several faculties working together and bearing on one another. Its proper subject is then neither this faculty nor that but simply the man, insofar as he uses his intellect and will in a certain way. We take this view too, since a man is free not simply insofar as he wills, nor simply insofar as he judges, but insofar as he desires and wills on the basis of his mind's deliberate judgment and a settled counsel of reason.
translator_notes: Josuam Placeum is Josué de la Place (Placaeus) and Mosis Amyraldi is Moïse Amyraut, both of the Saumur academy; the Latin gives only their names.

title: On the nature of freedom: whether it opposes necessity or only compulsion is a verbal or minor dispute
english: On the nature of freedom, as the earlier disputations also make clear, opinion varies no less in both schools. First, we showed at length that in each school some teach, against the protests of others, that freedom of choice is opposed not to necessity as such but only to compulsion.

We also showed that the dispute here is either a mere matter of words or at least of little weight. Those who say that freedom in general is opposed only to compulsion, not to necessity, concede to theologians of the other view that being free from compulsion is not enough for freedom and is not, properly, what freedom consists in. It consists rather in the free agent's moving and acting itself, in a way peculiar to an intelligent agent and found neither in lifeless things nor in animals.

title: They also grant that most free acts are not fixed on one course but contingent
english: Besides, although they think that in a rational agent only compulsion stands in the way of freedom, and necessity does not, they still recognize that in most of their acts free agents are not only free from compulsion but are also not fixed on one course by any necessity.
So, on their account, some of a free creature's acts are necessary, but most are contingent.

title: Three freedoms: of contrariety or specification, of contradiction, and simple freedom or complacency
english: They therefore distinguish three kinds of freedom in free agents. The first, called in the Schools freedom of contrariety or of specification, is the power to do this, or its contrary, or something else.

The second, called freedom of contradiction, is the power, even where one cannot do this and its contrary, at least to act or to stop acting. Both of these are opposed to necessity and to being fixed on one course, and both go together with a certain contingency in one's acts.

To these they add a third, called simple freedom or freedom of complacency. Here a free agent's will and intellect turn back on themselves, tacitly or explicitly, approve their own acts, and in a way give orders to themselves, and so move and act themselves in a manner all their own: the intellect judges that it is judging rightly and that it ought to judge as it does, and the will wills its own willing and fixes and settles itself in its own act. This freedom can exist without freedom of contrariety or of contradiction, and it is compatible with a necessary and unchangeable determination to one course.

title: Freedom extended to necessary acts is taken in a broader sense
english: They admit that when freedom is stretched to cover acts that are necessary and unchangeable, the word is being used in a broader sense.
Taken more strictly, freedom deals only with what is contingent: with what may turn out one way or the other.

title: Those who oppose freedom to necessity grant some necessary acts and a willingness or complacency in them
english: Those who hold the opposite, that freedom is opposed not only to compulsion but to necessity as well, concede to the theologians who disagree that the will, or free agent, stands necessarily toward some of its acts, though it stands contingently toward most of the others.

They also think the will is free only with respect to the acts it produces contingently rather than necessarily. Yet they recognize that even in the acts on which the will is fixed unchangeably and necessarily there is a certain willingness and complacency of the will. When the will turns back on its act it approves it and gives itself the order, since it does not simply will but also wills its own willing and rests content in its act.

title: Hence the contention is verbal: both agree on how the matter stands
english: [The 1675 print sets this thesis twice. The first setting joins the opening words below to a repeat of the second half of X, adding only 'tacitly or explicitly'; the full thesis follows.]

This shows, as I said, that the dispute here is about words, not substance. Both sides agree on how the matter actually stands: the will stands necessarily toward some acts and contingently toward others. Toward some it enjoys freedom of contrariety or contradiction, while toward others it is fixed on one course, that is, it cannot do the opposite or stop acting.
And yet in the acts it produces necessarily, the will is pleased with itself and supremely wills and approves its own acts.
translator_notes: The duplicated setting (book 422-423) is kept in the locked Latin and marked in brackets, not removed; the rendering follows the full setting of XI.

title: The only remaining question, whether necessary acts should be called free, concerns a name
english: Only one question remains: should the acts the will produces necessarily and inevitably, toward which it is entirely fixed on one course, be called free? Some say no. They hold that such acts are in no way free and should be called only voluntary, because the only freedom they recognize is that of contrariety or of contradiction.

Others grant that these acts are not free in the stricter sense of freedom, the sense in which we can will and refuse the same thing, or will something different or contrary, or at least will or not will, that is, stop willing. But they insist that the same acts can and should be called free in a broader sense, namely simple freedom, or freedom of complacency.

The question therefore comes down to this: does the simple complacency that belongs to the will in all its acts, necessary and contingent alike, deserve to be called freedom in some broader sense or not? Plainly that is a question about a name only.

title: Strang concedes it would be a mere war of words (De voluntate Dei III.14, p. 687)
english: Among those who teach that freedom in general is opposed not to necessity but to compulsion, the Reformed teacher John Strang says this in so many words. He first argued at length that the will is free not only in dealing with means but also in dealing with the end, so that God loves himself freely and men freely will to be happy, since freedom of the will in general is nothing but intellectual spontaneity.

He then admitted that freedom is also used in a narrower sense, for what concerns τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, the things in our power, and limited to means ordered to the end, or to things that contribute little or nothing to the end. In that respect freedom includes a certain indifference, and free acts are purely contingent. He further noted that many deny, in this sense, that God loves himself freely or that the blessed in heaven love God freely.

He finally concludes: 'We do not think this matter worth a quarrel, since it would otherwise be a mere war of words (λογομαχία). For we do not deny that the term free choice is properly used in that way, although in another sense we have called those actions free.' (De voluntate Dei, book 3, chapter 14, page 687.)
translator_notes: Strangius is John Strang of Glasgow; Le Blanc cites his work as 'De voluntate Dei'.

title: Estius on Bonaventure: free choice as free and as deliberating; Bonaventure differs only in wording
english: Among those who teach that freedom is opposed not only to compulsion but also to necessity, the Roman theologian William Estius grants the same point. Replying to passages of Bonaventure brought against his own view, he says:

'In question 2 Bonaventure teaches that free choice can be considered in two ways, as free or as deliberating. As free, he says, it can bear on what is necessary, as is plain in God and the blessed, for although in them it has a necessity of unchangeableness, it has none of compulsion. As deliberating, he says, it concerns only the contingent, since no one deliberates about what is necessary or impossible.

This distinction shows well enough in what sense he said that free choice, as free, also looks to necessary things and can have a necessary act. For "as free" means nothing other than "as voluntary and not compelled". It is as if he said that the will, insofar as it is free from compulsion, deals even with necessary actions.

"As deliberating", on the other hand, meaning, as he explains, as weighing whether to choose this or that, refers to the freedom that belongs to free choice as such. Bonaventure therefore does not disagree with the others in substance; he merely spoke less aptly and against common usage.'

title: Within the Reformed School: whether every necessity properly so called conflicts with freedom
english: The dispute that remains within the Reformed School, among the very theologians who admit that freedom of choice is opposed not only to compulsion but also to necessity, seems no weightier.

Some of them teach without qualification that every necessity in the proper sense conflicts with freedom. Others grant that freedom is opposed to natural necessity but insist that necessity of many kinds can coexist with that same freedom of choice. A free agent, they say, can have a certain necessity of acting laid on it by the efficacy of God's grace and providence, or even by the mind's practical judgment, and that necessity does freedom no harm.

title: What the first party means by necessity properly so called: removal of the power to act otherwise
english: Those who insist that every necessity properly so called conflicts with freedom mean by that phrase only a necessity that does more than determine the agent to act. It also removes his power not to act or to act otherwise; it puts him in a condition where he not only acts surely and infallibly but really cannot fail to act, and that not only in the composite sense but in the divided sense too.

Such a necessity would leave the agent, whether he is acting or is on the point of acting, without the kind of power not to act, or to act otherwise, that a seated man has to walk even while he sits, and a walking man has to sit even while he walks.

title: Grace, providence and the last practical dictate determine infallibly, yet the power not to act remains
english: So they do grant that the motion of God's grace, the efficacy of his providence too, or even the practical judgment's last dictate, determines a man to act and to will in such a way that the act called free follows necessarily. Once God's grace and providence are at work with their motion and efficacy, the act toward which God prepares, moves and determines the man, whether by the motion of grace or by the efficacy of common providence, cannot fail to be put forth.

But they do not count this as necessity in the proper sense, because a real power not to act coexists with it. When God calls a man according to his purpose, he moves him to believe God and to love God and his neighbour in such a way that faith and love follow infallibly, and with that motion in place the man cannot fail to believe and love. Yet God does not take away his power not to believe and not to love. The act contrary to the divine motion cannot coexist with it, but the power to that contrary act does.

In the same way a seated man must be sitting while he sits and a walking man must be walking while he walks; it is impossible for a seated man not to sit or for a walking man not to walk. Yet the seated man keeps a real power to walk and the walker a real power to sit. This holds not in the composite sense, as if they could walk and stand at once, but in the divided sense, because any act, while it excludes the opposite act, does not exclude the potency for it.

title: So the man moved acts by a necessity of infallibility yet keeps a real power not to act
english: On this teaching, then, a man whom God effectively moves to do this or that, or whom the dictate of his own judgment drives to it, does act necessarily, with a necessity of infallibility, while still keeping a real power not to act.
He is able not to act, yet he will surely act; and the absence of the act can never be found together with such a judgment or with such a motion from God.

title: What the second party means when they say the man so moved cannot not act
english: Those on the other side, who teach that necessity of many kinds is compatible with freedom, and that a man moved by grace or driven by his own judgment's dictate to act cannot fail to act, mean only this. When God moves a man to some act, whether by the grace said to work in men both to will and to do, or at least by the efficacy of common providence, or even by the judgment of his own reason, the man cannot fail to produce the act he is assumed to have been moved and stirred to.
So once such grace and help, and such a judgment, are given, it follows necessarily that the man will act in this way or that.

title: They readily grant that the power to the contrary stands with the act itself
english: Still, they will readily admit that when grace moves someone to pray, say, or to give alms to a poor man, his power not to pray and not to give those alms is not removed on that account.

Indeed, the power to leave those acts undone, or even to do the opposite, coexists with the very act of praying and of giving alms just as much as the power to keep silent coexists with the act of speaking, and the power not to sit, or even to walk, coexists with the act of sitting.

title: Both agree: the act cannot be separated from God's motion, yet a power to cease or to the opposite remains
english: Both sides, then, agree on two points. A man whom the force and efficacy of God's grace or providence, together with his own reason's dictate, moves and drives to act must act, because his action cannot be separated from that motion of God and that determination of his own judgment.
And yet with such an act, and so with God's motion toward it, there coexists a power to stop it or even to do the opposite, in the way that has been explained and repeated more than once.

title: They differ in words but agree in substance
english: So when one party says that a man whom God moves to a given act acts necessarily, and the other insists that no necessity in the proper sense drives him to act, their words differ but their meaning is the same.

The first party says such a man acts necessarily because his act cannot be separated from God's motion, and the second does not deny it. The second says he is bound to act by no necessity in the proper sense, because a power to the opposite act, or at least to leaving the act undone, sits perfectly well with the act itself and still more with the motion toward it, and the first party readily grants that.

title: The Reformed dispute over indifference can likewise be settled
english: The same considerations show that the disagreement still apparently left among teachers of the Reformed School can easily be settled.

Some of them hold that freedom of choice includes a certain indifference in the free agent, by which, given everything required beforehand for acting, it can act or not act, and do this or that. Others deny that any such indifference is included in freedom or has anything to do with it.

title: What the defenders of indifference mean: not equipoise, but a true intrinsic power to act otherwise
english: Those who hold that freedom never exists without some indifference in the free agent do not mean by indifference a state in which the agent leans no more one way than the other and hangs in the balance, equally ready to be pushed either way. That is the very thing their opponents most object to.

None of the defenders of this indifference fails to hold that it is present even in someone who has decided, with firm and sure judgment, that he must do this and nothing else, and whose will is carried with great force in one direction by deep-rooted habits he could shake off only with the utmost difficulty.

In this matter, then, by indifference they mean simply a real, intrinsic power not only to act but also to stop acting, not only to do this but also to do something else or its opposite. That power is found not only in someone who is unsure and torn over whether to act, but also in someone who has no hesitation or doubt about what he should or should not do, and who sets himself, with a fixed and steady purpose, to act in this way and no other.

title: Nor do they mean the act can fail to follow upon efficacious grace and a settled judgment
english: Further, when they say that a free agent, given everything required beforehand for acting, can act or not act, and do this or that, they do not mean that the will's act can fail to follow once everything required for some act of will is in place, including the motion of God's grace and the practical judgment of the mind, so that the absence of the act could coexist with everything that moves and disposes the will to act.

They admit it is impossible for God to move someone by his effective grace to an act of godliness and for that act not to be produced, or for someone, having weighed everything, to judge that he must do and seek something here and now and then not do and seek it.

All they mean is this. The man who is moved to act in the way described will act infallibly and surely, and it cannot happen that he does not act; yet he still keeps in himself a real power not to act and to act otherwise. That power remains not only in someone fully prepared and ready to act but in someone actually acting. For although an act cannot coexist with its own absence or with a contrary act, the power to the contrary act can perfectly well coexist with it, as has been stressed many times already.

title: What the deniers of indifference mean: equipoise, in which no Christian theologian ever placed freedom
english: Those who argue the other way, that freedom of choice does not require any indifference in the agent, seem to mean by indifference the will's equal balance (ἰσοῤῥοπία), when it leans no more to one side than to the other and can be swayed no more this way than that.
Yet no one who bears the name of theologian in the Christian Schools has ever made freedom consist in that.

title: Nor do they deny the power to act otherwise: neither the act nor grace removes it
english: In the same way, when they say it is false that a free agent, given everything required for acting, can act and not act, and do this and that, they do not mean that whatever prepares and drives him to act takes away his ability to act otherwise or to hold the act back. They acknowledge that the act itself does not remove that ability, much less the things that drive him to it.

They do not deny that someone who by God's grace shows mercy to the needy always keeps in himself the power not to show it, or that someone who scorns this world's pleasures keeps the ability to pursue and embrace them; God's grace does not take that ability from him.

Their only point is that once everything required for acting is in place, a free agent cannot fail to act, even though he otherwise keeps an ability by which he could refrain or act differently. For instance, once everything needed on God's side to produce a man's faith and conversion is in place, the man cannot fail to be converted and believe, though always, even while he believes and is converted, he keeps an ability by which he could fail to believe and be converted.

title: So the deniers reject only two things, and the defenders of indifference grant both
english: This makes it plain that when these theologians deny that freedom consists in some indifference of the agent, they have only two things in view. First, freedom does not consist in a wavering state in which the person called free leans no more toward acting than toward not acting. Second, once God's grace and providence are at work with their motion and efficacy, and the agent's own judgment has given its dictate, the free agent cannot fail to do what God's effective motion and his own judgment drive him to. Both points are readily admitted by those Reformed who teach that freedom of choice includes a certain indifference toward acting.

What has been said shows just as clearly that the teachers who defend that indifference have only this in mind: God's motion and the mind's practical judgment move a man to act in such a way that, on the one hand, he acts surely and infallibly and, on the other, he is not deprived of the ability not to act or to act otherwise. In the same way, when a man actually acts, the act he has been moved and driven to does not take that ability from him.

title: Rightly understood, the Reformed doctrine agrees in substance with the more received Thomists
english: From all this it is clear that the Reformed teaching on this point, correctly stated and understood as its own exponents intend it, does not in fact differ from the view of those in the Roman School called the more widely received Thomists.

These Thomists maintain that freedom is opposed not only to compulsion but also to natural necessity, necessity in the proper sense. Even so, they recognize that once everything required for acting is in place, the free creature's act follows necessarily, with a necessity of infallibility.

A free agent always keeps in itself the power not to act, even while it is actually acting, and all the more when it is on the point of acting. But once everything required on God's side and on the intellect's side for the will to act is in place, the will acts surely and infallibly, and its action cannot fail to follow. On their teaching, then, the power not to act or to act otherwise can perfectly well coexist with everything required for acting, but the absence of the act cannot, and still less a contrary act.

title: Their indifference is only the true power not to act, as Alvarez states (De auxiliis IV.14)
english: By the indifference to acting or not acting in which, on their view, freedom must be placed, or which at least necessarily goes with freedom, they mean nothing other than what was described above.

It is not an indifference that would picture a free cause as unsure and torn over whether to act, nor one by which, given everything required for acting, the free agent might just as well not act as act. It is simply a real power not to act and to act otherwise. That power remains in a free cause when, with everything required for acting in place, it is not only on the point of acting but will act infallibly and surely.

Alvarez sets out his view on this very clearly and explicitly in the summary of his work on the helps of divine grace, book 4, chapter 14, the source of the words of his that we quoted in the preceding disputation.
translator_notes: Alvarez is the Dominican Diego Álvarez; the work is his De auxiliis divinae gratiae.

title: Rivet's account of free choice is taken word for word from Alvarez
english: That the view of this Diego Alvarez, and of the others called with him the more recent Thomists, is here exactly the same as that of the teachers of the Reformed Church is well attested by the very learned Andrew Rivet, some years ago professor at the University of Leiden. When he set out his own mind on the freedom of human choice, he used no words but those taken from Alvarez himself, in his Summa of controversies, treatise 4, question 3.

He grants that one may accept the definition of free choice as 'a faculty of the will by which, given everything required beforehand for acting, it can act or not act', provided this is taken in the divided sense, not the composite. 'That is,' he says, 'if someone says that, given everything required beforehand for the act in the order of reason or of time, free choice can act or not act, meaning that together with those same prerequisites there is in free choice the ability and power by which it could act or not act if it wished, as Diego Alvarez distinguishes. For even God's effective motion, by which the will is determined to such an act, does not take from free choice the ability to perform that act or the contrary one; it only brings it about that, while free choice is able to perform such an act or not, it performs it infallibly and yet freely. When it does so, the power to another act remains, because it is not determined by nature to such acts.

For, as the same author says, in a contingent and free cause there is at once a power to either of two opposites, but not a power to have the opposites at once. A power to one act does not conflict with a power to the contrary act, nor even with the contrary act itself, though contrary acts do conflict with each other in the same subject. Hence created free choice, not only before it is determined to one act but in the very instant in which God determines it and it determines itself to that act, has at the same moment a power by which it can produce the contrary act if it wishes. It has no power to have the contrary act at the same moment, because two contrary acts cannot be in the same power at once, only one after the other.'

All these words are either quoted outright or at least borrowed from Diego Alvarez. So is what Rivet adds as that teacher's conclusion, which he endorses: that it does not belong to the nature or definition of free choice that, given everything required beforehand in the order of causality for performing such an act, it can leave that same act undone in the composite sense, if the composition is made between those prerequisites and the absence of the act or a contrary act. In other words, with God's effective help it cannot at the same time be true that free choice does not produce the act of love, or that it produces an act contrary to the love of God.
translator_notes: Andreas Rivetus is André Rivet, the French Reformed theologian who taught at Leiden.

title: The only real controversy left to the Reformed is with the Molinists
english: So no dispute of substance or of any weight is left for the Reformed except with those in the Roman School called Molinists, after the famous Jesuit Luis de Molina, who wrote and taught about a century ago.

They understand the indifference to acting and not acting in which freedom of choice consists, and the familiar definition that calls it 'that by which, given everything required beforehand for acting, the will can act and not act, do this or that', very differently from the more recent Thomists, as we showed in the preceding disputation.

title: What the Molinists grant: not equipoise; habits; the composite sense; not a power of good and evil
english: They do agree with the others that the indifference in question here does not mean a condition of the will in which it leans no more one way than the other and hangs between two opposites as if balanced on scales. They grant that freedom suffers nothing from habits that strongly incline the will to do this rather than that and make it hard for it to go another way.

Nor do they deny that, in a certain composite sense, it is false that the will can act and not act, or do this and that, namely if someone takes this to mean that an act and its absence, or two contrary acts, can be present and combined in the will at once.

They also accept that the indifference in which the essence of freedom consists is not the power to act well or badly. They acknowledge that freedom of choice remains even in one who cannot act well, as in the damned spirits, and is present still more in one who cannot act badly, as in the saints who see God's face and reign with him in heaven.

title: What the Molinists defend: the act may fail to follow upon all prerequisites; Reformed and recent Thomists deny it
english: What they do defend, and strongly, is that the will is in itself so undetermined and indifferent that, given everything required beforehand for acting, whether on God's side, the object's, or the intellect's, the will can fail to act, and often actually does. Nothing, then, that moves and stirs the will to act beforehand is such that, once it is in place, the will's act cannot fail to follow; quite often it really does not follow.

So everything that precedes the will's act and is required for it can really be combined not only with a power not to act or to do something else but with the very absence of the act, and even with the contrary act.

As the foregoing shows clearly enough, both the Reformed and those more recent Thomists deny this. They hold that a power not to act, or to do the opposite, can indeed coexist in the will with what God's side or the intellect's side requires for acting, but that once those are in place the will always acts and nothing else can happen. On that supposition the will acts surely and infallibly, though it keeps in itself the power not to act.

title: Rome has not defined the dispute; Paul V and Clement VIII seemed to favour the Thomists, Innocent X and Alexander VII the other side
english: The dispute has often been raised and argued before the popes of Rome and before a body of cardinals appointed for the purpose, yet so far they have not settled it, and they have allowed their people to hold and defend either view as they choose.

Around the turn of this century, at the close of the last, Popes Paul V and Clement VIII seemed to favour the Thomists' view. In these last years their successors Innocent X and Alexander VII seem to have leaned rather toward the opposite teaching. As a result it has now become by far the more common view in the Roman School and is held by most of its theologians.
translator_notes: The body of cardinals is the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1598-1607), which ended without a definition.

title: Alignment: Jansenists and recent Thomists with the Dort Reformed; Remonstrants with the Molinists
english: On this point, moreover, some teachers of the Roman Church, namely the so-called Jansenists and those more recent Thomists as well, join forces against the Molinists with the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort.

On the Molinists' side, by contrast, stand those Reformed in the Netherlands called Remonstrants or Arminians, along with others who do not follow the Synod of Dort, and they defend the Molinist teaching on this question very vigorously.

title: First Reformed objection: the Molinist view lessens the efficacy of grace (1 Corinthians 4:7)
english: The Reformed teachers reject their view mainly because it lessens the efficacy of God's grace and gives free choice more than its due in the matter of salvation.

Scripture teaches that every good thing in us must be credited entirely to God's grace, as the Apostle says: 'What do you have that you did not receive?' On this teaching, however, the fact that a man is able to believe and love God is indeed owed to the helps of grace, which move and stir him to faith and love. But the fact that he consents to the grace that moves him and settles himself to believe and love God depends so much on his freedom of choice that it is not, properly, an effect of God's grace, since the consent often fails to follow when grace is given. God's grace could then be called only a condition of it, a cause without which it would not happen.

title: Second objection: the will, not grace, would distinguish believers from unbelievers
english: Scripture also teaches that it is God's grace that sets people apart from one another: those who are converted from those who are not, believers from unbelievers, those who obey God's call from those who resist it. As Paul says, 'Who makes you different?'

The doctrine we are now examining, however, implies that the difference between people is made not by God's grace but simply by the human will. It assumes that when equal grace is offered to several people, one believes and another does not, one is converted and another is not.

It follows that one person's believing and being converted rather than another's must be traced not to any efficacy of grace but only to the free self-determination of the human will, because this one chose to consent to the grace that moved him and came first to him, while that one refused.

title: Third objection: grace would give only the powers, not the willing and doing (Philippians 2:13)
english: Moreover, if God's grace merely moves, prepares and stirs people to will and to carry out what he commands, in such a way that the willing and doing themselves can fail to follow in a person once grace is given, and in fact often do fail, then grace produces in a person the strength or the dispositions needed for willing and doing good, but not the willing and doing themselves.
The Apostle testifies the opposite: it is God who works in us both to will and to do for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13).

title: Fourth objection: Christ teaches a grace that brings all who receive it to him (John 6:45)
english: Finally, if the will can always fail to act even when everything required for acting is in place, on God's side too and with no efficacy of grace whatever left out, then there is no grace of God, at least no ordinary grace, that a person's conversion follows infallibly and surely, and that brings everyone who receives it, without exception, to Christ.
Christ himself teaches the opposite: there is a grace of God that no one receives without coming to him. 'Everyone,' he says, 'who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me' (John 6).

title: Christ's argument in John 6:43-45 would fail if many who are drawn do not believe
english: Surely, if many of those whom the Father's grace draws and God teaches inwardly still do not believe in Christ or come to him, how could Christ give, in that same passage, this as the reason why not everyone who hears the gospel comes to him, namely that those who come to him must be drawn and taught by the Father?

'Do not grumble among yourselves,' he says. 'No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. It is written in the Prophets: And they will all be taught by God. Everyone, then, who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me.'

If the very people who do not believe the gospel are drawn by the Father's grace, it would make no sense to say: 'Do not be surprised that this person and that, to whom the gospel was preached, have still not believed it, since those who believe the gospel must be drawn by God's grace.'

title: Conclusion: freedom is wrongly placed in a power not to act even in the composite sense
english: There is, then, a divine grace, shared indeed by all the elect, whose motion and impulse a person's conversion follows infallibly and surely; and yet everyone agrees that a person's conversion to God is a free act of the will.

It is clear, therefore, that freedom is wrongly located in the will's always being able, with everything required for acting in place, including grace's ordinary motion, as much not to act as to act, and that not only in the divided sense but also in the composite sense, so that grace's motion could coexist with the absence of the act toward which it moves a person.

title: Safer definitions of free choice: those of Alvarez and of Bellarmine
english: So, rather than the familiar description of free choice as 'a faculty by which, given everything required beforehand for acting, a person can act and not act, do this or that', it is safer to use the one Alvarez put in its place: 'Free choice is a faculty of will and reason for acting or not acting, as one pleases, and for doing one thing or the other.'

Or else Bellarmine's: 'Free choice is a free power, given or granted for the great glory of God, to choose one thing over another among the things that lead to some end, or to reject or accept one and the same thing as we decide.'

title: Durandus: God concurs with secondary causes only remotely and mediately
english: Durandus, a well-known figure among the older scholastics, held and taught that God concurs with secondary causes only remotely and mediately.

On his account God gave everything its own nature and essence, bestowed the power to act, and keeps both in being by his continual power. He did so on the understanding that each creature, by the power God once placed in it and always sustains, then carries out its own motions, without God touching its acts and effects directly and of himself. It follows that God is only the remote cause of what creatures do, and the creature alone is the proximate and immediate cause.

title: Among recent writers Louis of Dole, a Capuchin, follows Durandus (as reported by Rutherford)
english: Among more recent writers, a certain Louis of Dole, of the Capuchin order, whose book appeared with many approvals from theologians, comes over to Durandus's view.

He says that God's concurring with man in action amounts to nothing more than creating free choice, in natural acts, or, in supernatural acts, giving a power or habit of acting by which the will itself does the entire work in every supernatural act, without any further immediate concurrence of God actually advancing the action. His words are reported in this form by Samuel Rutherford, professor of theology at the University of St Andrews, in his Scholastic Disputation on Divine Providence, chapter 25.
translator_notes: Ludovicus a Dola is the Capuchin Louis of Dole; Samuel Retorfortis is Samuel Rutherford, whose Disputatio scholastica de divina providentia Le Blanc cites.

title: On this view there is no difficulty in reconciling concurrence with freedom
english: For these teachers, then, reconciling God's concurrence with the freedom of human acts poses no problem at all.
God does not concur in those acts immediately, but only mediately, through the free choice he created once and keeps in being without interruption.

title: The Roman School commonly rejects this: God gives being to every act of the creature immediately
english: The Roman School, however, generally rejects this view. With very few exceptions, the teachers of the Roman Church, old and recent alike, agree that God cooperates with secondary causes in such a way that every action of a secondary cause comes proximately from God as well as from that cause.
No action can be performed by a creature unless God, together with the creature, gives that action its being, and does so of himself and directly.

title: Their proof from Acts 17:28: in him we live and move and are
english: They draw this from certain passages of Scripture, chiefly Acts 17:28: 'In him we live and move and have our being.'

When the Apostle says that we exist and live in God, that is, through him, he makes it clear enough that God gave us our nature and all our powers at the start and constantly sustains them. And when he adds that we also move in God, he appears to teach outright that all our movements and actions, like our nature itself, come directly from God and are carried out by his power.

title: John 5:17: my Father works until now
english: They also cite Christ's words in John 5:17: 'My Father is working until now, and I am working.'

The unceasing work ascribed to God there, they argue, is best explained as the continual influence by which God concurs in every action of created things and produces those actions together with them. This is all the more so because Christ clearly has in mind a work like the one he had just done in healing the lame man.

title: Texts that ascribe to God what happens daily in nature
