english: They also think the same can be inferred from every passage in which Scripture assigns to God, one by one, the things that happen daily in nature through secondary causes.

So in Psalm 104 God is said to water the mountains from his upper rooms and to make grass grow for the cattle and plants to serve mankind. In Psalm 135 he brings up clouds from the ends of the earth, makes lightning for the rain, and brings the winds out of his storehouses. In the New Testament he clothes the grass of the field, that is, decks it with flowers, and gives each kind of seed its own body (Matthew 6:30; 1 Corinthians 15:38).

Scripture would hardly have spoken this way, they argue, if no particular and immediate act of God were involved in such things and they had no proximate and immediate cause other than nature itself as God created it.

title: An argument from natural reason: what preservation needs, first production needs still more
english: To these scriptural testimonies they add an argument from natural reason, which runs as follows. No created substance can continue to exist unless God keeps it in being by his immediate influence. Much more, then, do the motions and actions of substances need such influence, for how could accidents depend less on God for their preservation than substances do?

Moreover, whatever a thing needs in order to be kept in being, it needs all the more in order to be produced in the first place. It follows that secondary causes can produce nothing whatever unless an actual and immediate influence of the first cause is present at the same time.

title: Hence the common Roman conclusion: God concurs proximately and immediately with every act; but how is disputed
english: From these and like arguments the teachers of the Roman Church now conclude, almost unanimously, that God concurs and cooperates with every secondary cause, necessary, free or contingent, in each of its acts, and does so proximately and immediately.
But when one asks what this cooperation of the first cause with the secondary cause is and what it consists in, the scholastic teachers turn out to hold widely different views.

title: Thomas and the Dominicans: God premoves and applies secondary causes to their work (Estius)
english: Thomas and most of his followers, chiefly the Dominicans, teach that to explain God's concurrence it is not enough to say simply that God flows into the various acts and effects of secondary causes and gives them and keeps them in being, as he created and keeps in being the secondary causes themselves and their powers.

They insist that something more is needed: God must premove the secondary causes and apply them to their work, without which they would do nothing whatever. This, they say, is what the dependence of secondary causes on God as first mover requires.

On their view God is called the first mover precisely because he moves all other causes beforehand and applies them to their operations, and so produces all the effects of secondary causes first in the order of nature, though not of time. So Estius puts it on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 24, paragraph 14.

title: This seems to be the teaching of the Roman Catechism (on the first article of the Creed; Wisdom 8:1)
english: This appears to be the teaching of the Roman Catechism itself, published by order of the Council of Trent. Toward the end of its explanation of the first article of the Creed it says:

'God not only protects and governs by his providence everything that exists. He also so drives the things that move and act, by an inward power, to their motion and action that, while he does not hinder the efficiency of secondary causes, he goes before it, since his most hidden power reaches to every single thing and, as the wise man testifies, "reaches mightily from one end to the other", and so on.'

title: God stirs and applies the secondary cause; with the premotion given, it cannot fail to act in the composite sense
english: They hold, therefore, that God rouses and applies the secondary cause to act, and that before the creature works, in the order of reason and nature, God effectively moves it in each of its actions. It is God who acts and brings it about that the creature acts and does whatever it does.

Without this premotion from God the creature can do nothing at all; and once the premotion is given, it is impossible, in the composite sense, for the secondary cause not to do and make what the first cause premoves it to.

title: The difficulty: how can premotion consist with created freedom?
english: Since on their view this divine premotion applies to free agents no less than to necessary ones, a considerable difficulty arises: how can it be reconciled with the freedom of creatures?

If our will can do nothing unless God first moves it and applies it to its work, how can it be considered mistress of its own act and indifferent to acting or not acting, when the divine motion and application required beforehand for each of its acts is not in its power? And again, when God moves the will and applies it to its work, how can the will be said to act freely, when it can neither refrain from acting nor resist the divine motion?

title: Bellarmine: the divine motion is received according to the will's negative determination (De Lib. Arb. IV.16)
english: To resolve that difficulty Bellarmine says that God's influence or power, by which the will is moved and applied to its work, is received in secondary causes according to their disposition.

For Bellarmine the disposition according to which God's motion is received in the will is simply a kind of negative determination that comes before both God's influence and the will's elicited act. In his sense it consists in the will's letting itself be moved by the object that reason sets before it, or not letting itself be moved by it. He calls the determination negative because it lies not in a positive act but in the absence of one, though the will is no less free to act than not to act.

This, he thinks, is how the will is truly free and determines itself even though God moves it and applies it to its work: God's motion itself is in the will's power. 'If it lets itself be moved by the object set before it,' he says, 'God applies it and moves it to produce the act; if it does not, God neither applies it nor moves it. God freely bound himself to this when he created a free will.' (De libero arbitrio, book 4, chapter 16.)

title: So, for Bellarmine, the will remains mistress of its act because the motion is in a way in its power
english: On Bellarmine's view, then, the answer to the objection is this. Although the will needs God's prior motion and application in order to act, it is always mistress of its act, because it has that motion in its power to some degree, in the way just explained.

Once God's motion is given, the will cannot fail to be moved; yet it is always free in acting, because it was in its power not to be moved by God, namely by not disposing itself, through that negative determination, to receive his motion. That was up to the will.

title: Many Thomists reject Bellarmine's solution: God moves the will at his own choice, prior by nature to its self-determination
english: Bellarmine's solution does not satisfy many of those who hold with Thomas that the will, like every other secondary cause, needs a certain prior motion and application from God in order to act.

They maintain that God moves the will as he chooses, without any regard to a negative determination of that kind that may have preceded in the created will. He does not merely move it but efficaciously impels it to act in this way or that, so that the will is determined by God to do this and not something else, to will this and refuse that, first in the order of nature, before it determines itself.

title: This is their 'physical predetermination': physical as opposed to moral causality
english: This is what they call predetermination, and they also call it physical, not in the sense in which the physical, meaning the natural, is opposed to the supernatural, but in the sense in which the physical is opposed to the moral.

They hold that God predetermines created wills to act not merely by presenting an object, urging and attracting, which is what a moral cause does, but by moving the will itself directly and exerting on it a true, real action in the proper sense, which is what belongs to a cause called physical.

title: They extend predetermination to evil acts as well as good
english: They hold that predetermination of this kind takes place not only in the good acts of free causes but in their evil acts too.

Since they think that the secondary cause depends on the first so completely that it can do nothing unless the first moves it and applies it to act as its instrument, they teach, consistently with that doctrine, that even for acts tainted with some malice and depravity the created will is premoved and predetermined by God in such a way that, once God's motion is given, it must do this or that.

title: Yet they deny God is the author of sin: he effects only what is positive; the depravity is a privation
english: They deny, however, that it follows that God is the author of sin. In an act of sin God brings about only what is positive in it, and therefore good, and moves and determines the will to nothing beyond that.

The depravity and corruption attached to such an act is nothing positive requiring a cause that properly produces it. It is only the absence of the rightness the act ought to have, and it arises from the failure of the created will.

title: Alvarez teaches this exactly (De auxiliis II.7): God physically predetermines the will to all its good acts
english: Diego Alvarez sets out this teaching accurately and clearly in the Summa of his work De auxiliis divinae gratiae, book 2. The heading of chapter 7 there reads: 'That God, by a prior motion inhering in the created will, moves, applies, or predetermines it in the manner of a physical cause to all its good acts in particular, without prejudice to its freedom.'

In that chapter he writes: 'By this motion and application God really changes the will from one state to another and makes it willing instead of unwilling.' And again: 'By this actual, efficacious motion, in the manner of a physical cause, that is, truly as an efficient cause, God predetermines man's will to free good acts, so that the will, moved by God through help of this kind, determines itself freely and infallibly to produce its second act freely.'

title: Alvarez II.9: God premoves free choice to the act of sin as act and being; the malice is from the deficient will
english: The heading of chapter 9 reads: 'That God, by a prior motion, truly as an efficient cause or in the manner of a physical cause, premoves free choice to the act of sin insofar as it is an act and a being.'

The chapter opens: 'What has been said about the predetermination of the will to good acts must be extended to the act of sin insofar as it is an act and a being. Hence whatever being is found in any act of sin, even one otherwise intrinsically evil, must be traced back to God as the first cause who premoves and, by an actual motion, predetermines the created will to that act insofar as it is an act and insofar as it is a being.'

Then, to show why it does not follow from God's being the first cause who premoves and predetermines the created will to an intrinsically evil act, such as blasphemy or hatred of God, that God causes the moral malice in such acts, he says this: the deformity of sin, or moral malice, does not follow intrinsically and by the nature of the case from the act of blasphemy or hatred of God in its essence as an act, nor as a being in the order of nature, even taken individually. It follows from the act as it comes from a created will that fails. The moral malice and the defect of sin must therefore be laid on the failing will, not on God.

title: Estius states the same and raises against himself the objection from freedom
english: What Estius writes in the passage cited above agrees with this. Having set out the same view and brought many arguments to support it, he concludes as follows and raises against himself the objection from the freedom of the human will:

'Since, then, what has been said makes it clear that our will is efficaciously moved and determined to its actions by God as first cause, first agent, mover and deliberator, and is therefore anticipated and predetermined by him, it remains to explain how the freedom of our will is consistent with that efficacious motion and determination, indeed with divine premotion and predetermination. For what a prior cause efficaciously moves and determines to one side does not seem to be left free to go either way.'
translator_notes: 'deliberante' is printed as it stands in the 1675 text; it is not emended.

title: Estius's answer: freedom requires choice from a judgment that could have been otherwise; only uncreated will has its choice from no prior
english: His answer is that for the nature of free choice it is enough that the will, on a prior judgment of the practical intellect, chooses one of two opposites in such a way that it could choose the other on a different judgment of the same intellect. The root and foundation of freedom of choice lies in the intellect, insofar as it can weigh different aspects of good in opposite options and set them before the will.

The nature of free choice does not require that a free agent, when it chooses on a prior judgment, should not be moved by some higher cause to judge and choose as it does. So, since God's motion predetermining the will does not prevent a man from having a full and complete judgment of reason, judging one means contingent and another necessarily connected with the end, and being able to choose differently on a different judgment, that motion does the freedom of our will no harm. It belongs only to the uncreated will not to receive its choice from something prior.

title: Alvarez's other reconciliation: the premotion is needed to act actually, not to be able to act
english: Alvarez, however, tries another way to reconcile the physical predetermination of the human will to each of its acts by the impulse of God moving it with the will's free choice.

He sets himself this objection: 'If God's prior influence on the cause is necessary for the will to act, it follows that without it the will cannot act, and so its freedom is lost.' He replies: 'That prior motion, or immediate influence on the cause, is not needed for the will to be able to act if it wishes; it has that through its own power, or through supernatural habits. It is needed only for the will actually to act. So from the fact that God does not move the will by that prior motion, it does not follow that the will cannot will or act; it follows only that it will not in fact act.'

title: Alvarez II.6: power to the contrary stands with predetermination in the divided sense; the omitter sins by his own fault
english: In chapter 6 of the same book, answering the second argument, he denies that because God has predetermined someone to will this or that, it is not, absolutely speaking, in his power to will something else, although on the supposition of that divine predetermination it is impossible, in the composite sense, for him to will another object.

In short, he distinguishes between willing and acting on the one hand and being able to will and act on the other. He grants that without that predetermining influence the will never acts, and that with it the will always acts. But he insists that with it the will has the power not to act, and without it the will has the power to act, in the divided sense. On his view the will's power not to act or to act otherwise coexists with the predetermining influence, but the opposite act, or ceasing from the act, does not. Conversely, without that influence the power to act remains in the will, though without it that power is never brought into act.

From this he concludes that someone who omits an act that is commanded omits it freely and sins. Through sufficient help he could have kept the command; by God's mercy he could have had the motion needed to act; and by his own fault he prevented God from giving it to him.

title: Most Roman doctors now reject predetermination: it destroys freedom and makes God the author of sin
english: The great majority of the Roman Church's teachers, however, now reject this view. They argue that an influence premoving and predetermining human wills to each of their acts completely destroys the freedom of human choice.
They add that it would make God the author of sin, since on that view he predetermines people even to intrinsically evil acts and lays on them a kind of necessity to do wrong.

title: Their view: God concurs by acting on the action and effect, not on the faculty
english: They therefore reason about God's concurrence quite differently. First, they hold that when God concurs and cooperates with secondary causes he does not do or impress anything on the faculty that acts, our will, for instance.
He only flows into and acts directly on the action itself and on the effect of the secondary cause, producing it at the very moment the secondary cause produces it.

title: God's action is the creature's own action as receiving its being from God, not a distinct action on the will
english: Next, and consistently with this, they teach that the action of the first cause concurring with the secondary cause is not an action really distinct from that of the secondary cause. It is that same action, considered as receiving its being from the first cause.

So when God concurs with the will in an act of willing or refusing, he does not, on their view, exert on the will an action distinct from the will's own. He only gives being to the will's action together with the will, and keeps that action in being. God's cooperation here is therefore not something other than our act of will; it is our act of will itself, insofar as its production and preservation depend directly on God.

title: So the secondary cause is not moved or determined by God; God's concurrence is indifferent and is determined by the creature
english: They also deny, as plainly follows from the foregoing, that the first cause moves the secondary cause to act or determines it, in acting, to produce a given action.

On their view, then, the secondary cause, and so the will, does not act because God moves it and applies it to act; rather, God cooperates with it because it sets itself to act. God's concurrence and influence is of itself indifferent, and it is the secondary causes that determine it to the various kinds of action.

title: Molina's account in the Concordia (q. 14, disp. 26): one action, from God by general concurrence and from the creature by particular influence
english: These points, and more of the same kind, are worked out and explained at greater length by Luis de Molina in his Concordia of free choice with the gifts of grace, question 14, disputation 26.

He states, first, that God concurs with secondary causes in their operations and effects in this way: just as the secondary cause directly produces its operation and through it brings about its result or effect, so God, by a general concurrence, flows directly together with it into that same operation and through the operation or action brings about its result or effect.

Second, when God concurs with secondary causes he acts as a universal cause, by an influence indifferent to various actions and effects, and that general influence is determined to different kinds of action and effect by the particular influence of secondary causes, which differs according to the different power each has to act. The sun's influence, which is likewise universal, is determined by a man's influence to produce a man and by a horse's influence to produce a horse. If the cause is free, it is in its power to exert its influence so that this action rather than that results, say willing rather than refusing, or walking rather than sitting, and this effect rather than that, this artefact rather than another. Or it can withhold its influence altogether, so that there is no action at all.

Third, God's influence through universal concurrence is not enough to produce any effect without the influence of the particular secondary cause that determines it. Nor, conversely, is the particular cause's influence enough without God's influence through universal concurrence, which helps it and which by ordinary law God has resolved never to withhold. These two influences depend on each other in order to exist in reality; indeed they are not two actions but numerically one action. As it comes from God acting in that way it is called general concurrence; as it comes from the secondary cause, say from fire heating something, it is called the concurrence or influence of the fire. And that action is of this kind, heating rather than cooling, not because it comes from God through universal concurrence but because it comes from the fire, with God cooperating, through the fire's particular power.

title: On the Molinist account concurrence harms neither freedom of exercise nor freedom of specification
english: These teachers believe that their account of divine concurrence lets them show easily how it can be reconciled with the freedom of human acts.

Two kinds of freedom are usually ascribed to the will: freedom as to the exercise of the act and freedom as to its specification. Concurrence understood in their way takes nothing from either. It does not impair freedom of exercise, since it lays no necessity of acting on the will. The will does not act because God acts; rather, God acts because the will acts, even though God and the will begin to act at the same moment of time and of nature. In the language of the Schools they put it this way: the will acts prior by nature to God, not with the priority of the instant 'in which' but of the instant 'from which'.

title: God has decreed to concur whenever the will determines itself; the kind of act comes from the will
english: The will can do nothing at all without God's concurrence. Yet under the law God laid down when he made it free, that concurrence is always ready for it, because God willed, and decreed from eternity, to concur in every work of the free will once the will has determined itself to act.

The will is no less free as to the specification of its act. Whether it acts well or badly, whether it shuns a thing rather than seeks it, does not come from any force in the divine concurrence but from the will's own determination. In producing an action of this kind rather than that, the will freely makes use of God's concurrence, which of itself is indifferent.

title: The Remonstrants (Arminius, Grevinchovius, Corvinus) admit only a general, indifferent concurrence
english: Among the Reformed, those in the Netherlands called Remonstrants or Arminians acknowledge no concurrence of God with secondary causes other than the general, indifferent one that is determined by the concurrence of the secondary cause.

This can be seen in Jacobus Arminius, after whom all the rest are named. Arguing against Perkins, he not only asserts that this concurrence of God is indifferent in itself, but also that it 'contributes nothing to the creature's will by which it is inclined, helped or strengthened to act', and that 'the created will has God's concurrence in its own power before it acts, ready and laid out for it' (Antiperkinsus, p. 733). Grevinchovius teaches much the same against Ames (section 32, p. 368), and Corvinus against Tilenus (chapter 9, p. 354).
translator_notes: The Antiperkinsus is Arminius's Examen of William Perkins's treatise on predestination; Grevinchovius is Nicolaas Grevinckhoven, Corvinus is Johannes Arnoldus Corvinus, and Tilenus is Daniel Tilenus.

title: Some who subscribe to Dort agree here with the Molinists and Remonstrants
english: Even among the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort, some seem to agree on this point with the Molinists and the Remonstrants.

They recognize no general concurrence of God with secondary causes other than a simultaneous and indifferent one. By it God acts not on the cause itself but, together with the cause, on its act. It does not determine the secondary cause to one kind of act or another; instead the secondary cause shapes it in various ways according to its nature, or even its freedom.

title: Robert Baron of Aberdeen holds the same view as Fonseca and Suarez
english: This at any rate is beyond all doubt the view of the Scot Robert Baron, professor of theology at the University of Aberdeen during his lifetime, as can be seen in his Metaphysics adapted to the use of theology.

On God's concurrence, and so on its agreement with the freedom of our choice, he declares that he holds exactly the same as Fonseca and Suárez. The concurrence is indifferent in itself and is determined by the secondary cause to a particular kind of action. God has no need to premove secondary causes; it is enough that he acts together with them on their effects and actions. God's concurrence and influence is thus in reality nothing other than the secondary cause's action itself, insofar as that action receives its being from the first cause together with the second and depends on it (Section 8, Disputation 3, 'On the concurrence or cooperation of God').

title: John Strang of Glasgow: God's influence is prior by nature and special, yet Thomist predetermination is not needed for every act
english: The Scot John Strang, himself also a professor, at the University of Glasgow, does not seem far from this view.

He holds that the action in which God and the creature concur comes from God prior by nature to its coming from the creature, and that God's influence on that action is prior by nature to the creature's influence (De voluntate et actionibus Dei circa peccatum, book not numbered in the print, chapter 11). He also denies that God concurs only by a general influence, as the sun concurs in the same way in generating a man and a horse (book 2, chapter 3); he posits a special influence of God for special effects, as these differ in kind, and that physically, not morally. Even so, he argues at length, and proves, that the premotion and predetermination of God which the school of Thomas maintains and defends is not necessary for each and every act of creatures.
translator_notes: Joannes Strangius is John Strang of Glasgow. The print's first reference reads 'lib. cap. 11.' with no book number; it is left as printed.

title: What Strang means by premotion, and where he allows it
english: By that premotion and predetermination, he explains, he means the action by which God stirs and applies the secondary cause to act. Prior by nature and by reason to the creature's acting, God really and efficaciously moves it to each of its actions, acting and bringing it about that the creature acts and does whatever it acts and does. Without this premotion of God the creature can do nothing whatever; once it is given, it is impossible in the composite sense for the secondary cause not to do what the first cause premoves it to.

Strang grants that God does use premotion and predetermination of this kind for the works of grace and for very many other operations of the will, whenever he pleases and there is need. But he denies that it belongs to God's common concurrence or is applied across the board to all the actions of creatures, especially those to which sin is necessarily attached (book 2, chapter 4, near the end).

title: Strang's and Baron's chief reason: otherwise our sins would be imputed to God
english: Strang says he holds this view chiefly because, if God necessarily determined devils and wicked men to every action of sin, it would follow, in his judgment, that our sins could rightly be charged to God.
Robert Baron, cited above, says this was the reason that weighed most with him as well.

title: Both reject predetermination as contrary to freedom; Strang's two senses of freedom
english: Both men also hold that this predetermination should be rejected because it damages the freedom of the will and does not seem capable of being reconciled with it.

Strang does, however, distinguish two senses of freedom (De voluntate Dei circa peccatum, book 2, chapter 8). Freedom in the broader sense is essential to the will and is found in any act done willingly and with reason. Freedom in the stricter sense consists in a certain indifference on the agent's part and belongs to the will with respect to most of its acts. On his view, the divine premotion and predetermination by which God moves human beings gently, in a way suited to an intelligent creature, does not overturn the first kind of freedom. It cannot, however, coexist with the stricter kind, since that freedom lies in indifference, which any prior determination not within the will's own power contradicts.

How God's simultaneous concurrence, always ready for the created will, does no harm to freedom of that kind has been explained above. These theologians reconcile it with freedom in the strict sense in just the same way as the teachers of the Roman School.

title: Very many Reformed side with the Thomists: efficacious premotion to every act, good and evil
english: Very many Reformed theologians, however, side with the school of Thomas. They hold that God not only concurs and cooperates with creatures in each of their acts, but that creatures can do nothing unless God efficaciously premoves and predetermines them to this act or that.

This holds, they say, for free causes as much as for necessary ones, and for evil acts as much as for good ones, although God does not move or predetermine to the malice and depravity of the act, only to what is positive and naturally good in it. And just as on their view the secondary cause can do or perform nothing without such predetermination, so too, once it is given, the cause cannot fail to act and perform.

title: William Ames: without predetermination man would be God's partner, not his subject
english: William Ames holds that premotion and predetermination of this kind must be admitted for secondary causes, and above all for the human will. Otherwise, in his judgment, the subordination of secondary causes to the first cause in their operations would be done away with.

Every operation of the human will would be removed from the rule of providence and from God's efficacious government. Man would be God's partner rather than his subject. Indeed God would hang on man's nod even in matters that weigh most in governing the whole world. Man would no longer have to say, 'If God wills, I shall do this or that'; rather God would have to say, 'If man wills, I shall do this or that' (Bellarminus enervatus, tome 4, book 4, chapter 2).

title: Samuel Rutherford rejects an indifferent concurrence as injurious to God (De divina providentia 25)
english: The Scot Samuel Rutherford, who was professor of theology at the University of St Andrews a few years ago, holds the same view. He attacks with many arguments, as fictitious and impious, a concurrence of God that is general and indifferent in itself and is determined by the concurrence of the secondary cause.

In his judgment such a concurrence wrongs God. It robs God of freedom in his decrees and makes God shamefully dependent on the fickle nod of his creature, since it supposes that God is determined by the creature rather than the creature by God. It also removes the point of the prayers in which we ask God to bend our hearts and the hearts of others as our salvation and theirs requires, for that cannot happen except through an operation by which God determines human wills. For the same reason it would be pointless to thank God for good things obtained through free agents. Nor would the wealth that comes to people through their free acts of trade be from God. Finally, God's particular providence, which Scripture so often commends, would have to be denied (De divina providentia, chapter 25).

title: Rutherford: the real question is indeclinable predetermination, not the word 'physical'
english: In his Exercitationes apologeticae pro divina gratia Rutherford maintains that in all acts, of nature and of grace alike, God determines the will by a truly real impulse, in the manner of a physical cause. He adds, though, that the main dispute is not whether this predetermination should be called physical, but whether God predetermines free acts in a way that cannot be turned aside.

'The question,' he says, 'is whether God does not so move the will that, under that motion, once moved it cannot fail to be fully moved; or whether God's action on the will does not so bend it that it cannot fail freely to bend itself where God inclines it. We, for our part, prove from Scripture that the will is necessitated by God's motion, by which it is moved beyond turning aside.' If anyone grants this, he adds, he is ready to bid farewell to physical predetermination, although in reality God does determine the will in the manner of a physical cause (Exercitation 3, chapter 1).

title: William Twisse distinguishes concurrence from predetermination and rejects the Jesuits' indifferent concurrence
english: The English theologian William Twisse distinguishes God's concurrence from his predetermination, though he thinks both necessary for every action of the creature. He grants that the concurrence is simultaneous with the creature's operation in both nature and time, but he insists that it is joined with a certain prior motion on the will itself.

'We too admit a concurrence on the act,' he says, 'simultaneous both in nature and in time; but we say that this concurrence involves a prior motion on the will itself, prior, I mean, not in time but in nature' (Vindiciae, book 2, part 3). In the same book, at page 18, he rejects an indifferent and undetermined concurrence of the kind the Jesuits teach: 'For my part I think it can be shown that this indifferent and indefinite concurrence is wrongly posited, as plainly as that the sun shines at noon.'
translator_notes: Tuissus is William Twisse; the Vindiciae is his Vindiciae gratiae, potestatis ac providentiae Dei.

title: What Ames and Rutherford chiefly deny; the other side also grants a strong providence beyond general concurrence
english: From the reasons Ames and Rutherford give, it is clear that what they chiefly mean to deny, and shrink from as the gravest error, is that God's operation and efficacy concerning the creature's act consists in nothing more than a concurrence that is indifferent and indefinite in itself.

Those who otherwise hold that God's general concurrence, needed for each act of creatures, is indifferent in itself and variously determined by secondary causes have no intention whatever of asserting that. Besides that general concurrence of God, they recognize the great power and efficacy of divine providence in bringing about, furthering, regulating and directing all kinds of events, especially where human wills and the acts freely elicited by them are concerned. Strang points this out carefully in many places.

title: Ames (with Alvarez) and Twisse: predetermination leaves the power to act otherwise, in the divided sense
english: As for reconciling this predetermining concurrence with freedom of choice, on Ames's view one must say with Diego Alvarez that God's predetermination does not prevent the will from acting freely. It does make the will act certainly and infallibly, yet it does not take from the will the power to act otherwise.

Twisse likewise says that God moves human wills to do something in such a way that whatever happens comes about in keeping with the condition of their free will, so that at the very moment they act they are able not to act, in the divided sense, that is. 'In the composite sense it is utterly impossible.'
translator_notes: The print gives the last word in Greek, ἀδύνατον ('impossible').

title: Rutherford's two indifferences, objective and internal; all these theologians allow only hypothetical necessity
english: According to Rutherford, two kinds of indifference go to make up freedom. One is objective: the intellect puts before the will something it may choose, as a means that is not necessary to the highest good intended absolutely. The other is internal, vital and elective: by it the will of itself is able as much to will a thing as to refuse it, with both the essence of freedom and its own most natural way of acting kept intact.

God's predetermination prejudices neither kind of indifference in any way. Not the objective kind, since it does not prevent the intellect from setting before the will an object it may choose, one suited to reaching the end but not necessarily connected with it. Nor the internal kind, since when God determines the will to refuse this, he does not stand in the way of its being able by nature to will it.

Finally, all these theologians agree that God's premotion and predetermination does impose some necessity on the acts of the will, but only a hypothetical necessity. That does not conflict with freedom, which is overturned only by necessity arising from external force or from natural determination.

title: Some Reformed side with Durandus: Moise Amyraut's concurrence is only conservation
english: Among the teachers of the Reformed School there are also some who, regarding God's general concurrence needed for every act of creatures, seem to think as Durandus and Louis of Dole, teachers of the Roman School, do.

The distinguished Moïse Amyraut, for instance, seems to recognize no general concurrence of God, by which he concurs with all secondary causes, beyond the continual efficacy by which he keeps and sustains the nature of each thing and the powers nature has given it. From this he concludes that such concurrence has no bearing on freedom. 'Suppose,' he says, 'that nature and its powers could subsist without the help of such concurrence; they will certainly act freely. Now add a concurrence that does nothing more than keep in their natural state, and preserve, things that would otherwise collapse and vanish: freedom will suffer no harm from it.' These words show clearly enough that on this point the distinguished author holds, as already said, the same view as the old scholastic Durandus (De libero arbitrio, chapter 4, near the end).

title: Amyraut's providence in good acts: presenting the object and disposing the subject
english: Even so, besides that general concurrence Amyraut recognizes a great efficacy of God's providence, by which God determines in time the acts of our will, good, bad and indifferent alike, in keeping with his eternal decree.

But he reduces the whole efficacy of divine providence that shows itself in good acts to two operations. The first is the presenting of the object, which plainly does no violence to freedom. The second is the inner disposing of the subject, which consists in freeing the faculties from the hindrances that have come upon their native constitution, or even in raising them in some way above the lot of nature. Here too it is no less evident that human freedom suffers no prejudice.

title: Amyraut on evil acts: an external and an internal act of providence
english: In the same way, with respect to evil acts, he teaches that Providence acts in two ways, one external and the other internal. The external act, he says, concerns two things. 'Either it is engaged in presenting objects fitted to stir the faculties, or it consists in this: God does nothing himself, but allows and permits the devil to exercise his working, so as to add to the force of the objects.'

God's internal act in the evil deeds of human beings consists, according to him, in this: out of the many objects leading to evil that a person turns over in his mind, God either obscures one or removes it from the mind altogether, or else arranges for some one object to be presented from the side on which it is most apt and suited to move. In none of this, likewise, can there be anything harmful to human freedom.
translator_notes: The print has the Greek ἐνέργειαν ('working, activity') for the devil's operation.

title: Amyraut on indifferent acts: all human acts are efficaciously determined through the objects
english: Finally, for indifferent acts he traces God's efficacy in the same way to three things: the presenting of objects, the management of causes that can lend those objects force, and an inner operation that makes one object prevail over another and present itself to the mind in the way best suited to move it.

Yet through these operations, which by everyone's admission do no harm to freedom, he holds that all human acts are efficaciously determined by God and that God's eternal decrees about them are fulfilled with complete certainty. The reason is that the human faculties, mind and will, are determined to particular actions by the objects set before them in a way that fits their inclination and disposition. From this arises a kind of necessity in their operations which agrees perfectly well with freedom, and which is still enough to ensure that what God has most surely planned in his eternal counsel and determined shall be done is carried out by human beings with equal certainty and without swerving.

title: Josue de la Place declines to define the dependence of secondary causes on the first
english: Josué de la Place, a most learned and very subtle theologian, agrees with the other theologians that the will in acting depends on God as on the first cause, as other secondary causes do. But being a modest man he does not venture to define what that dependence is or how great it is, and he declines to give his judgment on the various questions about God's concurrence and cooperation with all secondary causes that are commonly debated in the Schools.

These are his words: 'The will depends on God as on the first cause, on which all secondary causes depend in acting. How far secondary causes depend on the first cause in their causing is fiercely disputed among the papists. That God concurs with every cause, so that it acts in keeping with its faculties, is admitted by all. But nearly all of them maintain that this concurrence is immediate, proximate, and simply the same as the action of the secondary causes themselves, though some others object. And over that very immediate concurrence the Dominicans and the Jesuits fight each other stubbornly with all their might, the former for what they call physical predetermination, the latter strenuously opposing it. For our part, out of the reverence we owe to God's infinite majesty, we do not venture to define how great the dependence of the secondary cause on the first is. It is enough for us that, provided it does not cast on God even the slightest stain of our sins, it cannot be made too great' (Treatise on free choice, p. 174).
translator_notes: Josue Placeus is Josué de la Place of Saumur.

title: De la Place reconciles that dependence with freedom as immunity from a threefold necessity
english: A little further on he reconciles this dependence of the will on the first cause with the will's freedom. He writes:

'However our will may depend on God, and whatever God may work in it, it always keeps the freedom that we said lies in exemption from a threefold necessity: of coercion, of determination by matter, and of determination by the senses.'

title: Pareus: the manner is past finding out; God governs the will as a master guides a pupil's hand
english: Pareus's view is not very different. He condemns the rashness of the scholastic teachers who raise and settle various questions about God's concurrence, 'in which', he says, 'they have dared with rash curiosity to investigate and define what cannot be adequately known or explained.' He judges safest the view of Cajetan, who found the agreement of free choice with divine providence inexplicable and beyond understanding in this life, because God's judgments are unsearchable and his ways past finding out.

In general he wants only this held as certain: that the human will is governed by God's nod and inclined wherever he wills. To reconcile this with our freedom, he says that what is governed from outside, without its own deliberation and choice, does not act freely. But when God governs by showing the intellect an object, and through it efficaciously moving and affecting the will to choose this or that of its own accord, the will still chooses freely, even though it is inclined by God's nod wherever he wills. 'In the same way,' he says, 'a beginner learning to form his letters writes freely, though his hand is guided by the schoolmaster.'

This is also the point of what he adds a little later and often repeats: that God by his concurrence does determine the human will, 'but not by a physical, brute, violent determination; rather by a spontaneous one, joined with its own judgment and choice' (Animadversions on Bellarmine's fourth book on free choice, chapter 14).
translator_notes: 'Quis' in the quotation is the old form of 'quibus' ('in which'). The print reads 'cap. 14.' in the reference.

title: Le Blanc: their modesty deserves praise; to define the manner of concurrence is rash
english: For my part, I think the modesty of these very learned men deserves the highest praise. To define with certainty the manner of divine concurrence by which the first cause cooperates with secondary causes seems to me rash and far too bold.
Our feeble understanding cannot penetrate and search out the abyss of God's power and wisdom, and the matter is neither adequately grasped by reason nor revealed clearly enough in Holy Scripture.

title: Physical predetermination to intrinsically evil acts seems to make God the author of sin
english: Above all, I cannot see how anyone can hold that God physically premoves and predetermines free causes even to acts that are intrinsically evil without its following that God is the author of sin.

Who could understand, for instance, that God, by an influence preceding every motion of the human will, laid on the first man a necessity of desiring the forbidden fruit and an appetite for eating it; and that every day, by an efficient causality in the proper sense, he predetermines people, and, to use a barbarous word, 'necessitates' them to blaspheme God and hate him; and yet that the guilt, which cannot be separated from those acts, is not to be laid back on God himself?

title: With de la Place: the dependence cannot be too great, so long as God is not made author of sin; immediate concurrence most probable
english: But as long as God is not made the author of sin, I judge with the most learned de la Place that the dependence of secondary causes on the first in their acting cannot be made too great.
It also seems to me highly probable that God, as the Schools commonly hold, concurs immediately in each and every act of creatures.

title: Providence, even over evil acts, is not confined to a general, indifferent concurrence
english: What I hold as most certain of all, and what I think all theologians grant, is that the power and efficacy of divine providence, even in regard to evil acts, must in no way be confined to a concurrence that is general and indifferent in itself.
In many ways known to his own wisdom, God brings about, furthers, directs and regulates the varied course of events, including those in which human wickedness plays a part.

title: However God works in free causes, he leaves them the power to act otherwise
english: I am no less certain that, in whatever way God acts and works in free causes, he always does so in keeping with their nature and without any prejudice to their freedom.
So when he efficaciously moves human wills to one act or another, he does not take from them the power to act otherwise.

title: Socinus and his followers deny that God has certain foreknowledge of future contingents
english: Socinus and his followers cannot understand how future contingents, things that have no necessary and determinate cause, can be known in advance with certainty.
They therefore deny that God himself has any certain foreknowledge of future events of this kind.

title: Scripture plainly teaches God's foreknowledge: the prophets are its witnesses (Tertullian)
english: It is astonishing that people who grant Scripture divine authority can persuade themselves of this. Nothing is gathered more plainly from Scripture than that God knew beforehand every future thing, as the prophecies recorded in it make clear.

As Tertullian neatly puts it, 'God's foreknowledge has as many witnesses as God has made prophets.' The prophets, inspired by God, could not have foretold things that happened only many ages later and were done freely by human beings unless those things were known to God from eternity.
translator_notes: The Tertullian saying is from Adversus Marcionem, book 2, chapter 5.

title: God foretold free acts centuries ahead: the oppression in Egypt (Genesis 15)
english: Countless examples from Scripture prove that God foretold many things that human beings would freely do many ages later.

In Genesis 15 God foretold that the Egyptians would oppress Abraham's descendants for four hundred years, and that in oppressing that people they would sin gravely and bring God's wrath on themselves. 'Know for certain,' God says to Abraham, 'that your descendants will be strangers in a land that is not theirs; they will be enslaved and oppressed for four hundred years. But I will judge the nation they serve.'

title: Deuteronomy 31: Israel's future idolatry foretold to Moses
english: Likewise in Deuteronomy 31 God is recorded as saying to Moses: 'You are about to sleep with your fathers. Then this people will rise up and prostitute themselves to the foreign gods of the land they are entering to live in. They will forsake me and break my covenant that I made with them.'
The outcome, matching these predictions in every respect, showed that they were certain and infallible.

title: The Jews' unbelief and the rejection of the Messiah foretold (Isaiah 53) and Christ's own predictions
english: In many places the prophets also foretold that the Jews would not believe in the time of the Messiah, and that this people would therefore be rejected. This is especially so in Isaiah 53: 'Who has believed our message, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?'

There the prophet foretells that their unbelief would go so far that they would despise their King, the Messiah, even wound him, remove him by a most cruel and shameful death, and count him among transgressors and criminals. And the Messiah himself, Jesus our Lord, while he lived on earth, foretold one by one all the crimes and outrages that the leaders of the Jewish nation would commit against him. He added that all this must happen so, and that everything written by the prophets about the Son of Man must be fulfilled in this way.

title: Judas's betrayal foretold by Christ and, ages before, by David (Psalms 41 and 109)
english: Christ's prediction about Judas, that he would betray him, is especially striking, and it came long before Satan had put that into Judas's heart. Indeed, many ages before Christ's coming God had foretold the same betrayal through the prophets.

Christ testifies that this is what David's words in Psalm 41 refer to: 'He who eats bread with me has lifted his heel against me' (John 13). And Peter, with an eye to what is written in Psalm 109, says: 'The scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand through the mouth of David concerning Judas,' and so on (Acts 1).

title: Antiochus Epiphanes (Daniel) and the man of sin (Paul): such predictions require certain knowledge of contingents
english: To these may be added what Daniel foretells of the impiety, pride, lust and cruelty of Antiochus Epiphanes, with which he would rage against the Jews and profane God's own temple. Paul likewise foretells the coming of the son of perdition, who would sit in God's temple, exalt himself above God himself, and lead very many astray by lying signs.

All these things were to be done freely by human beings. The Spirit of God, speaking in Scripture, could not have foretold them certainly, clearly and one by one, as we see was done, unless God has certain and distinct knowledge of all future events, however contingent they may be.

title: Without foreknowledge of free acts God would not be omniscient
english: Certainly, if God does not know every future thing from eternity, but is ignorant of what creatures will freely do, omniscience can no longer be ascribed to him.
Nor can he truly be said to know all things, since some things would be hidden from his knowledge.

title: It would also make God mutable and his knowledge imperfect
english: It would also follow that God is not free from all change. Since God knows present things, if he was ignorant of them before they existed, he learned something from the outcome itself and passed from not knowing to knowing, which cannot be conceived without some change in God.
It further follows that God's knowledge is not perfect, since on this hypothesis it grows and advances in what it knows every day.

title: The Socinian objection: Scripture says God grieved and repented that he had made man (Genesis 6)
english: Against so plain a truth the objections the Socinians usually raise have no force. One is that Scripture presents God as saddened by human sins and moved to repentance: 'The Lord saw that human wickedness was great on the earth and that every thought of the heart was set on evil all the time, and he repented that he had made man on the earth. Grieved to the heart, he said, I will wipe man, whom I created, from the face of the earth' (Genesis 6).

From this they infer that before human beings plunged into every kind of crime God did not know for certain that their wickedness would be so great. Otherwise, they say, there seems to be no reason for saying that on seeing it he was grieved and repented of having created man. No one repents of what he has done unless some new knowledge comes to him, or something happens to him that he did not expect and had not foreseen.

title: A second objection: 'Now I know that you fear God' (Genesis 22)
english: And certainly it seems plainly to follow from God's own words to Abraham in Genesis 22 that he learns something new about the free actions of human beings.
After Abraham had shown himself ready to sacrifice his son at God's command, the Lord says: 'Now I know that you fear God, because you have not spared your only son for my sake.'

title: A third objection: God 'expected' grapes and got wild grapes (Isaiah 5)
english: Scripture even seems to teach that some things turn out otherwise than God himself had supposed, since it says that people do some things contrary to what he had expected.

So God complains of the stubbornness and rebellion of the Jewish people in Isaiah 5: 'What more should I have done for my vineyard that I have not done? Why, when I expected it to yield grapes, did it yield wild grapes?'

title: Reply: Scripture speaks of God's repentance figuratively; it signifies an effect, not a feeling (1 Samuel 15)
english: The answer is that Scripture often ascribes human limbs and feelings to God by a figure of speech, not because they belong to him literally and properly. Much that is said of God in human terms (anthropopathos) must therefore be understood in a way fitting for God (theoprepos), in a manner worthy of him.

So when Scripture says that God repented, there is no more need to take this literally than what we read elsewhere, that God's heart was stirred or that smoke rose from his nostrils. Indeed, when Scripture speaks of repentance in the proper sense, it expressly denies it of God, as when Samuel says to Saul: 'The Glory, or Strength, of Israel will not lie or change his mind, for he is not a man, that he should repent' (1 Samuel 15).

In God, then, repentance means not a feeling but an effect. When Scripture says God repented, it puts the antecedent for the consequent: it means that God did what a man does who regrets something he has made. God resolved to wipe from the earth, because of their wickedness, the human beings he had made, as a man destroys a work he regrets.
translator_notes: The print gives two words in Greek: ἀνθρωποπαθῶς ('with human feelings') and θεοπρεπῶς ('as befits God').

title: God's 'sorrow' likewise puts the consequent for the antecedent
english: In the same way God is said to be grieved by human sins, not because he feels in himself any emotion like our sadness. It is simply a way of saying that God strongly disapproves of human sins and is displeased by them, and that they are such as would bring him sorrow if he were like us and subject to the same passions.
Here the consequent is put for the antecedent: sorrow stands for what is apt to produce sorrow in a subject capable of it.
translator_notes: The print gives ὁμοιοπαθής ('of like passions') in Greek.

title: The vineyard: God was not in doubt, but had used means from which a man could rightly hope for fruit
english: Similarly, in Isaiah the Lord is said to have expected grapes from his vineyard when it yielded wild grapes. This is not because God was uncertain or in doubt about what the Jewish people, represented by that vineyard, would do after so many means had been used to form them to true godliness.

It is because he had done what ought plainly to have brought that people back to the right path. Had one man used such means toward another, he could rightly have hoped and expected that the other's heart would be softened by them and turned to love and willing obedience.

title: 'Now I know': Abraham gave certain proof of his fear of God
english: When God says to Abraham, 'Now I know that you fear God, because you have not spared your only son for my sake,' he does not mean that he had previously doubted Abraham's godliness or had not known him well enough.

He means only that Abraham, by being ready at God's command to sacrifice his own son, gave a sure and unquestionable proof of his love and fear toward God. It was proof enough to convince anyone who had so far doubted the matter and had not been fully certain and persuaded of it.

title: The objection from God's oath in Numbers 14
english: The argument our opponents draw from Numbers 14 has no more force. There God is said to have sworn that he would bring his people into the land of Canaan, and yet, because of their sin and unbelief, he swears again that he will no longer do so: 'As I live, says the Lord, I will do to you just as you have spoken in my hearing. Your corpses will lie in this wilderness. None of you who were counted, from twenty years old and upward, and who grumbled against me, will enter the land I swore with raised hand to settle you in, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.'

'For what man,' they ask, 'is so mad as to swear in earnest that he will do something he already knows full well he will not do, or for which he already has thoroughly established reasons why he will by no means do it? And what is more unworthy of God than to swear that he will do something only in words and not in intention?'

title: Reply: the oath concerned the nation, or was conditional; even a good man may swear so
english: It is true that God often swore to give the land of Canaan to Abraham's descendants, and the words just quoted refer to those oaths, which are recorded in many places. But the quoted words, 'You will not enter the land I swore with raised hand to settle YOU in', do not prove that the oath was aimed specifically at those Israelites who rebelled in the wilderness. There the word 'you' refers to the Israelite nation in general, not to the particular persons who made it up at the time.

Even so, there would be nothing absurd in saying that God promised those men in particular, on oath, that they would enter the land of Canaan, not absolutely but on a condition, though he foresaw that they would not meet it. All that is required is that the condition was part of their duty and was one they could and ought to fulfil.

Among human beings, too, no one would be mad who swore to someone that he would do this or that provided the other kept to the duty of a good man, even though he was sure the other would not do his duty at all.

title: The Socinians' chief motive: certain foreknowledge would make God's earnest exhortations pointless
english: Those who today maintain that God has no certain foreknowledge of future contingents are moved chiefly by this. If God foresees with certainty, and from eternity, what human beings will freely do, then in their view he cannot seriously warn, exhort and implore them to turn and repent.

'What need is there,' they ask, 'to exhort and press someone earnestly to do what you know for sure he will do? And what is the good of much pleading and imploring with someone who, as you well know, will do none of the things you ask?'

title: Reply: God foresees obedience or defiance only as following his earnest warnings, which are means to obedience
english: Far from preventing God from earnestly warning, asking and exhorting human beings, their foreseen defiance or obedience is something God cannot foresee without first foreseeing, and resolving within himself, that he will deal with them earnestly in this way.

God's warnings, exhortations and pleas are the means by which human obedience is brought about. They are also presupposed conditions without which people cannot be, or be called, rebels against God and defiant toward him.

title: Even the Socinians grant that God pleads with the hardened, as with Pharaoh
english: Our opponents themselves can be convinced that it is not unworthy of God's wisdom to urge, exhort and invite to repentance, by every means, those he knows for certain will never obey his warnings, exhortations and commands. They admit that some, by God's judgment punishing their stubborn wickedness, are so blinded and hardened that they cannot repent.

Yet they cannot deny that toward those very people, whom he knows perfectly well to be in that state, God uses the warnings and pleas by which he ordinarily calls human beings to their duty, as the example of Pharaoh alone makes plain.

If, then, by our opponents' own admission, God's earnest pleas, threats and complaints can have a place with such people, without any breach of his justice or loss to his wisdom, why can the same not hold for all the others whom God knew from eternity would not obey, out of the free purpose of their own will and mind?

title: The objections from Scripture fail; the real difficulty: foreknowledge seems to make every event necessary
english: All the arguments drawn from Scripture against God's eternal foreknowledge, by which he knows certainly and distinctly whatever creatures will freely do at any time, are therefore empty.

We must now consider how the freedom of creatures in acting can coexist with that eternal foreknowledge of God. There is no small difficulty here, one that has long exercised the minds of learned teachers. Since God's foreknowledge cannot be mistaken, what God foresaw would happen cannot fail to happen. So everything happens necessarily, and the human will cannot fail to produce and elicit the acts God foreknows from eternity that it will produce. In that case the freedom of human actions seems to vanish entirely. For how can something be called free if it is impossible for it not to happen, or to happen otherwise?

title: The common answer: foreknowledge imposes no necessity, for things are not future because foreknown
english: Very many theologians of the Christian schools answer this, and in my judgement rightly, that God's foreknowledge places no necessity on things. Foreknowledge is not the cause of things; rather, in a certain sense the future things themselves can be called its cause.
Things are not future because God foreknows that they will be. On the contrary, God foreknows that they will be because they really are future.

title: Impossible that the foreknown fail to happen in the composite sense, not in the divided sense: Judas
english: The objection runs: what God foreknows from eternity as future cannot fail to happen; God foresees all future things; so everything happens necessarily. The common teaching of the schools replies that it is indeed impossible for what God foreknew as future not to happen, but only in the composite sense, not in the divided sense.

This means that two things cannot hold together: that something is foreseen by God as future, and that it does not happen. Yet, speaking simply and absolutely, the thing foreseen is able not to happen, if it is considered in its own nature and without reference to God's foresight.

Take Judas. God had foreseen that he would betray Christ, yet he could have refrained from betraying him had he wished. God's foreknowledge did not lay on him any necessity of betraying Christ. Nor does it follow that God's foreknowledge could have been mistaken. Had Judas not betrayed Christ, his betrayal would not have been foreseen; God would instead have foreseen that Judas was not going to betray Christ.

title: As our seeing does not change what we see, God's foresight changes nothing in future things
english: Once God's foresight is supposed, then, everything he foresees as future must indeed happen. In the same way, once our own seeing is supposed, everything we see happening must be happening.

Our seeing does not alter the nature of things. It does not make something necessary in itself that is free or contingent by its own nature, even though, given that we see it happening, it cannot fail to be. In just the same way God's foresight alters nothing in future things and does not take away their freedom or contingency. This holds even though what God foresees as future, being supposed future, cannot fail to be future.
If we suppose that a thing actually exists, it cannot fail to exist actually. In exactly the same way, if we suppose that a thing is future, it cannot fail to be future.

title: The necessity foreknowledge brings is hypothetical, of the consequence, of infallibility, not antecedent
english: In short, seeing present things brings a certain necessity upon them, but only a hypothetical one. The schools call it consequent necessity, or the necessity of the consequence, and it fits perfectly well with their freedom or contingency.

So too the foresight of future things means that they will necessarily happen, but only by a necessity that rests on a hypothesis, usually called the necessity of infallibility. It does not stop them being free and contingent in themselves and absolutely.
The only necessity that removes contingency and freedom is the one called antecedent and absolute, which is a necessity not merely of the consequence but of the consequent as well.

title: The later Thomists: God's knowledge is the cause of things, yet it foreknows the free mode of acting (Alvarez)
english: Others, however, try to reconcile God's foreknowledge with human freedom in another way. They hold false the proposition 'Things are known by God because they are future', and true the proposition 'Something is future because God foreknows that it will be'. On their view God's knowledge is the cause of things.
Yet they do not think this harms human freedom. From eternity God foreknows not only that people will do this or that, but also the manner in which they will act, namely freely and contingently.

So, given God's foreknowledge, it follows necessarily, to take an example, that Peter will speak. Indeed God's knowledge is, in its own way, the cause of Peter's speaking. But it follows that he will speak in a particular manner: contingently and freely. Hence, they say, God's foreknowledge implies the actual exercise of human freedom rather than destroying it. Such foreknowledge does not remove from Peter's will, as he speaks, the free power by which he could refrain from speaking if he wished; rather it places that very power in his will.
This is the teaching of those called the later Thomists, as can be seen in Didacus Alvarez, in the summary of his work on the aids of divine grace, book 1, chapter 11.
translator_notes: Didacus Alvarez (Diego Álvarez, d. 1635), Dominican, author of De auxiliis divinae gratiae.

title: Some Reformed answer more loosely: foreknowledge brings a necessity, but not of coaction or physical determination
english: Some Reformed teachers answer the difficulty in a still simpler and less precise way. They say that God's foreknowledge does bring a certain necessity upon all future things, but that not every necessity is at odds with freedom. Only necessity arising from compulsion or from physical determination conflicts with it.

title: The converse difficulty: how acts that may or may not happen can be foreseen certainly
english: In these various ways Christian theologians try to show how human freedom can stand alongside God's foreknowledge of all future things.

Yet it is no less difficult to explain the reverse. If creatures have freedom to act or not to act, how can God foresee their future acts with certainty and without fail? How can anything be known with certainty that has no certain existence either in itself or in its causes, and is as able not to be or happen as to happen and be?

title: The Thomists' first foundation: all futures present to God in eternity, as to one on a watchtower (Alvarez)
english: The scholastic teachers work hard to get out of this difficulty and try in various ways to explain how God foreknows future contingent and free things.

The first are the later Thomists just mentioned. They lay two foundations for the certainty by which God foreknows every future contingent from eternity. The first is that all future things are present to God in eternity, not merely in objective or known being, but in real being, in their own actual existences.

'God,' they say, 'stands toward future contingents like someone on a high watchtower who surveys the whole road and everyone travelling along it. One traveller follows another and the one behind cannot see the one ahead, yet the watcher on the tower sees them all at once and has them present to himself. So likewise God has present to himself, on the watchtower of eternity, all things past and future, though the one succeeds the other.' These are the words of Didacus Alvarez, book 1, chapter 8.

There he further proves this presence of future things in eternity from the fact that eternity is an indivisible duration that exists whole all at once. Whatever coexists with eternity at any time therefore coexists with all of it, and so is present to all of it.

title: Alvarez concludes that the real presence of things in eternity is the proper reason of God's certain knowledge
english: At the start of the next chapter he draws this conclusion: the actual existence of things in eternity, viewed from the side of God's eternity, is the proper reason why God knows all future things with certainty, contingent ones included.

The reason is that things present to a knower, though contingent in themselves, are already regarded as determinate. They are determinately true with respect to the measure in which they are present, and with respect to the knowledge by which they are known as present.

title: The second foundation: God's absolute decree predetermining good acts and permitting evil (Alvarez)
english: The second foundation on which they rest the certainty of God's knowledge of things that will happen contingently is the absolute decree of the divine will. In the same place Alvarez says that the certainty of God's knowledge of future contingents can also be drawn from another source. This is the absolute and efficacious decree of his will, which predetermines in detail every future thing, free ones included, with all their circumstances, if they are good, or permits them if they are evil.

To explain more clearly what this efficacious decree permitting evil is, he notes further on that God's infallible foreknowledge of sins presupposes two decrees on God's part. One is an absolute decree to produce the act of sin insofar as it is an act and a being. The other is a decree not to give efficacious help for avoiding the sin, that is, a decree to permit its wickedness, which is attributed to the created or defectible will alone.
In these two decrees, he says, all future sins are known with certainty. If God abandons the sinner and does not help him so that he will not fall, he will infallibly sin.

title: Others know futures in the decree alone: Scotus and others, Calvin, and Twisse against Penot and Suárez
english: There are, however, other teachers in the Roman school who reject this presence of future things in eternity in their own existences as empty and invented. They hold that every future contingent, whether it comes from free second causes or from other natural causes, is known with certainty and without fail in God's decree alone, by which he decreed that it should happen. This view is usually attributed to many of the older scholastics, such as Scotus, Richard, Hervaeus, John Major and a good number of others.

Very many Reformed theologians also embrace it, teaching with Calvin that God foresees what will happen for no other reason than that he decreed it should happen. William Twisse, among the most celebrated English theologians, sets out, defends and illustrates this teaching of Calvin at length, through almost the whole of his dissertation on middle knowledge, written against Penot and Suárez.
translator_notes: 'Ricardo' is presumably Richard of Middleton; 'Penotrum' is the Jesuit Guillaume Penot, whose work on middle knowledge Twisse answered alongside Suárez.

title: Recent Roman theologians reject both views; some say God knows futures in their proximate cause
english: Most of the more recent theologians of the Roman school approve of neither view. They reject the presence of future things in eternity in their real being, described above. Nor do they accept any efficacious decree of God by which the acts of free causes are defined in advance, before those causes determine themselves.

So to give some account of God's foreknowledge of future contingents they take refuge elsewhere. First, some hold that what will happen contingently and freely is known by God in its proximate cause. That cause is the will, taken not on its own but as it is engaged here and now: with this judgement, this object and this inclination, and finally with everything else that can either hinder it or determine it to will.

title: Bellarmine: God sees free acts in the human will, knowing its propensities and all that may meet it
english: Bellarmine comes close to this view. 'It seems probable to us,' he says, 'that God sees future free actions only in the human will.' A little later he adds: 'God knows perfectly all the inclinations and the whole temper of our mind. He is not unaware of everything that can present itself to it in each deliberation. Finally, he sees clearly what is most fitting and suitable to move such a mind, endowed with such an inclination and temper. Because of all this he infers without fail which way the mind will lean.'

He goes on to say that in the contingent cause, considered strictly by itself, there is no determination. Suppose, however, that someone takes the contingent or free cause together with everything that can present itself and get in the way. Suppose too that he sees the inclinations and aptitudes both of the cause and of all the objects and circumstances, which God alone can do. Then some determination will result, and because of it one will be able to say truly, 'This will happen at such a time.' On Grace and Free Choice, book 4, chapter 15, in the reply to the sixth argument.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 4, chapter 15.

title: Becanus: God knows futures certainly by the infinite reach of his intellect and their determinate truth
english: Others say simply that God foreknows future contingents with certainty for this reason: whatever exists at some time, whether contingently or necessarily, was true as a future thing before it existed. Whatever is true the divine intellect knows with certainty, because no truth can be hidden from an infinite intellect, and the divine intellect is infinite.

So, on their view, 'the certainty of God's foreknowledge is to be sought from two sources. First, from the infinite power and penetration of the divine intellect. Second, from the determinate truth of future contingents.' These are the words of the Jesuit Becanus in his Summa of Theology, volume 1, treatise 1, chapter 10, question 11, first conclusion.
translator_notes: Martin Becanus (1563-1624), Jesuit, Summa theologiae scholasticae.

title: Against the first view: future things cannot coexist with eternity before they exist (the post in the river)
english: Each of these views, however, seems to face no small difficulty. First, take the real presence of future things in eternity, meaning that they are thought to coexist with eternity itself from eternity. This is plainly a pure invention.
For one thing to coexist with another, both must exist; what does not exist cannot coexist. Since contingent things did not exist from eternity, they could not coexist with eternity from eternity.

The supposed indivisibility of eternity is no help here. Things that happen in time can coexist one after another with something that admits no division or succession within itself. A post driven fast into a river does not always have the same water flowing round it, but ever new water. It is no more necessary that what exists alongside God's eternity at some time should always coexist with it than that what coexists with his immensity in some place should coexist with it everywhere.

title: Against the decree view: an absolute decree to sins makes God the author of sin
english: Next, among the things God foresees as future are many sins and moral evils. It is therefore very hard to understand how God could have foreknown future things of every kind in some absolute decree of his will.

God can bring about and decree good things without any damage to his goodness and wisdom. But it is contrary to the divine goodness that he should move and predetermine the wills of creatures toward things evil in themselves.

Suppose someone says that God, absolutely and efficaciously, by a decree of his own, determined the will of the angels who fell to rise up in pride against God. Suppose he says God determined the will of our first parents to disregard God's command and covet the forbidden fruit. Who could say this without thereby making God the author of sin? And who could persuade himself of the following? By an eternal decree of God, preceding any determination of the created will foreseen in any way at all, human wills have been determined one by one to acts of blasphemy and hatred against God. And yet God is not the cause of those sins!

title: Against the proximate-cause view: certainty in circumstances implies a necessity, and would excuse Adam
english: Nor do I see how the future act of a free cause can be foreknown with certainty within that cause, considered in the circumstances that are to dispose it most immediately to act. That could only be if we presuppose that some necessity of acting in that way is laid upon it by the object being set before it in such circumstances. That too brings no small difficulty with it.
