It would follow that Adam, affected and disposed as he was before he sinned, had a necessity of sinning laid on him by the temptation put before him and the circumstances that went with it. This can scarcely be granted without his seeming to be excused from blame.

title: The fourth view states only what is certain: predictions are true, and the infinite intellect reaches all truth
english: The fourth view looks for the certainty of God's foreknowledge in the infinity of the divine intellect and in the determinate truth of things that will happen contingently. It asserts nothing that is not certain and beyond doubt.

It is clear that Scripture contains divine predictions about future contingents. That alone shows that true propositions can be framed about them, for God asserts nothing that is not true. Every true proposition must have truth corresponding to it in reality. So, since it can be said determinately and truly that this or that will happen freely and contingently, it follows that its truth is determinate.

It is no less clear that, once the truth of future contingents is granted, that truth is perceived and known by the divine intellect, which is infinite. Truth is the object of the intellect, so an infinite intellect reaches to all truth. Otherwise it would by that very fact not be infinite but would have bounds and an end, since it could not reach some truth.

title: Yet it leaves the main question: whence contingents become future, which points back to the decree
english: Yet although that view contains nothing but truth, it does very little to answer the question and does not remove the main difficulty. The hardest thing to understand here is where contingent things get their being future from. How do they pass from eternity out of mere possibility into the status of future things, so that God can perceive them as future?
It seems that no appeal is possible here except to the decree of God's will, since from eternity nothing existed outside God to which that change could be ascribed.

title: Nor can God see as certain what has no certain existence in itself or its cause (against Becanus)
english: There is a further serious difficulty. Suppose a thing depends on a cause that is undetermined in itself and is as able not to produce it as to produce it. How can the divine intellect still know it with certainty, when on this account it has no certain existence either in itself or in its cause?

The divine intellect, however infinite, cannot see what does not exist, and it does not alter the nature of its object. Nor would its perception and grasp be true if, as some say, it knew more in the cause than is actually there. See Becanus, volume 1, treatise 1, chapter 10, question 7.

title: The safest course is to confess our ignorance: 'Such knowledge is too wonderful for me' (Psalm 139, Sirach 3)
english: Anyone who searches into so great a matter finds darkness closing in on every side, and meets tangles and snares from which we cannot properly free ourselves. I therefore think nothing is safer or more honest than to confess our ignorance openly here and to take David's words in earnest: 'Your knowledge is too wonderful for me, too high for me to reach.'

I would not measure other people's minds by my own feebleness, nor condemn a modest inquiry into this matter. Still, I am readily persuaded that this mystery belongs among the things of which the wise man says, 'Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not search out what is too strong for you.'

It should not seem surprising if our mind, confined within such narrow bounds, cannot grasp how the divine intellect, which has no bounds at all, knows and reaches things that lie furthest from our knowledge.
translator_notes: The Psalm is quoted in the Vulgate form (Psalm 138:6); the wise man's saying is Ecclesiasticus 3:21 (Vulgate 3:22).

title: Our ignorance of the mode does not weaken certainty of the fact: light, the moving of limbs, the imagination of pregnant women
english: Yet this does nothing to weaken the certainty we ought to have both about God's foreknowledge and about human freedom. Each of them has a sure and unshaken foundation in Scripture, with the light of reason agreeing; and human freedom has our own experience besides.

How many things there are, not only in divine matters but in nature itself, indeed in ourselves, whose existence we cannot doubt! Yet our mind cannot investigate how and why they are without entangling itself in snares it cannot get free of.

What is clearer than that light and sight exist? Yet what is harder than to fathom and explain the nature of light and how sight happens? What is better known than that the limbs of the body move in countless ways at a mere nod of the will? Yet how hard it is to understand and teach how that comes about!

What is more firmly confirmed by daily experience than that pregnant women, by the power of the imagination alone, produce many extraordinary marks in their unborn children? Yet what have the philosophers worked out on the matter that would satisfy a sensible person even slightly?

So if in human matters the fact itself remains certain even when the manner of it is uncertain or entirely unknown to us, this must apply all the more to divine matters, which lie beyond the senses and far exceed the grasp of our mind.
translator_notes: The belief that a mother's imagination could mark her unborn child was a commonplace of early modern natural philosophy; it is rendered as Le Blanc states it.

title: Conditional knowledge, devised by Molina and Fonseca, is the starting point for reconciling freedom with God's decrees
english: Of all the devices the schools have produced for reconciling human freedom with the certainty and unchangeableness of God's decrees about human acts, the one that has spread most widely is so-called conditional knowledge. The Jesuits Luis de Molina and Fonseca were the first to hold that the key to this reconciliation must be sought there. Very many have followed them since, both in the Roman school and among the Protestants themselves.

So, God willing, as we take up the agreement of human freedom with the divine decrees and set out the various views of the teachers on the question, we have thought it right to begin with this knowledge.
translator_notes: Luis de Molina SJ (1535-1600), Concordia liberi arbitrii; Pedro da Fonseca SJ (1528-1599), Commentarii in Metaphysicam Aristotelis.

title: Most Roman doctors hold that God knows not only what will be, but what would freely happen under any condition
english: Most of the teachers of the Roman school hold that God foreknows not only what will happen freely and contingently, yet simply and absolutely. He also foreknows what will never actually happen but would happen freely if this or that condition were in place.

For example, God knows not only what each of us will do right up to the end of life in the various states in which his sure providence is to place us. He also knows what we would do if the future state of things were entirely different and other opportunities for action kept presenting themselves to us.

title: This knowledge of what would be is placed before every free decree of God's will
english: Foreknowledge of what will absolutely happen must follow some decree of God's will. By that decree he has resolved to create these or those agents, to place them in this or that order of things, and to concur with them in acting as needed.

By contrast, they hold that God's knowledge of things that will not simply happen, but would happen only on some supposition, comes before every free decree of his will. That is, to speak in our human way of conceiving, before God made any decree about anything at all, he knew with certainty and distinctness what any possible creature would freely do. He knew this on the supposition that he chose to create it, not to withhold his concurrence from it, and to set these or those objects before it in these or those circumstances.

title: Yet a decree is included in the condition: not one already made, but one supposed to be made
english: This knowledge comes before any free decree in God. Even so, as is clear from what has been said, the condition under which something is said to be future includes a decree. It is not a decree conceived as actually present in God, but one that would necessarily have to be posited in God for that thing to be able to exist.

So the conditional futurity that is the object of this knowledge still depends on a decree of God. It does not depend on a decree already made, but on one supposed to be made by God, so that the thing can truly be called future. In our human way, God is imagined reasoning with himself: 'If I decreed to create this angel or this man and not to withdraw my concurrence from him, in such an arrangement of things he would do this and nothing else, though he could act otherwise.'

title: Vasquez: a decree to concur is understood under the condition, but God has decreed nothing about that case
english: Gabriel Vasquez makes this point in his commentary on the first part of Thomas. 'Nevertheless,' he says, 'we must say that God knows future things under a condition with certainty in such a way that his decree to concur with the will is also understood within the condition. It runs like this. God knew well: "If on this or that occasion I gave Peter this or that call, and cooperated with it as it required, and did not miraculously withdraw my concurrence, such a deed would be done. Yet I could withdraw it if I pleased." But whether God would deny or grant his concurrence in that case, he himself decreed nothing.' Volume 1, disputation 67, chapter 4.
translator_notes: Gabriel Vázquez SJ (1549-1604), Commentarii ac disputationes in primam partem S. Thomae.

title: Suárez likewise includes God's will, to effect or permit and concur, in the antecedent of the conditional
english: Much the same is found in Francisco Suárez. 'Add further,' he says, 'that this whole effect depends simply on God's will for whether it absolutely exists or not. So in these conditionals too the divine will must be included in the antecedent: that is, if God wills such an effect, or at least wills to permit it and to concur with it. In this way that knowledge also has a relation to the divine will under the stated condition.'
This is in book 2, chapter 6, of his work on the knowledge God has of future contingents proposed under a condition, before, in the order of reason, he decrees anything about the condition itself.
translator_notes: Francisco Suárez SJ (1548-1617), Opuscula theologica: De scientia quam Deus habet de futuris contingentibus, book 2, chapter 6.
The italic 'absolute fit, vel non fit' is read with long s as 'sit ... sit', as the sense and Suárez's text require.

title: The decree on which futurity depends is not a predetermining one, but only a decree to supply concurrence
english: They do not think that free causes, in order to act in time, must be premoved and predetermined by God to this or that act. In the same way, they do not think the decree of God on which the futurity of free acts depends, whether absolute or conditional, is a decree to premove and predetermine free causes.

Rather, they hold that without any such decree, whether simply laid down or at least supposed, God foreknows with certainty whatever free agents will do, absolutely or under a condition. For a thing to exist and be foreseen as future, they say, it is enough that we posit or suppose in God a decree to supply concurrence. They hold that concurrence alone is necessary for acting. As they conceive it, it is always available to free agents and neither applies them to act nor predetermines them.

title: Why 'middle': between knowledge of vision (free, after the decree) and knowledge of simple intelligence
english: They call this knowledge 'middle knowledge' because, as they see it, it stands midway between what the schools call the knowledge of vision and the knowledge of simple intelligence.

By the knowledge of vision they mean the knowledge by which God knows things that exist outside himself at some point in time, whether past, present or future. God knows all these from eternity as clearly, certainly and distinctly as if they were actually present to him, just as we know things we see in front of us. That is why it is called the knowledge of vision, by comparison with bodily sight, by which we see things placed before our eyes.

This knowledge is also called free knowledge, because it follows the free decree of God's will to create and preserve things. Without that decree nothing can exist, and so nothing can be seen as present or foreseen as future. Had God decreed to create nothing, knowledge of this kind could not be ascribed to him.

title: Knowledge of simple intelligence: God's natural knowledge of all possibles, prior to every decree
english: By the knowledge of simple intelligence they mean the knowledge by which God knows and understands everything possible, the essences of things, and all their connections, whether necessary or possible in any way at all.

This knowledge is called natural rather than free. In our way of conceiving, it comes before every decree of God about the things to be made. It could not have been absent from God even if he had willed to create nothing outside himself.

title: Middle knowledge shares in both: free in its objects, natural in preceding every decree
english: They call God's knowledge of things that would happen contingently under some condition 'middle' because it neither fully matches the knowledge of vision nor the knowledge of simple intelligence, but shares something of each.

It is not about merely possible things considered apart from any question of existence, as the knowledge of simple intelligence is. Nor is it about things that will absolutely happen at some point in time by God's decree, as the knowledge of vision is.

In part it resembles free knowledge, because it concerns things that would happen freely if only the condition were met, and whether the condition is met lies in God's freedom. In part it resembles natural knowledge, because it comes before every decree of God, and God could not have been without it even if he had not decreed the world or decreed to create anything.

title: Vasquez and Valentia call it simply conditional, reducible to the other two; a dispute about words
english: Some, however, call this knowledge of future things under a condition not 'middle' but simply 'conditional'. They think it can easily be reduced either to the knowledge of vision, as some hold, or, as many more hold, to the knowledge of simple intelligence. Vasquez and Gregory of Valentia are among these.

Vasquez does note, though, that nothing prevents setting up some third category between those two kinds of divine knowledge for the sake of teaching and clarity. The disagreement, he says, is about words, not things, and it matters little if people speak differently on the point. Volume 1, disputation 67, near the end.

title: Scripture proof: David at Keilah (1 Samuel 23) — God foreknew what Saul and the Keilites would do
english: They think it can be proved, both from the testimony of Scripture and from arguments of reason, that God has knowledge by which he foreknows with certainty things that would happen contingently under some condition.

From Scripture they first cite various examples of predictions about things that did not actually happen but would have happened had certain things been in place. One is 1 Samuel 23:11-12. David asked the Lord whether, if he stayed in the city of Keilah, Saul would come to capture him, and whether, if Saul came, the men of Keilah would hand him over to Saul. He was told both that Saul would come and that the men of Keilah would hand him over, if he stayed in Keilah.

So God foreknew with certainty both these things, which depended on the free will of Saul and of the men of Keilah, under a condition that never came about. David fled, and for that reason neither thing actually happened.
translator_notes: The print spells the town variously (Kebela, Kebila; Kebilitae, Kehilitarum); the English uses Keilah throughout.

title: Scripture proof: the ban on mixed marriages (1 Kings 11:2) — fulfilled in Solomon, not in others
english: A similar case is God's command forbidding the Israelites to marry their sons or daughters to the daughters or sons of peoples outside God's covenant. God gives as the reason for this command that those foreign nations would otherwise lead the Israelites' hearts astray and turn them toward their gods: 'You shall not go in to them, nor they to you, for they will surely turn your hearts away to follow their gods' (1 Kings 11:2).

This shows that God foreknew with certainty that the Israelites' hearts would be led astray if they entangled themselves in unlawful marriages of this kind. It came true in Solomon, because the condition was met. It did not come true in most other Israelites, because in their case the prior condition did not occur.
translator_notes: '1 Reg.' in the print is the Vulgate's 3 Kings, i.e. 1 Kings in the English numbering.

title: New Testament: Tyre and Sidon would have repented (Matthew 11:21); Paul told to leave Jerusalem (Acts 22:18)
english: From the New Testament they make much of Christ's words in Matthew 11:21: 'Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.' Here Christ declares that the people of Tyre and Sidon would have repented if God had used the same means with them that he used with the Jews. So God had known from eternity that their repentance would have occurred under that condition.

They also lay weight on the passage where the Lord, in a trance of Paul's, tells him to leave Jerusalem quickly, because the people there would not accept his testimony about him. God foresaw that if Paul preached Christ to the Jews, they would not believe his testimony (Acts 22:18).

title: Argument from reason: conditional propositions about future contingents are determinately true or false
english: They also think many arguments from reason prove that God has such knowledge. The first is this. Propositions about a future contingent under some condition have determinate truth or falsity, just as much as propositions about things that will absolutely happen. So they too are objects of God's knowledge, since no truth can be hidden from an infinite intellect, which the divine intellect is.

That propositions about future contingents under a condition are determinately true or false follows from the fact that there can be genuine contradiction between them, just as between propositions about things that will absolutely happen. These two plainly contradict each other: 'If Peter is placed in such circumstances, he will sin' and 'It is not the case that if Peter is placed in such circumstances, he will sin.' In every pair of contradictories one side must be true and the other false.

title: The conditional truth holds before the decree: prior in reason to absolute futurity
english: Next, if it is true that Peter, placed in certain circumstances, sins, then it was certainly true that if he were placed in them he would sin. This was true not only before he was placed in them, but even before God decreed that he should be placed in them. So God knew, before his decree, that this would happen under such a condition.
And in the order of reason, before it is true that something will absolutely happen, it is true that it would happen conditionally.

title: A wise agent foresees consequences before deciding; so God knew what creatures would do before decreeing
english: Again, it is the mark of a wise person, before deciding anything, to form in his mind an idea of what will follow from the things he is to decide and do. Since God decreed all things with perfect wisdom, he must have known, prior in the order of reason to decreeing to create this or that creature, to set such things before it, and to concur with it in this or that way, what would follow from all of it.
He must have known what the creature would freely do or leave undone once all this was in place. That knowledge is precisely the conditional knowledge in question.

title: Without it, endless questions would have no answer from God, or would need infinite idle decrees
english: Besides, unless we ascribe such knowledge to God, countless questions could be put to him, like the ones David asked, to which God could give no certain and clear answer except that the matter cannot be known. That seems to take a good deal away from God's omniscience.

Suppose someone asks what a man who died peacefully in Christ would have done if martyrdom had been offered him. Or whether this or that man, had he sought the hand of a certain girl before the man she married, would have won her consent or not. Or how a certain person would conduct himself if he were elected king of Poland. There are endless questions of this kind.

Shrewd and experienced people can make guesses about such things, so it is unlikely that God is simply ignorant of them. It seems unworthy of God not to know for certain what a man can reach by probable conjecture.

Someone may say that God does know such things and can answer distinctly and clearly about them, but that such knowledge presupposes a free decree about whether those things would come about in this or that case. Then it will follow that there are in God countless decrees about things that will never actually happen. Those decrees would be pointless, empty and idle, which is quite absurd.

title: The later Thomists deny any middle knowledge besides natural and free knowledge
english: Yet a good number of teachers of the Roman school, especially those called the later Thomists, deny that God has any middle knowledge. Besides natural knowledge, called the knowledge of simple intelligence, and free knowledge, called the knowledge of vision, they admit no third kind.

They deny any knowledge by which God, before every decree of his will, would know things that are neither merely possible nor absolutely future, but that would happen under this or that condition, done freely by intelligent creatures given this or that.

title: Their reason: nothing is future, absolutely or conditionally, except by a decree predetermining the will
english: In their view, nothing becomes future, whether outright or on a condition, unless a decree actually comes first in God and gives it that status. Through such a decree God settles that what is called future will be brought about by him, or at the least allowed.

It follows that, until God's will has decreed to predetermine the human will toward one of two contradictory or contrary options, no one can know what a particular person will do. Nor can anyone know what he would do in such circumstances; all that can be known is what he is able to do. Before such a decree the thing is not yet future and not yet non-future. It is simply possible, and open either way.

title: They grant conditional predictions (Keilah) but make them follow a decree to permit and predetermine (Alvarez)
english: They do not deny that some things that would happen contingently and freely under a condition are foreknown by God with certainty and foretold in Scripture. God foretold to David that if he stayed in Keilah, Saul would come to seize him, and that if Saul came to that city, its inhabitants would hand David over to him.

But they insist that this certain foreknowledge of God follows a free decree in God, by which he determined that this or that should happen if this or that condition were fulfilled. Thus God foreknew that if David stayed in Keilah, Saul would come and the people of Keilah would hand David over. He foreknew it because, given that condition, he had decreed both to permit those acts and to predetermine to their substance the wills of Saul and of the inhabitants of Keilah.

This can be seen at greater length in Didacus Alvarez, On the Aids of Divine Grace, book 1, chapter 6, titled 'That besides merely natural and merely free knowledge, no middle knowledge is to be posited, even in God.' See also the next chapter, where he answers the objections of the teachers who hold the opposite view.

title: Among Protestants, the Remonstrants by common consent approve middle knowledge
english: Protestant views on this matter also vary. First, those in the Netherlands called Remonstrants seem by common consent to approve of middle knowledge as described so far.
They acknowledge that God foresees not only what will absolutely happen, but also whatever would happen freely in any order of things in which God might choose to place free agents.

title: Episcopius on the threefold knowledge, approving the distinction as useful for teaching
english: First, Simon Episcopius reports with approval the threefold distinction of knowledge in God that has been standard since Molina. 'It should be noted,' he says, 'that a threefold knowledge is usually ascribed to God.

One is necessary and practical and is called the knowledge of simple intelligence. By its nature it comes before every act of the free will, and by it God understands himself and everything else that is possible.

The second is free and is called the knowledge of vision. It comes after the act of the free will, and by it God knows everything he has decreed to do or permit, in the same order in which he decreed to do it or permit it to happen.
The third is middle knowledge, by which God knows what men or angels would do in their freedom under a condition, if they were placed in these or those circumstances, in this or that state or order.

Whether this distinction of divine knowledge is correctly drawn we do not examine. That it can be drawn usefully and for the sake of teaching we do not doubt at all.' Theological Institutions, book 4, chapter 19, On the order and manner of divine knowledge.
translator_notes: Simon Episcopius (1583-1643), Institutiones theologicae, book 4.

title: Grevinchovius argues for it at length (answered by Ames); Courcelles praises Gomarus for admitting it
english: Nicolaas Grevinchoven argues at length for this knowledge in the reply he wrote against the Dissertation on Universal Redemption and Election from Foreseen Faith, page 393 onward. William Ames examined that reply in his book titled A Brief Scholastic Rescript to Nicolaas Grevinchoven's Reply.

Courcelles likewise makes it plain that he approves of the middle or conditional knowledge that the schools ascribe to God. He praises Gomarus because, taught by Arminius, Gomarus acknowledged a conditional knowledge in God in his later theses On the Eternal Decree of God and On Predestination.

'With its help,' Courcelles says, 'he removes from his position that great absurdity which would make God the author of the first man's sin, and so of all the other sins thought to flow from it.' This is in the preface to the book titled James Arminius's Examination of the Theses of Francis Gomarus on Predestination.
translator_notes: Greek ἄτοπον (atopon), 'something out of place, an absurdity', rendered 'absurdity'.
Étienne de Courcelles (Curcellaeus) edited Arminius's Examen thesium Gomari (1645) with a preface.

title: Even some Reformed who signed Dort admit it: Gomarus on Tyre's repentance (Matthew 11:21), cited by Walaeus
english: Even among the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort, some acknowledge in God this conditional knowledge, by which, before every decree of his will, he knows what any free cause would do in any order of things, according to its innate freedom. Francis Gomarus seems to come first among them, and Courcelles has already cited him for this view.

Commenting on Matthew 11:21, Gomarus first notes that the repentance of Tyre that would have followed Christ's miracles is to be understood as the kind common to elect and reprobate, believers and unbelievers. In his view the sackcloth repentance of the Ninevites was of this kind. He then adds these very words:

'What Christ asserts about this repentance of Tyre that would have followed under that condition is true by virtue of the unbounded foreknowledge of his divine nature. By it he knows what would have followed given an antecedent, even if neither came about. Given that condition, everyone knows that one or the other would have happened, that they would either repent or not, from the principle that two opposites cannot both be true at once. But which of them would have happened, since the matter was contingent, only he foresaw who sees all things by his infinite knowledge and foretells with certainty not only necessary things but future contingents too. A similar passage is Ezekiel 3:6-7.'
So Balduinus Walaeus reports in his commentary on the historical books of the New Testament, at the passage of Matthew cited.
translator_notes: Balduinus Walaeus (Boudewijn de Waele, 1630s-1680s), son of Antonius Walaeus, published a Commentarius in libros historicos Novi Testamenti; the Ninevites' sackcloth is Jonah 3.

title: Baron approves Fonseca: God knew conditionally what Adam would do before decreeing to permit the fall
english: Robert Baron also expressly approves Fonseca's view, which posits in God a certain conditional knowledge before his free decree, preceding his absolute foreknowledge of future things.

For example, God at first knew only conditionally what would happen if Eve, led astray by the serpent, tempted Adam. Once he decreed to permit Adam to obey his wife's persuasion, he foresaw no longer conditionally but absolutely that Adam would fall.
translator_notes: Robert Baron (c. 1596-1639), Aberdeen divine, Metaphysica generalis.

title: Baron: like a wise builder, God deliberated what would follow, including free causes given their occasions
english: He states his own and Fonseca's view on the matter like this. 'Those who wisely undertake a great work first consider what will follow from it before they decide absolutely and definitely to do it. In the same way God, best and greatest, before he willed with an absolute and definite will to create the world, considered, as if deliberating with himself (to speak in our human way), what would follow if he set up heaven and earth and everything in them in the very manner and order in which he later actually arranged them.

By a kind of hypothetical knowledge he knew which events would come about, and of what kind, if all things were arranged in the manner and order in which they are now arranged. God knew not only what would happen if natural causes were set up in the order and manner in which they are arranged. He also knew what would happen if free causes were offered the opportunities to act or not act that they now have, or that free causes which existed earlier had.

For God, whose judgements are beyond understanding, knew with certainty what would happen if these or those opportunities were offered to men or angels. For example, by this conditional knowledge God knew what would happen if Adam's wife, led astray by the serpent, persuaded Adam to eat the apple.'
General Metaphysics adapted to the use of theology, section 12, disputation 2, numbers 55 and 56, and many other places in the same disputation.

title: Antonius Walaeus admits middle knowledge, proving it from Matthew 24 (days shortened; the elect not deceived)
english: Antonius Walaeus, professor at the University of Leiden, is especially notable. He acknowledges in God a middle knowledge by which future things are known on a hypothesis, even though they are not absolutely future, or not yet.

He holds, for example, that God foreknew that Adam would misuse his freedom if God made him such as he was, endowed him with such gifts, allowed him to be tempted, and so on. The same holds, he thinks, for the other outcomes of free choice that depend on the choice of angels or human beings.

He proves this knowledge from the passages of Scripture cited above and from many others, such as Matthew 24: 'Unless those days had been cut short, no flesh would be saved', and 'if it were possible, even the elect would be led astray', that is, unless they were preserved by special grace. From these and similar passages, he says, it is clear that God has some such knowledge, before any decree of his, of what was certainly going to happen. Loci communes, under the knowledge of God, page 160 of the quarto edition.
translator_notes: Antonius Walaeus (1573-1639), Leiden professor and delegate at Dort; Loci communes.

title: Walaeus: it need not be a third species, for it belongs to simple intelligence
english: In the same place, however, he warns that this hypothetical knowledge need not be set up as a third kind of knowledge, since it belongs to the knowledge of simple intelligence.

'It is absolutely necessary,' he says, 'that God from eternity surveyed all the possible ways in which second causes act, alone or together with others. So he also surveyed what would infallibly happen or not happen given each particular hypothesis: if he produced those causes, preserved them, and concurred with them in this or that way, or arranged them in this or that way, or allowed them to be arranged. No Christian will deny this.'

title: Walaeus' warning: it must not be used to make election depend on free choice, or to deny physical grace
english: But he teaches that we must take special care that no one misuses this knowledge. One misuse is to weigh the decree of election by the good use of a person's free choice. Those who do this hold that God, before electing someone, foresaw how that person would respond if this or that preventing and accompanying grace were offered him in this or that order of things or state. He foresaw whether the person would assent to it by free choice or not. On this view free choice determines God's grace for them, not the other way round.

The other misuse is to deny that God works efficaciously in the will of the person being converted, beyond moral instruction. As Walaeus expects to show later, God acts in a person's will not only morally but also physically when he converts him.

title: Paul Ferry of Metz: God foresaw by conditional knowledge that man, created fallible and tempted, would fall
english: Paul Ferry, the celebrated minister of God's Word at Metz, also admits in God this conditional knowledge of future things, which comes before the free decree. 'By what they call his conditional knowledge,' he says, 'God foreknew that man would do this or that, in whatever way he made him. So he foreknew that man would fall if God created him able to fall, allowed him to be tempted, and left him to himself, given his innate freedom to go either way and the weakness of a creature.
If man fell, God foreknew that all would perish, if he so willed; or he could rescue some from it, so as to display his justice in the one group and his grace in the other,' and so on.

Later, setting out the reasoning of God's providence regarding the fall, he says: 'First, God foresaw that man would fall if he were created able to fall and were tempted. Next, because he saw that it was fitting, it pleased him that this should happen. He did not force man, but created him that way and left him to temptation and to himself.'

A little further on he adds that God determined nothing about man's fall without first foreseeing that, given freedom and temptation, man would infallibly fall. Vindiciae pro Scholastico Orthodoxo, pages 203, 209 and 210.
translator_notes: Paul Ferry (1591-1669), Reformed pastor at Metz; the work cited answers the Jesuit François Véron's Scholastique orthodoxe.

title: Many Reformed reject it: God knows conditional truths, but from his free decree, not before it
english: Many other Reformed theologians, however, reject this middle and conditional knowledge in God as empty and superfluous. They do not all do so in the same way, though, or rely on the same grounds.

First, some grant that every proposition denying or affirming that something will happen contingently, under any condition, is determinately true or false, and so knowable by God. No one doubts that God knows and grasps every truth with certainty. So they affirm that no question about free and conditional future things that a human or angelic mind can imagine is one God cannot answer clearly: given this or that condition, the matter will turn out thus.

Yet they deny that it follows that God has any conditional knowledge preceding his free decree. God does know these things, but from the free decree of his will. By that decree he predefined with himself from eternity the modes and connections not only of things that will happen in time but also of things that never will and are merely possible. There is this difference: the former he willed to happen, the latter he did not. Yet if he had willed them, they would happen just as he had predefined.

These are the words of Matthias Nethenus, given in the work of the celebrated Gisbertus Voetius and approved by Voetius himself: Theological Disputations, part 1, theses on conditional or middle knowledge in God, section 3, number 18.
translator_notes: Matthias Nethenus (1618-1686) defended these theses under Gisbertus Voetius (1589-1676) at Utrecht; they are printed in Voetius, Selectae disputationes theologicae, part 1.

title: Voetius' disputants: two states of the object of God's knowledge but three moments; conditionals belong to free knowledge
english: To set out their view on the matter more distinctly, those very learned men say that in the object of God's knowledge they consider two states, possibility and futurity, but three moments. In the first, God, looking at his own omnipotence, saw what he could do without contradiction. In the second, by an absolute decree he fixed beforehand within himself the modes, connections and sequences of everything that could be made: what would or would not be cause, effect, means and end, what would come before, together or after. He did this with one proviso: if he willed them to be future.

In the third, among the things fixed beforehand under that condition, he made a distinction. For some he left the condition standing and added the decree 'I do not will them to be future.' For others he removed the condition and put in its place the decree 'I will them to be future.'

Only in the third moment, they say, is a thing finally brought out of the state of possibility into the state of futurity. In the first two it stays in the state of possibility. The difference is that God knows things in the first moment by nature, before any act of his will, and in the second after an act of his will. These too are their words, in that third section, number 13.

Their words make it plain that they treat contingent futures under a condition not as truly future but as merely possible. Yet they want the knowledge of them to belong not to God's natural knowledge but to his free knowledge.
translator_notes: 'Viri illi Doctissimi' are the authors of the Voetian disputation cited at XXXII (Gisbertus Voetius with Matthias Nethenus); 'tertia illa sectione, num. 13' refers to that disputation.

title: They take this from Samuel Rutherford: God's will is determined from eternity toward every being, so conditionals are true by his will
english: They admit that they took this doctrine from the Scot Samuel Rutherford, and in the same place they lay down, as a most certain foundation drawn from him, the following. God's will is not undetermined, doubtful or suspended toward any being, whether actual or potential, and whether it is to be actualized at some time or never brought into act.
Nor does his will contain potentiality, suspension and the lack of a second act, as a created will does. By the eminence of its act it is determined from eternity with respect to every being.

From this they infer that God necessarily wills or does not will every possible sequence and connection of beings. So in every conditional proposition about a contingent future, it is true by God's definite and certain will that if this or that condition were in place, this and nothing else would follow.
translator_notes: Samuel Rutherford (c. 1600-1661), professor at St Andrews; Latinised 'Retorfortis'.

title: Rutherford: God knows the Keilah and Tyre conditionals by free knowledge in a predetermining decree
english: Rutherford himself, lately professor of theology at the University of St Andrews, also a learned and subtle man, uses the same principle. He states that God knew by free knowledge, in a predetermining decree, that the people of Keilah would hand David over to Saul if he had stayed with them, that the Tyrians would have repented if they had seen the signs, and other things of the kind.

By that decree, he says, God absolutely fixed beforehand the sequence of all possible beings. 'This certainly,' he says, 'belongs to the wonderful providence of God, whose will is undetermined and suspended toward no beings, whether actual or possible.' Exercitationes Apologeticae pro Divina Gratia, chapter 5, on middle knowledge.
translator_notes: Rutherford, Exercitationes apologeticae pro divina gratia (Amsterdam, 1636; Franeker, 1651), cap. 5.

title: Others hold that many conditional propositions about free futures are neither true nor false, and so fall outside God's knowledge
english: Others, however, think that many, or rather countless, propositions about contingent futures under some condition can be framed and made up that do not fall under God's knowledge. They express nothing that God himself can know or understand.

This is not because God is ignorant of any truth, or because something is really future that God does not know to be future. It is because, in their view, such propositions signify nothing that is determinately true or false. What they affirm or deny as future under a certain condition is no more future than not future; it is open either way.

title: Example: angels in another world; such a conditional is neither true nor false, and omniscience loses nothing
english: Suppose someone says that if God created another world and placed certain angels in it in these or those circumstances, those angels would persevere in their duty and in the love of God. On their view, what that conditional proposition asserts is neither true nor false, and so God cannot know it as true or false.

The matter is of itself merely possible and open to being so or not being so, and God knows that this is how it stands. So if it is said that the proposition contains no truth God can know, God's omniscience loses nothing.

title: They reject as absurd infinite decrees about connections of possibles (Rutherford, Voetius); so Strang and Twisse
english: They consider absurd the view of those who ascribe to God countless decrees about contingent connections between any one possible thing and another. This includes cases where no order, subordination or coherence appears. It is as though God had decreed whatever would happen in the countless worlds he could create, under countless different conditions.

This is the view just reported from Samuel Rutherford and from Voetius's theses. John Strang expressly rejects it in his treatise On the Will and Actions of God concerning Sin, book 1, chapter 5, and book 3, chapter 13. So does Twisse in his dissertation on middle knowledge, book 3, page 472.
translator_notes: John Strang (1584-1654), principal of Glasgow University, De voluntate et actionibus Dei circa peccatum (Amsterdam, 1657); William Twisse (1578-1646), Dissertatio de scientia media (Arnhem, 1639).

title: They do not deny all knowledge of conditional futures, but derive it from absolute decrees about what really happens
english: Even so, they do not deny that God has any knowledge of things that would be or would have been contingently future under a condition that has never been, and never will be, fulfilled. They grant that some things of this kind are foretold in Scripture and so were known to God and clearly seen by him. What they insist on is that this knowledge did not come before the free decree of God's will.

This is not because they allow in God conditional decrees, by which he wills something to happen under a condition that will never obtain. Nor do they allow explicit, formal decrees about the connection of two events, neither of which will actually exist. Their reason is that, given this or that condition, it follows from certain absolute decrees of God about things that will really happen that these or those things would have come about.

title: Keilah: God knew the betrayal from his decree to save David by flight, without an explicit conditional decree
english: For example, God knew that Saul would come to the city of Keilah and that its people would hand David over to Saul if David stayed there. He knew it because he had decreed to rescue David from Saul's hands not by a miracle or by some extraordinary change of heart in Saul or in the people of Keilah, but by David's withdrawal and flight.

It follows that David would have been handed over to Saul if he had stayed with the people of Keilah. Yet we do not posit in God an explicit decree of the form 'I will that the people of Keilah hand David over if he stays with them.'

title: Ames: an implicit, virtual decree grounds conditionals that never occur; they belong to the knowledge of vision
english: William Ames explains the matter this way in his rescript to Grevinchoven's Response, chapter 15. 'This too,' he says, 'deserves careful consideration. A decree of God may be conceived either as a formal and explicit statute, or as implicit and virtual, contained by the force of another decree. Only the implicit kind applies to conditional contingent futures that never come to exist, because by the force of actual decrees they would exist if this or that were posited.

God had decreed to free David from the men of Keilah by means of flight, not by changing their minds outside the usual order. From this actual decree flows the conditional contingent: if David does not flee, he will be handed over.'

In this sense, Ames says, the conditional future rests on the free decree and so is understood by the knowledge of vision. That knowledge covers not only what will absolutely happen, but also what would flow from an actual decree already made, given this or that condition.
translator_notes: William Ames, Rescriptio scholastica et brevis ad Nic. Grevinchovii responsum (Harderwijk, 1615), cap. 15.
The print reads 'quia virtute actuali decretis'; rendered as 'by the force of actual decrees' (Ames's sense: by virtue of an actual decree). Not emended.

title: Their main foundation (Twisse): nothing is future before God decrees it, since futurity from eternity needs an eternal cause
english: Twisse, Rutherford, Voetius, Ames and others deny that God knows, before his free decree, what would contingently happen under some condition. The main foundation they rely on is that, on their view, nothing is future until God has decreed that it shall be. It follows that before God's decree nothing can be conceived or known as future.

They prove that nothing is future, absolutely or conditionally, before God decrees it, on these grounds. No cause can be imagined or thought of, other than God's decree, by which a thing passes from being possible to being future from eternity. Nothing temporal can cause what is eternal.

So the futurity that exists from eternity cannot be traced to anything that happens in time. It must have some eternal cause, and that can only be God's free decree. Twisse repeats this a thousand times in his dissertation on middle knowledge.

title: Voetius (Nethenus): the whole controversy turns on whether conditional futures can become future except by God's decree
english: Voetius, or rather Nethenus in Voetius's work, after arguing at length against middle knowledge, finally concludes: 'From what has been argued so far against middle knowledge, it is clear that the whole difficulty of the present controversy comes down to this point.

Could free conditional futures, which by their own nature are open to being future or not future, have passed from eternity into the state of something future in any way other than by the divine decree, which is the cause of every kind of futurity whatever? This is the foundation of foundations, on which the whole weight of the case rests. It is the postulate that we cannot grant our opponents and they cannot prove to us.'
translator_notes: Matthias Nethenus (1618-1686) defended disputations under Gisbertus Voetius at Utrecht; the print spells 'Nathenus'.

title: Strang's argument: conditionals without necessary connection cannot be known with certainty, so not by God
english: Strang does not agree with the theologians just named that the futurity of every event from eternity depends on nothing but God's free decree. He tries to prove by another argument, which he considers unanswerable, that God cannot know free contingents as future on any supposition from which the determination of the created will does not necessarily follow.

His argument runs like this. Conditionals whose consequent has no necessary connection with the antecedent cannot be known with certainty, and so God cannot know them either, since his knowledge is entirely certain and infallible. The conditionals said to be the object of middle knowledge are of this kind, and so on.

He proves the major premise as follows: 'Unless the object is certainly true, it cannot be known with certainty. As long as the matter is uncertain, it cannot be known with certainty. But nothing is certainly true that is not necessarily true, necessarily, I mean, either absolutely or on a hypothesis.

So for conditional knowledge to be certain and infallible, its object must be a necessary conditional proposition. And no conditional proposition is necessary unless the inference in it is necessary.' Treatise on the Will of God concerning Sin, book 3, chapter 11.

title: Le Blanc's view, first: no conditional free future is knowable unless the condition includes God's decree not to deny concurrence
english: To state briefly what I myself think: first, it is certain and, as is clear from what has been said, granted by everyone, that nothing is freely future under any condition, or can be known as such, unless God's decree not to deny the creature the concurrence necessary for acting is included in the condition under which it is said to be future.

That is, if any proposition about conditional futures is to be capable of truth, it must be explained and understood like this: this or that creature, placed in such an order of things, will do this or that, provided God wills to concur with it as he usually does. He must concur if the creature is to be able to put forth its action.

title: Second: such conditionals are determinately true or false; even the later Thomists cannot deny it on their own premises
english: Second, I think it must also be granted that every proposition about free and contingent conditional futures, where a condition of that kind is understood, is determinately true or false. At any rate the later Thomists cannot deny this, nor can others who agree with them on this matter while otherwise attacking middle knowledge fiercely.

On their view, for a creature to act God must premove and predetermine it, and once God's predetermination is posited the creature's action follows necessarily. So on their assumptions this conditional is infallible and necessary: if God willed to place such a creature in this or that state and to deny it nothing it needs to act, it would do this or that. For that condition contains God's decree to predetermine the creature to act.

title: The reasons for determinate truth in absolute future propositions hold for these conditionals too
english: The reasons that lead us to hold that absolute propositions about contingent futures are determinately true or false seem to apply to these conditionals as well. One is that of two contradictories one must be true and the other false. Another is that in every true disjunction at least one part must be true.

For this disjunction is true: if Peter is placed in such an occasion and God does not deny him his usual concurrence, he will sin or he will not sin. These two propositions also contradict each other: 'If Peter is placed in that order of things and God is not unwilling to concur with him in acting, he will do this,' and 'If Peter is placed in that order of things and God is not unwilling to concur with him in acting, he will not do this.'

title: Objection that nothing is future before God's decree: absolute futurity needs a decree, conditional futurity only a supposed one
english: Someone may object that nothing is future except in dependence on God's decree. Before God's decree, then, a thing is no more future than not future, but open to being either, so that neither can truly be said of it.

My answer is this. For a thing to be absolutely future, some decree of God on which its futurity depends is indeed required beforehand. But for a thing not to be simply future, only future under some condition, no decree actually present in God is needed. It is enough that there be a decree that would have to be posited in God on that hypothesis.

title: No truth escapes God's intellect; so these determinately true conditionals are objects of his knowledge
english: Again, it is certain and granted by all that no truth whatever escapes God's intellect. Propositions about free futures, under the condition explained more than once, have determinate truth, so they too are objects of God's knowledge.
God therefore knows what every possible creature would do if he willed to establish it in this or that state and to deny it nothing it needs in order to act.

title: Even predeterminists must grant it, as Twisse concedes on Suarez's reading of the conditionals
english: Those who hold that creatures can perform no action without God's prior, predetermining concurrence cannot deny this proposition either, which follows from the one before. Plainly God cannot fail to know what each possible creature would do if he willed not only to create it but also to apply it to act and predetermine it.

Twisse admits as much. He notes that Suarez teaches that the conditional propositions about contingent futures that are the object of God's knowledge include God's will in the antecedent: that is, if God himself willed such an effect, or at least willed to permit it and to concur with it. Twisse then adds: 'In this sense we grant that the conditionals the Jesuits invent do hold.' Dissertation on middle knowledge, book 3, page 465.
translator_notes: Francisco Suarez SJ (1548-1617).

title: On their principles too, this knowledge is in God prior in reason to any decree
english: It is just as clear, on the principles of those same teachers, that the knowledge by which God knows what any possible creature would do in this or that state of things, if he willed to supply it with the concurrence it needs to act, exists in God prior in the order of reason to any decree of his about things.

Before we conceive of God decreeing anything, it is true that if God willed to move and predetermine some creature to act by his concurrence, it would certainly do what it was moved and determined to do. The truth of this proposition does not depend on some earlier decree of God fixing the connection between that possible decree and the event that would follow from it.

title: A prior decree fixing all connections of possibles is fiction, idle, and unworthy of God's goodness and justice
english: Indeed, the decree some posit, as reported above, by which God fixed within himself the connections and sequences of everything that could be made before he decreed anything to be future, seems pure invention. It seems contrary not only to God's wisdom but also to his goodness.

If it were so, God would have had to form decrees like these within himself before resolving to create this world: 'If I will to create Adam, I will that his fall be necessarily bound up with his temptation. If I will to create David and that he see Bathsheba, I will that lust for that woman be joined to that sight.'

Or again: 'I will that such occasions of sin be followed by such sins, if I decree that such occasions shall exist.' Or even: 'I will that in the countless worlds I could create, these or those contingently possible events be inseparably linked with these or those events of the same kind.'
Such decrees are not only plainly idle, trivial and pointless. They are utterly unworthy of the goodness and justice of the one who is a God who does not will iniquity.
translator_notes: 'Deus nolens iniquitatem' echoes Psalm 5:5 (Vulgate 5:5; English 5:4), 'non Deus volens iniquitatem tu es'.

title: So all must grant conditional knowledge before any actual decree; the only question is what decree the condition includes
english: So it cannot reasonably be denied, and everyone ought to grant, that God has a certain knowledge of what is freely and contingently future under a certain condition, before we conceive of any actual decree in God about future things.

The whole difficulty is this. Must the condition under which something is said to be future include a decree to premove and predetermine the second cause to act? Or is it enough that the decree which that condition would require in God be simply a decree to provide a concurrence that is of itself indifferent and is determined by the second cause to a particular kind of action?

title: Predeterminists require a predetermining decree in the condition; Le Blanc denies predetermination to evil acts lest God author sin
english: All the theologians who think nothing happens without God's concurrence applying and predetermining the second cause to act insist that no proposition about contingent conditional futures has any truth, or can be known as true, unless a decree to premove and predetermine the free agent is assumed in the condition.
They hold that the futurity of every action depends on such a decree, and some even make it the sole and only cause. Without such a decree, they say, no action of a second cause can be future.

Our view, however, is that second causes do many things in time to which God does not predetermine them. We do not see how God would escape being the author of sin if he predetermined free causes to acts that are vicious in themselves and intrinsically evil, such as blasphemy and hatred of God.

But if a free cause can perform some action without God's premotion and predetermination, then for an action to be future, or to be such that it would be future, there is no need to posit or suppose in God a decree to premove and predetermine the creature to act. A decree to provide the concurrence without which the creature can do nothing, and which its action really needs, is enough.

title: Le Blanc rejects Twisse's claim that God's decree is the sole cause of every event's futurity: it makes God the author of sin
english: Above all, I cannot accept in any way what William Twisse asserts in many places: that God's decree and will is the one and only cause of the futurity of every event.

What then? Is God's decree the only reason why Adam was going to disobey God, and likewise why the angels who fell were going to exalt themselves against God in pride? Who could bear to hear anyone say so? Or who could say it without plainly making God the author of sin?

title: Twisse's argument from eternal futurity; reply: futurity is only a relation of reason, an extrinsic denomination
english: 'But,' says that learned man, 'no cause can be given for a futurity that existed from eternity unless the cause itself existed from eternity. Nothing temporal causes what exists from eternity. But nothing existed from eternity except God himself, who acts outside himself only through his free will.'

My answer is that this argument assumes that futurity is something real, distinct from the future thing itself and having a cause other than that thing. That is entirely false. Futurity is nothing but a certain relation of reason, an extrinsic denomination of the thing said to be future. It is not some being distinct from the future thing that needs a cause different from the cause of the future thing itself.
The argument itself makes this plain. It rightly assumes that nothing existed from eternity except God. So the futurity said to have existed from eternity was either nothing real or God himself.

title: The cause of a thing's existing in time is the cause of its having been future from eternity, as of its being past for ever
english: So whatever causes a thing to exist at some point in time is exactly what causes it to have been going to exist from eternity. In the same way, whatever is the cause of a thing's having been at some time is the cause of its being called past for ever.

A cause existing from eternity is no more needed for a thing to have been future from eternity than a cause lasting for ever is needed for a thing to be past for ever. A future cause is enough for a future effect, just as a past cause is enough for a past one.

title: Since God does not cause sin in time, his will is no cause of sin's futurity; it depends only on his decree to permit
english: Since God is not the cause of sin in time, I am far from thinking we should say that God's will is the only cause of sin's futurity. On the contrary, I judge that we must deny plainly and without qualification that it is the cause of that futurity at all, whether on its own or together with the second cause.
It is true that man sins only in dependence on God's will, since he could not sin unless God permitted him to. In that sense the futurity of sin also depends on God's decree to permit sin.
But God's will is not for that reason to be called the proper cause of man's actually sinning. In the same way, it does not follow that God's decree is the proper cause of the futurity of sin.

title: Strang, though no predeterminist, still denies that free contingents are knowable from a hypothesis that does not necessitate
english: Even some who hold that certain free acts are absolutely future, and are foreknown as such by God without any decree predetermining free causes to those acts, still deny that God can know free contingent futures on any supposition that does not necessarily entail the determination of the created will, and so does not include an absolute decree that these acts shall be future. The very learned Strang is one of them.
This can be seen in Strang himself, On the Will of God concerning Sin, book 3, chapter 11.

title: Strang's reason proves too much: by it God could foreknow no absolute contingent he had not decreed, which Strang denies
english: His reason, as reported above, is that nothing can be known with certainty that is not certainly true, and nothing is certainly true that is not necessary either absolutely or on a hypothesis. He concludes that conditional futures cannot be the object of God's knowledge, which is infallible and entirely certain, unless the condition includes something from which what is called future follows necessarily.

But if this argument held, God could foreknow no contingent thing as absolutely future except what he had first decreed to be absolutely future. Yet Strang does not accept that, since he grants that people freely do many things to which God does not predetermine them.

title: Strang's answer: whatever is absolutely future is necessary on the hypothesis that it is future
english: 'But,' says that learned man, 'whatever God foresees as absolutely future, however contingent it may be in itself and able, strictly speaking, not to be, is still necessary on a hypothesis. The hypothesis is not some divine predetermining decree, but simply that it is future.
Just as whatever is, is necessarily while it is, so whatever is future, by the very fact that it is assumed to be future, is necessarily future. And so God can know it with certainty.'

title: The same answer serves conditional futures: given that the agent would so act, it must so act under the condition
english: What that very learned man thinks must be said of absolute futures can be applied with no less reason to conditional futures. I will say in the same way that God foresees with certainty what would freely happen under some condition.

He foresees it because, although the free cause could act otherwise and the condition would not force it to act, it would in fact act in this way. On the hypothesis that it would act in this way, it must act so once the condition is in place. So it is something God can know with certainty.

title: So there is no reason to deny God this knowledge without a predetermining decree; the objections strike absolute foreknowledge too
english: I therefore see no reason to deny God knowledge of what would freely happen under a certain condition, even though the condition does not include a decree predetermining the free cause to this or that.

If any arguments seem to overthrow that knowledge, for instance that it cannot be grasped how God infallibly knows something to be future that could fail to be, those arguments also conflict with the foreknowledge of contingents that are absolutely future, and God's word puts it beyond all doubt that God has that foreknowledge.

title: We must not limit God's knowledge because we cannot grasp how he knows; it is safer to err on the side of his knowing
english: We certainly ought not to presume so much on ourselves as to dare to set limits to God's knowledge and deny that he knows something because we cannot understand how he would know it. God's intellect, infinite in every way, doubtless knows more than we can grasp or reach.

At any rate, someone who thinks God knows things that perhaps are not knowable errs less dangerously than someone who denies that God knows what he really does know, things that fall within the object of his omniscience.

title: Conditional knowledge has no necessary tie to the errors it is used to defend, nor to reconciling efficacious grace with freedom
english: I add that the knowledge of conditional futures, as described so far, has no necessary connection with the various errors that very many misuse it to defend and gloss over.

Above all, we maintain that it in no way conflicts with grace that is efficacious of itself, and that we do not need it to reconcile the efficacy of God's grace with the freedom of human choice. With God's help, we will show this in what follows.

title: Common doctrine: God's eternal will is the cause of all things, and human acts too fall under his immutable decrees
english: It is the common, accepted teaching of theologians, drawn from the plain witness of Scripture, that God's eternal will is the cause of all things. Everything, human acts included, is subject to the unchangeable decrees of God's providence.
Nothing happens, whether by brute and lifeless causes or by men and angels, except in accordance with God's eternal preordination and determination.

title: The difficulty: no one resists God's will, so freedom and the will's indetermination seem lost
english: Yet this seems to destroy freedom entirely, in angels and in men alike. No one can resist God's will. If God wills that angels and men do what they do, they cannot act otherwise; so they do not act freely and are not masters of their own acts.

Again, if the actions of the human will are determined by God's unchangeable decrees, the will seems to lose all indetermination, and with it the indifference in acting in which the essence of freedom consists.

title: Some scholastics confessed it beyond reason in this life, notably Cardinal Cajetan
english: Some scholastics found this difficulty so hard that they frankly confessed their ignorance on this point. They judged it beyond the reach of the human mind so long as the mind is burdened with this mortal body.

One of them was Cardinal Cajetan, a very famous figure among the scholastics. Sharp and subtle as he was, he could never satisfy himself here. He held that the harmony of free choice with God's providence cannot be explained or understood in this life, as his commentary on the first part of Thomas, question 22, article 4, shows.
translator_notes: Thomas de Vio, Cardinal Cajetan (1469-1534), commentary on Aquinas, Summa theologiae I, q. 22, a. 4.

title: Other Roman theologians think they can untie the knot, though they differ on decrees and on freedom
english: Other theologians of the Roman school, however, are confident that they can untie this knot, and to that end they seek out and invent a variety of solutions.
They do not all agree, either about the divine decrees or about what human freedom consists in.

title: The later Thomists: every free act predetermined by absolute decree before any foreseen determination (Alvarez)
english: To begin with the so-called recent Thomists: on their teaching, everything that occurs and is carried out in the world, and so also every free act of the will, was individually predetermined and predefined by God. God did this by an absolute and efficacious will, prior in reason to his foreseeing any determination of the created will, whether it was to come about absolutely or only on some condition.

This is the express view of Diego Alvarez, Archbishop of Trani and Salpi, among others, in the summary of his work on the helps of divine grace, book 2, chapter 5, which begins: 'From the sacred writings, if they are carefully weighed, we have it that God by his absolute and efficacious will predetermined all acts in particular, free ones included, that are to come about in time.

He did so prior in the sign of reason to the divine intellect's knowing that those acts would come about, even on the hypothesis that the created will were placed in such an order of things and in such circumstances.'
translator_notes: Diego Alvarez OP (d. 1635), Archbishop of Trani; De auxiliis divinae gratiae (Rome, 1610), with its summary; book 2, chapter 5.

title: So Matthaeus de Rispolis, and Estius agrees
english: Matthaeus de Rispolis teaches the same doctrine in his treatise entitled The State of the Controversy over Predefinitions and Predeterminations in Relation to Free Choice. In book 1, question 1, he argues at length that there are in God eternal predefinitions and predeterminations of the will's acts, in particular and by an absolute decree.

That decree, he holds, presupposes no conditional knowledge of how the will would determine itself if placed in such a state of things. William Estius agrees with them too, as is clear from what he writes on distinction 39 of the first book of the Sentences and on distinction 24 of the second book.
translator_notes: Matteo Rispoli OP, Status controversiae praedefinitionum et praedeterminationum cum libero arbitrio (1620s); Willem Hessels van Est (Estius, 1542-1613), commentary on Lombard's Sentences, I d. 39 and II d. 24.

title: Evil acts too are predefined as to their positive reality; their malice only permitted (Alvarez)
english: These authors do not exempt even the will's evil acts from this eternal predetermination of God. They hold that these too were predefined by an absolute and efficacious decree, at least as to what is real and positive in them. The malice itself, which is nothing but the privation of due rightness, they admit God did not efficaciously decree but only permitted.

This is seen especially in Diego Alvarez, in the summary on the helps of grace already cited, book 2, chapter 9, which begins: 'What has been said about the predetermination of the will to good acts must be extended to the act of sin insofar as it is an act and a being.

Hence whatever entity is found in any act of sin, even if that act is otherwise intrinsically evil, must be traced back to God as the first cause, who premoves and predetermines the created will to such an act insofar as it is an act and insofar as it is a being.'

title: Yet they hold this leaves contingency intact: God decreed not only the event but its free mode
english: On their view, God by his eternal decree predetermined and predefined whatever is done in time by any cause. Even so, they maintain that nothing prevents many things from happening not by necessity but contingently and freely.

God's eternal providence did not provide necessary causes for every event and effect; for some it provided free or contingent causes. Nor did it determine only that this or that should happen; it also determined the way each thing should happen. So God willed some things to happen necessarily, and others contingently and freely.

Far from removing the freedom of human acts, then, God's eternal providence is the first cause to which whatever freedom and contingency there is in things must be traced. For God willed not only that things should be, but also by his will settled and defined the mode and manner in which each should be.

title: God decreed not only that men act but that they act freely, choosing by their own judgement with power for the opposite
english: So, in these doctors' view, God's having decreed from eternity that men should do this or that, and that their wills should be drawn to these or those objects, is no obstacle to human freedom. God did not decree simply that they should do this or that, but that they should do it freely.

That is, they were to choose this or that by the judgement of their own reason as most fitting and advantageous for themselves, and in such a way that, judging differently, they could choose the opposite. On their view human freedom properly consists in this, so the determination made by the divine decree does not overturn it.

title: It is irrelevant to free choice whether its choice is impressed by a prior cause, so long as it follows practical judgement
english: In their phrase, it is 'irrelevant' to free choice whether its choosing is impressed on it by a prior cause or not.
What matters is that the choice comes from a judgement of the practical intellect, which is able to weigh different kinds of good on opposite sides and set them before the will.

title: Independence from a prior cause belongs to God alone; free creatures depend on the first cause as necessary ones do
english: Someone may say that 'free choice' means a cause that, in its free action, is independent of any prior cause. They reply that this is assumed as true falsely and without warrant.

Free choice of that kind belongs to God alone, who is wholly independent of any higher cause. Free creatures depend on the first cause in their free acts no less than necessary causes do in their necessary acts.

title: The decree determines the act but leaves the faculty flexible: true in the divided, not the composite sense
english: It is objected that once God has decreed some act of the human will, the will cannot act otherwise, so its indifference in acting, where freedom lies, is removed. They answer that it cannot both be true that God decreed the will should do something and that the will does not do it or does something else.

Yet God's decree does not prevent the will from keeping the power to act otherwise. The decree determines the act, but leaves the faculty able to turn to the opposite. So when a man does something in keeping with God's decree, it can truly be said that he is able not to do it and to act otherwise. God decreed that he should do this, but should do it in such a way that he remains able to act otherwise.

Thus, granted the divine decree, it is not true in the composite sense that the will can act or not act; but it is true in the divided sense. The opposite act cannot stand together with the divine decree, but the faculty for the opposite act stands with it perfectly well.

title: If pressed that God's decrees would be frustrated, they deny it: had man acted otherwise, God would have decreed otherwise
english: Someone may press the point: granted God's decree about some action, it cannot be said at all that a man can act otherwise, since it would follow that God's decrees could be thwarted and made void, which is utterly impossible. They deny the inference. If the man acted otherwise, which is assumed to be possible, God would have decreed otherwise.

They do not think it conflicts with the unchangeableness of God's decrees that a man, while carrying them out, keeps the power to act otherwise. It would conflict only if someone said that a man can end up doing the contrary of what God has decreed, and these theologians say no such thing.

title: Estius and Alvarez: being able to will differs from actually willing; the decree is needed only for the act
english: Much of the same kind can be read in William Estius in the places cited above, and in Diego Alvarez, summary on the helps of grace, book 2, chapter 6. There Alvarez answers the objections against a predetermination of the will that comes from God's external decree.

He raises this objection against himself. On his view, man can will only what God by an efficacious decree wills him to will, and can perform only acts God has predetermined. So we do not will freely what we will, but by absolute necessity, since we cannot do otherwise if God wills that we do it.

By the same reasoning, the acts commanded of us are not freely left undone. For if God's having predetermined our will to an act is required for us to do it, we cannot do it unless God by his absolute and efficacious decree has predetermined that we shall do it.

He answers that being able to run is one thing and actually running another. In the same way, being able to will or to produce some particular act is one thing, and actually producing it is another. For a man truly to be able to will an object, it is not required that an absolute and efficacious decree should have preceded in God from eternity, predetermining his free choice to will that object. That is required only for him actually to will it.

So from the absence of such a decree in God it does not follow that, absolutely speaking, the man cannot will the object; it follows only that he does not in fact will it. Nor does it follow that, if God has predetermined me to will this particular thing, it is not in my power, absolutely speaking, to will something else. Granted God's efficacious will, however, it is impossible in the composite sense that I should will another object.

title: Indifference opposed to necessity is of freedom's essence; indetermination implying potentiality is not
english: It is objected that the predetermination of the divine decree to this or that act takes from the will its indifference to acting, in which freedom lies. Alvarez answers that the indifference opposed to being determined to one thing by necessity does belong to the essence of freedom.

Free choice has this indifference even at the moment when God efficaciously predetermines it to act, indeed at the very moment it acts. What does not belong to the essence of freedom is indetermination in the sense that implies potentiality and the lack of a second act, and that is opposed to being determined to one side in the manner proper to freedom, which consists in a capacity for either side.
translator_notes: The print divides 'in determinationem'; read as one word, 'indeterminationem', which the sense and the contrast with 'Indifferentiam' require.

title: A free power can act or not act absolutely speaking, though not in the composite sense under God's efficacious will
