english: Someone may insist that a free power, by its nature, is able to act and not act once everything required for acting is in place. Yet once God's efficacious decree predetermines our free choice to do this particular thing, the will cannot fail to do it, for no one can resist God's will.

Alvarez answers that a free power, by its nature, is able to act and not act, with everything required for acting in place, speaking absolutely and without qualification. It is no absurdity, however, that granted God's efficacious will, it cannot in the composite sense fail to perform the act to which God predetermines it.

title: Predetermined acts are necessary only by necessity of inference, and the decree itself infers the exercise of freedom
english: Lastly, someone may say that necessity is opposed to freedom; and if God by an efficacious will predetermines us to act, every one of our actions will be necessary, since whatever God wills to happen must happen. Alvarez answers that all acts God has predetermined do come about necessarily, but by necessity of inference, given the supposition of that decree.

They do not come about by absolute necessity, which overturns freedom. In fact, the same predetermination implies the actual exercise of our freedom. For God predetermined not only that the will should will such an object, but also predefined that it should will it freely.

title: Objection: a supposition outside the will's power makes the act simply necessary; answer: not when the supposition is on God's side
english: Someone may press further that the necessity introduced by the divine decree removes the freedom of the created will. What is necessary on a supposition becomes simply necessary for a given agent when it is not in his power to remove or establish the supposition from which the act, called necessary on that supposition, follows necessarily.

But it is not in the created will's power to remove or establish the supposition of God's efficacious decree predetermining created free choice to act. That decree comes from God alone and in no way depends on the free working of our choice, not even as foreknown by middle knowledge. So the will's acts that are called necessary on the supposition of that decree are necessary absolutely and simply, and therefore not free.

Alvarez answers that when the supposition preceding an act lies on the side of the first and most universal cause, namely God, something can be necessary on a supposition with respect to the created will and yet free for it without qualification. This holds even though it is not in the will's power to establish or remove the supposition from which the act necessarily follows by the necessity of infallibility.

It is otherwise, he says, when the preceding supposition lies on the side of some created cause external to the will. Only God, the author of the created will, can by his infinity and omnipotence change it in keeping with its nature, move it efficaciously, and apply it to produce a particular act, not only as to its substance but also as to its free mode. A created cause cannot do this, because it is limited, finite and lower than the will itself.

title: Many Roman doctors are not satisfied; some cut the knot by denying that any free acts are predefined (Suarez, per Strang)
english: This way of reconciling human freedom with the decrees of God's providence, however, does not satisfy a great many doctors of the Roman school. Some of them, to cut the knot, deny that any free acts, whether of the natural or the supernatural order, were predefined by God from eternity.

Nor, on their view, does God predetermine any such acts in time, since they think predefinition and predetermination alike are incompatible with the freedom of the will. Suarez mentions these men, as John Strang reports, in book 3 of his work on the helps of grace, chapter 17, numbers 1 and 2.
translator_notes: Francisco Suarez, De auxiliis (Opuscula theologica), book 3, ch. 17, nn. 1-2, as reported by John Strang of Glasgow (1584-1654), De voluntate et actionibus Dei circa peccatum.

title: Vasquez reports some who say God foreordained our works only in general, lest necessity or a lack of the decree follow
english: Gabriel Vasquez attributes a similar view to some of his own school, in volume 1 on Thomas, disputation 99, chapter 5, where he reports their various positions on this question. 'Finally,' he says, 'some, overwhelmed by this difficulty, say that God from eternity did not will our works one by one, but only in general, and determined in a universal way that he is ready to act with anyone according to that person's determination.'

Vasquez adds that they adopt this view in order to maintain that God's foreordination imposes no necessity on our will against its freedom. A further reason is this. If God had to foreordain and will from eternity even the works of grace one by one, those who do not act and do not consent to the call would lack something necessary for acting, namely that decree. It would then be no wonder that they did not act, since without it they could not.
translator_notes: Gabriel Vasquez SJ (1549-1604), Commentarii ac disputationes in primam partem S. Thomae, vol. 1, disp. 99, ch. 5.

title: Others grant God foreordained each act, but after foreseeing the will's absolutely future determination (Lessius)
english: Not far from these are certain others. They do grant that God foreordained from eternity each single act of men, but say that this foreordination follows his foresight of how the will itself would determine itself.

On their view no human works, not even supernaturally good ones, were predefined in particular by an absolute decree of God before he foresaw our will's determination as future, not only conditionally but also absolutely. This is the teaching of the Jesuit Leonard Lessius in his treatise on predestination.
translator_notes: Leonard Lessius SJ (1554-1623), De praedestinatione et reprobatione (Antwerp, 1610; in Opuscula, 1626).

title: Vasquez assigns the same to Catharinus, Cordoba, Sirenus, Osorio: free choice the first root; three instants in works of grace
english: In the same place Vasquez attributes the same view to Ambrose Catharinus, Antonio de Cordoba, Julius Sirenus, Osorio and some others. They teach, he says, that God did not foreordain our acts, good or evil, as to their substance, before he foresaw how our choice would determine itself. The determination to one side rather than the other, in good or evil acts as to their substance, comes indeed both from us and from God, but its first root and cause is free choice.

From this, Vasquez says, they infer that our determination is understood to come before God's predestination and foreordination. They assign the same order, he says, in the works of grace as regards consent and cooperation, though they grant that operating and arousing grace, that is, the call, comes before both our cooperation and God's.

As Vasquez reports, they distinguish three instants. In the first our will is anticipated by grace. In the second it determines itself to consent to the call or to resist it. In the third God concurs with it. So on their view God foreknows what the will is going to determine itself to, in works of grace as in works of nature, before he decrees to concur with it in this or that act, and so before he foreordains any of our acts.
translator_notes: Ambrosius Catharinus Politus OP (1484-1553); Antonio de Cordoba OFM (1485-1578); Julius Sirenus (Giulio Sireno, fl. 1560s), De fato; 'Osorius' is probably Jeronimo Osorio (1506-1580), bishop of Silves. All as reported by Vasquez, disp. 99, ch. 5.

title: These easily reconcile freedom with the decrees: the decrees follow the foreseen determination, so only consequent necessity arises
english: These men find it easy to reconcile the freedom of our choice with God's decrees. On their view the divine decrees follow God's foresight of the determination that will come from our will as its first root and cause.

So the divine decrees, no more than God's foreknowledge, give rise to any preceding necessity in our actions. They produce only a consequent necessity, which does not remove our freedom but presupposes it intact.

title: Others distinguish absolute and conditional foreknowledge; the latter is the middle knowledge treated above
english: Others, however, use a twofold distinction here. The first is between absolute and conditional foreknowledge of future things. Absolute foreknowledge is that by which God foresees this or that as simply and really future.

Conditional foreknowledge is that by which God foresees not what is simply and absolutely future, but what would be future if this or that were in place. An example is the direction in which Adam's will would of its own accord lean and tend if it were created in such a state and these or those objects were put before it. This is the knowledge the schools call middle knowledge, which we dealt with at length in the preceding theses.

title: They grant the decrees to permit or effect acts precede foreknowledge of the absolutely future determination (Adam, Paul)
english: On this basis they grant that God's decrees about human acts, whether to permit them or to bring them about, come before his foreknowledge of the human will's absolutely future determination, according to our way of conceiving things in God.

On their view, for example, God decreed to permit Adam to desire the forbidden fruit, and to concur with him in that act, before he absolutely foresaw that Adam's will would determine itself to it. Likewise he decreed to anticipate Paul with his grace and to cooperate with him in the act of conversion before he absolutely foresaw that Paul's will would determine itself to it.

title: But God decreed nothing about free acts before foreseeing which way the will would incline in a given state
english: They maintain, however, that God decreed and settled nothing about men's free actions before he foresaw which way the human will would lean and determine itself if it were placed in this or that state of things.

Nor, they say, did God absolutely will that the will should produce these actions rather than those before he foreknew what each individual would do and will if this or that occasion for acting were put before him.

title: Their doctrine: before any decree God foresaw what would follow under every condition, and above all with free creatures
english: Their teaching, then, is this. Before any decree about creating and bringing about things, God foresaw from eternity what would come about and follow given any condition at all. He had before his eyes countless forms, arrangements and modes of things, and for each of them he knew what would result if it were put in place.

In particular they teach that God could not be ignorant of what would happen if he created free causes, namely men and angels, and saw to it that they were offered the occasions for acting that were later offered and will be offered hereafter, and placed them in the circumstances in which they were later placed and will be placed in future. Nor could he be ignorant of what would happen if such circumstances had been varied in countless ways and quite different occasions for acting had been offered.

title: Only after this foresight did God decree to create, to arrange the occasions, and to concur; absolute foreknowledge follows the decree
english: God thus foresaw and considered what would happen if men and angels were placed in these or those circumstances and prompted to act by these or those objects, what good he could bring out of it, and how he could direct these things or those to the display of his glory. Only then, I say, on these doctors' view, did God resolve to create men and angels in the state in which they were afterwards created.

He resolved also to arrange that these occasions for acting rather than others should be put before them, and to concur with them in the actions to which he foresaw their wills would determine themselves, provided he did not withhold his concurrence. Finally, this decree was followed by the absolute foreknowledge by which he foreknew that they would act in this way or that.

title: So God foreordained men's acts only by placing them in states and supplying aids and occasions, imposing no necessity
english: They hold, therefore, that God preordained and predefined men's actions only in this sense: he willed to create them in that state and to supply them with the motives, aids and occasions for acting from which he foresaw that they would act in such a way and would produce these volitions rather than those.
All the while it remained in their power to act this way or otherwise, since none of these things imposed on them any necessity of acting this way rather than another.

title: They call good acts predefined but evil ones not; only their permission, which is good, is predefined
english: On this account it might seem that nothing prevents us from saying that God predefined all free acts, whatever they may turn out to be. The authors of this view, however, distinguish between good and evil acts. Good acts, they grant, can rightly be said to have been predefined by God's eternal decree. About evil acts they think otherwise.

God did decree to place men in the state in which he foresaw, by conditional knowledge, that they would act badly. Yet he neither wills nor approves their evil acts, and God's predefinition includes or presupposes the approval of the divine will. So although evil acts are not predefined by God, their permission is predefined, because permitting them is good.

title: This is Fonseca's teaching
english: Fonseca, among others, teaches this. He holds that before any foreknowledge of free acts, none of them were predefined from eternity, since otherwise the freedom of the created will would be removed.

After God foreknew future free acts in the conditional state, only the good ones were predefined by him, because only they have his approval. Evil acts are not predefined, but their permission, which God approves, has been predefined. Commentary on Metaphysics 6, chapter 2, question 5, section 7.
translator_notes: Pedro da Fonseca SJ (1528-1599), Commentarii in libros Metaphysicorum Aristotelis, on book 6, ch. 2, q. 5, s. 7.

title: They hold the decrees easy to reconcile with freedom: providence moves the will only by proposing objects and reasons; certainty rests on middle knowledge
english: These doctors also think that, once their hypothesis is admitted, it is not hard to reconcile the decrees of providence with the freedom of our choice. On their view God's providence lets our wills act according to each one's own inclination.

God has not decreed to lead men's minds and turn them in various directions by any means other than setting objects before them, within and without, and other inducements that do not take from the will its power to act this way or otherwise. These leave to the will, as the schools put it, the specification of its action.

So the whole certainty of God's decrees rests on the infallibility of that middle knowledge, by which, they claim, God foreknows before any decree of his will which way the created will would lean and tend if these or those occasions for acting were put before it. It does not rest on any force or efficacy by which the will is necessarily moved to act so.

title: Vasquez accepts conditional foreknowledge but not that the decrees precede absolute foresight, lest antecedent necessity follow
english: Gabriel Vasquez, however, is not satisfied with this solution of the difficulty. He accepts what the authors of the view just set out say: that before God frames his decrees about free acts, he foreknows by a kind of conditional knowledge which way the will would lean and what it would determine itself to, if these or those circumstances were in place.

What he cannot accept is what they do not hesitate to grant, namely that God's decrees about free acts come in God, according to our way of conceiving, before his absolute foresight of that same will's determination. If it is granted that God in any way foreordained the acts of our will before he absolutely foreknows what its inclination and determination will be, Vasquez thinks there arises from this a kind of antecedent necessity that is incompatible with the freedom of future acts.
translator_notes: The print reads 'ejusdem voluntas', a slip for 'voluntatis' (governed by 'determinationis'); the lock and translation read 'voluntatis'. Vasquez, disp. 99, ch. 5 as above.

title: Nor does Vasquez side with those who put absolute foreknowledge of the will's determination before God's decree to concur
english: Yet he does not join those who think God absolutely foreknows what the will is going to determine itself to before he decrees to concur with it in this or that act, and before he in any way foreordains its act. His reason is that he judges it impossible for our will to act or determine itself prior in nature to God's acting with it. It follows that not even in eternity can the will's determination be understood apart from God's decree to concur with it.

A further reason is that this view seems to take something away from God's cooperating grace. 'Our will,' he says, 'needs for acting not only to be aroused but also the cooperation of grace in order to consent to that arousing. So it will need that cooperation in order to determine itself to consent as well. How then can it be understood as determined at some prior moment without the cooperation of grace?'

title: Vasquez's own view: God's definition of our acts neither precedes nor follows the will's determination but accompanies it
english: So Vasquez devises something else of his own. God's definition, which foreordains our works one by one, neither comes before the determination of our will in the order of causes nor follows it, but accompanies it.

From this he concludes that the necessity which follows once God's decree is posited is not antecedent to our freedom and determination but accompanies them. So our freedom is neither hindered nor harmed by that necessity, since only a preceding necessity damages freedom, not one that follows or accompanies it.

title: His ground: God's cooperation is simultaneous with our consent, so decree and foresight of our determination are conceived together
english: The basis of his view is this. On God's side, no working that precedes our will's consent imposes on the will a necessity to consent. The cooperation of God by which he brings about our will's very consent in no way precedes our will's determination; it exists together with it in time, in nature and in reason.

It follows that God's decree to bring about that consent cannot come before his foresight of the human will's determination. Things that exist wholly together in time cannot have an order of prior and posterior in God's foreknowledge and decrees.

From this he concludes that no free work of our will was predefined by God before he foresaw our will's free determination. Rather, the foresight of that determination and God's decree predefining our will's act must be conceived as together in God.

title: Arminius and the Remonstrants side with Molina; Arminius's two senses of determination
english: James Arminius, and those in the Low Countries who followed his teachings and are called Remonstrants, agree with Molina and his disciples in explaining the nature of human freedom. They also seem to reconcile that freedom with the decrees of God's providence in the same way. Arminius's teaching in his Response to Article 7, Works page 143, at least points that way.

There he does not deny that God by his eternal decree predefined and predetermined future contingents. But he distinguishes two kinds of divine determination by which God settles that something shall happen. In the first, whatever action, motion or impulse of God is in place, the free second cause remains free both in its power and in the use of that power to act or not act, so that it can suspend its action if it wishes.

In the second, once God's action, motion and impulse are in place, the second cause does not remain free, at least not in the use of its power so as to be able to suspend its action. Instead it is necessarily bent to one side, its indifference to either side being removed, before the determined act is produced by the free creature.

If 'determination' is taken in the first sense, he does not deny that God so determines future free and contingent things. If it is taken in the second sense, he flatly denies that God by his decree determined future contingents to one side or the other.
translator_notes: Jacobus Arminius (1560-1609), 'Apologia adversus articulos XXXI', art. 7, in Opera theologica (Leiden, 1629), p. 143.

title: Arminius does not say how determination and indifference cohere; his disciples (Grevinchoven) use middle knowledge
english: He does not clearly explain how these two things fit together: that an action is determined by God's eternal decree, and yet, with that determination in place, the will always remains indifferent to the action and always able to produce it or not.

From what he adds, however, he leaves us to infer that it works like this. To carry out his decrees about human acts, God moves men's wills only by supplying and setting before them objects and arguments that do induce them to will, yet in such a way that it always remains in their power not to be moved by those objects.
His disciples, such as Nicolaus Grevinchoven among others, expressly bring in middle knowledge to untie this knot, as most Jesuits do, in the way set out in the preceding theses.
translator_notes: Nicolaus Grevinchovius (Grevinchoven, d. 1632), Remonstrant minister of Rotterdam.

title: Some Reformed who subscribe Dort take the same way, notably Robert Baron of Aberdeen, who follows Fonseca
english: Yet even among the Reformed who otherwise seem far from the Arminian teaching and subscribe to the Synod of Dort, some follow this same way of reconciling the decrees of God's providence with the freedom of human choice.

One of them is Robert Baron, some years ago professor of theology at Aberdeen in Scotland. In his Metaphysics adapted to the use of theology he praises Fonseca's teaching on this point and openly endorses it: section 12, disputation 2, number 65.
translator_notes: Robert Baron (c. 1596-1639), professor of divinity at Marischal College, Aberdeen; Metaphysica generalis (published posthumously), sect. 12, disp. 2, n. 65. On Fonseca see De Decretis Pars Secunda XXXI.

title: Baron cites Fonseca's two conclusions: nothing predefined before foreknowledge; concurrence decreed after it (Adam)
english: Baron there cites two conclusions of Fonseca which, by his own account, strike him as especially helpful for showing that God's providence and the freedom of human choice agree. First: none of our free acts was predefined from eternity prior to every foreknowledge of them.

He glosses this as follows. Until God had foreknown or foreseen in which direction human wills would turn, were this or that occasion put to them, he neither willed absolutely that the will should elicit one set of actions over another, nor decreed to concur in eliciting one set rather than another.

Second: once God, as we must conceive it, had foreseen the direction our wills would take when given this or that occasion, he decreed from eternity to concur with them at the relevant times in eliciting precisely the actions he saw they would turn toward.
Thus, to take an example, God foresaw from eternity that Adam, if tempted by his wife, would desire the fruit, and for that reason decreed to concur with Adam in eliciting that desire.

title: Baron's four steps in God's decree about the first sin
english: So he thinks the order of God's decree about that first sin can be explained as follows. 'First,' he says, 'God has a conditional foreknowledge by which he foresees that Adam will desire the fruit if such an occasion is offered him. He also has a foreknowledge by which he knew that he could direct that act of Adam to his own glory.

Second, he foresaw that from the wicked act Adam would perform if such an occasion were offered him, he could bring a great good, namely the display of his glory. Because of this, I say, he willed that the occasion be offered to Adam; that is, he willed to permit Eve, deceived by the serpent, to tempt Adam.
Third, by a foreknowledge that is not conditional but absolute, he foresaw that Adam's will would lean toward desiring the fruit at the time when Adam was to be tempted.
Fourth, partly so as not to take from Adam the use of his free choice, and partly to display his glory, he decreed to concur with Adam's will in producing that volition.

From this it plainly follows that Adam was not going to fall, or to desire the fruit, because God decreed to concur with his will in producing the desire. On the contrary, God decreed to concur in producing that action rather than another because he foresaw that Adam's will would lean that way when such an occasion was offered him.'

title: Hence, says Baron, the decrees impose no causal necessity, only necessity of consequence, no more than foreknowledge
english: From this, he goes on to say, it plainly follows that God by the decrees of his providence does not impose on us a necessity of willing this or that. Nor are God's decrees the causes why we produce this or that volition at this or that time.

So it does not follow from the infallibility of the divine decrees that all our free actions come about necessarily by a causal necessity. From that infallibility it follows only that our free actions come about necessarily by the necessity of consequence, which is neither causal nor motive.

Thus the decrees of God's providence will no more remove the freedom of our choice and the contingency of our actions than God's foreknowledge does. A thing will not come about because it is foreknown; likewise we shall not act in these or those ways because God decreed to concur with us in producing these or those actions. Rather, God decreed to concur in such actions because he foresaw that we would act so.

title: John Strang: decrees cover all acts, but not in the same way; evil acts are objects of a non-efficacious permission
english: The Scot John Strang, a few years ago one of the most celebrated men of his own side, reasons here in a way of his own. He grants that God's eternal decrees concern each and every human act, but not all in the same way.

First, evil acts, in his view, are objects of the divine decrees not because God decreed and predefined that they should be done, but because God decreed to permit them to be done, then to bring good out of them and order them to various ends. He denies, however, that this permission is efficacious, that is, such that once it is in place whatever is permitted follows necessarily.
translator_notes: John Strang (1584-1654), principal of the University of Glasgow; De voluntate et actionibus Dei circa peccatum (Amsterdam, 1657).

title: Strang: acts not evil in themselves are all decreed, some absolutely, some respectively
english: As for acts that are not by their nature joined to malice, he holds that all of them can be said to be decreed and predefined by God, but again not all in the same way. Some, on his view, God decreed absolutely, others respectively.

By 'absolutely' decreed and predefined he means those that God decreed before considering our will, indeed those to which he resolved to predetermine our will. By 'respectively' he means those that God decreed would come about according to our free choice, in matters where he grants us a free option, so that we may lawfully choose this or that.

title: In the first way God decreed all truly good acts and many indifferent ones (Cyrus, Pharaoh and Joseph)
english: In the first way, he judges, God decreed and predefined all truly good acts, those that of themselves contribute to man's eternal salvation. To these God resolved from eternity to predetermine our will efficaciously, just as in time he actually does predetermine it.

Besides men's good works, he also thinks there are many other acts of a kind to which malice does not necessarily cling, to which God predetermines men's wills in time. These were therefore decreed and predefined by God absolutely from eternity: for example, the heroic deeds of Cyrus, what Pharaoh king of Egypt did for Joseph, and countless things of the same kind.

title: Yet many acts not evil are left to free option, and are predefined only respectively, with regard to the will's determination
english: Even so, he thinks that for many acts which are not evil in themselves, men's wills are not absolutely predetermined by God in time; they are left a free option between two or more alternatives, all of them lawful.

Likewise he does not think that all acts of the will, even those without the character of sin, were absolutely predefined by God in his eternal decrees. They were predefined, in his phrase, only 'respectively': not before and apart from considering how the created will would determine itself, but with regard to that determination.

title: Strang's example: David's three options (2 Samuel 24); God decreed what David would choose
english: He offers an example, saying: the three things God left to David's choice in 2 Samuel 24 were all lawful options; David could rightly pick any of them, since God's leave here was moral and not merely physical.

God left him free to take whichever of the three he liked best, did not confine him to one, and so made no decree that he should choose only one. Yet because God knew in advance what David would choose and took that into account, one may rightly say that God simply decreed that pestilence should come and that seventy thousand men should be killed.

God decreed to carry out whatever David would choose; he had foreseen that David would choose this; so it was this that God decreed to carry out. (Strang, On the Will of God concerning Sin, book 3, chapter 2.)

title: His simile: a king who lets a servant choose a reward decrees to give whatever he chooses
english: In the same place he illustrates the point with a comparison from human life. 'If a king,' he says, 'gives his servant the option of choosing and asking for this reward or gift, or that one, or a third, he certainly has not decreed to restrict him to one of them. He has decreed to give him the particular reward or gift that the servant chooses or asks for.

This can be said of God much more. The king gave the servant the option perhaps without knowing, and uncertain, what he would choose. But to God, from whom nothing can be hidden, it was certain from eternity what David would choose.'

title: Strang: with the decree of permission joined to foreknowledge, God predefined each lawful act, foreknowing and decreeing in one instant
english: Toward the end of the chapter he explains the matter more precisely in these words. 'Whenever God leaves to the choice of the created will an election and option between two or more things, or between acting and not acting, we must not think that God restricts it to one side only.

But if we join to the decree of permission God's foreknowledge of the future event, it can be said that God predefined each lawful act that comes about. For he himself grants that freedom to the will, cooperates with it, and decreed the same from eternity.

This is not because God first foresaw the future event and then decreed that it would be; that would be absurd, to decree as future what he already foreknew to be future before the decree. Nor is it because God first decrees absolutely and then foreknows the thing as future. In that case he would not have permitted, or decreed to permit, the will's free choice to do and not do this and other things. It is because in one and the same instant he both foreknows and decrees, or predefines.

In eternity there is certainly nothing prior or posterior. Since foreknowledge and predefinition are both from eternity, neither comes before or after the other. In our way of conceiving we do distinguish different instants of reason in God's eternal acts. But even by instants of reason we do not call one of these prior or posterior to the other.'

title: Strang's two freedoms: the essential freedom of spontaneous rational motion survives absolute decrees; indifference does not
english: To reconcile the divine decrees with the freedom of the human will, he distinguishes two kinds of freedom of the will. One, taken more broadly and commonly, is essential to the will: it consists in the will's being moved by its own motion and by a definite judgement of reason. The other, taken in a stricter sense, he locates in a kind of indifference of the will toward two or more opposites.

He admits that the decrees of God by which acts of the will are absolutely predefined remove this second freedom, since they predetermine the will to one thing and no longer leave it indifferent to act or not act.

But on his view they do not deprive the will of the first freedom. It fits perfectly well that the will should follow the judgement of reason and be carried by a motion in keeping with its nature, and yet be predefined by God to act and predetermined in time. For God moves the will gently, in a way that suits and befits the will's nature.

title: Decrees of permission and respective decrees leave the will free in both senses
english: The decrees of God by which he permits evils to be done, or by which he predefined certain acts of the will not absolutely but only respectively, leave the will free, on his view, not only in the first and broader sense but also in the second and stricter one. Prior to the will's own determination they do not take from it the indifference to act or not act.

God's permission leaves the will in a state where it can do or not do what is permitted. And what God decreed respectively was not, as already said, predefined before and apart from considering how the will itself would determine itself. This is set out at greater length in Strang, book 2, chapter 8.

title: So for Strang, in conversion and works of grace man keeps only essential freedom, not indifference
english: On this man's teaching, then, in most of what he does in this life man enjoys the freedom that consists in the power to determine himself to either of two opposites. But with respect to many other acts that are absolutely predefined by God's decree he does not keep that freedom, only the freedom that consists in acting willingly and by the judgement of his own reason.

He thinks this holds above all in man's conversion to God and in the works of grace. 'Without God's predetermination,' he says, 'a man cannot be converted and cannot act piously; and once the predetermination of grace is in place, he cannot fail to be converted and cannot fail to act piously. So although we acknowledge that the freedom essential to the will remains in those works, we deny that freedom in the stricter sense has any place there.'

title: Moses Amyraut: all human acts, good, evil or indifferent, designated by decrees executed unfailingly, without violating freedom
english: Moses Amyraut, a man of renowned and most celebrated memory, also seems to follow a way of his own here. He holds that whatever men do, whether good, evil, or of the kind counted indifferent, is designated and predefined by God's eternal decrees.
Those decrees, he holds, are carried out with complete certainty and without fail, yet in such a way that human freedom is not violated and God is not made the author of sin.
translator_notes: Moise Amyraut (1596-1664), professor at Saumur; 'Inclytae memoriae' marks him as deceased.

title: Amyraut: the free faculties are determined by objects; the will follows the intellect, the intellect the object as proportioned
english: To explain how these things fit together, he assumes that man's free faculties, which on his view are the intellect and the will, are determined by their objects. He holds that the will necessarily follows the dictate of the intellect, and that a man cannot will otherwise than he judges ought to be willed.

Suppose an intellect affected and disposed in this or that way, and suppose this or that object is put before it in a certain light, that is, equipped and backed by these or those weighty reasons, so that there is a proportion and fit between such an object and the intellect as it then stands. Then the intellect must necessarily be determined to assent or dissent.
It must then pronounce this or that definite judgement about the object offered to it, as required by the proportion or fit assumed to hold between the intellect and the object.

title: Amyraut: this necessity does not harm freedom, which is not indifference; only physical force or the loss of deliberation does
english: Nor does he think that this necessity or determination, which on his view arises from the fit between object and faculty, hinders freedom at all, since he does not place freedom in the free faculty's indetermination, indifference and immunity from all necessity.

He thinks freedom conflicts only with the necessity that comes from external force, from matter or from sense, which we may call physical and brute necessity, or at least with the necessity that removes all consultation and deliberation.

title: Amyraut: providence executes the decrees by conserving the faculties and arranging the objects offered
english: Next, with respect to human actions in general, he locates the efficacy of God's providence, by which the divine decrees are carried out, in this: God preserves man's faculties and, in various and countless ways, either allows or arranges that various objects be offered to them or withdrawn.

From this the actions designated by God's decrees arise necessarily and infallibly. Yet they suit the nature and disposition of the free faculties and the condition of the objects put before them, and so they are free. No force is brought to bear on the faculties, and the offering and presenting of objects of any kind in no way violates their freedom.

title: For good actions Amyraut adds only the cleansing, strengthening and raising of the faculties
english: With respect to good actions in particular, beyond what has already been said, he ascribes to God only this: that he cleanses the faculties themselves of their inborn faults, or supplies them with new strength and raises them above their native, original condition.
Plainly such acts do not harm the faculties' freedom at all, but rather help it.

title: For evil actions God neither inclines nor corrupts, but arranges objects; the result follows necessarily yet freely
english: As for evil actions, however fully they are subject to the divine decrees, he thinks it can easily be shown from his principles that God can in no way be called their author. God does not incline men's minds and wills to evil or corrupt them in any way; he only allows them to put forth their own motions of their own accord.

Divine providence is involved with these actions only in arranging or permitting that these objects rather than others be offered to them, and in this way rather than that. From this, nevertheless, these or those actions necessarily result, as the relation of proportion and fit between such objects and faculties disposed in this or that way requires.

So the divine decrees about them are carried out without fail, and meanwhile the faculties themselves move freely, since no force is applied to them and they act only as their own nature and disposition lead.

title: Amyraut's conclusion: men act freely and yet inevitably accomplish what the decrees appointed
english: God, then, does nothing to men's faculties, whether they are carried toward good or toward evil, that conflicts with their native freedom. Yet upon God's working these or those acts, good or evil, follow infallibly, and God decreed things from eternity exactly as he carries them out in time.

From this Amyraut concludes that it fits perfectly well that men act freely and that, while acting freely, they inevitably accomplish what God's eternal decrees have appointed and designated. This is worked out more fully by that most learned man in his disputation on free choice, chapter 4.
translator_notes: Amyraut, disputation on free choice (De libero hominis arbitrio), ch. 4.

title: Many Reformed add physical and real premotion and predetermination of the faculties
english: To deal with this difficulty, however, a good number of theologians of the Reformed school take a somewhat different path. They teach not only that whatever men do is predefined by God's eternal decrees, but also that those decrees take effect by more than that most learned man holds.

They do not work only through some change in the free faculties, consisting in their restoration or the addition of new strength, together with the presenting of various objects from within and from without. They also work through a physical and real efficacy by which the faculties themselves are premoved and predetermined to these and those free acts.

title: Their teaching: all events, even free and contingent ones, are decreed by an absolute, energetic decree that cannot fail
english: Their teaching is this. By an absolute and, as they call it, 'energetic' decree of God, whatever is done even by free and contingent causes has been decreed and ordered. This decree can never fail, and what God has so decreed must without exception be fulfilled.
So the very things that contingent and free causes do are done necessarily with respect to this decree, and cannot turn out otherwise.

title: The decree covers good and evil actions; the energetic decree divided into effective and permissive
english: They further contend that not only the good actions of free causes but also the evil ones fall under a decree of this kind, since both are done by God's decree and will. They divide that absolute and energetic decree into an effective decree, by which God resolved to bring something about, and a permissive decree, by which God resolved to permit something.

Under God's effective decree they place not only the good actions of creatures but also the evil ones, considered in themselves, according to what is positive in them, and as distinguished from the malice that gives them their name. They think both kinds are done not only by God's decree but also by his stirring and moving the second causes, applying and determining them to do this or that.
The malice of free actions itself, however, they teach is not brought about by God but only permitted.

title: The permissive decree, though not effective, is efficacious; God wills that evil come about
english: Yet they hold that the decree by which God resolved to permit evil as such, though not effective, is nevertheless efficacious. That is why they ascribe everything that is done, good and evil alike, to God's decree which they call, with a Greek word, 'energetic', and which they then subdivide into effective and efficacious.

On their view, once God's permissive decree is in place, it is no less necessary that evil be done with God permitting it than, once his effective decree is in place, that good be done with God approving and bringing it about.

So they insist that it can and should truly be said not only that God wills to permit evil, but also that he wills evil to be done by his permission. The reason is that the divine will is directed not only to permitting evil but also to the actual outcome of the evil action.

title: Their defence: evil comes by God's decree but not his efficiency; the creature fails; the entity of the act is good
english: They deny, however, that this makes God the author of sin. Evil happens as God has decreed, yet God is not the one who works it: it comes from the creature falling short, under a definite permission of God.

And although what is positive in an evil action is traced to God as its efficient cause, God is not for that reason the cause of evil. The being of an action, however evil, is good, whereas malice formally consists in a certain lack of rectitude.

title: Objection that God authors what he wills; reply: to will a thing in itself differs from willing its outcome
english: If someone objects that God plainly appears to be the author of what he wills to be and to be done, since God's will is the cause of things, they reply that willing a thing for its own sake is one thing and willing a thing as to its outcome is another.
They add that God first and properly wills not to hinder sin, and wills the outcome of sin only as a consequence. For what God does not hinder comes about precisely because he does not hinder it.

title: Special and general will: by the general will God wills sin only because he wills it to come about
english: They also distinguish two wills in God, one general and the other special. The special will, for them, is that by which God both approves and brings about something. Its object depends on it and follows from it as an effect follows its cause. By this will, on their account, God wills what is good and is unwilling toward evil as evil, as in the verse, 'You are a God who does not will iniquity.'

The general will, on their view, is that by which God wills something not to be, and also, for definite reasons, wills not to forbid certain things and so wills them to come about, though he does not simply approve them. Or it is God's decree by which he wills something not as approving it or doing it himself, but only as a permitted doing by others.

And so, they say, the thing to be done depends not on God's will but only on the will of the failing creature. By this will, they say, God wills sin, the fall of Adam for example, not simply but only in that he wills it to come about.

title: Distinctions of necessity: absolute and hypothetical; of coaction and of infallibility
english: To reconcile the necessity that God's decree places on every event with the contingency and freedom of those events, they first distinguish absolute necessity from necessity on a hypothesis. Absolute necessity is that by which something simply cannot be otherwise. Necessity on a hypothesis is that by which something that in itself and simply can fail to be, or be otherwise, cannot be otherwise once a certain condition is given.

Next they divide necessity into the necessity of coercion and the necessity of mere infallibility. The necessity of coercion is that by which a cause acting from outside applies force to things and drives them by compulsion to do this or that.

The necessity of infallibility is that by which a thing is certainly and unchangeably going to happen, yet such that, if we look at the thing's cause in itself, it could fail to happen or happen otherwise. This is the necessity meant in the axiom, 'Everything that is, while it is, is necessarily.'

title: Free acts are necessary only on the decree's hypothesis and by infallibility; freedom and necessity do not clash
english: With these distinctions in place, they say that what free and contingent causes do does indeed come about necessarily with respect to the divine decree. But it does so not absolutely, only on the hypothesis of that decree; and the necessity is not one of coercion but only of infallibility, because God foreordained that these things should be done.
This kind of necessity, they say, does not remove the freedom of second causes but rather secures it, since it is not freedom and necessity that cancel each other out but freedom and coercion.

'For,' they say, 'God's decree makes it necessary not only that a contingent and free cause act, but also that it act contingently and freely. By his decree God determined not only each event but also its mode and manner.'

title: God moves free causes congruously; power to the opposite remains in the divided sense (Perkins, Twisse)
english: They add that God moves free causes in a way suited and agreeable to their nature: by gently bending the will and inclining it through objects shown to it by the intellect, and only in such a way that a man consults and deliberates with himself about what he will do, and chooses by his own judgement what seems to him the course to follow.

They say further that a free cause is so determined to do this or that by God's decree, and by the motion that follows the decree, that there still remains in it the power not to act and to act otherwise, not in the composite sense but in the divided sense.

For although the opposite act, or ceasing from that act, cannot stand together with God's preordination to this or that act, the power to the contrary act, or to suspending the act, stands with it perfectly well.

This is the teaching of William Perkins in his little book on the mode and order of predestination, of Twisse who defended him, and of many other very distinguished men among the Reformed. It can be seen at length in Twisse, throughout the second book of his defence of Perkins's little book.
translator_notes: William Perkins (1558-1602), De praedestinationis modo et ordine (Cambridge, 1598), answered by Arminius; William Twisse (c. 1578-1646), Vindiciae gratiae, potestatis, ac providentiae Dei (Amsterdam, 1632), a defence of Perkins against Arminius.

title: Le Blanc: none of these opinions satisfies; each labours under a notable difficulty
english: For all my respect for the talent and learning of all these doctors, I cannot rest in any of the opinions described. They do not remove every doubt, and every one of them seems to me to struggle with some serious difficulty.

title: Against the middle-knowledge view: hard to reconcile with victorious, efficacious grace taught by the orthodox School
english: Take first the opinion that sets before the divine decrees a conditional knowledge of how the will would lean and incline, one way or the other, if a given occasion for acting were offered it. It holds that God foreordained men's actions only in that he willed to create them in that state and offer them those occasions for acting.

From this he foresaw that, with his general concurrence, they would act in such a way and would produce these volitions rather than those. They would do so not by any necessity laid on them by the objects themselves or by some action of God, but because they would so determine themselves of their own accord, the contrary being in their power.

This opinion, I say, does avoid many of the awkward consequences that press on the others. But it can hardly be reconciled with the grace that conquers and is efficacious of itself, which brings free choice under itself and is by no means to be made subject to free choice, as the orthodox School proclaims.

title: Besides, God's absolute predefinition before the will's determination is foreseen brings an antecedent necessity
english: Add this. Suppose that before decreeing anything about us God foreknows what the will would do on the supposition that it is placed in such circumstances and such motives are brought to bear. Still, if God foreordains something as simply going to happen before the absolute determination of our will is foreseen, an antecedent necessity arises from it, since what God predefines must without fail come to be.
This necessity seems no less at odds with freedom than if no such conditional knowledge had gone before, since that knowledge does not put such a decree of God in our power.

title: Against Strang: no ground to grade deliberate acts as more or less free
english: In John Strang's opinion, what seems to me quite improbable is the difference he sets up, as regards freedom, among things men do on purpose and after deliberation. As he has it, only some acts are free with the freedom that lies in indifference, by which a man can act or not act, do this or that, while others are free only with a simple freedom that does not require the will's indetermination, only that a man act willingly and with judgement.

To this second class, he thinks, belong not only all good actions but also many that in their kind are neither good nor evil. Yet we find by experience that we use our reason, judgement and power of choice in the same way, not only in all the actions of civil life but also in good ones. Why, then, should we think that some acts are freer than others, and that the same kind of freedom does not belong to them all?

title: Nothing forces us to say grace removes the power to act otherwise; it can be efficacious without that
english: Besides, what forces us to say that when God moves us to good works he takes from us, by his grace, the power to act otherwise? Divine grace can have its efficacy without this.
Nor does divine wisdom lack ways to ensure that we do the good, and do it certainly and infallibly, even though it does not take from us the power to the opposite act, or even to suspend our act.

title: Against Amyraut: if objects necessitate rational powers as brute ones, freedom differs not from brute spontaneity
english: In Moses Amyraut's opinion, too, I am not satisfied with his assumption that in all their acts the mind and will are so determined by objects that, if these or those are set before them in a certain way and manner, they necessarily do this or that and cannot act otherwise or stop acting.

If rational powers, no less than brute ones, are determined to a given action by their objects, what difference will there be between the spontaneous motions of animals and the free actions of rational creatures?
And how can free agents be called masters of their acts and be said to have their own acts in their power, if objects impose a necessity of acting on them no less than on other agents?

title: Applied to Adam: if the objects God arranged necessitated his eating, where is his guilt, and how is God not author?
english: This is especially so if we suppose that a necessity of eating the forbidden fruit was laid on the first man through objects offered to him according to God's decree, with divine providence arranging and managing it. Suppose too that Adam could not refrain from it, given both the strength he had received from God and the incitements by which he was led to it.

Then I do not see what fault there was in him that deserved punishment, or how God is not the author of his sin. That unlawful eating would have followed necessarily from the match between the strength God had granted him and the temptations and various objects set before him, not by any fault of his but because God so ordained and arranged it.

title: Against the last view: God cannot be said to will what he does not approve; willing evil's existence is incoherent
english: Finally, in the last opinion, though it is held by many illustrious doctors, we cannot accept their saying that God wills evils to be done, even though he does not bring them about but only permits them. We do not think God can rightly be said to will what he does not approve, and it cannot be said that evils are done with God's approval.

Nor can we see the sense of the distinction they draw between evil and the outcome of evil, when they say that God does not will evil yet does will the outcome of evil; that God refuses evils themselves yet wills that evils should happen; or, what amounts to the same, that he wills the existence of evils.
How can the existence of a thing be distinguished from the thing itself? And how can anyone refuse something and at the same time will that it exist?
translator_notes: The print runs 'velle malorum existentiam quomodo potest enim' without a stop; the translation breaks the sentence before the question 'quomodo potest enim'.

title: Harder still: acts to which malice is necessarily joined, predefined by the effective decree, make God author
english: No less harsh is their claim that the very actions to which malice is necessarily attached were predefined by God's effective decree.

How will God not be the author of sin if by his eternal decree he predefined the act by which someone hates God himself and blasphemes his name, and in time, in line with his decree, premoves and predetermines the man to that kind of act?

title: The same absurdity from an efficacious decree of evil as evil: was Adam's rebellion necessary by God's decree?
english: The same absurdity seems plainly to follow from their saying that evil, even as evil, was foreordained by a decree of God which, though not effective, is nevertheless efficacious, such that once it is in place evil necessarily follows.

What then? Shall we say that God's decree made it necessary for the first man to rebel against God and break the command he had received from him? How could he justly be punished for sin if a necessity of sinning was laid on him without any prior fault?
And should not the guilt of that transgression rather be thrown back on him from whose decree so harsh a necessity is supposed to have arisen?

title: These men soften their phrases, but such harsh speech needlessly troubles the people; it is neither Scripture's nor the Fathers'
english: I know that the great men who use expressions of this kind do not admit these consequences, and bring their statements, as far as they can, to a sound and acceptable sense.

But however much such harsh expressions are softened by charitable interpretation, they cannot fail to offend the ears of Christian people and to plant various doubts in the minds of those who hear them, and that without any need. What need is there to cling tooth and nail to ways of speaking that are neither stated outright in Scripture nor used by the ancient doctors of the Church?

title: What Le Blanc holds certain: all things governed by providence; good from God, guilt the creature's; evil only as God permits
english: Someone will say: 'Why do you pick at other men's opinions? If you have something better, bring it out, or else take orders.' I answer that in this matter some things are certain and beyond doubt for me, while others I do not know.

It is clear from Scripture, and reason itself agrees, that all things are governed by God's providence and are so subject to the divine decrees that nothing happens without God's knowledge or against his will. Whatever is done well is to be credited to him as the author of all good things, while the guilt of all evils lies with the creature alone.

Yet nothing evil happens except so far as God, by a settled plan, allows it and does not hinder it. And God so governs men's evil actions, and uses them in such a way, that he draws many good things from them and directs them to various excellent ends.
translator_notes: Horace, Epistles 1.5.6 ('vel imperium fer'), proverbial for 'propose something better or accept the terms'.

title: Equally certain: men use their freedom, and are rightly praised or blamed, rewarded or punished
english: It is no less certain by reason and experience, and confirmed also by the authority of Scripture, that men use their freedom whether they act well or badly. They are moved so freely that they are rightly held to deserve praise or blame, punishment or reward, according as they have acted well or badly.

title: Hence both are to be held together; providence cannot be overstated so long as freedom is safe and God not made author of sin
english: It follows that human freedom must be acknowledged in a way that takes nothing away from divine providence, and that the power and efficacy of divine providence must be exalted in a way that still affirms the creature's freedom.

But provided the rational creature's freedom in acting is kept intact, and great care is taken not to shift the creature's guilt onto God, as if he were the cause or author of sin, one cannot ascribe too much to the decrees and efficacy of divine providence.

title: How God governs rational creatures so that they always act freely exceeds Le Blanc's grasp; he confesses ignorance
english: But to explain point by point the nature of the divine decrees, and how God so governs and moves rational creatures that they always act in keeping with their nature, that is, freely, is, I confess, beyond my understanding.

I do not doubt that divine wisdom and power, both of them infinite, have ample means of achieving this. But I do not think it lies within my small capacity to grasp them. In all I have been able to read or think out, I have found nothing that satisfied me on every side, nothing in which the mind could rest as in something found out and understood.
So I would rather frankly confess my ignorance on this point than boast that I know what I am aware I do not know, or press on others as true things whose truth I am not fully convinced of myself.

title: No shame in ignorance where Scripture is silent: it teaches that God rules all, not the mode
english: I am not ashamed of this ignorance of mine. It is safe not to know what God has not openly revealed in his word and what human reason cannot search out by itself.

Holy Scripture does plainly teach that all things are governed by divine providence, that nothing happens unless he deliberately allows it, and that all his works are known to God and settled from eternity.

But how God moves second causes, what the nature of his decrees is, how he carries them out and brings all things to their appointed end, Holy Scripture does not disclose, nor does it seek to satisfy human curiosity on the point.

title: Scripture rather shows it hidden: Isaiah 55:8-9 and Romans 11:33-34
english: Indeed, it shows clearly enough that this is something God willed to be hidden from human minds and closed to them, a depth our mind's sharpest sight cannot reach.

This is what God says in Isaiah: 'For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways. For as the heavens are high above the earth, so are my ways high above your ways and my thoughts above your thoughts.'

So too the Apostle in the letter to the Romans: 'O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgements, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?'
translator_notes: 'Investigabiles' follows the Vulgate of Romans 11:33, where it means 'unsearchable'.

title: Learned attempts are not condemned if modest and charitable; but keep such questions in the School, not before the people
english: Not that I therefore condemn the efforts of learned men who try to bring some light into this darkness and to test for themselves how high our mind can rise in so great a matter, provided it is done with proper modesty and a true and serious recognition of our weakness.

Let each put forward the conjectures and inventions of his own mind in such a way that he also listens to the reasoning of others. Let him not think he alone is wise, nor fight and quarrel bitterly and with hostility against those who will not at once submit to his pronouncements.

But such things, whatever they are worth, should be kept for the School. Difficulties should not lightly be raised among the people, for they plant doubts in men's minds that the obscure and weak solutions offered with them cannot clear away.

title: Rome and the Protestants agree in words that fallen free choice can do nothing without grace, yet speak differently of it
english: Our earlier theses established a verbal agreement, at any rate, between Rome's doctors and the Protestants: once nature has fallen, a man's free choice achieves nothing whatever apart from Christ's grace where true piety and the things that of themselves lead to eternal salvation are concerned.
But when they turn to fallen man's free choice as it stands toward saving, spiritual good, Rome's doctors and the Protestants use different language.

title: Rome: even before grace man has free choice in spiritual things, since aided he can embrace or reject the good
english: First, the theologians of the Roman School, however much they acknowledge that the help of divine grace is necessary for works of piety, still want it said that man has free choice in divine and spiritual things even before grace.

They do not mean that he can do anything of that kind without grace, but that, with the help of grace, he can freely embrace spiritual good, and in such a way that he has a real power to reject it and turn away from it.

title: Bellarmine states this as the common Roman teaching (De libero arbitrio 6.15 and 6.9)
english: Bellarmine sets this out, as the shared view of the entire Roman School, at many points in the sixth book of his treatise on free choice, above all in chapter 15. His first proposition there is: 'Prior to any grace, man possesses free choice not merely for natural and moral works but for works of piety and supernatural works too.'

What he means by this emerges from chapter 9 of that book, where the question is framed as follows: 'Since the first man's fall, does man really have free choice in matters of salvation? That is, granted he can do nothing without grace's help, once prevenient grace has stirred him and God assists him, can he act in such a way that he is also able not to act?'
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine SJ (1542-1621), Controversiae, De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 6, chapters 9 and 15.

title: Trent, Session 6, canon 4
english: Trent's sixth session, in its fourth canon, has the same aim. It runs: 'If anyone says that man's free choice, moved and roused by God, cooperates not at all by assenting to God who rouses and calls, whereby it disposes and prepares itself to obtain the grace of justification; that it cannot dissent if it wishes; but that like some lifeless thing it does nothing whatever and is merely passive: let him be anathema.'
translator_notes: Council of Trent, Session 6 (1547), Canons on Justification, canon 4.

title: Roman doctors differ on how grace is efficacious, but all agree it leaves the power to refuse
english: The doctors of the Roman School differ widely among themselves on how divine grace is efficacious. Some hold that grace not only gives free choice new strength, invites and urges man to do good, or even helps him in doing it, which all grant, but also that its efficacy is so great that it bends and determines the will to do good infallibly and irresistibly. Others deny this, as we have shown more fully elsewhere.
But all agree that, however great the efficacy of divine grace, it still does not take from free choice the power to reject the good to which it moves and draws a man.

So even those who maintain that grace is efficacious of itself and works the act of conversion in man infallibly still admit, in line with the canon of Trent, that man always keeps the power to dissent from grace and resist it. Thus all agree that free choice, once grace has gone before it and roused it, can do good in such a way that the contrary remains within its power.

title: Free choice not extinguished but weakened (Trent, Session 6, canon 5)
english: So they maintain that free choice, even with respect to saving good, was not extinguished and lost through sin, but only weakened, wounded and diminished. Here they follow the teaching of the Synod of Trent, whose canon on this point is the fifth of the sixth session:

'If anyone says that man's free choice was lost and extinguished after Adam's sin, or that it is a thing in name only, indeed a name without a reality, in short a fiction brought into the Church by Satan: let him be anathema.'
translator_notes: Council of Trent, Session 6, canon 5.

title: A remote and imperfect power for works of piety remains, but no proximate power (Bellarmine 5.15)
english: Their reason for calling free choice wounded and weakened rather than wholly lost and extinguished, even in spiritual matters, is this: after sin, and still prior to grace, there survives in man some remote, imperfect capacity for works of piety. What he lacks for such works is a complete, proximate capacity; so on that side he can accomplish nothing whatever by himself.

See Bellarmine on free choice, book 5, chapter 15. Proposition two there reads: 'Prior to any grace, man has a remote, imperfect capacity for doing works of piety.' Proposition three reads: 'Prior to any grace, man lacks a proximate, complete capacity for works of piety; hence by himself he can do absolutely nothing of that kind.'
translator_notes: The print gives 'libro quinto' here though III cites book 6, chapter 15 for the same propositions; kept as printed.

title: Bellarmine's meaning: no feeble good without grace, only a capacity that new strength makes able; his answer to Chemnitz
english: These words of Bellarmine, in which he says that man can do nothing at all of himself in what concerns salvation and piety, show in what sense he ascribes to the sinner who lacks God's grace an imperfect power for spiritual and saving good.

He does not think that without grace a man can achieve something of that kind, if only feebly and imperfectly. He means only that after sin there remains in man a certain power which, once it receives new strength through grace, can move freely toward spiritual good, though before, left to itself, it could do nothing at all about it.

Bellarmine himself makes this point in answering Chemnitz's dilemma: 'Either man has some strength of his own, however slight, or none at all. If he has some, then he can do something without God's grace; if none, then free choice is extinguished.' He replies that man has only a remote power and imperfect strength, and so can do nothing by himself; but if that power is perfected and strength is added, he can achieve a great deal.
translator_notes: Martin Chemnitz (1522-1586), Lutheran theologian, Examen Concilii Tridentini.

title: Freedom before grace is bound, like sight in the dark until the object appears
english: To show how man before grace has free choice even in spiritual things, though before grace he cannot do good, he says that in that state man's choice is indeed free in that respect, but its freedom is, as it were, bound and hindered. It is untied and released when the proximate power to act is given to it by God's prevenient grace.

He illustrates this: 'We find something like it in the power of sight. When the sensible image is absent, a man has the power and freedom to see, for that image is not the cause of the freedom or of the power of seeing. Yet the power is remote and the freedom bound until the image is received, the power is completed, and it can go out into act.'

title: Bellarmine denies that freed choice acts by strength it already had; he rejects Chemnitz's account (cap. 13)
english: It should also be noted that when Bellarmine says man's freedom regarding spiritual good was bound by sin, not extinguished, he does not mean that free choice, set loose by grace and consenting to good and pursuing it, does so by strength it already had and not by strength newly supplied by grace. That would be like a man whose chains are taken off: when he walks, he does so by strength he already had, which was not newly added to him, only its use held back by some hindrance.

In fact he complains that Chemnitz fraudulently and deceptively attributes something like this to the Catholic doctors. 'Chemnitz writes,' he says, 'that the Catholics hold that free choice, roused by grace, puts forth the strength it had even before it was roused, and by that strength of its own consents to God's call, so that prevenient grace does not give strength to free choice but only wakes it, as it were, from sleep.

The Catholics do not think this. They do acknowledge free choice in man even before divine grace goes before him, since free choice is a natural thing and is not lost through sin. But they do not say or think that free choice has any power, at least any proximate power, for acts of piety; it receives that from God through prevenient grace.' Chapter 13, answer to the first argument.
translator_notes: The print reads 'quatum usus' (page image); read 'quarum usus', which the relative clause requires.

title: Free choice of itself cannot cooperate in its conversion, but can receive the power, as a stone cannot
english: So Bellarmine teaches in the same place that a sinner's free choice does not have from itself the ability to cooperate in its own conversion, but receives the power to cooperate from grace.

'Just as a stone,' he says, 'does not have from itself the ability to cooperate if it should happen to be turned into flesh, so free choice does not have from itself the ability to cooperate in its own conversion. Yet it can receive from God, through prevenient grace, the power to act, which a stone cannot.'

title: Molina: consent to prevenient grace is wholly supernatural, yet free (Concordia, disp. 40)
english: This is the teaching of Luis de Molina himself. He holds that the consent our will gives to God calling it through prevenient grace comes from God not only as one who attracts, invites and rouses, but also as one who cooperates through the help of grace. So there is nothing in that consent that is not in fact supernatural, and in what is needed for justification the adult has nothing to boast of that he has not received from God through grace.

He reasons this way from earlier premises: 'Hence in the consent of free choice to God, who rouses and calls through prevenient grace, there is in fact nothing that is not supernatural and does not also come from God, not only as attracting, rousing and inviting our choice to it, but also as cooperating through the help of grace.

So the adult has nothing at all, among the things needed for justification and by which he is set apart from the unjustified, that he can boast of as though he had not received it from God; even though in many of the things needed for justification he freely cooperates and contributes, so that it is in his power not to cooperate or contribute, and so to prevent them from coming into existence.' Disputation 40, on article 3 of question 14.
translator_notes: Luis de Molina SJ (1535-1600), Concordia liberi arbitrii cum gratiae donis (1588), disputation 40, on Aquinas, Summa theologiae I, q. 14, a. 13.

title: Molina's double anathema: on those who make the consent natural, and on those who deny it free
english: So he at once pronounces anathema on those who affirm that the consent we give to God rousing us through prevenient grace is natural, or can be produced without the help and cooperation of that prevenient grace.

'In our judgement,' he says, 'anyone who affirms that the consent of our choice to God rousing and calling us through the help of prevenient grace is a natural act, or can be produced without the help and cooperation of that prevenient grace, must be held anathema. But anyone is also anathema who says that this consent is not within the free power of our choice, in the way explained, and that the free cooperation of our choice is not necessary for the supernatural acts by which we are disposed to grace and set apart from those who are not justified.'

title: Yet they confess the beginning of justification is from God alone, man merely passive (Angles)
english: The doctors of the Roman School, with the Council of Trent, hold that man's free choice cooperates with God as he calls and rouses it, and that the human will acts not only actively but freely in the first acts by which we turn to God, so that it can not only consent to grace that attracts and draws it but also dissent from it.

All the same, they concede that our justification and conversion start from God alone and not from our free choice, and that in this respect man is merely passive. This can be seen in Joseph Angles, Bishop of Bosa, whose conclusion reads: 'The beginning of our justification lies not in our free choice. It lies solely in God himself, while we are merely passive.'

He goes on to support it with a number of scriptural texts: 'You did not choose me'; 'Apart from me you can do nothing'; 'No one can come to me unless my Father draws him.' (Flores theologicarum quaestionum, on free choice, the single question, article 3, difficulty 7, conclusion 1.)
translator_notes: Josep Anglès OFM (d. 1588), Bishop of Bosa in Sardinia, Flores theologicarum quaestionum in secundum librum Sententiarum.

title: Angles's three kinds of works: antecedent, extreme, intermediate
english: To illustrate the point, in the same article he distinguishes three kinds of works bearing on our justification. Some works, he says, go before our justification, some are final, and some lie between.

To the first kind belong, on his account, predestination itself, the inward call through inspiration and the outward call through the preacher, the call through scourges, the fear of punishment, the desire for glory, and so on. To the second belong the infusions of supernatural qualities, such as the infusion of faith and of the grace that makes us pleasing to God, that is, justifying grace.
To the third belong the intermediate works, which follow the prevenient helps and come before justifying grace: acts of faith, hope, love and penitence that dispose us to grace.

title: The first two kinds are from God without us; in the third man acts freely with God
english: He teaches that these three kinds of works differ with respect to their efficient cause. Works of the first and second kind, such as the prevenient helps and habitual grace, are from God without us. So Peter and Paul were merely passive and contributed nothing when Christ called them, and so the air is passive when it receives light from the sun; in this way the infused virtues, which are supernatural qualities, are put on us while we do nothing.

But as for works of the third kind, the intermediate dispositions to grace, the man who is to be justified is not merely passive toward them but also active. In this respect he cooperates freely with God, as the will produces the act of penitence and of love, and the intellect produces the act of faith. Seventh difficulty, on article 7.

title: Jansenius: free choice remains, but freedom for true good is lost; the sinner can only sin
english: Jansenius does grant that after sin there remained in man the faculty called free choice, by which we will and act rightly or wrongly; which, just as it is now of itself inclined to evil, can also be bent to good by grace and embrace it freely.

Yet he maintains, following Augustine and the truth of the matter, that the freedom of choice with respect to true and saving good can rightly be said to have been destroyed and lost in man through sin. Sin has not stripped man of the freedom essential to the will, which is opposed to compulsion and to determination by nature. What perished entirely in man through sin is the freedom for good that is opposed to bondage, until man's will is set free by the grace of Christ the Saviour.

In his view, sin has made man such a slave of sin that whatever he does, he can no longer do anything but sin. He can indeed refrain from particular sins, but when he refrains from one he falls into another and trades sin for sin, not for true acts of virtue.

For his will, turned from God by a perverse affection and seeking its good in creatures, always and everywhere strays from the true end until God's grace lifts it up, and so whatever it does cannot be free of sin. This is set out at length by that author in his book on the grace of the first man, chapters 6 and 7, in On the State of Fallen Nature, book 2, likewise chapters 6 and 7, and in many other places.
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansen (Jansenius, 1585-1638), Bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (Louvain, 1640): De gratia primi hominis et angelorum; De statu naturae lapsae, book 2.
