title: Protestants: fallen man is not weakened but dead toward works of piety
english: The Protestants, both the theologians of the Augsburg Confession and those specifically called Reformed, teach by common consent that fallen man, before the grace of Christ, lacks all strength in what pertains to works of piety, which of themselves serve and are directed to salvation, and to the inward and spiritual acts of the Christian and theological virtues.

They do not think it enough to say that our free choice in this respect is faint, weakened, broken and diminished; they hold that it is entirely extinguished and lost. So man before grace must be compared not to a sick man or a captive but to a dead man, after the manner of Scripture, which often insists that men of themselves and without grace are dead in sins.
Hence they will not allow it to be said that man before grace has free choice for works of piety and supernatural works; they hold that to that extent he has been stripped of his freedom.

title: The Formula of Concord, Epitome article 2: as a corpse cannot revive itself
english: The doctors of the Reformed School repeat and press these and similar points everywhere, and so do the theologians of the Augsburg Confession already mentioned, especially in the book they call the Book of Concord.

'We believe,' they say, 'that just as a dead body cannot bring itself to life or restore bodily life to itself, so a man who is spiritually dead because of sin has no ability whatever to call himself back to spiritual life.'

So they condemn the errors of those who teach: 'Although unregenerate man, as to free choice, is before his regeneration too weak to begin his conversion, turn himself to God by his own strength and obey God's law with his whole heart, yet once the Holy Spirit has made a beginning by the preaching of the word and offered his grace to man in the word, man's will by its own natural strength can in some way contribute something, however small, weak and feeble, to help and cooperate in conversion, apply and prepare itself for grace, grasp it, embrace it and believe the Gospel.' Epitome of the articles in controversy among the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, article 2.
translator_notes: Formula of Concord (1577), Epitome, article 2 (Of Free Will), affirmative thesis 2 and negative thesis 4 (rejected errors).

title: The Solid Declaration condemns the synergists
english: The Book of Concord also contains the Solid Declaration, a fuller restatement of those articles, and there they condemn the synergists' doctrine. The synergists picture man in spiritual matters as not altogether dead to good, merely badly hurt and half dead.

They grant that free choice is too feeble to start, to turn itself to God by its own strength, or to obey God's law wholeheartedly. But once the Holy Spirit starts the work, summoning us by the Gospel and holding out his grace, forgiveness of sins and eternal salvation, free choice (they say) can go out to meet God with its own natural powers.

On this view it can contribute something to its own conversion, at least a little and weakly. It can assist and cooperate, ready and apply itself to grace, lay hold of it, embrace it and believe the Gospel. And as the work is continued and kept up, it can work alongside the Holy Spirit with its own powers. (Article 2, rejected errors, no. 4.)
translator_notes: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, article 2.

title: Lutherans with the Reformed: in conversion the will is purely passive
english: So the same doctors of the Augsburg Confession teach, with the Reformed, that in a man's conversion his will is purely passive: it does nothing but only receives into itself the motion and action of the Holy Spirit. Luther himself held this, among others, as the same doctors acknowledge in the place already cited.

title: Yet the sinner's omission of faith and love is free and punishable
english: The Protestants do not therefore deny that when a sinner fails to perform the acts of faith, hope and charity and the other virtues commanded him in the Gospel, the omission is free and so deserves penalty and punishment.

According to the Reformed, this is because man, though without grace, still knowingly and willingly leaves undone the acts God prescribes. No outside force or physical obstacle keeps him from performing them, only the perverse disposition of his own will, which does not remove his native freedom in acting.

To this may be added that, according to the doctors of the Augsburg Confession, the grace of God needed to do good is in some way available to all men, and God is ready to give it to each and every one if they do what lies in them.

title: Protestants grant the corrupt will is free from coercion and physical necessity, only not from bondage to sin
english: Again, although the Protestants deny that man in the state of sin has his freedom with respect to divine and spiritual acts, they grant that his will, however corrupted by sin, can be called free in various ways with respect to those acts.

On their view, the corruption brought in by sin does not prevent man's will, with respect to any acts whatever, from being free not only from outside force and compulsion but also from any physical necessity and brute determination.

They hold only that the will of corrupt man, until it is set free by God's grace, is not free from bondage to sin, that is, from the necessity of sinning that comes from vice; and so, regarding spiritual good, it lacks the freedom that is opposed to bondage.

title: Pareus: Bellarmine's question is slippery; which freedom does he mean?
english: David Pareus sets out the Protestant teaching this way. Taking up the question as Bellarmine frames it, 'whether man after the fall of the first man truly has free choice in the things that pertain to salvation', he calls the question slippery and sophistical.

'For,' he says, 'it is unclear what freedom of choice for divine actions he means: freedom from compulsion, from physical necessity, from brute determination, which we readily grant; or freedom from bondage to sin, that is, from the necessity of sinning that comes from vice, or from dependence on God's motion, which cannot be claimed for man in the state of sin without blasphemy.' On Bellarmine, book 6, On Grace and Free Choice, chapter 8.
translator_notes: David Pareus (1548-1622), Heidelberg professor, Castigationes in Bellarmini libros de gratia et libero arbitrio.

title: Placaeus: fallen man is free from three necessities but has lost the power not to sin
english: This agrees with what Josué de la Place teaches in his treatise on man's free choice, chapter 4, which deals with man's free choice in the state of sin. 'In Adam's descendants,' he says, 'there is a faculty of judging and willing that is free from a threefold necessity: from compulsion, such as our body can suffer; from determination by matter, chiefly as seen in stones and logs; and from sense, as belongs to brute animals. Because of this faculty man is a subject capable of either vice or virtue, and answerable to God's law.'

He then adds: 'What freedom of choice, then, did Adam lose? He lost the absolute power of not sinning that lay in original righteousness. This lay partly in the natural integrity of the moral faculties, their perfection and rectitude, free of any vice, disease, disorder or error; partly in the desire for the true last end and in the habits of good living that sprang from that desire, which by the order of nature would have grown little by little to the highest degree of perfection.

In place of this freedom came the bondage of sin, which lies in the corruption and crookedness of the moral faculties, especially the will. That corruption consists in turning away from the true last end and turning toward a last end that only falsely appears to be one.

Since whatever is desired is either the last end or a means to it, it follows that nothing sound is left in our moral faculties. And more than that: as long as we are in that condition, we cannot help sinning.'
translator_notes: Josué de la Place (Placaeus, c. 1596-1655), professor at Saumur; treatise De libero hominis arbitrio, chapter 4.
The print has the Greek 'δεκτικὸν' (receptive, capable) and 'ἀταξίᾳ' (disorder).

title: The Reformed distinguish proximate and active power from remote and passive power (Pareus)
english: A further point: on this question the Reformed doctors separate two kinds of capacity, the proximate and active kind and the remote and passive kind.

Man in the state of sin and before grace, they allow, keeps some remote, passive capacity for spiritual and supernatural acts; what they refuse him, so considered, is any proximate, active capacity for them. Pareus draws exactly this line when commenting on Bellarmine's sixth book on free choice, chapter 15.

title: The Leiden Synopsis, disputation on free choice, theses 18-19
english: The Leiden theologians use the same distinction in their Synopsis of Purer Theology. 'In the state of corruption,' they say, 'that is, in man begotten only by nature and bound by original sin, he has not lost the act of understanding in the intellect, nor the natural freedom of choice in the will; he has kept, with the substance of the soul, its natural faculties, which are the sources of actions, and the remote and passive power of receiving the contrary.

Yet he has lost rectitude and goodness from the intellect and likewise from the will, and has even acquired the contrary, vicious habit. So free choice, by its proximate and active power, at the prompting of the devil, under whose power and dominion it lies, no longer moves toward the good that is truly good but only toward evil, though under the appearance of good.

It still keeps a choice among the kinds and degrees of evil, and it moves necessarily as regards its proximate principle, yet spontaneously, voluntarily and willingly. For it chooses evil and rejects good.' Disputation on free choice, theses 18 and 19.
translator_notes: Synopsis purioris theologiae (Leiden, 1625), disputation 17 (De libero arbitrio), theses 18-19.

title: Alexander Morus: a remote and imperfect power means only the natural capacity of willing
english: Close to this is a passage in Alexander Morus, De Victoria Gratiae, disputation 3, thesis 15. He allows that man before grace may be said to have a remote and imperfect power for works of piety and supernatural works, so long as that phrase means the natural power of willing and refusing. That power gives man a proportion to such works and so a capacity for them, which you would not find in stones or in beasts.

His point is that man, however corrupted by sin, has natural faculties that God's grace can move to works of piety; beasts and lifeless things have no such faculties. Others mean the same by a passive and remote power: man is by nature able to receive the helps of divine grace, and through them his faculties take on new strength and move toward spiritual and saving works.
translator_notes: Alexander Morus (1616-1670), Reformed theologian at Geneva, Middelburg and Paris; De Victoria Gratiae (theses).

title: Placaeus: fallen man could not sin if he willed as he ought, so the power not to sin belongs to nature
english: Josué de la Place seems to go further, though in substance he arrives at the same place. However deep man's corruption, he teaches, man could avoid sin if he willed to, that is, if his will were set against sinning as it ought to be. So the ability not to sin, given a serious and proper willing, is to be credited to nature and not to grace.

He holds that even corrupt man has this ability: he can sin if he wishes, and he can also not sin, provided his will recoils from sin as it should. 'So,' he says, 'those who credit grace with the ability not to sin, on the condition that the will were rightly set against sinning, seem not to have weighed the nature of things well. It belongs rather to nature, which makes the notions of the involuntary and of sin conflict with each other.'
From this he concludes that it is useless to cite against us the scriptures that grant man the ability to do good if he wills, meaning if he wills as he should. Treatise on free choice, chapter 4.
translator_notes: Josué de la Place (Placaeus), De libero hominis arbitrio, chapter 4.

title: Placaeus distinguishes conditional and absolute power not to sin
english: To make his meaning plainer, that learned man separates a conditional from an absolute power of not sinning and of doing saving good.

The conditional power is the one by which a man is able to refrain from sin and do good if he wills, and on condition that he wills as he ought. The absolute power is the one by which a man simply is able to refrain from sin and to act well.

title: Absolute power divided into first (the natural faculty) and second (habits)
english: He divides this absolute power further into a first and a second. The first is simply the natural faculty that makes man able to act well or badly, something beasts do not have. The second absolute power of acting well consists in habits that determine or incline the natural power toward acting well.

title: The first power is the material principle of moral acts, the second the formal
english: In a moral action one can tell apart its matter or substance from its form, which is its moral goodness or badness. Accordingly he calls the first power the material principle of moral actions and the second the formal principle.
The bare act of willing comes from the will, the natural power by which we are able to act well or badly; willing well or willing badly comes from the habits that incline or determine the will.

title: In fallen man the first power remains, the second is lost and turned into its contrary
english: On these premises he holds that in us, corrupted by sin, the first power remains, the material principle of acting either well or badly. The second power, the formal principle of acting well, was lost through Adam's sin.

It was not merely lost but changed into the opposite power. So all our moral faculties carry a universal resistance to the one thing that finally is acting well according to God, and it is all the more stubborn because it is ingrained from birth and reinforced by constant habit, like a second nature.

title: Physical and moral inability (Placaeus); the demons cannot love God
english: Another distinction belongs here, used by Placaeus and many others with him: physical power or inability against moral. Physical inability to act well exists when the natural power of understanding and willing, without which nobody can act either well or badly, is absent or not in its own control.

Moral inability exists when mind and will are present and in their own control, but have been fixed by certain habits on acting badly. Placaeus also puts it another way. Physical inability lies outside the will: it is what keeps you from doing a thing however much you want and try. Moral inability lies in the will itself: you cannot do something because you do not want to, your will being fixed on the opposite by a firm and deep-rooted habit.

This is the inability we see in the demons with respect to loving God. They cannot love God, not for want of any natural faculty needed to love him, but because of their own free will they are entirely hardened in hatred of God.
translator_notes: The print reads 'impotentia moralis est quae posita est extra voluntatem' for the first member of Placaeus's restatement; the sense and the contrast with 'Impotentia vero moralis ... in ipsa voluntate' require 'Physica', read here.

title: Fallen man has physical power for works of piety but is morally unable without healing grace
english: These theologians teach that man, even corrupted by sin and lacking any inherent or subjective grace, has a physical or natural power for works of piety. He lacks no natural faculty needed to perform such works, and no physical obstacle keeps him from attending to them.

Yet morally he is wholly unable to do them, because his natural faculties, mind and will, are so hemmed in and obstructed by vicious habits that he can do nothing of this kind without grace that heals and sets free.

title: Morus rejects the distinction: man's inability is physical, better called voluntary and malign
english: Some of the Reformed, however, seem to reject this distinction, Alexander Morus among others. He judges that man's inability for good is physical and should be called so, since it is born in us and passes into us together with our nature.

Calling it moral is careless, in his view, because in ordinary speech 'morally impossible' means not what simply cannot be done but only what is extremely hard and happens scarcely, with difficulty and seldom.

On this question he would rather divide man's inability into two kinds. One is involuntary, brought in from outside, or arising from weakness; the other is inward and voluntary and arises from malice, not weakness. To the second kind he assigns the inability ascribed to man regarding saving good. De Victoria Gratiae, disputation 6, thesis 13.

title: Those who speak otherwise mean the same: a mere dispute about words
english: Those who use different language here do not hold a different view. They call man's inability regarding spiritual good moral because it is voluntary and comes from vice, not because they think that man can do or even attempt anything of this kind by himself, however hard, rare and difficult the attempt.

They readily grant that this inability is ingrained in man from birth. Their only reason for not calling it physical is that it does not come from the lack of some natural power or faculty but solely from that faculty's vicious and blameworthy corruption, which the others do not deny at all. Among the Reformed, then, this is purely a quarrel over words.

title: Passivity in conversion concerns only the first helps and new strength, not the acts of conversion
english: The Protestants commonly teach that man is merely passive in his first conversion. They do not mean that the first acts by which a man turns to God, beginning to hate and loathe sin, to love God and to believe and trust him, are not living acts produced by man's faculties and so coming actively from him.

They mean only that God's grace goes ahead of our will, and that our will is merely passive with respect to the first helps by which God begins to move it toward good, and with respect to the new strengths God pours into it freely. Without these it cannot begin or attempt anything good, nor even cooperate with divine grace.

title: Perkins: in the first conversion the will concurs with grace as a companion
english: Perkins takes care to make this point. 'We say,' he writes, 'that in the sinner's first conversion man's free choice concurs with grace in a certain way, as a partner and a co-worker. Three things are needed for conversion: the word, the Holy Spirit and man's will. Man's will is not simply and in every respect passive; it has some working of its own, even in the soul's first conversion.

When anyone is converted, God does it, but not by forcing an unwilling man; he so inclines his will that the man himself wills his own conversion. For when a man is being converted, he too wills his conversion, by the grace of God.'

A little later he adds: 'We must remember that even at the very first moment of conversion the working of the Holy Spirit's grace and man's will that desires it occur in man together. The difference is that the Spirit's working comes first in order and as cause, and moves and rouses the will; the will, once moved and roused to act by grace, then also moves itself and works.' The Reformed Catholic, controversy 1, chapter 1, conclusion 5.
translator_notes: William Perkins (1558-1602), A Reformed Catholike (1597), Latin as Catholicus Reformatus; controversy 1 (free will).

title: The Lutheran Epitome: Luther's 'purely passive' concerns the kindling of new motions
english: The teaching of the theologians of the Augsburg Confession comes to the same thing. 'Luther's statement,' they say, 'that man's will is purely passive in conversion must be taken in the right and proper sense: with respect to divine grace kindling new motions. It refers to the moment when God's Spirit, through the word heard or the use of the sacraments, takes hold of man's will and works conversion and regeneration in him.

Once the Holy Spirit has done and accomplished this, and has changed and renewed man's will by his divine power and working alone, then man's new will really is an instrument and organ of God the Holy Spirit: so that it not only lays hold of grace but also cooperates with the Holy Spirit in the works that follow.' Epitome of the articles in controversy among the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, article 2, on free choice.
translator_notes: Formula of Concord, Epitome, article 2, negative thesis on Luther's 'pure passive'.

title: The Solid Declaration explains Luther: conversion wholly the work of the Spirit, not without the word
english: They confirm the same afterwards in the Solid Declaration, a full and clear restatement of certain articles of the Augsburg Confession that had for a time been disputed among some theologians who adhered to it; like the Epitome before it, this is included in the Book of Concord.

'When Luther affirms,' they say, 'that man is purely passive in his conversion, that is, does nothing at all but only undergoes what God works in him, he certainly does not think conversion happens without the preaching and hearing of God's word. Nor did he want this taken as if in conversion the Holy Spirit stirred up no new motions in us at all and began no spiritual working in us.

What Luther meant is that man cannot contribute anything, or bring any help to his conversion, of himself or by his natural powers; and that man's conversion is not partly but entirely the working, gift and work of the Holy Spirit alone.'
translator_notes: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, article 2.

title: The Lutherans hold conversion resistible (the Rinteln-Marburg colloquy at Kassel)
english: Even so, the same theologians hold that man's conversion is free in such a way that a man can resist the Holy Spirit as he sets about the work of conversion in us, and can put an obstacle in his way; indeed sometimes a man actually does resist and obstruct. There is no efficacy of the Holy Spirit, on their view, that a man cannot by his stubbornness and defiance rob of its fruit and effect.

This is the drift of what the Rinteln theologians affirm in their colloquy with the Marburg theologians, held at Kassel by the authority of the Landgrave of Hesse. To the question 'Is the grace of conversion such that a man, by the strength of grace, can equally obey the Gospel and, through inborn malice, resist it and put an obstacle in its way?' they answered yes; the Marburg side said no.
translator_notes: The Kassel colloquy of 1661 between Lutheran theologians of Rinteln and Reformed theologians of Marburg, convened by Landgrave Wilhelm VI of Hesse-Kassel.

title: The Reformed: grace converts infallibly, yet conversion is a truly free work
english: The Reformed deny that the grace by which God turns men to himself is such that a man may sometimes block it and prevent its effect. They maintain that when God takes up the work of conversion it never happens that a man resists so as to stay unconverted, because divine grace is so powerful in the sinner that it brings about his conversion infallibly and irresistibly.

Yet they admit that this power does not stop man's conversion from being a truly free work, one that comes from the man not only actively but freely. The reason is that divine grace, however effective in itself, moves a man only in a way that suits and fits a rational and free creature.

It infallibly secures not just that the man acts and wills but that he acts and wills freely, so that in the good works to which grace moves him he acts from his own judgement, choice and deliberation no less than if he were acting without grace.

title: The Reformed admit a true power of not converting, alongside efficacious grace
english: They do maintain that once the grace by which God converts men is given, conversion cannot fail to follow, and that the motion and push of converting grace cannot coexist with a resistance of the human will strong enough to block the act of conversion.

Still they recognize that, together with the efficacy of grace, a power remains for the opposite act and for not performing the act grace drives a man to. A man who is converted infallibly still always keeps a real power not to turn himself and to produce the contrary act.

title: Ames on 'able to work and not to work': true in one sense, false in the other
english: Ames teaches this plainly in his Bellarminus Enervatus. Explaining the sense in which man, roused by prevenient grace and helped by God, can act in such a way that he can also not act, he notes that 'can act and not act' may be read in two ways.

In the first reading, the power not to act exists in the same subject at the same time as grace and the help needed for acting; this sense, he says, is entirely true. In the second reading, grace and the help given for a particular act, together with the absence of that act or the contrary act, sometimes exist or can exist in the same subject at once; this sense, he says, is false.
translator_notes: William Ames (1576-1633), Bellarminus Enervatus, tome 4, book 4 (De libero arbitrio).

title: Ames: free choice acts as 'principle which' in pious works, not as 'principle by which'
english: So when asked whether men act through free choice in works of piety, he answers as follows. If 'acting through free choice' means that free choice acts in those works as the principle that acts (principium quod), we accept it.

If it means that natural freedom is the principle by which (principium quo) a spiritual action is done, and does not receive both its ability and its willing from grace, we reject it as Pelagian. Book 4, on free choice, chapter 3, on the powers of free choice.

title: So Protestants do not deny a remote and imperfect power in man before grace
english: What has been set out so far shows that the Protestants do not deny that after sin and before grace man has a remote and imperfect power for works of piety and supernatural works.
By that name they mean the natural faculty of willing and refusing, which gives man a certain proportion to such works and capacity for them, of a kind found neither in stones nor in beasts.

title: The remaining power is free from coercion and physical necessity; many call it a physical power to do good
english: They also grant that the power left in man after sin is free with respect to those works, not only from compulsion but from all physical necessity and brute determination.

That is why many of them do not hesitate to say that man before grace has a physical power to do saving good and can do good if he wills, though he is morally unable to do it because his will is hardened in evil by perverse habits.

title: Free choice is the material principle of pious acts; freed by grace it cooperates even in first conversion
english: What has been said also makes clear that the Protestants recognize free choice, which survived in man after sin, as the principle that acts (principium quod), or as others put it the material principle, of pious and spiritual actions. Before grace, however, it lacks the freedom that is the principle by which (principium quo), the formal principle of those actions.

Once that freedom to act well has been regained through the helps of grace God supplies, free choice cooperates with divine grace, not only in the acts that follow a man's first conversion but in the very acts that make up that first conversion.

So the Protestants do not deny that all of man's good works, which must be credited to grace, come actively and freely from man's will as grace moves and rouses it. Nor do they deny that man uses his inborn and essential freedom both when, driven by his own malice, he leaves undone the acts the Gospel commands him, and when, with grace helping, he performs them.

title: Lutherans: man can and does hinder grace; Reformed: grace determines infallibly, yet in the divided sense he can dissent
english: We have shown just as clearly that the doctors of the Augsburg Confession ascribe to man a freedom by which he is able not only to hinder the effect of divine grace but often does hinder it in fact.

The Reformed teach instead that grace moves and determines man's free choice to act well infallibly and irresistibly, yet does not for that reason remove its real power to act otherwise and to stop acting. Given grace, then, a man cannot dissent from it in what the Schools call the composite sense, though he can in the divided sense.

title: Bellarmine's state of the controversy is falsely laid down
english: All this plainly shows that Bellarmine and other doctors of the Roman School argue against the Protestants to no purpose, as though the Protestants flatly denied that man cooperates with divine grace in his conversion, and that conversion itself is a free work that man performs freely as divine grace moves and rouses him.

It also shows that the state of the question Bellarmine sets up between all Protestants and the Roman Church is empty and falsely stated. His question is: 'After sin, does man have free choice in matters of salvation in such a way that, though he can do nothing without the help of grace, yet when roused by prevenient grace and helped by God he can act in such a way that he can also not act?'

title: No controversy between the two sides taken collectively; the divide runs through each school
english: Between the Protestants taken as a whole and the Roman School taken as a whole there is no dispute at all on this point, although within each school theologians argue over the sense in which man, once grace is given, can act and not act.

Many in the Roman School hold that, whatever helps of grace are given, man can act well and not act in such a way that this is true in the composite sense too, not only in the divided sense. In other words, there is no help of grace whose effect a man may not sometimes block by his defiance and frustrate. Many Protestants hold and profess the same: all the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, and also those called Remonstrants.

Those specifically called Reformed disagree with them here. Their doctrine is that every help of grace necessary and prerequisite for a man's actual conversion always takes effect, and that it infallibly overcomes all the defiance and resistance of the human heart.

In the same way the Roman School has not a few who agree with the Reformed on this point in substance and part company with the other Roman theologians. They teach that divine grace is so effective in itself that it determines the sinner's free choice to good unswervingly and irresistibly, though it does not take away his power to dissent and act otherwise. Among them are not only Jansenius and his disciples but also the so-called later Thomists, such as Diego Alvarez and William Estius.
translator_notes: Diego Álvarez OP (c. 1550-1635), De auxiliis divinae gratiae; Willem Hessels van Est (Estius, 1542-1613), Louvain commentator on the Sentences.

title: Rome too confesses free choice before grace a slave of sin, and the beginning of justification from God alone
english: Conversely, we have shown that the theologians of the Roman School admit with the Protestants that man's free choice before grace is so enslaved to sin that it can do nothing in the things that make up true and saving piety toward God.
They even admit that the very beginning of our justification and conversion comes from God alone and not from our free choice, and that in this respect man is merely passive.

title: Bellarmine and Molina ascribe cooperation not to nature but to new supernatural strength
english: What has been said makes it just as clear that the doctors of the Roman Church, Bellarmine and Molina himself among them, credit free choice's cooperation with grace not to the powers of nature but to the new powers our will has received through the help of grace.

They do not mean that free choice, when it consents to grace and follows its lead, does so by powers it already had, whose use was merely blocked until grace set it loose; Bellarmine complains that this is falsely charged against his side. They mean it does so by powers God has added to it beyond nature, so that the consent man's will gives to grace as it calls and rouses is a supernatural work, not a natural one.

title: Perkins's state of the controversy is also mistaken
english: We must therefore admit that the state of the question between the Protestants and the Roman Church is not the one Perkins sets out here: whether man's will has a natural power to cooperate with divine grace in spiritual things. He says the doctors of the Roman Church affirm this and ours deny it, because on our view the will has its cooperation from grace, and on the Roman doctors' view from itself.

'They say,' he writes, 'that man's will concurs and cooperates with God's grace in the sinner's first conversion by itself and by some natural power of its own, and is only helped by the Holy Spirit. We say that man's will does cooperate with grace in the first conversion, but not as moved by itself; it is moved by grace, which must first move and lift it up before it can move itself or will anything well.'

What we reported above makes clear that Perkins is mistaken here, since the doctors of the Roman School teach expressly that the human will cooperates with grace not by its own powers but by those grace has newly supplied to it. The Reformed Catholic, controversy 1, chapter 2.

title: Objection: what then is disputed? Answer: on this precise question, words
english: 'Then what,' you will ask, 'is the dispute between the Protestants and the Roman School, when the latter affirms that man before grace has freedom of choice not only for natural and moral works but also for works of piety and supernatural works, and the former deny it?'
My answer: many doctors of the Roman Church do give free choice too much in various ways, as we showed in earlier disputations. But on this precise question the quarrel seems to be over words.

title: What each side means by affirming or denying freedom before grace
english: When the Protestants deny that man before grace has his freedom with respect to spiritual and supernatural works, they do not mean to deny that man before grace has the freedom essential to the will, opposed to physical necessity and brute determination, even regarding spiritual and supernatural things.

So they allow that man in that state leaves undone freely the supernatural acts the Gospel commands; and that when grace moves him he performs those acts freely and has a real power to act one way or the other, at least in the divided sense. All they mean is that man in that state is not free from bondage to sin or from dependence on God's motion through supernatural help, and that without such help he can do nothing whatever in the matter of salvation.

When the Roman School, for its part, affirms that man before grace is free in spiritual things and things of piety, it does not mean to deny that man before grace is a slave of sin and can do nothing at all without grace in the things that make up true piety toward God. It means only that man is by nature so made, and so endowed with that essential freedom, that with grace helping he moves freely toward good and always has a real power to do it or not do it.

title: Likewise 'extinguished' and 'wounded' mean the same in substance
english: In the same way, when the Protestants say that man's free choice was extinguished and lost through sin, not simply wounded and weakened, with respect to saving and spiritual good, they mean only that after sin no strength is left in man by which he could move toward good of himself. Whatever he is able to do and does in the matter of eternal salvation must not be credited in any part to free choice's own powers, but only to those Christ's grace has newly supplied.

When the theologians of the Roman School, on the other side, contend that man's free choice is not wholly lost but only taken captive, bound and wounded, even in what furthers man's eternal salvation, they do not mean that a sinner's free choice can do anything in pious and saving works without grace, even with difficulty and effort.

They do not even mean to teach that man, roused and helped by grace and as it were freed from chains, cooperates with grace by his own powers rather than by the new powers grace adds. Their meaning is only this: man's natural freedom was lost through sin with respect to no object at all. What happened is that his mind and will are obstructed by perverse qualities sin brought in, so that they do not move toward true and saving good as they should.

On this view those faculties need not be given to us afresh, nor a new free choice created in us. Mind and will need only to be healed of the wounds of sin and helped by grace with new strength added, so that we can act well.

title: Reformed doctrine does not differ: the dispute is about words, not the thing
english: The Reformed doctrine set out above is not far from this. On it, all the physical powers needed for acting well, which are simply free choice considered absolutely, remained in man after sin.

Sin brought in only a moral inability, consisting entirely in perverse habits that so besiege mind and will that they can neither know nor love saving good, nor move themselves the least step toward it, until Christ's grace sets them free from those habits.

All this makes plain that the Protestants contradict the Roman School in words but do not in fact deny what the Roman School means to affirm. As we have already said, the dispute here is not about the thing itself but about words.
translator_notes: The print reads 'abladit'; read 'abludit'.

title: Even in the Roman School the Protestant way of speaking is owned as Augustinian
english: Yet the Protestant way of speaking, when they say that through sin man lost freedom of choice for true and saving good, is not rejected everywhere in the Roman School: famous and learned men there recognize that it is taken from Augustine and agrees with the language of Scripture and the ancient Church. Jansenius and his disciples admit this honestly, as we showed above.

title: Two senses of moral good
english: On the necessity of grace and the strength of free choice in human nature corrupted by sin, with respect to moral good, opinions in the Roman School vary widely. To understand this variety we must note that the Schools use 'moral good' sometimes in a wider and sometimes in a stricter sense.

In the wider sense, moral good is everything that depends on will and reason and shapes them both in such a way that a man is owed praise or reward for it and can be called good without qualification. So that good lies entirely in virtue and in acts done according to virtue, whether the virtue is acquired or infused, natural or supernatural.

title: Moral evil, and physical good contrasted with moral good
english: Its opposite is the evil that deserves punishment and blame. This is usually called the evil of fault, and it includes all vices and sins.

Set against this good is the good called physical, or the good of nature. It does not depend on our will, and it perfects our nature without earning us any praise or reward; it does not make us good without qualification.

title: What physical good includes
english: Physical good includes nature itself and its faculties, and every advantage and gift that perfects nature apart from the character of virtue, of whatever kind, whether it springs from natural principles or is granted by God above nature.
So this good is called physical, or the good of nature, not to set it against supernatural good, but only to set it against moral good as just described.

title: The stricter Roman sense of moral good: the natural law kept without rising above nature
english: Protestants often use 'moral good' in this sense, as can be seen above all in the Saumur theses. In this dispute, however, the theologians of the Roman School take it a little more strictly. They set moral good not only against the good of nature, or physical good, but also against supernatural good.

So they do not include under moral good the theological or infused virtues and the acts that flow from them, which belong to the supernatural order. They include only what agrees with right reason and the law of nature without rising above nature. On their view the whole of that good consists in keeping the law written by nature on the human heart, which God summed up in the Decalogue and which is nothing other than the dictate of right reason.
translator_notes: The Saumur theses: the Theses theologicae disputed in the Reformed academy of Saumur (Amyraut, Cappel, La Place), published as Syntagma thesium theologicarum in Academia Salmuriensi variis temporibus disputatarum (1641; 2nd ed. 1664-65).

title: Two ways of keeping the precepts: as to the substance of the work, and as ordered to salvation
english: The precepts of that law can be kept in two ways: first, only as to the substance of the works; second, in the manner by which they are ordered to eternal salvation and the blessedness promised to us.

A man keeps a precept as to the substance of the work when he freely refrains from what a precept forbids, such as theft or murder, or freely does what the law commands, such as honouring a parent, caring for his own family, or helping the needy from his own means.

For such works to profit us toward eternal salvation, more is needed: they must be done out of charity, from the love of God that the Gospel commends, and directed to God's glory. So to keep the precepts in this second way is not only to do the work the law commands, outward or inward, but also to do it out of charity.

title: A precept kept as to substance can still be sin; or it can have a natural moral honesty
english: The doctors of the Roman Church further observe that those who keep the precepts as to the substance of the works, but not out of charity, still fall into two classes.

'A precept of the law,' they say, 'can be kept as to the substance of the work and still be kept with sin, so that the act should not be counted praiseworthy or honourable. This happens when someone acts from a corrupt desire and for a bad end: for instance, if he returns a deposit to a friend or gives something to the needy, but to please a harlot and serve an unchaste passion.

But a man who is not moved by the love of God can still keep a precept as to the substance of the work, not from corrupt desire but from a natural affection that is not evil, and without aiming at a bad end, because he thinks it his duty and agreeable to reason. Then he commits no new sin in doing it, and the work he does has a certain moral honesty.' The good the Schoolmen call moral consists in keeping the commandments in this way, and they set it against both natural and supernatural good.

title: All agree: no keeping of the precepts in the way ordered to salvation without special grace
english: The doctors of the Roman Church agree that without the help of special grace no one can keep God's precepts, wholly or in part, in the way that orders them to life and eternal salvation. That is, no one can keep them so that the keeping of itself advances his salvation and merits grace or glory for him.

title: All agree: no grace is needed to keep some precepts as to substance with a vicious motive
english: None of them denies, either, that some precepts can be kept as to the substance of the work without grace, but only so that the act is not morally good and honourable, being spoiled by a bad end and corrupt desire. That is obvious in itself.

title: The question in dispute: can the precepts be kept without special grace so that the act is morally good?
english: The question among them is this: can God's precepts be kept without special grace, by the general help alone, in such a way that, although the act is not done out of charity and does not merit eternal life, sin is still avoided and the act is morally good and honourable? On this their opinions differ widely.

title: First opinion: Durandus, all the natural precepts can be kept without grace
english: First, many of the older Schoolmen maintain that man in the state of corrupt nature can, by his own strength and without the help of special grace, keep each and every precept of the law of nature as to the substance of the works, and so achieve the whole of what they call moral good.

This is the view of Durandus on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 28, question 4. There he affirms, and tries to prove with several arguments, that a man without grace can fulfil God's precepts, those of natural law though not those of supernatural law. So he grants that someone might, without grace, be free of every sin of omission and of commission, though original sin would remain in him and would shut him out of salvation.
translator_notes: Durandus of Saint-Pourçain OP (c. 1275-1334), In Petri Lombardi Sententias commentarium, book 2, distinction 28, question 4.

title: Durandus answers his own objection: without grace a man would be damned for original sin alone
english: He first argues against his own view: 'No one is damned except for a sin of commission or omission. Whoever fulfils the precepts of the law omits nothing, and whoever avoids all evil commits nothing. So if man could fulfil the precepts without grace, he could avoid sin without grace, and so avoid damnation without grace. But whoever is not damned is in glory. So a man without grace could be in glory.'
His answer is that, even without any sin of omission or commission, man would be damned for original sin alone unless grace set him free.

title: Vázquez says Durandus meant only habitual grace
english: Vázquez does maintain that Durandus is speaking there not of any grace at all but only of habitual and justifying grace. He does not think any Catholic doctor has taught that man can resist every temptation against natural law, and so keep the whole natural law, not only for a short time but for a long time too, without any help of grace through Christ.

When Durandus and the other older Schoolmen debate the overcoming of temptations and the keeping of the natural precepts, and ask whether a man can overcome all temptations and keep all the precepts without grace, by 'grace' they mean, he says, not the help of moving grace but habitual grace, by which we are righteous. On the Prima Secundae, vol. 2, disputation 189, chapter 2.
translator_notes: Gabriel Vázquez SJ (1549-1604), Commentariorum ac disputationum in Primam Secundae S. Thomae tomus secundus (1606), disputations 189-191 on the necessity of grace for moral good.

title: Le Blanc: Vázquez is wrong; Durandus meant no grace through Christ at all
english: Anyone who reads Durandus carefully can see that Vázquez is wrong here. Durandus means that man, by the strength of nature and without any help of grace through Christ, can fulfil God's precepts. He proves his view with this argument: 'What man does naturally he can do of himself without grace. But the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things of the law, as Romans 2 says. So the precepts of the law can be fulfilled without grace.'

So for Durandus to act without grace is the same as to act naturally and of oneself. But a man who does something through some help of grace from Christ cannot be said to do it naturally and of himself, even if he lacks habitual and justifying grace.

Besides, in question 2 of the same distinction Durandus raises against himself Christ's words, 'Without me you can do nothing.' He replies that they must be understood of God's general influence, by which he keeps the principles of things in being, and without which nothing would exist or happen.

title: Scotus and Biel follow Durandus; the view now rejected as Pelagian
english: Scotus and Gabriel Biel took the same view as Durandus. With him they hold that man, even corrupted by sin, can by his own strength and without grace keep all the moral precepts, the precepts of the law of nature, as to the substance of the works, though not as ordered to the supernatural end. So Estius reports on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 26, paragraph 40, proposition 8.
But the Roman School today commonly rejects this view, and in Estius's judgement it plainly leans toward the heresy of Pelagius and is contrary to the Catholic faith.
translator_notes: John Duns Scotus OFM (c. 1266-1308); Gabriel Biel (c. 1420-1495), Collectorium on the Sentences. Willem Hessels van Est (Estius, 1542-1613), In quatuor libros Sententiarum commentaria, book 2, distinction 26, §40.

title: Second opinion: Tapper, each precept one by one but not all together
english: Some in the Roman School, in the past and still today, admit that man in his present state cannot keep all the precepts and overcome every temptation taken all together, or, as they say, collectively. Yet they hold that, one by one and without any help of grace through Christ, he can keep any natural precept, however hard, and overcome any temptation, however strong.

In chapter 2 of the disputation just cited, Vázquez ascribes this view to Ruard Tapper, the Louvain theologian, on the seventh article of the Academy of Louvain, at the paragraph 'Haec confirmantur'. And there that doctor does say of works that by their kind do not exceed the strength of our nature, as is true of everything the natural law commands, that each of them is in our power, weak and without grace though we are.

'There is no one,' he says, 'who cannot refuse, and even avoid, murder or any other sin, even venial. No passion and no fear of death can make it necessary to follow it in such a way that willing and refusing do not stay in our power, so long as reason is not overwhelmed and its judgement stays free.' He adds at once: 'So the necessity of sinning that comes from our weakness is set against inevitability as to all sins together, not as to each; nor is it a necessity of committing any particular sin.'
Vázquez reports, in the disputation cited above, chapter 2, that some more recent writers of his time held the same view, and adds that twenty years earlier it was quite common in Spain.
translator_notes: Ruard Tapper (1487-1559), dean of Louvain, Explicatio articulorum venerandae facultatis sacrae theologiae generalis studii Lovaniensis (1555-57), article 7.
'Collective / sigillatim': the Schools' distinction between all the precepts or temptations taken together and any one taken singly.

Tapper's 'opponitur inevitabilitati quoad universa, non quoad singula' is rendered literally ('is set against inevitability'); his argument shows the sense: the necessity of sinning that comes from weakness holds for all sins taken together, not for each one taken singly.

title: Third and commonest opinion: no precept kept without special grace under grave temptation, but easier works can be
english: Far more common in the Roman School is a third view. It holds that man in the state of corruption cannot, without the special help of divine grace, keep the precepts of the natural law, either all together or even one by one, because some of them exceed the strength of corrupt nature: such as the precept against coveting, and the command to love God as the author of nature with all our heart. Those who hold this view admit that under grave temptation no commandment of the moral law can be fulfilled and no moral good achieved.

But when no grave temptation arises, they maintain that with God's general concurrence alone, without any particular help of grace, the easier works of the moral law can be kept as to the substance of the work in such a way that every new sin is avoided.

For example, a man not moved beforehand by any inward grace from God can honour his parents, help the needy, answer truthfully when asked, and return a deposit to a friend. He does it not from corrupt desire, for then the acts would be vicious, but from a natural inclination that is not evil; and not for a bad end, but simply because he judges it reasonable and part of his duty. On that basis they hold that such an act contains no sin and is truly morally good and honourable, though it does nothing for eternal salvation and merits neither grace nor glory in any way.

title: Bellarmine and Estius: all the precepts kept for a short time without grace
english: Bellarmine and Estius, with very many others, defend and explain this view at length. They admit that some of the harder precepts of the moral law cannot be kept without grace. Yet they grant that man in the state of corrupt nature can, for a short time, keep without grace all the precepts of the law of nature that fall to be kept in that time.

Their reason is this: the affirmative precepts do not bind at every moment, and they do not all arise to be fulfilled at once; and the negative precepts, such as 'You shall not kill', are kept even by doing nothing. For a time, then, a man can hold back with respect to such precepts, if no temptation to the contrary arises. See Estius on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 26, paragraph 40.

title: Bellarmine's explanation: not for a longer time
english: Bellarmine says much the same. Explaining in what sense he had denied that all the moral precepts can be kept as to the substance of the work by the strength of nature alone, he writes: 'We do not mean that no one can keep them all for a very short time. It can happen that for a while no affirmative precept arises and no temptation urges us to break the negative ones.

So the sense of the proposition is that over any longer time, in which various precepts present themselves to be kept, they cannot all be fulfilled by the strength of nature alone in such a way that sin is wholly avoided.' De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 5, chapter 5.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine SJ (1542-1621), De gratia et libero arbitrio (Controversiae, vol. 4), book 5, chapter 5.

title: Fourth opinion: Vázquez and Alfonso de Castro, no wholly good moral work without grace
english: Yet not a few in the Roman School affirm that no moral work good in every circumstance can be done without the help of grace. This is Gabriel Vázquez's view on the Prima Secundae, vol. 2, disputation 190. There he cites very many Schoolmen, older and more recent, on his side.

Among them is Alfonso de Castro, who lays down as Catholic the assertion: 'Man's free choice, by its own power alone, even with God's common and general co-causation added, cannot do any good without some special help from God. For every such good is always preceded by some warning, drawing, inspiration, or some gift added over and above nature, which God himself gives purely as a gift to whom he pleases.' Adversus haereses, book 7, under 'Grace', heresy 1, assertion 3.
translator_notes: Alfonso de Castro OFM (1495-1558), Adversus omnes haereses (1534), book 7, s.v. 'Gratia', heresy 1.

title: John Fisher: the Fathers against the Schoolmen
english: John Fisher, bishop of Rochester in England, teaches the same. 'I have preferred,' he says, 'to follow the Fathers rather than the Schoolmen, since on this matter they contradict each other. The Fathers assert that no one can will anything good without God's special help, and that the general influence is not enough.

Some Schoolmen, on the other hand, contend that it is enough: that without that help a man can act morally well and do good, not only good in kind but also good furnished on every side with the proper circumstances.' Against Luther, article 36, at the paragraph 'Neutrum sane potest'.
translator_notes: John Fisher (1469-1535), bishop of Rochester, Assertionis Lutheranae confutatio (1523), article 36 (on free choice after sin).

title: On this view every act without grace is flawed; Vázquez states the precise question
english: On these doctors' view, then, man in the state of sin can do nothing without God's grace that is truly a work of virtue and deserves to be called good and honourable without qualification. In that state, whatever works a man does, however fine and outwardly honourable they look, are made vicious by the lack of some circumstance and take on something of the character of sin.

What grace is needed for corrupt man to act well and give true obedience to the moral law, Vázquez explains carefully in the disputation just cited. At the start of chapter 1 he points out that the question is not whether habitual grace, the grace that makes acceptable and justifies, which he places in charity, is needed for acting well by the moral law. Nor is it whether all the works of a man in sin are sins, nor even whether faith is needed to act well; it is only whether man can act virtuously without some help of grace.

'In this controversy,' he says, 'our question will not be whether an unbeliever can do some good things. We will not dispute whether some good can be done without charity, or whether all the works of a man in sin are sins or he can do some good ones. The controversy now is whether man can do any good work according to virtue without the help of God's grace; and that is a very different question.'

title: Vázquez: neither charity nor faith is needed for a morally good work, only some help of grace
english: So he grants that neither the charity the Holy Spirit pours into the hearts of believers nor faith itself is needed for someone to act well and give true obedience to the moral and natural law. A morally good work can come from a man who is not only lying in sin but is still an unbeliever.
The one thing he denies is that a sinner, without any help of divine grace at all, can act well, even by the standard of natural virtue and honesty.

title: Vázquez's two helps of grace through Christ: supernatural and natural
english: What that necessary grace is, he explains more fully in chapter 12 of the same disputation. There he distinguishes two helps of grace through Christ: one supernatural by its own nature, the other natural. He does not think the first is needed for any work of moral virtue; only the second is, which belongs to the natural order.

His view is that man can do particular works of moral virtue without the help of grace through Christ that is supernatural by nature, the kind needed for the works of the infused virtues. But he cannot do any moral work that is virtuous and good in every respect without some help of grace through Christ that is natural by nature and is prepared for us through natural causes by God's eternal mercy.

title: That natural help consists in a good thought God sends us
english: Although on his view this help belongs to the natural order, he affirms that it is distinct from the gift of creation and from the common influence by which God concurs with all natural causes. He places it chiefly in a holy thought by which, he holds, God must go before us for each good work. He proves that grace is needed for each good work from the thought prepared for us beforehand for each one.

'Although we have free choice,' he says, 'and our will moves freely either way, it cannot be moved at all without a thought, and something outside it must bring it to this first thought rather than the opposite one. So whenever it is stirred to good by a thought, when it might not have been, it receives from God a particular grace distinct from the grace and gift of creation.

Since God was free not to bring us to this or that good thought, he does us a particular kindness in it, whether he applies it directly himself or through other outside causes. However it happens, it must finally be traced to God, because divine providence and foreknowledge so order all the causes that stir this thought that contrary causes could have been ordered, or these arranged otherwise.' So he traces to this good thought, prepared for us by God's free will, the particular grace of God by which we do all good works, moral ones included.

title: Good thoughts before faith; how a natural help is 'somehow above nature'
english: So that doctor holds that not every holy thought either is faith itself or begins after faith or from it. He maintains that God inspires holy thoughts in men through natural causes even before they believe and come to faith.

Yet he notes that this kind of help, though it belongs to the natural order, since it consists in good thoughts that do not go beyond the light of nature, can be called in a sense above our nature. It is above our own effort and care: God prepared and granted us such a thought without them, when he could have sent us the opposite one.

It can also be called so because the helps he gives us for living rightly in any kind of virtue, and for overcoming temptations and desires, are given us by God with our blessedness in view, which is our supernatural end. Vol. 2 on the Prima Secundae, disputation 189, chapter 16.

title: Why Vázquez calls this natural help grace of Christ
english: That is why he contends that this help, needed for any good moral work, belongs to the grace of Christ, even though in substance it is of the natural order. Morally good works done through such help, even by unbelievers, in some way dispose men to justification and so to eternal salvation, and they serve to obtain justifying grace.

'Christ died,' he says, 'that the ungodly might be justified, and also that they might live rightly. For by good works and an upright life, even in moral virtue, we obtain from God the spirit of compunction and of justification.' By this reasoning he thinks it sufficiently shown that this help of grace, distinct from the gift of creation and required for each good moral work, comes through Christ. Disputation 190 already cited, chapter 12.

title: With most of the Roman School, Vázquez holds such grace can be given to those without faith
english: So although that doctor thinks some help of the grace of Christ is needed for anyone to act morally well, he holds with by far the largest part of the Roman School that this grace can be given to someone who has no faith. By 'faith' he means not only true faith in Christ but any knowledge at all of the one true God, which can be found not only in heretics but also in many unbelievers and pagans.

His view is that among every kind of unbeliever, even pagans who do not know the one true God, there can be, and sometimes are, works of the moral virtues, though this happens rarely. Disputation 191, chapter 2.

title: Estius: some acts of pagans are not sins but imperfectly good
english: Estius takes this view on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 41, paragraph 3. He asserts there that some actions of unbelievers are not only not sins but are morally good, though imperfectly. He notes that by 'unbeliever' he does not mean a Jew or a heretic, even though such a person in truth has no faith, since faith is the name of a whole virtue. He means a pagan or heathen, who has no knowledge even of the one God to whom he might refer his actions.

He thinks such an unbeliever sometimes acts from a natural affection that of itself tends toward good, and directs some actions not to a bad end but to the good and to the last end, known in general and vaguely. In his judgement that is enough for them not to have the character of sin.

The righteous in this life do not refer all their actions to God, whom they hold as their last end; they do not so refer those in which they stumble daily. Likewise, he thinks, the unrighteous, even unbelievers, need not refer all their actions to what their corrupt will has set up as the thing to love above all.

Just as desire sometimes slips into the righteous some movements of the will that are not referred to God as last end, and cannot even be, so, on his view, the natural instinct for good sometimes draws from unbelievers actions that a man does not refer to what he loves in particular as the highest good. He refers them to the good and to the last end, at least in general, though he does not know what that end is in particular and distinctly.

title: Vázquez: an act is referred to God by its nature, without a further intention
english: Close to this is Vázquez's teaching. For our works to be good and honourable, he says, they must indeed be referred to God as last end, but not by some prior act of will by which they could be said to be referred habitually; they are referred by the very nature of the work, without any further movement of the will.

So for an unbeliever to do a good work it is enough that he knows it is good and loves it for the sake of virtue's own honesty; by that very fact the work is sufficiently referred to God. Disputation just cited, chapters 2 and 3.

title: The popes' bull against the Louvain doctor confirms Estius and Vázquez
english: The popes of Rome have given their verdict for this view of Estius and Vázquez. The contrary teaching appears to stand condemned in Pius V's bull, which Gregory XIII later confirmed.

That bull, aimed at a Louvain doctor, condemns several propositions, and one of them reads: 'All the works of unbelievers are sins, and the virtues of the philosophers are vices.' Vázquez reports this in the passage cited above.
translator_notes: Pius V, bull Ex omnibus afflictionibus (1 October 1567), condemning propositions of Michael Baius of Louvain, confirmed by Gregory XIII in Provisionis nostrae (1579); the proposition quoted is no. 25 in the usual numbering.

title: Some Roman theologians still hold that no work of unbelievers is morally good
english: Yet some in the Roman School, against what the bull decrees, affirm that no work of unbelievers is morally good. Their reason is that for a work to be virtuous and morally good, it is not enough to do what ought to be done; it must also be done when, as much as, and for the sake for which it ought to be done.

The end for whose sake every work must be done is God, loved by the one acting, and everything else is referred to him. Since God alone is to be loved for his own sake, every affection not directed to God as its end is evil. So they conclude that no work of unbelievers is good, because they do not know the true God and so refer none of their acts to him as last end.

title: Gregory of Rimini: only pagans who lack knowledge of the one God; Grosseteste requires faith in Christ
english: Vázquez, in the often-cited disputation 191, ascribes this view to Gregory of Rimini, a celebrated Schoolman. He notes that by the unbelievers from whom no good work can come Gregory means unbelievers in the plain sense, that is, Gentiles who have no knowledge of the one true God. He does not mean schismatics and heretics, or those unbelievers who by some faith believe and know that there is one God.

So for someone to act well, that doctor does not think infused and supernatural faith necessary, only some faith and knowledge of the one true God. Still, there are some in the Roman School who require for acting morally well not just any faith but the faith of Christ itself. Among them, Vázquez again reports, is one 'Lincolniensis'.
translator_notes: Gregory of Rimini OESA (c. 1300-1358), Lectura super primum et secundum Sententiarum, book 2, distinctions 26-29.
'Linconiensis': the bishop of Lincoln, Robert Grosseteste (c. 1175-1253), as cited by Vázquez; the print spells it Linconiensis.

title: Jansenius and his disciples: only supernatural grace and Christian faith make a work morally good
english: It is above all Jansenius and his disciples who embrace this last view. They all hold that grace is needed for a morally good work, and not just any grace: it must be grace of the supernatural order, through which faith is first created in men. Nor is it faith of any sort, but Christian and infused faith, which out of devout affection we give to God speaking in his word.

They will have every good volition begin from faith of this kind, without which no good work can exist. So all the works not only of Gentiles but of everyone who lacks faith in Christ, such as heretics, are true and mere sins, however praiseworthy and good they look to men.
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius (1585-1638), bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (Louvain 1640), volume 2, De statu naturae lapsae; Le Blanc cites it by book and chapter.
'This last view': that of XIX-XXI and following, that no morally good work can be done without some grace.

title: Jansenius on Augustine: before faith, man's choice is captive and every act a sin
english: Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, hands this doctrine down as Augustine's and sets it out carefully in the volume he entitled Augustinus, in book 3 of On the state of fallen nature. In chapter 14 there he contends that this was the view of Augustine and his disciples, and so of the Catholic Church, which took up their teaching on this point against the Pelagians: after the fall man's choice is so captive and so stripped of the freedom to do good that whatever it does before grace, that is, before faith, from which freedom from sin begins, not only contributes nothing to piety and salvation but is not even morally good, since it is a true sin, properly so called.

In the same place he sets out as the undoubted view of Augustine and his disciples that no work that is good, even morally, can be done by human choice unless it is set free by grace, and not by any grace but by the grace of faith. Before faith, then, choice is not free to abstain from sin when it is thinking of acting here and now; whichever way it turns, it is held by a necessity of sinning that human strength cannot undo.

So, on this view, through Adam's fall man's freedom for good perished in such a way that before grace he cannot fulfil the whole law of moral righteousness, nor even one work of it. And his freedom to abstain from sin perished in such a way that he cannot escape the guilt of sin even in a single work. A necessity of sinning was therefore brought in, not in some acts only but in all.

For before grace, he holds, man not only cannot live wholly without sin, in that he necessarily falls at some time, but every act of his before he believes is a sin, whether he seems to flee the temptation to sin or to embrace it.
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius (1585-1638), bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (Louvain 1640), volume 2, De statu naturae lapsae; Le Blanc cites it by book and chapter.
Le Blanc gives the first sentences as Jansenius's own words (set in italic in the print); they are rendered here as reported teaching.

title: Works before faith are sins; the philosophers' virtues were vices
english: In chapter 1 of the next book he sets out to prove, expressly and specifically, following Augustine and the truth itself, that all works done before faith, from which the Christian religion begins, are nothing but sins, and that moral goodness is ascribed to them falsely and in error.
And, as follows from this, in chapter 8 he shows that the virtues of the philosophers were not true virtues but vices.
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius (1585-1638), bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (Louvain 1640), volume 2, De statu naturae lapsae; Le Blanc cites it by book and chapter. The 'following book' is book 4.

title: Only a faith working through love, from heavenly charity, gives a good work
english: Nor does he think an inert and idle faith is enough for someone to be able to act morally well. He holds that an active faith is required, one that in some way works through love. For he does not think any work is morally good, or escapes the character of sin, unless it proceeds from the love of God and from a kind of heavenly charity.

This is seen especially in chapter 16 of the third book already cited, On the state of fallen nature. There he sets out to teach from Augustine that no good work, that is, no work without sin, can be done by man unless the good deed itself is loved: that is, unless the righteousness of the precept itself delights the mind. For him, to delight in the righteousness of the precept is nothing other than to pursue a good work out of heavenly charity, since God is righteousness, and righteousness is loved by charity alone. So to do good by loving the righteousness of the law is nothing other than to do good by loving God himself with the charity of the Holy Spirit, because God is righteousness itself and truth.

So, in Augustine's own words, he affirms that there is no good fruit that does not spring from the root of charity, and that only then, and not otherwise, does anyone begin to delight in the righteousness of the law, when the faith that works through love is present. In chapter 16 of the next book he teaches that faith is needed for a good work because it is faith that obtains the help to love God. There too he affirms that there is no good work and no good will except from the intention of a good faith, that is, of the faith that works through love.
translator_notes: 'The faith that works through love' is Galatians 5:6 (fides quae per dilectionem operatur), Augustine's constant text on the point.

title: Every good work must be referred to God as its end
english: And as on his view every good work must proceed from a sincere love of God, so too it must be referred to God as its end. However good what someone does may be in its substance, unless he does it for God and with regard to God, he cannot avoid sin in it.

He sets out to prove this in chapter 17 of the third book of On the state of fallen nature, often cited, where his thesis is: 'No good work at all, that is, no work without sin, can be done unless it is referred to the end to which true wisdom commands that it be referred, that is, to God loved for his own sake. Otherwise it is neither done rightly nor a good work, but is polluted by the contamination of true sin.'
Hence also in that book and the next he everywhere draws the necessity of faith for acting well from this: faith is what directs the intention in acting toward that end.
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius (1585-1638), bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (Louvain 1640), volume 2, De statu naturae lapsae; Le Blanc cites it by book and chapter.

title: Against the common Roman view: a natural, not-bad affection is not enough
english: So he does not at all approve what most theologians of the Roman School take as certain and lay down: that for a morally good work it is enough that it proceed from a natural affection that is not bad, and that the agent does not intend a bad end, even if he does not think of God, and indeed does not even have knowledge of and faith in the one true God.

As when someone among those who do not know God is moved by some natural compassion to help a person in need, or honours his parents, and returns a loan or a deposit to a friend, because he judges it fair and just and in keeping with reason. Yet he does not refer it to God's glory, either habitually or actually, but rests in the mere honesty of the action, seeking virtue for its own sake and not for anything else.
translator_notes: 'Habitually or actually': the Schools' distinction between an intention still in force from an earlier act (habitual or virtual) and one present in the act itself.

title: No middle between charity and cupidity
english: For he does not think there is any affection that is not bad if it does not flow from a sincere and chaste love of God. Every affection of man, he holds, belongs either to charity and the love of God or to concupiscence and depraved cupidity, and there is nothing in between.

For it is absolutely necessary that all our affection and love either tend toward God and finally end in God, or end and come to rest in some creature, whatever that creature is supposed to be. If it is of the first kind, it belongs to charity and so is good; if of the second, it belongs to cupidity and so is bad.

title: Jansenius, book 3 chapter 19: every love but charity is blameworthy cupidity
english: This is seen especially in chapter 19 of that third book of On the state of fallen nature, already cited often. Its title is 'There is no middle between charity and blameworthy cupidity'. There he proves it from the fact that there is no middle between the love of God and the love of the creature.

'All the affections of the mind,' he says, 'turn on the love of some thing as on a hinge. That love can only be love of the Creator or love of the creature. The first is good; the second is blameworthy, since the Apostle calls it love of the world and, according to Augustine, it is the very character of sin, which rules in every kind of wrongdoing. So it is surely clear that every love other than that charity is that blameworthy cupidity.'
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius (1585-1638), bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (Louvain 1640), volume 2, De statu naturae lapsae; Le Blanc cites it by book and chapter.
'Love of the world': the phrase of 1 John 2:15 and of James 4:4; Jansenius gives it simply to 'the Apostle'.

title: Works not referred to God serve the creature, not the Creator
english: In the previous chapter he proves at length that all love of the world and of the creature is vicious, that is, when any creature is loved for its own sake and not for God. From this he gathers that all works not referred to God, to be possessed in eternal life, are bad by the very fact that in them men love the world, not God. So they serve the creature, not the Creator, and obey concupiscence, or cupidity, which the devil planted in man, not charity, which God planted.

'For,' he says, 'no middle can be imagined between the Creator and the creature, between the world and God, for them to pursue in acting; nor any middle way between cupidity and charity by which they are moved in their morally good actions. Only an ungodly man would deny that it is a sin to serve the creature by cupidity rather than the Creator, and to love the world rather than God while acting.

So in those works, however good and philosophical, and however free of sin they may seem, if they are done without faith in God, a Christian may not doubt that those who lack the faith that directs the intention serve the creature, not the Creator; for it is impossible that in acting they serve no one. A man serves whatever he looks to and loves as the end of his work, whether that is his work itself, or the object of the work, or (which is always so, and does not exclude the other two) the very man who seems to be doing a morally good work.

For by the very fact that in acting he looks either to the empty splendour of the work, as the Stoics did, or to honour, riches, pleasure or his own curiosity, as other philosophers did, he seeks for himself whatever he regards as final, not for God, whom he does not know at all. So no evasion can excuse him: in that very work he serves the creature, not the Creator.'
translator_notes: 'Serve the creature rather than the Creator' echoes Romans 1:25.

title: Seeking virtue for its own sake is the height of pride
english: So on his view it is a very great vice to seek virtue itself for its own sake and to perform the duties of virtue only for the honesty and beauty by which they win our mind's approval and commend themselves to it.
