For whoever rises no higher, and does not aim in this at serving God and proving himself to him, holds his own excellence as his highest end and thinks of serving and pleasing himself alone, who is a creature. That is beyond doubt the height of pride and the greatest departure from the true end, and so a very grave sin before God, however much such actions shine in men's eyes.

Those who pursue virtue in this way cannot be excused at all on the ground that virtue by its nature can be referred to God, even though the one who seems to act from virtue does not look to that. For all the other goods of human life, which are never sought for their own sake except viciously, can also be referred to God when considered in themselves.

title: Jansenius on the philosophers' self-pleasing; only the will to please God saves virtue from pride
english: That learned man discusses this at length in book 4 of On the state of fallen nature, chapter 11 and several chapters after it. 'This, then,' he says, 'was the evil proper to the philosophers' virtue, even when it was at its most refined: delighted by a kind of ruinous loftiness of virtue, they sought it so that they might excel in their own eyes, take delight in themselves and please themselves, when through it they ought to have pleased God, or, as Augustine puts it, the truth. This evil of self-pleasing clings so closely to those who desire to please neither God nor men that they cannot possibly avoid falling into it.'

For, as he adds a little later, 'Whoever does not lift his eyes to God, to please him by the beauty of virtue, but admires virtue alone as the end of good, most beautiful and most lofty, cannot seek it without pleasing himself by it, nor seek it without wishing to please himself by it. Since the human mind must take delight in something, in what else, I ask, can a mind estranged from God, which looks down on the other, lower creatures, as we are supposing, take delight than in what it believes most excellent among created things? That is the mind itself, now adorned with virtue, an adornment of its own that it judges the most beautiful of all. So whoever does not desire through virtue to please God or other men necessarily pleases himself by his virtue.'

From this he concludes that only by the will to please God through virtue can it be avoided that virtue, not only the philosophical virtue of the Gentiles but Christian virtue too, should please itself through pride and become a vice, which had been thought to be a virtue.
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius (1585-1638), bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (Louvain 1640), volume 2, De statu naturae lapsae; Le Blanc cites it by book and chapter.

title: So every good work belongs to piety and in its way profits salvation
english: Further, since in Jansenius's mind there is no good work that does not flow from a kind of heavenly charity and is not referred to God, to be possessed in eternal life, it also follows that there is no good work that does not belong to the worship of God and to piety and in its own way profit the soul's salvation.

So the Schoolmen divide good works in vain into those that are only morally good, cannot be counted among acts of piety and religion, and so profit the doer nothing toward eternal life, and those in which piety and religion consist and which in this way contribute something to the soul's salvation and eternal life.

title: Jansenius: every good work is meritorious; no virtue is barren
english: Jansenius himself draws this corollary from his doctrine in book 4 of On the state of fallen nature, chapter 2, where his words are: 'It is in no way possible that a work born of faith and the love of God should not by that very fact also be a work of piety, of righteousness, of the worship of God, meritorious and beatific. For what piety, righteousness and worship of God is more excellent than the love of God from faith? What is more meritorious and beatific, that is, more conducive to blessedness, than the love of God from faith?'

Later he declares that he holds with Augustine that there neither is nor can be any good work which, just as it requires faith and the love of God as its principle, is not by that very fact also a work of piety and of the worship of God and in its own way meritorious of eternal life.

In chapter 15 he criticizes the division of virtues and affections that Julian the Pelagian once used, saying that there are some through which we are good barrenly and others through which we are good fruitfully, that is, those which, as the Schoolmen teach, either help toward obtaining eternal life or do not. 'Since there neither is nor can be any virtue,' he says, 'that does not do its work from faith and love of the true God, to whom every work of virtue must be referred, and if it is not so referred it is a sin by the very fact that its end is not right, no virtue can possibly be barren. For faith and the love of God can in no way be barren; if it is barren, it is no longer virtue but must be vice.'
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius (1585-1638), bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (Louvain 1640), volume 2, De statu naturae lapsae; Le Blanc cites it by book and chapter.
Julian of Eclanum (c. 386-c. 455), Augustine's Pelagian opponent; the distinction is reported in Augustine, Contra Julianum 4.3.

title: Yet Jansenius allows that sinners can do some good works, with Trent
english: Although that man acknowledges no good work except what proceeds from charity and from faith working in some way through love, he does not deny that sinners, that is, those in mortal sin, who have not yet been justified and obtained the forgiveness of their sins, can do some good works.

In this he subscribes to the Council of Trent, which pronounces anathema on those who affirm that all works done before justification are true sins: 'If anyone says that all works done before justification, in whatever way they are done, are true sins or merit God's hatred, let him be anathema.' Session 6, canon 7.
translator_notes: Council of Trent, session 6 (13 January 1547), canon 7 on justification.
'Not yet ... justified and obtained remission': 'nondum' governs both 'justificati sunt' and 'adepti', which share the verb; the English keeps 'not yet' over both.

title: Believing sinners differ from unbelievers: they can do good works from faith
english: This is seen in Jansenius, On the state of fallen nature, book 4, chapter 4. 'Although it is most true,' he says, 'that the works of all sinners, and even of the righteous, which are not referred to the end to which they ought to be referred, that is, to God, but stick fast in creatures, are true sins, it is false that the case is the same for believing sinners as for unbelievers.

For by the very fact that sinners are imbued with faith, even though they lack that perfect charity which loves God above all, that is, justification, they can still do many good things from that faith: first of all, believing itself and willing to act, and, if they still lack the strength, groaning over their weakness and obtaining from faith justification or the strength to act. Augustine always ascribes works of this kind to sinners.'

Later, wishing to prove that believers, however enslaved to sins, do not lack a certain imperfect love of God, which is nonetheless sincere and the beginning of true piety, a love of God that unbelievers wholly lack, he says: 'By the very fact that they still remain believers they cannot fail to have that affection of true piety and love from which they believe God, from which they hope for blessedness in due course, from which they pray to obtain perfect charity and righteousness, and from which they also do some other good things with a sincere regard to God, although they do not yet love him so as to prefer him to all earthly loves and delights.'
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius (1585-1638), bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (Louvain 1640), volume 2, De statu naturae lapsae; Le Blanc cites it by book and chapter.

title: Two charities: perfect charity in the justified, imperfect charity in believing sinners
english: For he distinguishes charity properly so called, by which God is loved above all, from a certain imperfect charity, by which God is loved freely indeed and for his own sake, yet not above all.

In his mind the first charity is our very righteousness and can be found only in the justified, and so in those no longer stuck in sin. The second can be found even in sinners not yet freed by God's grace from the guilt of their sins. In them, through helps supplied by Christ, certain acts of faith and love are stirred up, by which sinners are disposed to receive righteousness from God and the forgiveness of their sins.

title: That imperfect love is a true and formal love of God, not a merely implicit one
english: Yet on his view that imperfect love is not merely, as some more recent Schoolmen think, an implicit love of God wrapped up in the intention of some moral honesty. It is a true and formal love of God; without this love of the Creator no one, according to Augustine, uses creatures well, whether he is a believer or an unbeliever, righteous or a sinner; and a believer, even a sinner, by no means lacks it in certain works.

So in that man's view the charity, or love, now in question, which believers do not wholly lack even when lying in sin, is an imperfect love of God, or a certain imperfect delight in God. It goes before the charity commonly known, the charity that loves God above all, and it begins all righteousness. This can be seen more fully in that author, in that chapter 4 of book 4 of On the state of fallen nature.
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius (1585-1638), bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (Louvain 1640), volume 2, De statu naturae lapsae; Le Blanc cites it by book and chapter.

title: Despite all this, the whole Roman School grants fallen man free choice in moral matters
english: Not a few theologians of the Roman School think that no morally good work can be accomplished without the grace of Christ. Most doctors of that School hold that at least the harder precepts of the moral law cannot be kept without the help of that grace, and that not even one of the easier ones can be obeyed without Christ's help if some heavy temptation presses.

Yet in this they all agree: man, even in the state of fallen nature, has freedom in moral matters; he has free choice and ought to be said to have it, not only in civil and natural matters but in moral ones too.

title: Bellarmine: Catholics, against all the heretics, hold free choice in moral good as dogma
english: This is seen in Bellarmine. 'The controversy,' he says, 'is between all Catholics on one side and all the heretics of this time on the other (for on this point there is no variety of opinion either among our own or among our adversaries): whether man in the state of fallen nature has free choice in choosing moral good and avoiding evil, or, what is the same, in keeping or breaking the precepts of morals.
And all Catholics, both the old and the more recent, proclaim the affirmative as a dogma of the Catholic faith.' On free choice, book 5, chapter 13.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine (1542-1621), Controversiae, De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 5 (on free choice in fallen man); Le Blanc cites the chapters as printed.
The print spells 'Hereticos' in the quotation; kept.

title: So the Roman dogma: fallen man acts well or sins freely, whatever is said of grace
english: So among them it is Catholic dogma that man, even when corrupted by sin, uses his freedom when he acts morally well, and transgresses the precepts of the moral law no less freely, whether by doing what they forbid or by leaving undone what they command, whether or not grace is supposed necessary for acting morally well.

That is a different question from this one, and on it, as we have seen, the doctors of the Roman School are not of one opinion; yet none of them denies that fallen man has his free choice with regard to moral good.

title: Bellarmine's state of the question: free choice with the necessary help supposed
english: Bellarmine himself explains the sense of this question as follows. 'We are not disputing here,' he says, 'whether the law can be fulfilled by the strength of nature alone. Nor are we unaware that the help of grace is in every way necessary, since the law alone does not make men righteous; rather, those justified through grace do the law.

Our question is whether, once the help of grace is supposed, man truly has free choice, so that he can fulfil the law or, if he prefers, transgress it. Just as, if someone asks whether a man can see or not see at will, one should not object, "What if there is no light?", for the question is understood with everything supposed that is necessarily required.
We say, then, that once the necessary help is supposed, whatever it may be, man is truly and properly free in moral matters.' On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 18.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine (1542-1621), Controversiae, De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 5 (on free choice in fallen man); Le Blanc cites the chapters as printed.
'Those justified ... do the law' turns Romans 2:13 ('the doers of the law shall be justified').

title: Two ways of keeping the moral law: as to the matter of the work, and as truly good
english: Thesis I. According to the common doctrine of the Protestants, the precepts of the moral and natural law can be kept in two ways. The first is absolute: as to the matter of the work, that is, as to doing the work considered in itself. The second is the way required if an action is to be truly good and upright in God's sight.

To keep the law as to the matter of the work is to do what the law commands in general, or to abstain from what it forbids: to help the needy, honour one's parents, refrain from murder, theft and adultery, without regard to the principle the work flows from or the end it is referred to. For an action to be truly good and upright, it must in addition be done from a proper principle and be referred to the end God requires. If these circumstances are missing, the action is judged vicious before God and takes on the nature of sin.
translator_notes: The Latter Part opens with its own title heading (print p. 490): Theses theologicae de Gratiae necessitate, et Liberi Hominum Arbitrii viribus circa bonum morale, in statu Naturae lapsae. Pars Posterior, in qua Protestantium Doctrina exponitur, et cum Scholae Romanae Doctrina comparatur (the Latter Part, in which the Protestants' doctrine is set out and compared with the Roman School's). The heading is kept in the Latin lock ahead of Thesis I.
'Upright' renders honestus, the moral worth of an act, throughout.

title: Some precepts cannot be kept even outwardly without grace
english: Thesis II. The first question the Protestants ask, then, is whether man, corrupted by sin, can by the powers of his own free choice and without God's grace fulfil the precepts of the moral law, at least as to the matter of the work.

They answer with one accord that some precepts of the moral law cannot be kept by fallen man without grace, not even as to the matter of the work, or, in the Roman School's language, its substance. Such are the precept not to covet, and the precept to love God with all one's strength and above all things.

title: Others can be kept outwardly without saving grace: Ames and Melanchthon
english: Thesis III. They agree no less that corrupt man can keep certain precepts of the law without the saving grace of Christ, at least absolutely and as to the matter of the work. This can be seen in Ames's Bellarmine Disarmed: 'We also grant that a man without faith, with special help and even without it, can perform some moral good, if "perform" is taken to mean doing the work considered in itself, without regard to the principle it flows from and the end to which it ought to be referred' (book 4, On free choice, chapter 3).

What Melanchthon teaches in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession agrees with this: 'The human will can in some measure achieve civil righteousness, or the righteousness of works. It can speak of God, offer God a certain worship by outward work, and obey magistrates and parents in choosing an outward work. It can keep its hands from murder, adultery and theft.'
translator_notes: William Ames (1576-1633), Bellarminus enervatus (Amsterdam 1628), book 4, on free choice, chapter 3.
Philip Melanchthon, Apology of the Augsburg Confession (1531), article 18, On free will.

title: Alexander Morus: honest civil acts are possible in the state of sin
english: Thesis IV. Nor is this far from what Alexander Morus teaches: that moral goods, taken absolutely, can be performed by man in the state of sin. 'Anyone can,' he says, 'live chastely and soberly as far as outward acts go, keep his hands from theft and murder, govern his power of movement, attend the gatherings of the Church, and hear the Gospel gladly instead of stopping his ears like the deaf adder.

All these things are upright and civil, and God finds them less displeasing when they are practised in whatever way than when they are left undone out of profane contempt' (On the Victory of Grace, second disputation, thesis 41).
translator_notes: Alexander Morus (1616-1670), Disputationes de victoria gratiae (Geneva); Le Blanc cites the second disputation by thesis number.
'Govern his power of movement' (locomotivam regere): to control where one's body goes, that is, to carry oneself to church.

title: Experience shows pagans capable of civil righteousness
english: Thesis V. Experience itself makes it plain that a man, even a pagan with no saving knowledge of God, can repay a deposit or a loan, care for his relatives, honour his parents, give alms to the poor, live temperately and soberly, and do many other such things.

In this way he can do many things that look fine and praiseworthy before men, who cannot see what lies within, and from them arises a kind of righteousness and civil uprightness. Such was found in Socrates, Epaminondas, Phocion, Scipio, Cato and many other men praised among the Gentiles, whose examples ought to make most Christians blush.

title: Yet even civil righteousness is owed to a special help of God
english: Thesis VI. Although in the Protestants' view the grace of Christ is not needed for civil righteousness and uprightness of this kind, many of them point out that it is to be ascribed to a special help of God.

Men left wholly to themselves, they say, could not attain even this civil righteousness, and those praised among the pagans for virtue did no praiseworthy actions without God helping them in a singular way and restraining their native corruption. Without this they would have rushed, no less than very many others, into every abominable crime.

title: Amyraut: without providence's restraint every man would be a Nero
english: Thesis VII. This is the view of Moïse Amyraut in his disputation On free choice. 'In my opinion,' he says, 'if God abandoned all men to their native corruption and withheld all the efficacy of his providence, both the providence at work in moderating the temperament of the body and the providence that exerts itself in each man's mind, ruling or restraining it or spurring it to some kind of pursuit of virtue, there would be no one who would not equal or surpass the Neros, Caligulas and Sardanapaluses, or any others among the most desperate, in injustice, lust, cruelty, avarice and every foulness of vice' (page 173).
translator_notes: Moïse Amyraut (1596-1664), Disputatio de libero hominis arbitrio (Saumur); Le Blanc cites page 173.

title: Morus: freedom for civic virtue is God's gift, not nature's
english: Thesis VIII. What Alexander Morus teaches in the disputation already cited agrees with this. 'Further,' he says, 'the liberty by which men make laws, govern the state, take counsel for the common good, win victories and shine in various virtues, even those who live in the state of sin, is not present in them as if it arose from the very cradle of nature. It comes from God, the Father of lights, from whom every good gift comes down. They acknowledged this themselves when they wrote that no distinguished man arises without divine inspiration, and reason itself convinced them. Otherwise why would the sons of heroes so degenerate, why would twins born together turn out so unlike, and why would men trained in the best education become savage beasts?' (thesis 46).

In the next thesis he adds: 'God's provident hand scatters, as it were, certain seeds of a good disposition at a man's very birth, and then puts opportunities for cultivating them in his way. These would do little good, though, unless God curbed men's wickedness with the reins of his Spirit. Since he wills that human society be held together in lawful order, he does not let everyone's insolence run wild alike, but restrains some by fear of punishment and kindles others by love of reward. Otherwise everything would be in utter confusion, if men broke out into evils of every kind as far as they are all inclined to them.'
translator_notes: Alexander Morus (1616-1670), Disputationes de victoria gratiae (Geneva); Le Blanc cites the second disputation by thesis number.
The dictum that no great man arises 'sine aliquo afflatu divino' is Cicero, De natura deorum 2.167.
'Naturae' is read for the print's ligature in 'ipsius naturae incunabulis'.

title: All are born equal in corruption; the difference lies in God's restraint
english: Thesis IX. So, in the opinion of these divines, if man's nature is considered in itself, all men are born equal, and none is better or worse than another. Whatever difference appears between them in this respect is to be ascribed to God's secret dispensation, by which men's passions are not cleansed within but are held in check so that they do not boil over more violently.

For although a Lerna of every kind of evil lies hidden in each person's breast, God lets some indulge their vices and be driven as if by furies. Others he moves by shame, respect for the laws, and the love of a good name and of undying fame, and keeps them to some extent within their duty. So the fact that not all emperors were Caligulas, nor all other men like Timon, is not something we should credit to nature, as if she were a mother to some and a stepmother to others. We should recognise God, who leaves some to their lust and curbs and holds back others in various ways.
translator_notes: Lerna: the marsh of the many-headed Hydra, proverbial for a mass of evils.
Timon of Athens, the proverbial misanthrope.

title: Civil goods are owed to providence, and God sometimes rewards them in time
english: Thesis X. In the Protestants' view, then, many things that are civilly good and upright can be done by man in the state of sin and without the grace of Christ, and they deserve to be ascribed to a singular efficacy of divine providence. Such acts make those in whom they are found less bad, and among men they can be judged praiseworthy. Indeed, God sometimes rewards things of this kind with some temporal reward.

'In this way,' says Alexander Morus, 'he shows how much truly good things please him, since he does not let even that faint shadow of goodness go unrewarded. Then he acts so as to make it an example, inviting the rest to do better.

Moreover, if all the godly prospered in this world, men would hardly look for the judgement to come. So when they sometimes see plainly that things go better for those who have some concern for godliness, they are reminded of the providence of God. Finally, God measures out a temporal reward in proportion to the goodness that shines in the work. He repays outward virtue with short-lived and passing goods, he who has appointed a heavenly and eternal kingdom for the spiritual course' (the disputation already cited, thesis 45).
translator_notes: Alexander Morus (1616-1670), Disputationes de victoria gratiae (Geneva); Le Blanc cites the second disputation by thesis number.

title: No act without Christ's grace is truly good before God: 'splendid sins'
english: Thesis XI. The Protestants, however, hold with one accord that in this state of corrupted nature no moral good can be performed by man without the grace of Christ in such a way that the act is held truly good and just before God and is not to be counted among sins. So whatever men do without the grace of Christ, however much it has the look of virtue and some outward goodness and uprightness, does not escape the character of sin in God's judgement. Thus the finest and most glorious deeds of heroes are splendid sins, masks and likenesses of virtues, as Morus, often cited already, puts it with Augustine in thesis 42.

'By moral works,' he says, 'Bellarmine meant works that please God and such as God requires. In that sense we readily believe Augustine that man can do nothing at all, and that even his finest and most glorious deeds are splendid sins, masks and likenesses of virtues.' What we read in David Pareus agrees with this: 'We say that the moral virtues of the unregenerate, of whatever kind, done without faith and with an unclean heart, however upright, just and worthy of praise and reward they may be before the world, are nonetheless sins before God, not in their kind but by accident' (on Bellarmine, On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 4).

He calls such virtues sins by accident because, though they are good things in their kind, they fall short in certain essentials. They do not arise from the proper principle, and they are not referred to the lawful end.
translator_notes: Alexander Morus (1616-1670), Disputationes de victoria gratiae (Geneva); Le Blanc cites the second disputation by thesis number.
'Splendid sins' is the traditional summary of Augustine's teaching (cf. De civitate Dei 19.25), not his own phrase.
David Pareus (1548-1622), commentary against Bellarmine's De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 5, chapter 4.

title: Why: such acts neither proceed from love of God nor are directed to his glory
english: Thesis XII. The reason why, on Protestant doctrine, the acts of a sinner done without the grace of Christ really have the character of sin, though they are good in their kind and as to the matter of the work, is that they neither proceed from the love of God nor are directed to his glory.

The Protestants hold that both of these are plainly necessary for any work that is truly good and good in God's judgement, and they consider that neither can be found in fallen man without the saving grace of Christ.

title: The law of nature requires that all be done from love of God above all
english: Thesis XIII. That no work can be truly good by the law of nature unless it flows from the love of God, they prove from the fact that this law of nature requires man to love God his creator, from whose goodness he has all that he is and all that he can do, with all his strength and above all things.

Whoever is moved to act by love of creatures alone, and not by love of God, shows by this that he does not love God above all creatures. He prefers love of the creature to love of God, and so he acts viciously.

title: Against a 'virtual and implicit' love of God in the ignorant
english: Thesis XIV. It is useless for some to distinguish here between a virtual, implicit love of God and a formal, explicit one, as though someone who does not formally love God, and is even ignorant of him, could still be reckoned to love him implicitly when he loves certain actions God has commanded, actions that must for that very reason be reckoned pleasing to God.

For whoever does not know God, or does not act from love of God, whether actual or habitual, undoubtedly acts from love of himself and loves himself above all things. He loves an upright action only so that he may take joy in it and be pleased with himself. Every love of self not subordinated to the love of God is vicious and sinful, and it is wholly unreasonable to find a praiseworthy implicit love of God inside a vicious love.

title: The same law requires every act to be referred to God's glory
english: Thesis XV. In the same way the law of nature requires the rational creature to direct all its actions to the glory of God. God's glory is the natural end of all things, for 'the Lord has made all things for himself', and 'of him, through him and to him are all things'. Paul's precept, 'Do all to the glory of God', therefore belongs to the law of nature.

So no act that the agent does not refer to the glory of God can be truly good and just, since the goodness of actions is to be measured chiefly by their lawful end (Proverbs 16:4; Romans 11:36; 1 Corinthians 10:31).

title: A good end that is not God himself is not enough
english: Thesis XVI. Nor can anyone say that acts done for some end that is not bad are in some way referred to God's glory even if the agent does not think of it. Suppose, for example, that someone who does not know the true God gives money to a person in need in order to help him. It would be argued that such an act looks to God's glory, since all the goodness in created things looks to God of itself and is referred to him.

But for an act to be counted as done for God's glory, it is not enough that its end is something naturally good, which by its nature could be referred to God. Otherwise a man who works for no other end than to get rich could be said to work for God's glory, since wealth is in itself a good thing and not a bad one. Yet such work is undoubtedly wicked, and tends toward vice, not virtue.

title: Love of God and reference to his glory need the grace of Christ
english: Thesis XVII. To love God above all things and to refer one's actions to his glory belongs above all to the spiritual worship of God and to godliness. It follows that the saving grace of Jesus Christ must certainly be wholly necessary for it, since without that grace, as the whole Roman School admits, the free choice of fallen man can do nothing at all toward willing and doing spiritual good.

From all this the Protestants rightly conclude that a man without the grace of Christ, in the bare state of fallen nature, can do nothing that has the true character of moral good and is held truly just and upright before God. Men left wholly to themselves both miss the true end in what they do and act from a bad principle, namely love of self.

title: Placaeus: the unregenerate always miss the true scope and so sin
english: Thesis XVIII. With these agree what we read in Josué de la Place's treatise On man's free choice. He first teaches that Adam lost the absolute liberty of not sinning, and that the bondage of sin took its place. That bondage lies in the depravity and crookedness of the moral faculties, especially the will, and the depravity consists in turning away from the true last end and turning toward a last end that only appears to be one.

It follows, since whatever is desired is either the last end or a means to it, that nothing sound is left in our moral faculties, and that as long as we are in this condition we cannot help sinning. He then gives the reason in these words: 'Whether we seek the last end or the means, we always miss the true mark, however brightly the unregenerate man may seem to shine with virtues. For whatever he desires, says or does, he aims at a last goal that falsely appears to him to be the goal, though it is very far from the true one. By that very fact he sins, and he cannot help sinning as long as he judges wrongly about the goal' (page 199).
translator_notes: Josué de la Place (Placaeus, c. 1596-1655), De libero hominis arbitrio (Saumur), page 199.

title: Morus: four defects in the works of the graceless
english: Thesis XIX. Alexander Morus likewise observes that a sinner who lacks God's grace falls short in many ways in all his works, however excellent they may otherwise seem. So before God, who judges by the truth of the matter, they are really counted not good but bad, since good comes from a cause that is whole, and evil from the lack of even one circumstance.

He notes four defects in works of this kind, in their principle, their subject, their manner and their end. Their principle is not the Spirit but the flesh, that is, carnal affection, and the fruits of the flesh cannot please God. Their subject is a man without the grace by which 'we serve God acceptably', that is, offer God a worship that pleases him. Their manner is drawn from some generosity of spirit, not from faith, and without faith no one pleases God. Finally their end, the salvation of one's neighbour and the glory of God, is wholly missing (On the Victory of Grace, disputation 2, thesis 43).
translator_notes: Alexander Morus (1616-1670), Disputationes de victoria gratiae (Geneva); Le Blanc cites the second disputation by thesis number.
The Greek is Hebrews 12:28, 'let us serve God acceptably' (print: εὐαρέστως λατρεύομεν τῷ Θεῷ).

title: Defects in the works of the godly are accidental; in the graceless, essential
english: Thesis XX. It is true that even the works of the godly and righteous, done through God's grace, have their own blemishes and defects. But those defects are only accidental and do not take away the essence of a good work. The defects that spoil the works of those without the grace of Christ are essential ones, and the very nature and essence of a good work cannot survive them. A work's goodness depends chiefly on the end it tends to and the principle it springs from.

Yet all the works of a man without the grace of Christ, as shown above, miss the true end, which is God's glory, and take their origin from a bad principle, earthly desire. That ruins a work that would otherwise be good in its kind. The works of the godly and righteous proceed from love of God and tend to his glory. Their only shortfall is that God's glory is not sought in them as purely as it should be, and the love of God they flow from is not as fervent as it ought to be.

So the works of the godly are good, imperfectly but truly. Whatever works are done by those who lack the grace of Christ, however brightly they shine in men's eyes, are really bad before God and do not keep the nature of a good work, though some are less bad than others.

title: Morus: the works of unbelievers are only less bad
english: Thesis XXI. Alexander Morus notes this in the disputation already cited so often, thesis 44. 'The works of unbelievers,' he says, 'are not good; some are only less bad than others. The works of the faithful, though stained with spots, maimed in various ways and imperfectly good, are still good, truly good.

They go forward feebly, but on the way of salvation; they throw with weak motion, but at the mark. The others race along at speed, but off the road; they draw the bow hard, but do not aim at the true mark.'
translator_notes: Alexander Morus (1616-1670), Disputationes de victoria gratiae (Geneva); Le Blanc cites the second disputation by thesis number.
The image of runners off the road echoes Augustine, Enarrationes in Psalmos 31.2.4 ('bene currunt, sed in via non currunt').

title: No Protestant room for works naturally good but not saving
english: Thesis XXII. From what has been said it is easy to gather that, on the Protestant view, no work is truly good in the moral order unless it is also ordered to eternal salvation and forms part of worship and godliness toward God. For they count nothing worthy of the name of a good work unless it aims at God's glory and springs from love of him.

So the distinction among good works that holds in the Roman School has no place with them: that some works are merely naturally and morally good, yet still truly good even in God's sight, though they do nothing toward eternal salvation, while others help toward salvation and have a supernatural goodness. On their view all truly good works originate in a supernatural principle, namely the grace of Christ, and also contribute something toward eternal life.

If they sometimes ascribe a moral goodness to the works of those outside the grace of Christ, they mean by it a goodness that is only outward and civil. It does not make the work acceptable and pleasing to God, and it does not stop it from really being a sin and deserving the name.
translator_notes: The print places a comma after 'moralem' ('extra Christi gratiam moralem, aliquam bonitatem'); the sense requires 'moralem aliquam bonitatem' together and the rendering follows the sense.

title: What the Protestants mean by the grace of Christ
english: Thesis XXIII. In this question, however, they do not give the name 'grace of Christ' to the helps of the natural order that God does not refuse even to unbelievers who remain in their unbelief.

They call grace of Christ only the grace that begins with faith, and not with faith of just any kind, but with Christian faith infused by God, which is not idle and dead but begins to work through love.

title: All works of unbelievers are sins; Pareus requires justifying faith
english: Thesis XXIV. They therefore count all the works of unbelievers, however fine they look, among sins. And they reckon as unbelievers not only those wholly ignorant of the true God but all who lack true faith in Christ and do not know the one true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. They hold that the works of all such people, however excellent and upright they seem, are not acts of true virtue but sins painted in its colours, as is clear enough from what has already been said.

For without faith nothing can please God, and whatever is done without faith is sin. By faith here they mean not only the faith opposed to a wavering conscience, but the faith that shapes the conscience from God's word as it should, makes it certain, and is even able to justify a man.

This is David Pareus's teaching: 'We say that a morally good work, one ordered to God's law, worship and good pleasure, requires not only the special help of God's singular providence, and not only the special grace of a singular divine motion, but also the special grace of justifying faith' (on Bellarmine, On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 4).

title: The grace required is regenerating grace itself: Placaeus and Ames
english: Thesis XXV. The Protestants do not merely say that the grace by which faith is produced is needed for every good work, and that no one can offer the natural law a true obedience pleasing to God without it. They also teach openly enough that the grace without which no one can act well, or do even one truly good work, is regenerating and justifying grace itself.

This can be seen especially in Josué de la Place, who denies that a man can avoid sinning without the grace of regeneration. His words are these: 'As for moral actions, those the law commands or forbids, Bellarmine multiplies questions needlessly. We bring our whole dispute with the Papists over free choice in the state of sin back to this one question: can an unregenerate man avoid sinning without the grace of regeneration? The Papists say yes; we say no' (treatise On free choice, page 201).

What we read in Ames's Bellarmine Disarmed agrees with this. 'First,' he says, 'our divines teach that man can do nothing of spiritual good before he is born again, whereas Bellarmine requires only the help of a grace that persuades and assists. Second, our divines require for spiritual good the help that is proper to those effectually called, whereas Bellarmine means a general help that is lacking to no one at the right place and time' (book 4, On free choice, chapter 3).

There Ames includes under 'spiritual good' everything truly good in the moral order. For, as I showed above, the Protestants count nothing in this order as truly good unless it proceeds from a sincere love of God and so belongs in some way to godliness and the spiritual worship of God.
translator_notes: Josué de la Place, De libero hominis arbitrio, page 201.
William Ames, Bellarminus enervatus, book 4, on free choice, chapter 3.

title: No good work before justification: Trent's canon censured
english: Thesis XXVI. That on the Protestant view no one can do any truly good work before justification is plain from their censure of the Council of Trent's canon 7 of the sixth session: 'If anyone says that all works done before justification, in whatever way they are done, are truly sins or deserve God's hatred, or that the harder anyone strives to dispose himself for grace, the more grievously he sins, let him be anathema.'

They also often praise and approve Augustine's saying: 'Good works follow the one who is justified; they do not go before the one who is to be justified.' This can be seen especially in Calvin's Antidote to the Council of Trent on that canon, and in Chemnitz's Examination of the same council, where he treats of preparation for justification.
translator_notes: Council of Trent, session 6 (1547), canon 7 on justification.
Emendation against the print: the print reads 'tanto eum gravis peccare'; the canon's text is 'gravius', and the rendering follows the canon.
Augustine, De fide et operibus 14.21.
John Calvin, Acta synodi Tridentinae cum antidoto (1547); Martin Chemnitz, Examen Concilii Tridentini, part 1, on justification.

title: The difficulty: living faith and some love of God precede justification
english: Thesis XXVII. On this point, however, Protestant doctrine does not seem free from difficulty. Those among them who reason most exactly about theological matters acknowledge that faith, and a living and active faith, is a prerequisite condition of a man's justification.
Yet believing in God is a truly good work, and living faith does not exist without some love of God, which is itself a good work too. So some works that precede justification are truly good.

title: Repentance too is a prerequisite condition: Maresius, Ames, Chemnitz
english: Thesis XXVIII. They also acknowledge that repentance, or penitence, is the condition on which the forgiveness of sins, in which a sinner's justification consists, is offered in the Gospel. So the celebrated Maresius teaches that forgiveness of sins belongs to repentance 'conditionally, inasmuch as it is offered to us in the Gospel on the condition of repentance and faith' (disputation On repentance and Christian liberty, thesis 32).

Likewise Ames, in Bellarmine Disarmed, book 5, on justifying faith, chapter 3, grants that penitence precedes justification as a disposition prerequisite in order, but not as a cause. The same can be seen in Chemnitz himself at the place just cited.

Yet penitence and repentance involve many good works, such as the resolve to live a new life, hatred of sin, and even some love of God, which arises from the hope of obtaining pardon from him. So a good number of good works precede justification. Indeed Ames, at the place already cited, expressly acknowledges that 'some love of God comes before the forgiveness of sins, or justification, as a prerequisite disposition', though 'no love precedes forgiveness as a causing disposition'.
translator_notes: Samuel Desmarets (Maresius, 1599-1673), Disputatio de resipiscentia et libertate Christiana, thesis 32.
William Ames, Bellarminus enervatus, book 5, on justifying faith, chapter 3.

title: Davenant: good works as concurrent or preparatory conditions
english: Thesis XXIX. Hence Davenant does not hesitate to assert that certain good works are necessary for justification as concurrent or preparatory conditions, though not as efficient or meritorious causes. Among these good works he counts inward ones that weigh much with God though men do not see them: grieving for sin, hating sin, humbly submitting to God, fleeing to God's mercy, setting one's hope on Christ the Mediator, resolving on a new life, and the like.

'For God's mercy,' he says, 'does not justify blocks of wood, that is, people who do nothing, nor horses and mules, that is, people who kick back and cling stubbornly to their lusts. It justifies men, and men who are pierced and contrite and follow the guidance of God's word and Spirit' (On actual righteousness, chapter 31).
translator_notes: John Davenant (1572-1641), Disputatio de justitia habituali et actuali (Cambridge 1631), on actual righteousness, chapter 31.

title: If good works precede justification they precede regeneration too
english: Thesis XXX. If some good works precede a man's justification, they must also precede his regeneration, since by the common doctrine of the Protestants regeneration comes after justification in the order of nature. Besides, a man's regeneration and his sanctification are in fact one and the same, so the Spirit by whom a man is regenerated is the same as the one by whom he is sanctified.

But the Spirit of sanctification, as the most learned and celebrated Protestants expressly teach, is promised to us in the Gospel only on the condition of faith, a living and effective faith, which cannot exist without many good works. Nor is that Spirit given except to those who earnestly want to rise out of their vices, who hunger and thirst for true righteousness, and who ask God for him in constant prayers made in faith.
As the Lord Jesus says, 'How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?' (Luke 11:13). And to pray to God in faith is certainly a truly good work.

title: Pareus: acts of faith, fear and love dispose to sanctification
english: Thesis XXXI. To the same point is the fact that Protestants of great name acknowledge certain dispositions to sanctification, aroused by the power of God's Spirit in people who are to be sanctified and regenerated. These are various acts of faith, fear and love, as can be seen in Pareus on Bellarmine's On justification, book 1, chapter 3.
Acts of faith and love cannot fail to be good works. And since they are taken to be dispositions to sanctification, or regeneration, they cannot fail to come before it in some way as well.
translator_notes: David Pareus, commentary on Bellarmine, De justificatione, book 1, chapter 3.

title: How then can they require regenerating grace for every good work and condemn Trent?
english: Thesis XXXII. So if, by the Protestants' own doctrine and admission, some good works precede a man's regeneration and justification, how can they hold that the very grace by which we are regenerated and justified is necessary for every good work?
And how can they condemn the canon of the Council of Trent that pronounces anathema on those who say that all works done before justification, in whatever way they are done, are truly sins?
translator_notes: Council of Trent, session 6 (1547), canon 7 on justification.

title: The difficulty resolved: grace of justification taken widely and strictly
english: Thesis XXXIII. To solve this difficulty we must note that the Protestants use 'the grace of regeneration and justification' sometimes in a wider and sometimes in a stricter sense. In their usage, justification taken strictly and precisely is nothing but the absolution of a sinner for the sake of Christ's satisfaction, which is given and imputed to him. Understood in this way it is a benefit distinct from faith, the faith by which we share in it and which is therefore called justifying faith.

Taken more widely, though, the grace of justification includes the very faith by which we are justified. This is the sense the Protestants have in mind when they deny that any truly good works precede justification. For them, to come before justification is the same as to come before justifying faith, and nothing precedes justification that does not also precede faith.

So when they say that everything done before justification is sin and not a good work, they mean only that no good work can exist in a man before faith, and that all the works of unbelievers are sins.

title: Chemnitz: Trent's canon read in the wide sense; preparations granted in the strict
english: Thesis XXXIV. This can be seen in Calvin and Chemnitz, where they censure the canon of the Council of Trent already mentioned. Chemnitz, condemning that canon, takes it to pronounce anathema on those who deny that unbelievers dispose themselves for grace by their works: 'In the seventh canon,' he says, 'they pronounce anathema on those who deny that unbelievers dispose themselves for grace by their works' (Examination, part 1, page 157, column a).

But earlier in the same work, taking justification in the stricter sense, he admits that penitence, faith, contrition and the resolve not to go on in sin are, according to Scripture, certain preparations for justification. 'God wills,' he says, 'that we begin from knowledge of his word and assent to it. And contrition must come before justification: that is, a serious acknowledgement of our sins, the terrors of a conscience that recognises God's wrath against our sins and grieves over sin. In this contrition the resolve to persist and go on in wickedness is not kept but thrown away.

Faith must be added to this, so that by knowing and trusting the mercy God has promised for the sake of his Son the Mediator it may raise up and comfort the mind again, and we may not be crushed by despair and rush into eternal ruin. Faith must rather come to God, seek, desire, ask for, lay hold of and receive the forgiveness of sins' (page 155).
translator_notes: Martin Chemnitz, Examen Concilii Tridentini, part 1, on justification; Le Blanc cites pages 157 (column a) and 155 of his edition.
Council of Trent, session 6 (1547), canon 7 on justification.

title: Calvin: Trent's canon refuted by arguments about faith alone
english: Thesis XXXV. Calvin likewise, refuting the same canon of the Council of Trent, uses no arguments except those that prove nothing good can be done without faith. God does not care for outward masks but looks at the faith of the heart; hearts are purified only by faith; whatever unbelievers do, they do not refer their deeds to God; and finally, as Augustine says, if any good fruit in a man is praised, its root must be looked for in faith.

And 'our religion distinguishes the just from the unjust not by the law of works but by the law of faith itself, without which what look like good works are turned into sins' (Antidote, on canon 7 of the sixth session). It is plain, then, that for Calvin in this place doing something before justification is the same as doing it before faith and in unbelief, and that he means only that all works before faith are bad and not good.

This fits very well with the view that justification, taken as the forgiveness of sins or the sinner's absolution, is preceded by certain acts, not only of faith but also of fear, hope and love, and by the resolve to live a new life, which are good and pleasing to God.
translator_notes: John Calvin, Acta synodi Tridentinae cum antidoto (1547), on session 6, canon 7.
The law of faith set against the law of works is Romans 3:27.

title: Regeneration too taken strictly and widely
english: Thesis XXXVI. In the same way regeneration, or sanctification, is sometimes taken strictly, for a habitual change in a man through infused habits of righteousness and holiness. Sometimes it is taken more widely, for all the effects of divine grace in us by which we are brought from the state of sin into the state of righteousness and of the children of God.

Taken so, the grace of regeneration or sanctification includes the beginning, the progress and the completion of the efficacious grace by which God abolishes the dominion of sin in us and makes us servants of righteousness. In Scripture's words, it makes us put off the old man and put on the new, created after God in righteousness and true holiness. This is what Ames means when he says that regeneration is sometimes taken for the whole series of helps by which we are moved toward it (Theological disputation on the preparation of the sinner for conversion, thesis 11).
translator_notes: William Ames, disputation De praeparatione peccatoris ad conversionem, thesis 11.

title: Good acts precede regeneration strictly, not regeneration widely
english: Thesis XXXVII. Regeneration taken in the first, stricter sense is preceded by many acts of faith, hope, fear, sorrow for sin, love too, and prayer for God's help. These are undoubtedly good works, acceptable to God, by which a man is prepared, as God has ordained, to receive the gift of the sanctifying and regenerating Spirit. So the grace of regeneration in that strict sense is not needed for doing them.

But without the grace of regeneration taken in the second and wider sense, no one can do anything good. A man cannot possibly act well before God begins to work in him by his grace, to free him from the chains of sin and set him in the liberty of God's children. As already said, the first beginnings of that grace belong to regeneration taken more widely.

title: Necessary grace does not stop the sinner sinning freely
english: Thesis XXXVIII. Grace is wholly necessary if corrupt man is to do any good work, and without grace he can do nothing well and in conformity with God's law.

Yet in the Protestants' view this does not prevent man in that state from acting freely when he does evil, whether by committing what the law forbids or omitting what it commands; in doing so he exercises the native power of his free choice.

title: Necessity of sinning does not remove essential liberty
english: Thesis XXXIX. Without grace man is the servant of sin, as Scripture says, and whatever he does he cannot help sinning. Yet this necessity of doing evil does not take away the natural freedom of his choice. The freedom that belongs essentially to every agent with intellect and will does not consist in being indifferent between acting well and acting badly, with an equal power for either. Otherwise neither the demons in hell nor the angels in heaven would act freely, since the demons are fixed on doing evil and the angels, conversely, on doing good.

That natural freedom of choice consists rather in acting without compulsion and without any brute impulse of nature, choosing what one pleases and thinks fit after a prior judgement and deliberation of the mind. So this freedom is opposed to coercion and to natural or brute determination, but not at all to the bondage of sin. That bondage does not stop a man, when he sins, from acting deliberately and at the dictate of his own reason, without any coercion and without natural or brute determination.

title: The sinner is determined to evil in general, not to each act: Perkins's prisoner
english: Thesis XL. Add that man in the state of sin, left to himself, is indeed determined to evil in general, but not to each particular evil action: he can abstain from this one or that one, just as a man locked in prison can walk about freely inside it. William Perkins uses this comparison to illustrate the point.

'I will show by an example,' he says, 'that some things are done necessarily and freely at the same time. Suppose a man has been thrown into prison, so that he must stay there and cannot leave for wherever he wants. He can still move about and walk freely within the prison. It is the same with the human will. Bound by the chains of sin, it naturally does nothing but sin, and so sins necessarily; yet it sins of its own free will' (The Reformed Catholic, first controversy, On free will, fourth conclusion).
translator_notes: William Perkins (1558-1602), A Reformed Catholike (1597; Latin Catholicus reformatus), first controversy, On free will, fourth conclusion.

title: Grace moves the will without prejudice to its freedom
english: Thesis XLI. Likewise, in the Protestants' mind, the presence and efficacy of grace, when it is at work, does no harm at all to human freedom. Actions done with grace moving and helping are no less free than they would be if they were supposed done without grace.

Grace does no violence to the human will; it moves it in a way suited to a free faculty, with a deliberate judgement of the mind going before and accompanying the act, and without taking from the will the power to act otherwise. So all good works are effects of divine grace in such a way that they are also acts of a free choice set free by grace, which acts not by its own powers but by those grace has supplied.

title: Pareus: in this life the freed will can still do good and evil
english: Thesis XLII. Nor is man's choice so freed by grace in this life that he cannot always act badly as well as well, as Pareus, disputing against Bellarmine, freely admits. 'What Christian,' he says, 'ever doubted that a man endowed with grace has a choice that is set free and free to choose good and do it by the power of grace, and also to choose evil and do it out of the weakness of nature, which grace neither regenerates nor governs perfectly in this life? Hence the reborn use their freedom of will in this life both to do well and to do badly.

So there can be no question whether a man, given the help of grace, truly has free choice' (on Bellarmine, On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 13). The same author repeats this in chapter 28 of that book: 'In the state of grace the renewed will chooses good freely, in such a way that while it is effectively moved by grace to choose it, it can indeed choose the opposite through the defect of nature, but does not will to, because of the efficacy of grace.'
translator_notes: David Pareus (1548-1622), commentary against Bellarmine's De gratia et libero arbitrio; Le Blanc cites book and chapter.

title: In what sense the Protestants deny free choice for moral good
english: Thesis XLIII. If someone asks whether man in the state of fallen nature is free, without grace, to choose moral good and keep God's commandments, the Protestants answer no. So most of them deny that free choice remained in man after sin with regard to moral good.

All they mean by this, though, is that by his fall man became the slave and captive of sin, and his choice lost the freedom that is opposed to the bondage of sin. The freedom essential to an intellectual agent still remained in him, the freedom from which man's choice, considered absolutely, is called free.

title: Bellarmine's question answered by a distinction
english: Thesis XLIV. To the question Bellarmine poses, then, whether man in the state of fallen nature has free choice in choosing moral good and avoiding evil, or, which is the same thing, in keeping or breaking the moral precepts, they answer with a distinction. In that state, before grace, man has free choice in violating and breaking the moral precepts. Once grace is given, he can use the freedom of his choice both to keep them and to break them.

Without grace, however, he does not have free choice to keep those precepts. Without grace he can do nothing good, not through the lack of some physical faculty, for he always has a mind and a will, which are never stripped of their essential freedom, and no other natural faculty is needed for doing good. The reason is that his will is set fast in evil until God frees it by grace and releases it from the bondage of sin, a bondage that can coexist with the freedom just described.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 5, where he states the question of free choice in moral good.

title: Pareus: the charge that Protestants deny free choice altogether is a calumny
english: Thesis XLV. So they complain that Bellarmine and others slander them by charging that they teach that man never has free choice in moral matters, whether with grace or before it.

'Who could say without flagrant slander,' asks Pareus, 'that on our view man never has free choice? In the state of sin choice is free only for evil, because it is captive as regards good; in the state of grace it is free for both. Does it never have free choice, then?' (on Bellarmine, On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 28).
translator_notes: David Pareus (1548-1622), commentary against Bellarmine's De gratia et libero arbitrio; Le Blanc cites book and chapter.

title: Rome and the Protestants agree on two points about keeping the law
english: Thesis XLVI. From what has been set out at length both in this disputation and in the one before it, it is plain that the Roman School agrees with the Protestants on one point: fallen man cannot without grace keep the precepts of the moral law in the way in which they are ordered to heavenly happiness, so that keeping them gains him a right to eternal life and furthers his everlasting salvation.

In turn the Protestants agree with the Roman School that fallen man can keep certain precepts of the moral law without the grace of Christ, at least as to the outward work, or absolutely and as to the matter or the doing of the work itself, as the Protestants put it. The Roman School says 'as to the substance of the work'. The two come to the same thing, though some Protestants reject the second way of speaking because the substance of a thing includes both its matter and its form. The question here concerns only the matter of the moral work, not its form, which depends on its end and principle.

title: Pareus: the outward act is not the substance of the work
english: Thesis XLVII. This can be seen in David Pareus, already cited so often. 'So Bellarmine deceives and is deceived,' he says, 'when he takes the outward act of a work and the substance of the work to be the same thing, though they differ as part and whole. The substance of a work requires matter and form, no less than the substance of a man requires body and soul.

The outward act the law commands serves as the matter. The inward conformity and purity that comes from faith serves as the form of the work, and a lawful end is also required for it. The Philosopher himself praises an act of virtue only on account of its end, if it is done for the sake of the noble. So whoever performs the outward act of a work has not performed the substance of the work' (on Bellarmine, On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 5).
translator_notes: David Pareus (1548-1622), commentary against Bellarmine's De gratia et libero arbitrio; Le Blanc cites book and chapter.
The Greek 'tou kalou heneka' (for the sake of the noble) is Aristotle's formula for the end of virtuous action, e.g. Nicomachean Ethics 3.7, 1115b12.

title: All Protestants condemn the view that every precept can be kept without grace
english: Thesis XLVIII. But there is no Protestant who does not condemn what some in the Roman School have taught: that each and every precept of the moral law can be kept without the grace of Christ as to the substance, or matter, of the work.
For, as we saw above, the Protestants except from this certain precepts that concern inward acts of the mind, such as the precept not to covet and the precept to love God above all things.

title: They also reject the common Roman view of the easier precepts, and the Spanish view reported by Vázquez
english: Thesis XLIX. It is also clear from what we have said that the Protestants by common vote reject what by far the largest part of the Roman School teaches: that the easier precepts of the moral law can be kept by corrupt man without the grace of Christ in such a way that the act is truly good and sin is avoided in it, even though it does nothing for eternal salvation.

Much more do they reject the view of those in that School who held that fallen man can fulfil the whole law of nature without grace, or, if not all its precepts together, at least each one taken singly. Many in Spain thought so toward the end of the last century, as Gabriel Vázquez testifies.
translator_notes: Gabriel Vázquez SJ (1549-1604), commentary on Aquinas, Prima secundae; cited in Pars Prior for the Spanish opinion.

title: Even Vázquez differs from the Protestants on what the grace of Christ is
english: Thesis L. Indeed it follows easily from what has been said that Gabriel Vázquez himself, who admits that no morally good work can be done without the grace of Christ, still differs a great deal from the Protestants here. By the grace of Christ he means certain helps of the natural order that can come even to unbelievers who remain unbelievers. Consequently he teaches, with a great many theologians of the Roman School, that any unbeliever at all can do some truly morally good works by means of such helps.

The Protestants, however, mean by the grace of Christ only the grace that begins with faith in Christ, a faith that is living and effective. So they deny that any unbeliever, that is, anyone not filled with true faith in Christ, can do any work that is truly good and good before God and that lacks the character of sin, however upright and praiseworthy it may look to men.

title: Rome has not defined that faith is unnecessary for a morally good act: Jansenius
english: Thesis LI. It also appears from what we reported above that the opposite view, which holds that faith in Christ is not necessary for someone to act morally well, is not so certain and defined in the Roman Church that it is forbidden to hold the contrary.

For Jansenius, and a good number of distinguished men who follow him, openly teach the same as the Protestants on this point, and yet Jansenius's book was not publicly censured for this, as it was for many other things.
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius (1585-1638), Augustinus (1640), as set out in Pars Prior XXXIII-LIII.
Augustinus was condemned by Urban VIII's bull In eminenti (dated 1642, published 1643) and five propositions from it by Innocent X's Cum occasione (1653).

title: No real difference between the Protestants and Jansenius
english: Thesis LII. Indeed, in this whole question of the powers of free choice in fallen man and the necessity of grace for moral good, there seems to be no true and real difference between the doctrine of the Protestants and that of Jansenius.

Jansenius acknowledges with them not only that the grace of Christ, and an effective and active faith in him, is necessary for any morally good work. He also holds, as follows from this, that no work is truly good unless it proceeds from some sincere love of God and tends to his glory. And so he holds that the Scholastics distinguish good works to no purpose, into those that belong to godliness and further eternal salvation and those that neither concern godliness nor help toward eternal salvation.
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius (1585-1638), Augustinus (1640), as set out in Pars Prior XXXIII-LIII.

title: Jansenius admits good works before justification, which the Protestants seem to deny
english: Thesis LIII. It is true that Jansenius nonetheless holds, with the Council of Trent, that a man can do certain good works before he is justified, and that not all the works done before justification are sins and displeasing to God.

The Protestants seem commonly to assert the opposite when they censure the canon of Trent that pronounces anathema on anyone who says that all works done before justification, in whatever way they are done, are sins.
translator_notes: Council of Trent, session 6 (1547), canon 7 on justification.
Cornelius Jansenius (1585-1638), Augustinus (1640), as set out in Pars Prior XXXIII-LIII.

title: The Protestants mean only that nothing good precedes justifying faith
english: Thesis LIV. But it is clear from what was set out above that when the Protestants teach that whatever is done before justification is sin and not a good work, and say with Augustine that good works do not go before the one who is to be justified but follow the one who is justified, they mean only this: that nothing good at all can be done before justifying faith, and that they include under justification the very faith by which we are justified. For them, then, a good work's being done before justification is the same as its being done by someone who is still an unbeliever.

If, however, someone distinguishes justification from justifying faith itself and takes it precisely for the sinner's absolution and the forgiveness of his sins, the same Protestants do not deny that certain good acts, works that please God, precede our justification.

First among these is the act of the faith that justifies the ungodly, the sinner's flight to God's mercy. Others are sorrow for past sins and hatred of them, the resolve to live a new life, prayer for God's grace, the hope of obtaining pardon, and similar acts. These exist in a man, in the order of nature, before his sins are forgiven and before he can be counted as justified.
translator_notes: Augustine, De fide et operibus 14.21.

title: Jansenius and Bellarmine read Trent's canon narrowly; the dispute is verbal
english: Thesis LV. On Jansenius's reading, the Council of Trent does not define that good works are done before faith, but only before justification. It pronounces anathema not on anyone who says that all works done before faith are sins, but only on anyone who says that everything done before justification is sin. Bellarmine himself explains the canon in just this way.

'The Council does not define,' he says, 'that the works of unbelievers are not sins, but that not all works that precede justification are sins. Even the works done by believers after they have fallen into sin precede justification. For the Council does not follow Luther's rules, who held that faith is lost through every mortal sin, but the Lord's rules, who in Luke 18 approved the prayer of the tax collector, who prayed in faith for the forgiveness of sins.

Nor does the same Council define that the works of sinning believers are not sins without qualification; it added "done in whatever way". So we are to understand that the Council defines only that certain works of sinning believers are not sins, namely those done with God's special help. Only about these did the Council properly mean to define anything, since its purpose was to treat of justification and of the works that dispose to it. And, as the same Council holds, only those works dispose to justification that take their beginning from God's prevenient grace' (On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 4).

From all this we may conclude that the dispute between the Protestants, who deny, and Jansenius, who affirms, that certain good works are done before justification is only about words. Indeed the same holds between the Protestants and the canon of Trent so often cited, as Jansenius and Bellarmine explain it.
translator_notes: Council of Trent, session 6 (1547), canon 7 on justification.
Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 5, chapter 4.
'Prevenient' renders gratia excitans, the grace that rouses the will first (Trent, session 6, chapter 5).

title: The bondage of sin leaves the sinner free in sinning
english: Thesis LVI. We have also shown clearly enough that the Protestants teach that in the state of fallen nature man without grace is the slave of sin and a kind of captive. On their view, though, this bondage to sin does not prevent him from being carried freely into sin, and from turning away from and neglecting the good the law commands.

In this he fully exercises the freedom of his choice, since he acts without compulsion and from the deliberate judgement of a corrupt reason, and when he commits this sin or that one, he has the power to refrain from it.

title: Grace leaves freedom intact, even for the strict Reformed
english: Thesis LVII. We also saw that they freely grant the doctors of the Roman School that divine grace, without which man can do nothing good, moves the human will in such a way that it does no harm at all to its freedom. Good works done by man through grace are also acts of free choice, acting not by its own powers but moved and roused by grace.

Indeed the same Protestants do not deny that, once grace is given, a man can act well or badly. Even the strictest defenders of grace among them, those called Reformed in a special sense, ascribe to grace an efficacy that bends and determines the will toward good, but still does not take from it every power of acting otherwise.
translator_notes: 'Those called Reformed in a special sense': the Calvinist churches, as distinct from the Lutherans.

title: Bellarmine's chief controversy is empty
english: Thesis LVIII. So the controversy Bellarmine calls the chief one, and imagines to lie between all the Protestants on one side and all the doctors of the Roman School on the other, is empty and amounts to nothing.

It is whether a man, given the help needed for acting, whatever that help may be, is truly and properly free in moral matters; or whether, given the help of grace, he truly has free choice, so that he can break or keep the precepts of the law. The Protestants deny neither of these; they gladly affirm both with the theologians of the Roman School.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 5, where he names this the principal controversy.

title: 'No free choice for moral good' means only the will's bondage to sin
english: Thesis LIX. Nor does it conflict with this that we often read in their writers that man after sin and before grace does not have free choice with regard to moral good.

By this, as we have said, they mean only that before grace the human will is the slave of sin and has no strength of its own for good. Yet the freedom essential to the will always remains in it, a freedom which, as the Roman School itself admits, the bondage of sin does not remove, as the example of the demons makes plain.
translator_notes: Thesis LIX closes De Gratiae necessitate; the next treatise, Theses in quibus exponuntur Variae distinctiones & acceptiones Gratiae, begins on print p. 500.

title: Why the distinctions of grace must be set out
english: Thesis I. Many questions about grace and free choice are argued with great heat, and to understand and clear them up it helps a great deal to know the various senses and distinctions of grace used in the Christian schools.
Our aim is to throw some light on the controversies that occupy and divide those schools. So it will serve that aim well if we set out these senses and distinctions as briefly and clearly as we can.
translator_notes: Before Thesis I the print has the heading: THESES THEOLOGICAE In quibus exponuntur Variae distinctiones & acceptiones Gratiae, quae apud Doctores Scholae Romanae sunt in Usu (Theological theses in which are set out the various distinctions and senses of grace in use among the doctors of the Roman School). Pitt 1675, book p. 500 (PDF 516); the English omits the heading, which is kept in the Latin lock.

title: Grace taken most generally: God's love, and any free gift
english: Thesis II. To begin with the Roman School: its theologians, Bellarmine and William Estius among others, observe that the word 'grace', taken in its most general sense, is used in two ways.

First it means God's own love and goodwill, by which he wishes men well and does them good. Second, it means any free benefit from God, anything he grants us graciously. They acknowledge that both senses are current in Holy Scripture, in the church writers, and in the scholastic doctors themselves.
The first they call eternal and uncreated grace, the second temporal and created grace. What others say with Estius comes to the same thing: grace can be understood either on God's side or on ours.
translator_notes: The print's footnotes: Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 1, chapters 1 and 2; Estius on the Sentences, book 2, distinction 26, section 1. They are kept in the Latin lock at the end of the thesis.
Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio (Controversiae, De gratia primi hominis ... et de libero arbitrio), book 1.
Guillaume Estius (Willem Hessels van Est, 1542-1613), commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences, book 2, distinction 26.

title: Grace taken most widely includes nature itself
english: Thesis III. God gives us freely not only what surpasses nature: the goods of nature themselves we also have from his free kindness, without any merit of ours. So grace in its widest sense, as the same doctors observe, is not set against nature but includes nature itself, which is sometimes called grace because it is a free benefit God has given us for nothing.
This sense is common enough in ordinary speech, where we credit the gifts and advantages of nature to God's grace. In Scripture and in the schools it is very rare and little used.

There grace is usually confined to those benefits of God that go beyond the order of nature: they do not flow from nature and are not needed to make it what it is or to preserve it, but are added to it by God's free kindness.

title: Grace opposed to nature: owed neither to merit nor to nature
english: Thesis IV. In this sense grace is set against nature. The gifts God confers on us above nature are free in a special way: they do not fall under the person's merit, and they are not owed to nature either.

God, absolutely speaking, owes nothing to anyone and is bound to nothing. Yet once he wills that a creature should exist and act, he must in a way supply it with whatever it cannot exist or act without.

title: Adam's grace and Christ's grace
english: Thesis V. Some doctors of the Roman School take care to divide this grace that is set against nature into two: the grace given to man before the fall, and the grace given to fallen man through Christ's merit.

They call the first the grace of Adam and the second the grace of Christ; the first the grace of health and the second healing grace. The first was given to a man who had not earned it, the second to one who was actually unworthy of it.

title: Jansenius: Adam's help 'without which', Christ's help 'by which'
english: Thesis VI. Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, presses this distinction again and again as of the greatest weight in the book he titled Augustinus, where he collects and explains the difference between the two graces at length from Augustine.
He puts the difference here. The grace given to man before the fall was a help without which the first man could not will good, but it did not make him actually will it.
The grace Christ gives fallen man makes him actually will. It is not merely a help without which, but a help by which the willing of good is itself produced in him.
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (1640), De gratia Christi salvatoris.
The 'help without which' and 'help by which' (adjutorium sine quo non, adjutorium quo) come from Augustine, De correptione et gratia 11.31-12.34.

title: Jansenius on the two kinds of help (De gratia Christi 2.4)
english: Thesis VII. For he observes that the will's helps are of two kinds. One is a help without which the will cannot will, yet in such a way that willing or not willing, using the help or not using it, is left to its free choice. The other is a help by which it is determinately brought about that the will wills.

He holds that the grace of man in his integrity was a help of the first kind, and that the grace by which Christ heals corrupt man is a help of the second kind. 'The difference between the two graces, of health and of healing,' he says, 'lies in this: the help of that first integrity so helped the will that the will itself might work with it, if it chose; now the help itself makes it will.

That is, before the ruin the help was such that its influence on the work, just like the will's, hung on the free will's own nod, so that the indifference of liberty, able to bend either way, remained intact. Now, after the ruin, it is such that it makes the will assent, and flow into the work, and will' (De gratia Christi salvatoris, book 2, chapter 4).
