translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (1640), De gratia Christi salvatoris. The print repeats 'in eo' ('In eo ... differentia in eo sita est'); the lock keeps it and the English renders it once.
'Influere' is rendered 'flow into the work', matching 'influxus ... in opus' earlier in the quotation; 'annuere' is 'assent' (literally 'nod assent').

title: Jansenius' contrasts between the grace of the first and second Adam
english: Thesis VIII. In keeping with this he teaches throughout the work that the chief difference between the grace of the first Adam and that of the second is this: the first gave man the power to do good if he willed, while the second gives him besides the willing itself.

The first was subject to the will's nod and to its power of command; the second subjects the will to its own nod and command. The first followed the will's lead with the obedience of a servant at its heels; the second, ruling with authority, draws the will after it like such a servant.
The first went along with the will as the will went ahead, and could be overcome and turned aside. The second leads and drives the will as it follows, and can be neither overcome nor turned aside.
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (1640), De gratia Christi salvatoris.

title: Molinists against Jansenius: grace in the will's power
english: Thesis IX. On this point Jansenius has many followers, namely those who call themselves disciples of Augustine in a special sense. Even so, this teaching of his is rejected by most of the Roman School. Both the followers of the method and teaching of Molina the Jesuit and those called the recent Thomists openly oppose it.

The first group hold that the grace of Christ, no less than the grace given to the first man before he fell, is in the will's power in such a way that, by its inborn liberty, the will can use it or not use it, and in fact often does not.
So, on their view, it depends on free choice whether Christ's grace is efficacious or not, and whether it achieves its effect in a man's conversion or fails to.
translator_notes: Luis de Molina SJ, Concordia liberi arbitrii cum gratiae donis (1588).

title: The recent Thomists: physical predetermination even in Adam
english: Thesis X. Those called the recent Thomists, on the other hand, think that a grace which predetermines the will and applies it efficaciously to good was not foreign to the state of innocence.

If Adam did any good before he sinned, as he certainly did, he did it, they say, by the power of a grace that physically predetermined his will: a grace that did not merely give his will the ability to do good but efficaciously moved it to good beforehand.
On their principles, without this efficacious premotion from God man's will cannot be carried toward good in any of its states.

title: Grace freely given and grace that makes pleasing
english: Thesis XI. The grace conferred on corrupt man through Christ is commonly divided in the Roman School into what they call grace freely given and the grace that makes pleasing.
In the minds of that School's doctors the division is not meant to imply that some grace is not freely given, for they grant that the grace that makes pleasing is also given freely.
Rather, as often happens elsewhere, one species that has no name of its own is left with the name of the genus, as Bellarmine points out in the place cited above.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio (Controversiae, De gratia primi hominis ... et de libero arbitrio), book 1. (chapters 1-2, cited in Thesis II).

title: The two defined: for others' salvation, or chiefly one's own
english: Thesis XII. So for them grace freely given is a supernatural gift, given without any debt, chiefly for the spiritual salvation of others. The grace that makes pleasing is a supernatural gift, given without any debt, chiefly for each person's own spiritual salvation.

Both kinds serve the salvation of the receiver and of others alike. The difference is that the grace that makes pleasing is given chiefly for the salvation of the one who receives it and only secondarily for others: first we ourselves are to be made holy and righteous, and then others are to see our good works and glorify our Father in heaven.

Grace freely given, by contrast, looks chiefly to the salvation of others. It consists of gifts that do not of themselves directly serve the salvation of the person in whom they are, but are a great help in bringing others to repentance and faith.
translator_notes: 'That others may see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven' is Matthew 5:16.

title: What belongs to grace freely given (1 Corinthians 12)
english: Thesis XIII. Grace freely given therefore includes the word of knowledge, the word of wisdom, the gift of prophecy, the discerning of spirits, kinds of tongues, the working of miracles, the gift of healing, and the other gifts of this kind that the Apostle lists in 1 Corinthians 12.

Some of these gifts bring bodily benefits, as the gift of healing brings good health. But since the chief and final end of all grace freely given is the eternal salvation of the soul, the definition given above said that all such grace is conferred for the spiritual salvation of others.
translator_notes: The list follows 1 Corinthians 12:8-10 in the Vulgate's terms (sermo sapientiae, sermo scientiae, gratia sanitatum, operatio virtutum, genera linguarum, discretio spirituum).

title: What the grace that makes pleasing includes, up to eternal life
english: Thesis XIV. Under the grace that makes pleasing they include everything in which any part or beginning of salvation and righteousness consists: everything that either makes a man pleasing to God and his friend, or disposes him to reconciliation and friendship with God and is of itself directed to that end.

To this class belong faith, hope and good will, indeed any beginning at all of faith and good will; repentance, the forgiveness of sins, charity, righteousness, good works, the virtues and their growth, perseverance, and finally eternal life itself. Those earlier benefits of God are destined for eternal life as for grace brought to completion, and of it the Apostle says, 'The grace of God is eternal life' (Romans 6). So Estius on the Sentences, book 2, distinction 26, paragraph 1.
translator_notes: Guillaume Estius (Willem Hessels van Est, 1542-1613), commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences, book 2, distinction 26.
'Gratia Dei vita aeterna' is the Vulgate of Romans 6:23.

title: Why 'makes pleasing': both effect and object of God's love
english: Thesis XV. They call it the grace that makes pleasing because it places in a man something that pleases God and wins his approval, and so makes the man, at least to some degree and in some respect, pleasing and acceptable to God.

They do not mean that the grace they place in man under that name comes before every act of God's love toward us, or is strictly the cause of the love God bears him. They teach that this grace is at once the effect and the object of God's love.

It comes from the love by which God wishes man well, being the greatest good God bestows on him, and to that extent it comes after God's love. At the same time it is something highly pleasing to God, and because of it a man cannot fail to be pleasing to him. To that extent it is the object of God's love and in some way comes before his love for us.

title: Actual and habitual grace; Bellarmine's 'grace of special help'
english: Thesis XVI. The Roman School divides the grace that makes pleasing into actual and habitual grace, or, which comes to nearly the same thing, into permanent grace and the grace of special help, as Bellarmine prefers to put it (De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 1, chapter 2).

There is in fact some difference to be noted between actual grace and this grace of special help. The grace of special help means not our good actions themselves but rather a kind of principle of them, whereas our good works are themselves a kind of actual grace and fall under that term.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio (Controversiae, De gratia primi hominis ... et de libero arbitrio), book 1.
'Eorum' (plural masculine) refers loosely to the actions; rendered 'of them'.

title: Habitual grace once doubtful: Vienne and Trent
english: Thesis XVII. Commonly accepted as this division is, someone has nevertheless rejected it. No theologian of the Roman Church has ever doubted that there is some actual grace of God in man. Habitual grace is another matter.

The scholastic doctors admit that in the Roman Church the point was not formerly so settled. It seems to have been defined only at the Council of Vienne under Clement V and at the Council of Trent in the last century; before that it was somewhat doubtful and open to dispute whether any habitual grace is given.
translator_notes: Council of Vienne (1311-1312) under Clement V, constitution Fidei catholicae, preferring the opinion that infused grace and virtues are given to infants in baptism.
Council of Trent, session 6 (1547), on justification; 'the former century' is the sixteenth, Le Blanc writing in the seventeenth.

title: Pighius against habitual grace
english: Thesis XVIII. Indeed Albert Pighius, a doctor of some fame, dared on this point to set himself against the common view of the Roman School a little before the time of the Council of Trent.

As Bellarmine reports, these are his words in the fifth book of his work On Free Choice: 'We shall look for the various senses of grace not in the schools but in Holy Scripture. For in the schools they generally imagine some quality created in (increatam) our soul by God, either the same as the habit of charity or distinct from it. I judge all this to be invented, with no authority from Scripture.'
translator_notes: Albert Pighius, De libero hominis arbitrio et divina gratia libri decem (Cologne, 1542), book 5, fol. 76r, as reported by Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 1, chapter 3 (Opera omnia, Vives ed., vol. 5).

'Increatam' is read as the participle of increo, 'created in', not 'uncreated'. Pighius's own text (1542, book 5, fol. 76r) and Bellarmine's quotation of it both read 'imaginantur gratiam Dei qualitatem aliquam increatam animae nostrae a Deo' (Le Blanc drops 'gratiam Dei'). The word describes the scholastic view Pighius rejects: a quality put into the soul by God, either the habit of charity or distinct from it. In the same chapter Bellarmine defends that view as 'habitum supernaturalem a Deo nobis infundi' and grace as 'habitum, sive qualitatem creatam'. Pighius's own view was that grace in Scripture is God's favour (his next pages gloss 'finding grace in someone's eyes' as being loved freely), and Bellarmine groups him with Calvin's 'gratuita acceptione'. In scholastic terms that favour is 'gratia increata' (Thesis II; Lombard's uncreated charity, the Holy Spirit), but here the word qualifies the created quality Pighius denies, not his own view.
'In illis' ('in those') refers back to the schools; the English makes this explicit.

title: After Trent: is habitual grace of faith? Soto denies
english: Thesis XIX. Since the Council of Trent nobody follows Pighius, and his view is commonly condemned, at the least as very rash. Even so, the theologians of the Roman School still argue among themselves whether it is a matter of faith that habitual grace is given, and whether those councils meant to define the point as of faith.
After the Council of Trent, Domingo de Soto, a distinguished doctor who had been present at it, denied that they did. Others commonly hold it more probable that this teaching is of faith.
translator_notes: Domingo de Soto OP (1494-1560), theologian at Trent, author of De natura et gratia (1547).

title: Habitual grace includes infused virtues and justifying grace
english: Thesis XX. Under habitual grace they include all the infused habits of the virtues, and above all the grace in which, on their view, consists the righteousness by which we are formally justified before God.
They call this justifying grace, and usually just 'grace' with nothing added, and in common usage the name 'grace that makes pleasing' is usually confined to it.

title: The stricter sense of 'grace that makes pleasing'; is it charity?
english: Thesis XXI. It should be understood that writers of the Roman Church ordinarily take the grace that makes pleasing in a far narrower sense than in the division just given. There it is set against grace freely given in such a way that it covers every inward gift that of itself helps the receiver's salvation and is directed to it.
In the narrower sense they mean by it a habit, a kind of quality, by which a man is properly and formally made righteous and so simply pleasing to God and his friend.
They debate many questions among themselves about this grace. The chief is whether it is a habit distinct from charity or entirely the same as charity.

title: Thomas: grace really distinct from charity, seated in the soul's essence
english: Thesis XXII. Thomas, the prince of the Roman School, and very many others teach that this justifying grace that makes pleasing is a quality really distinct from charity and from all the other habits of the virtues.

They hold that the subject of grace is the very substance of the soul, where it has its seat directly, while the subject of charity and the other virtues is the soul's powers, that is, the mind and the will. In their view grace stands to the infused virtues as the soul stands to its powers.

The soul gives natural being to the body, and from it flow the powers that are its instruments. In the same way the grace in question gives the soul a kind of supernatural being, and from it flow, in a manner, the habits of the infused virtues, which are the proximate principles of supernatural action.
translator_notes: Thomas Aquinas, Summa theologiae I-II, q. 110, aa. 3-4.

title: Durandus: grace and charity differ only in name
english: Thesis XXIII. Some, on the other hand, such as Durandus, hold that there is no difference at all between grace and charity. They say the two are not distinguished even in concept, only in name.

Charity and grace, on this view, are no more distinct than being dear and being pleasing: it is called grace because by it a man becomes pleasing (gratus) to God, and charity because by it he is made dear (charus) to God.
translator_notes: Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, on the Sentences, book 2, distinction 26.

title: Bellarmine's middle way: one habit, distinct only in reason
english: Thesis XXIV. A great many others take a kind of middle way. They say that grace and charity are not wholly indistinct, yet are distinguished not in reality but only in concept.

Their view is that one and the same habit is called grace insofar as it looks to its subject, adorns the man in whom it dwells and makes him pleasing and lovable to God. Insofar as it looks to the work and makes the will ready to love God above all things, it is properly called charity. This is Bellarmine's view (De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 1, chapter 6).
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio (Controversiae, De gratia primi hominis ... et de libero arbitrio), book 1.
The verb under a blot in this copy is read 'exornat' (adorns); 'exo...t' is visible and the djvu text supports the length.

title: Actual grace: internal, not external, helps
english: Thesis XXV. As for actual grace, or the grace of special help as Bellarmine calls it, to see what they mean by the term we must first note that the schools usually divide the helps by which God assists a man in acting into internal and external.

External helps are occasions and opportunities for acting, examples, counsels, precepts, exhortations and many others it would take too long to go through one by one. Internal helps consist in certain motions of the soul. External helps have nothing to do with the grace now in question, which is confined to the internal ones.

title: General and special help; Bellarmine's definition
english: Thesis XXVI. The Roman School further divides this internal help of God, which men need in order to act, into general and special. General help is the help by which God concurs with all creatures and works with them in their acting, whether they act well or badly, and whether what they do lies within the powers and scope of nature or goes somewhat beyond it.

For in the common view of the Roman School whatever is positive even in evil acts is good, and cannot come about without God's cooperation. Special help is help that God gives only for good acts that exceed the powers of nature.
So Bellarmine defines the grace of special help as 'the motion of God by which man is helped toward actions that in some way surpass his nature'.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio (Controversiae, De gratia primi hominis ... et de libero arbitrio), book 1.

title: Three ways an act surpasses nature's powers (Bellarmine)
english: Thesis XXVII. Bellarmine observes that an action can surpass the powers of nature in three ways. The first is simply and absolutely, when the action is by its kind of a higher order than natural things. Such are the acts of the theological virtues of faith, hope and charity, which are not acquired by repeated practice but are infused into the soul by God.
The second is not simply but because of the state of sin, since man, weakened by sin, cannot easily do many things without such help.

The third is because of manner, place, time or some other circumstance: something that does not exceed nature's powers by its kind or because of man's state may still exceed them because of the circumstances. 'So,' he says, 'a righteous man will easily be able to keep some commandment of the Decalogue if no temptation from the devil comes upon him from outside. But if such temptation comes, he will not be able to do it without special help.'
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio (Controversiae, De gratia primi hominis ... et de libero arbitrio), book 1. Le Blanc paraphrases the three modes and then quotes.

title: Actual grace: the good motions God stirs in us
english: Thesis XXVIII. In the view of the doctors of the Roman School, then, actual grace covers all the good and saving motions God stirs up in our souls.
These motions are God's, because they come from him. They are ours too, because they are vital acts drawn out of our own faculties as God moves them in a special way.

title: Motions of intellect and of will
english: Thesis XXIX. These good motions concern either the intellect or the will. Those of the intellect are inward illuminations and devout thoughts sent by God, in a word any enlightenings and inspirations that lead the mind to know saving truth.
Those of the will are devout desires and saving motions and affections that touch the will directly.

title: Gregory of Valencia: God's motions and our responses
english: Thesis XXX. Gregory of Valencia, to make the teaching clearer, divides the motions that belong to actual grace into two kinds.

'One kind,' he says, 'consists of the motions by which God rouses, calls and invites our minds to turn to him through faith, hope, charity, repentance and acts of that sort. The other consists of the motions or acts by which we answer God as he rouses, calls and invites us, and open the door of our mind when we turn to him' (tome 2, disputation 8, question 3, point 2).
translator_notes: Gregory of Valencia SJ, Commentarii theologici, tome 2, disputation 8, question 3.
The 'door of the mind' echoes Revelation 3:20, cited in Thesis XXXII.

title: Indeliberate and deliberate motions
english: Thesis XXXI. According to him, the motions of the first kind are indeliberate: our faculties produce them only physically, not freely. Those of the second kind are free and deliberate.

The first kind covers devout thoughts and devout desires that God sends directly, without our consent. The second covers all the acts of the Christian virtues that we bring forth with the help of God's grace.
translator_notes: Gregory of Valencia SJ, Commentarii theologici, tome 2, disputation 8, question 3.

title: Rousing and assisting grace: Bellarmine and the Jesuits
english: Thesis XXXII. The grace of special help, or actual grace as others call it, is usually divided into rousing grace and assisting grace, or in Bellarmine's terms into rousing help and assisting help. The theologians of the Roman School do not all explain this distinction the same way.

Bellarmine and all the Jesuits with him, and very many others, say that rousing grace, which they also call calling grace, covers the divine enlightenings and inspirations by which God knocks at our heart to wake us from the sleep of sin or of slackness in good works.

Assisting grace, or the grace of assisting help, they say, covers God's cooperation, guidance and protection, by which we are helped both to choose and to do what God, going before us, has inspired. So Revelation 3: 'Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice, I will come in to him', and so on. These are Bellarmine's words (book 1, On Free Choice, chapter 2).
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio (Controversiae, De gratia primi hominis ... et de libero arbitrio), book 1. Le Blanc cites it here as 'lib. 1. de lib. Arbitrio'; it is the same work cited in Theses XVI and XXIV.
Two words under blots in this copy are read 'eligamus' (el...amus visible) and 'sto' (Ecce sto, the Vulgate of Revelation 3:20).

title: Gregory of Valencia agrees: calling and assisting grace
english: Thesis XXXIII. Gregory of Valencia's account comes to the same thing. 'Theologians,' he says, 'give the name calling or rousing grace to certain divine inspirations, motions stirred up by God in a man's mind, by which God draws and invites the man to himself and moves him to devout and saving actions, so that he may turn to God by acts of faith, hope, charity and repentance.

They call assisting grace those gifts and benefits by which God helps a man who consents to the divine calling and rousing: both in the very act of consenting and turning, and in the other acts of devotion by which one presses on toward blessedness.

So this assisting grace includes first of all God's special concurrence with man in conversion, that is, in believing, hoping, loving, repenting and so on. It also includes his guarding man with particular care and providence, protecting him from evil, directing and spurring him to good, and giving him strength through various inspirations to overcome temptations and keep the commandments' (tome 2, disputation 8, question 3, point 3).
translator_notes: Gregory of Valencia SJ, Commentarii theologici, tome 2, disputation 8, question 3.
The print reads 'stimulat ab bonum'; the lock keeps it and the English follows the evident sense 'ad bonum' (to good).

title: Rousing grace on the first view: enlightenment and stirrings before consent
english: Thesis XXXIV. On the view of these doctors, then, rousing grace consists in an enlightening of the mind and in devout thoughts, feelings and desires that God stirs up directly in human souls without waiting for their consent.

The human mind and will do take a physical part in these, since they are living acts that come from those faculties. But they do not take part freely, because these are undeliberate acts, which come before the mind has weighed anything and before the will has chosen.
translator_notes: 'These doctors' are Bellarmine and Gregory of Valencia, quoted in Theses XXXII-XXXIII.

title: Assisting grace on the first view: a partial cause, not prior in nature
english: Thesis XXXV. Assisting grace, in the opinion of the same doctors, consists chiefly in a gift and help of the supernatural order by which the will is lifted up and helped to produce acts beyond its natural strength.

This help moves the will physically and effectively. Yet it does not concur in the supernatural work before free choice in the order of nature, and with regard to the supernatural act it is not, strictly, the total cause but only a partial one.

title: What rousing grace includes: inner hearing and sudden divine flashes
english: Thesis XXXVI. Those who list more precisely what this rousing grace consists of include in it, first, an inner hearing and preliminary grasp of the truths of faith, which comes before assent.

Next they include certain divine flashes that strike our mind so suddenly that, in a new and unfamiliar light, we find ourselves knowing and seeing the greatness and worth of divine things, or else the foulness of sin, the smallness of human affairs and the like. When these are noticed and weighed with more attention, they move a person powerfully to turn wholly to God.

title: Delight in the will and movements of the appetite
english: Thesis XXXVII. Under this heading they also place an inner delight in the will, which usually follows such enlightenments.

They add various movements that God stirs up in the appetite, such as love, fear, hope, sorrow, shame and similar feelings. By these the higher reason is sometimes drawn and inclined to pursue virtue and turn away from vice.
translator_notes: Two words are blotted in the print. The lock reads 'illustrationibus' (visible '...lu...rationibus'; Le Blanc uses 'illustrationes' in Theses XXXIX and XLIV) and 'appetitu' (visible 'appe-'; compare 'tam in intellectu, quam in appetitu' in Thesis XXXVIII).
'Confusio' is taken in its moral sense, shame.

title: Outward occasions counted as rousing grace (Valencia, Alvarez)
english: Thesis XXXVIII. Indeed, although that special help, which they divide into rousing and assisting, strictly consists in inward movements of the soul, as has been said, many also count certain outward things as rousing grace. These are the occasions and opportunities that God's providence supplies to a person so that such movements may be stirred in him, in both the intellect and the appetite.
Examples are sickness, dangers, good companions, misfortunes and various other events, as may be seen in Gregory of Valencia at the place just cited.

Alvarez likewise notes that rousing grace includes both an outward rousing, which comes through creatures and signs perceived by the senses, and an inward one, which comes directly from God when he puts devout thoughts into the mind and sets before it what can lead free choice to the act of faith and charity and to other supernatural works (De auxiliis divinae gratiae, book 8, disputation 75).
translator_notes: Gregory of Valencia SJ, Commentarii theologici, tome 2, disputation 8, question 3.
Diego Alvarez OP (d. 1635), De auxiliis divinae gratiae et humani arbitrii viribus (Rome, 1610).

title: The second view: knocking is not yet rousing (Revelation 3:20)
english: Thesis XXXIX. Other theologians of the Roman school, however, explain and understand the division of grace into rousing and assisting in quite another way. From what has been said it is clear that for the first group rousing grace is the grace by which a person is roused and urged toward good even though he does not yet will it, and assisting grace is the grace by which he is helped to will it and then to do it.
To this they apply the text of Revelation: 'Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door to me, I will come in to him,' and so on.

The second group, whom we are now discussing, holds that this text should not be taken of rousing grace, because knocking and rousing are not the same thing. Many people are knocked at, both through the outward ministry of preaching, exhortation and rebuke and through inward enlightenments and inspirations, and yet are not roused from the sleep of sin or neglect. They do not wake up but stay sound asleep, and so they cannot yet be said to have rousing grace.
It is the same with people held by bodily sleep: someone knocks, yet they do not wake at once.

title: Estius: rousing grace actually wakes the sinner
english: Thesis XL. By rousing grace, then, they mean the grace by which a sinner, or one who has stopped doing good and lies as if sunk in a kind of sleep, is given the thought, desire and will to do a good work, in such a way that he can now be said to be truly roused from the sleep of sin or from neglect of good works.
By assisting grace they mean the grace by which someone already roused is helped to will more perfectly what he has begun to will, and to carry out what he has already willed.

'Grace,' they say, 'rouses us to will and assists us to do. Willing belongs to rousing grace; doing and completing belong to assisting grace.' This is the interpretation of William Estius on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 26, paragraph 11.
translator_notes: Guillaume Estius (Willem Hessels van Est, 1542-1613), commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences, book 2, distinction 26.

title: Jansenius on rousing and assisting grace
english: Thesis XLI. Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, explains this division of grace into rousing and assisting in the same way, in book 4, chapter 16 of his treatise on the grace of Christ the Saviour.

'Rousing grace,' he says, 'is properly the grace that stirs up a good movement in the will's power where there was only a bad one, or that wakes the will's power, which is dead and asleep toward God, so that once it has received the movement of willing well it may begin to live and stay awake.

In the same way Augustine and the Fathers properly give the name assisting grace to the grace that, once the movement of good will has been stirred and received, helps the man who already wills and strives, either to carry out what he has willed, or to will more strongly what he has begun to will, and to overcome the desire of the flesh that stubbornly resists the will he has received.'

To explain this more clearly, he teaches in the preceding pages that rousing, in this division, is not so much any urging or prompting to act as the first awakening, rousing or flaring up of a good volition that was asleep, dead and extinguished.
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (1640), De gratia Christi salvatoris. Book 4, chapter 16.

title: Operating and cooperating grace: Augustine's words
english: Thesis XLII. In the Roman schools, too, the division of grace into operating and cooperating is familiar and very well known. It is drawn from Augustine's words in On Grace and Free Choice, chapter 17: 'He works at the start, so that we may will; and he cooperates with those who will, to bring the work to completion.' A little later he says: 'He works without us so that we may will; but when we will, and will in such a way that we act, he cooperates with us.'
So on a common and rather loose understanding, operating grace is the grace that works alone, without us, and cooperating grace is the grace that does not work without us but with which we cooperate.
translator_notes: Augustine, De gratia et libero arbitrio 17.33.

title: The older scholastics: operating grace as the habit of grace
english: Thesis XLIII. The theologians of the Roman Church, however, do not agree on which grace it is that works without us, or which grace cooperates with us, or how and how far we cooperate with it.

The older scholastics, according to Bellarmine, give the name operating grace to the habit of grace itself, insofar as it formally makes us righteous and pleasing to God, since God does this in us without us. They take cooperating grace to be the same habit insofar as it is the source of meritorious works: when we do good works, grace is not the only thing at work in us, but we ourselves also truly cooperate.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 1, chapter 14 (Opera omnia, Vives ed., vol. 5), checked against the Vives text. Bellarmine has 'gratiam operantem vocant ipsum habitum gratiae, ut formaliter nos justos et gratos Deo facit; id enim Deus in nobis sine nobis facit'.
Two words are blotted in the print; the lock reads 'esse' ('Gratiam cooperantem esse volunt') and 'bona' ('Quum enim bona opera facimus') from Bellarmine's text of the same passage.

title: The moderns: operating grace produces undeliberate movements
english: Thesis XLIV. Most present-day doctors of the Roman Church, however, take operating grace to mean the grace by which those movements of the soul are produced in us that are undeliberate and do not depend on our will's free consent.
These are devout thoughts, enlightenments of the mind and also certain devout desires, by which God moves and urges us toward faith and conversion.

title: 'Without us': not physically passive, but not freely concurring
english: Thesis XLV. They point out that this grace is rightly said to work in us without us, not because our mind and will are merely passive toward the movements it produces in us, for since these are living movements they must, they say, come efficiently from a living power.
It is said so rather because by this grace God works in us without our concurring morally, that is, freely, though not without our acting physically.

For, as they say, the actions usually credited to us are not those that happen without freedom, which are called acts of a man, but only those to which we freely determine ourselves, which are properly called human acts.
translator_notes: Actiones hominis and actiones humanae: the scholastic distinction between 'acts of a man' (anything a human being does, including undeliberate acts) and 'human acts' (free, deliberate acts).

title: The moderns: cooperating grace produces free consent
english: Thesis XLVI. Accordingly, by cooperating grace they mean the grace that produces in us the free consent of the will by which we obey God's call, and the further acts of our will by which we keep on in good and turn more and more to God.
They say it is called cooperating rather than operating because we concur with it freely, and the acts credited to it come not from grace alone but also from our free choice.

title: How the Jesuits read Augustine (Becanus, Peter of Saint Joseph)
english: Thesis XLVII. Augustine's statement that grace works without us so that we may will, they take to refer to the undeliberate act of the will, an imperfect sort of desire. His addition, that when we will he cooperates with us, they take to refer to the completed act of the will, a choice that is perfect and deliberate.

This is how the Jesuits commonly explain operating and cooperating grace today, together with very many doctors of the Roman Church who side with them against the Dominicans and the more recent Thomists.

This may be seen in Becanus's short treatise De auxiliis gratiae juxta Catholicos, which is among his minor works, and in Peter of Saint Joseph, Idea theologiae speculativae, book 4, chapter 6, resolution 4.
translator_notes: Augustine, De gratia et libero arbitrio 17.33.
Martin Becanus SJ (1563-1624); the treatise is among his Opuscula theologica.
Pierre de Saint-Joseph (Petrus a Sancto Joseph, Feuillant, 1594-1662), Idea theologiae speculativae.

title: Vasquez: the holy thought before consent; merit in the consent
english: Thesis XLVIII. Gabriel Vasquez teaches in agreement with them that operating grace is the holy thought itself, which comes before consent, and likewise the sudden movement of the will that arises from that devout thought without our freedom, by which we are held back from evil and urged toward good.
Cooperating grace, he says, lies in the free consent, in which some merit is already found, either merit that strictly deserves eternal life or merit that obtains some gift by asking.

For God works in us without us the holy thought and the first undeliberate movement of the will, which together are the beginning of good action and of our salvation; but the consent itself that we give to this call God works with us (on Thomas, part 1, tome 1, disputation 88, chapter 6, number 20).
translator_notes: Gabriel Vasquez SJ (1549-1604), commentaries on Thomas Aquinas's Summa.
Meritum condignum and impetratorium: merit that deserves its reward in strict justice, and merit that obtains a gift by way of petition.
The reference is given as printed ('in 1. Thom. to. 1.'); the mark after '1' is damaged in the print.

title: Andres de Vega: man wholly passive, with the Nominalists
english: Thesis XLIX. Andres de Vega, however, a man of no small note among the doctors who attended the Council of Trent, assigns to operating grace the same things as the doctors just named, namely the holy thought and the first movement of the will by which a person is suddenly moved toward good. But he holds that God is said to work these in us without us for a different reason.

His reason is that in producing that movement and that holy thought God alone acts physically, while the man is entirely passive: in it he not only does not act freely, but does not even produce any action physically.

What led this doctor to that view is that, with the scholastics called Nominalists, he thought that God, as sole efficient cause, could produce in a man an act of understanding or of willing while the intellect and will were wholly passive and did nothing at all, even though the man shaped by that quality is said to understand and to will.

Though these are expressed grammatically as a man's actions, in that case they are not really actions or products of the mind and will, but only qualities that by their formal effect make the man understanding and willing. On this see Vasquez, chapter 3 of the disputation just cited.
translator_notes: Andres de Vega OFM (1498-1549), theologian at the Council of Trent, author of De justificatione doctrina universa.
The print reads 'Mominales'; the lock keeps it, and the English follows the evident sense 'Nominales' (the Nominalists).

title: A third view: operating grace effects the first deliberate act
english: Thesis L. Others, however, think that operating grace means the grace that produces in a person the first act of deliberate will, such as conversion, whether from unbelief to faith or from other sins to repentance.

By cooperating grace they mean the grace that produces the later acts of the will, such as willing to pray, willing to do good works and the like. On this view operating grace is simply special, efficacious help with regard to the will's first act, and cooperating grace is likewise special and efficacious help with regard to the acts that follow.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 1, chapter 14 (Opera omnia, Vives ed., vol. 5), checked against the Vives text. The definition is Bellarmine's own ('Dicendum igitur est, gratiam operantem illam esse, quae efficit in homine primum actum deliberatae voluntatis').

title: Bellarmine: God alone is the moral cause of the first willing
english: Thesis LI. This is Bellarmine's view. He argues that God can rightly be said to work in us without us that first deliberate act of willing by which we turn to God, even though our will produces it freely and not merely physically.

'If we consider the efficient cause of this act,' he says, 'it is not only God through special help but also the will through free choice, and in this sense God does not work it without us. But if we consider its moral cause, that is, the cause that persuades, urges and advises, that cause is God alone.
For the will does not drive itself by persuading and urging itself to will what it does not will; it is God who, speaking inwardly to the soul by his inspirations, urges and persuades it to will.'

On his view, then, operating grace is the grace that comes before our effort and diligence and brings it about that we will what we did not will before. It does so without our working to make ourselves will, though not without our freely consenting when we will.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 1, chapter 14 (Opera omnia, Vives ed., vol. 5), checked against the Vives text.

title: Bellarmine: cooperating grace for the later acts
english: Thesis LII. In his view the grace needed for the will's later acts, after the first, is called cooperating, because once we have begun to turn to God we not only produce the later acts through free choice with God's help, but also spur and drive ourselves to them, with God cooperating.

'So operating grace,' he says, 'is the grace that makes us will to believe, since this happens in us without our asking for it, much less toiling and striving for it; and cooperating grace is the grace that makes us will to pray, fast and give alms, since this does not happen except with our effort and diligence cooperating.'

From this he concludes that God does not work our willing without us, but only works without us the fact that we will. For we cooperate with God in willing, that is, in freely producing the act of willing, but we do not cooperate in bringing it about that we will, because we do not ourselves move and spur ourselves to will; he alone moves and drives us by an inward inspiration.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 1, chapter 14 (Opera omnia, Vives ed., vol. 5), checked against the Vives text.

title: Estius: the first good movement and Paul's conversion
english: Thesis LIII. Estius's teaching comes to the same. Operating grace, he says, is commonly said to work in us without us because the first act of conversion, the first good movement of the will, which is the effect of that grace, does indeed come from the will as from an active and free source. Yet God works it by his grace without any earlier movement of the will in us by which we strive or aspire toward that first movement, or by which the will commands it of itself.

Indeed a good disposition of the will is sometimes breathed into a person even while he strongly resists, as happened with Paul. His conversion, as regards that change from evil to good brought about by operating grace, is the pattern and model for the conversion of all sinners, since by God's grace they are turned from being averse and made willing from being unwilling.

The later acts of the will that follow that first one, by which we go on clinging to God, are also worked in us by God's grace. But our will, now turned to God, not only produces them freely but also commands them of itself through other earlier acts.
In this way it cooperates with divine grace in a special manner, and for this reason the grace is called cooperating in this respect (on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 26, section 11).
translator_notes: Guillaume Estius (Willem Hessels van Est, 1542-1613), commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences, book 2, distinction 26. Section 11.
'Peccatorum' is read as the genitive plural of peccator (sinners), as the next sentence ('ex nolentibus volentes redduntur') requires.

title: Jansenius: operating grace makes the first good will
english: Thesis LIV. Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, explains operating and cooperating grace in much the same way. 'Operating grace,' he says, 'is the grace that by itself, with no prior effort, prayer or merit on man's part, works the will, or the willing, by which the will is made good from bad and just from unjust.

Cooperating grace is the grace that cooperates with a man who already wills and strives, by enlarging that will and strengthening it to firmness, so that he may accomplish and complete what he has willed and is striving for.'

In the same place he teaches from Augustine that operating grace is the grace by which, when we did not will before, we are brought to will; and cooperating grace the grace by which, when we already actually will, we are brought to will more strongly, so that by overcoming every obstacle we also actually do it. The first works so that we have a good will, a willing of good, in some way or other; the second, so that this good will may be enlarged and strengthened.

From this he concludes that cooperating grace is never spoken of with respect to the first good will, when the will's power breaks out into it, since that first will, or good volition, is the effect of operating grace alone. It is spoken of only with respect to good will after a person has begun to will, so that this willing may last, grow and be enriched with good works as with fruit.
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (1640), De gratia Christi salvatoris. Book 4, chapter 15 (cited at the end of Thesis LV).

title: Jansenius: no merit before the first good will; cooperating grace and growth
english: Thesis LV. Operating grace, then, as he carefully observes, alone produces the first good will in a person. This is not because the person does not at the same time contribute his own influence to that will, that is, to the will's movement and consent, but because grace works that movement while we contribute nothing toward having it, whether by asking, desiring, striving or meditating, and so bring no good merit whatever with respect to that will.
Such merit is impossible, he says, for the very reason that this is laid down to be the first good will, to which one turns from a bad will.

Cooperating grace, in turn, is so called because it works something in us not alone but with us cooperating at the same time. It does so not merely by a simultaneous influence, by which we cooperate with operating grace too, but ahead of that grace's effect, by willing, believing, desiring, asking, knocking, taking pains and so even meriting.
Thus the effect of cooperating grace is the whole growth of that first good will, up to the height of human perfection (On the Grace of Christ the Saviour, book 4, chapter 15).
translator_notes: Cornelius Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (1640), De gratia Christi salvatoris. Book 4, chapter 15.

title: Alvarez: both graces in every devout work, by physical predetermination
english: Thesis LVI. Diego Alvarez's view differs from all of these. He holds that in every devout work, whether inward or outward, whether it is the first by which we turn to God or any later one, operating and cooperating grace always both take part.

Operating grace is the grace by which God physically predetermines our will to consent to any good work; cooperating grace is the grace by which God works any devout action together with us. Both are needed: God must premove our free choice physically and efficiently to any supernatural act, and he must also act together with that same free choice, which, once premoved by God, moves itself to the good work.

Grace is called operating with regard to the first effect, in relation to which our will is only moved; and cooperating with regard to the second, in which the will, having been moved, moves itself. This is because our will is passive toward the prior motion by which God moves it to supernatural acts, since that motion is produced not actively by our free choice but by God alone, from whom that help of operating grace comes.

The will, moved by God, then actively and freely produces supernatural works, with God's grace acting together with it. So in the first respect God's grace works without us, and in the second we cooperate with it (De auxiliis divinae gratiae, book 9, disputation 81).
translator_notes: Diego Alvarez OP (d. 1635), De auxiliis divinae gratiae et humani arbitrii viribus (Rome, 1610).

title: How operating differs from rousing grace: the Jesuit answer
english: Thesis LVII. Here the doctors of the Roman Church raise the question how operating grace differs from rousing grace, and cooperating grace from assisting grace. From what has been said it is easy to work out how each party must answer, according to its own positions.

Some, with Vasquez, Molina and most of the Jesuits, take rousing grace to mean only the grace that knocks and urges, and that indeed often in vain; assisting grace, the grace by which God concurs by special help with free choice while free choice consents to grace and obeys it; operating grace, the grace that produces in us devout thoughts and undeliberate movements, in which we take part physically but not freely; and cooperating grace, the grace that produces in us the free acts of the will by which we answer God when he calls and invites.

These people hold that operating grace is the same as rousing grace, and assisting grace the same as cooperating grace. For them one and the same grace is called rousing insofar as it urges and rouses us to good through the holy thoughts and devout desires it puts into us, and operating insofar as it works these in us without our freely concurring and consenting.

Likewise one and the same grace is called assisting insofar as it helps us while we consent to grace's invitation, and cooperating insofar as it does not work without us, as we freely give our consent.
translator_notes: Luis de Molina SJ (1535-1600), Concordia liberi arbitrii cum gratiae donis (1588).

title: The same identification for Jansenius and Estius
english: Thesis LVIII. Rousing grace is likewise the same as operating grace, and assisting grace the same as cooperating grace, for all who, with Jansenius and Estius, take rousing grace to be the grace that actually wakes the sinner from the sleep of sin, and assisting grace the grace by which a person is helped to complete the good he has already begun to will.

They also take operating grace to be the grace that produces in us the first act of conversion, and cooperating grace the grace that produces the acts that follow, in which we cooperate not only by a free contribution of the will but also by some prior effort and striving of our own.

title: Bellarmine's mixed view: rousing grace is wider than operating
english: Thesis LIX. Others agree with Jansenius and Estius that operating grace is the grace that works the first conversion in us, and cooperating grace the grace that moves us to the good works that follow from it.

But they maintain with the Jesuits that rousing grace is the grace by which we are knocked at so that we may wake from the sleep of vice, even if through our own fault we often stay asleep, and assisting grace the grace that strengthens and helps us while we actually shake off that sleep.

These, like Bellarmine, distinguish rousing grace from operating grace, and so assisting grace from cooperating grace, since for them rousing grace covers more ground than operating grace. They therefore divide rousing grace into sufficient and efficacious, and efficacious grace again into operating and cooperating, as may be seen in Bellarmine, book 1 On Grace, already cited many times.
translator_notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio (Controversiae, De gratia primi hominis ... et de libero arbitrio), book 1.

title: Alvarez: rousing grace is sufficient, operating grace efficacious
english: Thesis LX. Alvarez likewise distinguishes rousing grace from operating grace. For him rousing grace is a grace that draws and attracts the will toward good only morally, while operating grace not only morally but also physically premoves and predetermines the will toward good.
So on his view rousing grace is the same as sufficient grace, whereas operating and cooperating grace belong to efficacious grace.
translator_notes: Diego Alvarez OP (d. 1635), De auxiliis divinae gratiae et humani arbitrii viribus (Rome, 1610).

title: The chief dispute: is assisting grace prior in nature? (Jesuits)
english: Thesis LXI. Among the theologians of the Roman school, however, the main dispute here concerns the way in which God's grace cooperates with our will.

The Jesuits and many other doctors of the Roman school deny that assisting or cooperating grace concurs in the supernatural work before free choice in the order of nature. They do so in order not to admit that grace predetermines free choice, since in their judgment the freedom of the will would then perish: on that supposition divine grace would lay on the will some necessity of acting that could not stand with freedom.

Peter of Saint Joseph, among others, thinks and argues this way in his Idea theologiae speculativae, book 4, chapter 6, where his third resolution begins: 'Assisting grace does not concur in the supernatural work before free choice in the order of nature.'
translator_notes: Pierre de Saint-Joseph (Petrus a Sancto Joseph, Feuillant, 1594-1662), Idea theologiae speculativae.
The print reads 'Der gratia' and, in the quoted resolution, 'uon concurrit'; the lock keeps both, and the English follows the evident 'Dei' (of God) and 'non' (not).

title: Alvarez: assisting grace prior in the order of causality
english: Thesis LXII. Others, on the contrary, maintain that assisting and cooperating grace comes before free choice in the order of causality and acts before it does. Although grace and free choice act on the devout work at the same time, the influence of grace is in some way prior in nature, and is not simultaneous with the influence of free choice in the order of causality.

This is the view of Diego Alvarez in the Epitome of his work on the helps of divine grace, book 3, chapter 19, whose heading is: 'That cooperating grace, as cooperating, is prevenient, or premoves free choice to consent, and does not merely act on the devout work equally and simultaneously with it.'

The chapter itself begins: 'From what has been laid down it is clear that cooperating grace, insofar as it is distinguished from rousing grace, goes before the free cooperation of created choice, not by priority in time but only in reason and causality.'
translator_notes: Diego Alvarez OP (d. 1635), De auxiliis divinae gratiae et humani arbitrii viribus (Rome, 1610). The Epitome is his summary of the larger work.

title: Freedom kept: the power to act otherwise in the divided sense
english: Thesis LXIII. They do not think this harms the freedom of the human will in any way. God's grace moves and determines created free choice to act in such a way that it does not remove its power to act otherwise.
So when grace is given, the will does act without fail, yet in the divided sense it always remains able not to act or to act otherwise.
translator_notes: In sensu diviso: the scholastic 'divided sense', in which the will's power is considered apart from the grace actually given; taken together with that grace (the composite sense), the will does not fail to act.

title: Molinists: assisting grace only a partial cause
english: Thesis LXIV. Further, those who follow the method and teaching of the Jesuit Molina hold that assisting or cooperating grace is not, strictly, the total cause of the supernatural act, but only a partial cause.
Their reason is that, in their view, assisting grace produces the supernatural act only in dependence on free choice.
translator_notes: Luis de Molina SJ (1535-1600), Concordia liberi arbitrii cum gratiae donis (1588).

title: Totality of effect, not of cause: the two horses
english: Thesis LXV. They grant that the whole supernatural act depends on grace, but add that it depends on grace not totally but only in part, because grace cannot produce it except in dependence on the will's concurrence.

Grace can therefore be called the total cause of the good act by totality of effect, but not by totality of cause, which is the point at issue here. The whole effect does depend on grace, but as on a cause that does not produce it without another cause acting with it at the same time.

That is why they compare grace and free choice to two horses pulling the same cart together. Neither of them acts first and moves the other to act, and each is only a partial cause of the pulling, although the whole pulling can be said to depend on each horse, since each contributes something to all of it.
translator_notes: Totalitas effectus and totalitas causae: a cause is total 'by totality of effect' if the whole effect depends on it, and 'by totality of cause' if it produces the effect with no co-cause.

title: On their view rousing grace imposes no necessity either
english: Thesis LXVI. On their view, then, assisting grace taken strictly and as such does not move a person to act, but helps him in the actual working.

Rousing grace, though it does move a person to act, does not lay on him any necessity of acting. It leaves him his own part to play, namely to determine himself to the devout work, since otherwise he can refrain from it, if he wishes, and determine himself differently.
So it too should not be called the total or adequate cause of the good work, as may be seen in the same Peter of Saint Joseph at the place cited above.
translator_notes: Pierre de Saint-Joseph (Petrus a Sancto Joseph, Feuillant, 1594-1662), Idea theologiae speculativae. Book 4, chapter 6.

title: Estius and the recent Thomists: grace the total cause
english: Thesis LXVII. Estius and the more recent Thomists, by contrast, hold that God's grace is the total cause of a good work in such a way that it produces all the good there is in the work. The whole work must therefore be credited to divine grace as its total cause, and not merely as a partial one.
translator_notes: Guillaume Estius (Willem Hessels van Est, 1542-1613), commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences, book 2, distinction 26.

title: Wholly from grace and wholly from free choice: subordinate causes
english: Thesis LXVIII. Yet although, speaking absolutely and strictly, they assert that the whole good work comes from God's grace, they also teach that the same good work comes wholly from free choice as well.
Nothing prevents a thing from coming wholly from two causes when one is subordinate to the other, that is, when the lower cause receives all its power to act and all its motion from the higher.

This, they teach, always holds between the first cause and a second cause, whatever kind of second cause it may be and whether it acts freely or by nature, because whatever a second cause does must be traced back to the first.

Between these causes no division of the work can be admitted in any way, as if some part of it were thought to be done by the second cause that is not also done wholly, in every part, by the first cause, which applies the second cause to all its working.

title: God makes man act, not the reverse
english: Thesis LXIX. They therefore say that the whole good is carried out by grace and free choice together, in one undivided work. What comes from free choice is not distinct from what comes from grace, just as what comes from the first cause is not distinct from what comes from the second.

Between the two agents, they teach, the difference is this: as free choice has its being from God, so it has all its good working from God's grace, which works in it and through it; but God, in what he works, does not in turn depend on man's free choice, either wholly or in part. For God causes man to act; man does not cause God to act.
The same holds in every work or action done by any second cause whatever.

So on the view of these doctors divine grace and free choice do not cooperate as partial causes that depend on each other in acting, but as total causes ordered one under the other, the lower depending on the higher and moved by it, not the reverse. This may be seen at more length in the same Estius on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 26, paragraph 29.
translator_notes: Guillaume Estius (Willem Hessels van Est, 1542-1613), commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences, book 2, distinction 26. Paragraph 29.

title: Prevenient and subsequent, leading and accompanying; sufficient and efficacious deferred
english: Thesis LXX. Some other divisions of grace coincide with those already given and differ little or not at all from them, as when grace is divided into prevenient and subsequent, and into leading and accompanying.

By leading and prevenient grace the theologians mean the same grace they call rousing and operating, and by accompanying or subsequent grace the grace otherwise called assisting or cooperating. The grace that rouses us to good, and to that extent works in us without us, also goes before us; the grace that helps us in the actual working and cooperates with us is held to accompany our wills in doing good, and comes after that first grace.
Some, however, look for certain subtle distinctions among these divisions of grace, but recounting and mentioning them would not do much for our purpose.

What chiefly remains to be considered here is the well-known division of grace into sufficient and efficacious. But since a careful account of it calls for a longer inquiry, it has seemed best to put it off to the next disputation.
translator_notes: This closes the Roman School locus; the book continues with its Reformed counterpart, 'Variae distinctiones & acceptiones Gratiae, quae usitatae sunt in Scholis Reformatis' (book p. 511).

title: Grace mostly means God's favour, sometimes his created gifts
english: Thesis I. In the common understanding of the doctors of the Reformed school, grace usually means God's own love and favour, with which he pursues us though we do not deserve it. Sometimes, though, it also means certain created gifts and effects of that favour.

So Tilenus, in the first disputation of his theses on the various names of the divine will (thesis 20), teaches that God's grace is taken both actively and passively. In the first sense, he says, it means God's kind and well-disposed will, which, far from acting out of our merit or as a debt, rather bestows everything generously and freely. In the second it means some gift given freely.
translator_notes: The print reads 'non ex merito nostro, vel ex debito, imo largientem'; 'imo' ('nay rather') sets the participle 'largientem' against the denied grounds of merit and debt.

title: Peter Martyr: grace as favour toward the elect, and as the gifts it gives
english: Thesis II. Peter Martyr says the same in his Commonplaces. The word grace, he writes, is used in two ways in holy scripture. First and chiefly it means God's goodwill toward people and the free favour with which he pursues the elect.
Then, because God endows his elect with outstanding gifts, grace sometimes also means the gifts that God bestows on us freely (class 3, locus 2, paragraph 7).

title: Aretius and Polanus: mercy in God and gifts of the Spirit
english: Thesis III. Likewise Aretius, in locus 25 of his commonplaces, teaches that when scripture speaks of grace, it means by the word first God's free mercy, by which he shows himself in reconciling and justifying a person.

Next, it uses grace for the gifts of the Holy Spirit as well, and he grants there that these gifts may rightly be called infused grace. Polanus's distinction comes to the same thing. The grace of God, he says, is spoken of homonymously, that is, in two senses: it is either grace that resides in God or grace given by God (Syntagma of Christian Theology, part 1, book 2, chapter 21).
translator_notes: The Greek word was checked against an enlarged scan of the page (PDF 527); the djvu text garbles it.

title: Polanus: saving grace is not anything created in us
english: Thesis IV. The Reformed theologians do grant that in holy scripture the grace of God sometimes means the gifts and effects of God's favour and love toward us. Still, they think grace is to be taken that way in only a few places.

For they hold that every passage saying we are chosen, called, justified or saved by God's grace must not be explained of some gift that inheres in us. These passages refer only to God's free love and goodwill. This can be seen especially in Polanus.

Grace that makes us pleasing and acceptable to God, he writes, and so saving grace as well, by which we are chosen in Christ for eternal salvation, effectually called, justified and regenerated, and by which in the end we are saved forever, is not a quality infused into us. It is not something created and inhering in us, not the love with which we love God, nor any other virtue in us (Syntagma, book 2, chapter 21, cited just above).

title: Tilenus: natural and supernatural gifts; gifts for one's own salvation and for the Church
english: Thesis V. Tilenus also notes that when grace is taken for the gifts and effects of God's favour, in a broad sense it covers nature itself together with its endowments and gifts. Properly, though, it is limited to certain supernatural gifts that God grants to people.

He holds that these gifts are in turn of two kinds. Some bear properly and directly on the salvation of the one who receives them, as effects of that active grace by which God justifies us; faith, love and hope are of this kind. Others concern not so much the personal salvation of those who receive them as the common use and building up of the whole Church, such as the gifts of prophecy, tongues and miracles and others like them.

title: Zanchi: gifts that belong to eternal life and gifts that do not
english: Thesis VI. Zanchi's teaching in book 4 of On the Nature of God (chapter 2, question 1) comes to the same thing. The gifts of God that are sometimes called grace either belong to eternal life, like faith, hope and love and the virtues joined to them, or do not belong to eternal life, like the gift of tongues, of miracles and the others Paul lists in 1 Corinthians 12.
Similar statements can be read in Polanus at the place already cited.

title: Cameron's division of the gifts
english: Thesis VII. Cameron's distinction, in the digression on grace in the first volume of his lectures, is not far from this either. He says that some gifts of grace come to no one who is not also saved, while others come even to those who are not saved.

He also divides God's gifts into those that help others only and not ourselves, such as all of God's gifts bestowed on the ungodly, and those that often help others and sometimes do not, but always help the people on whom they are bestowed. Faith, hope and love are of this second kind.

title: These divisions match the scholastic pair, yet the Reformed fault it
english: Thesis VIII. These divisions of the gifts of grace accepted among the Reformed differ little or not at all from the scholastics' standard division of grace into grace freely given and grace that makes pleasing. Tilenus admits as much in thesis 22 of the first disputation on the various names of the divine will, cited above.

Even so, most Reformed theologians criticize and find fault with this distinction of the Roman school. First, they object that some of God's gifts are singled out and called grace freely given, since there is no grace that is not given freely. Hope, faith and love are no less God's free gifts than the gift of prophecy, of healing and the like.

title: Second objection: no created gift first wins God's favour
english: Thesis IX. Second, they do not accept that anything created and inhering in us should be called grace that makes us pleasing and acceptable to God, as can be seen in Polanus, Aretius and Peter Martyr at the places cited above.

They do not deny that the gifts which the doctors of the Roman school mean by grace that makes pleasing are something that pleases God, something he delights in and finds acceptable. Their point is that these gifts are not what first wins God's favour for people. The gifts are themselves effects of God's favour and love, and they come from God already favouring and loving us even before we received them. As John says: not that we loved God, but because he first loved us.
translator_notes: Le Blanc's 'John' conflates 1 John 4:10 and 4:19, as was common.

title: Peter Martyr's own words against habitual grace that makes pleasing
english: Thesis X. That this is what those doctors hold is clear from their own words. Peter Martyr, in his Commonplaces (class 3, locus 2, paragraph 8), speaking of the scholastics' infused grace, writes: It is no small error that they want us to be made pleasing to God by this habit or created thing. When he has endowed us with such a gift, he must have loved us first, for God's love comes before all his gifts.

And in paragraph 13 he says: Those who chatter in the schools that grace freely given is one thing and grace that makes pleasing another are just as wrong. All grace has to be given freely, for otherwise, as Paul says, it would not be grace. And since by grace that makes pleasing they mean a habit, as we showed above, they are wrong to lay down that people become pleasing to God through such gifts. With him we are received into favour by his mercy alone and for Christ's sake.

title: Cameron: love for the gifts is human; God's love makes the gifts
english: Thesis XI. Cameron says much the same in the digression on grace mentioned above. It must be noted, he writes, that God's gifts are never called grace in the sense that they win God's favour, as if those gifts made us pleasing and acceptable to God.

If God's gifts are ever called grace in that sense, the reference is to human beings, who are drawn to love by such gifts, and not to God. To see this, one must understand that human love won by these gifts does not make the gifts but finds them. Divine love both found and made them, like a painter who delights in his work: he takes joy in its beauty and was also the one who produced that beauty.
So, strictly speaking, no grace should have been called grace that makes pleasing. It should rather have been called the grace of the one who makes pleasing.
translator_notes: 'gratia gratum facientis' is a play on the scholastic 'gratia gratum faciens': the grace belongs to God who makes pleasing, not to a gift that makes pleasing.

title: So the Reformed grant the gifts please God but do not precede his favour
english: Thesis XII. It is clear from this that the Reformed doctors do not deny that faith, hope, love and similar gifts of the Holy Spirit are things pleasing to God, on account of which the person who has them pleases God and is acceptable to him.
They deny only that these gifts come before God's favour and goodwill toward us. Rather, they are its effects and its gifts.

title: Tilenus: the schools confuse the gifts with justifying grace
english: Thesis XIII. On this point Tilenus seems to fault the scholastics for one thing only. They confuse the gifts they call grace that makes pleasing with justifying and saving grace, which in the view of the Reformed theologians is not anything inhering in us but simply God's active and external grace.

Speaking of hope, faith and love, he says: The scholastics call this grace that makes pleasing, and most dangerously confuse it with that active grace. This is in thesis 22 of the often-cited disputation on the various names of the divine will.

title: Testard: grace freely given invites; grace that makes pleasing transforms
english: Thesis XIV. Some doctors of the Reformed school do accept the distinction of grace into grace freely given and grace that makes pleasing, but in a different sense from the one the scholastic doctors accepted. Testard, in his Irenicum, takes grace freely given to be the grace by which God invites a person to salvation, and grace that makes pleasing to be the grace by which God effectually changes, converts and sanctifies a person.

Alternatively, for him grace freely given is a genus, and grace that makes pleasing is the species of that genus through which faith is produced in a person, sins are forgiven and holiness is infused. This can be seen in thesis 300.

The distinction of grace into grace freely given and grace that makes pleasing, he writes, can be accepted in this way. Grace freely given is the grace that only goes before by inviting on God's side, like general grace. Grace that makes pleasing, which is also freely given, effectually changes a person and turns someone abhorrent into someone pleasing and acceptable to God. Or else grace freely given is the most general genus of grace and covers every grace, while grace that makes pleasing is the species of it that produces faith, forgives sins and sanctifies; in a word, it prepares the subject.
translator_notes: 'qualis est generalis' refers to Testard's general (universal) grace that invites all; 'subjectum' is the person who receives grace.

title: Rivet and Ferry: grace that makes pleasing is God's favour itself
english: Thesis XV. Rivet, however, in his Summary of Controversies (tractate 4, question 2), takes grace freely given to mean all the gifts of grace. By grace that makes pleasing, which he also calls grace that gives freely, he means God's favour itself, from which those gifts come.

Paul Ferry uses the same distinction in this sense in chapter 30 of his Specimen of an Orthodox Scholastic. By grace that makes pleasing he means grace that remains within God, which places nothing in the one who is favoured but is simply God's love. Under grace freely given he includes all the benefits of calling, justification and so on, which flow down to us from the grace that gives freely as from an overflowing spring.

title: Actual and habitual grace: older Reformed reject, later ones accept
english: Thesis XVI. Most Reformed doctors do not explicitly state a distinction of grace into actual and habitual. Indeed some of the older Reformed seem to reject it: Peter Martyr, at the place cited above, sets out to refute the scholastics, who imagined, as he puts it, that grace is a habit infused into the soul.

But the more recent doctors of the Reformed school, like most of the older ones too, acknowledge that there is a habitual grace. They speak of the theological virtues as habits infused by God. Robert Baron, a Scot and professor of theology at the University of Aberdeen, testifies that on this point the consensus of the modern theologians, as he calls them, is unanimous. William Ames also defends this view of habitual grace at length against Grevinchovius in chapter 10 of his reply to Nicolaus Grevinchovius's response.

title: The older Reformed meant justifying grace only
english: Thesis XVII. Indeed, I think that even those older writers who seem to disagree do not really disagree. When they argue against the scholastics that grace is not a habit infused into the soul, they are plainly dealing with justifying grace.

So their meaning is not, without qualification, that God infuses no habits of virtue into believers' souls through the Holy Spirit, or that such habits are never called grace. They mean only that the grace by which scripture says we are saved and justified does not consist in those holy habits at all, and that this grace means God's mercy and goodwill alone.

The proof is this. At times they deny that the grace by which we are saved, justified and even regenerated is a habit and infused quality, and they also deny that it is anything created and inhering in us, as we reported of Polanus above. Yet Polanus himself, in the same chapter, grants that there is an inhering grace. This, he says, is faith and also the grace of conversion and regeneration, which people call the grace of Christ the Redeemer, and likewise Christian grace.

So when he denies that regenerating grace is anything created and inhering in us, he is speaking only of the efficient and impelling cause of our regeneration, not of what the scholastics call its formal cause.

title: Habitual grace in the soul's essence: Ferry admits it
english: Thesis XVIII. Many scholastics hold that, besides the habits of the virtues, there is a habitual grace that directly penetrates and affects the very essence of the soul. Most doctors of the Reformed school do not deal with this question explicitly. Yet it seems not far from what they do acknowledge, namely the new and supernatural being and the habitual renewal of all the faculties that are given to a person in regeneration.

Paul Ferry, however, pastor of the church at Metz, who recently died in the Lord, explicitly admits a grace of this kind. He holds that before the act of conversion itself God infuses into the very substance of the soul a habitual grace. It pervades the whole soul like a spiritual light and from the soul's substance works its way into all its faculties.

In this way it prepares them to follow the leading of efficacious grace and to obey it readily and willingly, as can be seen in the homily on Hebrews 12:28 that he published. But I know that many people dislike this view.
translator_notes: 'esse illud novum & supernaturale' is read as the scholastic noun esse ('that new and supernatural being'), paired with 'habitualis ... innovatio'. Ferry died in December 1669, which dates this locus.

title: Rousing and assisting grace among the Reformed
english: Thesis XIX. The distinction of grace into rousing and assisting grace is less common in the Reformed school than in the Roman. Still, the very learned Ferry mentions it in the homily just cited and seems to approve it.
The British theologians at the Synod of Dort use it as well.

title: Operating and cooperating grace, taken with the later Thomists
english: Thesis XX. The doctors of the Reformed school do not object to the scholastics' distinction of grace into operating and cooperating grace. But, with the more recent Thomists, they take operating grace to be the grace by which a person is first converted to God, and cooperating grace to be the grace by which someone already converted to God is moved to act well.

So Aretius, at the place cited above: Grace, he says, is sometimes operating and sometimes cooperating. The first is said to heal our will and change it for the better; the second strengthens the will once changed and brings it about that it acts rightly.

title: Martyr: one grace, passive at first, then active and passive
english: Thesis XXI. Peter Martyr likewise, at the place mentioned several times, says that operating grace is the grace that heals and changes our will at the start, and cooperating grace is the grace that makes the will, once changed and healed, act rightly. He adds that operating and cooperating grace are one grace, not two.

He explains that the two names arise because the will, when it is first healed, concurs with grace passively. For, he says, it is said to be changed, and we are said to be regenerated. Afterwards it is both active and passive, because, moved by God, it too wills and chooses.

title: Yet the first act of conversion is vital and free
english: Thesis XXII. Still, neither he nor the other Reformed deny on this account that the first act of conversion is a vital act, an action produced by the faculty in us called the will. Indeed they do not deny that it is a free action and one of those the schools call human acts.

Their only point is this: when God converts a person, the first thing grace works in us is something that goes entirely before the person's free movement toward good. On this point, then, the Reformed seem not to differ from the sounder scholastics, though they put their meaning in other words.
translator_notes: 'humanae' is the scholastic actio humana: a deliberate act proceeding from reason and will, as distinct from a mere act of a human being (actus hominis).
The last word 'exprimant' is broken across the line in the print ('ex-/primant'); the djvu text drops its second half, which was read from the scan of PDF 530.

title: Prevenient and subsequent grace: Aretius
english: Thesis XXIII. The doctors of the Reformed school also accept the distinction of grace into prevenient and subsequent, though not all in the same sense. Aretius holds that prevenient grace is the same as operating grace, and subsequent grace the same as cooperating grace, as a great many scholastics also hold.
