Grace is called prevenient, he says, because it goes before the will, so that the beginning of conversion is not from us but from God in his mercy. It is called subsequent because new impulses and good works follow conversion, and we cannot do any of these without grace.

title: Martyr: each grace goes before the next and follows the last
english: Thesis XXIV. Martyr, on the other hand, holds that grace is called now prevenient and now subsequent because God's mercy adorns us in a certain order with many different gifts. So any grace that comes earlier can be called prevenient with respect to a later one.
First, he says, the will is healed. Once healed, it begins to will what is good; having willed the good, it begins to carry it out; then it perseveres in doing good; and at last it is crowned.

So grace goes before our will by healing it and follows by making right things pleasing to it. It goes before so that we may will, and follows by driving us to accomplish what we have willed. It goes before by moving us to good works and follows by granting perseverance. It goes before perseverance by bestowing it and follows it by crowning it.
translator_notes: Martyr's chain echoes Augustine, Enchiridion 9.32 and De natura et gratia 31.35.

title: New Reformed divisions: Tilenus's decreeing and executing grace
english: Thesis XXV. Besides the standard divisions of grace used in the Roman school, the Reformed doctors have devised many of their own. Tilenus, for example, distinguishes God's grace into decreeing and executing grace.

The first, he says, means God's eternal purpose to choose us before the foundations of the world were laid. The second covers the whole working out of this wonderful mystery through its various times and stages (On the names of the divine will, disputation 1, thesis 24).
translator_notes: The scan is low-resolution here; 'mundi' and 'complectitur' could also be read as 'muidi' and 'camplectitur'. The ordinary forms are kept, and the sense is the same either way.

title: Universal and particular grace: Polanus
english: Thesis XXVI. Many theologians of the Reformed school also commonly distinguish grace into universal and particular grace, though not all in the same sense.

In his Syntagma (book 2, chapter 21), Polanus opens the chapter by dividing grace into the grace residing in God and the grace God gives. Near its close he writes that the grace God gives to people is of two sorts. Universal grace includes natural grace, bestowed on everyone without exception, and supernatural grace before the fall. Particular grace is supernatural grace after the fall, granted only to part of humankind.

title: Polanus: natural and supernatural grace, before and after the fall
english: Thesis XXVII. Earlier he had distinguished grace into natural and supernatural. By natural grace he means nature itself and all the gifts both of unfallen nature and of what remained in corrupted nature. By supernatural grace he means any gifts above nature that God has bestowed on human beings.

So he divides supernatural grace again into supernatural grace before man's fall, meaning the gifts above nature bestowed on man while still whole, and supernatural grace after man's fall, a name that covers all the gifts above nature bestowed on man as a sinner.

title: Polanus: no supernatural grace is universal after the fall
english: Thesis XXVIII. By universal grace, then, he means the gifts, natural as well as supernatural, that were bestowed on our first parents before sin. They belonged to the whole human race, which then consisted of those two alone, and they were to be passed on to all their descendants had they persevered in obedience to God.

He also allows that after the corruption of the human race, the benefits and gifts of nature that remained after sin and are common to all people may be called universal grace. But after sin he admits no supernatural gift or benefit as universal, and so he says that after the fall all supernatural grace is particular.

Accordingly he divides what he calls particular grace into two. One kind is common to elect and reprobate and is given by God for the salvation of others, such as the charisms the scholastics call graces freely given. The other is proper to the elect and meant for the salvation of those who receive it: faith, regeneration, repentance, love, the hope of eternal life and the gift of perseverance, which the scholastics class under grace that makes pleasing.

title: Testard: general grace offers, particular grace applies
english: Thesis XXIX. Paul Testard, some years ago pastor of the church at Blois, uses the distinction of grace into particular and universal in a very different sense in his synopsis of the doctrine of nature and grace (thesis 300).

Grace toward sinners, he says, is of two kinds, general and particular. General grace is given to the whole world: it is the offer of salvation and the power to be saved. Particular grace belongs to the elect alone: it is the application of salvation. Its nearest foundation is free election, its middle stage effectual calling, and its crown justification, preservation and glorification.
He immediately adds that this particular grace is either prevenient, such as election and calling, or mercifully rewarding, such as justification, preservation and glorification.
translator_notes: 'custodia' is rendered 'preservation' (God's keeping of the elect).

title: Testard's universal grace: salvation made possible for all
english: Thesis XXX. In his view, then, universal or general grace is the benefit of God by which salvation is offered to all people and so made possible for each and every one of them: they can be saved if they will, and it is due to themselves alone that they do not obtain salvation.

For he holds that God provided Christ as Redeemer for all, and that by his death the sins of all people were expiated in such a way that, on God's side, nothing further prevents anyone who turns from sin and is converted to God from sharing in salvation and being freed from perdition, since Christ's death made full satisfaction to God's avenging justice for the sins of all.

Nor is that all. He holds that God calls all people to share in salvation in Christ: some by the explicit word of the Gospel, others by the voice of creation and by the many signs of God's kindness and patience that shine out in the works of nature and providence and invite people to repentance, and so to salvation.

title: Testard's particular grace: salvation effectually applied to the elect
english: Thesis XXXI. By particular grace he means the grace by which God makes certain people actually share in salvation, not merely offering them Christ's benefit but applying it to them effectually and in fact.

He calls this grace particular because, unlike the first, it does not reach everyone but belongs to a few, namely the elect, since it consists in election itself and in the benefits that flow from it: internal and effectual calling, justification, the gift of perseverance and glorification.

title: Amyraut and his followers; the opponents in the Netherlands, France and England
english: Thesis XXXII. The very distinguished Moise Amyraut uses and explains this division of grace into particular and universal in the same way in the two treatises he entitled On Universal and Particular Grace.

All those in France who follow Cameron's method and teaching agree with him and support him, as do a great many in Germany and Poland who seek and pursue peace and concord with the Lutherans. But most of the Reformed in the Netherlands, and not a few in France and England, reject and attack this distinction and admit no universal grace of Christ at all.

title: Universal grace is an external benefit; particular grace works within
english: Thesis XXXIII. From what has been said it is clear enough that these theologians do not mean by universal grace any grace inhering in people. They mean only an external benefit of God: he handed his Son over to death so that divine justice might be satisfied for the sins of all, and, his justice being thus appeased, he calls people from outside to share in the salvation that Christ won for them by his death.

By particular grace, on the other hand, they chiefly mean the gifts and helps of God by which he acts within people, works conversion and faith in them, and in the end makes them actually share in eternal salvation.

title: Amyraut: objective and subjective grace
english: Thesis XXXIV. This gave rise to another distinction of grace, into objective and subjective grace, which the very distinguished Moise Amyraut sets out at the beginning of his dissertation on particular grace.

There he teaches that two graces are needed to produce faith in human souls. One functions as an object: the mercy of God offering itself from outside in Christ's satisfaction. The other affects and enlightens the mind from within so that the object may be received.

He calls the first objective because it is external and of itself places nothing in a person; it is only set before him as an object that he ought to embrace by faith. He calls the second subjective because it changes a person within and is received in him as in a subject. He holds that objective grace is universal and belongs to absolutely everyone, while subjective grace is particular and meant specially for the elect.
translator_notes: 'misericordiam Dei ... offerentis' is read with the participle in agreement with Dei: God's mercy as God offers it outwardly in Christ's satisfaction.

title: The Remonstrants philosophize about grace like the Molinists
english: Thesis XXXV. Those in the Netherlands called Remonstrants or Arminians reason about grace in much the same way as the doctors of the Roman school now called Molinists.

For they use the distinctions of grace into rousing and assisting, prevenient and subsequent, and operating and cooperating grace, and in the same sense as those doctors. This can be seen in the Remonstrants' declaration of their opinion on the third and fourth articles, which is contained in their synod.
translator_notes: 'in eorum Synodo' refers to the Remonstrants' Acta et scripta synodalia, their own record of the Synod of Dort, where the declaration on articles 3 and 4 is printed.

title: Remonstrant rousing grace: illumination of the mind acting on the will
english: Thesis XXXVI. There they say that by rousing grace they mean the gracious and unmerited working of God and the Holy Spirit.

First it fills the intellect with knowledge of the things of salvation and enlightens it, and so brings it to assent to divine truth. Second, it acts on the will itself through that same enlightenment and through the meanings contained in the word.

title: Remonstrants: the Spirit acts on the will, but not irresistibly
english: Thesis XXXVII. Still, they add, they do not in the least deny a direct working of the Holy Spirit on the will, in which he pours into it the strength and supernatural ability to believe. That ability, though, neither forces the will nor settles its choice irresistibly.

They note that this grace is called rousing because it draws, attracts, invites and urges the will toward free assent and, provided the person puts no obstacle in the way, makes it actually will. The same grace is also called prevenient, because it goes before our will, and finally operating, because it is also the cause of the act of willing.

title: Why rousing grace is needed: supernatural acts exceed the will's native power
english: Thesis XXXVIII. They point out that the need for this grace arises because supernatural acts, such as those that make up a person's conversion, far exceed the will's inborn and native power.

So supernatural strength and a special grace that goes before the act of the will itself are needed to produce such an act, which is not the case for the will's other, natural acts that are proportioned to its power.

title: Remonstrant assisting grace: concurrence 'more than moral'
english: Thesis XXXIX. Assisting grace, for them, is the grace that helps the will and concurs with it effectively in producing the act, and does so not only morally but also physically, or rather more than morally.

For the word 'physically' seems to them most unsuitable in this matter, because the acts in question are supernatural; yet no other proper word occurs by which they could state the point positively. They observe that this grace is also called cooperating, because it works together with the will, and subsequent in relation to prevenient and rousing grace.

title: Remonstrants reject habitual grace infused without our acts
english: Thesis XL. The distinction of grace into actual and habitual they reject as a scholastic invention with no basis in scripture, provided that habitual grace is taken to mean an infusion of faith, hope and love into the will such that a person is said to acquire those habits without any intervening act of the will.

For they hold that habitual faith, love and hope are finally produced in us through frequent acts of faith, hope and love that come from God's special grace, just as habits of liberality and justice are produced in us through repeated acts of justice and liberality.

To think that the habits of the theological virtues are produced directly by God without any act of the person's own is, they say, the view of people who want all those habits poured into them at one stroke, because they find it too much labour to acquire them by frequent acts.

title: Yet they admit an infused permanent supernatural power
english: Thesis XLI. But if habitual grace is taken to mean a supernatural power given to the will so that it can believe and act well, they declare that they gladly accept it.

So it is clear that, although they deny habitual grace, they still acknowledge a permanent quality and supernatural power infused by grace. That comes to almost the same thing and differs little or not at all from the view of those who speak differently.

title: Both sides grant both senses of grace; mutual accusations are groundless
english: Thesis XLII. From what we have set out so far about the various divisions and senses of grace in both the Roman and the Reformed school, it is plain that the theologians of the Roman Church freely teach and grant that in holy scripture grace is not always taken for gifts and helps of God that inhere in us, and that grace sometimes means God's favour itself, from which those gifts and helps come.
In turn, the Reformed doctors do not deny that scripture often gives the name of grace to the gifts and effects of God's favour.

So some of the Reformed are wrong to accuse the doctors of the Roman school of meaning nothing by grace but some supernatural gift infused into us. And the doctors of the Roman school have no reason to attack the Reformed and complain of them as if they acknowledged no grace inhering in us.

title: Grace freely given: only a dispute about words
english: Thesis XLIII. It is also clear from what was said about the distinction of grace into grace freely given and grace that makes pleasing that this is nothing but a dispute about words.

The Reformed contend that no grace is given otherwise than freely, and that every grace is called grace precisely because it is given gratuitously. The doctors of the Roman school accept this. They explain that they call one species of grace grace freely given in a special sense, not because the other species is not freely given too, but because the school found it convenient to call that species by the name of the genus, since it has no name of its own.

title: Grace that makes pleasing does not precede God's love
english: Thesis XLIV. When these doctors name the other species grace that makes pleasing, their reason is not that it precedes every act of divine love toward us, or that it is the cause by which God is first moved to wish us well.
The Reformed rightly judge that to be false and absurd, since God loves us before we love him.

title: The Reformed grant that faith makes one pleasing to God
english: Thesis XLV. Yet the Reformed school does not therefore deny that what the Roman school means by grace that makes pleasing, namely faith, hope and love, is something on account of which a person is pleasing and acceptable to God in a special way.

Paul has this in view when he says to the Hebrews that without faith it is impossible to please God, and the theologians of the Roman Church have the same in view when they call that grace the grace that makes pleasing.

title: God's love both precedes the gifts and follows them
english: Thesis XLVI. So both sides will readily grant that there is an act of God's love that comes before the gifts and virtues the scholastics call grace that makes pleasing, since God wishes us well before we have them. They will also grant that there is an act of the same love that those gifts come before, since without them we cannot please God or win his approval.

Such gifts and virtues formally make the person adorned with them pleasing and acceptable to God. As Peter says in Acts 10: Truly I have found that God shows no partiality, but in every nation whoever fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.

title: The Reformed admit infused habits; the charge against them is unjust
english: Thesis XLVII. Next, it is clear from what was set out earlier that the doctors of the Reformed school admit certain divinely infused virtues and certain gifts of saving grace that exist in the soul as a habit and permanent quality.

So the theologians of the Roman communion unjustly charge them with denying that there is any habitual grace that is a quality inhering in the soul, since few or none of the doctors of the Reformed Church deny it.

title: The real question: what 'grace' means in the texts on salvation
english: Thesis XLVIII. The only point in question is this. In the passages of scripture that say we are saved and justified by God's grace, does grace mean God's external favour and goodwill, or some grace that inheres in us, whether actual or habitual?
The Reformed school affirms the first, the Roman school the second.

title: Not whether inherent grace exists, but how to read those texts; locus closed
english: Thesis XLIX. So the question is not simply whether there is a saving grace that inheres in us, either as an act or as a habit. It is only whether the passages of scripture that ascribe our salvation and justification to God's grace are to be understood of such grace.
The doctors of the Roman Church say yes and the Reformed say no. How much this question matters we have considered more fully elsewhere.
translator_notes: The print's 'Quae quaestio ... expensum est' mixes genders; the English follows the sense. 'Elsewhere' points to Le Blanc's theses on justification (De Justitia per Gratiam Fidelibus inhaerente).
The last lines of this thesis are missing from the djvu text and were read from the page image (PDF 533).

title: Jansenius: what sufficient and efficacious grace mean
english: Thesis I. Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, and his followers give the name sufficient grace only to a grace after which God need supply nothing further, by way of principle, for a person to will and act. Efficacious grace, for them, is only the grace that does more than give created nature the strength to will: it produces the willing itself in that nature, and of itself bends and determines the faculty of will to will.

On their principles, then, no grace is truly sufficient and yet not efficacious except one that gives the creature the ability to will so fully that no further divine help toward willing is needed beforehand, and that is yet so subject to the creature's freedom that whether to use that grace or not rests with its free choice. Conversely, the only truly efficacious grace is not one that the will's act happens to follow somehow, but one that brings the creature's will under itself, moves it of itself effectively to will, and by its own force infallibly produces the act of willing in it.

title: Jansenists: in the state of innocence grace was only sufficient
english: Thesis II. They hold that grace sufficient in the sense just described was given to angels and to human beings when they were created. In their view God gave both what they needed to act rightly, but left it to their free choice whether to make use of those aids.

In that first state of unfallen creatures efficacious grace had no place, since neither humans nor angels needed it before the fall. So although the blessed angels did persevere in good after receiving grace from God, that is no reason to say they had efficacious grace; theirs was merely sufficient. Conversely, the apostate angels and our first parents lacked no aid of God's grace that was needed for them to persevere in good.

title: After the fall: a prior grace that determines the will
english: Thesis III. Once a person has fallen into sin, these doctors hold, he cannot turn to God, nor, once converted, set himself to any good work, without some prior aid of grace. This aid does not merely invite and urge him toward the good, or assist him while he does a good work; it bends and determines his will toward the good and effectively produces in it a good act of willing.

They say the weakness of the will demands this. Corrupt concupiscence, clinging to a person after sin, keeps dragging the will down toward earthly things by its constant weight, so that for every single impulse of heavenly love it must be lifted upward by God's actual and efficacious help.

title: Hence no grace is sufficient without being efficacious
english: Thesis IV. It follows that everyone who does not actually turn and do good lacks some divine aid that action requires and presupposes. Such people, then, should not be said to have sufficient grace for turning and doing good, since only what includes everything needed deserves the name sufficient.

Whoever has every aid that a good work requires beforehand will infallibly and surely perform it. So every grace that can truly be called sufficient is efficacious as well, and the Schools' custom of dividing the saving grace of Christ the Redeemer, which fallen humanity needs, into efficacious and sufficient is pointless.

title: Christ's healing grace is efficacious of itself
english: Thesis V. On their view, then, all true grace of Christ, properly and specifically so called, the grace suited to heal sick humanity and needed for every devout affection and movement of the will, is efficacious of itself. No hard heart ever rejects it, because it always grants the willing and removes hardness of heart in proportion to the divine gift.
A person can withhold consent from it if he chooses; yet it always ensures that he does not withhold consent, and does not want to.
translator_notes: 'A nullo duro corde respuitur' echoes Augustine, De praedestinatione sanctorum 8.13.

title: Not every such grace converts: the ineffective desires
english: Thesis VI. They do not, however, claim that this grace proper to Christ always actually converts a person and produces true and earnest repentance in him. For someone moved by it does not always will or do, effectively and fully, what ought to be willed and done.

A sinner often gets stuck in the merely ineffective desires that grace has shaped in him, and through his own weakness and fault does not carry them through to the deed. He may even cast those desires aside, and as concupiscence fights back and wins, fail to turn from sin, or to repent as he should and as much as he must to rise from sin and receive God's forgiveness.

title: That grace still reaches the effect God intended; the Saint-Amour exposition
english: Thesis VII. Even so, they hold that this same grace of Christ is efficacious in such a person and achieves the very effect for which it was precisely and immediately given and which God intended, namely nothing other than the stirring of a good desire that has only begun. If that desire falls short of its final and complete effect, the accomplishment of the work it was urging and stirring him toward, the fault lies with the person alone, not with God; the cause is in the human being, not in God.

Yet if God chose to give as much grace as suffices and is needed for this person to repent as he ought, rise from his sin and attain God's justifying grace, he would most surely repent, rise from sin and attain that grace. But God shows mercy to each person as he wills, as much as he wills, and where he wills. This is set out in the 'true and Catholic exposition' of the five propositions on grace included in the book titled Journal de Saint-Amour.

title: Jansenius, book 2 chapter 27: velleities and the gentle breeze
english: Thesis VIII. Jansenius states his view on this point in the same way in De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 2, chapter 27. Having argued at length that no grace of Christ is without effect, and hence that there is no grace of Christ that is sufficient and yet not efficacious, he meets at the start of that chapter a difficulty he puts to himself:

"No one should be troubled by the fact that many people are, by God's doing, given light in their minds, and are even stirred in their wills by movements of divine grace, and yet refuse their consent to its inward persuasion and leaning, and so conclude that it is false that grace always produces, in the person who receives it, the effect for which it is given. One must bear in mind that the effects of divine grace come in many kinds, just as those of the will do. There is complete willing, which Augustine calls 'ability'; there is also incomplete willing, which people usually call velleity; and velleity itself comes in various degrees, down to the very first and faintest delight in the good. This, then, is the first effect of that heavenly dew, which it produces at the very least in everyone on whom God pours it.

"A flood of divine grace sweeps the whole human will along with it like a raging torrent, so that it tears apart, as if in a violent storm, every tie of the human heart that snares it in earthly things. In the same way that gentle breath, like a faint breeze, softly wins from the will a faint delight, matched to so beautiful a thing set before it for contemplation, and swiftly, almost by stealth, draws the will after it.

"So although this grace by no means suffices for a person to carry out God's command, to love God above all things, to hope, to pray or to believe, it still contributes something: it stirs up free velleities, not full willings, toward these or some other heavenly thing, which no one can gain by human power unless God pours them in. For not every grace suffices to produce every effect, as some have imagined; the powers must be matched to the difficulty of the actions."
translator_notes: The print reads 'Hec ergo primus est'; normalized to 'Haec', and taken as 'this [delight] is the first effect'.

title: The second of the five propositions is not Jansenius's
english: Thesis IX. This shows that Jansenius is wrongly credited with the proposition: 'In the state of fallen nature, inward grace is never resisted.' Yet this is the second of the five notorious propositions that the Roman pontiffs Innocent X and Alexander VII condemned as heretical, as being those of Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, in constitutions they issued on the matter.

Apart from the fact that the wording of this proposition appears nowhere in his works, he plainly teaches the opposite in the passage just quoted, where he states outright that many people are, by God's doing, given light in their minds and even stirred in their wills by movements of divine grace, and yet refuse consent to its inward persuasion and leaning.

title: Their 'cannot' means: lacks proximate and complete power
english: Thesis X. These theologians teach that after the fall a person cannot perform even one good work without such efficacious aid from God bending and determining the will toward the good. They mean this of proximate and complete power. All they intend is that, so long as the efficacious grace that a sick and listless will needs for a given good work is missing, a person is not proximately and completely able to do it.
Since this grace, efficacious of itself, grants both the willing and the proximate and fullest ability together, anyone without it lacks the willing and the proximate ability that it supplies.

title: Senses of 'being able' (1): remotely, through free choice
english: Thesis XI. They readily grant, however, that even without Christ's efficacious grace people can be said in many ways to be able to keep God's commandments and do good works. Jansenius sets this out at length in De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 3, chapter 15. There he notes that, in matters of the good or devout life, a person can be said to be 'able' to do something in several senses.

The first and most remote is through the mere capacity of free choice to be turned toward good or toward evil. This power is grounded in the bare nature of free choice, so long as it has not yet been hardened in evildoing by the penalty of eternal damnation. Only demons and the damned, then, should be said in this sense to be no longer able to believe, love and do good, since they are no longer in a state where God's grace could bend them toward the good. Conversely, every human being without exception, for as long as he lives this mortal life on earth, is rightly said in this way to be able to believe and to love God, because through God's grace he can be bent toward these things.

title: Senses of 'being able' (2): through faith
english: Thesis XII. Second, according to the same doctor, we are said, in a somewhat closer sense, to be able through faith to live rightly, withstand every temptation and avoid sins, even though we lack love for God, God's actual help and the will's inner strength.

Faith of itself cannot do any of this. But it is the seed of prayer, and by prayer we usually obtain love, helping grace and strength of will; that is why we are said to be able to do these things through faith itself.

title: Senses of 'being able' (3): through justifying love
english: Thesis XIII. Third, in the same doctor's view, we are said in a much fuller and closer sense to be able to do what belongs to true devotion through the love by which a person is justified. That love is simply a good will, a good act of willing; while we lack it we cannot live rightly, and when we have it we are said to be able to.

The love that confers the power of doing good has various degrees and stages of growth, and the power is greater or lesser accordingly. Weak at first and not equal to every good work, it grows gradually until it gains enough strength to overcome every allurement, every threat and every torment.

title: Faith and love give ability as habitual gifts
english: Thesis XIV. What he says about the ability given through faith and love, he cautions, should be understood chiefly of these habitual gifts. Through them the righteous are said to be able to pray, love, live rightly and overcome temptations even when they are doing none of these things.
For they are virtues that remain in the soul and so make it strong enough to carry out certain works, though while still imperfect they are not enough for works of a higher order.

title: The fullest ability comes only from actual grace
english: Thesis XV. He insists, though, that we should not be said to be able in the fullest sense to do good and carry out the duties of devotion except when the Holy Spirit's inspiration so prepares the will that it does not merely have the power but actually wills. On his teaching, then, this fullest ability is had only when the deed is actually done as well. It is the proper effect not of faith or love, that is, of a habitually good will, but of the actual grace that Christ brought to weak humanity by his cross. That grace assists not only the ability but the doing itself, since it gives not merely 'the ability, if you will' but also 'the will to do what you can'.

So however great a person's faith and love, or habitually good will, may be, even of the strongest kind, if a temptation arises, however slight, and he is not fortified by such an inspiration of the Spirit, that is, by actual grace, he will certainly give way, because without it, since the first man's fall, the will or habitual love cannot pass into action. For the tinder of inborn concupiscence constantly presses the listless soul downward, and is itself constantly stirred up by visible objects presenting themselves from every side, inside and out, unless the gift of the Holy Spirit either heads off its stirrings before they rise or crushes them once they have risen.

title: The first of the five propositions, in Jansenius's sense
english: Thesis XVI. From this, as from what was brought forward earlier, it is plain in what sense Jansenius maintained this proposition: 'Some of God's commandments are impossible for righteous people who will and strive, given the strength they now have; they also lack the grace by which they would become possible.'

This is the first of the five propositions just mentioned, which the Roman pontiffs condemned some years ago as maintained by Jansenius, and indeed, as they put it, in the sense in which he maintained them, though they neither explain nor define the sense they mean to condemn.

title: What the first proposition meant: no proximate power without efficacious grace
english: Thesis XVII. Whatever they made of that sense, what has been set out shows for certain that by those words Jansenius meant only this. At times, by a judgment of God that is hidden but just, certain believing and righteous people do not receive from God grace efficacious of itself for praying, for overcoming a temptation, or for keeping some commandment.

In that case, though they do have some will to keep the commandment, it is slight, feeble and imperfect, not equal to keeping it fully and as it should be kept. With the strength they have at that moment they are therefore not proximately and completely able to pray as they should, to overcome the temptation, or to keep the commandment as it should be kept. This inability, then, is simply the one that comes from weakness of will and from the absence of the efficacious aid that gives at once both the proximate and fullest ability and the willing.

title: Two kinds of inability (1): lack of something the will cannot supply
english: Thesis XVIII. That doctor and those who share his view insist, however, that the inability to do good found in everyone who lacks the grace of Christ needed for this or that good work does not cancel their obligation to do it, nor excuse them from doing their duty in that respect. To prove it they point out that there are two kinds of inability to carry out a commandment.

'One kind,' they say, 'comes from the lack of something that no amount of will, that is, no strength of willing, can make up. Such is the inability of someone who has no worldly goods to give alms, or no knowledge to teach a person perishing for want of instruction, and countless cases like these. Of this inability it is perfectly true that God does not command the impossible. The moment such an impossibility arises, either the commandment lapses or at least the person commanded is no longer bound to fulfil it. In impossibilities of this kind the will is also counted as the deed, since the failure to act is not the will's fault but sheer lack of power.'

title: Two kinds of inability (2): defect of the will itself
english: Thesis XIX. 'The second kind of inability arises from a lack in the will itself, that is, in the act of willing. If that willing were present in the measure it ought to be, the commandment would be kept with the greatest ease, for it is kept simply by willing firmly. So if someone wills firmly, the commandment is thereby already kept and cannot fail to be kept, since such a will carries with it both full willing and the power to do what it has willed.

'This inability to act does not excuse in the least the person who fails to do what is commanded, for he could do it if he chose. If he did not choose to, and so could not, who would deny that he deserves blame for that very will, so perverse and hardened?'

title: Applied to sinners: inability is hardness of will
english: Thesis XX. Applying this to the case in hand, they say that the inability of sinners to carry out God's commands is such that they do not cease to be able to keep them if they choose. 'Let them will it,' they say, 'and will it fully, and the moment they have willed it the commands will be kept. If they will not, and therefore cannot, who would not hold against the unwilling the hardness of their wicked will and the loss of power that followed?

'In truth, lacking such power is nothing other than the hardness of a bad will; and being unable to retreat from a will once adopted is nothing other than willing stubbornly.' So Jansenius, that bishop of Ypres, philosophizes on the subject in De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 3, chapter 15.
translator_notes: 'a qua suscepta' taken with the (bad) will: being unable to draw back from a will once taken up, as in XXII 'a semel suscepta volitione retrocedere'.

title: Grace is justly withheld from the guilty
english: Thesis XXI. He adds that when God withholds grace from people he withholds it justly, because by their own fault they have made themselves unworthy of it. So its absence cannot excuse their inability to do good.

It would be different, he says, if God deprived a creature free of all sin of the aids it needs to act rightly. Then the creature would bear no blame, since in that respect it would simply be following the order God had set, and could not be said to have departed from it.

title: Inability without grace squared with freedom
english: Thesis XXII. Nor does he find it any harder to square the inability that comes from the absence of grace with the freedom of human choice. On his account that inability is simply the will's obstinacy in evil and its refusal to bend toward good, which began in an initially free choice.

God's own voluntary steadfastness, by which he cannot draw back from a decision once made, does not remove his freedom. In the same way the fixity of sinful humans or angels, by which they cannot take up a good will, in no way impairs their freedom. Nor is there any necessity here that conflicts with freedom or wipes out the guilt of a will gone astray. Whatever necessity there is springs entirely from hardness and stubbornness of willing, and this does not remove or lessen the guilt of those who will obstinately; it rather increases and compounds it, because through it the will clings more firmly to evil.

title: The Louvain doctors before Jansenius
english: Thesis XXIII. Moreover, toward the end of the last century and many years before Jansenius wrote, the doctors of Louvain likewise recognized no grace sufficient for a person's conversion except the grace that actually converts him.

They maintain that the help sometimes given to those who neither believe nor turn to the Lord is not sufficient for faith and conversion, because grace sufficient for conversion converts of itself, and grace that does not convert does not suffice. Justificatio of the censure against the Louvain Jesuits, chapter 16.

title: The Roman School accepts the division: Thomists and Molinists
english: Thesis XXIV. Apart from Jansenius's followers, who style themselves disciples of Augustine, the whole Roman school today accepts this division of the grace of Jesus Christ into sufficient and efficacious. The so-called recent Thomists defend it, and so do those who follow Molina's method and positions.
They do not, however, all explain and understand it in the same way.

title: The recent Thomists: efficacious grace really distinct from sufficient
english: Thesis XXV. Those called recent Thomists give the name sufficient grace to grace that confers the ability to act, even though, for a good action actually to follow, a fresh aid on God's part is still required beforehand. Efficacious grace, for them, does not merely confer the ability to act; of itself it effectively moves a person to act well, and so gives ability together with its effect.

On their view, therefore, efficacious grace is really distinct from sufficient grace in its being, since it adds to sufficient grace a further divine aid that must precede the good action and is needed for it.

title: Thomists: sufficient grace gives proximate and complete power
english: Thesis XXVI. Although the grace they distinguish from efficacious grace does not include that final requirement for doing good, they still insist it is rightly called sufficient. It may not suffice for anyone actually to act, but it gives the strength to act well and suffices to make a person able to act well. Indeed they say such sufficient grace confers not just some power to do good, but a power that deserves to be called proximate and complete, even though, as they admit, a fresh aid from God must necessarily come before the good action.

Just so, a healthy person with sound eyes has, on their view, proximate and complete power to see even while he stays in darkness, although for sight actually to happen he needs, besides sound eyes, light to illuminate the objects before him.
translator_notes: 'ex ipsorum sensu' taken as 'in their view' (the Thomists'), as 'ex eorum sensu' in II.

title: Sufficient grace given even to those who fail
english: Thesis XXVII. They maintain that grace sufficient for doing good in this sense is given even to those who in fact fail to do the good work. God gives them aids by which they are able to act well, aids that furnish them proximate and complete power to do good, 'in first act', as the Schools put it.

What they lack is a further aid, required beforehand for the good work itself, which infallibly moves everyone who receives it to that work, and which God graciously grants to all who actually do good. These, accordingly, are said to have grace for doing good that is not only sufficient but efficacious too.

title: Why it is still called sufficient: ability as such
english: Thesis XXVIII. The grace given to the others, in their view, is rightly called sufficient. Though it is not enough to give ability together with its effect, it is truly enough to give ability as such. No further aid is needed for those who have received it to be truly called able to do the works for which it is said to suffice, even though a fresh aid is needed for the action actually to follow.
That fresh aid does not add some new strength to the power, giving it ability in first act, as was said above. Its proper work is to move the power, already fit for acting, and apply it to the act.

title: Alvarez: complete and incomplete sufficiency
english: Thesis XXIX. As Alvarez observes, aid sufficient for a given operation is of two kinds. One is completely sufficient: beyond it no other aid is absolutely necessary for the operation actually to be produced. The other is not completely sufficient, yet truly sufficient, in that it confers the ability with respect to that operation. No other aid is then absolutely necessary for the person to be truly said to be able to produce it, just as to say that someone can see requires only that he have the power of sight, though many other things beyond that power are needed for him actually to see.

In this sense he maintains that through the aids of the grace which he calls sufficient, a person truly can perform the act in relation to which the grace is called sufficient, even if he will never perform it unless God, by efficacious aid, brings it about that it is reduced to second act. So aid sufficient for believing is aid by which a person can believe, and aid sufficient for persevering is aid by which he can persevere if he wills, though for him actually to will it efficacious aid is further required. Epitome de auxiliis divinae gratiae, book 3, chapter 17.

title: On Thomist premises the division held even before the fall
english: Thesis XXX. Indeed, on these doctors' assumptions, the division of divine grace into sufficient and efficacious must have applied even to unfallen nature. On their teaching, for any creature to act it is not enough to have the power of acting granted by the Creator; the first cause must also apply that power to acting and move it beforehand.

So for the unfallen creature actually to do good it needed not only an aid that gave it the strength to do good but also another by which God would effectively move and predetermine its faculties to do good. It follows that the apostate angels did have sufficient aid for persevering but lacked the efficacious aid required for actually persevering, while the good angels were given aid for persevering that was not only sufficient but efficacious of itself.

title: A grace sufficient for one act is efficacious for another
english: Thesis XXXI. They do grant, however, that a grace which in one respect is only sufficient is efficacious in another. A grace that is sufficient for some complete act, toward which it disposes a person and to which it is directed, is efficacious for the incomplete acts by which a person is usually prepared for that complete act.

Indeed, on their view, although every sufficient grace is inefficacious for the full work for which it is called sufficient, it is most fully and most abundantly efficacious for the proximate and immediate act for which God gives and appoints it.

title: Alvarez: sufficient for faith, efficacious for its preparations
english: Thesis XXXII. Diego Alvarez, among others, teaches this expressly in section 3 of the chapter already cited: 'Every aid that is sufficient with respect to one act is always efficacious with respect to another, which an absolute decree of the divine will has appointed it to bring about.

'For example, aid sufficient for the act of faith effectively produces in a person devout thoughts and knowledge of what is to be believed, or devout desires to have faith, and other incomplete acts of this kind which, as a rule, come before the assent of faith. Likewise aid sufficient for the act of contrition effectively produces in a person reflection on the pains of hell, or attrition, or other incomplete acts of this kind which as a rule come before perfect contrition.'

title: Sufficient grace lies in different things for different works
english: Thesis XXXIII. Since the grace called sufficient is so called in relation to the various works toward which it disposes a person and for which it gives him the ability, according to which work is in question, that sufficient grace must be located in various things. The same grace does not make a person sufficient for everything.

So in a righteous person, the grace sufficient for works of true piety, worthy of eternal life, consists both in habitual grace itself and in the gifts of the Holy Spirit he already possesses, and in the various illuminations and enlightenings by which he is invited and urged toward this or that work. In a believer not yet justified, faith together with such movements of the Holy Spirit is sufficient aid for praying, asking and obtaining from God justifying grace and the gift of the Holy Spirit. And in one who does not yet believe, the grace sufficient for the act of faith consists, as Alvarez has already said, in knowledge of what is to be believed, devout thoughts, devout desires to have faith, and the like.
translator_notes: The print's plural 'sunt' with 'gratia sufficiens' (the subject is a list) is kept; the English follows the sense.

title: Alvarez: grace in the intellect alone is not simply sufficient
english: Thesis XXXIV. Be that as it may, that doctor holds that no grace is sufficient for any good work or devout action unless it not only enlightens the intellect inwardly but also in some way moves and affects the will.

'Rousing grace,' he says, 'by which only the intellect is enlightened or moved, is not the same as sufficient grace, speaking without qualification, but only in a certain respect. For not only the intellect but the will too needs divine motion and prevenient grace to be made able to perform works of piety, since sin has corrupted the will more than the intellect.'

title: Alvarez's proof: grace in the intellect is external to the will
english: Thesis XXXV. He proves it as follows: 'For salvation it is necessary not only that the intellect know what to do and what to avoid, but also that the will will to embrace good and avoid evil, and to love God above all things. But by rousing grace received in the intellect alone, the will cannot will anything that leads to salvation, nor love God above all things.

'For grace present in the intellect is external to the will, and so it does not give the will a sufficient principle for performing works of piety.' He concludes that grace received only in the intellect is not grace sufficient for salvation. Epitome de auxiliis, book 3, chapter 16.

title: The recent Thomists: efficacious grace as God's physical operation (Estius)
english: Thesis XXXVI. These recent Thomists locate the aid proper to efficacious grace in a gratuitous and gracious working of God that, properly speaking, produces conversion itself, or any other act of true piety, within a person's free choice. It does so by acting efficiently on the will's very movement, that is, by applying the will itself and determining it to will and to choose. This working is called physical, meaning working in the proper sense, such as is recognized in God with respect to all the other effects that come from him.

Since it is impossible for God to determine the will without its being determined and doing what God applies it to as a secondary cause, it follows that this grace cannot fail to have its effect. 'Hence, on this view, the grace of God is called efficacious with an efficacy not moral but physical, and in the most proper sense.' These are the words of Estius on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 28, paragraph 2.
translator_notes: The print numbers this thesis 'XXVI'; corrected to XXXVI (between XXXV and XXXVII).

title: Efficacious of itself: infallibly, insuperably, indeclinably
english: Thesis XXXVII. That is why they call this grace efficacious of itself, that is, grace that by its own force moves and determines free choice, and does so, in their own words, 'infallibly, insuperably, indeclinably'. For the human will cannot cheat it of its effect or prevent it from accomplishing what God properly gives it for, because this divine grace overcomes all human resistance, and its power consists in making a person willing who was unwilling.

title: Its efficacy is absolute and does not wait for consent
english: Thesis XXXVIII. For this reason they also say that this grace's efficacy is absolute with respect to the good action and does not hang on the consent of free choice. For the good action to follow, it does not wait for free choice to consent but brings about that consent by its power, since it brings free choice under itself and is in no way subject to free choice's power.

title: Freedom kept: the practical judgment could have been otherwise
english: Thesis XXXIX. Yet they do not think that this efficacy of grace removes or lessens the freedom of the human will in any respect, or that a person's good actions, which depend on that grace as their cause, are any less free for it. For through his grace God does not merely cause us to do good works in keeping with his will; he also causes us to do them in the way that suits human nature, and therefore freely.

That efficacious motion of divine grace brings it about in us that we choose the good on the basis of a prior judgment of the practical intellect, and in such a way that, on a different judgment of the same intellect, we could choose evil; and this is enough for freedom in the full sense. Although grace surely and infallibly ensures that our will is carried toward this or that good, with the mind's practical judgment going before, it does not prevent the intellect, while following that guidance, from keeping the power to judge otherwise, nor the will from keeping the power to choose otherwise; and freedom consists in this. A person is wholly free who of himself is so indifferent to acting or not acting that while he acts he has the power not to act or to act otherwise.

title: The power to dissent: composite and divided sense (Alvarez)
english: Thesis XL. For although grace works effectively so that free choice consents to the grace that moves it and follows its lead, it does not take away its power to dissent. The efficacious aid of Christ does ensure that a person's will always and most surely embraces the good toward which it is moved; but it does not prevent the will, while grace is moving it, from always having the power not to do that good, and even to do the opposite evil.

In these doctors' view, the created will's actual dissent cannot coexist with the actual motion of efficacious grace, but the power to dissent coexists perfectly well with that same motion. And this is what Alvarez says: that free choice moved by God with efficacious aid cannot dissent from it in the composite sense, but can in the divided sense.

title: Jansenius agrees with the Thomists on how efficacious grace works
english: Thesis XLI. Jansenius and his followers, moreover, teach the same as the recent Thomists about the way in which Christ's healing and efficacious grace works in human wills and moves them to act. With them they hold that the efficacy of this grace is absolute, and that it does not depend on, or wait for, the consent of free choice in order to achieve its effect.

It is, they say, the conqueror of the human heart, and such that no one can resist it. The effect for which God supplies it is inseparably joined to it, and no heart, however hard, rejects it, since it is given precisely to take away the heart's hardness. It does not leave the will evenly balanced but carries it off with the greatest power, and so rules the human will inseparably and indeclinably. Much to the same effect can be read in Jansenius throughout the eight books of De gratia Christi Salvatoris, above all in the third.

title: Jansenius: grace physically predetermines the will
english: Thesis XLII. Indeed Jansenius asserts with the Thomists that the task of physically predetermining the will truly belongs to this aid of Christ. It is such that it draws the will to act, not if the will chooses, but by most effectively granting it to will. It does not wait for the will to act together with it; it makes the will act together with it, applying the will to will and do whatever God has resolved should be willed and done through it.

For since, as he says, the will has been set by earthly desires toward not willing, and even toward resisting, this aid removes that downward pull and that bent in the opposite direction and turns the will back toward the good, not merely if free choice sees fit and wills, but by its own inexpressible light and sweetness, causing it to see fit and to will. So, on his account, God makes willing and consenting people out of unwilling and resisting ones, by inclining, applying and determining the will, and, because he anticipates the will's own determination, by predetermining it too: not only morally but by a true, real and physical determination.

For moral predetermination is the kind that works only from the side of the object, by way of something that allures, coaxes, asks, counsels and so on, whether from outside or within. This predetermination, by contrast, works in the will's power itself, which it properly applies to willing by the greatness of its sweetness, and by applying it determines it, since it causes in the will this very act of determining itself, and therefore predetermines it. De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 8, chapter 3.

title: Jansenius: freedom saved in the divided sense (book 8, chapter 4)
english: Thesis XLIII. On the same reasoning as the Thomists, that bishop and those who hold to his teaching maintain that the efficacy of Christ's grace just described can be reconciled with the freedom of human choice in this state. The grace of Christ that determines the will to act in no way removes its power to act otherwise, even though it infallibly causes it to act. An agent should be judged free if it acts in such a way that it has the power not to act or to act otherwise. Freedom does not require that the will's not acting be compatible, at the same moment, with everything needed for action being present; it requires only that the will be able not to act.

So on their assumptions, once the motion of divine grace is given, the soul must indeed follow it in the composite sense; the will cannot resist God as he moves it, or dissent from what God wills to accomplish through it, and in that respect the force of divine grace is rightly called indeclinable and insuperable. In the divided sense, however, it is true that the will, even while grace moves it, can resist God, dissent from grace and turn aside elsewhere than God is leading it. For in consenting to grace it does not thereby lose the power to dissent; in yielding to God's motion it does not lose the power to resist; and in following God's lead it does not lose the power to turn aside where concupiscence draws it.

This is set out in Jansenius, De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 8, chapter 4: 'As in the composite sense those expressions are true which say that the will, acted on by divine grace, cannot resist God, cannot dissent from what God wills to accomplish through it, cannot turn aside, cannot overcome; so, conversely, in the divided sense those are true which say that it can turn aside, can dissent, can overcome.'

title: Jansenius, book 8, chapters 20-21: powers to opposites are not opposed
english: Thesis XLIV. He repeats and presses the same point in chapter 20 of the same book: 'We say that free choice, however strongly and effectively it has been anticipated and determined to do good by the delight of grace, can still not only fail to do the good but even do evil. This is true not in the composite sense, as the common phrase has it, but in the divided sense.

'At the very time when the will's choice is placed under the delight of grace that moves it effectively, and even while it is performing the good act of will, there is in that same will the power not to perform it, and even to sin. This is not because ceasing from the act it is then eliciting, or an actual sin, could coexist with the influence of delighting grace (which the composite sense would require), but because the power to cease and to sin can be joined with that same grace at the same time in the same choice of the will.

'Two contrary acts are opposed and cannot be in the same will at once; but powers for opposites are not opposed, either to one another or to the opposite acts, and they dwell together in the same subject at the same time, whether it is acting or at rest. So the will, however much it is captivated by the sweetness of grace, can refrain from doing what it is drawn to, since it keeps a real power of not acting even under the grace that draws it, although not acting itself cannot be combined with the working of grace in the same will at the same time.'

In the next chapter he puts it more briefly: 'The power of dissenting does not conflict with the actual motion of grace and with consent, although actual dissent cannot be joined with God's actual motion.'

title: Jansenius's preferred concord: freedom as acting from one's own reason
english: Thesis XLV. Jansenius and those who share his view do acknowledge that the efficacy of divine grace must be reconciled in this way with indifference, that is, with the power toward good and evil, toward acting and not acting, which they do not deny is found in all who live in this mortal body, and in which many seem to place the very essence of freedom. Even so, they insist that the true and genuine harmony of divine grace with free will is not to be sought there, because Augustine and his first disciples set out that harmony differently.

To reconcile grace with free choice, they say simply that grace does not take away free choice, since it causes free choice not to lie idle like a stone and do nothing, nor to be forced to the good against its will, but itself to will and act. For they defined as free what is in our power, and they said that what is in our power is what happens when we will it, or what someone does if he wills and does not do if he does not will. On these premises it follows that every act of will whatever, that is, every rational volition, is free. Just as it is impossible for it not to happen when we will it and to happen when we do not, so it is impossible for it not to be in our power and thereby not free.

Since grace, then, does nothing but cause us to elicit a good volition from the right judgment of reason, by that very fact it causes us to act freely, and so it does not destroy our freedom but establishes it. Jansenius judges this way of reconciling human freedom with the infallible efficacy of divine grace to be the best and most genuine of all (De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 8, chapter 19). For on his view the essence of freedom considered in general does not consist at all in the indifference by which one can will or not will, will this or its contrary, but rather in being moved to will and act not by some external force or brute necessity but by the judgment of one's own reason, and so far being master of one's own act.

title: Same working, different essence: Jansenius and the Thomists part
english: Thesis XLVI. Jansenius and the recent Thomists agree that the grace of Christ by which people are converted and do good is grace efficacious of itself, which brings free choice under itself and is in no way subject to it, and which does not wait for the human will's consent for its effect to follow but brings that consent about infallibly and powerfully.

Yet they disagree about the nature and substance of that grace, and do not explain in the same way what it consists in and where it lies. For both, the way this grace works is the same; what it is differs.

title: Agreed: an immediate motion of the will, not an abiding habit
english: Thesis XLVII. Both sides agree that the grace without which no one turns to God and does good, and whose recipients are all surely and infallibly converted and do good, is an aid that moves and affects the will itself, of itself and immediately, and not the intellect alone; and that it is not to be located in any abiding habit.
But what it is, the two sides do not fully agree; indeed, not even the Thomists agree among themselves.

title: Three Thomist accounts of the premotion; Alvarez's 'virtual motion'
english: Thesis XLVIII. All of them call this efficacious aid by the name of physical predetermination, and say that it is a gratuitous and prior motion of God that moves the created will and applies it to doing good. Yet some say that this premotion of God, by which human wills are moved to do good, is in the manner of a quality that does not remain but passes away with the will's own operation.

Others say that the actual motion by which God moves the will and applies it to act is really the will's operation itself, insofar as it comes from God, who applies the will to act and efficaciously premoves it.

Finally, others hold that this prior motion is neither in the manner of a quality received in the will nor the same as the will's operation, but something with a kind of incomplete being, as colours are in the air and the power of the craft is in the craftsman's tool, which may properly and fittingly be called a 'virtual motion'. So Diego Alvarez, De auxiliis divinae gratiae, book 3, disputation 19, who defends this last opinion as true and as his own.

title: Alvarez: the will is passive to the premotion, active in its act
english: Thesis XLIX. From this he infers that this aid of God, which precedes the created will's action, is produced in the will effectively by God alone and in no way depends efficiently on any influence of the will itself. So with respect to that prior aid of God the will is passive, although the same will is active and free with respect to the free act to which that prior aid moves it. The disputation just cited, section 6.

title: Not in our power, yet we can hinder it: Alvarez's man commanded to fly
english: Thesis L. These doctors also acknowledge that this motion of God, prior to and necessary for every good work, is not in a person's power, since it is given and withheld at God's good pleasure. Yet they maintain that our will has the capacity to prevent itself from receiving that motion.

From this they infer: 'If a person does not perform the act that is commanded, it will be counted against him as a fault, because by his own fault he prevented the efficacious aid from being given him, which he needed in order actually to perform the act of virtue that is commanded. It is as if God laid on someone a command to fly and, as far as lay with God, offered him wings and the help he needed to fly, and the man answered in his freedom, "Lord, I do not want to take wings or to fly": he would rightly be held guilty and a breaker of the command, even though he could not fly without wings, because by his own fault he prevented their being given him by God.'

These are the words of the same Alvarez in the book just cited, disputation 18, section 20, where he supports his teaching with Augustine's saying: 'That people are not helped by God's grace, the cause lies in themselves, not in God.'

title: Why premotion is needed: dependence on the First Cause, not only the fall
english: Thesis LI. These doctors do not derive the need for this aid, which effectively premoves and predetermines the will to every devout action, simply from the corruption and weakness of the human will. They derive it in general from the dependence of every secondary cause on the First Cause, without whose impulse and prior motion, on their assumptions, no cause can do anything at all; and further from the indifference of the free will, which is not fit to do anything unless a higher agent determines it.

title: Physical premotion presupposes a moral motion through the object
english: Thesis LII. Although they place this efficacious aid in a motion that physically predetermines the will, they acknowledge that it presupposes a moral motion, brought about by a fitting presentation of the object through which that object appears lovable and suited to the will. For the will cannot desire anything unless the intellect first presents it to the will as suited to it.

So no one is physically determined by the aid of grace to pursue the good unless his mind has been enlightened with knowledge of that good, and his will invited to desire it and morally inclined by the inward persuasions and promptings of the Holy Spirit. Yet on their teaching the will's consent never follows from this unless that other aid is added which moves the will effectively and physically to consent.

title: Jansenius: efficacious grace is a heavenly delight
english: Thesis LIII. Jansenius holds that the grace of Christ which, once a person has been enlightened with knowledge of the good and in various ways prompted, drawn and urged to embrace it, finally determines him effectively and surely to pursue it in fact, is nothing other than a heavenly and inexpressible sweetness, or spiritual delight. By it the will is anticipated and bent to will and do whatever God has resolved that it should will and do.

For there is no kind of good action or good will, and no effect of efficacious grace, that is not to be ascribed to this heavenly delight as to the true grace of Christ and its true cause. It is by this delight that we begin to desire the good preached to us, and by it that, with devout will, we believe and take up the good we have already thought of.

Without such a delight poured in from heaven, no prayer pleasing to God can be offered, God cannot be loved purely and chastely, the temptations of our desires cannot be resisted, and in short no good work can be done. So that doctor labours at length to prove from Augustine: De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 4, chapters 1 and following.

title: Three acts of the appetite: love, desire, delight
english: Thesis LIV. To explain what this heavenly sweetness and delight is, which in his own view and Augustine's is the true grace of Christ, he distinguishes three acts of the appetite and of the will with respect to the good. The first is simple love, or complacency: a kind of adjusting of the appetite to the good as suited to it.

The second is a movement that follows from this, called desire, by which the appetite reaches out toward the good that suits and fits it. The third is rest in a good one has already gained; and this act is properly called joy and delight, by which the mind settles in a present good with a certain satisfaction and enjoyment.

title: Even love and desire share in delight
english: Thesis LV. Although delight properly consists in that third act, he observes that a certain delight is present even in the earlier acts of simple love and desire. Since every love tends by way of desire toward delight, as to its rest and centre, the movement itself cannot fail to share something of that sweetness. As soon as a movement begins it has a share in rest, inasmuch as even the first moment of a movement has its own partial end.

title: Love of spiritual goods already possesses and enjoys them
english: Thesis LVI. This holds good most of all, by far, in the love and desire of spiritual things: wisdom, truth, holiness, righteousness and charity. Whoever loves earthly things does not gain them simply by loving them, nor rest in them as things gained, nor take delight in enjoying them in his mind.

But whoever loves righteousness, truth, wisdom or charity by that very fact gains, has and possesses those goods, and so enjoys them with delight and delights in enjoying them. So whoever loves God, who is eternal wisdom itself, truth, charity and righteousness, enjoys God and delights in him by the very act of love, which possesses its object.
It follows that the names of delight and sweetness are rightly given to acts of love and desire as well, especially when they concern God and divine things, as Augustine does throughout.

title: Deliberate and indeliberate acts of love and desire
english: Thesis LVII. Note also that the acts of love and desire that affect the will are of two kinds. Some are deliberate and free, drawn out after weighing the matter, from a definite judgment of reason. Others are indeliberate and therefore not free: they spring up in the will all at once when some object is put before it, before the mind is able to weigh and deliberate.

title: The heavenly delight is an indeliberate act sent from heaven
english: Thesis LVIII. With these points in view, the same doctor observes that the heavenly delight in which he places Christ's efficacious aid, needed for every devout action and good act of the will, is not delight in the proper sense, by which the will rests in a present good and enjoys it and which is the end point of the desire by which the will is carried toward the good. Nor is it any free and deliberate movement of the will.

It is an indeliberate act sent into the will from heaven, through which the good put before the will either simply pleases it sweetly or even stirs it to desire that good. Although the will does not elicit this heaven-sent act freely, the act still proceeds from the will actively and is a vital movement of the will.

title: Not a free love or desire (book 4, chapter 11)
english: Thesis LIX. On that doctor's principles it is plain that this delight does not consist in any free love or desire. It is needed even in order to desire and love God, or any true spiritual good, by a free movement of the will, since such desire and love are good acts, which cannot come from the will without the grace of sweetness.

Jansenius deals with this more fully in De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 4, chapter 11, whose heading is: 'This heavenly delight, in Augustine's mind, is a vital and indeliberate act of the soul; that is, an act of the love and desire that come before consent and before the delight that is also called the mind's rest and joy.'

title: Why delight is needed: the will moves only toward what delights
english: Thesis LX. In that author's view this divinely infused delight is needed for every good act of the will because, by Augustine's express statement, the will cannot be moved in any way unless something comes before it that delights and invites the mind. The will embraces nothing unless it is first touched toward it by some sense of delight.

This holds not only for good things but for evil ones too. The will is not carried toward evil unless some prior delight prepares and drives it, through which evil coaxes it under a false show of good.

title: Two delights in conflict: the stronger carries the will
english: Thesis LXI. A person's mind is often touched at once by some sense of delight toward opposite things. Especially in believers, as long as they carry this mortal body, there is a struggle between two delights, one earthly and the other heavenly, one harmful and the other helpful; and whichever wins draws the mind after it, inclined and consenting.

It can never turn out otherwise than that the greater delight carries the will off toward what delights it more. Wherever the mind stands between righteousness and sin and is pulled two ways, it must act according to whatever has delighted it more.

title: Augustine on Galatians: whatever delights us more, we must act on
english: Thesis LXII. Jansenius illustrates his view with these words of Augustine from the commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, where, treating the fruits of the Spirit (joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control), he says: 'These spiritual fruits reign in the person in whom sins do not reign. These goods reign if they delight so much that they hold the mind firm in temptations, so that it does not fall into consenting to sin. For whatever delights us more, we must act according to it.

'For example, the form of a beautiful woman comes before us and stirs us to the delight of fornication; but if that inner beauty and the pure face of chastity delight us more, through the grace that is in faith in Christ, then we live by it and act by it. So, with sin not reigning in us to make us obey its desires, but righteousness reigning through charity, we do with great delight whatever we know pleases God in it. What I have said of chastity and fornication I mean to be understood of the rest.'

title: The efficacious help is the delight that is greater: victorious delight
english: Thesis LXIII. So he places that efficacious aid of divine grace not in just any delight in the good, but in a delight that, in the person to whom it is given, is greater than every opposing delight and overcomes it; and for this reason he calls it, with Augustine, 'victorious delight'.

If the delight of the flesh is greater, the delight that the spirit pours in will never win the will's consent. A lesser delight cannot overcome a greater; the mind follows whichever delight has held it more strongly by the sweetness with which it touches it. De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 4, chapter 6.

title: Victorious in one person, overcome in another
english: Thesis LXIV. Although, on his teaching, that victorious delight in which Christ's healing and efficacious grace consists drives the will to the good infallibly and makes it surely consent to the good that is so sweet, nevertheless a delight that wins in one person, because the delight of the flesh opposing it there is weaker, and so brings the will to consent, will in another person be overcome by a greater and stronger delight of the flesh. There it will not bend the will, which a mightier and stronger earthly delight will lead away captive.

title: Why the victorious delight is needed: the will's weakness; Augustine to Simplicianus
english: Thesis LXV. He traces the need for that victorious delight, which must be poured in from heaven to overcome temptations and to carry out the works of righteousness, to the weakness of the will, which makes it unable to embrace anything good unless it delights. The will by itself, with only its freedom of willing, cannot overcome the inner obstacles of pleasure or pain; nor is a person able of himself, as the Pelagians claimed, to lay down laws for the impulses born in him.

Earthly delights arising from the concupiscence innate in human beings so weigh down the will and call it back from the true good that it cannot lift itself up and break out into actions worthy of heaven, unless God sends a heavenly delight and sweetness, greater and stronger than those earthly ones. By it the will is freed from the birdlime of carnal desires and set at liberty from that captivity. Without it the will cannot will the good so strongly and intensely as to overcome the opposing temptation.

Nor is it in the will's power to take delight in heavenly things at its pleasure, as Augustine says to Simplicianus: 'Who has it in his power that his mind should be touched by a sight that would move his will to faith? Who embraces in his mind anything that does not delight him? Or who has it in his power either that something able to delight him should come before him, or that it should delight him when it comes? So when the things by which we advance toward God delight us, this is inspired and given by God's grace; it is not obtained at our own bidding and by our own effort, or by the merit of our works.'

title: Jansenius's conclusion (book 4, chapter 7)
english: Thesis LXVI. From these and many similar passages Jansenius draws this conclusion: 'This weakness of willing, which arises from the delights of earthly things that press the will down to love created and carnal things, is the true reason why the delight of righteousness, that is, of the good work commanded, is necessary. Lifted up by it, the mind can either will strongly what it already wills feebly, or even will what it does not will.

'Unless God has softened the will with the sweetness of this delight, it will never be able either to fulfil or to will the righteousness of the commandment itself; and if it seems to perform some acts concerning the commandment, they will end only in the fruit of earthly desires and delights, or of its own pride. That heavenly sweetness smooths the way so that the will can get free of the birdlime of carnal things and fix itself on loving righteousness.

'It follows that if this delight is lacking, the will, as if numb and dead, can embrace nothing good at all; just as, conversely, in loving carnal things it can pursue nothing except what has delighted it.' De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 4, chapter 7.

title: This need comes from the will's punishment, not its nature
english: Thesis LXVII. That author is careful to point out that this need of heavenly delight for willing and acting, and the weakness of our will that makes it unable to be moved to the good unless something has delighted it, or to choose between two delightful things anything other than the one that has prevailed by delighting, comes not from the essence and nature of the will but from its punishment.
