He does not think that the nature of the human will, considered in itself, is such that it cannot freely pursue a good object unless that object has first delighted it. Still less does he think it necessary that, when a good object is seen, the will be touched with some delight.

title: Before the fall no delight ruled the will; the first sin had no delight before it
english: Thesis LXVIII. So he ascribes all this to a weakness of the will contracted through sin, which is to be counted among the punishments of sin. On his assumptions, before sin no delight ruled the will, bending and determining it to one side or the other by effectively drawing out its consent.

Before man fell from his original integrity through sin, no delight in earthly things urged and enticed his will toward evil, since every such delight is born of concupiscence, which is the fruit of sin. The first sin of the first man was therefore committed with no delight going before it: the first delight followed the perverse will, not the will the delight. For every resistance to a good will is the punishment of an evil will, and God does not inflict it on a rational creature that has not deserved it.

title: Adam's grace was not victorious delight
english: Thesis LXIX. As for good actions, the first man was indeed endowed with grace so that he could perform them and carry them out duly and perfectly. But that grace was not such as to make him will and act, since it was subject to his free choice and it lay with him to use it or not to use it. So the victorious delight that brings free choice under itself and moves the will to the good effectively and infallibly had no place in him.

It plainly follows that the present need of victorious delight for acting well does not arise from the nature of the will itself. Otherwise it would have had to be permanent in man, whereas in man unfallen it had no place and was not even necessary to him.

title: The cause is the will's corruption; delight as its one medicine (chapter 9)
english: Thesis LXX. On this doctor's view, then, what makes that heavenly delight necessary for good acts is nothing other than the corruption and depravity of the human will, which through the first man's sin has been thrown headlong under the rule of lusts. So in every action before grace it is roused by some lustful delight that goes before it and tickles it; by consenting to that delight it sins, and if left to itself it cannot fail to consent.

To cure this evil God sends the delight of the good, that is, of righteousness, as the sick will's one medicine. Because it runs directly against the disease afflicting the will, it wrings from the will the consent to the good that God requires of it. So the will is turned back upward, so that, fastened to the spirit that soothes and delights it and, as it were, hanging from God, it is no longer dragged down into its old slavery to lust. Jansenius develops this at length in chapter 9 of the book already cited several times.

title: Where Jansenius and the Thomists agree on sufficient grace
english: Thesis LXXI. From all this it is easy to see how Jansenius's view agrees with the Thomists' and how it differs from theirs on the grace they call sufficient and the grace they call efficacious. As for the grace called sufficient, Jansenius grants with them that even those who are not converted and do not act well receive manifold grace from God, and that not only is their intellect enlightened but their will too is struck by various motions of grace.

Nor does he deny that, once such aids of grace are received, a person is truly said to be able to be converted and to act well. Conversely, the Thomists admit that all those who are not converted and do not act well lack an aid that is plainly necessary for anyone actually to be converted and act well.

title: The difference: a battle of words about the name 'sufficient'
english: Thesis LXXII. The difference is this: the Thomists say that grace which good action does not in fact follow is nevertheless sufficient, and that through it a proximate and complete power of acting well is given. Jansenius and his followers deny this.

Here the dispute is plainly a mere battle of words, a question about a name. For Jansenius denies that such grace is sufficient, and that it gives the proximate power of acting well, for one reason only: it lacks an aid that is plainly necessary for good action, as the Thomists themselves concede.

title: Where Thomists and Jansenius agree on efficacious grace
english: Thesis LXXIII. On efficacious grace, the Thomists teach together with Jansenius that no grace of Christ exists that is not efficacious in some respect: there is none that fails to bring about, surely and infallibly, some effect, the very effect for which God precisely gives it and to which his absolute decree has destined it. Jansenius, for his part, grants with them that Christ's grace determines the will physically as well as morally.

With one accord and equal insistence both sides maintain that divine grace is efficacious from itself and of itself. Its efficacy is absolute and does not hang on the consent of free choice, and grace is master over free choice rather than subject to its power.

title: First difference: a passing motion received, or a vital act of the will
english: Thesis LXXIV. On the nature of efficacious grace, however, they differ in many respects, as Jansenius notes and reports at length in De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 8, chapter 1. For the recent Thomists, the grace that physically predetermines the will is, as explained above, a 'virtual motion' with a kind of incomplete being, present in the will in the way colours are present in the air and impetus in a thing that has been pushed.

For Jansenius, that grace is a real and true affection of the will, consisting in a love and desire for heavenly and spiritual good, by which the human mind is carried upward sweetly and with immense joy. So for the Thomists this efficacious aid is only received passively in the will, while for Jansenius it is something that proceeds actively from the will and is a vital movement of it.

title: Second difference: absolute premotion against relative delight
english: Thesis LXXV. Next, in the Thomists' view the physically predetermining aid is such that, whatever the circumstances in which the will is placed, it always makes it act, produces its effect, and overcomes all resistance. If the same aid that moves and determines this or that person to act well were given to everyone else, it would move them all alike, and would move this same person too, whatever impulses of concupiscence he were supposed to be shaken by.

In Jansenius's sense, however, Christ's efficacious aid works otherwise. The victorious delight in which he places that aid is relative: it is victorious only when it is greater than the opposing delight. If the other delight happens to be more ardent, the mind will cling only to ineffective desires and will never effectively will what ought to be willed.

So a delight that wins in one person, because the impulses of concupiscence are weaker, will be overcome and prove inefficacious in another, because the impulses of the same concupiscence are more violent. Nor will what is enough for this person to overcome a present temptation be enough at another time, if a stronger and fiercer temptation presses on him.

title: Third difference: why the aid is needed
english: Thesis LXXVI. Further, the recent Thomists hold that physical predetermination is necessary for the human will to act well because the will, like all other secondary causes, needs to be premoved by God, the First Cause, in order actually to act. They also derive this necessity from the will's indifference, which on that account must be determined to act by a higher cause.

Jansenius, however, thinks the efficacious aid of divine grace necessary to the human will for one reason only: the wound inflicted by sin, and the weakness contracted from the concupiscence that clings to fallen man.

title: Hence: premotion in Eden for the Thomists, not for Jansenius
english: Thesis LXXVII. On the Thomists' assumptions, then, the physically predetermining aid was necessary even for man unfallen, quite apart from any thought of sin. On Jansenius's view, by contrast, the efficacious aid by which a person comes to will and act had no place in the state of innocence.

There was only the aid without which man could not act well, and which could easily coexist with his not acting well, since it was subject to free choice and in no way brought man's free choice under itself.

title: Molina departs from both; sufficient aid given to all
english: Thesis LXXVIII. The teaching of the most celebrated Jesuit Luis de Molina, whom many others follow, is far removed from the view of Jansenius of Ypres and of the recent Thomists as well. To make this clearer, the substance of his view on efficacious and sufficient grace should be briefly restated from his writings.

He will not have any aid of grace called sufficient except one which, once given, requires nothing further on God's part for the action actually to follow. In this sense he teaches that God grants sufficient aid of grace both to those who do not act well and do not turn to God and to those who are converted and act well.

title: Sufficient aid divided into efficacious and inefficacious by its outcome
english: Thesis LXXIX. Hence he divides sufficient aid into efficacious and inefficacious aid. Efficacious aid is the aid that its effect follows, that is, the good work to which it moves a person. Inefficacious aid lacks its effect: through it a person is not actually converted and does not act well.

title: Molina: efficacy from the aid itself would destroy freedom
english: Thesis LXXX. On his view, an aid's being efficacious does not depend on a special motion of God which, once given, always brings free choice to consent and cooperate, and which, once withdrawn, leaves it never consenting or cooperating. Indeed he thinks those who hold this err in faith.

He reports the view of those who say that free choice's consenting or not consenting is to be ascribed to God's aid itself, or to God moving efficaciously or inefficaciously through it: so that whenever God moves through an aid that has its efficacy from the manner of the divine motion and from God himself, free choice consents and cooperates toward salvation, and whenever he moves through an aid that does not have its efficacy from him, free choice does not consent or cooperate toward salvation. Then he adds: 'I would certainly not hesitate to call this view, explained in this way, an error in faith.'

His reason is that in this way, as he sees it, freedom of choice is lost, since a person's conversion and perseverance will then depend not on his own innate freedom but on the quality of the aid and of the divine motion. 'For if,' he says, 'our choice has from the efficacy of the divine aid that it consents or does not consent to God's call, cooperates or does not cooperate toward salvation, and perseveres or does not persevere in grace, then this certainly depends not on its own innate freedom but on the quality of the aid and of the divine motion; and so there is nothing that could be credited to it for praise and merit, but rather freedom of choice toward salvation is lost altogether.' Concordia liberi arbitrii cum gratiae donis, question 23, articles 4-5, disputation 1, member 6.

title: Efficacy depends on free choice, even in the composite sense
english: Thesis LXXXI. On his view, then, the division of sufficient aid into efficacious and inefficacious is taken from the effect, and the effect depends on the freedom of choice. So it lies with human choice, and is placed in its power, whether the aid of grace, sufficient of itself, becomes efficacious or remains inefficacious.

Sufficient aid is called efficacious when choice is converted with it by its own freedom, although, with nothing in the aid preventing it, choice could have remained unconverted, and that in the composite sense and not only in the divided sense. It is called inefficacious when choice, by the same freedom, is not converted with it, although it could have been converted and could actually and in fact have elicited the act of conversion without any further aid of God's grace.

'We assert,' he says, 'that whether the aids of prevenient and assisting grace granted by the ordinary law to those still on their pilgrimage are efficacious or inefficacious for conversion or justification depends on the free consent and cooperation of our choice with them. It is therefore in our free power either to make them efficacious, by consenting and cooperating with them toward the acts by which we are disposed for justification, or to make them inefficacious, by withholding our consent and cooperation, or even by eliciting the contrary dissent.' Same book, question 14, article 13, disputation 40.

title: Named from the outcome: more grace may convert no one
english: Thesis LXXXII. On his assumptions, then, efficacious and inefficacious aid are so named from the outcome, and efficacious aid has nothing more in itself than inefficacious aid. It can therefore happen, and often does, that of two people anticipated by equal grace from God one is converted and the other is not.

Indeed it sometimes happens that someone who has received greater aids of grace remains impenitent or neglects to act well, while another, to whom God has granted fewer and lesser aids, truly repents and is eager for good works, because the first refused to use the greater grace God granted him and the second, in his freedom, made good use of the lesser.

It also sometimes happens that of two people in whom grace is efficacious, the one helped by lesser grace acts more fervently and with greater zeal, while the one helped by greater grace acts more sluggishly and slackly.

title: Molina's own words (disputation 12)
english: Thesis LXXXIII. This is Molina's express teaching in question 14, article 13, disputation 12: 'It can happen,' he says, 'that of two people inwardly called by God with equal aid, one is converted through the freedom of his choice and the other remains in unbelief. It often happens, too, that one person is converted with the same aid with which another is not.

'Indeed it can happen that someone anticipated and called with far greater aid is, in his freedom, not converted, while another is converted with far less. For God often calls, and sinners refuse and scorn all God's counsel.'

title: Molina need not reconcile efficacy with freedom: grace is subject to choice
english: Thesis LXXXIV. Plainly, then, Molina has no need to labour at reconciling the efficacy of divine grace with the freedom of human choice. He makes God's grace subject to man's free choice, and will not allow any aid of grace to be so efficacious that it determines free choice to act of itself.
Whatever aid from God is supposed to precede a good action, the human will's dissent can always coexist with it, and it remains in a person's power to use it as he pleases or not to use it.

title: Yet the consent is supernatural: grace cooperates as a habit with its power
english: Thesis LXXXV. Even so, he holds that the act of free choice by which it consents to divine grace is not merely natural but supernatural, and must be ascribed to God's grace. This is so not only insofar as grace is called prevenient, alluring and inviting a person to the good and in a way supplying him with new strength, but also insofar as through that same grace God, together with man's free choice, flows into its act; in this respect it is called cooperating grace.

On his view, the grace by which God anticipates a person helps the will in acting and cooperates with it in the way a habit inhering in a power concurs with that power toward its act. So this cooperation of grace itself depends on the free will, and must not be thought of as moving the will or as prior to its action. In the same way, a habit's influence on an act depends on the power: the habit does not move the power to act, but, as the power moves itself to act, the habit flows together with it into the power's act.

title: Molina, disputation 40: prevenient grace as the Spirit's instrument
english: Thesis LXXXVI. This is how Molina reasons on the matter in various places, but above all in disputation 40 on question 14, article 13: 'Third, we assert that prevenient grace, by which the Holy Spirit anticipates, rouses, allures and invites an adult's choice to the acts of believing, hoping, loving and repenting just mentioned, is an instrument of the Holy Spirit, by which he further concurs efficiently and flows in together with choice itself to produce those acts, when choice consents to that grace and, with it, flows into and cooperates in those acts. Such acts therefore come at once efficiently from choice itself, through its own influence on them, and from God, who flows into them by a new influence or new action through prevenient grace as through an instrument.

'For just as the habits of the virtues, natural and supernatural alike, incline the powers to their acts and so make them apt for them, and therefore concur efficiently with the powers toward those acts by flowing into them with their own partial influence, so, since prevenient grace allures, invites and inclines the powers to elicit those supernatural acts, whenever the powers consent to rousing grace and flow into the acts to which grace allures and invites them, grace itself will also flow in and cooperate with the powers in those acts.

'Again, just as the actual existence of the habits' influence on the acts of virtue that the powers elicit depends on the powers' own influence on those acts, since a habit is not a sufficient cause for producing such acts without the powers' concurrence, so the actual existence of that new influence of prevenient grace on the acts of believing, hoping, loving and repenting depends on the cooperation and influence of our free choice on those acts through intellect and will, since prevenient grace likewise is not a sufficient cause of those acts without our choice's cooperation in them and influence on them.'

title: Molina's two anathemas
english: Thesis LXXXVII. From this he concludes that the consent of free choice to God, who rouses and calls through prevenient grace, is nothing in reality that is not supernatural and does not at the same time come from God, not only as from one who allures, rouses and invites choice to it, but also as from one who cooperates through the aid of grace. On his view, therefore, 'anyone who affirms that the consent of our choice to God, who rouses and calls through the aid of prevenient grace, is a natural act, or can be elicited without the aid and cooperation of that prevenient grace, must be held anathema.'

Yet he declares in turn that 'anyone is also anathema who says that this consent is not in the free power of our choice in the way he has explained', namely so that it lies with free choice to make such prevenient grace of the Holy Spirit void or not. These are his words in the same disputation 40.

title: Molina, disputation 37: what each cause contributes to the act
english: Thesis LXXXVIII. He explains more precisely what grace contributes and what free choice contributes to the good acts in which a person's conversion consists in disputation 37 on the same article. There he assumes that three things concur in any good act: first, God's general concurrence as first agent; second, the particular influence of divine grace; and finally, man's free choice.

He then teaches that a good act, for example the act of believing, hoping or repenting, has from God's general concurrence that it is an act at all, but not that it is this act rather than that one; from free choice, that in its substance it is this act and not another; and from grace, that it is a supernatural act.

'For,' he says, 'it comes from God, flowing in through the general concurrence alone, as from a universal cause, and so it has from that cause no more reason to be an assent of belief or sorrow for sins than to be the opposite act or an act of some other power. From the influence of free choice, together with the knowledge and other things needed for the act to be produced in its substance, it has, as from a particular cause, that in the substance of the act it is an assent of faith or sorrow for sins rather than some other act.

'From prevenient grace, that is, from God as he flows into the same act through it, as through his instrument, together with free choice, it has that it is a supernatural act, specifically distinct from the purely natural act of believing or of sorrowing for sins that free choice would then elicit by its own strength alone, if prevenient grace did not flow in together with it.'

title: Grace and free choice as two parts of one complete cause
english: Thesis LXXXIX. On his view, then, God's grace and man's free choice are two parts of one complete cause of the act of believing, hoping or repenting as salvation requires it, and each such act depends on the influence both of free choice and of divine grace. From free choice they have that in their substance they are believing, hoping and repenting; from the influence of grace, that they are supernatural and of the kind needed for salvation.

So each of these acts is wholly from free choice and wholly from grace, but from neither as from the whole and complete cause, only as from a part of the complete cause. This is how that author sets out his view at the beginning of the disputation just cited.

title: Equal aids: true of prevenient grace, not of cooperating grace
english: Thesis XC. When Molina says that if God gives two people equal aids, one may be converted by his own freedom and the other not, he warns that he means the aids of prevenient grace, taken as prevenient. If we speak of that same grace as cooperating, that is, as the grace through which God flows into the act a person freely elicits, it is no longer true that with equal aid one is converted and the other is not. It is impossible for someone not to be converted while God is nevertheless producing in him, together with his free choice, the act of conversion.

Yet prevenient and cooperating grace are in reality one and the same, and the cooperation of grace depends on the cooperation of our free choice, just as the concurrence and influence of any habit depends on the working of the power it resides in. So, speaking simply and absolutely, he thinks one must say that a person is converted and saved by his freedom with equal or even smaller aids, while another is neither converted nor saved. Speaking with the utmost strictness, though, one should not say that with equal aids of grace one is converted and the other not, since in the one converted there is an influence of grace not present in the other: the influence that depends on the consent of our free choice.

title: Not converted by freedom alone
english: Thesis XCI. In the same way, according to this Doctor, one must not say that when two adults have equal aids of prevenient grace, the one who is converted is converted by his freedom alone. That conversion does depend on freedom and is brought about by choice in its freedom. But it is not brought about by that freedom alone: the aid of prevenient grace cooperates with it at the same time, through the influence by which it takes on the character of cooperating grace.

Even so, when that influence is present and accompanies prevenient grace in dependence on the cooperation of choice, nothing more is required than the free cooperation of our choice. This is in disputation 40 on article 13 of question 14, in the paragraph 'Ad secundam'.

title: Able not to be converted: composite and divided sense
english: Thesis XCII. It follows from his assumptions that, whatever aids of prevenient grace are given, taken as prevenient, a person is able not to be converted, in the composite sense as well as in the divided sense. Given the aid of the same grace as cooperating, however, a person can indeed fail to be converted in the divided sense, but not in the composite sense.

For the influence of cooperating grace cannot be present, as cooperating in conversion, without the sinner being converted through his own choice. This takes nothing away from the freedom of choice, because, as has been said many times already, that influence of cooperating grace depends on the consent of human choice. This can be seen in the same disputation, in the paragraph beginning 'Hinc patet'.

title: Molina's account of the nature of grace: illumination and motions
english: Thesis XCIII. Molina explains at length, in disputation 45 on article 13 of question 14, the nature of this divine grace, which is prevenient in one respect and cooperating in another, and which man's free choice makes efficacious or inefficacious. To begin with, he places that grace in general in an illumination of the mind and in certain motions of the will.

title: Illumination: acquired knowledge helped by God's influence
english: Thesis XCIV. For him this illumination of the mind is simply a set of notions received from an external preacher or from some other source, and helped by a special, supernatural influence of God so that they are in some way already fitted for salvation. He observes that when God enlightens people in the ordinary way he does not send into them new species and ideas from which that knowledge arises, the knowledge through whose intervention their minds are enlightened.

That knowledge arises through species acquired in the human way and stirred up by preachers or by some other means. God inserts himself into them by his influence, so that this knowledge becomes more or less fitted for salvation, in proportion as his influence is greater or smaller. On Molina's view, then, for God to enlighten is nothing else than to cooperate in this way, by his influence, in the kinds of knowledge that rouse the will.

title: The motions of the will in prevenient grace arise naturally
english: Thesis XCV. On his view the motions of the will that make up prevenient grace are certain affections. Once knowledge has gone before, they raise and invite the will to elicit hope, to love God or to grieve for sins, before it elicits the act of hope, or of love, or of grief arising from love of him.

The will does not cooperate in these motions and affections as free choice, but only as will, that is, as a kind of nature. Whether it wants them or not, they rise up in it naturally once the knowledge is present. They have the character of grace only if God at the same time flows specially into them, so that they become supernatural and are also fitted in a certain way for salvation.

title: The natural motion that precedes volition: Lucifer and Eve
english: Thesis XCVI. To make this clearer, he observes that when we contemplate something very lovable and well worth obtaining, a motion rises naturally in the will by which it is drawn toward that thing. This motion is not a volition. It is an affection of the will toward the thing, whose goodness, so to speak, touches it and entices it to will it.

According to Molina this motion normally comes before volition, in angels as well as in men, and in the state of intact nature as well as in that of fallen nature. Lucifer's will was drawn toward what he sought to gain through pride before, in time or in nature, he freely willed it. In the same way Eve was drawn toward the forbidden fruit before she willed to eat it against God's law.

title: The will can hinder this motion only indirectly
english: Thesis XCVII. Once such a motion has arisen in the will from contemplating the thing, it is in the will's power simply to will the thing or not to will it. The motion by which the will is drawn toward the thing, however, does not arise freely, as was said; it arises in the will purely by nature once the thing is contemplated.

Still, the will can hinder that motion in itself indirectly: by keeping the thought away, by turning to other matters, and by seeing to it that the mind sets before the will other things that usually draw it toward the very opposite.

title: The natural motion toward hope
english: Thesis XCVIII. Suppose there is an affection toward something that the mind conceives as lovable and presents to the will, and the mind then sees a way and an approach by which it believes the thing can be obtained. A motion then also rises naturally in the will, a kind of uplift toward hoping, which comes before the free act of hope in time or in nature.

That motion is produced by the knowledge of the object's goodness and the knowledge of the way it is believed it can be obtained, with the will cooperating not as free but as a kind of nature. It rises naturally in the will, and it is the stronger, the greater and more probable is the knowledge of the object's goodness and of the way to obtain it. The same holds for the will's affection toward an object known simply as good.

title: Grace only perfects and helps nature
english: Thesis XCIX. Molina gives grace no other role than to perfect nature and help it in its own motions, so that each person becomes, through supernatural aid and grace, what salvation requires. To identify and explain the motions of grace, therefore, he wants us to look at the course and order that nature itself, or the knowing and desiring powers, would follow if they produced, by their own strength alone, the substance of the same acts that are attributed to grace. He thinks this can happen.

In this way we are to understand how God, through the aids and gifts of grace, inserts himself into nature, cooperates with it and helps it, so that it produces beyond its own strength such acts as are necessary for salvation.

title: Prevenient motions are vital operations, not free acts
english: Thesis C. So he holds that the motions in which he places prevenient grace are vital operations proceeding actively from our faculties. Yet they are not elicited freely by those faculties, and strictly speaking they should not be called acts of free choice, though they depend a great deal on free choice.

The reason is that free choice can help or hinder those acts in various ways, can desire them and ask God for them, and can in some way fit and dispose itself so that, by the common course and order of divine providence, they may be given to it by God more readily.

title: How free choice helps or hinders prevenient grace
english: Thesis CI. For example, the notions of things to be believed, through which, with a supernatural influence added, our mind begins to be enlightened for salvation, can be acquired freely: by listening to preachers, by reading devout books, or in some similar way. Equally, a person can freely turn away from them and so put an obstacle in the way of God's illumination. Even so, those notions get the character of prevenient grace only from God's supernatural influence, not from man's free choice.

The same is true of the devout affections that result naturally and necessarily in the will once God's illumination is given, and that have the character of prevenient grace on the will's side if some special influence of God is added to them. Man's free choice can hinder them, when he freely stops thinking devout thoughts or brings up and looks for reasons that draw the will the other way. It can also help them, when someone of his own accord keeps his mind fixed on that devout thought.

title: Molina in his own words: the motions of prevenient grace toward faith
english: Thesis CII. To show Molina's view more clearly, it will be to the point to set out in his own words the order and pattern of the motions of prevenient grace by which we are called to faith, hope, love and contrition, in which a person's conversion consists. In the disputation already cited he reasons about this as follows.

'While a person not yet inwardly called to faith in a supernatural way thinks over and weighs the things to be believed, through notions acquired by a preacher's ministry or from some other source,' he says, 'God flows into those notions by a particular, supernatural influence. By it he helps that knowledge, so that the matter is weighed better and more clearly and is penetrated, and also so that the knowledge now reaches the level of supernatural knowledge, fitted in its order and degree to a supernatural end.

When the mind weighs and enters into the things that belong to faith, that is, how worthy they are of assent and how much it matters to assent, a motion of affection toward the things so known arises naturally in the will. By it the will is drawn and, so to speak, invited to command the intellect to assent to them. God too, as it were, inserts himself into this motion. He flows into it through a particular aid and with that aid as it were sharpens it, so that it presses and draws more strongly, and he makes it supernatural, so that in its order and degree it is fitted for salvation as well.'

title: The free acts of faith and the infused habit
english: Thesis CIII. 'Even when these two motions of prevenient grace have helped and roused it, free choice remains free to command the assent of faith or to withhold that command. Suppose the will decides to embrace the faith and orders the intellect to believe. Then, as the motion of prevenient grace it possesses flows in alongside, the will produces within itself a supernatural act: in that act it wills to embrace the faith, and by that act it orders the intellect to assent.

In the same moment the intellect, set in motion by the will's supernatural command and aided by God's light, produces a supernatural act of assent to what God has revealed. A person rightly prepared by these two supernatural acts, one of intellect and one of will, then receives from God alone the infused, supernatural habit of faith, which enables him afterwards to produce further acts of the same supernatural kind.'

title: The motion of grace toward hope
english: Thesis CIV. On the motion of grace that rouses us to the act of hope, he explains his view as follows. 'When the intellect, already enlightened by the light of supernatural faith, thinks about the eternal happiness God has prepared for man, about its goodness and excellence, about God's many other glorious works and the benefits he has conferred on man, among them Christ's incarnation and passion, and considers the other means most abundantly supplied to it for gaining eternal life, there arises naturally in the will not only an affection toward happiness, by which the will is drawn and invited to want it with love of desire, but also a motion of uplift, by which it is attracted and drawn to hope for that happiness from God.

This motion does depend on free choice, if choice turns away from the thought from which the motion arises. Nevertheless, once obstacles are removed, it rises purely by nature, and God, as it were, thrusts himself into it with a special influence. He sharpens it and makes it supernatural, so that in its order and degree it is what salvation requires, and through it he raises the will supernaturally and, so to speak, invites it to elicit the supernatural act of hoping for eternal happiness and for the means needed to gain it.

Through such grace, then, our free choice, anticipated and roused by God, elicits, if it wishes, the first free act of supernatural hope. Duly disposed by that act, it receives from God the habit of supernatural hope, through which it can afterwards elicit other similar supernatural acts whenever it chooses.'

title: The motion of grace toward love of God
english: Thesis CV. In keeping with this he also discusses the grace needed for the act of love of God and of contrition for sins. 'Next,' he says, 'when the intellect, enlightened by the light of faith, with an act of supernatural hope already present in the will, considers God's goodness both in itself and toward us, and the many great benefits with which he has gone before us so gently, a motion of the love of friendship toward God is stirred up naturally in the will.

By that motion the power is drawn and invited to love God. God inserts himself into this motion too, and by his supernatural influence he not only sharpens and kindles it but also makes it supernatural, of the kind, that is, which in its order and degree is necessary for salvation.'

title: Contrition as the last disposition to sanctifying grace
english: Thesis CVI. 'If, at the same time, knowledge is added of how great, how many and how ungrateful are the sins by which we offend God, then free choice, anticipated by the same grace, just as it can elicit the act of supernatural love of God, so will be able to elicit the act of true sorrow for sins, felt on account of God, who is loved with an affection of supernatural love.
That sorrow is true contrition and the final disposition for sanctifying grace, which follows contrition in the same instant, though later in the order of nature.'

title: The aid of prevenient grace distinguished from prevenient grace itself
english: Thesis CVII. Molina also distinguishes the aid of prevenient grace from prevenient grace itself. By prevenient grace he means the knowledge in the mind and the affections in the will that God sharpens and helps by a particular influence so that they become supernatural and, in their degree and order, what salvation requires.

By the aid of prevenient grace he means the supernatural influence by which God sharpens, helps and kindles that knowledge, mostly acquired by human means, and those affections, which, as described, rise purely by nature in the will once such knowledge is present. Through it they become supernatural and of the kind that serves man's eternal salvation.

title: The recent Thomists and Molina diametrically opposed
english: Thesis CVIII. From all this it is easy to see that the doctrine of the recent Thomists, as Diego Alvarez presents it, stands diametrically opposed to Molina's teaching about the grace called efficacious, the grace to which a person's conversion is ascribed. The two are in complete conflict, whether we look at the way grace moves a person to the acts by which he turns to God, or at the nature and quiddity of grace itself and where it is to be located.

title: On how grace works: efficacious of itself, or by consent
english: Thesis CIX. On the way grace works, the recent Thomists, Alvarez among them, hold that the grace by which a person is converted is efficacious of itself. It is not made so by the consent of free choice; rather, as was explained earlier, it determines free choice to consent, powerfully and infallibly.

Molina and his followers maintain the opposite: the grace that converts a person is subject to free choice in such a way that its efficacy depends on free choice's consent. It lies in a person's free power to make it efficacious or inefficacious, and in fact each of these quite often happens.

title: On what grace is: a virtual motion, or affections of the will
english: Thesis CX. As for the essence of the grace by which the will is moved to the acts of conversion and which actually brings conversion about, the recent Thomists, as was said above, place it in a virtual motion. This motion has an incomplete kind of being and is in the will as colours are in the air, or as impetus is in a thing that is being driven along.

Molina places the grace that moves a person efficaciously to conversion, when free choice consents, in certain affections of the will that arise from a prior illumination of the mind. God inserts himself into them by his influence, draws the will to will, gives it the strength to will, and concurs with the will at the same time, if it wills.

title: Jansenius nearer Molina than the Thomists on the nature of grace
english: Thesis CXI. On this point, then, Jansenius stands closer to Molina than the recent Thomists do. He agrees with the Thomists entirely on the way efficacious grace works, contending that the efficacy of Christ's saving grace in no way depends on the consent of human choice but produces that consent of itself, infallibly and insuperably. Yet on the nature and substance of the grace called efficacious, his view is less far from Molina's doctrine than from the Thomists'.

As is clear from what was said earlier, he places this efficacious grace, to which in his view a person's conversion and all the good works of the faithful must be wholly ascribed, in certain affections of love and desire. These proceed from the human will, not freely but actively; they are its vital acts, and by them the will is carried and led to embrace the good freely. Such are the affections he means by the name of heavenly sweetness and delight, in which he places efficacious grace.

title: Where Jansenius differs from Molina: natural affections or heaven-sent
english: Thesis CXII. He differs from Molina, however, in this. On Molina's doctrine such affections arise in the will purely by nature once the mind is illuminated, and God does no more than thrust himself into them by a special influence and make them supernatural.

On Jansenius's view, whatever illumination of the mind is given, these affections do not rise by nature in the will of fallen man. They must be sent into it wholly from heaven, and not merely sharpened and heightened by some divine motion so as to become supernatural.

title: Molina: a natural affection precedes every free act of the will
english: Thesis CXIV. Molina further holds that it belongs to the nature of the will, considered absolutely, that as soon as the intellect presents it with some object as good and delightful, it is moved toward that object by a certain motion and touched by an affection. That affection entices and provokes the will to embrace such an object freely. He does not think the will is ever borne freely toward any object as good unless a motion and affection of this kind, arising naturally in it, has gone before.

So when man and the angel, still unfallen, began to turn away from the true good and to prefer an earthly, private good to the spiritual and divine, in each case, on his view, the evil will was preceded by such a motion and affection. By it the man was roused and drawn to eat the forbidden fruit, and the angel to admire and look up to his own excellence.

title: Jansenius: delight is not of the will's nature, nor preceded the first sin
english: Thesis CXV. Jansenius, by contrast, does not hold that the love and desire he calls delight necessarily precede every act of the will, when the will is considered absolutely and apart from the weakness contracted through sin. This is the delight by which the will is now drawn before it freely wills and embraces anything, and by which above all it must be touched before it pursues the heavenly and spiritual good.

On his doctrine it is not simply part of the will's nature that it cannot freely embrace a good object unless the object has first delighted it. Still less does it belong to the will's nature to be touched by some delight whenever a good and pleasant object is presented to it. Above all, he teaches that the first sin, of men and of angels alike, was committed without any preceding delight, and that neither men nor angels in their unfallen state had any affection by which they were solicited and invited to the will's first evil act.

title: A middle way between Molina and the recent Thomists
english: Thesis CXVI. Among the doctors of the Roman Church, however, many take what is in a sense a middle way between Molina's view and that of the recent Thomists, which seem to stand, as it were, at the extremes. For although on the substance of the question they agree with Molina, they depart from him on some points and try to soften his doctrine. Among them are Bellarmine and Vasquez, and above all Peter of Saint Joseph, a Feuillant monk.

title: First: sufficient grace suffices for actual conversion
english: Thesis CXVII. First, they hold with Molina that a sufficient grace is given for a person's salvation and conversion. Even if he is not actually converted, he can still be actually converted through it, if he chooses to use it, without any further prior aid from God. A grace that needs some other preceding aid of God before the good action really follows is not, in their view, properly called sufficient.

title: Peter of Saint Joseph on sufficient grace
english: Thesis CXVIII. Peter of Saint Joseph teaches this in his theological treatise on divine grace, disputation 6, section 6, where his first assertion reads: 'It is certain from faith that some grace sufficient for salvation is given, a grace by which a person can be converted even though he is not actually converted.' His second is this: 'That grace is called sufficient which is enough not only for a person to be able to act, but also for him actually to act if he chooses.'

title: Sufficient means enough to act, if one wills
english: Thesis CXIX. He repeats and confirms this doctrine in his Idea of speculative theology, book 4, chapter 7, where his second resolution reads: 'Only that grace is called absolutely and truly sufficient for some operation which is enough not merely for a person to be said to be able to act in some fashion, but also for him actually to act, if he chooses.'

He says he lays this down against the authors of physical predetermination. They hold that an aid is truly sufficient for operation if it gives the ability to act, even though another aid, really distinct from the sufficient one, is necessarily required for anyone actually to act. For, to take an example, a person is said to have sufficient and proximate power to see only because he has everything needed to see in fact, if he wants to see.

title: Second: no grace physically predetermines the will
english: Thesis CXX. Second, they maintain with Molina that no grace of God is efficacious in the sense of physically predetermining the will to act well and so imposing a necessity of acting that comes before the good action itself. In their view no such necessity can coexist with the freedom of human choice. They do not deny, on the other hand, that grace moves and inclines the will physically toward good operations.

title: Peter of Saint Joseph against physical predetermination
english: Thesis CXXI. This can be seen in Peter of Saint Joseph, in the seventh disputation of the treatise already cited, which he devotes almost entirely to refuting the physical predetermination of grace, and also in the same seventh chapter of book 4 of the Idea of speculative theology. His sixth resolution there reads: 'Although, on the probable view, efficacious grace really and physically moves and inclines the will to the good work, it does not physically predetermine it to that work.'

He proves the first part of this resolution from the claim that efficacious grace is a real motion existing in the soul, inclining it to the good work after the manner of an impressed impetus. In bodies an impetus concurs effectively and really in local motion; so, by proportion, the impetus impressed on the will must really cooperate in the soul's spiritual and supernatural motions.

title: Third: efficacious grace placed in the same things as Molina's
english: Thesis CXXII. Further, when they explain what efficacious grace is, the grace by which people are actually converted, they place it in the same illumination of the mind and the same motions and affections of the will in which Molina places it. They will not have efficacious grace be anything really distinct from exciting or prevenient grace.

On their account that grace consists, on the one hand, in various inspirations and illuminations of the intellect, by which the mind begins to think about the reward of eternal life, the pains of hell, the beauty of virtue and so on; and, on the other, in various affections sent by God into the will, by which it begins to love heavenly goods, to fear the pains of hell, to be drawn toward virtue and so on. So one reads in Peter of Saint Joseph, treatise on divine grace, disputation 7, section 1: 'These motions,' he says, 'entice the will, give it the strength to consent, and help it, once it consents, to give its consent, by concurring with it effectively.'

title: But efficacy does not consist in consent
english: Thesis CXXIII. These writers locate efficacious grace in the very things Molina names, but they give a different account of where its efficacy lies. Molina, as shown at length earlier, has grace called efficacious on account of its result, namely that the human will works along with it. His assumptions therefore make the efficacy of grace hang simply on man's free choice, which can turn a grace that is in itself merely sufficient into an efficacious or an inefficacious one; and it follows from his principles that efficacy consists in the human will's assent and cooperation.

That conclusion is flatly rejected by the doctors whose position is being described here. They insist that the grace called efficacious is efficacious of itself, before the will consents. Properly speaking, grace is not efficacious because the will gives its consent; the will gives its consent because grace is efficacious.

title: Bellarmine and Peter of Saint Joseph against efficacy from cooperation
english: Thesis CXXIV. This is Bellarmine's express doctrine in book 1 of On Grace and Free Choice, chapter 12. He first reports the view of those who place efficacious grace in human assent and cooperation, so that grace is called efficacious from its outcome because the human will cooperates, and who think it lies in a person's power to make grace efficacious when of itself it would be only sufficient. Then he adds: 'This opinion is wholly foreign to the teaching of blessed Augustine and, as I judge, to the teaching of the divine Scriptures as well.'

Peter of Saint Joseph likewise lays down this assertion: 'The efficacy of grace does not consist in the cooperation of the will' (On divine grace, disputation 7, section 9, number 61). He proves it on the ground that grace is not efficacious because the will acts; on the contrary, the will acts because grace is efficacious. The efficacy of grace therefore cannot formally be taken from the will's cooperation, since that efficacy is the cause of the cooperation and comes before it (Idea of speculative theology, book 4, chapter 7, on the seventh resolution).

title: Efficacy as congruity of the call with free choice
english: Thesis CXXV. On their view, then, 'the efficacy of grace consists in a certain congruity and attunement of the divine call with free choice; given this, the effect follows infallibly, in accordance with God's foreknowledge.' These are Peter of Saint Joseph's words in his Idea of speculative theology, book 4, chapter 7, resolution 7.

In the treatise on divine grace he notes that this congruity is not to be drawn merely from place or time, as though grace were efficacious just because it comes at a fitting place and time. Congruous and efficacious grace is certainly given only at a fitting time. Still, its congruity and efficacy are not mainly derived from the time; something must be found in the call itself that makes it take effect at that time and place, since a different call, though sufficient, would achieve nothing at that very moment. In his sense, therefore, 'that congruity of grace is simply a certain proportion and fit between grace itself and the will in such a state that the act follows infallibly' (disputation 7, section 9, number 66).

title: God fits the call to each person's temper and moment
english: Thesis CXXVI. He explains this in the next paragraph: 'Through his infinite knowledge God knows with complete certainty what each person would do in this or that state of affairs: whether he would consent or not, and what manner of calling would be suitable for him not merely to be urged but to be won over. Plainly the ambitious man is moved one way and the greedy man another, and so with the rest. To the ambitious it is useful to point out how unstable human affairs are, since many have been suddenly thrown down from the very height of honour; to the greedy, the shortness of life and the uncertain hour of death, and so on. And because temperaments differ among the ambitious, and likewise among the greedy, some must be shown examples, others reasons drawn from philosophy or theology, others comparisons taken from more familiar things, so that each is brought to repentance by his own route.

Indeed one and the same person differs from himself from day to day, from hour to hour, from moment to moment. Now anger grips him, now joy, now sorrow; so today he must be moved and stirred in another way than yesterday, and reasons that would have persuaded him effectively in one hour may prove useless in the next. So true is it that whatever is received is received in the manner of the one receiving it, and that things do not always look the same to us; the end appears to each of us according to how we are disposed. At times, then, because of circumstances of place or time and because of the various passions that stir him, a person is so disposed that a given thought or illumination of the mind, and a given affection or motion of the will, are duly fitted to him and attuned to bringing about his conversion. The efficacy of grace must therefore be located in this attunement between the aid and the will so disposed.'

title: The supposition: God's middle knowledge
english: Thesis CXXVII. The authors of this view therefore assume that God foreknows from eternity, by what the Schools call middle or conditional knowledge, what this or that person would do if he were called in one way or another, and if such illuminations and inspirations and other means, outward and inward, were used to convert him. If Peter, say, is called in this way, God knows he will follow; if in that way, not at all. Yet whichever way he is called, he can follow or not follow, as he wills.

title: Tyre and Sidon called incongruously, Ephesus congruously
english: Thesis CXXVIII. On that basis they say that God decreed to call and stir certain people to conversion, the Tyrians and Sidonians for example, by means and in a manner that did truly give them power to turn to God if they wished, but that he foresaw with certainty would have no effect on them. He did not call them by the means he foresaw would convert them if used.

The Ephesians, by contrast, he willed to call not in a manner they would reject, but in the one by which he foreknew for certain they would be led to faith. It follows that God decreed to give the first a grace by which they could be converted if they wished, and the second a grace by which they would in fact be converted.

title: Sufficient and efficacious differ only morally
english: Thesis CXXIX. The first grace is the one they call sufficient, the second the one they call efficacious. Those called in the first way are said to be called incongruously; those called in the second, congruously. The second calling originates in a decree by which the conversion of those called has been predefined; the first does not.

Even so, on these doctors' view, the grace conferred through the first calling and named sufficient is not really distinct from efficacious grace, whether in physical entity or in power to act. It differs only morally, that is, in its relation to the act that is to follow. A person may lack the efficacious aid by which he is in fact converted, yet through the aid called sufficient he can actually be converted if he wishes, with no new aid serving as the source of the good work.

title: Yet the one given efficacious aid receives far greater grace
english: Thesis CXXX. These theologians hold that the aid called efficacious does not differ from the aid called merely sufficient physically, in real entity or power to act, but only morally, or as they put it, in relation to the act to follow. Even so, they consider that whoever is given efficacious aid receives a far greater grace from God than one granted sufficient aid alone. This is because the worth and size of a gift or grace are to be measured chiefly by the intention of the giver and by the benefit and fruit that come to the receiver.

Efficacious aid is given by God with a settled purpose of converting the person; sufficient aid cannot be traced to any such purpose. Moreover, the conversion that efficacious aid brings about is the greatest good its recipient gains from it. Sufficient aid, however great in itself, is assumed not to suit or fit the disposition of the one who receives it, so it stays entirely useless to him; indeed, incidentally, it turns to his greater condemnation.

title: Against Molina: equal grace, unequal outcome is impossible
english: Thesis CXXXI. These doctors therefore refuse to say with Molina that of two people forestalled by equal grace, one may be converted and the other not. Whoever is converted has always received more grace from God than the one who is not. Granted grace equal in every respect among several people, either all will be converted or none will.

In their opinion it may well be that, as regards the divine aid that goes before him, the convert has no brighter illumination of mind and no stronger motion of the will than the one who is not converted. They even allow that the mind of someone who stays rebellious may be lit more clearly by the divine Spirit, and his will struck more forcefully and keenly, than in someone actually brought to conversion and faith by efficacious grace. Yet in the convert the divine motion, whether greater or smaller, always counts on their view as greater grace, because it is suited and attuned to the disposition of the one receiving it. It thus springs from a more striking goodwill of God toward him and works to his greater benefit.

title: Bellarmine: equal inward motion, unequal grace
english: Thesis CXXXII. This is Bellarmine's teaching, comparing his own view with that of Molina and Lessius, though without naming them. 'The first view,' he says, 'makes the efficacy of grace depend on the human will; ours makes it depend on the will of God. Suppose the question is put: if two people have entirely the same exciting and assisting grace, at least in first act, hear the same preacher and see the same signs, can it happen that one believes and the other does not? The first view will answer that it can, since the will remains free and can follow grace or resist it at its own choice.

Our view will answer that it can indeed happen that two people receive the same inward motion, hear the same preacher, see the same signs, and that one believes while the other does not. But it cannot happen that two people receive entirely the same exciting grace and one believes while the other does not. Grace includes not only the inward motion or stirring but also the circumstances of place, time, person and so on. If the same motion is received and one believes while the other does not, then beyond doubt the one received it in the manner, place and time that God foresaw would suit his temperament, and the other did not; and so the believer had a far greater grace of God than the unbeliever.

The one who did not believe had grace by which he could believe if he would; the one who believed had grace by which he could and would believe. For God works the willing in us when he calls people in such a way as he sees they will follow. So the believer truly has no ground to boast or swell with pride over the unbeliever, since what chiefly sets him apart from the unbeliever is not he himself by free choice but God by the efficacious grace he gave him and did not give the other' (On grace and free choice, book 1, chapter 13, near the end).

title: Peter of Saint Joseph: aid as being and as benefit
english: Thesis CXXXIII. Peter of Saint Joseph teaches much the same at the end of the seventh disputation of his treatise on divine grace. 'Divine aid,' he says, 'can be viewed in two ways: as a being or as a benefit. Viewed the first way, it can happen that one person is not converted with equal or even greater aid while another is converted with less. The reason is that grace does not determine the will; when equal aid, considered as a being, is offered to two people, each stays undetermined between consenting and not consenting, so one of them may freely consent though the other does not consent at all.

But if the aid is viewed as a gift and benefit, it cannot happen that, given equal aid, one is converted and the other not. For aids are called equal in the order of benefit when they benefit equally; so if one aid benefits to the point of actually taking effect and the other not at all, they are already unequal in the order of benefit.'

title: In what sense efficacy depends on free choice
english: Thesis CXXXIV. The authors of this view hold that the efficacy of grace is something in the divine aid that comes before the will's working, and so does not hang on the will's consent and cooperation in the way Molina and his followers claim, as though it lay in a person's power to make grace efficacious or inefficacious. Even so, they do not deny that the efficacy of grace depends on free choice in some way. On their account it can be considered in two ways, in first act or in second act. Taken the first way, it is simply the power to bring about the effect, which is not distinct from the aid itself; in this respect it depends not on free choice but on God.

Taken the second way, efficacy means the actual working itself, the actual influence of grace on the supernatural work; and in this respect too it depends on God. Just as an instrument's influence on a work depends on the principal agent using it, so the influence of grace on a supernatural work depends on God as primary agent, who works through grace as through an instrument of his own. Yet this actual working of grace depends not only on God but also on free choice itself, as a partial cause without whose operation grace would not act. In this respect, then, that is, in second act, they say the efficacy of grace also depends on free choice. So Peter of Saint Joseph explains his mind on the matter in the treatise on divine grace, disputation 7, number 62.

title: Given efficacy in first act, consent follows infallibly
english: Thesis CXXXV. Whatever this dependence of efficacious grace on free choice in second act may be, on their view the efficacy of grace is such that, once it is in place in first act, the effect follows infallibly, namely the consent and cooperation of free choice. For an aid is called efficacious when it 'moves the will efficaciously and infallibly to give its consent, and makes it act', as the same Peter of Saint Joseph puts it in the disputation cited, number 61. Given that efficacy of the divine aid, which it has from God alone and prior to the will's consent, it can never happen that a person fails to do what such aid moves him to do.

Conversely, take that efficacy away, and however much sufficient grace is supposed, the good work for which it is called sufficient simply cannot follow. Here too they part from Molina. On his assumptions, whatever grace of God is given ahead of the will's actual consent, the effect it is directed to may follow or may not, and the outcome is infallible neither way.

title: Infallibility reconciled with freedom
english: Thesis CXXXVI. Nor do they find it hard to reconcile this infallibility of outcome, whether the aid called efficacious is given or withheld, with the freedom of human choice. It never happens, they say, that the will refuses consent to the motions that make up efficacious grace, that is, to motions which, according to God's foreknowledge, so suit the will and are so attuned to it that they will bend it.

Even so, the will, forestalled and stirred by those motions, is not predetermined by them. It determines itself to act in such a way that, while they are present, it could refrain from acting and withhold consent, or even settle on refusal, if the nature of such motions is considered in itself.

title: A consequent necessity, from consent foreseen under condition
english: Thesis CXXXVII. They admit that in a way it is necessary for someone who has received efficacious grace to consent to it and do what it moves him to, since it is a contradiction for a grace to be efficacious and yet for the effect not to follow once it is given. But that necessity does not impair freedom, because on their teaching it is consequent, not antecedent.

For them, efficacious grace is precisely grace made up of aids so fitted to the will for the place and time that God foresaw from eternity that, if they were offered, the will would freely let itself be moved by them, though it could also resist. So the congruity that makes grace be called efficacious includes the will's future free consent, foreseen by God from eternity through conditional knowledge. Saying that a person must consent to efficacious grace therefore does no harm at all to his freedom. Only that grace is called efficacious to which the will is assumed to be about to consent freely if God applies it to the person; and so that necessity does not go before the will's consent, foreseen under a condition, but follows it.

title: Moral, not metaphysical, infallibility
english: Thesis CXXXVIII. They add that efficacious grace is infallible in producing its effect not absolutely and metaphysically but rather morally. Being supremely congruous and proportioned to the will's disposition, it moves the will infallibly, yet in a very gentle way that agrees with the will's own temper.

It is like a man struggling with the direst want and poverty: physically he could turn down a hundred gold coins offered to him, but morally speaking, things being as they are, or given his state, situation and misfortune, he will infallibly accept them, because they are so well suited to relieving his distress.

title: The claim to square with predestination too
english: Thesis CXXXIX. Lastly, those who hold this opinion pride themselves that the efficacy of grace, as they explain it, fits perfectly not only with the freedom of human choice but also with the certainty of divine predestination. On this view predestination achieves its effect through aids that can in themselves be rejected, yet are so suited to the will's temper that, in line with God's foreknowledge, they will take effect infallibly.

title: Close of the four Roman opinions
english: Thesis CXL. So we have set out briefly, as clearly as we could, the four opinions on the sufficiency and efficacy of divine grace that are most established and accepted in the Roman School. Others could be reported as well. But they seem highly improbable, their authors are less known and their followers fewer, and it would be far too long and tedious to note the finer differences on which individual doctors partly disagree among themselves. We may rest content with these four, and it does not seem worth the effort to look more minutely into such details.

title: Appendix: Gregory of Valencia on efficacious grace
english: Thesis CXLI. So that some pages are not left blank here, we will add in brief, as an example, the opinion of Gregory of Valencia, a Jesuit of some note, which a number of learned men report and refute. He holds that efficacious grace consists in a gift that a person already forestalled by calling and stirring grace can obtain, with God's help, through devout use of his free choice. In one order of cause, the efficient, this gift is by nature prior to the free conversion itself; in another, the material and dispositive, it is posterior.

title: The gift: infused habits of grace and the virtues
english: Thesis CXLII. He places this gift in the infusion of habits of grace and of the virtues, since the human mind, strengthened by those habits, elicits the act of conversion. On his view, then, efficacious grace is either habitual grace as it is infused, or the infusion itself, insofar as through that infused grace free choice elicits its own conversion, with God concurring in it at the same time.

title: Valencia on sufficient grace
english: Thesis CXLIII. On his view, for someone to count as having sufficient grace for a devout action, he must have either all the gifts and aids that the action requires as its principles or starting points, or else one or more of those gifts, such that, forestalled and stirred by it or them, he can acquire all the remaining gifts or aids of that kind through some use of his free faculty, with God's help. This can be seen in Gregory, already named, tome 2, disputation 8, question 3, point 4.

title: Between the Thomists and the later theologians
english: Thesis CXLIV. Clearly, then, this doctor denies that sufficient and efficacious grace are the same real entity. Efficacious grace, for him, adds to sufficient grace a new aid that comes before the person's conversion; here he sides with the recent Thomists and parts from Molina and the authors of congruous grace.

Yet at the same time he denies that the efficacy of divine grace is absolute, making it depend instead on the use of our free choice; here he leaves the Thomists and sides with those later theologians.

title: Le Blanc's objections to Valencia
english: Thesis CXLV. His opinion runs into a difficulty of its own: what he says about efficacious grace can apply only to the sinner's conversion to God, not to the good works of someone already converted. Those works need no new infusion of habitual grace, and yet efficacious grace extends to them as well.

Besides, for my part I cannot understand how the infusion of habitual grace can be prior to a person's conversion as efficient cause and yet at the same time posterior to that same conversion as dispositive cause.

title: The Lutherans reject the division of grace into sufficient and efficacious
english: Thesis I. The theologians of the Augsburg Confession known as Lutherans reject the familiar division of grace into sufficient and efficacious. Their reason is that the grace of God at work in believers is one and the same as the grace that unbelievers drive away.

On their view, therefore, the very grace that the unbelieving and impenitent scorn and tread underfoot is efficacious of itself and in itself. It should not be called merely sufficient, as if set against some other grace that is efficacious.

title: One grace converts Peter and leaves Simon Magus unconverted
english: Thesis II. They teach that God, so far as it rests with him, wants to convert everyone to whom the word is preached, and offers the same grace to all and to each. Many, however, resist divine grace and the Holy Spirit as he sets about the work of conversion, so in them grace does not achieve its effect. Others let divine grace in and put no obstacle in its way, and in them grace is efficacious and actually brings about conversion.

Since, on God's side, the grace that converted Simon Peter is the same grace that failed to convert Simon Magus, the difference being only that one resisted and the other did not, they see no reason to distinguish one grace from the other.

title: Gerhard: one grace, worked in believers and repelled by unbelievers
english: Thesis III. This can be found in Johann Gerhard, theologian of Jena, in his second tome, in the treatise on free choice, chapter 6, section 1. 'We readily grant,' he writes, 'that many resist the Holy Spirit as he undertakes the work of conversion, reject God's counsel against themselves, and judge themselves unworthy of eternal life, so that by their own fault they drive the grace of conversion away from themselves.

Yet we deny that grace itself must for that reason be split into sufficient and efficacious, because the grace of God that works in believers and the grace that unbelievers drive away are one and the same.'

title: Gerhard: two extremes to avoid, and a middle way
english: Thesis IV. To explain where the efficacy of divine grace comes from, he first notes two extremes to be avoided. The efficacy of grace for conversion must not be credited to the cooperation of the human will, nor to an absolute decree of God choosing certain particular people. One must take a middle way instead.

That many are converted and saved is to be put down to divine grace alone; that many are not converted and are lost must be recognized as happening only through the fault of those who are lost. In this devout simplicity, he says, a Christian mind can rest secure, even if it cannot find its way out of every difficulty.

title: Gerhard: grace does not determine the will by physical action
english: Thesis V. He then tries to show how two claims fit together: that the efficacy of divine grace is not to be credited to the cooperation of the human will, and yet that it is not to be credited either to some physical action of God that determines the will to will and choose the good which stirring grace has inspired in it. He sets out his view as follows.

'In the work of conversion,' he says, 'the Holy Spirit finds a subject with no strength to cooperate, for the mind of one not yet reborn is blind and the will turned away from God and hostile to him. So the Spirit acts with every kind of healing and helping grace, to turn the one he wants to convert from unwilling to willing, from enemy to obedient. This does not happen as though he converted someone who neither thinks nor knows, or even someone unwilling, by forcing him. Rather, the Holy Spirit gives new strength by which the person can assent to the call, yet does not in one instant take away that old liberty, or better, that wretched slavery, by which he can refuse the grace offered.

We must not say, then, that the grace of the Holy Spirit in conversion determines the will by some physical action to will and choose the good. The Holy Spirit allows himself to be resisted, lets his work be hindered, and sees many judge themselves unworthy of conversion and of its fruit, eternal life itself.

After the fall every person has a will, but the will does not have from its own strength the power to will spiritual good, for it is enslaved to sin. In conversion, then, the Holy Spirit renews a person's will and gives it new strength, so equipped that it can actually will and choose the good. Even so, because of the depravity of nature that still clings to him, a person can refuse the good and can obstruct the Spirit's work. So it must not be said that in conversion grace determines the will by some physical action to will and choose the good.' Otherwise, as the same doctor says, all whom the Holy Spirit wants converted would be converted by unchangeable necessity, which he holds to be absurd.

title: Calixtus: God works through the preached word unless men love darkness
english: Thesis VI. Georg Calixtus, formerly professor of theology at the Academia Julia, teaches the same doctrine and explains it more clearly in his Epitome of Theology, taken down as he dictated it. In the treatise on the ministry of the word, page 241, he teaches that when a minister of the word puts the teaching of the Law and of the Gospel before people, God is at work through this means and instrument of his.

Through it God rouses in human hearts sorrow for sins committed, trust in Christ's merit, hatred of sin, and eagerness for a new life, unless people, through their own stubbornness and obstinacy, love darkness more than light.

title: Calixtus: man can resist grace, yet can care for the means of salvation
english: Thesis VII. On his view there is no doubt that a person can scorn and reject the grace offered and resist the Holy Spirit when he is about to produce faith, since God does not draw and convert people by his absolute power but according to the order and pattern he laid down once for all.

On the other hand, he holds, it is certain that a person can be anxious for his salvation and can take trouble over the means to it, as in the saying, 'Many will seek to enter and will not be able.' A person can hear God's word, and even receive it with all readiness and study it in an effort to learn and come to know the truth.

title: Calixtus: those who do this receive greater aids
english: Thesis VIII. In this doctor's view, God judges those who do this worthy of greater aids, so that they understand the word, recognize their sins from it, and put faith in the promises of the Gospel.

This is not because such effort, whatever its worth, has any great dignity or merit. It is because God wants his word honoured in this way, wants this order kept, and wants the person to do this much before God himself provides greater and more particular aids, supernatural in kind.

title: Calixtus: supernatural acts and acts within man's power
english: Thesis IX. That author draws a distinction. On one side are actions supernatural in kind: they exceed human strength by their nature, are not in human hands, and so must be credited to the Holy Spirit. Believing, fearing and loving God, and the like, in which true conversion to God consists, are of this sort.

On the other side are certain acts within a person's power, which God wants him to perform before any advance is made to supernatural aids and gifts, at least in the ordinary course. Such acts are hearing God's word, studying it, paying attention to it, and taking some care about the means of salvation.

title: Calixtus quoted: believing is supernatural; some prior acts are in man's power
english: Thesis X. 'Believing,' he writes, 'is an action supernatural in kind, that is, beyond human strength by its nature. We credit it to the Holy Spirit because he rouses the human mind to believe and brings it about that a person believes, loves and fears God, and indeed wants to believe, fear and love.

So we assign to God the supernatural acts that enter into, or make up, true conversion, and we deny that they lie in human hands. We do not deny, however, that some acts lie within a person's power, which God wants him to perform before any advance is made to supernatural aids and gifts, at any rate in the ordinary course.'

title: Calixtus: hearing and weighing the Gospel is not above nature
english: Thesis XI. What the same author teaches elsewhere agrees with this. 'Note,' he writes, 'that once God has revealed the Gospel and has it preached by people far and wide among people, it is not beyond the strength of nature for someone to hear the Gospel, grasp it, think it over, and set it beside what others, Jews for instance or Muslims, put forward as revealed by God.'
This is in his judgment on the theological controversies in dispute between the Lutherans and the Reformed, number 33.

title: Those who hear and do not choke the word are led to faith
english: Thesis XII. According to him, then, all who hear the word, do not reject God's counsel against themselves, and do not smother God's word with the worries, riches or pleasures of this life experience God's help and working, and are brought to faith and life by his free goodwill.
Those who act otherwise must lay it to their own carelessness and defiance that God does not give them faith.

title: God provides means even for those who have not heard the word
english: Thesis XIII. God's word is the instrument he ordinarily uses in converting people, yet Calixtus does not hold that those to whom the word has not been preached are left without any means of salvation. God, he says, so acts toward them and is so disposed that if they are lost it is their own fault, not for want of the aids they needed.
