If they make right use of the faculties and powers that remain in fallen nature, God stands ready to supply means by which they can be brought to fuller knowledge and so, in the end, to true and saving faith.

title: Calixtus on those who never hear: Cornelius and the eunuch of Candace
english: Thesis XIV. He puts this question to himself: 'How will people come to faith who neither live among Christians nor have ever heard a word about Christians, from whom alone one can hear the word? Are they not lost without any carelessness on their part, simply because God did not provide for them to hear the word as other nations do?'

Among other things he replies that 'all people keep some powers of intellect and will and some natural knowledge. If any have used these rightly, cared for their salvation, and worked at it as far as they can, God will provide them with means to bring them to a fuller and more complete knowledge, one that rests on divine revelation.' He finds an example of this in Cornelius the centurion and in the eunuch of Queen Candace.

title: Those who neglect the means are kept from the light by their own fault
english: Thesis XV. 'But if others, unlike these,' he continues, 'have neglected the means and aids within their reach, put out the sparks born in them, and, as Paul says, held down the truth in unrighteousness, then it is no fate or divine decree but their own fault that shuts them out from the clearer light.'
This is in the Epitome of Theology already cited, page 244.

title: Conclusion: the Lutherans keep what the Roman school means by sufficient grace
english: Thesis XVI. It is clear, then, from what has been said, that the theologians of the Augsburg Confession reject the division of grace into sufficient and efficacious, so common in the Roman school, yet affirm what most doctors of that school mean by sufficient grace.

That is: those who are not converted by the preaching of the Gospel lack no aid from God's side that their conversion requires and without which they could not be converted. And so even unbelievers who reject God's word are offered a grace fully enough to bring them to repentance and faith, if they do not refuse to use it.

title: Conclusion: no physical predetermination, so little difficulty over freedom
english: Thesis XVII. It is just as plain that, given their own principles, these doctors have little trouble reconciling the efficacy of grace with the freedom of human choice. They hold that grace does not physically predetermine the will to good and lays no necessity of acting well upon it.

A person, rather, is free either to let divine grace be efficacious, by doing through nature what divine wisdom requires of him beforehand so that grace may exercise its efficacy in him, or to set a barrier and hindrance in the way of that grace, by neglecting what grace does not usually act without, namely hearing God's word, studying it, and reflecting on it.

title: Calixtus: the power to believe is given, but no necessity
english: Thesis XVIII. This is Georg Calixtus's doctrine in the judgment already cited on the controversies in dispute between the Lutherans and the Reformed, number 32. There he first establishes that the Gospel is God's appointed instrument for imparting faith and salvation to people. With it, as it enters the mind through the ears, supernatural divine grace is joined, and through that grace a person who, left to himself, could not before give assent and faith is now able to.

Then he adds: 'He thus gains the power of believing that he lacked before, yet no necessity binds him, for if he gives free rein to his disposition and depravity, he can resist and struggle against the Holy Spirit and drive away the word of God ...

That a person who hears and weighs the Gospel believes, or even can believe, must be credited not to the powers of nature but to the grace bound up with the Gospel and supplied through it. That he can withstand grace must be blamed on his inborn depravity and disposition. Since God is indeed efficacious and at work through his grace, though not by absolute power but by a power that allows for conditions and order, it follows that he can be thwarted in the result and outcome.'

title: Conversion the work of the Spirit alone, without denying vital acts
english: Thesis XIX. None of this conflicts with what the same theologians say: that a person's conversion is the work of the Holy Spirit alone, and that in conversion the human will is purely passive.

They do not mean by this to deny that the acts of faith, hope, fear and love that make up true conversion to God are living acts freely produced by a person's will. They mean that the will's natural powers count for nothing at all toward producing those acts, and others like them. Nor can the will, from those natural powers of its own, cooperate in any way with the divine grace that converts a person, or add anything of its own to it, when the Holy Spirit, through the word heard, sets about changing and renewing the will and supplying it with new strength.

title: The Formula of Concord: the will passive in the kindling of new motions
english: Thesis XX. The Book of Concord comes to the same thing in the Epitome of the articles in controversy among the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, toward the end of the chapter on free choice. 'Luther's statement,' it says, 'that in conversion the human will is purely passive must be taken rightly and properly, that is, with respect to divine grace in kindling new impulses. It refers to the moment when the Spirit of God, through the word heard or through the use of the sacraments, lays hold of a person's will and works conversion and new birth in him.

Once the Holy Spirit has worked and accomplished this, and by his divine power and working alone has changed and renewed the person's will, then that new will really is the Holy Spirit's instrument and organ: it not only lays hold of grace but also works together with the Holy Spirit in the deeds that follow.

Before a person's conversion, then, only two efficient causes remain that are effective for conversion: the Holy Spirit, and God's word, the Holy Spirit's instrument by which he brings about conversion. A person must certainly hear this word, but he cannot by any strength of his own manage to embrace it with true faith; that comes only by the grace and working of the Holy Spirit.'

title: The Remonstrants keep the division of grace
english: Thesis XXI. The Remonstrants of the Low Countries, also called Arminians, strongly approve the distinction of grace into sufficient and efficacious and hold firmly to it. They think it rests on many passages of Scripture and is plainly needed to defend God's justice.

So they deny that sufficient grace is only the grace that is efficacious, the grace that actually produces a converted person. 'Although,' they say, 'sufficient grace has the greatest efficacy and energy (energeia) for working conversion in a person, it does not always, through the person's own vice and fault, take effect and reach the actual outcome (apotelesma) of conversion.' This can be seen in their Synod, in the declaration of the Remonstrants' opinion on the third and fourth articles, page 15.

title: Enough grace given to all who hear the word
english: Thesis XXII. They explain more precisely what this sufficient grace consists in at the beginning of the same declaration, in the sixth thesis. 'Although,' they say, 'by God's entirely free will there is the widest inequality in divine grace, the Holy Spirit still gives, or stands ready to give, to each and every person to whom the word is preached as much grace as is enough to advance their conversion step by step.
So grace sufficient for faith and conversion comes not only to those whom God is said, under the decree of absolute election, to will to save, but also to those who are not in fact converted.'

title: Where the Remonstrants place efficacy
english: Thesis XXIII. They refuse, however, to place the efficacy of grace in some all-powerful force of action and an unavoidable determination of the will to good, or, as some Scholastics do, in the congruity of the call.

They place it rather in an operation of grace that most surely achieves its effect whenever a person sets against it no new obstinacy and rebellion, which he could have set against it of himself. These are their words, on the same page 15 of the declaration cited.

title: Grace acting on the mind
english: Thesis XXIV. On the following page, to set out the acts of divine grace one at a time, they note that three things in corrupt man need correcting and regenerating: the mind, the will and the affections. To this threefold subject they match three kinds of act of divine grace.

First, in their own words: 'By his word and the enlightening of his Spirit, God assures the mind of his saving will and brings it to assent to the truth of the word. Through carelessness or through malice of will, a person can spurn and scorn this enlightening and revelation when it first comes to the mind, outwardly or even inwardly, and can refuse to take it deep into his soul, and from this comes affected ignorance.

Even so, once the truth is set clearly and plainly before the mind by the Holy Spirit, the intellect cannot fail to assent or hold back its judgment. It is determined to assent by the object so presented and by the Spirit who instils it, and the intellect cannot of itself resist that enlightening, since its object determines it.'

title: Grace acting on the will
english: Thesis XXV. 'God also bends the will to obey him, and through his Holy Spirit, who uses the word, he so inclines it to acts of faith and obedience that through that working the will not only is able to obey but actually obeys, every time it obeys, through that same working, and not of itself, by itself or from itself.'

title: Supernatural power given to the will
english: Thesis XXVI. To magnify grace in every way they add that a supernatural power is also given to the will, and that in this way God acts directly on the will, so long as that action does not necessitate the will beforehand or remove its freedom and its power of not willing.

title: Grace acting on the affections
english: Thesis XXVII. They go on to say that once the mind has been enlightened and the will given supernatural power, partly by enlightening and partly by a direct infusion of strength, God also corrects our affections and that sensitive part of us. He moves them with good desires, whose objects the intellect points out and whose acts the will commands.

As those affections are corrected, disciplined and brought into order more and more, the will becomes readier, easier and less hindered in practising acts of devotion, since the affections and that law at war in our members no longer fight back as much as before.

title: The word persuades through the Spirit, not beside it
english: Thesis XXVIII. To show what parts the word of God and the Holy Spirit who uses the word each play in this efficacy and working of grace, they say that the word urges but the Spirit using the word persuades.

They add that it is always safer to hold that the Spirit's action on the will has the word's action under it, than to make the Spirit's action run alongside the word's action on the will and say that he works beside the word rather than through it. This is so that we do not seem to hand the Enthusiasts the principles of their teaching, and who knows what hidden motions, drawings and impulses, which anyone can easily imagine for himself.

title: Is God's converting action only moral?
english: Thesis XXIX. To make their mind on the force and efficacy of divine grace clearer still, they raise many questions and answer them briefly and precisely. 'If we are asked,' they say, 'whether God's converting action is only moral, working by urging, setting before, inviting, we answer that it is more than moral.

If we look at stirring grace, we say that a supernatural power, distinct from enlightening, is poured into the will itself as well; if at cooperating grace, we say that it can be called physical and has a real and proper efficiency.'

title: Immediate action on the will, but resistible
english: Thesis XXX. 'If it is asked whether the Spirit has no direct action on the will, we do not deny that there is one. If it is asked whether grace works with the same kind of efficacy in quickening the intellect, the affections and the will, we answer that it does not: its way of acting on the will is resistible.'

They do not, however, seem to deny outright that grace produces some motions in the will irresistibly. On their assumptions this seems to be limited to the efficacy by which the will is made, without qualification, good from bad.

title: Grace acts beyond illumination and invitation
english: Thesis XXXI. 'If it is asked whether, beyond enlightening the mind, stirring the affections and inviting the will, grace does nothing by way of principle or in advance of conversion, we answer that it does something.'
What grace does besides this seems, on their view, to be the infusion of the new strength they spoke of earlier.

title: When conversion follows grace
english: Thesis XXXII. 'If it is asked whether, when God has put in place every working he uses to bring about conversion in people, conversion often fails to follow or never fails, we answer: with antecedent and prevenient grace in place, it often does not follow; with cooperating grace in place, it never fails to follow.'

title: Conversion contingent, yet infallibly foreknown
english: Thesis XXXIII. Their next question is whether conversion is a contingent and uncertain thing, or whether, in the person converted, it comes about infallibly through a necessity of cause or of outcome. Their answer: 'Being free, conversion is contingent; being known to God in advance, it is not uncertain to him.

Its necessity is not that of the cause, or of the consequent, for the person was able to resist. Its necessity is that of the consequence, or of foreknowledge, and in that way it comes about without fail in anyone God foreknew would be converted.'

title: Why one is converted and another not
english: Thesis XXXIV. 'If it is asked why this person is converted and that one not, we answer: this one is converted because God converts him while he sets up no new obstinacy; that one is not converted because he sets up new obstinacy. You will ask why this one sets up new obstinacy and the other does not. We answer: this one sets it up because he wants to; that one does not, because grace moves him not to want to.

You will ask whether the one who sets up no new obstinacy, and so is converted, does not have greater grace than the one who sets it up, and so is not converted. We answer that their antecedent and prevenient grace can be equal, but the first has cooperating grace and the second does not.'

title: The Remonstrants reconcile freedom and efficacy easily
english: Thesis XXXV. It is clear from this that the Remonstrants, on their own principles, can easily reconcile freedom of choice with the efficacy of grace. They assume that the grace moving the will to conversion acts in a resistible manner: the will can give way to grace and accept its working, and can also block grace and hinder its working. They say so themselves on page 17 of the declaration so often cited:

'To this conversion of his, to which grace moves him, a person, from his inborn depravity and his attachment to worldly things, can freely set a barrier and hindrance, and often does. His will may neglect the outward preaching of the Gospel and treat it as of no account when he has the chance to hear it; or handle the word he has heard carelessly, being more taken up with worldly things; or in some other way prevent the Holy Spirit from persuading it of the truth, necessity and usefulness of the Gospel teaching.

Or he may assent to the word and its truth, yet refuse to shape his will by what that word prescribes and to obey it; and, giving the flesh free rein, he quenches the Spirit, resists the Spirit, and wilfully crushes and roots out good desires and thoughts often poured in and offered from heaven. So we say that the human will is not necessitated to will good, but that a person can resist of himself, that is, refuse to will, often actually refuse, and resist the workings of sufficient grace.'

title: Testard: sufficient grace as universal, efficacious as particular
english: Thesis XXXVI. Apart from the Remonstrants, some of the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort also divide grace into sufficient and efficacious, though in a quite different sense. Paulus Testardus, pastor of the church at Blois in his lifetime, uses this distinction in his Irenicum, thesis 300, and in many places in his book on nature and grace.
By sufficient grace, however, he means what he calls universal grace, and by efficacious grace what he names particular grace.

title: Testard: sufficient grace is objective, not subjective
english: Thesis XXXVII. In his view, then, this sufficient grace is not a subjective grace that inwardly disposes a person to faith and repentance. It is only an objective grace, which consists in salvation being made possible for a person.

This happens in two ways: through Christ's satisfaction, which took away the barrier that divine justice set against people obtaining forgiveness of sins, and through God's outward call and invitation to faith and repentance, given either by the preached word or by the works of nature and providence.

title: Why Testard calls this grace sufficient
english: Thesis XXXVIII. He calls that grace sufficient because it gives a person the ability to be saved if he wills. So if someone does not come to share in salvation, the cause lies only in his own depravity and malice, and he cannot complain of God as though God had denied him something without which he simply could not be saved.

For he has the object set before him in sufficient light, and he has a mind and will that of themselves can and should embrace and accept it. Only his own perversity, of which he himself is the cause, prevents this, and for that reason he has no ground to complain of God.

title: Testard: why particular, efficacious grace is needed
english: Thesis XXXIX. He admits, though, that unless something more is added, no one can ever be saved by this sufficient grace alone. The reason is man's inborn depravity and wickedness, which keeps him from making good use of the means God sets before him, means otherwise sufficient for salvation in themselves.

So that depravity makes faith and repentance morally impossible for him, although his physical faculties equip him adequately for them. Hence the need for a particular grace to correct man's depravity and so to dispose and move his mind and will from within that, once his corrupt habits are shaken off, he embraces the salvation offered from outside and takes refuge in God's mercy by faith and repentance. This particular grace Testard therefore calls efficacious.

title: Other Reformed reject the division
english: Thesis XL. Other Reformed theologians, however, generally reject the distinction of grace into sufficient and efficacious. In their judgment no grace is really sufficient, or can be called so, unless it is also efficacious.

Their reason is that for a person to be actually converted, God must give a help that does more than simply move and draw him toward the good: it must bend and determine his will to will the good and hold to it. Without such help the will would never be carried there, since man's inborn depravity blocks the way.

title: Dort: grace efficacious of itself (rejection of errors 8 and 9)
english: Thesis XLI. All the Reformed who follow the Synod of Dort hold in common that the grace of God, to which man's conversion and all the good works that follow it must be credited, is efficacious of itself. Its efficacy in no way depends on the cooperation or consent of the human will, since grace itself causes that infallible consent or cooperation.

This agrees with the decrees of that Synod. In the rejection of errors on the third and fourth articles, canon 8, it condemns those who teach 'that in regenerating a person God does not use those powers of his omnipotence by which he would bend the person's will to faith and conversion with power and without fail; but that, with every working of grace that God uses for converting a person in place, the person can still resist God and the Spirit who intends and wills to regenerate him, and often actually does, so as to prevent his own regeneration entirely, and so it remains in his own power whether he is regenerated or not.'

In canon 9 it also condemns those who teach 'that grace and free choice are partial causes acting together at the start of conversion, and that grace does not come before the will's own working in the order of causes'; that is, 'that God does not effectively help a person's will toward conversion before that will moves and determines itself.'

title: Dort: how God works true conversion in the elect (article 11)
english: Thesis XLII. The same Synod explains how God works true conversion in the elect: 'He not only has the gospel preached to them outwardly and powerfully enlightens their minds by the Holy Spirit, so that they rightly understand and judge the things of the Spirit of God.

By the power of the same regenerating Spirit he also reaches into the innermost being of a person: he opens the closed heart, softens the hard one, circumcises the uncircumcised, and pours new qualities into the will. He makes the will alive where it was dead, good where it was bad, willing where it was unwilling, obedient where it was stubborn, and he moves and strengthens it so that, like a good tree, it can bear the fruit of good actions.' This is in the head of doctrine on man's corruption and conversion and its manner, article 11.

title: Dort: this working is supernatural and infallible (article 12)
english: Thesis XLIII. In the next article the Synod adds that this working of God is wholly supernatural, both most powerful and most gentle, wonderful, hidden and beyond words, and no less in power than creation or the raising of the dead. So all in whose hearts God works in this wonderful way are regenerated surely, infallibly and effectively, and actually believe.

title: Hence no sufficient grace for those who do not believe
english: Thesis XLIV. Since that working of God does not show itself in those who do not actually believe and repent, the theologians who subscribe to that Synod deny that such people are given sufficient grace, however much the outward preaching of the word invites them to repentance and faith, and even though some inward motions of the Holy Spirit stir them.

title: Yet grace works to some degree in the unconverted
english: Thesis XLV. Note that the Reformed who deny that everyone who is not converted has grace sufficient for conversion do not deny that God's grace works to some degree in many who harden themselves in their sins and do not come to God by faith and repentance.

In their view there are certain things that go before conversion or regeneration, common to the elect and the reprobate, which the power of the word and Spirit rouses in the hearts of both alike: knowledge of God's will, a sense of sin, fear of punishment, thoughts of deliverance, some hope of pardon, and other motions of that kind.

title: Many resist and perish by their own fault
english: Thesis XLVI. They admit that many whom God calls to faith and conversion in this way refuse to follow God's call, resist the Holy Spirit as he prompts them toward what makes for their salvation, and in the end entirely stifle the motions that the word and the Holy Spirit stirred in them, and so are lost for ever through their own fault.

title: The British theologians at Dort on preliminary effects
english: Thesis XLVII. Among others, this is the teaching of the British theologians, included in the Acts of the Synod of Dort. Setting out their opinion on the third and fourth articles and dealing with what comes before conversion, they state in their second thesis and those that follow:

'There are certain inward effects that go before conversion or regeneration, which the power of the word and the Spirit rouses in the hearts of people not yet justified, such as knowledge of God's will, a sense of sin, fear of punishment, thoughts of deliverance, and some hope of pardon. Those whom God moves in this way by his Spirit, through the word, he calls and invites to faith and conversion truly and in earnest.
Those whom God so moves he does not abandon, nor does he stop leading them forward on the true road to conversion, until they abandon him by wilful neglect or by refusing this initial grace.'

title: The British theologians: preliminary effects can be stifled
english: Thesis XLVIII. 'These preliminary effects, produced in people's minds by the power of the word and Spirit, can be smothered and entirely put out through the fault of a rebellious will, and in many they usually are.

So some people, in whose minds the power of the word and Spirit has stamped a measure of knowledge of divine truth, some grief for their sins, and some longing and concern for deliverance, are turned completely the other way: they reject the truth and hate it, hand themselves over to their desires, grow hardened in their sins, and rot in them with no longing or concern for deliverance.'

title: The British theologians: God's special mercy toward the elect
english: Thesis XLIX. They add that even the elect never behave in these acts that go before regeneration so well that God could not justly abandon and forsake them for their negligence and resistance.

But God's special mercy toward them is such that, though they push away or smother this stirring and enlightening grace for a time, he presses them again and again and does not stop leading them forward until he has brought them wholly under his grace and set them in the state of regenerate children.

title: The Reformed differ on how grace moves the will
english: Thesis L. Further, the teachers of the Reformed school all agree that grace exerts its efficacy not just on the human mind but on the will as well, and that it bends and settles the will toward the good with power and without fail.
Where they part company is over how grace moves our will so that it turns toward God and gives its assent to what is good.

title: Testard, Amyraut and Camero's followers: grace works by persuading the mind
english: Thesis LI. Paulus Testardus, Moses Amyraldus and the others who follow Camero's method and teaching on grace hold that the efficacy of God's grace, which turns a person to God, plants faith in Christ in him and sets his heart on fire with love for God, works like this. The saving truth set out in the Gospel is presented to the mind in a certain way, and the Spirit's hidden power so shapes the mind from within that the person comes to be utterly and effectively convinced of that truth.

He concludes that nothing is better, and nothing does more to bring a person to true happiness, than holding fast to Christ and obeying his Gospel. On their premise the will must follow where the practical intellect leads and what it judges, so the will takes up the saving good that the Gospel offers and the intellect points out, and grasps it eagerly. Turned away from empty and earthly things, it turns wholly to God, and in this its renewal and sanctification consist.

title: On this view grace reaches the will only through the mind
english: Thesis LII. So they hold that the efficacy of God's grace exerts itself first and directly on the mind alone, and on the affections and the will only as a result and at second hand. The will and affections are renewed only through the renewing of the intellect, as the fruit and working (energeia) of the light that renews the mind passes on to those faculties, which are subject to the intellect's lead.
This can be seen in Paulus Testardus, Irenicum, thesis 424 and following.

title: This differs from mere moral suasion
english: Thesis LIII. It is clear from this that their view is quite different from that of people who place the whole efficacy of grace in a kind of moral persuasion, one that leaves the will undecided and can be either accepted or rejected by it.

In those who are converted by God's grace they recognize not only some persuading by God's Spirit working through the word, but a truly forceful and strong persuasion that sweeps the will along and moves it with the greatest effect: very gently indeed, yet surely and without fail it settles the will on the good and draws its consent out of it, instead of waiting for consent as if from a will still doubtful and undecided.

title: Other Reformed: grace works in the will itself
english: Thesis LIV. Other theologians of the Reformed school, however, hold that grace acts directly not only on the mind, enlightening it and flooding it with new light, but on the will itself as well.
In the will, they say, grace really and physically produces the consent that the will gives to God's admonitions.

title: Ames: a real working of God joined to moral suasion
english: Thesis LV. Amesius sets out and explains this view in Bellarminus enervatus, book 3, on grace, chapter 3. 'We say,' he writes, 'that along with moral persuasion there is also a real causal working of God.
By it a new source of spiritual life is planted in the heart of the person who is effectively called, and at the same time he is roused to perform the acts of this life.'

title: Ames adopts Alvarez on physical predetermination
english: Thesis LVI. In the same place he fully approves Didacus Alvarez's view and owns it as his own: through the efficacious help of grace God physically predetermines the created will, that is, in the manner of a physical cause, so that it consents without fail and works together with God as he calls and rouses it.

Then, in Alvarez's own words, he says that to predetermine physically is nothing other than truly, efficiently or really to make the will itself work together with God without fail. He adds that 'help of grace efficacious of itself', as it comes from God ahead of the will's free cooperation, and 'help that predetermines physically' mean the same thing.

title: Both parties keep the will's freedom
english: Thesis LVII. Yet however much both groups of Reformed teachers stress the efficacy of God's grace, they deny that it in any way harms the freedom of the human will. Whatever good works a person does by God's grace, he does freely.
So the very first act of conversion is just as free as the acts that follow it: it is not merely a living operation of our will but one the will freely brings forth.

title: Ames' reconciliation: the power not to act remains
english: Thesis LVIII. Not all of them, however, show in the same way how these things fit together. Amesius, just cited, following Didacus Alvarez, tries to reconcile that direct and effective working and determining of God's grace in the will with the will's own freedom in acting and in obeying grace.

He says that someone acts freely if, while acting, he keeps the power not to act. Grace moves and determines the will to act, yet it does not take away its power not to act. The power not to act exists in the same subject together with the grace and help needed for acting, the help that makes someone act.

Yet the grace and help given for a particular action and the absence of that action never are, and never can be, in the same subject at once. Others say the same thing this way: grace does determine the act, but it does not remove all indifference and indetermination from the faculty.

title: The Cameronians: certainty from the mind's nature
english: Thesis LIX. The first group, Camero's followers, think their premise makes it easy to show how a working of grace that is sure and infallible, and in no way depends on our will's consent, fits perfectly with human freedom.

On their teaching that working is sure and infallible because a mind in the right state, acting in keeping with its nature, cannot fail to embrace the truth when it is offered and recognized, or fail to judge good what is plainly shown to be good. When an object is fittingly brought to bear on a faculty that is in good order, an action in keeping with its nature follows by necessity.
In the same way the will cannot fail to will and follow what the intellect, having weighed everything, judges is to be willed and followed.

title: The Cameronians: no harm to the intellect's freedom
english: Thesis LX. Nothing here harms freedom, they say, either in the intellect or in the will. Not in the intellect, since grace does only two things for it: it sets the Gospel truth before it in a fitting light, and it restores it to a fitting condition, or even lifts it somewhat above its natural lot.

The intellect cannot withhold assent from a truth it has recognized, but the truth put before it does it no violence when it assents, since in assenting it acts entirely in keeping with its nature. So if the intellect has any sort of freedom, that freedom suffers no harm here.
Still less can the inward working of grace, which gives back to the intellect the powers it had lost or even supplies new ones, damage whatever freedom the intellect is thought to have.

title: The Cameronians: no harm to the will's freedom
english: Thesis LXI. As for the will, the working of grace described above does necessarily draw out its consent, yet it in no way takes its freedom away, since it moves and determines the will only through the judgment of the practical intellect.

In these learned men's view, the necessity and determination of the will's acts that come from the mind's practical judgment do not stop those acts from proceeding freely from the will. The will's freedom is not opposed to every necessity, only to necessity that comes from outside force, from matter or from the senses.
This is argued more fully in Moses Amyraldus' treatise on free will, especially section 4, and likewise in Josua Placeus' posthumous book on the same subject.

title: The older Reformed answer more simply
english: Thesis LXII. The older teachers of the Reformed school give a simpler answer. Grace does not take freedom away from the will, even though it lays a certain necessity on it, because not every necessity is at odds with freedom, only the necessity that comes from outside force or from natural determination.
Grace does not compel the will or do it any violence; it bends it gently, in a way that suits its nature.

title: A difficulty: free first act, yet merely passive
english: Thesis LXIII. The Reformed teachers also admit that a person converted by God's grace freely performs the very first act of conversion. At first sight this does not seem to fit well with what they commonly teach, in agreement with the theologians of the Augsburg Confession: that in the work of his regeneration and conversion a person is merely passive.
How can the human will freely perform the act of conversion and yet be merely passive in its own conversion? Can a will that is assumed to act freely be merely passive?

title: The British theologians: conversion in two senses
english: Thesis LXIV. The British theologians untie this knot in the explanation of their opinion on the third and fourth articles that is included in the Acts of the Synod of Dort. They point out that 'conversion' is used in two senses.

First, it means the direct work of God by which he regenerates a person; second, the act by which a person turns himself to God through faith and saving repentance. In conversion or regeneration in the first sense, on their account, a person is passive, and it is not in the human will's power to hinder God as he thus directly converts and regenerates.
In conversion in the second sense the will, moved by God, does act, and it performs the acts that make up our turning to God.

title: The British theologians: regeneration first, then our act of faith
english: Thesis LXV. Conversion in the sense of God's direct work, they say, is the work by which God, through an innermost and wonderful working, regenerates the souls of his elect, which various acts of his grace have already stirred and prepared, and as it were creates them anew, pouring in the life-giving Spirit and filling every faculty of the soul with new qualities.

In their view this conversion is followed, not in time but in order of nature, by our actual conversion: God draws the act of believing and turning out of the changed will, and the will, moved by God, then acts too, turning itself to God and believing, that is, producing its own living act.

They add that this divine action does not damage the will's freedom but strengthens it. It does not tear out by the roots the corrupt possibility of resisting, but effectively and gently gives the person a firm will to obey.

title: The Hessian theologians teach the same
english: Thesis LXVI. The Hessian theologians teach the same thing in the exposition of their opinion on the third and fourth articles, which is also included in the Acts of that Synod. Their sixth thesis, on man in the state of grace, reads:

'The human will is therefore merely passive in receiving supernatural qualities, or faculties and powers, and new inclinations. The action of the Holy Spirit, who pours those supernatural powers into the will and bends and inclines it effectively and powerfully to conversion and faith, does not depend on the human will or on its cooperation or consent.

But with respect to the acts of faith, love, hope and so on, and to good motions, the will is not purely passive but both passive and active. Moved and stirred by God's preceding grace and helped by his following grace, it acts too, and produces acts of faith, love, hope and the other virtues. That is why it is not said that God believes, hopes and loves in us or through us, but that we do so by God's grace.'

title: Remonstrants and Augsburg theologians agree in substance
english: Thesis LXVII. From what has been set out so far it is easy to conclude that the Remonstrants and the theologians of the Augsburg Confession differ somewhat in method and in their ways of speaking about sufficient and efficacious grace, but agree on the substance.

The Augsburg theologians deny that grace is properly divided into efficacious and sufficient; the Remonstrants affirm it and strongly approve the distinction. Yet the Augsburg theologians do not mean that those who hear God's Word and are not converted lack some help on God's part without which they cannot be converted; nor, therefore, that the grace given and offered them falls short of producing faith and repentance in them.

On the contrary, they say that the grace offered to these unbelieving and impenitent people deserves to be called not only sufficient but efficacious too, because of itself it is efficacious to bring them to repentance and faith, unless they go on of their own accord putting an obstacle in its way.

title: Why the Remonstrants call such grace merely sufficient
english: Thesis LXVIII. The Remonstrants, for their part, do not divide grace into sufficient and efficacious because they think that the grace received by those who stay unbelieving and go on in their sins lacks the force and efficacy needed beforehand for their conversion to follow, so that it earns only the name 'sufficient' and not 'efficacious'.

They grant that those who reject the Gospel preached to them lack no help they need to come to faith. They refuse the name 'efficacious' to the grace these people share in for one reason only: it does not in fact produce in them the effect it is meant for, because of the hindrance such people set up, not because grace itself lacks the force and efficacy required.

title: What both sides confess
english: Thesis LXIX. So both sides confess and teach that the grace given to those who will not obey the Gospel has enough strength to convert them, and that it fails to take effect in them only because they resist its motions and willingly put an obstacle in its way.

Conversely, they hold that believers, and those who are converted to God in earnest, could have blocked the grace that is efficacious in them if they had wished, and could have hindered its effect by their obstinacy, and that this grace laid on them no necessity of believing and turning to God.

title: The Remonstrants' view is tolerable
english: Thesis LXX. On this point, then, the Remonstrants think nothing worse than those called Lutherans. The Reformed do not avoid communion with the Lutherans; they even invite them, unasked, to peace and brotherly concord.

So, unless the Remonstrants err in something more serious, the Reformed should not shut them out of their communion over this head of doctrine, but should regard their opinion on it as tolerable and not harmful to piety.

title: The Remonstrants and the Molinists agree
english: Thesis LXXI. Anyone who compares what we reported about Molina in earlier theses with the Remonstrant doctrine set out in these will see clearly that on the efficacy and sufficiency of grace the Remonstrants hold in fact just what many teachers of the Roman school who follow Molina today hold.

Both agree that of two people given equal preventing grace, one can be converted and the other not, because one freely put an obstacle in grace's way and the other did not. Both agree, too, that God gives even those who are not converted helps of grace so fully sufficient for their conversion that nothing more is needed beforehand on God's side for their conversion actually to follow.

title: Dort, the recent Thomists and the Jansenists agree
english: Thesis LXXII. We have shown just as clearly that those who subscribe to the Synod of Dort think and teach in substance the same thing on efficacious and sufficient grace as the more recent Thomists and the followers of Jansenius.
Where they seem to disagree on some points, the dispute is either about words or of little weight.

title: What the Reformed grant with these Roman doctors
english: Thesis LXXIII. The Reformed who approve that Synod confess and acknowledge, together with these teachers of the Roman school, that those converted by God's grace perform the acts of conversion freely.

They hold that God's grace does make sure, infallibly, that they believe and repent, yet in a way that suits a rational and free nature, one that does not take away from them absolutely the power to act otherwise and to leave those devout acts undone.

title: The Reformed grant inward helps to the unconverted
english: Thesis LXXIV. They also freely grant that those who hear the Gospel and are not converted or do not give up sin receive, besides the outward grace of preaching, many inward helps of grace. God knocks at their hearts from within in various ways and enlightens their minds, so that they may turn from sin and give the Gospel the faith it deserves.
So they perish only through their own fault, and it is their perversity and obstinacy alone that keeps them from sharing in salvation.

title: Jansenists and recent Thomists on efficacious grace
english: Thesis LXXV. In turn, both the so-called Jansenists and the more recent Thomists acknowledge that grace is so efficacious that it does not merely invite and urge the will toward the good but also bends and determines it with power.

Its efficacy, they say, is not to be made to hang on the consent of free choice, since in those it converts grace itself draws out and produces that consent, infallibly and in a way that cannot be overcome.

title: They admit that the unbelieving lack a necessary help
english: Thesis LXXVI. They admit just as openly that everyone who refuses to believe or is hardened in sin lacks some help on God's part that is entirely necessary, and needed beforehand, if a person is actually to come to faith and truly repent of his sins.

title: The dispute over 'sufficient grace' is verbal
english: Thesis LXXVII. The recent Thomists hold that people in whom grace fails to convert nonetheless possess grace sufficient for conversion; the Reformed, siding with Jansenius, reject this. The quarrel is purely verbal.

What the Thomists intend is not the claim that the unconverted are missing no help from God that would have to come first. Only that claim is what Jansenius and the Reformed reject in saying such people lack sufficient grace. Apart from it, they would happily concede to the Thomists that the grace these people receive may be termed sufficient after a fashion, within its own kind.

title: The Nassau-Wetterau theologians at Dort
english: Thesis LXXVIII. A clear case is the Nassau-Wetterau theologians' judgment on the third and fourth articles, preserved in the Acts of the Synod of Dort. In setting out their thesis on what God intends when he calls people, they grant that preaching and enlightenment, a grace hypocrites have in common with the godly, suffices for conversion in one respect: at the level of secondary causes or means, in that conversion requires no further means beyond these, whether of outward preaching or of inward enlightenment.

Taken without qualification, though, it does not suffice, that is, without the grace of being drawn from within; and without that grace, Scripture declares, it is impossible for anyone to be converted and come to Christ.

title: Differences on the nature of efficacious grace are scholastic
english: Thesis LXXIX. There are differences between the Thomists and Jansenius, and among the teachers of the Reformed school themselves, over how to explain the nature of efficacious grace and in what to place it.

The Thomists place it in a certain motion with power in it, present in the will as an impetus is present in a thing that is driven; Jansenius in feelings of love and longing for the heavenly and spiritual good, by which the human soul is gently swept upward; Camero's disciples in a most powerful enlightening and persuading of the mind, which sweeps the will and affections along with it; others in an all-powerful and most effective working of God, by which a new source of spiritual life is put into the heart of the person called and he is at the same time roused to perform the acts of this life.

All this belongs to purely scholastic debate, on which learned men may speak and think one way or another; and what most learned men put forward here seems to call for reconciling rather than setting against each other.

title: A plea to leave arduous questions aside
english: Thesis LXXX. The great variety of opinions and views on the nature and essence of efficacious grace, and on how it works in people's souls, which has occupied the Christian schools for so many centuries now, shows that the matter is tangled and obscure and full of difficulties on every side.

There is no hope that the disputes will end unless some limit is put to curiosity and hard, unnecessary questions are dropped. It would indeed be far wiser, and better for Christian peace and piety, to keep away from such questions altogether than to quarrel endlessly over matters that overwhelm the human mind by their difficulty and on which hardly anyone can satisfy himself.

title: What should be preached to the people
english: Thesis LXXXI. These questions in particular are brought before ordinary Christians in homilies and sermons not only to no profit but often to great harm, since they plant scruples in simple minds that the skill and eloquence of the disputants cannot properly clear away afterwards.

So when these matters are spoken of, especially before the people, the safest course, and the one that best suits Christian prudence and sobriety, would be to keep to what Christian teachers agree on, which is also enough to shape piety and faith.

For example: whatever good is in us and is done by us is owed to God's grace; it is God who works all good in us; without Christ and the help of his Spirit we can do nothing at all in what furthers our eternal salvation; we have nothing that we have not received freely from God and could boast of over another; and so we must ask for God's grace in everything, and thank him for whatever we have done well and rightly.

title: Grace leaves freedom and effort intact; the wicked have no excuse
english: Thesis LXXXII. Yet God, the author and maker of our nature, who knows best how the human soul is to be moved, works in us by his grace in such a way that our freedom loses nothing, and he moves us to do good not as if we were logs or posts but as befits rational creatures.
So the necessity and efficacy of God's grace in no way remove our care and concern for good works, and we must not work and watch any less because we need God's help in everything.

However necessary grace is, the wicked who do evil and refuse to obey God's word have no grounds for complaint against God. He invites them to repentance and gives them the means of salvation in such a way that they rush to ruin only through their own fault, and their failure to gain eternal salvation must be put down to their obstinacy and rebellion alone.

title: Enough for Christians; moderation in the schools
english: Thesis LXXXIII. In my judgment these points, which no one questions, ought to be enough for all Christians, without further and more curious inquiry into the inmost nature of human freedom, into how grace works in us, or into how its efficacy is to be reconciled with the freedom of our choice; on these Scripture gives no distinct, clear and express pronouncements.

If anyone insists that it is permissible to philosophize about these matters further and more precisely in the schools, it would at least be desirable to do so with the greatest restraint, and with a sincere admission of our own darkness and ignorance in such hard matters. That would take all bitterness out of the debates on a subject so weighty and difficult in itself, and would train minds to mutual Christian and brotherly tolerance. May God, by that same grace of his, be pleased to bring this about in those who preside over the Christian schools.

title: Appendix: the Socinians on grace
english: Thesis LXXXIV. By way of appendix, it seemed right to add what the Socinians of today ascribe to the helps of God's grace in a person's conversion and in the practice of piety. They assume that the human will is not so bound by sin by nature that it cannot will or refuse to do something in matters of religion and eternal salvation, and also, once a person has heard the Gospel teaching, actually believe and obey God's commands.

God, they say, willed that our will, from which piety of life springs and by which it is judged, should lie within our choice and power, though he commonly furthers, hinders or permits its outward act as he chooses. From this they conclude that the willing of good that is in us is ours, not God's.

title: Socinians: God's government and the inward act
english: Thesis LXXXV. If anyone objects that on this view much will be taken away from God's government as seen in his ruling of the world, they answer that the inward act of our will, the only thing God has ordinarily put in our power, carries no weight in the government of the world.

What matters there is its outward effect, which is so subject to God's power that nothing can happen unless God decrees and helps, or permits it. Free choice reaches far enough, they say, that with God sometimes helping and sometimes only permitting, a person can not only conceive a plan to do something but carry it through to the end.

title: Socinians: God's help is never refused to those who ask
english: Thesis LXXXVI. As for good actions that the will commands and God wants us to carry out, they grant that these very often cannot be done without God's help. They do not think this prevents them from being in our power in their own way, because God refuses his help to no one who comes to him as a suppliant.

So if someone without God's help has not obeyed his commands, he must blame himself and has no excuse for his sin, because he did not earnestly ask for God's help, or would not take up the aids God gave him for practising piety. That evil comes only from the person's own wickedness, which makes him not bring his will into line with what God approves.

If he did, there would be no doubt that he would try every way and means of carrying it out, and would therefore always turn to God's help; protected by it, he would easily gain knowledge of divine things and fix his whole mind on devotion to God.

title: Socinians: God's outward and inward help
english: Thesis LXXXVII. They say, further, that God aids human efforts in two ways. One is outward and lies in threats or in promises, though promises have more power to fire people with devotion to God.
The other is an inward help that God gives us when, by divine power, he engraves more deeply on our minds the promises made to us and confirmed by outward proofs, or teaches us his will more fully.

title: Socinians on Philippians 2:13
english: Thesis LXXXVIII. Someone may say that where saving good is concerned Scripture ascribes to God our very willing, no less than the outward deed, as in Paul's words to the Philippians: 'It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, for his good pleasure.'

They answer that these words, and others like them that ascribe a person's conversion to God, do not mean that God wholly and necessarily brings about in people what the words say, but that God leaves out nothing that serves to bring it about while our will's freedom stays intact.

God draws and invites us to will the good by the greatness of his gifts and by the certainty, surpassing worth and breadth of his promises. By these he makes us not able to will, which we have by nature, but actually willing; yet he does it in such a way that it always lies in our power to resist that divine efficacy. This is set out more fully in Volkelius the Socinian, On True Religion, book 5, chapter 18.

title: Man was created able to obey the law perfectly
english: Thesis I. God created man in a condition in which he could give the law God laid on him a complete and perfect obedience, free of any stain or fault. It would not have been fair for God to require of an innocent creature what he had given it no strength, or not enough strength, to do.
Scripture confirms this when it teaches (margin: Eccl. 7:29) that God made man upright; and no one could count as upright who was unable to conform himself to God's law, the very rule of uprightness.

title: Fallen man cannot keep the law of himself
english: Thesis II. But man broke God's law of his own accord and lost the gifts and helps by which he had been able to keep it. He thus became the slave of sin, so that of himself he cannot satisfy the law fully in even a single work, or offer God an obedience that pleases him and that he accepts. Much less can he fulfil the law as anyone must who wants to reach life by the law.

Holy Scripture teaches this plainly enough. It says that people outside Christ's grace are dead in sins (margin: Eph. 2); that without him we can do nothing (margin: John 15); that we are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as if from ourselves (margin: 2 Cor. 3); and that the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, is not subject to God's law and cannot be (margin: Rom. 8).

title: Christ came to free us from sin's slavery as well as its penalty
english: Thesis III. But God took pity on the human race, lost through its own fault, and sent his Son Christ into the world. Christ was not only to free people from the punishments their sins had justly earned, but also to release them from slavery to sin.
He was to give them the grace by which they could once more serve God in true righteousness and holiness and make a start on a new obedience to his commandments.

title: The grace of the new covenant promised in Ezekiel
english: Thesis IV. God often promised this grace through the prophets, as belonging to the new covenant to be made in Christ. In Ezekiel 11 he says: 'I will give them one heart and put a new spirit within them. I will take the heart of stone out of their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, so that they walk in my precepts, keep my judgments and do them, and so that they are my people and I am their God.'

And again in chapter 36: 'I will pour clean water on you, and you will be made clean from all your defilements; from all your idols I will cleanse you. I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you. I will take the heart of stone out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you and make you walk in my precepts, keep my judgments and carry them out. You will live in the land I gave your fathers; you will be my people, and I will be your God.'

title: The same promise in Jeremiah
english: Thesis V. What we read in Jeremiah 31 agrees with this: 'The days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah. It will not be like the covenant I made with your fathers on the day I took them by the hand to lead them out of Egypt, a covenant they broke, and I was lord over them, says the Lord.

This is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my law within them and write it on their hearts; I will be their God, and they will be my people.' And in the next chapter: 'I will give them one heart and one way, so that they fear me all their days, and that it may be well with them and with their children after them. I will make an everlasting covenant with them and never stop doing them good, and I will put the fear of me in their hearts, so that they do not turn away from me.'

title: Moses foretold the same
english: Thesis VI. Moses too had foretold something similar. In Deuteronomy 30 the promise runs: the Lord your God will circumcise your heart and your offspring's heart, so that you love him with all your heart and all your soul, so that you may live.

Shortly afterwards come the words: 'Then you will return, hearing the Lord your God's voice and carrying out every commandment I command you today; and the Lord your God will make you abound in all the works of your hands.'

title: Without such grace no one could be saved
english: Thesis VII. Certainly, if God did not give people a grace by which they could offer his commandments true and sincere obedience, none of them could be saved, or have good grounds for trusting that God will show him the kindness and mercy he offers and grants us in Christ. God promises to deal mercifully and kindly only with those who keep his covenant and carry out his commandments.

So Psalm 103: 'The Lord's mercy is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him, and his righteousness reaches their children's children, those who keep his covenant and remember his commandments so as to do them.' Ezekiel 18 agrees: 'If the wicked man repents of all the sins he has committed, keeps all my precepts and does what is just and right, he will surely live; he will not die. I will not remember any of the wrongs he has done; he will live by the righteousness he has practised.'

title: Christ in Revelation blesses those who keep the commandments
english: Thesis VIII. The same point is made when Christ in the Book of Revelation calls blessed, in the end, those who keep God's commandments, and declares that all who give themselves to vice and who love and practise falsehood are to be shut out of God's city.

'Blessed', he says, 'are those who keep his commandments, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and enter the city through its gates. Outside are the dogs, the sorcerers, the impure, the murderers, the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practises falsehood' (Rev. 22).

title: No one belongs to Christ who does not keep the commandments
english: Thesis IX. No one who fails to keep God's commandments is in communion with Christ or can be thought truly to know and love him. John says: 'By this we know that we have known him, if we keep his commandments. Whoever says he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him' (1 John 2).

In chapter 3: 'Whoever keeps his commandments remains in him, and he in him'; and in chapter 5: 'This is the love of God, that we keep his commandments.' That is why Paul (1 Cor. 7) teaches that in Christ nothing counts for anything but keeping God's commandments: 'Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing; what counts is keeping the commandments of God.'

title: The saints of Scripture kept God's commandments
english: Thesis X. Experience itself proves most clearly of all that the faithful can keep God's commandments through God's grace, since Scripture testifies that many holy and devout people actually kept them. David does not hesitate to say so of himself in Psalm 119: 'I made haste and did not delay to keep your commandments' (margin: Pausa Heth); and again, 'My soul has kept your testimonies and loved them dearly. I have kept your commandments and your testimonies, for all my ways are before you' (margin: Pausa Schin).

Luke the Evangelist gives the same testimony of Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth: 'Both were righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord.' Indeed, Scripture often describes all the devout and faithful as those who keep God's commandments, as when David says in the same psalm, 'I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments.'

title: God's commandments are not burdensome
english: Thesis XI. John is therefore right to say, in the fifth chapter of his first epistle, that God's commandments are not burdensome. They require nothing of us that is not in close accord with nature and reason and very much to our good.
Besides this, God gives his own people the strength to carry out his commandments, and by his grace he ensures that the devout and faithful keep them.

title: In some sense the regenerate fulfil the law
english: Thesis XII. Since Scripture says that the faithful, in whom God's grace is at work, keep God's commandments, they can no doubt also be said in some sense to fulfil God's law. God's commandments are the same thing as his law, and to keep God's commandments and to fulfil them mean one and the same.

Nor can it be denied that true and sincere charity, the love of God and of one's neighbour, is found in those reborn by God's Spirit. Those who believe in Christ and have been born again by his Spirit have passed from death to life, and, as the apostle John testifies, 'whoever does not love remains in death' (1 John 3).
So all who live the spiritual life necessarily love God and their neighbour. Love is the fulfilment of the law, and whoever loves has fulfilled the law, as Paul expressly teaches in Romans 13.

title: The righteousness of the law fulfilled in us
english: Thesis XIII. Again, 'the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in us' and 'we fulfil the law and its righteousness' seem to say exactly the same thing. Now the apostle teaches that Christ came into this world so that the law's righteousness would be fulfilled in us, who live by the Spirit and not by the flesh.

'What the law could not do,' he says in Romans 8, 'because the flesh made it weak, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin: he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the justification, or righteousness, of the law would be fulfilled in us, whose walk follows the Spirit and not the flesh.'

title: But the regenerate cannot fulfil the law perfectly
english: Thesis XIV. In Scripture's way of speaking, then, those led by God's Spirit may truly and fittingly be said to fulfil God's law and keep his commandments.
Still, they are far from able to fulfil the law perfectly, or to give God's precepts an exact obedience that is complete in every part.

title: What it is to fulfil the law perfectly
english: Thesis XV. To fulfil the law perfectly is to satisfy it in every respect and in all its rigour, falling short in nothing that the law, strictly taken, requires of a person. Such a person could then reach life by virtue of the legal covenant, under its clause 'Do this and you will live', and claim as his right the happiness the law promises, with no fear of the penalties it threatens against those who break it.

No one fulfils the law in that sense and in that respect except someone entirely free of sin who has never broken it. All who have sinned even once are judged, condemned and handed over to the curse by the law strictly taken, under its other, terrible clause: 'Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of this law, to do them.'
The law justifies and acquits no one freely, but only as a matter of debt, as Paul teaches in Romans 4. Every sinner, whoever he is, needs God's grace and mercy and can be justified only freely.

title: No one has never broken the law
english: Thesis XVI. Yet there is no human being who has not broken the law at some time. All are born in sin; by nature they are slaves of sin, indeed dead in sins, and would lie for ever in that death and slavery unless Christ's grace raised and freed them. We showed this briefly above, and Scripture drives it home so often and so plainly that collecting its testimonies on the point would seem superfluous.

Paul above all presses the doctrine in his epistles, especially in the first four chapters of Romans. There he proves by many arguments that all have sinned and that all, Jews and Greeks alike, are under sin, in line with the scriptural sayings: 'No one is righteous, no one understands, no one seeks God. All have turned away; together they have become worthless. No one does good, not even one.'

From this he concludes that no one is justified before God by works of the law, but that all are justified freely by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. It follows that no one fulfils God's law perfectly and in every respect. If anyone did, he would surely be justified by works of the law, and that as a matter of debt, not of grace.

title: Even the holiest sin daily
english: Thesis XVII. Not only are people sunk in sin by nature and convicted of sin by the law; even after they are reborn by grace, they are far from giving the law a perfect obedience in every respect. Even the holiest fall into many sins every day.

So James says, 'We all stumble in many things' (margin: Jas. 3), and John in chapter 1 of his first epistle, 'If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.' The wise man agrees in Ecclesiastes 7: 'There is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.'

title: The regenerate also fall into grave sins
english: Thesis XVIII. Those reborn by Christ's grace remain liable not only to lighter and smaller sins; hardly any of them fail at some time to fall into grave sins. Through these they are held bound by a fresh guilt of eternal death and lose their present fitness for the kingdom of heaven, until God's special grace stirs them and they rise again by a particular repentance.

The frequent falls of the saints recorded in Scripture show this, such as David's, who fell into adultery and murder, and Peter's, who denied Christ three times with an oath. The daily experience of the faithful confirms it all too often.

title: Even the obedience of believers has its defects
english: Thesis XIX. Even the obedience believers give the law has its own defects and flaws. In the very works they do in conformity with the law they fall short of the law's full exactness (ἀκρίβεια), so that in this respect there is always room left for progress, always something still to strive toward.

Paul's example makes this plain. It would be hard to find anyone to whom Christ gave so large a measure of grace, yet Paul admits he is not yet perfect and keeps reaching for what lies further on. In Philippians 3 he writes: 'Not that I have already grasped it, or am already perfect; but I press on, if somehow I may take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of me. Brothers, I do not consider that I have taken hold of it. One thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching out toward what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal, for the prize of God's upward call in Christ Jesus.'

title: Objection: Scripture calls some saints perfect
english: Thesis XX. Someone will object that in that very passage the apostle assumes some people are perfect and counts himself among them. Right after the words just quoted he adds, 'Let as many of us as are perfect think this way.' In 1 Corinthians 2 he says, 'We speak wisdom among the perfect.'

Scripture also testifies of many holy men that they were perfect. Of Noah, Genesis 6 says: 'Noah was a righteous man and perfect in his generations, and he walked with God.' Of Job, God himself says to Satan in chapters 1 and 2: 'Have you considered my servant Job, that there is no one like him on earth, Isch Tham, that is, a man of integrity, or perfect, and upright, who fears God and turns away from evil?'

David in Psalm 18 does not even shrink from claiming such perfection: 'I was blameless, or perfect, with him, and kept myself from my iniquity. And the Lord repaid me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in his sight.'

title: Absolute perfection and comparative perfection
english: Thesis XXI. To resolve this difficulty we need a twofold distinction of perfection. One kind is called perfection absolutely; the other is perfection only in a certain respect, by comparison. What is absolutely perfect lacks nothing in its kind. Things are called perfect by comparison when, though far short of the highest perfection, they still surpass many other things of the same kind with which they are compared.

When we say that no one in this life is perfect, that is, no one gives God's will a perfect obedience, we mean absolute perfection: perfection that has reached the top and can receive no addition. In this sense Paul admits he is not yet perfect, since he had not yet reached the degree of love and obedience toward God to which the blessed spirits reigning with Christ have been raised. Their knowledge, and their obedience and love as well, can grow no further, because they are carried toward God with all their powers and the whole affection of their will.

None of this stops believers who outstrip others in virtue, and who have advanced further in knowing divine truth and in striving after piety and righteousness, from being called perfect. They are perfect not simply, but relative to those who fall well behind them here: those who are still, in Paul's words, infants in Christ and in some way carnal, compared with others who are called spiritual in a special sense (see 1 Corinthians 3). These are, so to speak, the grown-ups among Christians, of a riper age and stature, if one may put it so. They are the ones Paul calls perfect in the passages cited, when he says, 'We speak wisdom among the perfect,' and, 'Let as many of us as are perfect think this way.'

title: Perfection of parts and perfection of degrees
english: Thesis XXII. Close to this distinction is another, which commonly divides perfection into perfection of parts and perfection of degrees. Obedience perfect in degree reaches the highest degree of perfection: through it a person conforms and submits himself to the law so perfectly that nothing at all can be found lacking in him and he can make no further improvement in that respect. In this sense, as we maintain and as is self-evident, no one fulfils the law perfectly in this life.

Obedience that falls well short of the highest degree can still be, and be called, perfect in its parts. As to its parts, essential or integral, it lacks none of what is needed for true obedience acceptable to God. In this sense the obedience of the godly in this life is perfect, and in this respect believers renewed by Christ's grace and led by his Spirit can fulfil God's law perfectly: that is, they can give his commandments a true, sincere obedience that pleases God. The essential perfection of such a thing is simply its being true and sincere.

title: Three requirements of true obedience
english: Thesis XXIII. To make this clearer, note that three things above all are needed for our obedience to be true and sincere. First, it must be given not only with the body and outward action but with the inner affection of the mind as well. Doing what the law commands profits nothing unless it springs from love of God and from zeal to carry out his will and advance his glory. Equally, a certain wish to obey God is not enough unless his commandments are actually carried out in deed when the situation calls for it.

Second, true obedience is not satisfied by keeping some of God's commandments while neglecting the rest. We must earnestly submit to every precept of the divine law and try to fulfil each one as occasions arise. Third, our obedience must be steady and lasting. Obeying God for a while is not enough; we have to persevere in obeying him to the end, in hard times as in good ones.

title: The regenerate lack none of these
english: Thesis XXIV. On all these counts, the obedience of the truly godly, those reborn by God's Spirit, lacks nothing. They serve God not with the body alone but bring mind and affections under his will. They not only do in deed what the law commands; in doing it they aim at God's glory and are moved by love for him.

Their concern is not to obey merely this or that commandment; they try to conform themselves to God's whole law and to every one of its commandments. And they do so not merely for a while, as long as things go well, but also when temptations and persecutions break upon them: to their last breath they keep God's commandments before their eyes and measure their actions by that rule.

title: This is the perfection of parts Scripture praises
english: Thesis XXV. So the perfection the Schools usually call perfection of parts can rightly be ascribed to their obedience. They try to bring both the acts of the body and the affections of the mind into line with the whole law and every one of its precepts, and to do so steadily and with perseverance.

If this were not so, Scripture would certainly not credit believers with true righteousness and holiness, as it does in Ephesians 4 when it says they put on the new man, created after God in the righteousness and holiness of truth. A righteousness maimed and mutilated in the parts that belong to its very essence is no true righteousness.

This is the perfection for which Job and Noah are praised and which David has no qualms about claiming for himself. In those places 'perfection' means only the integrity and sincerity of these holy men; the Hebrew word Tham or thamim, which translators there render 'perfect', properly means whole and sincere.

title: The orthodox position stated
english: Thesis XXVI. So we deny that believers can fulfil God's law perfectly, if the perfection meant is the one called absolute, the perfection of degrees. All of them, no less than other people, are sinners by nature; even after receiving grace they keep stumbling in many things and stay exposed to serious falls; and in their good works themselves they fall short of the full exactness (ἀκρίβεια) the law demands in its strictness.

Yet with Scripture we say and teach that believers keep God's commandments by Christ's grace, and in a certain way fulfil the law as well, since they give the divine law a true obedience, approved by God, that covers all its precepts. That obedience sits far below the highest perfection, but in Scripture's usage it can still be called perfect, because it is true and sincere and lacks nothing that the nature and integrity of true obedience, acceptable to God, necessarily requires.

title: Roman doctors misstate the Reformed doctrine
english: Thesis XXVII. This account of the orthodox view needs careful attention because of the doctors of the Roman Church, who on this question, as on many others, either fail to understand the teaching of the Reformed school or twist it deliberately. They ascribe to Protestant theologians a flat denial that Christ's faithful can keep God's commandments and fulfil the law in such a way that any of their works can be called righteous.

They even claim that Protestants teach that the law is simply impossible for someone justified by Christ's grace, so that he can do no good works at all and has no true actual righteousness. This can be seen in Bellarmine, De justificatione, book 4, chapter 10, and in Becanus's Summa of scholastic theology, volume 2, tractate 4, chapter 4, which is titled 'On the merit of good works according to the opinion of the Calvinists'.

title: A state of the question that does not exist
english: Thesis XXVIII. Hence, resting on this false assumption, they frame between us and them a state of the controversy that does not exist at all, namely 'whether justified people, helped by the Lord's grace, can fulfil the divine law in such a way that their works not only should not be called sins but truly and properly deserve to be called righteous.' These are Bellarmine's words in the chapter 10 already cited.

In line with them is what we read in Gabriel Vasquez, volume 2 on the Prima Secundae, disputation 212, whose title asks 'whether righteous people can fulfil the law in such a way that their works are not only not sins but are to be called righteous.'

title: What Protestants do and do not deny
english: Thesis XXIX. Protestants never meant to deny any of this. They do not teach that God's law is simply impossible for the justified. They do not deny that believers give God's commandments true obedience, or that by Christ's grace the godly fulfil God's law to the extent of doing good works.

Nor do they say that the works by which believers, moved by the divine Spirit, try to conform themselves to the law must be called sins and are really sins by nature; they grant that such works can and should be called holy and righteous. The one thing they have always denied is that believers can fulfil the law perfectly, since their obedience, however true and sincere, always falls far short of the highest perfection.

title: The testimony of Pareus
english: Thesis XXX. So that no one can falsely allege that Protestants think otherwise, or that we are pinning on them a doctrine not their own, we will cite a few of their statements on the matter as a sample. To go through them all would be endless labour, and needless; besides, the matter is plain enough to anyone who pays attention.

Pareus, then, writing on Bellarmine's De justificatione, book 4, chapter 10, says: 'The question is whether the justified can fulfil the divine law. Our opponent affirms it absolutely; we grant it of an imperfect, begun fulfilment and deny it of a perfect one.' Later, explaining what fulfilling the law means, he says: 'To fulfil God's law, speaking absolutely, is to give the divine law a perfect obedience without any defect, and I confess we teach that the justified cannot do this.'

He goes on to say that we teach fulfilling the law is impossible for a justified person, not outright, as Bellarmine falsely charges us, but with respect to the law's exactness (ἀκρίβεια), which rules out every defect. A person in the state of grace can therefore fulfil the law in a begun way, that is, begin the new obedience of the law according to all its precepts, but cannot fulfil it absolutely, without any sin.
